en: Having prostrated before the Lord, the cause [of all], and the sage Kaṇāda,
the *Padārthadharmasaṅgraha*, which leads to great exaltation, will hereafter be expounded.

Furthermore, because it establishes an immediate succession qualified by valid cognition (*pramiti*), the absence of such [cognition] is excluded. Thus, the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*), functioning as a reason, refers to a student born of a distinguished lineage and family, produced from an unimpaired Brāhmaṇa father and an unimpaired Brāhmaṇī mother, who possesses a desire to hear, the capacity for hearing, retention, comprehension, reasoning, and critical discernment, and is intent upon the truth—such a disciple he addresses. And so, according to the passage: "The Brāhmaṇa Sumati went to the venerable Ulūka... For there is no cessation of pleasure and pain for one who possesses a body; but for one who has become bodiless, pleasure and pain do not touch him" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.1), one experiences the constant absence of pleasure and pain in the state of being bodiless. [He received] the vision of the [six] categories, just as [the sage] Kaṇāda did. And having seen that [student] was a fit recipient, the Blessed One, through the power of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), attained the knowledge of the reality of the six categories within a single atom, was instructed by Maheśvara, and proceeded to compose the Sūtras.

To achieve that purpose, [one might argue] that because the collection of aphorisms (*sūtra-sandarbha*) is extremely concise, or perhaps due to its profundity, the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) would not arise for people such as ourselves; thus, there would be no qualified audience (*adhikārin*), just as [there is none] for the *Praśastapāda-saṃkṣepa* (the *Padārthadharmasaṃgraha*). This is incorrect. For [the meaning] is manifested through instruction (*upadeśa*). To explain: just as in the case of substances (*dravya*) and so forth, for one who has established a linguistic convention (*kṛta-samaya*), there arises a pervasive cognition (*anugata-jñāna*)—such as "this is a Brahmin"—which is subsequently uncontradicted (*bādhaka*). Since this is established as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the existence of an audience consisting of those learned in the categories (*padārtha*) is proven. Therefore, there is no fault regarding the lack of a subject matter (*nirviṣayatva*). Furthermore, the charge of being devoid of a denotable object (*nirabhidheyatva*) is unproven, since [the categories] such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth are indeed denoted. Moreover, the absence of a purpose (*prayojana*) has already been refuted by the presentation of that very purpose. Thus, [the objection is] dismissed.

Now, it must be stated: what, then, is consciousness, and what is the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*)? It is the absolute cessation of the specific qualities of the self (*ātma-viśeṣa-guṇa*), such as cognition and so forth, which persist as long as their substratum exists; it is not dharma, artha, or kāma, because these are accomplished by means that yield only limited results. {An Investigation into the Category of the Supreme Good}

Now, what is the proof for the existence of *niḥśreyasa* (the supreme good)? It is the portion of inference [establishing] the cessation of the conscious Viṣṇu. For instance: "The continuum of the nine specific qualities of the self (*ātmaviśeṣaguṇa*) is absolutely cut off, because it is a continuum (*santānatva*). Whatever is a continuum is seen to be absolutely cut off, such as the continuum of a lamp-flame; and this [continuum of qualities] is likewise a continuum; therefore, it is absolutely cut off. Since the property of being a continuum (*santānatva*) is present in the subject (*pakṣa*) by pervasion (*vyāpti*) within cognitions and so forth, there is no lack of establishment regarding its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). Furthermore, since it is observed in similar instances (*sapakṣa*) such as lamps, there is no contradiction (*aviruddhatva*). Nor is there any inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*), as there is no such [continuum] in atoms (*paramāṇu*) and the like which would belong to the subject. Since neither perception nor scripture presents a contrary conclusion, it is not a case of "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*) reasoning. Nor is this a case of a counter-balanced argument (*satpratipakṣa*), because it possesses the five required characteristics (*pañcarūpa*); thus, it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Now, since [ignorance] cannot be without a cause, a cause must be stated for that by which it is completely severed; and that cause has indeed already been stated. Furthermore, because of the instruction that "the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*)," this knowledge of reality does not depend on individual instances because it is non-specific; rather, it is defined as follows: "knowledge of reality arises with respect to those things characterized by the definitions of substance (*dravya*) and so forth."

Now, regarding the fact that the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*): if it were held that one who has produced the knowledge of reality immediately destroys [the afflictions] and so forth, then for people like us, the knowledge of reality would be impossible because of the non-existence of such [destruction]. Alternatively, if it is maintained that Kaṇāda composes the *sūtras* to bring about the knowledge of reality for people like us—who have already attained the knowledge of reality through merit born of yoga—this objection does not apply. For although the knowledge of reality exists as the cause of the supreme good, there is no fault here, because we accept that a *specific* knowledge of reality is the cause of the supreme good. To explain: even when the scriptural (*śrauta*) knowledge of reality has arisen for people like us, the supreme good does not occur because the knowledge of reality produced by the practice of yoga is absent. Indeed, when the scriptural knowledge of reality has arisen, one engages in the practice of yoga; through the power of that practice, a final knowledge of reality arises with respect to the self as it is characterized by all its specific attributes, and this is the cause of the supreme good.

For it is thus observed that right knowledge possesses the capacity to terminate false knowledge, as in the case of mother-of-pearl and similar objects. Since right knowledge is antagonistic to other cognitions, opposition to right knowledge is indeed possible even through false knowledge occurring at a later time. If what is intended is the cessation of the mental continuum (*manaḥ-santāna*), then just as the continuum of false knowledge is cut off by right knowledge, it is not the case that the continuum of right knowledge is cut off by false knowledge.

And when false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) has ceased, passion (*rāga*) and the other afflictions perish because they are rooted in it; for in the absence of a cause, the effect cannot arise. When passion and the others are absent, activity (*pravṛtti*), which is their effect, ceases. In the absence of that [activity], there is no production of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*). As for those [karmas] whose effects have already begun, they are exhausted through experience (*upabhoga*). [Question: How is it that the destruction of accumulated (*sañcita*) karma occurs through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) alone? [Answer: As it has been stated:
"Just as a kindled fire reduces fuel to ashes in an instant,
so does the fire of knowledge reduce all actions to ashes" (Gītā 4.37).
But surely, it is also stated in the scriptures that destruction occurs only through experience, as it has been said:
"Karma is not exhausted even in hundreds of millions of eons if it has not been experienced;
whatever karma, whether auspicious or inauspicious, has been performed must necessarily be experienced" (Devībhāgavata Purāṇa 9.29.69–70; 40.73).

And thus, since the two [scriptures] have contradictory meanings, how can both possess authority? Furthermore, there is also inference regarding the exhaustion [of karma] through experience: "Past karmas are exhausted solely through experience, because they are karma; whatever is karma is exhausted solely through experience, just like the karma that has already initiated the present body; and these [past] karmas are likewise; therefore, they are exhausted solely through experience. Moreover, if exhaustion occurs through experience, there must necessarily be other karma, and consequently, there would be no cessation of saṃsāra.

That is incorrect. For one who has produced knowledge of reality through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) knows the object to be accomplished by karma and, having manifested multiple bodies simultaneously, experiences [the results]. Furthermore, there is no production of further karma because of the absence of the auxiliary cause known as "recollective identification" (*anusandhāna*), which is generated by false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*).

Now, [an objection]: "If false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) is absent, then because desire (*abhilāṣa*) is absent, the experience of fruits (*bhoga*) would be impossible. This is not so. For without experience, karma... [is] impossible; even one who knows [the truth] still acts out of a desire for that [fruit], just as a patient proceeds to take medicine based on the instruction of a physician. Knowledge (*jñāna*) also functions in this same way. It should be explained that [knowledge] operates through the destruction of karmas by means of experience—which is the door to the production of all bodies—just as fire [acts]... and not directly. Nor should it be said that for those possessing the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñānin*), there is the destruction of karma through the knowledge of reality, whereas for others it is through experience; for there is no well-known example of the destruction of karma by knowledge alone.

Others, however, maintain that because of the absence of the auxiliary cause—the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by false knowledge—even existing *karmas* do not initiate a body in another birth. In this case, the objection is that the effect-substance would become eternal. Now, if there is a prohibition against the arising of future merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), how then can one who possesses the knowledge of reality perform obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites? It is for the sake of avoiding transgression (*pratyavāya*). For it is said: "By performing only the obligatory and occasional rites, one effects the destruction of evil."
And purifying his knowledge, he should bring it to maturity through practice.
Through practice, a person whose discernment has reached maturity attains liberation.

Thus [it is said]. However, in the case of optional (*kāmya*) and prohibited (*niṣiddha*) acts, there is a prohibition against engagement. Alternatively, for one who possesses knowledge of reality (*tattvajñānin*), the production of merit (*dharma*) does not cease during the performance of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, because the intention (*abhisandhi*) is exactly the same; or rather, there is the renunciation of the fruits thereof. For it is heard in scripture that "the offering of all actions to the Supreme Teacher" [is required]. Nor is there engagement for the sake of rebirth for one whose afflictions (*kleśa*) have been destroyed (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.65). Enough [of this].

Now, let it be granted that the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*); however, [the claim that it is] the sole cause is denied, because [scripture] declares that actions such as renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) are also causes of liberation. For instance:
"Upon seeing a twice-born man renouncing, the sun moves from its place, thinking:
'Having pierced my orb, he shall go to the imperishable world. (*Sannyāsopaniṣad* 2.6)
"Two persons in this world pierce the solar orb: the wandering mendicant disciplined in yoga, and he who is slain facing the enemy in battle. Thus it has been stated [in Parāśara Smṛti 3.37].

True. It is indeed accepted that the act of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) and so forth serves as the cause for ascending by means of piercing the solar orb. If it is described as "the world" (*loka*), its imperishability should be understood in relation to the lower worlds or in comparison to the fruits of other ritual acts. For in this way, the practice characterized by renunciation and the like is considered superior to other material actions.

Furthermore, it is not the case that *niḥśreyasa* (the supreme good) consists in the absolute destruction of the nine specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the self by means of piercing the solar orb; for that [supreme good] exists everywhere as the nature of the self disjoined from specific qualities. For this very reason, it should not be said that [the self] is non-eternal because it is an effect of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), since the cessation of specific qualities is of the nature of a destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*), and it is only the self characterized by that [destruction] which is eternal. Moreover, the non-eternality of an entity that is an effect applies; however, there is no such state of the substratum [the self] upon the destruction of cognition (*buddhi*) and the other qualities, because the denial of their identity (*tādātmya*) will be stated later.

Now, if you think that because consciousness itself would be annihilated in the state of liberation (*mokṣa*), those of cultivated intellect would not engage [in spiritual practice], and therefore liberation must be accepted as being of the nature of bliss (*ānanda*), as it has been said: "Bliss is the form of Brahman, and that is attained in liberation."

Likewise, the experience [of pleasure] is known through the otherwise inexplicable nature of the memory, "I slept happily," which occurs subsequent to the state of deep sleep. In that case, since the operation of verbal testimony and inference is not perceived, and the operations of the external senses are absent, the operation of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is known; thus, it is mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, there is the following inference: The self has happiness as its intrinsic nature, because it is the object of an absolutely dear cognition and because it is pursued for its own sake and not for the sake of anything else. Whatever is of such a kind has happiness as its intrinsic nature, like sensory pleasure; and the self is of such a kind; therefore, it has happiness as its intrinsic nature.

This is incorrect, because there is a subverting argument (*bādhaka*). To explain: if that [liberation] were impermanent, its cause of production would have to be stated. However, in the state of liberation, a connection between the self and the internal organ cannot possibly depend upon a connection with a body, since the body and so forth are absent. Furthermore, the production of an entity without an inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) is never observed.

Now, if it is argued that this bliss is eternal, then if its cognition is unperceived yet eternal, there would follow the consequence of non-distinction between the state of liberation (*mokṣa*) and the state of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), since [the bliss] exists in both states alike. Furthermore, recollection would be impossible because the experience itself would persist. Moreover, the formation of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) would be impossible because the experience is without degrees of intensity. Alternatively, if it is argued that in the state of worldly existence there is no perception of the existing experience due to preoccupation with other objects, whereas in the state of liberation there is perception because of the absence of such [preoccupation], and thus there is a distinction; [we reply: ... [The argument continues as follows: ...If the experience were not perceived in the state of worldly existence due to distraction by other objects, then upon the cessation of that distraction, the experience would be perceived in the state of liberation. However, this is untenable, for if the experience is eternal and its cognition is likewise eternal, how can there be a time when it is not perceived? If it is claimed that the experience is not perceived because it is not manifested (*aprakāśita*), then we ask: what is this "manifestation"? If it is the nature of the experience itself, then it must exist at all times, and thus its non-perception is impossible. If, on the other hand, manifestation is something distinct from the experience, then one must explain how this manifestation arises and ceases. If it is said to arise from the contact of the self with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), then we ask: does this contact produce a new quality in the experience, or does it merely reveal what was already present? In the former case, the experience would be non-eternal. In the latter case, since the experience is eternal and its nature is always manifest, there is no reason for its non-perception during worldly existence. Thus, the claim of an eternal, unperceived bliss leads to logical inconsistencies.

That is incorrect. For if eternal pleasure were [perceived], then because experience itself would be eternal, distraction (*vyāsaṅga*) would be impossible. To explain: distraction is the non-arising of cognition regarding another object when the self has produced a cognition whose objects are form and so forth. Likewise, distraction is the failure of a sense organ—engaged in producing a cognition of one object—to produce a cognition of another object. Now, it cannot be argued that when a cognition of an object such as form arises for the self, there is no possibility of a cognition of eternal pleasure, because that cognition too is eternal. Nor can it be said that there is no awareness [of it] because it is obstructed by the body and so forth, precisely because it is eternal. To explain: an obstructor is defined as that which causes the frustration of an effect. And the non-arising of the cognition of eternal pleasure is not possible. Furthermore, since the body and so forth exist for the sake of enjoyment, it is illogical for them to be obstacles to enjoyment. It is never observed that something which exists for the sake of a particular thing becomes an obstacle to that very thing. If it were an obstacle, then the killer of one who removes that obstacle would not incur the fruit of violence (*hiṃsā*). Indeed, it is observed that one who removes an obstruction is simply a benefactor. Therefore, for one who destroys the body and so forth—which are obstacles to the perception of eternal pleasure—there is an absence of the fruit of violence; this is sufficient.
If it is argued that this cognition is impermanent, we say no, because there is no cause for its production.

If it is further argued that the conjunction between the Puruṣa and the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), depending upon dharma produced by yoga (*yogaja-dharma*), is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*), we say no; for since the dharma produced by yoga is itself impermanent, once it has perished, there would be no causal basis for dependence.

Now, [the opponent argues that] a continuum (*santāna*) consists of a subsequent cognition arising in dependence upon a preceding cognition produced from a quality born of the first conjunction, and from that, yet another; this is not so, because there is no proof for it. Furthermore, it is not observed that cognition itself—without depending on a connection with the body—is the required cause for the conjunction of the self and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Nor can one accept what is contrary to what is observed. Moreover, an effect cannot be entirely accidental (*ākasmika*). For this very reason, since there is no eternal pleasure or cognition, the cognition "I slept happily" is not a memory (*smaraṇa*). What then? This cognition "I slept happily" is an inferential knowledge of the absence of that [pleasure], based on the absence of recollection of the causes of pain. Otherwise, just as there is eternal pleasure, there would also have to be eternal pain, because of the memory "I slept painfully. If you say that this cognition "I slept painfully" arises because one perceives the causes of pain during the intervals within the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), then, by parity of reasoning, the cognition "I [slept] happily" will arise because of the absence of those [causes of pain].

If that is so, then how is it that scripture says, "Bliss is the form of Brahman," and so forth? For [the primary sense] is set aside because a subverting argument arises; thus, it is used in a figurative sense. To explain: this word "bliss" (ānanda) is seen to be employed for the absence of suffering, just as the word "pleasure" (sukha) is used for the absence of suffering—as, for example, when the burden is removed from a porter who was oppressed by it.

As for the inference that the self (*ātman*) has pleasure as its intrinsic nature (*sukhasvabhāva*): if "having pleasure as its intrinsic nature" means being connected with the universal (*jāti*) of "pleaseness" (*sukhatva*), this is not possible in the case of the self, because [the self] is perceived only as a quality (*guṇa*). For no single universal other than [those like] "I-consciousness" (*ahaṅkāra*) and so forth is ever observed to be common to both substance (*dravya*) and quality. If, on the other hand, it means being the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of pleasure, that is not the case, because the dilemma of whether [pleasure] is eternal or non-eternal is untenable. Likewise, regarding the locus of "pleaseness" or the locus of pleasure, there arises the same dilemma of its cognition being eternal or non-eternal. Furthermore, the two means of proof—being the object of the notion of "extreme dearness" and being taken up for one's own sake without reference to anything else—are not valid proofs because they are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since they apply even to the absence of suffering (*duḥkhābhāva*). Moreover, "being taken up for one's own sake without reference to anything else" is unestablished (*asiddha*), because things are taken up for the sake of pleasure. Similarly, "being the object of the notion of extreme dearness" is also unestablished, because even in a state of suffering, there exists the notion of what is not dear. Thus, these two inferences are not authoritative.

Furthermore, if one were to engage [in spiritual practice] out of a desire that there is eternal happiness in the state of liberation, one would not be liberated, because attachment is of the nature of bondage. Alternatively, for one who engages even out of aversion—thinking, "I shall cut off the intellect and so forth"—the same fault applies, since [aversion] is not favorable [to liberation]. Thus, the refutation of the absence of defects in what is contrary [to liberation] is equally applicable to attachment to that [state]; therefore, this [objection] is no fault, and other points should be inferred accordingly.

Now, if you think that it is better to enjoy sensual pleasure—which, though it involves the destruction of all virtues—is to be experienced by avoiding the means to suffering, that is not so; for because it is accompanied by suffering and is thus of the nature of suffering, it is to be abandoned. This scripture is not intended for those for whom this [sensual pleasure] is acceptable. There are indeed persons who loathe sensual pleasure, and it is for them that this scripture exists. And if they require instruction, they do not understand the goal through other means and proceed to its practice. Furthermore, since the existence of liberation is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the remaining [objection] is merely words and is therefore disregarded.

Others, however, believe that liberation arises from a means that is of a different nature [than the state of bondage]. As it has been said: "The discernment (*viveka*) of the difference between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa* is the means to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). For indeed, primordial matter (*pradhāna*) proceeds by means of the purpose of the *puruṣa*. And the purpose of the *puruṣa* is twofold: the perception of sound and so forth, and the discernment of the difference between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*. Once the purpose of the *puruṣa* has been accomplished, primordial matter no longer transforms into the form of the body and so on because its task is fulfilled; thus, the seer remains in his own essential nature. Or, once she is recognized as the seer, she does not approach the *puruṣa* to provide him with enjoyment, just like a procuress (*kuṭṭinī*) who is no longer sought after.

All this is false, because the non-existence of *pradhāna* will be demonstrated later. For it is only if the existence of *pradhāna* were established that the Puruṣa’s perception of its distinction from it would be possible. Or, let us speak even while granting [the opponent's position]: if *pradhāna* proceeds without depending on any external cause residing in the Puruṣa, then it would proceed toward the production of a body and so forth even for a liberated soul (*muktātman*), since there is no difference [between the two states]. If it is argued that it depends on "non-perception" (*adarśana*)—that is, *pradhāna* proceeds toward one for whom the perception of the distinction between the *guṇas* and the Puruṣa has not arisen, and such perception does not exist in the case of the liberated soul—that is not so. Because even in the case of the liberated soul, since the perception of distinction has ceased, the consequence is that *pradhāna* would still proceed [toward him]. Nor do we perceive any distinction between non-arising and cessation in terms of their being "non-perception. If it is argued that it proceeds by depending on "unseen merit/demerit" (*adṛṣṭa*), that is incorrect. Since that too exists in *pradhāna* as a latent power (*śakti*), it would be present without distinction in both cases. Furthermore, there would be an absence of the diversity of bodies and so forth, because *pradhāna* is of a single uniform nature. Nor can the diversity of bodies and so forth arise from a diversity in transformation (*pariṇāma*), because there is no cause for such diversity [within *pradhāna* itself]. Moreover, how could that *pradhāna*, which exists in a state of equilibrium (*sāmya*), attain a state of disequilibrium (*vaiṣamya*) in the absence of the purpose of the Puruṣa (*puruṣārtha*) as a cause for its activity? Or, if the purpose of the Puruṣa were already present, activity for that purpose would not occur simply because it already exists. Furthermore, it is not logical for that which is active without a cause for activity to cease, due to the absence of a cause.

As for what was stated—that the seer abides in its own nature—that is indeed accepted, since we admit that it abides devoid of specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*). Now, as for the claim that it abides in the form of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), that is not so; because consciousness is impermanent, its nature as consciousness is destroyed. Nor is there any proof for the permanence of consciousness which follows the presence and absence of the eyes and other sense organs. If you say it is the very nature of the self (*ātmarūpatā*), then if that [consciousness] is identical with the self, it is merely a synonym. If, however, they are distinct, then the argument is inconclusive due to conjunction and other relations. Furthermore, we shall later refute the identity of quality and the possessor of quality.

As for the claim that this [Prakṛti] does not approach the Puruṣa because he has been known as the seer—this is incorrect, because [Prakṛti] is insentient. For, since Prakṛti is insentient, in the absence of the cognition "I have been known by him as the seer," its activity would remain no different than before; enough of this over-elaboration.

Others, however, maintain that the arising of knowledge free from passion and other defilements through the cultivation of [the four truths as] impermanent and so forth constitutes the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). To explain: for one who cultivates the thought that "everything is momentary," attachment to sense objects ceases because of the absence of a relationship such as "this is mine. Likewise, through the cultivation that "everything is selfless," when there is an absence of possessiveness and aversion—thinking "I am not another" and "this is not mine"—there indeed arises a pure continuum of consciousness. Furthermore, because objects such as cloth and the like are negated, [they conclude] that "everything is empty. Thus, specific knowledge regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path is the cause of the supreme good. To elaborate: suffering consists of the five aggregates, beginning with form; its origin is the cause, so called because [suffering] arises from it; the cessation of these two is their destruction; and the means to that [cessation] is the path. Therefore, it is logical that the supreme good is either a pure continuum of consciousness or the annihilation thereof, resulting from the power of specific knowledge regarding these [four truths].

This is not so, because the meditation on momentariness and the like is of a false nature. Furthermore, false knowledge cannot be the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). We shall explain later how neither momentariness, emptiness, nor selflessness [is established]. If it is argued that one must meditate in this way solely for the purpose of preventing attachment, that is not correct, because detachment occurs in other ways as well. For instance, it is observed that knowledge of the true nature of things is the cause of engagement, while the perception of defects is the cause of withdrawal. Just as one engages with food mixed with honey and poison due to a perception of its qualities from failing to see the defect, and withdraws from it upon seeing the defect—not because of a prohibition regarding the object—so too, in the case of a son and others, it must be said that the very perception of the deformity of what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*) is the cause of withdrawal, not the absence of a relationship. Therefore, it is the negation of that [relationship] which is to be meditated upon. And it has been stated by the author of the *Nyāyabhāṣya*: "Regarding form and the rest, the notion of their causal basis (*nimitta-saṃjñā*) should be cultivated, not the notion of secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana-saṃjñā*), such as 'the teeth are thus,' 'the hair is thus,'" and so forth. As for this meditation on suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, if it is intended in the sense that "suffering" is the thing itself, "its cause" is the cause of that, "their cessation" is the cessation of those two, and "the means" is the means for that, then we do not deny it. For suffering is suffering by its very nature; anything else is suffering because it is a cause of suffering. And whether that [cause] be the five aggregates (*skandha*) beginning with form—namely, form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—or something else, even pleasure is suffering because it is accompanied by suffering. Thus, it is precisely the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) that is accepted as the means for severing that [suffering].

As for the claim that this knowledge free from passion and the like arises from specific cultivation (*viśiṣṭabhāvanā*), that is not the case. This is because the refutation of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) in the context of momentariness will be stated later. However, it is said by way of a concessive argument (*upetyavāda*): it is not logical that something devoid of passion should arise from a consciousness possessed of passion. For instance, just as "the nature of awareness [arises] from awareness" in another cognition, so too would passion and the like [arise] from it, due to their identity (*tādātmya*). Alternatively, in the contrary case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its absence. Nor is there any valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the claim that "the nature of awareness [arises] from awareness" simply because we observe the production of a dissimilar effect from a dissimilar cause. For this very reason, the fact that this cognition exists at a prior time by virtue of being the cause of another cognition, nor its being of the same class (*samānajātīyatva*), nor its belonging to the same continuum (*ekasantānatva*), is not a sufficient reason, because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). To explain: existence at a prior time is deviant with respect to things occurring in the same moment, and being of the same class is deviant with respect to cognitions belonging to other continua. For although these possess existence at a prior time and are of the same class, they do not serve as causes for the intended cognition. Furthermore, belonging to the same continuum is deviant with respect to the final cognition. Now, if it is argued that a final cognition is simply not admitted because [consciousness] always begins anew, then even the cognition of the body at death would be the cause of the cognition of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) body, or the cause of the cognition of the womb-body; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence of producing cognitions in a different continuum, since there would be no restrictive cause. If it is argued that the teacher’s cognition is indeed [the cause], why then does it not become the cognition of another student? If it is argued that karmic impressions (*vāsanā*) are the restrictors, no; for those too cannot exist apart from cognition. To explain: if there were identity between them, then cognition—being distinguished by the nature of awareness—would produce cognition without distinction, since the nature of awareness arises from awareness. Enough of this!

As for the claim that the cognition of the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is the cause of the cognition of the waking state, this is incorrect. If cognition were present during the state of deep sleep, there would be no distinction from the waking state, because in both cases there is no difference in the presence of self-cognizable cognition (*svasaṃvedya-jñāna*). If it is argued that the distinction lies in being unoverpowered by sleep, this too is incorrect. Since that [sleep] is a property of that [cognition], it is impossible for it to overpower [the cognition] through identity (*tādātmya*). If, however, they are distinct, then since only objects such as color and form exist [in that state], their own nature must be defined. Furthermore, if "overpowering" means destruction, then either cognition does not exist or destruction is without a cause. If it means concealment (*tirobhāva*), then since cognition exists, its very existence is what constitutes perception; thus, [concealment] is untenable under that assumption. Alternatively, if it is argued that because cognition is absent in the state of deep sleep, the continuity of a single stream (*ekasantānatva*)—based on the existence of the final cognition—is subject to deviation.

As for the claim that the destruction of passion and other defilements occurs through the power of specific cultivation (*viśiṣṭabhāvanā*), this is incorrect. For destruction is causeless, and thus cultivation is impossible. Cultivation is indeed possible because it bestows excellence upon an enduring entity; it is not possible, however, in the case of mere momentary cognition. For this very reason, a cognition free from all conceptual construction arises in the yogi. Nor can there be excellence with respect to a continuum (*santāna*), because such a continuum is itself impossible, and because it is illogical for something distinguished to arise from something undistinguished. To explain: it must be considered how a subsequent state possessing excellence could arise from a preceding state that is undistinguished [from its predecessor].

And as for the claim that the cessation of the continuum is the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), that is not so; because destruction is causeless, the application of means would be futile, as it would be accomplished without effort.

Others, however, maintain that the attainment of an imperishable body and other such qualities in a specific location resulting from the cultivation of non-absolutism (*anekānta*) constitutes the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). Thus, since there is aversion toward both the cultivation of permanence and the impermanence of the planets, the cultivation of non-absolutism is for the purpose of avoiding both. This should be applied similarly to existence, non-existence, and so forth. Furthermore, perceptible reality possesses a dual nature: it exists by virtue of being supported by its own space, time, and causes, and it does not exist in terms of another’s space and so forth. Likewise, a jar or similar object is permanent in its form as clay and the like, because it is perceived in all its states; yet it is impermanent in its form as a jar and the like, because that [specific form] passes away. Similarly, the self (*ātman*) is permanent in its nature as a self because of its eternal existence, but it is impermanent in its form as the modes (*paryāya*) of pleasure, pain, and so forth, because those perish. In this way, agency is to be inferred in respect to one's own effects, while non-agency is to be understood in respect to other effects. Finally, there is the state of being denotable by its own word and the state of being undenotable by other words.

This is improper, because false knowledge is denied to be a cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). Furthermore, non-exclusive knowledge (*anekāntajñāna*) is indeed false, since there exists a subverting proof (*bādhaka*). To explain: because "permanent" and "impermanent" consist of affirmation and negation respectively, they cannot both exist in a single, undivided substratum (*dharmin*). The same applies to "existence," "non-existence," and so forth. As for the claim that a jar and the like are permanent by virtue of being of the nature of clay and so on—that is incorrect. For the nature of clay is something distinct from the jar. To elaborate: the nature of clay is distinct from the jar; "clay-ness" (*mṛttva*) is a universal (*sāmānya*), and because it is eternal, the jar does not possess that [permanence], since it is other than that universal. Moreover, because the dissolution of the jar is perceived following its cause, the jar is indeed impermanent. Furthermore, existence in one's own location and non-existence in another location is precisely what we accept, since mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) is admitted. To explain: the non-existence of the jar in another place is neither its non-arising nor its destruction, because it exists there at all times. If, however, [the jar] possessed a dual nature, it would follow that it could not be perceived in its own location. Likewise, the self (*ātman*) is indeed permanent. Since pleasure, pain, and so forth are its qualities, the self is not destroyed even when those qualities—which are distinct from it—are destroyed. Nor is its non-agency with respect to other effects denied. To explain: it is accepted that whatever is observed to be actively involved in the production of something through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is the cause of that thing, and not of anything else. Similarly, although a thing may not be denotable by a particular word, it is not accepted that everything must be denotable by every word.

Furthermore, there is no obstacle to obtaining a distinguished body and so forth from the cultivation of non-absolutism (*anekānta*). Nor is it logical that bodies and other things, which possess the property of arising, should be indestructible. Likewise, if non-absolutism does not cease even in liberation, it would follow that the liberated one is both liberated and not liberated. And this being the case, the undesirable consequence follows that the very same person is both liberated and a transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*). Such is the refutation regarding the acceptance of non-absolutism even within non-absolutism itself. For the nature of a thing as both existent and non-existent is non-absolutist; if one accepts that this too is non-absolutist, then another form must also be perceived, and likewise another form distinct from the nature of being eternal and non-eternal, and so forth, must be asserted.

Others, however, maintain that through the knowledge of the oneness of the self, absorption into the Supreme Self is accomplished. For they hold that the self alone is the ultimate reality, since there is no means of valid cognition for the difference of other things from it. Indeed, perception grasps only the existence of objects and not their difference; thus, they consider this difference to be merely superimposed by ignorance.

That too is incorrect; for since the knowledge of the oneness of the self is of a false nature, it cannot logically be a means to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). We shall demonstrate its falsity in the section concerning the self, by means of the sūtra: "The selves are many because of their distinct dispositions" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 3.2.20).

In this way, it should be understood that even the knowledge of the non-duality of sound (*śabdādvaita*) is not a means to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), because it is of a false nature. To explain: there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*) for the claim that all objects have the nature of sound. If it is argued that there is likewise a lack of evidence for their difference [from sound], that is incorrect; for objects devoid of the nature of sound are perceived by the eyes and other senses. Indeed, the "nature of sound" would mean that an existing object is audible. But this is not the case for objects, since they are not grasped by the ear. If it is argued that the variety of perceptions arises from different states of sound itself, that is not so. Such [variety] would exist only if the nature of sound were established, yet there is no evidence for that. If it is argued that the very perception [of objects] through contact with sound is the evidence, no; for air and the like are perceived even without such contact by one who has not made a linguistic convention (*samaya*). Furthermore, contact with another sound is not logical, as it would entail the futility of linguistic conventions. Thus, when the nature of sound is the probandum, the perception of an object in contact with sound is not the evidence. For this very reason, the presentation of distinctions such as *vaikharī*, *madhyamā*, *paśyantī*, and *sūkṣmā* is the talk of a madman. Nor is there any necessary connection (*pratibandha*) such that the subtle state (*sūkṣmāvasthā*) is attained through the knowledge of the non-duality of sound.

And since, when one form of non-duality is refuted, all varieties of non-duality are likewise refuted by virtue of the same underlying logical connection, this [objection] will be refuted simply by the refutation of the oneness of the Self; therefore, we shall desist.

Others, however, maintain that through the grace of Maheśvara, when impure sovereignty is destroyed, there occurs a transference of its qualities [to the soul]. But that is incorrect, because the functioning of the qualities of one thing in another is never observed. Furthermore, the grace of Maheśvara is not denied in the case of liberation, since liberation is dependent upon it; this remains established by the refutation of false doctrines. Thus, the knowledge of the true nature of the six categories through their similarities and differences is the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) for the liberated one.
[An investigation of the words "atha" and so forth found in the Sūtra.]

Some maintain that the phrase beginning with "atha" (now) is also connected to the [following] sūtra as another interpretation; however, this is incorrect. For in every interpretation, it is indeed accepted that the Bhāṣya demonstrates that [the meaning] has been formulated in the sūtra, as in: "Now, therefore, we shall explain Dharma" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.1), and "That from which the attainment of prosperity and the supreme good results is Dharma" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.2). In the preceding sūtra, the word *atha* also signifies immediate succession (*ānantarya*); since no other possibility exists, it is understood to mean "immediately after the salutation. And since the context concerns knowledge, that salutation must belong to Īśvara alone. Furthermore, the author of the Bhāṣya, having restated the salutation to the Supreme Guru intended by the author of the sūtras, performs a salutation to another [Guru]; thus it should be explained, but not as being directed toward Kaṇāda himself, because of the contradiction of an action being directed toward oneself.

Nor is he called Kaṇāda because he eats grains (*kaṇa*); for by the word *kaṇa*, one’s own fruit of action is denoted, and thus, through this difficult etymology, it would refer to the transmigrating self (*saṃsāryātman*). Consequently, there would be no purpose in paying homage to him.

The meaning of the word *atha* has already been expressed by the word *anu*. The word *ataḥ* also [indicates] that we shall explain *dharma* through the function of speech—that is, we shall demonstrate, up until its full comprehension, that which arises in various ways and from various sources, and that from which it does not arise. Thus, the description of the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*) is for the very purpose of explaining *dharma*. For this reason, it is said that "the categories are subsumed under *dharmas*," and thus it is called the *Padārthadharmasaṅgraha*. As for the explanation of the subsequent sūtra, it is called *mahodaya* because a great arising (*mahān udayaḥ*)—characterized by heaven and liberation—proceeds from it. Since happiness and knowledge [result] from *dharma*, and because of its primacy in the production of knowledge, the remainder is explained as being subordinate to it.

Now, the meaning of the individual words: "Having bowed to the Lord, the Cause" (*praṇamya hetumīśvaram*). By means of the prefix *pra-*, he demonstrates an excellence of salutation. "Cause" (*hetu*) refers to being the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). Since other beings also possess this quality, the word "Lord" (*īśvara*) is used [to specify]. Although the word *īśvara* occurs elsewhere, in this context of knowledge (*jñāna*), it refers specifically to Maheśvara, according to the scriptural statement: "One should seek knowledge from Śaṅkara."

[Objection: In that case, the word "cause" (*hetu*) is redundant, since its qualification is established by the context of the discussion concerning knowledge. [Response: This is not so. Because praise consists in the proclamation of qualities, it expresses the capacity to perform all effects. Otherwise, since the meaning would already be conveyed by the mention of either one alone, the mention of both would be redundant.

Thus, after paying homage to the Lord (Īśvara), he pays homage to the Sage (Muni). He provides the qualification "Kaṇāda" because other sages also possess distinguished knowledge and dispassion (*vairāgya*). That he possesses distinguished knowledge is understood from the fact that the categories (*padārtha*) expounded by him cannot be established by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Precisely for this reason, since false knowledge—which is the cause of attachment and aversion—is absent when true knowledge exists, his dispassion arising from the absence of aversion is ascertained. The term "Kaṇāda" is derived from "he who eats grains" (*kaṇān atti*); by showing this name based on a specific mode of eating, objections regarding his lack of existence are refuted. And that [is as follows]: *Note: The text provided ends mid-sentence; the translation reflects the available portion.*
"One may eat grains or, if one desires, buffalo curds," and so forth—this is consistent with reason (*yukti*).

Furthermore, the understanding of reason is not the cause of engagement (*pravṛtti*), because that understanding occurs only when engagement has already taken place. For instance, one who engages in listening understands whether [the teaching] is reasonable or unreasonable. Engagement does not precede that comprehension, as that would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). Therefore, engagement in listening at the outset is justified only when there is an awareness that [the work] was composed by a distinguished person (*viśiṣṭapuruṣa*). Indeed, people engage [in study] thinking, "This was composed by Manu," or "This was composed by Vyāsa."

Thus, when there is a specific property (*dharma-viśeṣa*) that depends upon the salutation of the supreme and subordinate gurus, the non-existence of various effects occurs due to the obstruction of that property; consequently, the completion of the treatise indeed takes place without impediment. Now, this may be argued to be incorrect. For even when a salutation is present, the completion of the treatise is not observed, as in the case of *Kādambarī* and other works. Conversely, its presence is observed even when a salutation is absent, as in passages such as "the cognition of an object through a means of valid knowledge" (*pramāṇato ’rtha-pratipattiḥ*, Nyāya-bhāṣya 1.1.1).

True. Since the completion of the treatise is an effect, its cause must necessarily be stated; and since no other [cause] is possible, a specific merit (*dharmaviśeṣa*) is the cause. Regarding this, some hold that it may arise either from the act of salutation or from something else, and thus it is not restricted. Others, however, maintain that it is distinguished by a specific means of accomplishment (*sādhanaviśeṣa*), such that the specific merit which serves as the cause arises solely from salutation.

Now, one might ask: "If there is no salutation (*namaskāra*), how then can the treatise be completed? No; for even in that case, the existence of the cause is established by the existence of the effect. Even in the absence of a verbal salutation, a mental salutation is understood to exist, because completion is observed whenever a specific salutation exists. Thus, a verbal salutation—when augmented by a mental one—is held to be the cause of completion, whereas a purely mental one is also sufficient. For this very reason, it is logical that in some cases, despite the presence of a verbal salutation, the work may not be completed due to the absence of a mental salutation; and the absence of that [mental salutation] is known precisely through the non-arising of the effect. Furthermore, the universal concomitance (*vyāpti*) is grasped from scripture (*āgama*), which states that merit (*dharma*) is produced from salutation. Likewise, even an ordinary person is seen to engage in performing an action only after having performed a salutation; how much more so, then, the Blessed Sage, who speaks only what is faultless?

Others, however, resort to alternative etymologies such as "he gives grains" (*kaṇān dadāti*) or "he protects" (*dayate*) in order to refute an unfounded objection. It should be considered whether this is indeed what is meant here by the composition of the Vaiśeṣika Sūtras; furthermore, [the term] was included merely to avoid ignorance of common usage. Enough with these erroneous explanations!

Thus, since the destruction of obstacles occurs through the salutation of the supreme and subordinate gurus, or because the disciple is endowed with the aforementioned characteristics, the *Padārthadharmasaṃgraha* will be expounded immediately thereafter, uninterrupted by any further counteractive action. Nor is a specific immediate succession understood from the suffix *-ktvā* alone; for that suffix merely indicates that an action occurs at a prior time when there is a common agent. For instance, even when an action such as lying down intervenes after eating, the expression "having eaten, he goes" (*bhuktvā vrajati*) is indeed used. In this context, [the sequence is]: immediately after the prostration to Īśvara, the salutation to the Sage (*muni*), and immediately after that, the act of exposition. Furthermore, the exclusion of non-counteractive actions is not established, since physical movements and the like do occur.

Regarding the title *Padārthadharmasaṃgraha*: it means "a compendium of the properties (*dharma*) of categories (*padārtha*). Even though the final member of the compound is predominant, since properties reside in their substrates (*dharmin*), the compendium necessarily pertains to them as well. It is not denied that properties hold predominance here, because when one understands the properties of being the means to pleasure or pain, engagement or withdrawal occurs. Furthermore, while the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is intended as the primary subject here, it is certainly obtained as being subordinate to the categories.

Alternatively, because both are connected to the primary action of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), they possess primacy; thus, the compound is *padārthāś ca dharmāś ca* (both categories and properties). For independence consists precisely in connection with the primary action, not in the identity of the properties with the substratum (*dharmin*), as we shall explain later. "The compendium of the categories and their properties" (*padārthadharmasaṃgraha*) refers to a concise statement of what has been explained at length in other treatises. Others maintain that, through a verbal derivation (*bhāvavyutpatti*), it means "the knowledge of reality."

And that [treatise] "will be proclaimed," meaning it will be explained. Of what nature is it? It is called "of great exaltation" (*mahodaya*) because from it arises great exaltation (*mahodaya*), which is its effect, namely the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).

[As stated: "The knowledge of the true nature of the six categories—substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence—by way of their similarities and differences, is the cause of the supreme good. (*PDhS*)

The statement beginning with "Padārthadharmasaṅgraha" is a general declaration; the subsequent sentences concerning substance (*dravya*) and so forth serve to classify it. Since that classification is intended to indicate specific categories while excluding the rest, and because a determination of the exact number is indeed achieved through such classification—as evidenced by the mention of exactly six—it follows that there are precisely six categories (*padārtha*).

Now, why is non-existence (*abhāva*) not enumerated separately? Because it appears as subordinate to existence (*bhāva*). For instance, one who has no prior knowledge of the existence of a thing—such as an inhabitant of the Coconut Island (*nārikeladvīpa*)—cannot have a cognition of its non-existence. Since non-existence depends upon the thorough cognition of existence, it is not enumerated separately; for once existence is known, its non-existence is indeed cognized. Thus, the cognition of its non-existence is obtained from the thorough cognition of the substance (*dravya*), and their predominance has already been demonstrated.

“*Tattvajñānam*” (knowledge of reality) is the substantive for *samyaktva* (rightness), meaning knowledge; it does not mean that which is both reality (*tattva*) and knowledge (*jñāna*). For if there were deviation between the two terms, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Indeed, in the case of earth, fragrance is the reality (*tattva*), but it is not knowledge. Furthermore, knowledge can also be false knowledge, but that is not reality. Thus, despite this deviation, there is no coreferentiality between words denoting a property (*dharma*) and its possessor (*dharmin*). For reality, in the form of rightness, is indeed a property of knowledge itself.

Others, however, maintain that [this knowledge] arises through both similarity and dissimilarity with respect to the self (*ātman*), because the self is the primary reality (*tattva*). The primacy of the self is due to its being among the categories such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth; for it is accepted that the [knowledge] arising there through the power of practice is the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). Nor does this entail the consequence of [applying it to] false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), because it is qualified by being the cause of the supreme good; since false knowledge cannot possibly be the cause of the supreme good. And how the cause of the supreme good is the knowledge of reality has already been stated in the opening sentence. Furthermore, since that knowledge of the self depends on the knowledge of other categories because it is distinguished from them, the knowledge of the similarities and dissimilarities of substance and the other categories is purposeful.
(“From dharma alone, manifested by the command of God. <PDhS>

Now, let it be granted that true knowledge (*tattvajñāna*) arises from summary (*saṃgraha*); however, there is a contradiction in the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). To explain: if true knowledge arises from summary alone, then the author of the Sūtras would not possess it, because he lacks such a summary. If, on the other hand, it arises [from summary] and only then, that is incorrect; for even when a summary exists, it is absent for one of dull intellect. If it is argued that from summary there is *only* true knowledge, that is not so, since suffering and the like are also observed; thus, the phrase "And that [comes] from the injunction of God" (*tacceśvaracodanā*) and so forth is intended to resolve this doubt. To explain further: for people like us, true knowledge arises from summary alone. As for the knowledge of the author of the Sūtras, that arises specifically from particular qualities (*dharma*) and so forth manifested by the injunction of God. Nor should it be said that [the author’s case] is the same as ours, because people like us lack such specific qualities. Likewise, true knowledge certainly arises from summary, provided that the restrictive particle (*evakāra*) is understood as a conjunction rather than an exclusion, as in: "And that [comes] from the injunction of God, manifested from dharma alone. For one who possesses specific qualities, true knowledge is achieved with very little effort. Alternatively, let it be that from summary there is *only* true knowledge and not suffering and the like, provided that it comes from dharma alone manifested by the injunction of God. For whomsoever there is the presence of specific qualities, for them true knowledge is accomplished with minimal exertion.

Alternatively, the purpose of describing *dharma* at the beginning of the Sūtra, or offering salutations to the Lord (*īśvara*), is to resolve the following objection: "How can the knowledge of reality arise? [The answer is: The knowledge of reality arises solely from *dharma* manifested by the injunction of the Lord. Therefore, there is a formal declaration of that [dharma] at the beginning, as well as salutations to the Lord. The injunction of the Lord is a specific volition (*saṅkalpa*) in the form: "Let this be accomplished for him from this. From *dharma* manifested and assisted by that [injunction], the knowledge of reality arises. Furthermore, in response to the inquiry, "What is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of *adharma*?", one should repeat this very same point: "The injunction of the Lord. For an injunction is an impelling statement; because it is the primary element, the Veda is called the injunction. And since it was composed by the Lord, it is a means of valid cognition. [The phrase] "from that manifested" means "from *dharma* alone, as revealed [by that injunction]."
(“Now, what are the categories such as substance (*dravya*)? What is their nature? And what is their similarity (*sādharmya*), and what is their dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*)?

<PDhS> Thus, having accepted that the knowledge of the similarities and dissimilarities of substance and the other categories is the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), [the author] says, for the sake of thoroughly understanding their nature: “Now, what are the categories such as substance? What is their nature? And what is their similarity, and what is their dissimilarity? This is stated because doubt arises due to the various ways in which substance and the others have been described by others.

For instance, some hold that the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is substance (*dravya*), while others maintain it is that which is fit for buying and selling, and so forth. Or, one might be mistaken, thinking that substances and the other categories do not exist at all. Now, what are these categories such as substance? He says they do not exist; because of their absence, there is neither similarity (*sādharmya*) nor dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).

For instance, since color and touch appear through sight and touch respectively, there exists no substance distinct from them. Furthermore, this cognition of a jar and so forth is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it is a conceptual cognition (*kalpanājñāna*). There is also a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) consisting of the dilemma of subsistence (*vṛttivikalpa*) and other arguments. Thus, it is not accepted that parts subsist in a whole. And when a whole subsists in its parts, does it subsist in one part or by pervading [all parts]? If it subsists in one part, there would be the consequence of further parts. If it subsists in all parts, there is a contradiction with its being manifold; moreover, it would become a single substance. In that case, due to the absence of division of parts, it would be eternal; and as a single entity, it could not be a producer [of effects] either successively or simultaneously, nor could color and so forth arise [from it], since you accept that it produces multiple colors and so on. Furthermore, there would be no appearance of a "whole" in the parts, because it would then be a single substance. Now, suppose it does not subsist in each part individually by way of complete presence, but rather that it is one and the same in all parts. Even in that case, if it functions in other parts by means of its own singular nature, there is the consequence of those parts becoming one, because the whole consists in the form of subsisting in those parts. If it functions by means of different natures, then there is multiplicity, because difference is defined by a difference in nature. Thus, because subsistence is untenable, [the whole] is non-existent. For existence is pervaded by subsistence; and as that [subsistence] is excluded, it excludes existence which is pervaded by it—this is the intended meaning. [The opponent might argue: "Others perceive [the whole] as occupying a different location, like a cow or a horse. Since the cognition of it does not occur when those [parts] are not perceived, [the whole must exist]. However, if the whole is non-existent, then jars and such are merely aggregates of color and so forth. An aggregate is not a separate entity from its constituent members; thus, it exists only as a conventional reality (*saṃvṛtisan*).

Thus, everything is consciousness alone; for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of anything other than that. In this way, even the doctrines of the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*) should be refuted as the occasion arises, and thus they are not elaborated upon here.

"In that regard, substances are said to be exactly nine, designated by the general and specific names [of the categories]: earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, self, and mind. This is because no other name is mentioned for anything distinct from these. <PDhS>

In order to establish the true nature of substance for those who are doubtful or lacking comprehension, he says: “Therein, the substances,” and so forth. For instance, because a substance distinct from color and the other qualities is determined through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), misconceptions are eliminated. Color is indeed perceived by the eye alone, and touch by the tactile organ; however, substance is perceivable by two organs. How is this so? Through synthesis (*pratisandhāna*). For example: “That very thing which I saw with my eye, that same thing I now touch”; and “That which I touched, that very thing I now see. And such synthesis is not logical without the apprehension of a single object by both organs. Furthermore, since color and touch are each restricted to their own specific sense organ, [the synthesis] would not be possible [if there were no underlying substance].

Now, if it is argued that this is a conceptual cognition (*kalpanājñāna*), what indeed is this so-called "conceptual cognition"? If it is argued that because of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), the object perishes at the same time as the non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpakajñāna*), and thus this [conceptual cognition] arises only after remembrance (*smaraṇa*)—and therefore, being without an object (*nirviṣayatva*), it is not a means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇa*)—we say no. Since momentariness is unproven, even for that which occurs immediately after remembrance, its status as being produced from the object (*arthajatva*) remains, because it follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with the object, just like the non-conceptual cognition. If it is argued that since it is produced from the object, the object must exist at the very same time as the non-conceptual cognition, and that this [conceptual cognition] could arise because the sense organs (*indriya*) are non-discerning (*avicāraka*), we say no. This is because of the absence of a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*). To explain: in the production of conceptual cognition regarding objects, the sense organ depends upon the remembrance of linguistic conventions (*saṅketa*). Now, in the case of remembrance, do you maintain that there is either the addition of some excellence (*atiśaya*) to the object and the sense organ, or the removal of a lack of excellence? No; for remembrance itself is that excellence. For instance, whatever brings about an effect when something else is present is an excellence of that thing. Since the sense organ produces its effect when remembrance is present, remembrance itself is its excellence. Alternatively, through remembrance, the completeness of the causal factors (*kārakasākalya*) itself becomes the excellence, while their deficiency—the lack of excellence—is removed. For it is only when there is completeness that the effect is produced. As they say: [The verse follows: *smṛtyanugrahādvikalpe yadi pratyakṣatocyate | saṅketasmaraṇopāyamanyathā tadanugrahaḥ ||* "If it is claimed that conceptualization is perception because it is assisted by memory, then that assistance would otherwise [be required] through the means of remembering conventions."* *Note: The verse cited here is from Kumārila Bhaṭṭa’s Ślokavārttika, Pratyakṣasūtra, verse 120.*
"That which was previously not a cause of cognition due to the lack of any distinction in its utility would likewise remain so later;

therefore, even when the object has disappeared, there would be visual cognition"—this [argument] is refuted, because the "lack of distinction in utility" is unestablished. For instance, in non-conceptual (nirvikalpaka) awareness, there is no recollection of linguistic conventions (*saṅketa*) regarding the sense organ, whereas in conceptual (savikalpaka) awareness there is; thus, there is a distinction in utility.

{An Examination of Whether Conceptual Cognition is Produced from an Object} Now, conceptual cognition has the form of a word. Yet, the nature of a word does not exist in the object, for otherwise it would follow that conceptual cognition arises even at the very first contact of the sense organ [with the object]. Furthermore, [if the object were the cause], there would be a determination by the eye and other senses, whereas [conceptual content] is seen to be determined by the ear; thus, conceptual cognition would be objectless. This is incorrect. Since the refutation of the theory of forms (*ākāravāda*) will be stated later, the nature of a word does not exist in cognition. Moreover, it has been said that the difference in the cognition itself is caused solely by the difference in its auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*).

If substances do not exist, another cause for the synthesis [of cognitions] must be stated. If it is argued that there exists a latent impression (*vāsanā*) nourished since beginningless time, we say no; for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its existence. If it is argued that conceptual cognition itself is the means of valid cognition, we say no; because it occurs otherwise as well. For instance, since it is possible even when an object exists, how can it serve as a means of valid cognition for the existence of a latent impression? Furthermore, the understanding of a causal relationship is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and these two are present here for the sense organ just as they are elsewhere. If it is argued that because the sense organ operates in the production of non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*), its operation appears to be present in conceptual cognition as well due to dependence on that [non-conceptual cognition], but not in reality, that is not so. If [the cognition] were non-momentary, its operation would be possible in both cases. Nor is there any necessary connection (*pratibandha*) such that non-conceptual cognition alone is the cause for the production of conceptual cognition by way of the recollection of linguistic conventions (*saṅketa*). This is because perception necessarily has the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object and does not have succession as its object, whereas inference has only the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object. And there is no probans (*liṅga*) that is necessarily connected [to the effect]. Since the effect can occur otherwise, there is no proof for succession.

Furthermore, for those who maintain the doctrine of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), consciousness is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) only with respect to its own determination, not with respect to another object. If it is argued that mental impressions (*vāsanā*) alone are the cause [of conceptual diversity], then these impressions are not distinct from consciousness, because no cause is admitted apart from the cognitions of form, taste, smell, touch, and sound. If, however, they were identical [to consciousness], then since there would be no distinction anywhere due to their being of the nature of awareness (*bodha-rūpatā*), the variety of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) would not exist. If it is argued that the variety of mental impressions arises precisely from the variety of conceptual constructions and not from [external] effects, then—given their non-difference from consciousness—the consequence follows that they must be one, just like consciousness; or else, consciousness itself would have to be manifold, due to its identity with multiple objects. Otherwise, if this were reversed, their identity would be untenable. If it is further claimed that mental impressions are both the cause of specific cognitions and external, then the only difference would be in name, as "object" (*artha*) and "mental impression" (*vāsanā*) would be synonymous. If, on the other hand, mental impressions possess the nature of real entities (*vastu-rūpa*), then they could not be the producers of cognition, because the definition of a real entity is its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*).

Now, if it is argued that being "conceptual" (*savikalpaka*) consists in arising immediately after recollection (*smaraṇa*), then since that [recollection] has already been established as being produced by the object (*arthaja*), this is not a valid objection. Or, if it were accepted [that recollection is conceptual], it would follow that even indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*) would be conceptual. For instance, when there is contact between the tongue and a taste immediately after the recollection of a color, a cognition of taste arises. In that case, because the recollection of the color occurred at a prior time, it possesses the status of an immediately preceding cause (*samanantara-kāraṇa*); thus, according to the principle that "from cognition [comes] the nature of cognition," that [recollection] too would possess the character of a conceptual construction (*kalpanātva*) due to its arising immediately after recollection. Nor can it be said that in this case the status of being an immediately preceding cause is due to its nature as cognition, whereas elsewhere it is due to its nature as recollection; for there is no existence of a form of recollection that is a different entity from cognition, such that they could be identical. And when there is non-difference, a distinction—wherein in one case there is the status of being an immediately preceding cause by way of the nature of cognition, and in another case by way of a different form—is not tenable. Therefore, arising immediately after recollection does not constitute being conceptual. Furthermore, once it is established that [perception] is produced by the object, the fact that it arises with the mention of name, genus, and so forth, is not a defect. Since the character of conceptual construction is impossible [in perception], the act of synthesis (*pratisandhāna*) is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for establishing substance.

In this way, the objective support (*ālambana*) of the cognition of a jar and so forth must also be stated, for that [cognition] is a correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*). It is not a collection of form (*rūpa*) and other qualities, because since form and the rest are each perceivable by specific sense organs, their collection cannot be the object of a single sense organ. Furthermore, a collection of form and the rest that does not exist in ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) cannot be a producer of cognition. Since such a collection is not perceived, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of atoms (*aṇu*), for they are only known through their effects. Nor does an unaggregated atom exist, because it is simultaneously joined with six [other atoms]; thus, even that [atom] is non-existent in ultimate reality. And that which is not being accumulated cannot at all be an object of our perception; therefore, it follows that the cognition of jars and so forth would be without an object. Moreover, a cognition that is not sublated cannot be without an objective support; thus, because [the cognition and its object] are not distinct, the object is the undivided whole (*avayavin*).

If it is argued that there is a sublation [of the opponent's position] by means of the dilemma regarding subsistence (*vṛtti*) and so forth, we say no; for that [dilemma] lacks validity (*apramāṇatva*). To explain: [the opponent claims] "non-existence [of the whole] follows from the impossibility of subsistence. Is this an independent proof (*svatantra-sādhana*) or a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga-sādhana*)? If it is an independent proof, then since the thesis statement—"the whole (*avayavin*) as the subject (*dharmin*) does not exist"—involves a contradiction between its two terms (like saying "this does not exist"), and because the reason (*hetu*) suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatva*) due to the non-establishment of the subject, [it is invalid]. Furthermore, according to our own view, color and other qualities do exist, yet they lack subsistence; thus, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*), since we do not admit *inherence* (*samavāya*). Now, if it is argued that this is a reductio intended to produce an undesirable consequence for the opponent based on the opponent’s own pervasion (*paravyāpti*), [we reply: the opponent has accepted the "whole" as the subject, since it is what is to be demonstrated. In that case, if the opponent has already apprehended the whole through a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then the opposing inference cannot even arise, as it would be sublated by that very same [valid cognition]. Nor can it be said that the whole is sublated by this [inference] alone, because the reason would lack the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) without that [prior valid cognition]. If, on the other hand, the opponent has apprehended it through an invalid means of knowledge, then one must state that an object of knowledge is not established without a valid means of knowledge; what is the point of presenting an inference, since it lacks the property of being a feature of the subject and is therefore not a valid means of knowledge? Moreover, existence is not pervaded by subsistence for the opponent, because [existence] is observed in space (*ākāśa*) and so forth even in the absence of [subsistence]; thus, the reason is inconclusive (*anekānta*). Furthermore, it is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*), because subsistence—namely, inherence—is indeed established [for us].

Furthermore, as for the claim that [the whole] exists neither partially nor by its entire self, this is because it does not exist in any single part. Nor is the application of the word "different" (bheda) appropriate to an undivided whole, since it is observed only in relation to many things. For instance, a "part" (ekadeśa) is the designation of one among many, whereas the meaning of the word "all" (sarva) is the state of being without remainder. Likewise, since the negation of a specific case implies the admission of the remaining cases, it follows that there must be a mode of existence other than those specified; otherwise, one would have to say simply that it "does not exist. Moreover, if there were existence in a part—as in the case of a bamboo stalk existing in its segments—it would lead to the undesirable consequence that designations could not apply to the whole. Furthermore, if atoms lacked such a mode of existence, no composite effect could arise through the process beginning with dyads (dvyaṇuka).

Now, if this refers to the meaning of "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*), then does it exist there by way of pervasion (*vyāpti*) or by way of non-pervasion? In that regard, the acceptance [of its existence] as pervading its own substratum—like color (*rūpa*) and so forth—or as non-pervasive through the mode of subsistence—like conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth—is [the case]. For thus, the conceptual construction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)—that the whole (*avayavin*) exists in its parts by way of inherence (*samavāya-vṛtti*) and not by way of another form—is also refuted.
