Now, if the whole (*avayavin*) is perceived by means of the perception of all its parts, then because the middle and rear parts are not perceived, the whole would not be perceived at all. However, if it were perceived through the perception of even a single part, then it would be perceived even when only the dewlap (*sāsnā*) is observed; but this is not the case. This is because the whole is perceived through contact with the sense organ aided by contact with many parts. Furthermore, since the investigation into causes proceeds from the existence of an effect, once direct cognition is established, one says that the whole has this [contact with many parts] as its cause. Thus, the argument "because it is not perceived due to spatial difference" is inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to color and so forth. For instance, color and other qualities are not perceived as having different locations, yet they exist and are distinct from one another, as there is a difference in their appearance. Even cows and the like are distinguished solely by the difference in their appearance, not by a difference in location, for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of no distinction between designations. Likewise, the argument "because in the absence of those [parts], there is no cognition of that [whole]" is also contradictory. For the meaning of "in the absence of the perception of those parts, there is no cognition of that whole" is precisely that the cognition of the whole occurs upon the perception of the parts, which establishes the existence of the whole. Thus, from the perception of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), there arises the cognition of the qualified (*viśeṣya*); therefore, there is neither non-existence nor identity [of the whole with its parts]. Similarly, the perception of the parts is unproven in the perception of the whole, since in dim light one perceives only the configuration (*saṃsthāna*) of the whole. This debate regarding the whole has been explained in detail by my teachers, and thus it is not elaborated here. Once the whole is established, its qualities and other attributes residing therein are also generally established.
The Section on the Enumeration of Categories such as Substance and the Rest.

In this regard, he makes a proposition concerning substances: "Substances exist in an ultimate sense (*paramārthasat*), because they are objects of non-sublated cognition. Whatever is an object of non-sublated cognition exists ultimately, just like consciousness; these [substances] are likewise objects of non-sublated cognition; therefore, they exist ultimately. Here, in the subject (*pakṣa*) under consideration, the property of being an object of non-sublated cognition constitutes the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*). Furthermore, since consciousness—which exists ultimately—is an object of cognition, we shall explain that the reason is present in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*); and its exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), such as a donkey's horn, is established. Since neither perception nor scripture presents a contrary meaning, the object is uncontradicted. And because there is no valid counter-argument, the argument possesses validity.

Thus, in the compound "earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, self, and mind," (*pṛthivyaptejovāyvākāśakāladigātmamanāṃsi*), a *dvandva* (copulative) compound is used because all members are independent. Here, regarding the proposition that these are "substances" (*dravyāṇi*), he will state that the proof is their connection with the genus "substanceness" (*dravyatva*); likewise, regarding the subdivisions of earth and so forth, he will state the specific definitions such as "earthenness" (*pṛthivītva*) and the rest. These have been "designated by general and particular names" (*sāmānyaviśeṣasaṃjñayoktāni*): the general name is "substance," and the particular names are "earthenness" and so on; they are designated by these. How many are there? "Exactly nine" (*navaiva*) is determined, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish fewer or more. For instance, since the existence of earth and the others will be demonstrated later, there is no deficiency.

Now, because it is perceived as having [additional] qualities, its absence [of being a substance] is unproven. For instance, shadow is a substance, because it possesses action and because it possesses qualities. Its possession of action is known even through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), since from the operation of the eye there arises the cognition "it goes," and because of its reaching another location. To explain: shadow possesses motion, because it reaches another location; whatever reaches another location is observed to possess motion, just like Devadatta; and shadow reaches another location; therefore, it possesses motion. Furthermore, it possesses qualities.
Sunlight is pungent and dry, while shade is sweet and cool;
such is the traditional teaching (āgama).

This is incorrect, because shadow (*chāyā*) is of the nature of the absence of light (*bhāsām-abhāva*). To explain: wherever the proximity of light is obstructed by an obscuring substance (*vāraka-dravya*), there the conventional usage "shadow" occurs. Furthermore, one perceives that "the shadow moves" by superimposing upon the shadow the motion belonging to the obscuring substance, [provided] there is an absence of sunlight. Otherwise, the dependence on the motion residing in the obscuring substance would not exist. As for this quality of reaching another location—is it conjunction (*saṃyoga*) with another location, or inherence (*samavāya*)? It cannot be conjunction, because that too is something yet to be proven. For instance, conjunction is established only when the status of being a substance (*dravyatva*) is established; since the status of being a substance follows from conjunction, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). If, on the other hand, reaching another location is taken as inherence, that too is unproven; for what is inherent in one place cannot be inherently present in another. Shadow, however, is perceived as connected in one place and is subsequently perceived in another location as well. Moreover, the possession of action does not follow from inherence in another location, because action exists only among things that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*); thus, the possession of action is not a proof [for its being a substance]. And as for the sweetness or coolness attributed to shadow based on scripture, that too is merely figurative (*upacāra*). For those qualities which belong to a sweet or cool substance arise from the contact with shadow; they are described as such because the shadow performs the function of producing those effects. Therefore, one should not say that shadow is a substance because it possesses action and possesses qualities. Nor is it logical to claim it is a different kind of substance, because of the definitive restriction that "there are exactly nine substances."

On this point, some state the following reason: "Substances are exactly nine, because—given the absence of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) to establish fewer or more—they possess nine defining characteristics that stand in a relationship of delimiting and delimited, just like the nine substances such as the jar and so forth accepted by both [parties]. To explain: the absence of evidence for a greater number has already been shown. As for the defining characteristics, we shall explain them in their proper place. Furthermore, since the Omniscient Sage did not mention any other designations beyond those such as "earth" and so forth, there is no existence of other substances. For the Sage’s formal proposition was: "Whatever exists here in the form of a positive entity, all that must be enumerated by me."

“Qualities (guṇas) are seventeen as explicitly stated: color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort. Furthermore, there are exactly seven others gathered by the word ‘and’ (ca): heaviness, fluidity, viscidity, mental impression (saṃskāra), unseen force (adṛṣṭa), and sound. Thus, there are twenty-four qualities. <PDhS>

Likewise, he makes a proposition regarding the qualities (*guṇa*): "The qualities are ultimately real (*paramārthasat*) for the very same reason as previously stated. Furthermore, he will state the proof for the connection with the nature of quality (*guṇatva*) in the conventional usage of "quality," and the specific definition of those [qualities] within the various distinctions such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth. These, however, have been explicitly mentioned by the author of the Sūtras as "color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort" (*rūpa-rasa-gandha-sparśa-saṃkhyā-parimāṇa-pṛthaktva-saṃyoga-vibhāga-paratva-aparatva-buddhi-sukha-duḥkha-icchā-dveṣa-prayatnāḥ*). They are thus expressed through the function of the words [of the Sūtra], and we shall explain them. Here, the compound is a copulative (*dvandva*). To exclude deficiency or excess, those [qualities] obtained by implication are stated again by way of number as "seventeen" (*saptadaśa*). And by the word "and" (*ca*), heaviness, fluidity, viscidity, mental impression (*saṃskāra*), unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), and sound are also included; since the term "unseen force" (*adṛṣṭa*) denotes both merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), they become seven [additional ones].

Now, could there be an excess [of qualities] due to the threefold nature of those residing in *saṃskāra*? No; because they are one with respect to the universal (*jāti*) of *saṃskāratva*. Nor is it the case that there exists no commonality (*sāmānya*) called "unseen-ness" (*adṛṣṭatva*). Nor should it be asked how there can be an addition [of other qualities], since the inclusion of others such as desire (*kāma*), anger (*krodha*), and so forth will be explained as being included within these very [twenty-four]. "In this manner" means by the method already stated. "The twenty-four qualities" is said for the purpose of excluding both deficiency and excess. Since there is an absence of any proof establishing more or less, [the number is fixed] because they possess twenty-four characteristics that stand in a relationship of mutual exclusion and exclusion, like the twenty-four substances such as the jar (*ghaṭa*) accepted by both [parties].

Now, if it is argued that because qualities (*guṇa*) are devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*), their connection with number is untenable, we say no; for this is accepted as a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). For a metaphorical designation is postulated only when there exists a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the primary sense. And since that [metaphor] depends upon a cause (*nimitta*), the connection with an uncommon property (*asādhāraṇa-dharma*) serves as the cause. For wherever number is perceived, there too is the connection with an uncommon property; thus, through the recollection of that [connection], superimposition (*adhyāropa*) proceeds. The pervading cause (*vyāpaka-nimitta*), however, is either the capacity to produce purposeful action (*arthakriyā-janakatva*) or [the presence of a substance]. Co-inherence in a single object (*ekārtha-samavāya*) is not the [pervading] cause, because it is non-pervasive (*avyāpakatva*). To explain: while co-inherence in a single object exists for qualities and actions, it does not exist for universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth; therefore, this [co-inherence] is a non-pervasive cause for metaphorical designation. Nor is number a form of a quality (*dharma-rūpa*), because its exclusion from that [quality] will be stated later.

Others, however, maintain that because number functions here solely as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) through the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) is impossible. For instance, since the relation of qualifier and qualified is perceived without distinction in qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, just as it is in substances (*dravya*), on the grounds that the cognition of a thing qualified by number would otherwise be inexplicable—how could there be any metaphor? Furthermore, they argue that no rule exists stating that a qualifier must be either conjoined (*saṃyukta*) or inherent (*samaveta*). This is not so. For we observe that qualities, actions, and universals function as qualifiers only when they are inherent. Moreover, since qualities are themselves devoid of further qualities, the inherence of number within them is impossible. If qualities, actions, and universals were to function as qualifiers while remaining non-inherent, there would be an absence of false cognitions (*mithyājñāna*) and the like; for we shall explain that the cognition of a thing qualified by such [non-inherent factors] would be indistinguishable in both cases (true and false). Therefore, the linguistic usage of "one" and so forth with respect to qualities and the like must be explained as being purely metaphorical.

“Throwing upward, throwing downward, contraction, expansion, and locomotion—these are the five types of action alone. Because of the inclusion of ‘locomotion,’ whirling, evacuation, flowing, upward flaming, horizontal blowing, falling, bending, stretching, and so forth are specific varieties of locomotion and do not constitute separate classes. (PDhS)

Likewise, he makes a proposition regarding action (*karman*): "Actions are ultimately real" due to the very same proof previously stated. He will state that the proof consists in the connection with the nature of action (*karmatva*) in conventional usage, and that within the divisions of throwing upwards (*utkṣepaṇa*) and so forth, there exists their respective generalities (*sāmānya*). Similarly, "throwing upwards, throwing downwards, contraction, expansion, and going" is a *dvandva* compound. And for the purpose of excluding fewer or more [categories], there is the restriction: "only five actions. Here, however, the proof—characterized by the possession of the five definitions and accompanied by its qualification—is as before.

Now, it might be argued that because whirling and other such motions are perceived, the restriction [to five types of action] is untenable. This is not so; for he states that they are included within "going" itself: "By the mention of 'going,' whirling, receding, flowing, upward flaming, horizontal blowing, falling, bending, stretching, and so forth are specific varieties of going (*gamanaviśeṣāḥ*); they are subsumed under going and are merely its subdivisions. They are not different classes (*jātyantarāṇi*).

However, others hold that whirling and the rest are not merely specific varieties of going, but rather constitute different classes altogether. We shall demonstrate that this is an incorrect interpretation in the *Karmaparīkṣā*.

“Generality (*sāmānya*) is of two kinds: the higher (*para*) and the lower (*apara*). It is the cause of inclusive cognition (*anuvṛttipratyaya*). Among these, existence (*sattā*) is the higher, because its scope is the greatest; and since that existence is the cause of inclusion alone, it is a generality only. Substantiality (*dravyatva*) and the like are the lower, because their scope is smaller; and since they are also causes of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), they are generalities while also receiving the name ‘particular’ (*viśeṣa*).”

Thus, he makes a general proposition: “The universal (*sāmānyam*) is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*); the proof for this is as previously stated. However, regarding the conventional usage of the universal, he specifies the distinction by stating that the definition to be explained hereafter serves as the proof: “It is of two kinds. To ask in what form [it is twofold], he says: “Higher (*param*) and lower (*aparam*). By stating “the cause of inclusive cognition (*anuvṛttipratyayakāraṇam*),” he demonstrates its existence through its effect. For we shall explain in the examination of that [universal] that an inclusive cognition which is not caused by substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), or action (*karman*) arises from a connection with something else. This very [inclusive cognition], because it is unique (*asādhāraṇa*), also serves to differentiate the universal from others. For indeed, an inclusive cognition that is not caused by substance, quality, or action, and which is non-contradictory, does not occur without a universal; thus, it is indeed unique. In this regard, while specifying the distinction between the higher and the lower, he says: “Existence (*sattā*) is the higher universal. Why? “Because its scope is greater (*mahāviṣayatvāt*). For instance, the property of substance (*dravyatva*) exists only in substances, the property of quality (*guṇatva*) only in qualities, and the property of action (*karmatva*) only in actions; since existence pervades the domains of substance and so forth, it is the highest because its scope is greatest. For whatever pervades the domain of another is higher in relation to it, just as that which has a greater scope is higher in relation to earth-elements that have a smaller scope. And since that existence is the cause of inclusion alone, it is indeed a universal. Even though it is excluded from non-universals and the like, it is still a universal because it is the cause of the inclusive cognition of a real entity; thus, it is indeed a universal. Likewise, “the properties of substance and so forth are lower. By the use of the word “and so forth” (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the properties of quality (*guṇatva*), action (*karmatva*), earth (*pṛthivītva*), and so on. These are “lower” because their scope is smaller in comparison to existence. Since they possess the characteristics of a universal, they are “universals” in reality, yet they also receive the designation “particular” (*viśeṣa*) here figuratively. And since a figurative usage does not proceed without a basis, he says: “Because they are also the cause of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). It is not only the cause of inclusion; rather, it is also the cause of exclusive cognition. For the production of exclusive cognition is observed in the case of a particular (*viśeṣa*), and since that is present here too, the figurative usage proceeds. The primary particulars (*mukhya-viśeṣa*), however, are those that possess the specific characteristics of a particular.

“Particulars (viśeṣas) are those ultimate [qualities] residing in eternal substances; and they are indeed called particulars because they are the cause of the cognition of absolute differentiation. <PDhS>

Thus, he makes a proposition regarding the particulars (*viśeṣas*): "The particulars exist in the ultimate sense. The proof is as before. Regarding the phrase "subsisting in eternal substances" (*nityadravyavṛttayaḥ*): since cognitions (*buddhi*) and so forth also subsist only in eternal substances, the restriction "subsistence in eternal substances only" is intended to exclude [the fallacy of] subsisting in only a portion of the counter-examples (*vipakṣa*). It is not the case that cognitions and so forth are like this. This sentence is restrictive, meaning: "Their subsistence is only in eternal substances. Substances, qualities, and actions, however, subsist both in eternal and non-eternal substances. And since universals (*sāmānya*) also subsist in what is not a substance, the restriction is justified. By means of the exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), the phrase "only in eternal substances" establishes that because they subsist in eternal substances, the particulars are distinguished from everything else.

Others, however, claim that since the definition is intended with respect to categories (*padārtha*), the reason is "residing only in eternal substances. But that is incorrect; for [a reason] that resides in only a portion of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is not a prover. Moreover, even with respect to categories, there can be no exclusion from a portion of the counter-example—such as cognition (*buddhi*) and so forth—unless there is an exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*).

This is an explanation of the final term [of the definition]: "subsisting in eternal substances. As he will state later: eternal substances are denoted by the word *anta* (end) because they are situated at the end of production and destruction; those which exist in them are their subsistents (*tadvṛttayaḥ*), and are thus explained as *antya* (ultimate). And these—namely the *viśeṣas* (particularities)—"particularize," meaning they distinguish their own substratum from other substrata. For the sake of examination, he asks: Are these *viśeṣas* indeed only particulars, because they are always the cause of the cognition of exclusion alone? Not even a universal (*sāmānya*). For instance: atoms, which are the substrata of common genus, quality, and action, are connected with *viśeṣas*, because they are objects of the cognition of exclusion. Whatever is an object of the cognition of exclusion is connected with a *viśeṣa*, just like a post or similar things; and atoms are objects of the cognition of exclusion; therefore, they are possessed of *viśeṣas*. Furthermore, since being an object of the cognition of exclusion is observed in jars and so forth, it is established for eternal substances as well by the very reason of their being substances (*dravyatva*). Nor is it the case that qualities or other categories are the sole cause of the cognition of exclusion in atoms, because they are specified as being substrata of common genus, quality, and action. Nor should it be argued that the *viśeṣas* are not established as distinct because qualities and so forth are observed in the example, thereby creating a disparity between the example and the subject of the inference; for this would apply equally to all inferences. Thus, it is established that *viśeṣas* exist in eternal substances by virtue of generating the cognition of exclusion. However, they will be examined in detail during the investigation of *viśeṣas*; so, enough of this.

“*Samavāya* is that relation between things that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*) and stand in the relationship of the supported and the support, which is the cause of the cognition ‘it is here’. (*PDhS*)

Now, with the words "of things that are not established separately" (*ayutasiddhānām*), etc., he makes a formal proposition regarding inherence (*samavāya*): "Inherence is ultimately real, for the very same reasons previously stated. Its definition is stated: "The state of being the cause of the cognition 'here' [is the definition], even in the case of not seeing an intermediate space"; this refers to the apprehension of a relation. To explain: for those who do not perceive the space between a village and a grove from a distance, the cognition "there are trees here in the village" is observed; nevertheless, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the relation between the sky and a bird. Therefore, it is said: "the cause of the cognition 'here' is a relation. To illustrate: the cognition "a bird here in the sky" is observed. To exclude such cases, the mention of "the supported and the support" (*ādhāryādhāra*) is made. Now, the sky possesses neither the state of being a support nor the state of being supported, because there is no spatial relation of above and below (*adharottarabhāva*). For the relation of support and supported is observed only in the case of conjoined substances where a relation of above and below exists, as in the case of a bowl and a jujube fruit; and that [relation] is absent in the sky, because, due to its all-pervasiveness, it exists pervading the bird.

Now, it might be argued that because space (*ākāśa*) is beyond the reach of the senses, the cognition "here" would not occur with respect to it, since such a cognition exists only in relation to things that are perceptible. That is incorrect. Even though space is beyond the senses, the cognition "here" regarding it is merely an error; for the purpose of excluding that [error], the terms "locus" (*ādhāra*) and "located" (*ādheya*) are appropriate. Furthermore, the term "relation" (*sambandha*) is intended to exclude erroneous cognitions of this kind.

Others, however, in order to resolve this objection, maintain that *ākāśa* (space) is so called because it shines (*kāśate*) all around; thus, by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), the rays are designated as "space. They consider it logical that there can be the cognition "there is a bird here in space" based on direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). But that is incorrect, because if one resorts to metaphorical construction even when a primary sense exists, it leads to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, it has been stated that even regarding space, which is beyond the senses, non-perceptual knowledge is erroneous; therefore, a qualification is used to exclude such [erroneous] cases. Moreover, since space is the absence of corporeal substance, there is simply no connection with it.

For instance, when it is said that "inherence (*samavāya*) is the relation between things that stand in the relationship of the supported and the support, which is the cause of the cognition 'here [is this],' " there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the relation between a bowl and its fruit; therefore, the term "of things not established separately" (*ayutasiddhānām*) is used. "Establishment separately" (*yutasiddhi*) is as will be explained hereafter; those in whom that exists are "separately established," and by the negation of that, they are "not established separately. Even so, if it were merely said that "the relation of things not established separately is inherence," would there not still be a lack of deviation? No, because there is deviation due to the relation of signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*) and the relation of object and subject (*viṣayaviṣayibhāva*). To explain: the "greatness of space" (*ākāśamahattva*) is inherent in space and is denotable by the word "greatness"; thus, there is a relation of signifier and signified between the greatness of space and the word for it, yet there is no "establishment separately," because there is an absence of inherence in different substrates. For the greatness of space is inherent in space, and the word denoting it is also in that very same place—thus there is "non-separate establishment. Likewise, consciousness (*vijñāna*), which has desire and so forth as its objects, is inherent in the self, and desire and so forth are also in that very same place; thus, while there is non-separate establishment, there is between these the relation of object and subject. To exclude these two cases, the phrase "between the supported and the support" is employed. And in this case, the word "greatness of space" is not the support of that greatness, nor is the consciousness having desire and so forth as its object the support of them.

But even so, there is still deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to these two very cases. For instance, even when it is stated that "inherence (*samavāya*) is the relation between things that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*) and stand in the relation of the supported and the support (*ādhāryādhārabhūta*)," there remains deviation on account of the signifier-signified relation (*vācyavācakabhāva*) and the object-subject relation (*viṣayaviṣayibhāva*). To explain: since the sky is denoted by the word "sky," there exists a signifier-signified relation between these two while they stand in the relation of the supported and the support; yet, there is no separable establishment (*yutasiddhi*) here. Similarly, the cognition "I" has the self as its objective support (*ālambana*), and thus exists in the self itself; so, while there is inseparable establishment (*ayutasiddhatva*) between the two standing in the relation of the supported and the support, there exists an object-subject relation. Therefore, in order to exclude those [two], the restriction is made: "Inherence is only that relation which belongs to things standing in the relation of the supported and the support. This excludes both the signifier-signified relation and the object-subject relation, because these exist not only among things standing in the relation of the supported and the support, but also among things that are the opposite of such.

[Objection: But in that case, the phrase "of things not established separately" (*ayutasiddhānām*) is indeed redundant. [Response: No, for this too is a distinct definition, being restricted by the particle *eva*. For it is thus: "Inherence (*samavāya*) is that relation which belongs exclusively to things not established separately. However, the relations of denoted and denoter, and of object and subject, belong to both things established separately and things not established separately.

In this regard, some raise an invalid objection: "If inherence (*samavāya*) is unestablished, then there can be no inherence in substrates that are not 'separately established' (*yutasiddha*). Those things in which such separate establishment exists are 'not separately established' (*ayutasiddha*). By the negation of that [separate establishment], if there is an absence of those things that are not separately established, then inherence cannot exist. This is an invalid objection, because a definition serves to exclude what already exists. For if a non-existent thing were produced by a definition, then this objection regarding "those that are not separately established" would hold. It is not the case that the definition is impossible—on the grounds that "if inherence is not brought about by a definition, then due to the absence of separately established things, there is an absence of those not separately established"—because a definition is merely indicative (*jñāpaka*).

Now, [the opponent might argue that] the definition of inherence (*samavāya*) as "the relation between things that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*) and which stand in the relationship of the supported and the support" is redundant, since the phrase "the cause of the notion *iha* (here/in this)" already completes the two-fold definition. This is not so, because it serves the purpose of examination (*parīkṣā*). To explain: the notion "the cloth is in the threads" and so forth is produced by a relation, because it is an uncontradicted *iha*-notion; whatever is an uncontradicted *iha*-notion is produced by a relation, just like the notion "the curd is in the bowl"; and this [notion of the cloth in the threads] is likewise an uncontradicted *iha*-notion; therefore, it is produced by a relation. Furthermore, it is not the fact of being preceded by inherence that is being proven here, for that would entail the fallacy of the example lacking the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*). Nor is it the fact of being preceded by conjunction (*saṃyoga*). What then? It is the fact of being produced by a relation in general. And we shall explain in its specific examination that this [relation], being distinct from conjunction and the like, is indeed inherence. Enough with this excessive detail.
{Conclusion of the Section on Enumeration} (“Thus, the enumeration of the substrata has been made without [specifying] their properties. <PDhS>

Thus, when the categories (padārtha) such as substance (dravya) have been stated, a doubt arises among the students upon hearing the definitions and examinations of generality (sāmānya), particularity (viśeṣa), and inherence (samavāya): "Was the preceding section intended for mere enumeration (uddeśa), for definition (lakṣaṇa), or for examination (parīkṣā)? To dispel this doubt, the concluding statement beginning with "In this way" (*evam*) is presented primarily. Its primacy is due to the fact that enumeration is established everywhere [as the first step]. Enumeration, moreover, is the naming of categories by means of their designations alone. As for definition and examination, since they apply specifically to generality and the others, they are mentioned here only as a secondary consequence. Alternatively, considering that the highest good (niḥśreyasa) results from the thorough knowledge of the categories such as substance, a student might become discouraged—thinking that the highest good cannot be attained through mere knowledge of the enumeration—and thus turn away from listening. To reassure him, the statement says: "In this way, without the properties (dharma), there has been an enumeration of the property-bearers (dharmin) alone, neither their definition nor their examination. Through those [categories], the knowledge of similarities and differences (sādharmya-vaidharmya) arising from hearing is produced; and by the power of practice, this brings about direct (aparokṣa) cognition within the self—which is not characterized by any remaining particulars—thereby generating the highest good.
An investigation into the logical validity of determining the number of categories.

[Objection: But surely, if one accepts the restriction that "there are only six categories," then since it is impossible for properties (*dharma*) to be distinct [from the category of substance], how can there be an enumeration of substrata (*dharmin*) without [the properties] such as existence (*astitva*)? [Reply: No, because we accept that the restriction refers to the substrata themselves. [Objection: That is not so; for even existence and the others are indeed substrata in relation to their own underlying properties. Thus, even with respect to those, the restriction is contradicted. For instance, existence is the locus of the property of being denotable (*abhidheyatva*) because it is itself denotable; likewise, the property of being denotable is the locus of existence, and so forth. This should be applied accordingly.

[Objection: "The restriction [to six categories] is purposeful because they are the substrata of unique properties (*asādhāraṇadharma*). [Response: That is incorrect, because even existence (*astitva*) and so forth are substrata of unique properties. For instance, existence is distinct from nameability (*abhidheyatva*), and nameability is distinct from existence. If you argue that since differentiation (*vyāvṛtti*) is not possible without contact with a unique property, such a restriction based on being a substratum of unique properties is impossible—this is not so. Just as the definition of substance (*dravya*) is "that which possesses action, possesses quality, and is an inherent cause" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.15), where the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) and the exclusion of connection with others (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) apply to its being dependent on qualities; likewise, action (*karman*) is defined by its residing in corporeal substances necessarily while being momentary; generality (*sāmānya*) by its existing in many things through inherence while being eternal and unitary; particularity (*viśeṣa*) by its residing only in eternal substances through the exclusion of non-connection and the exclusion of connection with others; and inherence (*samavāya*) by its relation of necessary inseparability (*ayutasiddha*). Thus, there is no fault in the restriction that there are exactly six substrata of such properties.

If it is argued that because even distinct things lack a finite measure, they are non-numerable and thus do not become objects of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), we say no. Just as in the case of the earth, even though there is infinity, they become objects of the knowledge of reality through the apprehension of a single defining cause (*nimitta*). In that regard, the cause is "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) in the case of the earth, and "the nature of being a property" (*dharmarūpatā*) in the case of properties.

Now, if it is asked whether there is permanence (*nityatva*) or impermanence (*anityatva*) in *dharmas*: if they are permanent, there is no fault, because it is accepted that even upon the destruction of the substratum (*dharmin*), [the *dharma*] persists like existence (*sattā*). If they are impermanent, there is likewise no absence of production in qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, because substance alone is the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*); for just as destruction occurs, production is accepted as arising from efficient causes (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) alone. To explain: it is observed that a body consisting of substance, quality, and action is produced from inherent and other types of causes, whereas its opposite (destruction) arises from efficient causes alone. And so too, *dharmas* arise from efficient causes alone, because they are effects distinct from substance, quality, and action. Whatever is an effect distinct from substance, quality, and action is observed to arise solely from an efficient cause, just as destruction does; and since *dharmas* are effects distinct from substance, quality, and action, they therefore arise from efficient causes alone. Furthermore, since impermanence is observed in things whose nature is to be produced, existence (*astitva*) and the rest are also impermanent. Existence is the ground for the cognition "it exists," by which the cognition "it exists" occurs. Or, denotability (*abhidheyatva*) is the cause of the cognition of the denoted, and so on—this should be applied in all cases.

However, in the case of non-distinction (*avyatireka*), the explanation is that the subjects (*dharmin*) have been enumerated without their distinct attributes (*dharma*). In the case of distinction (*vyatireka*), because there exists a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), the qualification "distinct" is indeed obtained by implication. For thus, restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) would be untenable in the position of distinction.

Now, if it is argued that the restriction [of the number of categories] is intended as being based on the substratum of specific properties (*viśiṣṭadharma*), that is not correct. For if the restriction "there are only six categories" is stated according to the definitions already given, then since other categories that serve as substrata for common properties (*sādhāraṇadharma*) would remain unenumerated, the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) would be impossible. Yet, the restriction is for the sake of knowing reality. Furthermore, it is not the case that other categories are unknowable, because the entire manifold of existence (*bhāvaprapañca*) has been introduced as being knowable. Moreover, regarding those [other categories], the knowledge of reality must be achieved through both their general and specific forms. Generality consists in the nature of being an existent (*bhāvarūpatā*), while specificity consists in the application of defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇayoga*), as in the case of substance and the rest. And regarding those categories distinct from these [six], there would be knowledge only in a general sense, not in a specific one.

Now, if it is argued that—just as there is a specific characteristic such as substantiality (*dravyatva*)—there is also a specific state of being an object of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) due to the existence of a specific nature of *dharma*, then, in that case, even when other categories (*padārtha*) exist, one could not say "there are only six" if one accepts a restrictive determination (*avadhāraṇa*) based on their respective fixed definitions. For even though inherence (*samavāya*) exists, one would have to say "there are only five" based on the previous definitions. Likewise, if one accepts a restrictive determination based on each preceding definition despite the existence of each subsequent category, there would be only a single category. To explain: when a thing possesses the definition of substance, it is only a single category and nothing else; for if it possesses the definition of substance, it is included within substance itself.

Now, since it would follow that there could be no knowledge of reality regarding qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth—which possess distinct characteristics and relations—such a restriction [to six categories] is not tenable. If that is the case, then because it would follow that there could be no knowledge of reality regarding properties (*dharma*) that are not characterized by the six [categories], the restriction "only six" is improper. Furthermore, it was asserted at the outset that there is a declaration of the similarities and differences among the categories (*padārtha*). {An Investigation into the Nature of Properties (*dharma*)}

Likewise, because the nature of being a property (*dharmarūpatā*) does not pervade all individual properties (*dharma*), there can be no knowledge of reality regarding those properties. To explain: regarding this nature of being a property, is there another nature of being a property, or is there not? If it exists, then that [second] one would require yet another designation, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore, since the nature of being a property would be manifold, and in the absence of a single unifying cause or grasper (*upagrāhaka*), there could be no knowledge of reality regarding properties.

Furthermore, there is no universal (*sāmānya*) among phenomena (*dharma*) that possesses a recurring form (*anugatākāra*) apart from "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*), because one does not perceive a recurring cognition such as "phenomenon, phenomenon. If the nature of being a phenomenon (*dharmarūpatā*) were to pervade all phenomena by means of a recurring form, then, since it would possess the nature of a universal, phenomena would be included within [the categories of] substance (*dravya*) and so forth due to their connection with it; for the three [categories] beginning with substance are said to possess universals and particulars (*sāmānyaviśeṣavat*). Nor is the distinctness (*vyatireka*) of "phenomenon-ness" established merely by its possessing the characteristic of a universal, because that would entail the distinctness of "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and the rest as well. Likewise, since the nature of non-phenomenon (*adharmarūpatā*) cannot be connected with "phenomenon-ness," it is impossible for it to be included even within "phenomenon"; thus, it would have to be a separate category of entity (*padārthāntaratva*). And just as the nature of being a phenomenon exists in existence (*astitva*) and so forth, so too would other existences and so forth exist in "phenomenon-ness," and yet another "phenomenon-ness" would exist in those; thus, one cannot escape infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Now, it is not tenable that the very nature of existence (*dharmatva*) which is the superstratum (*ādheya*) of "existence" (*astitva*) and so forth should be the substratum (*ādhāra*) of other things and also their superstratum. For it is never observed that at one and the same time, that which is the substratum of something is also its superstratum. Furthermore, if a single cause such as "existence" were to persist across multiple entities, it would be included within the category of a universal (*sāmānya*), because it possesses the defining characteristics of a universal.

If there were a single, eternal existence (*astitva*) that, being present in all categories of objects (*padārtha*), produced the cognition [of "is"], what would be the use of *sattā* (existence as a category), or of intrinsic existence (*svarūpasattva*)? Or, if it is argued that existence is manifold, with the nameability (*abhidheyatva*) and so forth belonging to each individual object, we say no. For [if existence were manifold], even upon the destruction of a substratum (*dharmin*), existence would persist just like *sattā*. To explain: even when one substrate is destroyed, *sattā* persists in its unity by producing the cognition "it exists" in other objects as well. However, since the properties (*dharma*) are restricted to their respective objects, a different property alone could produce the cognition "it exists" in another substrate; thus, there is no proof for the persistence [of a single existence] even when the substrate is destroyed.

Now, if it is argued that because substance alone is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), qualities and so forth—lacking an originating cause—persist even when their substratum is destroyed; then, in that case, qualities and so forth would be non-eternal with respect to substances but eternal with respect to [other] qualities and so forth. If you say, "This is indeed accepted," then it is contradictory to claim that existence (*astitva*) and the rest arise solely from efficient causes (*nimittakāraṇa*) while possessing destruction. Furthermore, since existence and the rest are restricted to each individual object and are infinite in number, and since we observe the usage of non-different terms such as "exists" applied to those very objects, the same previous refutation must be inferred: that there is one existence among all existences, one nameability among all nameable things, and yet other existences and so forth within those [categories].

Furthermore, in the absence of a connection with a determinate substratum (*dharmin*), the restriction of designation—namely, that "this is its property"—is not tenable. Now, if the connection with existence (*astitva*) is inherence (*samavāya*), then properties (*dharmas*) would be included within substance (*dravya*) and the other categories by virtue of being inherent; for it is stated that only the five categories beginning with substance are inherent. If, on the other hand, the connection is something else consisting of the nature of the property, then if it is a relation of inseparable existence (*ayutasiddha*), how can it be distinct from inherence? Or, if it is distinct, let that very property itself be the pervader of the substratum; there is no need for inherence. Moreover, if another relation were admitted for that [connection], there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*); therefore, it must be accepted that it subsists in its own self. And subsisting in one's own self is precisely what inherence is.

Regarding the inference that "entities (*dharma*) arise solely from efficient causes (*nimittakāraṇa*), because they are effects distinct from substance, quality, and action, like destruction (*vināśa*)," the reason (*hetu*)—being an "effect" (*kāryatva*)—is unestablished (*asiddha*) if it means "the relation with the existence (*sattā*) of its own cause. Furthermore, since destruction lacks a relation with the existence of its own cause, the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is devoid of the probans (*sādhanavikala*). Moreover, since there is no proof for their being distinct from substance and so forth, the reason has a doubtful qualification (*sandigdhaviśeṣaṇa*). If it is argued that the cognition "it exists" regarding the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*) is the proof for their distinction [from those categories], then: "The cognitions such as 'it exists' regarding substances and so forth are based on an efficient cause established as distinct from the six categories, because they arise in respect to the six categories; whereas those which are not based on an efficient cause established as distinct from the six categories do not arise in respect to the six, just like the cognitions of substance and so forth. Since the cognitions 'it exists' and so forth do not arise in respect to the six [categories], they must therefore be based on an efficient cause established as distinct from the six categories"—this is the negative inference (*vyatirekī*). To explain: the cognition "it exists" regarding the six categories, as well as the cognition "it is denotable" (*abhidheya*), is seen to arise [in this way]; thus, there is the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*). There is no similar instance (*sapakṣa*) because there is no cognition accepted by both parties that is based on an efficient cause in the form of an entity distinct from the six categories. The cognitions of substance and so forth, however, are not based on an efficient cause in the form of an entity distinct from the six categories; thus they are the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). Therefore, the property of arising in respect to the six categories is excluded from the dissimilar instances. For instance, the cognition of a substance arises only in respect to a substance and not in respect to qualities and so forth; similarly, the cognition of a quality arises only in respect to a quality and not in respect to actions and so forth. Thus, there is no arising in respect to all six, which constitutes the exclusion from the dissimilar instances. Since this is contradicted in the dissimilar instances by perception and scripture, the reason is not "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*). Since no specific non-perception (*viśeṣānupalabdhi*) is possible, it is not "equal to the point at issue" (*prakaraṇasama*). Therefore, since the negative concomitance is established, the reason does not have a doubtful qualification. This is not so. The property of "arising in respect to the six categories" is unestablished with respect to individuals (*vyakti*). For instance, a single cognition "it exists" arises in respect to all six categories, as does the cognition "it is denotable. If it is argued that a cognition of the type "there is a substance," "there is a quality," etc., arises in respect to the six, and thus there is no lack of establishment, then the cognitions of substance, quality, and so forth—which belong to the same class of cognition—also arise in respect to the six. Yet these are not based on an efficient cause in the form of an entity distinct from the six categories; thus, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Furthermore, regarding whether that efficient cause distinct from the six categories is pervasive (*anuvṛtta*) or exclusive (*vyāvṛtta*), the same previous refutation should be applied. Moreover, since the cognition "it exists" is seen to arise in respect to categories through the relation of existence (*sattā*), there is a contradiction between presence and absence. If it is argued that the cognition of existence arises from the property of existence itself, then one must state what proof there is for the actual existence of *sattā*; since there is no difference in the nature of the cognition, there is no proof for the distinction, and thus the reason has an unestablished qualification. This is true. Furthermore, if "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) were intended merely as "having come into being after not having been," even that is doubtful in the case of existence and so forth. For, since they are perceived when their substratum exists, it is not known whether existence and so forth are manifested as already existing—like a universal (*sāmānya*)—or whether they are produced, like color and so forth (*rūpa*). Nor can the efficient cause be specified specifically. If it is argued that their efficient cause is the substratum of the qualities (i.e., the substance), then, since qualities and so forth are inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) by virtue of being the substratum of their effects, their arising from an efficient cause alone is contradicted. For, the necessary relation between the supported and the support is precisely inherence (*samavāya*). Otherwise, the definition of inherence would be subject to deviation. And if there were no relation, the aforementioned refutation applies. Thus, it is established that "the enumeration of substrata has been made without [additional] properties" (*dharmairvinā dharmiṇāmuddeśaḥ*).

Others, however, state that the subject (dharmin) has been mentioned together with its attributes (dharmas). By what means? "Without" (vinā)—that is, without the bird, the owl. They further argue that a general term is used here in a specific sense due to the context. [The commonality among the six categories:
"All six categories possess existence, nameability, and cognisability; and they possess the quality of being dependent, except for eternal substances."

Now, since existence (*astitva*) and the other [general properties] are included within the categories (*padārtha*) themselves, he says "of all six categories" (*ṣaṇṇām api padārthānām*) in order to ensure their full comprehension as being of the nature of common characteristics (*sādharmya*), even though they are specific to those categories. The expression "existence, nameability, and knowability" (*astitvam cābhidheyatvam ca jñeyatvam ca*) is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). It is not only that existence and the others are the six properties of the six categories; rather, "dependence" (*āśritatva*) is also mentioned. He states "and dependence, except for eternal substances" (*āśritatvam cānyatra nityadravyebhyaḥ*) because dependence is impossible in the case of eternal things, and thus it is mentioned separately due to its non-pervasive nature (*avyāpakatva*).

Now, if it is asked where existence (*astitva*) and the other categories are included if they are not distinct [from knowledge], [the answer is: because verbal usage is intended, existence is the being (*bhāva*) of the word-form "is" (*asti*), which is simply knowledge; for it is by means of that which exists that the designation "it is" (*asti*) proceeds. And when the intention is that existence is the being of "is" in its form as knowledge, then either the nature of existence (*sattā-svarūpa*) or existence itself (*sattva*) is obtained, since the cognition "it is" is observed in substances and so forth when that [existence] is present. Furthermore, this word "is" applies to knowledge and to the designation whose object is that [knowledge].

Likewise, the state of being denotable (*abhidheyatva*) is simply the cognition that "it is denotable"; for we observe the linguistic usage: "This object is denotable" by virtue of that [cognition] existing. And that object is the cognition produced by the denotation. Similarly, the state of being knowable (*jñeyatva*) is simply the cognition that "it is knowable"; for we observe the linguistic usage: "It is knowable" by virtue of that [cognition] existing. And that object is the cognition produced by the qualifier, which is the [act of] knowing.

Likewise, the state of being dependent (*āśritatva*) for those things that are dependent is the relation characterized by the nature of the container and the contained (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*). And this [relation] does not exist in space (*ākāśa*) and so forth, because they lack a substratum (*āśraya*). Furthermore, if the relation between container and contained were of the nature of inherence (*samavāya*), then because inherence itself lacks [inherence], it would not pervade all six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*). If it is argued: "The state of being dependent for the five [categories] is the relation characterized as inherence, whereas inherence itself has its own self as its locus," then in that case, the statement "the five possess the state of being inherent" (*samavāyitva*) would be redundant. For indeed, the state of being inherent is the relation characterized as inherence, and since that has already been expressed by the term "state of being dependent" for the five, there is no fault here, because the word "dependent" denotes that which is characterized by dependence.

Now, since a distinct cause [for inherence] is impossible, how can there be an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) applied to inherence, such that the "state of being dependent" (*āśritatva*) refers to the state of inherence which itself is dependent? This is not so. Because inherence is of the nature of a subsistence (*vṛtti*), it is observed to be dependent upon that which possesses subsistence; thus, if one were to postulate another subsistence for it, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, a figurative subsistence (*upacaritā vṛtti*) is accepted. And since no other cause is possible, this very specific kind of subsistence within inherence is the cause for the cognition of its being dependent. However, if inherence were to subsist in itself, then because it is inherently of the nature of subsistence, it would not require another subsistence; by accepting this, its being dependent is established.

For if there were no distinction [between them], the conventional usage of "substratum" and "residing thing" would be impossible; therefore, we shall explain in the *Samavāyaparīkṣā* that it is precisely the negation of a co-occurrence characterized by identity. Enough of this.

**The Common Characteristics of the Five Categories:** "The common characteristics of all five categories, beginning with substance, are being inherent (*samavāyitva*) and being manifold (*anekatva*)."

Now, setting aside *samavāya* (inherence), he states the common property (*sādharmya*) of the five [categories] beginning with "of substance and the rest" (*dravyādīnām*). Those of which substance is the first are "substance and the rest" (*dravyādayaḥ*); [the word] refers to them. It is not known how many there are, so he says: "The common property of all five is being inherent (*samavāyitva*) and plurality (*anekatva*). Those in whom inherence exists are "inherents" (*samavāyinaḥ*); their state is "being inherent" (*samavāyitva*), which is a mode of existence characterized by inherence. And "plurality" (*anekatva*) means the distinction between individual instances (*vyaktibheda*) when they possess identical characteristics, or it is a figurative application (*upacarita*) of the number "many. However, in the case of inherence—which possesses identical characteristics—there is neither a distinction between individual instances nor the number "many."

(“Regarding the five beginning with quality (*guṇa*), there is the state of being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*) and the state of being devoid of action (*niṣkriyatva*). <PDhS> Now, setting aside substance (*dravya*), he demonstrates their common properties (*sādharmya*): [the phrase] “of the qualities and so forth” (*guṇādīnām*) means those for which quality is the first; they are described thus. It is not known how many there are, hence [he says] “of all five” (*pañcānām api*). Their common property consists in being devoid of qualities and being devoid of action, which is expressed as “the state of being devoid of qualities and the state of being devoid of action” (*nirguṇatvaniṣkriyatve*). Those from which qualities have departed are “devoid of qualities” (*nirguṇa*); the state of being such is “the state of being devoid of qualities” (*nirguṇatvam*), which is the absence of qualities.

If it is argued that non-existence (abhāva) cannot be a property (*dharma*) because it lacks the nature of existence, we say no; for its status as a property is established by way of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). To explain: since we observe the conventional usage "devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇa*) applied to substances such as quality-possessors based on the presence or absence of qualities through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is known that the absence of qualities functions as a property by virtue of being a qualifier. And because this [absence] is common to all five categories, it constitutes their commonality (*sādharmya*).

The restriction that "there are only six categories" (*ṣaḍeva padārthāḥ*) refers specifically to positive entities (*bhāva*); thus, there is no fault even if non-existence (*abhāva*) is excluded. Furthermore, although a dependent thing may be a property (*dharma*), we do not accept the restrictive rule that a property must necessarily be inherent (*samaveta*). As for "actionlessness" (*niṣkriyatva*): those from which action characterized by motion has departed are "actionless" (*niṣkriya*); the state of being such is "actionlessness," which is the common property (*sādharmya*) consisting in the absence of action. This is because we observe the conventional usage "they are actionless" based on that very [absence].

Others, however, maintain that "absence of qualities" (*nirguṇatva*) is inherence (*samavāya*) characterized by the absence of qualities, and "actionlessness" (*niṣkriyatva*) is inherence characterized by the absence of action. But this is incorrect; for since another inherence cannot exist within inherence as its substrate (*dharmin*), the conventional usage of "absence of qualities" would not apply. Indeed, when there is non-difference, we do not observe the conventional distinction between property and property-possessor. {The common characteristics of the three categories}: "The connection with existence (*sattā*), the possession of generality and particularity (*sāmānyaviśeṣavattva*), denotability by terms whose meanings are established by convention, and being the agent of merit and demerit—these belong to all three categories beginning with substance (*dravya*). <PDhS>

He states the common property (*sādharmya*) of the triad beginning with substance (*dravya*): [the phrase] “of substance and the rest” (*dravyādīnām*). Those things of which substance is the first are "substance and the rest"; [the term refers to] them. Since it is not known how many [are meant], he says: “the connection with existence (*sattā*) belongs to all three as well,” which is their common property. The connection with existence is *inherence* (*samavāya*) characterized by existence.
[This concludes the discussion regarding the doubt and its resolution concerning existence, which is the cause of the notions of ‘existent’ and ‘non-existent.’]

Now, what is the proof for the existence of *sattā* (existence) in substances and the other categories? It is simply the cognition: "substance exists," "quality exists," "action exists. For indeed, since the cognition "existent" is a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*), it cannot arise without a qualifier; thus, the existence of *sattā* is established. If this is so, then the statement that [the term "existent"] applies to "three" categories is incorrect, because the cognition "existent, existent" arises even with respect to universals (*sāmānya*) and the rest. For instance, one observes qualified cognitions such as "the universal is existent," "the particulars are existent," and "inherence is existent"; therefore, a connection with *sattā* must be asserted [for them as well].

If it is argued that the cognition "existent, existent" regarding universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth arises from their own intrinsic existence (*svātmasattva*), then in that case, let that very same [intrinsic existence] suffice for substances (*dravya*) and the rest; what is the use of a separate *sattā*? Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish two distinct causes for the cognition "existent, existent" apart from a difference in the nature of the objects themselves. Therefore, either *sattā* or intrinsic existence (*svarūpasattva*) must be accepted as the basis for this cognition in all cases. To illustrate: the cognition "existent, existent" regarding substances and the like arises from their own intrinsic existence, because it is a cognition of the form "existent, existent," just like the cognition "existent, existent" regarding universals and the like.

Alternatively, the argument that "the cognition 'existent, existent' regarding universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth is an effect of [inherence] existence (*sattā*), because it is a cognition of 'existent, existent,' just like the cognition 'existent, existent' regarding substances (*dravya*) and so forth," is incorrect. This is because there is a subverting proof (*bādhaka*) against the connection with *sattā* in the case of universals and the rest. To explain: if one postulates a connection with *sattā* in the universal, since the cognition "existent, existent" is observed even in the case of *sattā* itself, there would have to be yet another connection with *sattā* for that as well, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Furthermore, since doubt arises regarding particulars because they are connected with existence (*sattā*), another particular would be required for the sake of certainty; and in that case as well, there would be another connection with existence, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) of doubts and certainties regarding particulars. Moreover, since there is an absence of the occurrence of existence in inherence (*samavāya*), and because this constitutes a subverting argument (*bādhaka*), there is no connection with existence in universals (*sāmānya*) and the like.

[Objection: But surely this [problem] is the same even regarding intrinsic existence (*svarūpasattva*). To explain: if there were a single intrinsic existence in universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth, then, just as with [intrinsic] existence (*sattā*), there would be the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and the like. If, on the other hand, it is restricted to each individual object, then—given its excluded nature (*vyāvṛttarūpatā*)—it could not produce the cognition "existent, existent" (*satsaditi*), for that [production] is indeed accepted [by you]. [Reply: No, because it is established otherwise. To explain: since there are subverting arguments (*bādhaka*) against the inherence (*samavāya*) of *sattā* in universals and so forth, the cognition "existent, existent" is metaphorical (*upacarita*) in their case. And a metaphor, when occurring, requires a basis (*nimitta*). Thus, by means of its own common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) which serves as the basis for the metaphor, [the object] possesses existence and produces the cognition "existent, existent," for it is observed that *sattā* is a common property where [the cognition occurs]. Therefore, through the perception of that [common property], the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of *sattā* certainly proceeds. Since the cognition "existent, existent" occurs in universals and so forth even otherwise, the reason (*hetu*) is established "otherwise" (*anyathāsiddha*). Nor should it be said that the cognition "existent, existent" regarding substances (*dravya*) and so forth arises solely from a unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*). For there is no subverting argument against its being primary (*mukhya*). Nor is a metaphor ever seen to occur without a primary instance; thus, it is established that the cognition "existent, existent" is observed in substances and so forth precisely due to the inherence of *sattā*.

Others, however, maintain that the cognition "existent, existent" is primary in both cases because it is produced by the qualifier "existence"—in one case (the substance) by way of inherence (*samavāya*), and in the other (the universal, etc. by way of the relation between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*). For indeed, the relation of qualifier and qualified does not depend on conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence, as that would entail its absence in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*). Rather, it is the basis for the cognition of a qualified object; wherever there is a cognition of a qualified object, there is the relation of qualifier and qualified. Thus, since the qualified cognition "existent, existent" arises even with respect to universals and so forth, the relation of qualifier and qualified is indeed the connection there as well; therefore, the cognition "existent, existent" is primary in both instances.

But this is incorrect. For it is observed that wherever the status of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) for qualities, actions, and universals is accepted by both parties, there it occurs through inherence (*samavāya*). Since inherence—which is the pervader (*vyāpaka*)—is excluded from universals and the like, the exclusion of the qualifiedness (*viśeṣaṇatva*) which is its pervaded (*vyāpya*) follows. Therefore, it is logical that the superimposition of "Being" (*sattā*) arises merely from the perception of a property associated with it. Otherwise, figurative cognition (*gauṇapratyaya*) and false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) would be abolished everywhere. To illustrate: in the case of "The boy is a lion," even though "lion-ness" is a qualifier in relation to the boy, the cognition would have to be primary (*mukhya*) as "like a lion. Likewise, in the cognition "Silver in mother-of-pearl," since "silver-ness" would be a qualifier just as it is in real silver, falsity would not exist. Yet falsity does exist; we shall explain this in the section on that topic.

Now, if it is argued that [the cognition] is figurative (*gauṇatva*) because it arises through the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of "lion-ness" upon a young boy (*māṇavaka*) due to the perception of qualities concomitant with that [lion], and likewise that it is false (*mithyātva*) because it arises through the superimposition of "silver-ness" upon mother-of-pearl due to the perception of similarity to silver—how can this be so? For there is no experience of lion-ness in the boy by way of inherence (*samavāya*), nor is there an experience of silver-ness in the mother-of-pearl by way of inherence. Therefore, the operation of lion-ness upon the boy and of silver-ness upon the mother-of-pearl occurs through the superimposition of what is being remembered; thus, figurative and false cognitions are appropriately distinguished. If that is so, then the cognition "existent, existent" (*satsat*) regarding universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth, arising through the superimposition of "existence" (*sattā*), would be logical, since there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) in the case of the inherence of existence. But how can this be a figurative usage (*upacāra*) when the sense of "as if" (*iva*) does not appear in the cognition "existent, existent" regarding universals and so forth? For a cognition is figurative only where the sense of "as if" is manifested; otherwise, if there were no distinction from false cognition (*mithyājñāna*)—since the nature of superimposition would be the same—the two would be indistinguishable. This is not so. One who perceives a person who lacks lion-ness still perceives him as "this is a lion. However, one who perceives mother-of-pearl which lacks silver-ness does not apprehend it as "silver. Thus, in the case of false cognition, a sublation is experienced subsequently. In the case of figurative cognition, however, the sublation exists even previously; it is only for the sake of proclaiming his bravery that people use the expression "the boy is a lion. In false cognition, on the other hand, they think "this is that very thing" in regard to what is not that. And while the cognition "existent, existent" does occur regarding universals and so forth, there is no sublation for it even throughout the three periods of time; the rest should be inferred accordingly.

Now, let us grant that the cognition "existent" (*sat*) is figurative with respect to universals (*sāmānya*) and the like, while it is primary with respect to substance-ness (*dravyatva*) and so on; however, the connection with existence (*sattā*) is still subject to doubt: does existence belong to things that are already existent, or to those that are non-existent? If it belongs to things that are already existent, then there must be existence prior to the connection with existence, as well as existence without the connection with existence. If one accepts the connection with existence, then this same dilemma applies to that [existence] as well, resulting in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If you say it exists without [the connection], then what is the use of existence? If, on the other hand, existence arises for non-existent things through a connection with existence, then that existence is not ultimate (*apāramārthika*), because it depends upon an external adjunct (*upādhi*). Moreover, if non-existent things acquire existence through a connection with existence, then even things such as a donkey’s horn would possess existence, since they are equally non-existent. Furthermore, if existence itself were non-existent, then by its connection with it, substances and the like could not possess existence. If existence were existent by its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), then substances and the like would necessarily be existent in that same way [without needing a further connection]; yet, if it is through a connection with existence, the infinite regress remains.
Therefore, the Śākyas maintain that existence consists in the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*);
others hold that it consists in connection with the present time.

Regarding that which we asked: "Does existence arise from the relation of existing things with existence, or from non-existing things?"—that is incorrect. Because the completion [of the thing] and its relation [with existence] are simultaneous. For indeed, the very production of entities is their relation with the existence of their own causes. There is no prior existence, because the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) has been refuted. Nor does the admission of a relation between non-existent things and the existence of their own causes lead to the absurd consequence of such a state occurring for things like a donkey's horn; for the absence of such a state is certain precisely due to the absence of the causes for its production. In the case of eternal things, since a temporal sequence of prior and posterior is impossible, the aforementioned alternative is untenable.

Nor is existence (*sattva*) non-ultimate, because the connection with existence (*sattā-sambandha*) is ultimate. Furthermore, existence in substances and so forth is not adventitious (*aupādhika*), as in the case of the color of a hibiscus flower appearing on a crystal; for existence inheres (*samavāya*) in those [substances]. An adventitious factor is either that which is superimposed or that which inheres, and in some cases it is that which conceals the inherent form. Thus, in the case of a crystal and the like, when its own form is concealed by the proximity of a red substance, the cognition "the crystal is red" arises; therefore, its adventitious nature is logical. However, existence does not manifest itself by concealing the essential nature of substances and so forth, since even "substanceness" (*dravyatva*) and other properties are perceived. Nor is it non-inherent, because inherence is observed therein.

[Objection: But if, in this way, substance-ness (*dravyatva*) and so forth were distinct [from substances], then, because their own nature would be impossible [without a substrate], it would follow that substances and the like themselves could not be perceived. [Response: That is not so, because substance-ness and the like are precisely what constitute the unique [defining] character (*asādhāraṇatva*) of substances and the like. To explain: the designation "substance" occurs in relation to a substance by virtue of its substance-ness, and [the designation] "quality" occurs in relation to a quality by virtue of its quality-ness and so forth. Thus, although the distinction [of being a separate entity] is the same in both cases, substance-ness inheres (*samaveta*) only in substances; therefore, it is the cause for linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) only there, and not in qualities and the like. The same must be said for quality-ness and so forth: their inherence in a specific substratum (*niyatadharmisamavāyitva*) is the regulating factor. As for inherence (*samavāya*), even though it is distinct [from the related entities], it appears as the substrate of that which inheres; thus, it is the cause for the linguistic usage of "inherence. However, if there were no distinction [between the universal and the individual], then because the natures of substance-ness and the like would be non-different due to their identity with a single substratum, they could not be the causes for distinct linguistic usages. Or, if there were such a difference, the substratum itself would have to possess that [distinctive] state; otherwise, if the opposite were true, there would be an absence of identity.

Nor should it be said that the cognition of substance and so forth is conceptual (kalpanā), because if that which conforms to the presence and absence of causal efficiency were considered conceptual, it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). Thus, it is established that regarding substances and the like, there arises the cognition "existent, existent" due to the connection with existence (sattā).

If existence (*sattā*) is accepted on the grounds of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), this same refutation applies equally. Is causal efficiency the property of things that exist, or of things that do not exist? If causal efficiency belongs to things that exist, then in accepting existence, there is an unavoidable circularity (*itaretarāśrayatva*). For existence would consist in being a producer of causal efficiency, while causal efficiency would belong to what exists; thus, if one is not established, the other is not established either. Alternatively, if the production of causal efficiency belongs to an existing thing even without [prior] causal efficiency, then this same dilemma applies there as well, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If, on the other hand, only non-existent things were producers of causal efficiency, then the same would apply to things like the horns of a donkey. Furthermore, if the existence of a causal efficiency itself depended on another causal efficiency, there would again be an infinite regress. If you say it is by its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), then it follows that all entities would possess such a nature [independently].
By this, existence (*sattva*) as a relation to the present time has been refuted.

Now, suppose existence is the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*). Since that capacity pervades many distinct entities, if it were to produce the cognition "existent, existent," there would be nothing but a difference in terminology. If, however, it does not pervade them, it could not produce a uniform, inclusive cognition (*anugatajñāna*). Likewise, if it consists in the production of causal efficiency, the conventional usage would be "capable of causal efficiency" rather than "existent, existent," because the two are distinct; so enough of this. Therefore, it remains established that substances and the other categories possess a relation to *sattā* (the universal of existence).

Likewise, a universal (*sāmānya*) such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) is itself a particular (*viśeṣa*) because it serves as the cause for the exclusion [of other categories] from substance; those things in which that exists are "possessing universals and particulars" (*sāmānyaviśeṣavat*). Their state is "the possession of universals and particulars. Alternatively, it is inherence (*samavāya*), characterized by the inhering universal and particular. For we observe such linguistic usage as "substance possesses universals and particulars," and so forth, based on that existing [inherence].

Likewise, because they are designated by the word "artha" (object/meaning) in their own system (*svasamaya*) and their own treatises, they are called "designated by the word *artha* in their own system" (*svasamayārthaśabdābhidheyāni*).
