Their state is "the state of being designated by the word *artha* in their own system" (*svasamayārthaśabdābhidheyatvam*); this similarity consists precisely in the cognition that takes as its object both the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*). Furthermore, the purpose of applying the designation "artha" [to sound] is stated in the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra (2.2.21): "Sound is an object perceivable by the ear. For instance, if one were to say "sound is that which is perceivable by the ear," there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to [universals] such as "soundness" (*śabdatva*); therefore, the term "artha" is included to exclude those. However, an "artha" can also consist of substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), or action (*karman*). Yet, the combination of these two—[being an *artha* and] being perceivable by the ear—is not the definition of sound.

Likewise, they perform merit and demerit; thus, "the state of being the performers of merit and demerit" (*dharmādharmakartṛtva*) refers to those [entities]. This consists of the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of substances and so forth, as well as specific auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-viśeṣa*). Accordingly, the substance *ātman* is the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) of merit and demerit. Furthermore, the substance of the Golden Mountain (*Suvarṇādri*) is the instrumental cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) through the acts of giving and seizing. Similarly, the conjunction of the *ātman* and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*), while pure intention (*śuddhābhisandhi*) and corrupt intention (*duṣṭābhisandhi*) are the instrumental causes. In this way, specific songs and specific dances are instrumental causes according to their respective possibilities. The rest should be inferred. Now, one might object: "Is not even a universal (*jāti*), like the substance gold and so forth, a cause of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*)? Let it be so; for its purpose is fulfilled by way of being an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*).

“Productness and impermanence belong only to those things that possess causes. (*kāryatvānityatve kāraṇavatāmeva*). Productness and impermanence belong to all three categories beginning with substance (*dravya*). If indeed a cause exists for certain things, they are "those possessing causes" (*kāraṇavanti*); it is understood that these two properties belong only to them, whereas the former property (existence) belongs to all. Although there is no difference in their being subject to exceptions, the fact that these two are not compounded with the term *kāraṇavattva* is for the purpose of indicating their association.
Alternatively, the non-compounding is intended to distinguish between those possessing causes and those lacking causes, as in the expression “of those possessing causes and those lacking causes.”

{An Investigation into the Category of Effectness (kāryatva)} Now, what is this so-called effectness? It is the relation with the existence of its own cause, because of the conventional usage that "it is an effect" by virtue of being related to that which exists as its cause.
Some say it is "coming into being after having not existed. Even in this case, "coming into being after having not existed" is precisely the relation with its own causes and with existence (*sattā*).

**An Examination of the Category of Impermanence (Anityatva)** Impermanence (*anityatva*), however, is the existence (*vastusattā*) of an entity as characterized by prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and non-existence after destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*). Now, since prior non-existence and non-existence after destruction do not exist at the time when the entity exists, how can they function as its characteristics (*upalakṣaṇa*)? Furthermore, existence (*sattā*) cannot be the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) in the conventional usage of "impermanent," because it is of a different nature. To explain: if existence were the qualifier, there would be only the cognition "existent, existent"; if, however, existence were a qualifier in other cognitions, then existence alone would have to be the qualifier everywhere, which leads to the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the term.

Therefore, some maintain that whatever, having come into being, ceases to be and abandons its own nature, is impermanent (*anitya*). This too is incorrect. For destruction (*vināśa*), because it is impossible at the time the entity exists, cannot function as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). If it is argued that even though destruction is non-existent [at the time of the entity], it serves as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) by means of inference, even so, one would have to say "it is destroyed" (*vinaṣṭa*), not "it is impermanent" (*anitya*). This is not so, because they are synonyms. For instance, there is common usage such as "impermanent objects are perishable. Furthermore, if there were no other cause for the cognition of impermanence, we might accept that existence (*sattā*) qualified by both limits [arising and destruction] is the qualifier. Just as non-arising and destruction, though non-existent, serve as indicators of existence through a certain figurative turn of phrase, so too there is no contradiction in their serving as indicators of the entity itself. For instance, prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) when remembered, and posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) when inferred, serve as indicators of the entity.

If it is argued that non-arising of destruction and destruction of non-arising are qualifiers of existence because they exist, then let the ultimate reality itself be conceived as the qualifier for those two; why this excessive effort? Or, if it is argued that a qualified existence is postulated as a qualifier so that the cognition of impermanence is not colored by non-existence? No, for no coloring by existence is perceived. Rather, a cognition arises simply that "the impermanent" is colored by impermanence.

Regarding the concept of impermanence (*anityatva*) as the existence of an entity characterized by prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and non-existence after destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), as proposed by Uddyotakara in the *Nyāyavārttika* (2.2.13), there would be a complexity of conceptualization (*kalpanā-gaurava*). The author of the *Bhāṣya* maintains that impermanence is simply destruction itself (*pradhvaṃsa*).

Furthermore, among the things enumerated here, those [such as dimension] do not possess the status of being inherent causes (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) or non-inherent causes (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*); rather, "causality belongs to them, except for spherical dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*) and so forth. {PDhS}

Likewise, the state of being a cause is "causality" (*kāraṇatva*). Causality consists in being either an inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) or a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*), which are the respective essential natures of these two types of causes; it does not consist in being an efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*), because that exists even in universals (*sāmānya*) and other categories. And although this [causality] is restricted to specific instances, it is a common property (*sādharmya*) when its particularities are not intended to be expressed. To the question, "Does this apply to all [categories]? he says: "Except for sphericality (*pārimāṇḍalya*) and so forth. This means excluding sphericality and the rest. Atoms are spherical; their state is "sphericality," which is the dimension of the atom. We shall explain later, in the section on dimension, that this is not a cause for the production of the dimension of dyads or atomic dimensions. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), one should understand that all-pervading substances such as space, the final sound (*antya-śabda*), and [the qualities of] priority, posteriority, and separateness are not causes.

[The common property of those things under discussion that are distinct from eternal substances: “And [they possess] dependence upon substance, except for eternal substances. (PDhS) Nor is this merely a repetition of the previous common property. Dependence upon substance (*dravyāśritatva*) is the state of being dependent upon a substance. And this exists in all things except for eternal substances, because they lack a substratum (*āśraya*). Although the dependence of [categories] beginning with substance was already stated by the mention of the six [categories] as being dependent, it is not redundant here, because it is mentioned here specifically as characterized by [their relation to] substance.

{The commonality of the triad beginning with generality:} “The three—generality and the rest—possess existence by their own nature, the characteristic of being cognizable by the intellect, the state of not being an effect, the state of not being a cause, the state of not possessing further generalities or particularities, eternity, and being denotable by the word ‘existent’ (*artha*). <PDhS> Now, [this] commonality belongs neither to one nor to two; rather, it belongs to all three. Existence (*sattva*) consists in being characterized by their own common property (*svātmanā sādhāraṇadharmeṇa*), which serves as the basis for metaphorical designation (*upacāra-nimitta*), and is the capacity to produce the cognition “existent, existent. For if this were taken in its primary sense, there would arise subverting arguments such as infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Others, however, state that the essence (*sattva*) of things consists in their being the cause of the cognition "existent, existent" for those things that do not possess [the universal] existence (*sattā*). For in this case, if no specific cause were mentioned, to say "the essence of existents is existence" would amount to saying nothing at all. If, on the other hand, it is held that for those things which do not possess [the universal] existence, their own self (*svātman*) acts as the cause for generating the cognition "existent, existent," then a fault arises regarding its having a recurring form (*anuvṛttirūpatā*); and if it has a distinct form (*vyāvṛttarūpatā*), it could not generate a uniform cognition. Therefore, it is logical that [the self of the thing] is merely the basis for metaphorical designation (*upacāranimitta*).

But in that case, would existence (*sattva*) not be merely metaphorical (*upacarita*) with respect to universals (*sāmānya*) and the like? Indeed, existence is accepted as being metaphorical, insofar as it consists in the capacity to produce the cognition "existent, existent. Now, if metaphorical existence is admitted, does it not follow that there is non-existence in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*)? That is precisely what we accept. For, by virtue of accepting the metaphorical status, there is no cognition of "existent, existent" regarding universals and so forth in the ultimate sense.

Now, it might be argued that if existence (*sattā*) were not their locus, there would be an absence of universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth; but that is incorrect. For if one were to admit the non-existence of something established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as the locus of its own unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*), then such non-existence would apply to substances (*dravya*) and the rest as well. Therefore, there is no fault in the view that universals and the like possess an intrinsic existence (*svarūpasattva*) of the kind described.

Likewise, "having cognition as their characteristic" (*buddhilakṣaṇa*) means those things which are characterized by cognition; the state of being such is "cognition-characterized-ness" (*buddhilakṣaṇatva*). Although a general term is used, it is understood from the context that what is intended is "the state of being characterized by any one of the cognitions of inclusion (*anugata*), exclusion (*vyāvṛtta*), or presence (*iha*). For the cognition of inclusion does not apply to particulars (*viśeṣa*) nor to inherence (*samavāya*), and the cognition of exclusion does not apply to universals (*sāmānya*) or inherence. Similarly, the cognition of presence does not apply to universals or particulars. The mention of "any one" (*anyatama*) is because there would otherwise be a difference in nature (*vaidharmya*) due to the exclusion [of certain categories]. And since that [state of being characterized] is common to all [categories], it constitutes their similarity (*sādharmya*).

Alternatively, the definition is that cognition (*buddhi*) as qualified by another attribute is the differentiator from others; and this is a commonality (*sādharmya*) whose specific qualifications are not intended to be expressed. For instance, the capacity to produce a uniform cognition based on a pervasive universal (*sāmānya*) exists in substances, qualities, and actions; however, in the case of universals themselves, this occurs through their very nature, while in the case of ultimate particulars (*viśeṣa*), it occurs through absolute exclusion. Furthermore, the non-sublated cognition of "inseparability" (*ayutasiddha*) is inherence (*samavāya*) itself; thus, even in the case of exclusion, the state of being cognizable by cognition is a commonality because it is shared equally.
Thus, the existence of effects is "effectness" (*kāryatva*); their non-existence is "non-effectness" (*akāryatva*), which is the absence of a relation with the existence of their own causes.

Likewise, the existence of causes is "causeness" (*kāraṇatva*); their non-existence is "non-causeness" (*akāraṇatva*), which is the absence of being an inherent (*samavāyin*) or non-inherent (*asamavāyin*) cause. Furthermore, the status of being an instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇatva*) is indeed accepted in the production of cognition. Similarly, "not possessing generality and particularity" (*asāmānyaviśeṣavattva*) means the absence of another generality (*aparasāmānya*). It does not mean inherence (*samavāya*) as characterized by that [absence], for if it were so, it would follow that inherence itself lacks that [absence].
“Even upon the destruction of all substrata, there is no destruction of universals or inherence. (PDhS)

The existence (*bhāva*) of eternal things is their eternity, which is their indestructibility; or rather, it is the absence of a connection with existence (*sattā*) characterized by both temporal limits (*ubhayānta*). For instance, while it is observed that produced entities (*kāryavastu*) are destructible, universals (*sāmānya*) and the like are indestructible because they are unproduced (*akāryatva*). Nor is there destruction due to the destruction of the substratum (*āśraya*), because even when one substratum is destroyed, [the universal] continues to produce its own corresponding cognition (*svānuraktapratyaya*) in other substrata. Thus, even when one substratum is destroyed, existence (*sattā*) remains the cause of the cognition "existent, existent" in other substrata. And since inherence (*samavāya*) is the cause of the cognition "here," neither of these two is destroyed by the destruction of their substrata.

Is it not the case that the universal, having an impermanent substratum, will perish due to the destruction of all its substrata, since there can be no existence for that which is without a support? This is not so; because it is established as non-perishable by virtue of being a non-product (*akāryavastu*), its persistence is maintained even when all its substrata have perished. For this very reason, although its substrata are absent, it is not designated by such forms as "cowness" (*gotva*). Furthermore, if a non-product were subject to destruction, it would follow that even space (*ākāśa*) and other such things would be annihilated.

If it is argued that the state of not being an effect is unproven because that which has an impermanent basis is perceived immediately after the arising of its basis—just like form and so forth—we say no, because perception occurs in both ways.

It is not known whether an entity arises after [its cause] has already arisen, or rather, that it is manifested (*abhivyajyate*). Since there is a logical refutation (*bādhaka*) against its arising, it is accepted that it is manifested. For instance, since only a substance (*dravya*) is prescribed as an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), and qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*karman*) are excluded from being such, there is no arising of their substratum. This is because, for example, the substratum of a universal (*sāmānya*) cannot have a simultaneous arising due to the absence of an inherent cause. Indeed, wherever an effect inheres, that [substratum] must necessarily be an inherent cause; since the inherence of a universal is perceived in all its substrata which occur sequentially, every one of them would have to be an inherent cause. Consequently, if arising occurred only upon the completion of all substrata, there would be no perception [of the universal] in those preceding [substrata].

If it is argued that, at the beginning of creation, because its own substrata are produced in great number, the universal (sāmānya) that has arisen will subsequently inhere in those substrata as they appear in succession—this is not so. For it is not observed in other effects; indeed, we have never seen an effect such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth, having arisen inherent in its own substrata, being subsequently connected to another [substratum] by way of inherence (*samavāya*). Nor can it be said that there is some other universal in things arising sequentially, for there is no evidence for their difference. On the contrary, we shall demonstrate in the examination of the universal (*sāmānyaparīkṣā*) that the very cognition of persistence (*anugata-jñāna*) is the proof for non-difference.

Thus, since there is a logical refutation of the position that [the universal] arises, it is manifested immediately after the production of the substance; therefore, because it is not an effect, its eternity is established.

Likewise, its non-denotability by the word "object" (artha) means the absence of being denotable by the word "object" according to our own system (*svasamaya*). Although the status of being an effect and so forth is established here for substances and the like alone, nevertheless, this is stated because similarity (*sādharmya*) is intended to be expressed. The absence of being an effect and so forth is also a similarity among universals (*sāmānya*) and the rest.
{The similarity of the nine substances}

“Earth and the other nine substances possess the quality of substantiality (dravyatva), the capacity to originate within themselves, the possession of qualities (guṇavattva), and the non-opposition between effect and cause.”

Having thus stated the common properties (*sādharmya*) of categories (*padārtha*), he says "of earth and the others," etc., in order to define the common properties of substances (*dravya*). "Of those whose first is earth" means "of earth and the others. It is not known how many [substances] are meant; therefore, [the text states]: "The connection with substantiality (*dravyatva*) belongs to all nine" as their common property. Connection with substantiality is an inherence (*samavāya*) characterized by substantiality. Although inherence resides in all five categories, nevertheless, being characterized by substantiality, it serves as a definition precisely because it is unique [to substances].

Nor should it be said that when it is stated that "the state of being a substance is substanceness" (*dravyatva*), the connection (*yoga*) is understood by implication; for if one were to deny the primary denotation of a word on the grounds that its function is understood [indirectly], there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Nor is the definition faulty because it is unreal due to having a figurative distinction, since it produces a specific purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), just like the sense of hearing. Nor is there the fault of an ineffective qualifier (*asamarthaviśeṣaṇatā*), because without the term "connection," the suspicion that [the definition] is impossible (*asambhavitva*) would not be removed. We shall provide the rebuttal to the remaining criticisms of the definition in the section on Earth (*pṛthivī*).

And the definition serves both for the purpose of differentiation and for the purpose of conventional usage. To explain: earth and the other [elements] are differentiated from others, or they are to be conventionally designated as "substances" because of their connection with substantiality (*dravyatva*). For those things which are neither differentiated nor conventionally designated as substances are not connected with substantiality, such as color and so forth; yet earth and the others are not like that, insofar as they are not unconnected with substantiality. Therefore, they are either differentiated from others or are to be conventionally designated as substances.

Thus, regarding the application of the term "substance" (*dravya*), the connection with the universal "substanceness" (*dravyatva*) is the cause for all nine [categories] beginning with earth; therefore, this sentence is also connected as being intent upon defining the meaning of words. And so, we shall explain that there is no contradiction whatsoever in the view that the meaning of a word possesses a universal. Likewise, it is for the purpose of refuting the notion of a supersensuous power (*atīndriya-śakti*). For that [universal] is the innate power of all nine [categories] beginning with earth, namely, the connection with "substanceness. {An Investigation into the Universality of Substanceness}

Now, since a cognition of a recurring form (anugata-ākāra-jñāna) is impossible for one who has not established a convention—just as it is with a mass of cows—there is no such universal as "substantiality" (dravyatva). For instance, while a resident of Nārikela-dvīpa perceives a mass of cows, a single uniform appearance manifests; this does not happen when earth and other substances are perceived. If it is argued that there is indeed a cognition of "substance, substance" for one who has established a convention, that [cognition] will arise solely by virtue of linguistic convention (saṅketa).

That is incorrect. Since a universal is manifested by specific manifestors, it does not follow that it is non-existent simply because those manifestors are not perceived. For instance, "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) is manifested through the perception of properties such as possessing action; "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) through the perception of its being dependent on a substance characterized by excellence; and "action-ness" (*karmatva*) through the perception of the characteristics of action. This should be considered for the remaining categories as well, and their respective manifestors should likewise be inferred.

Furthermore, since the perception of a manifestor does not exist for all [individuals], the non-perception of a universal is indeed an obstacle. However, for one who has established a convention, there certainly arises a continuous cognition regarding substances and so forth due to the perception of their manifestors. Or, even by means of a dewlap and so forth for which a convention has been established, it is perceived; thus, it is logical that there is a cognition of a uniform form regarding cows and other such things.

And where a cause consisting of substance, quality, or action is not possible in a cognition that is uncontradicted and inclusive, there the universal alone is the cause. Nor is there any sublation in the case of the inclusive cognition of substances and so forth, as there is in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*). For instance, the inclusive cognition "non-existence, non-existence," although not caused by substance, quality, or action, does not arise from a universal; because a universal cannot exist in non-existence due to the absence of inherence (*samavāya*). And it is observed that a universal exists only as something inherent.

If it is argued that this very cognition—"non-existence, non-existence"—which is colored by the property of non-existence (*abhāvatva*), demonstrates the inherence (*samavāya*) of that non-existence with the property of non-existence, we say no, because of the lack of pervasion (*anekāntāt*). To explain: it has already been stated that in the case of universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth, the cognition "existent, existent" occurs even without the inherence of existence (*sattā*). Furthermore, if non-existence possessed a universal, it would necessarily be of the nature of an entity (*bhāvarūpa*). And in that case, since non-arising is beginningless, it would follow that it is eternal; whereas since destruction has a beginning, it would follow that it is non-eternal. Moreover, if prior non-existence were eternal, there would be no perception of the object, because the two [prior non-existence and the object] are mutually exclusive in their persistence as distinct natures.

Furthermore, it is not logical for an entity (*bhāva*) whose nature consists in the destruction of non-existence (*abhāva*) to arise; thus, the qualification "prior" (*prāk*) is impossible. Moreover, there is no arising of destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*), because that [destruction] necessarily depends upon something that has arisen. Even if such an arising were possible, if destruction were to perish along with its status as having an origin, the entity itself would have to be perceived. For just as the entity is perceived prior to the non-arising of destruction, so too it should be perceived when destruction has ceased, since there is no difference in the absence of contradiction. But this is not observed; therefore, like a universal (*sāmānya*), there is a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

Furthermore, it is not possible for there to be a cognition "absence is absence" without a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). What then? There is simply a distinction in the arising of cognitions such as "the absence of a jar" and "the absence of a cloth. If it is argued that there exists a recurring cognition "the absence of a jar is an absence of a jar," even here, due to the influence of a limiting adjunct, it must be understood that a universal (*sāmānya*)—acting as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*)—is the cause of the cognition, because a primary [universal] would be sublated. However, in the case of the cognition "substance is substance," there is no such sublation; therefore, since the universal is established, this definition is not impossible.

Thus, "svātman" (one's own self) refers to that which is both one's own (*sva*) and the self (*ātman*); "inherence in that" (*tasminn ārambhakatvam*) means the production of an effect inherent in its own self, which is to say, the state of being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇatva*). And this [quality] distinguishes earth and the other elements from others because it exists only in them. For instance, the inherence of an effect is not possible apart from earth and the other [elements].

Likewise, those which possess qualities (*guṇa*) are "quality-possessors" (*guṇavat*); their state is "quality-possessorhood" (*guṇavattva*), which is either inherence characterized by qualities or the qualities themselves as inherent. These too are differentiators because they are unique [to each substance]. We shall explain how there is no quality-possessorhood among qualities and so forth on the occasion of the discussion of qualities (*guṇa*). Similarly, the non-opposition between cause and effect is "causal non-opposition"; those in whom this exists are "causally non-opposed," and their state is "causal non-opposition. The single property consisting in the mutual non-opposition of cause and effect is one and the same.

Alternatively, if there are two properties—namely, non-contradiction with the effect (*kāryāvirodhitva*) and non-contradiction with the cause (*kāraṇāvirodhitva*)—then "non-contradiction with the effect" means that they are not contradicted by, nor destroyed by, the effect; their state of being such is "non-contradiction with the effect," which is the absence of destruction by the effect. And since this exists in all [substances] such as earth and so forth, it constitutes a common property (*sādharmya*), but it is not a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), because it exists even in a portion of the heterologous class (*vipakṣa*). For instance, sound, cognition, and so forth are contradicted by their effects, but not all qualities (*guṇa*) are so; likewise, actions (*karman*) are also contradicted by their effects, yet not by the effect alone, since they are destroyed even when their substratum (*āśraya*) is destroyed.

Furthermore, even if one intends the definition in terms of the referent (*padārtha*), that which exists in only a portion of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) cannot be a probans (*gamaka*). Likewise, regarding "non-opposition to the cause" (*kāraṇāvirodhitva*): if they are not opposed by a cause, they are "non-opposed to the cause"; their state is "non-opposition to the cause," which means the absence of destruction by a cause. This [non-opposition] exists in space (*ākāśa*) and so forth because of the absence of a cause; thus, although it exists in the subject (*pakṣa*), it does not exclude [the property] from the counter-example. Therefore, it is not a valid definition. For instance, qualities (*guṇas*) are not destroyed by a cause, nor is action (*karman*).

Now, "non-opposition to the cause" means that they do not oppose, nor do they destroy, the cause; thus, their state of non-opposition to the cause is their state of not destroying the cause, which is a property of the effect. In this regard, since there is no cause for eternal substances (*nityadravya*), one must consider non-opposition to the cause as the absence of destroying a cause. That which exists in only a portion of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is simply non-probative. For instance, although sound, cognition, and so forth do indeed destroy their causes, form (*rūpa*) and other qualities do not; thus, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*). Likewise, action (*karman*) also does not destroy its cause.

Nor is there a lack of distinction [between the two] by virtue of their non-contradiction with the effect; for in that case, the property of the cause is its non-destruction by the effect, while the property of the effect is its non-contradiction with the cause—that is, its non-destructiveness of the cause—and thus they are not redundant. Therefore, it is established that in both ways, the mere similarity (*sādharmya*) which does not exclude even a portion of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is not the definition of that [logical reason].
[The specific qualities of atoms: "Possession of ultimate particularity (*antyaviśeṣa*), non-dependence, and eternity, except in the case of composite substances. (*PDhS*)

Thus, those things which possess ultimate particularities (*antya-viśeṣa*) are "possessors thereof" (*tadvantaḥ*); their state is "the possession of ultimate particularities" (*antya-viśeṣavattvam*), which refers either to inherence (*samavāya*) characterized by ultimate particularities, or to the ultimate particularities themselves as inherent.

Likewise, "non-dependence" (*anāśritatva*) and "eternality" (*nityatva*) constitute "non-dependence and eternality. Non-dependence is the absence of dependence; eternality is indestructibility, or alternatively, the existence of a real entity not delimited by either temporal extreme [beginning or end].

He asks: "Do these three properties exist in all [substances], such as earth and the rest, and are they pervasive? He replies: "Except for composite substances (*avayavidravya*). This means that, excluding composite substances, they exist only in eternal substances (*nityadravya*).

Now, one might ask: even though there is no difference in the fact that all three properties are subject to exceptions (*sāpavāda*), what is the purpose of not forming a compound because the last one possesses a specific qualification? [The answer is: Because the ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣa*) are non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*), they are distinguished by the very knowledge of their uniqueness (*asādhāraṇatā*). As for "non-dependence" (*anāśritatva*) and "eternality" (*nityatva*), they are not compounded because they are common (*sādhāraṇa*) to other things as well. To explain: eternality is common because it exists in qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth as well. Non-dependence is common because, although it applies primarily to inherence (*samavāya*), since there are objections to its primary application, it must be understood through a figurative sense (*gauṇavṛtti*); thus, it does not exist in reality and is therefore common.
{The common property of the six substances}:
“Earth, water, fire, air, self, and mind possess plurality and the possession of a lower genus.

(*PDhS*) Thus, having stated the common properties of the nine [substances] beginning with earth as distinguished from other categories, he again shows their common properties as distinguished from their own internal subdivisions: “earth, water, fire, air, self, and mind. The compound is a *dvandva* in the sense of conjunction (*ca*). “Plurality and the possession of a lower genus” means the state of being plural and the state of possessing a lower genus.

Multiplicity (*anekatva*) refers to the distinction between individual instances (*vyaktibheda*) of earth and the other [elements], which possess specific characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*), or it is the number "many" (*anekatvasaṃkhyā*). Since such a distinction of individuals or the number "many" is not possible for space (*ākāśa*) and the others, there is therefore an exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). Precisely because of this multiplicity, they possess a lower genus (*aparajāti*). An "lower genus" is that which takes the form of "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth, in relation to "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*). Those in which this exists are "possessors thereof" (*tadvant*); their state is "possession of a lower genus" (*aparajātimattva*). This is either an inherence (*samavāya*) characterized by a lower genus, or the lower genus itself as inherent [in them]. {The common properties of the five substances}.
“Earth, water, fire, air, and mind possess activity, corporeality, priority, posteriority, and velocity.”

Thus, the common properties (*sādharmya*) of earth, water, light, air, and mind are stated as follows: possession of action (*kriyāvattva*), corporeality (*mūrtatva*), priority (*paratva*), posteriority (*aparatva*), and possession of velocity (*vegavattva*). In this context, "action" (*kriyā*) consists of motion; those things in which it exists are "possessors of action. Their state is "possession of action," which means either action inherent (*samaveta*) in them or the inherence (*samavāya*) of that action in them. Similarly, "corporeality" (*mūrtatva*) refers to a limited dimension of a substance (*avyāpi-dravya-parimāṇa*); those things in which it exists are "corporeal. Their state is "corporeality," which means either corporeality inherent in them or the inherence of that corporeality in them. It is precisely because of corporeality that there is the existence of priority, posteriority, and so forth, as well as possession of action. "Priority and posteriority" (*paratvāparatve*) refer to the state of being prior and posterior; when these exist in earth and the other elements, the conventional usage of "prior" and "posterior" occurs. This means either the qualities of priority and posteriority inherent in them or the inherence of those qualities in them. "Possession of velocity" (*vegavattva*) refers to those things in which velocity exists; their state is "possession of velocity," which means either the quality of velocity inherent in them or the inherence of that quality in them. These properties are restricted to earth and the others; they do not occur in them at all times.
The common properties of the four substances [space, time, direction, and self] are: their all-pervasiveness, their supreme magnitude, and their occupying the same location as all conjoined things.

Thus, space (*ākāśa*), time (*kāla*), direction (*dik*), and the self (*ātman*) possess the common property (*sādharmya*) of being all-pervading (*sarvagata*), and so forth. The word "all" (*sarva*) here refers only to the corporeal (*mūrta*) entities mentioned immediately prior. "All-pervading" means having gone to (*gata*) or reached (*prāpta*) all [corporeal things]; the state of being such is "all-pervasiveness. This is conjunction (*saṃyoga*) with all corporeal things. And that [conjunction] is either produced by the action of one of the two factors (*anyatarakarmaja*) or produced by conjunction (*saṃyogaja*). Although there is no distinction in its residing in both [relata], this is a common property of space and the others alone; for it is space that has conjunction with all corporeal things, whereas no single corporeal thing possesses conjunction with all corporeal things.

Likewise, the state of being supremely great is "supreme greatness" (*paramamahattvam*). This is either an unsurpassed dimension or the inherence (*samavāya*) thereof. Similarly, it is the state of occupying the same location as all conjoined things (*sarvasaṃyogisamānadeśatvam*). All those things that possess conjunction are corporeal substances; those which are common to them are their conjunctions, and the locations or substrata of those [conjunctions] are space and so forth. The state of these is "occupying the same location as all conjoined things," which is to say, being the substratum for the conjunctions with all conjoined things.

Nor should it be argued that because conjunction resides in both [relata], this property [of being a substratum] must also belong to corporeal things; for just as a single space (*ākāśa*) is the substratum of the conjunctions with all corporeal things, a single corporeal thing is not so—this distinction is obtained by implication. Furthermore, there is no lack of distinction on the grounds of omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*). For omnipresence consists in either (1) having conjunctions with all [things], or (2) inherence (*samavāya*) as characterized by that, or (3) being the substratum of the conjunctions of all things that possess conjunction.

Alternatively, "all those" refers to those things which possess conjunction; these are the "possessors of conjunction," such as jars and bowls. Their conjunctions are "common. The rest is as explained previously. Others, however, maintain that by means of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) or etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), the word "possessor of conjunction" (*saṃyogin*) actually denotes the conjunction itself. They argue that "conjunctions" (*saṃyogāḥ*) are so called because they are conjoined (*saṃyujyante*); those things in which these exist are the "possessors of conjunction," which are the conjunctions themselves, either through figurative extension (*sthāna*) or metaphorical usage. Furthermore, "the common places of all possessors of conjunction" refers to the locations (*deśa*) that are common to them; since they are one, they constitute the substratum (*ādhāra*).

In this context, since the qualification "provided there is oneness" is obtained through the function of the word itself, the objection regarding the non-hearing of the [logical] capacity (*sāmarthya*) is refuted. However, that is incorrect; because that very same [qualification] is already relied upon in the definition of the general characteristics of the sense organs and in the definition of specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*), here it is merely a redundant effort.
[The common properties of the five beginning with earth:

"For all five, beginning with earth, there are the properties of being elemental (*bhūtatva*), being the material cause of the sense organs (*indriyaprakṛtitva*), and possessing specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) that are grasped by each respective external sense organ. <PDhS>

Likewise, he states the common properties (*sādharmya*) of earth and the other elements: "of earth and the others" (*pṛthivyādīnām*). Those of which earth is the first are "earth and the others"; [the term refers] to them. It is not known how many [are meant], therefore [he says] "of all five. Their common properties are: being elemental (*bhūtatva*), being the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the sense organs, and possessing specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) that are perceptible by each respective external sense organ; thus they have been described.

The state of being existent (*bhūtatva*) is the very nature (*bhāva*) of existents (*bhūta*), and that is indeed a universal (*sāmānya*). For instance, it is observed that a non-sublated, recurring cognition arises from a universal when substances, qualities, actions, and causes are its objects—such as the cognition "cow" and so forth. And there exists a recurring cognition regarding earth and the other elements, such as "existent, existent"; therefore, it arises from a universal. Furthermore, there is no sublation for this [cognition] as there is for a recurring cognition [regarding] universals and the like. Moreover, if one were to postulate a universal within a universal, there would be an infinite regress. It has been stated that the cognitions "substance-ness is a universal" and "quality-ness is a universal" occur without [a further] universal; and there is no sublation for the cognition "existent, existent."

Now, why is it that the inhabitants of Nārikela-dvīpa do not have the appearance of a single form? Because their manifestor is not perceived. For just as the generality such as "quality-ness" (guṇatva), though existing, is not perceived by the inhabitants of Nārikela-dvīpa due to the non-perception of its manifestor, so too is "element-ness" (bhūtatva). What, then, is its manifestor? It is instruction, just as in the case of Brahminhood. For just as Brahminhood is known through instruction, so too is element-ness.

Now, let there simply be instruction; enough with the postulation of a general property (*sāmānya*). As it has been stated by others: "The state of being an element (*bhūtatva*) is the denotability of the word 'element' (*bhūtaśabda*); this is the comprehension of the application of the rule governing the relationship between signifier and signified (*abhidhānābhidheya-niyama-niyoga*), and that [comprehension] arises either from the usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*) or from the method of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*) regarding the word."

But this is incorrect. If one were to postulate another cause for a cognition that persists without being sublated, then even [categories] such as "substanceness" (*dravyatva*) would have to be considered non-existent. Furthermore, for one who has established the linguistic convention, there arises the cognition "the past is the past," just as there is the cognition "a Brahmin is a Brahmin," and like the cognition "a substance is a substance. Therefore, "pastness" (*bhūtatva*) exists as a universal (*sāmānya*).

If it is argued that, whereas in substances there exists a unique, pervasive property such as being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇatva*) which, for one who has established a linguistic convention, manifests "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*), but no such thing exists in the case of the elements (*bhūta*), we say: no. For properties such as being the material cause of the sense organs (*indriyaprakṛtitva*) are indeed unique [to them]. If it is further argued that even when those [unique properties] are perceived, there is no inclusive cognition (*anugata-jñāna*) for one who has not established a convention, then this is the same regarding "substance-ness" and so on. For even when being an inherent cause and the like are perceived therein, it is not observed that one who has not established a convention has the cognition "this is a substance, this is a substance."

Now, since [the quality] arises from that which has been established by convention, there exists a generality such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth; and since that is common even to the state of being an element (*bhūtatva*), enough of this.

Likewise, the state of being the nature of the sense organs (*indriyaprakṛtitva*) is the state of being the cause of the nose, tongue, eye, skin, and ear respectively. And we shall explain that in the section on earth (*pṛthivī*) by means of the aphorisms beginning with "Because of the predominance [of earth], because of possessing smell," and so forth (VS 8.2.5).

In the case of the ear, however, since the ether characterized by its conjunction with the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*) is an effect, ether is its cause in relation to that; or else, the word *prakṛti* has the sense of "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*).

But surely, since the sense organs are derived from *ahaṅkāra*, this [claim] is incorrect. Furthermore, since luminosity is a property of *sattva*, the emergence of the sense organs must be from the *sāttvika* *ahaṅkāra*. If one asks what the proof for this is, it is their non-contacting mode of operation (*aprāpyakāritva*). This is known from the simultaneous perception of the branch and the moon. For otherwise, because the contact with the moon would occur only after the contact with the branch and after some time had passed, there would be no simultaneous perception; yet such simultaneous perception does exist. Therefore, they operate without reaching their objects. And since this is not possible in the case of material things—such as lamps and the like, where it is not observed—it should be understood that the other senses as well are non-material, precisely by the force of the example of the eye.

Likewise, it is because [the eye] illuminates both the large and the small. For it is observed that whatever possesses a certain dimension performs an action only to that extent. Thus, for example, it is observed that an axe or similar tool, being of small dimension, does not produce a cut by pervading a large banyan tree; rather, it acts only within the area it itself pervades. If the eye were likewise material, it too—being of small dimension—would not be able to discern mountains and such objects, yet it is observed to do so; therefore, it is not composed of the elements (*bhautika*).

Furthermore, because they have restricted objects: for if the eye were composed of light (*taijasa*), it would perceive only color (*rūpa*)—since that is its specific quality—and not substance (*dravya*), generality (*sāmānya*), and so forth. In the same way, it would follow by necessity that the remaining senses would also perceive only their own specific qualities. But this is not observed; therefore, the senses are not elemental (*bhautika*). For this reason as well, the senses are not elemental: because they are senses (*indriyatvāt*). Whatever is a sense is observed to be non-elemental, just like the mind (*manas*); and such are the senses; therefore, they are not elemental.

As for the proof that [the eye] acts without reaching [its object] (*aprāpyakāritva*), that is unestablished (*asiddha*). This is because "reaching" (*prāpti*) is observed through the non-perception of objects that are obstructed. Otherwise, there would be no non-grasping of what is obstructed and grasping of what is near, since there would be no distinction between the two cases due to the lack of contact. Furthermore, the impossibility of an obstruction [would follow], because an obstruction functions as a negation of contact; thus, an obstruction is postulated for the sake of non-grasping precisely by negating contact. Moreover, the efficacy of an obstruction is observed: a lamp illuminates what is distant; therefore, like a lamp, it determines its object through contact. Thus, the eye determines its object through contact, because it does not illuminate what is obstructed. Whatever does not illuminate what is obstructed determines its object through contact, just like a lamp. The eye does not illuminate what is obstructed; therefore, it determines its object through contact.

Since the existence of *prāpti* (contact) is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the notion that the branch and the moon are perceived simultaneously—despite the actual perception occurring at different times—is due to extreme rapidity, just like the illusion of piercing a hundred lotus petals all at once. Furthermore, the argument that [the eye] cannot illuminate large objects is not a proof, as it is established otherwise: namely, that the eye, having gone outward, acquires the dimension of the object through its connection with external light; thus, it illuminates large objects and so forth, and not because it is non-material (*abhautika*).

As for the claim that, because it is composed of light (*taijasa*), [the eye] must illuminate only color (*rūpa*), this is incorrect. This is evident from the case of a lamp. Indeed, a lamp is not observed to illuminate only color simply because it is composed of light; rather, it illuminates color, substance (*dravya*), generality (*sāmānya*), and so forth. This is precisely the distinction of the eye; therefore, its being composed of light is not contradictory. We shall explain later that among color and the other qualities, the fact that it invariably illuminates color alone serves as the inference for its being composed of light. Likewise, we shall explain that the fact that the olfactory organ (*ghrāṇa*) and others invariably illuminate odor (*gandha*) and so forth serves as the inference for their being composed of earth (*pārthiva*) and so on.

Furthermore, since no fixed restriction of objects is observed if there were a single material cause, there must be multiple material causes. For instance, it is observed that various lamps produced from a single cause have the same object; likewise, the sense organs would also have to have the same object. However, a restriction is seen in the case of the nose and other senses regarding odors and so forth; therefore, they possess multiple material causes.

Likewise, the sense organs have multiple types of material causes (*upādāna*), because they are substances that possess restricted objects. Whatever is a substance with a restricted object is seen to have multiple types of material causes, as in the case of spices, wind, lamps, musk, and so forth. And these [senses] are substances with restricted objects; therefore, they have multiple types of material causes. For instance, there would be a fallacy (*vyabhicāra*) if one were to claim that cognition and sound have a single type of material cause while also possessing restricted objects; hence, the qualification "being a substance" (*dravyatve sati*) is added. Nor can this [inference] be invalid despite possessing the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and other criteria, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

As for the inference that [the sense organs] are non-material because they are sense organs (*indriyatvāt*), in that case, "non-material" means not being excluded from the material elements. Since the negation of that [materiality] implies arising from other causes—because the negation of a specific alternative implies the admission of the remaining one—the example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*). Thus, in the case of the mind (*manas*), there is neither materiality nor non-materiality.

Furthermore, if [the permanence of the sense organs] is established by the negation of their production from the elements (*bhūta*), there is a contradiction with your own tenet, because you also accept the permanence of the mind (*manas*). Moreover, the status of being a sense organ for that which possesses the aforementioned qualifications is established otherwise—by its being the producer of direct cognition and by the negation of its production from the elements. Furthermore, the claim that the sense organs originate from the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*) is rootless, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its existence. For this process [of evolution] would hold only if the primal matter (*pradhāna*) existed, yet its non-existence will be stated later.

Furthermore, for those whose sense-faculties pervade the entire sphere of cyclic existence (*saṃsāramaṇḍala*), there would follow the consequence that they apprehend all objects without exception. If it is argued that their activity (*vṛtti*) is manifested in a restricted location due to the power of unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), then if this activity were identical with the faculty itself, nothing at all would have been said [to resolve the problem]. If, however, there is a distinction between them, then it is merely a difference in nomenclature, as that [activity] is simply the sense-faculty itself.

Now, is it determined that the transformation of the sense organ occurs precisely by assuming the form of the object, because otherwise the cognition of a restricted object would be inexplicable? That is not so, because perception occurs even otherwise. For instance, perception is indeed possible even when there is contact with a restricted object. Furthermore, since all-pervasiveness (*vyāpitva*) is not what the opponent most desires to establish, it will not be elaborated upon here. Moreover, we shall explain later that the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmapakṣa*) is untenable; therefore, this is sufficient.

Likewise, those which are grasped by each individual external sense organ are "grasped by each individual external sense organ" (*bāhyaikaikendriyagrāhya*). These are also "specific qualities" (*viśeṣaguṇa*); thus, "possessing those" means that which has them. Their state is "the possession of specific qualities graspable by each individual external sense organ. For the aforementioned qualities are inherent (*samaveta*) in them, or rather, inherence (*samavāya*) is characterized by them. Since the mere possession of qualities exists in all [substances], the term "specific" (*viśeṣa*) is employed. Since the possession of specific qualities exists in themselves, the term "graspable by external sense organs" (*bāhyendriyagrāhya*) is used. For number (*saṃkhyā*) and so forth are also graspable by the senses, yet they are not specific qualities. Indeed, if it were otherwise, the inclusion of the word "each" (*ekaika*) would be redundant, because the possession of specific qualities graspable by external sense organs does not exist elsewhere [than in the four elements]. This is true; nevertheless, there is no fault, as this constitutes the second common property (*sādharmya*). For since number and so forth are graspable by two sense organs, the term "graspable by one sense organ" is used. Furthermore, being graspable by one sense organ would be impossible in the case of color-form (*rūpa*) and the rest [if they were not specific qualities]. Indeed, a single sense organ is not the illuminator of all [objects]; thus, the inclusion of "each" (*ekaika*) is necessary. Even so, since the operation of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is impossible without the mediation of the external sense organs and so forth, the term "external" (*bāhya*) is used. And thus, the possession of qualities graspable by each individual external sense organ—by omitting the word "specific" (*viśeṣa*)—constitutes the second common property.
{The common properties of the four substances}: “The four possess the qualities of being initiators of substance and possessing touch.

(*dravyārambhakatvasparśavattve*) Thus, [the phrase] “the four possess the qualities of being initiators of substance and possessing touch” means that they have the nature of initiating substance and the quality of touch. Since it is not known which [four] these are, due to the lack of a specific designation, the term “earth and the others” (*pṛthivyādīnām*) must be supplied by way of immediate proximity.

Furthermore, what is the nature of being a constituent of a substance (*dravyārambhakatva*)? It is the state of being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇatva*) in the production of a substance, which is the inherence (*samavāya*) of the effect-substance [in its cause]. For it is by virtue of that [inherence] existing that there is the conventional usage: "the substance is the inherent cause in the production of a substance. To explain: the nature of being a constituent of a substance is not intended here as that by virtue of which [the causes], while existing, produce a substance. What then? It is that by virtue of which [the causes], while existing, *begin* (initiate) a substance; thus, the conventional usage is that they are the inherent causes in the production of a substance. And since that [usage] occurs when there is the inherence of the substance [in its parts], the nature of being a constituent of a substance is simply the inherence of the substance itself.

Now, if the intention is that [substances] originate from a quality inherent in themselves, then even if it were argued that touch alone [is the cause] because we observe that only those possessing touch are initiators of substances, nevertheless, since the meaning would already be conveyed by the state of possessing touch (*sparśavattva*), the property of being an initiator of substances would be redundant.

Regarding this, some offer the following resolution: the initiation of substances occurs when touch has been augmented by specific auxiliary factors (*sahakāriviśeṣa*). "Possessing touch" (*sparśavattva*) is the state of having touch; it is an inherence (*samavāya*) characterized by touch. {This is the commonality among the three types of substances.}

(“The three [earth, water, and fire] possess perceptibility, possession of color, and possession of fluidity. <PDhS> Thus, he states the common properties (*sādharmya*) of the three beginning with earth: perceptibility (*pratyakṣatva*), possession of color (*rūpavattva*), and possession of fluidity (*dravatvavattva*). Perceptibility is the state of being perceived among those things mentioned; it consists in being the object of non-indirect (*aparokṣa*) cognition, because there is the conventional usage that “they are perceptible” when they exist as such. Alternatively, it is the conjunction with causes such as magnitude (*mahattva*). As for the self (*ātman*) and so forth, this is merely a point of similarity regarding their perceptibility, whereas in their imperceptibility, they are excluded [from this category].

Others, however, maintain that because [the soul] exists as an object, perceptibility is intended here with reference to the two sense-faculties; and since this does not exist in the case of the self (*ātman*) and so forth, they consider it an excluded common property (*vyāvṛtta-sādharmya*). Furthermore, being the object of both non-conceptual and conceptual cognition is not excluded, because it does exist even in the case of the self. Thus, the word "I" applies to the self because it differs from words such as "earth" and so forth; and for one who has grasped the linguistic convention, conceptual cognition indeed arises through the recollection of that [convention].

Likewise, those things which possess *rūpa* (color/form) are "possessors of *rūpa*" (*rūpavanti*); their state is "the possession of *rūpa*" (*rūpavattva*), which is either the inherence of *rūpa* or the *rūpa* itself as inherent. And this [possession] is intended without regard for specific distinctions; otherwise, it would refer only to that which is the substratum of *rūpa* as excluded from earth and the other [elements]. Similarly, the state of fluid things is "fluidity" (*dravatva*), which is either the quality of fluidity as inherent or its inherence. Here too, there is no intention to specify particularities; otherwise, there would be only a distinction, namely that fluidity is adventitious (*naimittika*) in earth and fire, and natural (*sāṃsiddhika*) in water. (The common property of two substances.)

(“The two possess gravity and possession of taste. Thus, gravity and possession of taste are the common properties (*sādharmya*) of both earth and water. For instance, the state of being heavy is gravity (*gurutva*); it is either the quality of gravity inhering [in them] or the inherence [relation] itself.

Likewise, those two in which taste exists are "possessors of taste" (*rasavatī*); their state is "possession of taste" (*rasavattva*), which is either the inherence characterized by taste or the taste itself as inherent [in them].

{The common property of the six substances}: “The elements and the selves possess specific qualities (*vaiśeṣikaguṇavattva*). Thus, those which are both elements and selves are so designated; their possession of specific qualities is their common property (*sādharmya*). Those qualities which possess *viśeṣas* (ultimate particulars) are called *vaiśeṣika* qualities. The state of being such is *vaiśeṣikaguṇavattva*. That which is characterized by this is inherence (*samavāya*), or they [the qualities] themselves as inherent.
{The common property of three substances}: “Earth, water, and selves possess fourteen qualities.

Thus, earth, water, and selves are so designated; their common property is the possession of fourteen qualities. For instance, those in which fourteen qualities exist are called "possessors thereof" (*tadvant*); the state of being such is "the fact thereof" (*tattva*). This refers either to those qualities being inherent in them or to the inherence (*samavāya*) in them. It should be understood that here, because the qualities of one thing do not reside in another, what is intended as the common property is merely the number.
The common property of two substances [is]: "The possession of particular qualities that are momentary and reside in a single part, as in the case of space and the self."

"Ākāśa and selves" (ākāśaścātmānaśca) refers to those [nine substances] mentioned in that manner. Their common property (*sādharmya*) is "the state of possessing particular qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) that are momentary (*kṣaṇika*) and reside in only one part (*ekadeśavṛtti*). They are called "momentary" and "residing in only one part," and these are their "particular qualities" (*viśeṣaguṇa*). Those in which these exist are "possessors thereof" (*tadvant*); the abstract state of being such is "that-ness" (*tattva*), which is either their inherence (*samavāya*) or the fact that they are inherent (*samaveta*). The inclusion of the term "particular" (*viśeṣa*) is because the mere state of "possessing qualities" (*guṇavattva*) exists in all [substances]. Since that [mere possession of qualities] is common even to earth and the others, the word "residing in only one part" (*ekadeśavṛtti*) is employed.

Nevertheless, the inclusion of the term "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*) would be purposeless, because the quality of possessing a particular quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) that exists in only one part is absent elsewhere. This is not so, because the intended similarity (*sādharmya*) is the second one. For instance, since the mere possession of a particular quality exists elsewhere as well, the term "momentary" is included. And "momentariness" means rapid destruction while the substratum still exists. Furthermore, since the possession of momentary qualities exists elsewhere in relation to disjunction (*vibhāga*), the term "particular" (*viśeṣa*) is included. Thus, the similarity consisting in the possession of momentary particular qualities is distinguished from other cases by its absence elsewhere.

(“Space and time possess five qualities, and they are the efficient causes of all things that originate. <PDhS> Thus, “space and time possess five qualities” (*pañcaguṇavattva*) refers to their similarity by way of specific properties (*viśeṣa*). Those two in which five qualities exist are “possessors of five qualities” (*pañcaguṇavantau*); the state of being such is “possession of five qualities” (*pañcaguṇavattvam*). This refers either to the inherence (*samavāya*) characterized by the five qualities, or to those [qualities] themselves as inherent therein. And this constitutes a similarity based solely on the equality of number.

And thus, all those things which possess origination are called "originating" (*utpattimant*); for them, [the Lord] is the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇatva*) in their origination. The term *nimitta* is also used here as a synonym for *kāraṇa* (cause) in order to exclude the inherent (*samavāyin*) and non-inherent (*asamavāyin*) causes. Otherwise, because it would be common to both the inherent and non-inherent causes, it would be impossible [to distinguish the efficient cause] in relation to them.

For instance, the state of being a non-inherent cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) is "causality as a non-inherent cause. That by whose existence there is the conventional usage "non-inherent cause" is the absence of the characteristics of inherent (*samavāyin*) and non-inherent (*asamavāyin*) causes when both [types of] causes exist; for it is by virtue of that existence that such a convention is applied. Although there is indeed the status of an inherent cause in the production of its own number and so forth, there is no fault because of the qualification "of all [substances].
("The conjunction with adventitious fluidity exists in earth and fire.")*PDhS*

Thus, earth and fire constitute "earth-and-fire"; their common property (*sādharmya*) is the possession of occasional fluidity (*naimittikadravatva*). That which is produced from a cause is called "occasional" (*naimittika*). Although the word "cause" (*nimitta*) is a general term, it refers here by implication to conjunction with fire (*agnisaṃyoga*). This "occasional fluidity" and its "possession"—that is, the connection (*yoga*), which is inherence (*samavāya*)—constitutes the common property.
("In this manner, in all cases, common properties and differences should be stated through the opposite [of what has been stated]. <PDhS>)

Now, under the guise of a conclusion, he instructs the student: that which has been explained by me as similarity (*sādharmya*) is itself to be stated as dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*)—either by being excluded from all [cases] through its opposite, or by way of another distinction.

Alternatively, "that which has been explained as similarity" constitutes the conclusion; "dissimilarity, which is the opposite, will be stated" is an indication of the subject matter yet to come. {The commencement of the section on dissimilarity}

(“Now, the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is stated for each one individually. Having stated the similarities (*sādharmya*) of the nine [substances] beginning with earth, and further of the five, and so forth, he states their dissimilarity for each one individually with the words beginning with “here” (*iha*). “Here” (*iha*) means in the contexts ranging from earth up to the mind. “Now” (*idānīm*) means at this present time. “The dissimilarity is stated for each one individually” (*ekaikaśo vaidharmyam ucyate*). Now, one might object: since the suffix *śas* is prescribed in the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*) by the rule *ekaikaśas*, the explicit mention of “repetition” (*vīpsā*) is redundant. [As it is said: “Objects, resembling poison, strike one down one by one (*ekaikaśas*). (*Viṣayā viṣasannibhā ekaikaśo vinighnanti.*) Why? Because the suffix *śas* itself already conveys that meaning. This is not so; for the suffix *śas* is prescribed here specifically to indicate a distributive sense (*vyāpti*), whereas the word “repetition” (*vīpsā*) is used to indicate a collective sense (*samudāya*). For example, in the phrase “he eats rice grain by grain (*taṇḍulaṃ taṇḍulaṃ bhuṅkte*)”, the suffix *śas* is not applied because it would result in an undesirable meaning. Therefore, the mention of “repetition” is not superfluous. Furthermore, the suffix *śas* is prescribed after the word *eka* when it signifies a distributive sense, as in the rule *ekaśa ekavacanācca vīpsāyām*. Thus, the meaning is: “the dissimilarity is stated for each one individually, one by one. What is this dissimilarity? It is that which distinguishes one thing from another. For instance, among the nine substances, earth possesses qualities such as smell, while the others do not. This is the dissimilarity of earth. Similarly, water possesses the quality of taste, while the others do not. This is the dissimilarity of water. Likewise, fire possesses the quality of color-and-form (*rūpa*), while the others do not. This is the dissimilarity of fire. Air possesses the quality of touch, while the others do not. This is the dissimilarity of air. Space possesses the quality of sound (*śabda*), while the others do not. This is the dissimilarity of space. Time, direction, and self possess the quality of number (*saṃkhyā*), while the others do not. This is the dissimilarity of time, direction, and self. Mind possesses the qualities of dimension (*parimāṇa*), separateness (*pṛthaktva*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), disjunction (*vibhāga*), remoteness (*paratva*), proximity (*aparatva*), and cognition (*buddhi*), while the others do not. This is the dissimilarity of the mind. Thus, the dissimilarity of each substance has been stated. What is the purpose of stating this? It is for the sake of establishing the specific definitions (*lakṣaṇa*) of each substance. For it is through these dissimilarities that the individual definitions of earth and the other substances are established. Alternatively, the purpose is to refute the views of those who hold that there is only one substance, or that all substances are identical. For if there were only one substance, then the distinction between the agent of action and the object of action would be impossible. Furthermore, if all things were identical, then the production of effects such as jars and cloths from clay and threads respectively would be inexplicable. Therefore, the dissimilarity of each substance is stated in order to establish their distinctness and to refute the doctrines of those who deny plurality. Thus ends the section on dissimilarity. Now begins the section on the examination of the qualities (*guṇaparīkṣā*). Therein, first, the qualities belonging to earth are examined. Among them, the quality of smell is examined first. What is the definition of smell? It is that which is perceived by the nose alone. This is the definition of smell. How is this known? Because it is never perceived by any other sense organ. For smell is never perceived by the eye or any other organ. Nor is it perceived by the mind independently of the senses. Therefore, it is known that smell is perceived by the nose alone. Furthermore, it is established that smell belongs to earth alone, because it is never found in the absence of earth. For smell is never observed in water or other substances where earth is absent. Therefore, it is concluded that smell is a quality of earth alone. Thus ends the examination of smell. Next, the quality of taste is examined. What is the definition of taste? It is that which is perceived by the tongue alone. This is the definition of taste. How is this known? Because it is never perceived by any other sense organ. For taste is never perceived by the eye or any other organ. Nor is it perceived by the mind independently of the senses. Therefore, it is known that taste is perceived by the tongue alone. Furthermore, it is established that taste belongs to earth and water, because it is found in both. For taste is observed in earth, such as in fruits and roots, and in water, such as in juices and liquids. Therefore, it is concluded that taste is a quality of earth and water. Thus ends the examination of taste. Next, the quality of color-and-form is examined. What is the definition of color-and-form? It is that which is perceived by the eye alone. This is the definition of color-and-form. How is this known? Because it is never perceived by any other sense organ. For color-and-form is never perceived by the nose or any other organ. Nor is it perceived by the mind independently of the senses. Therefore, it is known that color-and-form is perceived by the eye alone. Furthermore, it is established that color-and-form belongs to earth, water, and fire, because it is found in all three. For color-and-form is observed in earth, such as in flowers and fruits; in water, such as in the color of milk and curd; and in fire, such as in flames and light. Therefore, it is concluded that color-and-form is a quality of earth, water, and fire. Thus ends the examination of color-and-form. Next, the quality of touch is examined. What is the definition of touch? It is that which is perceived by the skin alone. This is the definition of touch. How is this known? Because it is never perceived by any other sense organ. For touch is never perceived by the eye or any other organ. Nor is it perceived by the mind independently of the senses. Therefore, it is known that touch is perceived by the skin alone. Furthermore, it is established that touch belongs to earth, water, fire, and air, because it is found in all four. For touch is observed in earth, such as in stones and wood; in water, such as in coldness; in fire, such as in heat; and in air, such as in wind. Therefore, it is concluded that touch is a quality of earth, water, fire, and air. Thus ends the examination of touch. Next, the quality of number is examined. What is the definition of number? It is the cause of the cognition of "one," "two," and so forth. This is the definition of number. How is this known? Because it is the basis for the application of such linguistic expressions. For without number, the cognition and expression of "one," "two," etc., would be impossible. Therefore, it is known that number is a quality. Furthermore, it is established that number belongs to all substances, because it is found in every substance. For number is observed in earth, water, fire, air, space, time, direction, self, and mind. Therefore, it is concluded that number is a quality common to all substances. Thus ends the examination of number. Next, the quality of dimension is examined. What is the definition of dimension? It is the cause of the cognition of "large," "small," "long," and "short. This is the definition of dimension. How is this known? Because it is the basis for the application of such linguistic expressions. For without dimension, the cognition and expression of "large," "small," etc., would be impossible. Therefore, it is known that dimension is a quality. Furthermore, it is established that dimension belongs to all substances, because it is found in every substance. For dimension is observed in earth, water, fire, air, space, time, direction, self, and mind. Therefore, it is concluded that dimension is a quality common to all substances. Thus ends the examination of dimension. Next, the quality of separateness is examined. What is the definition of separateness? It is the cause of the cognition of "this is separate from that. This is the definition of separateness. How is this known? Because it is the basis for the application of such linguistic expressions. For without separateness, the cognition and expression of "separate" would be impossible. Therefore, it is known that separateness is a quality. Furthermore, it is established that separateness belongs to all
Some say that there is no fault because of Vyāsa’s usage [of the word *vaidharmya*].

The teachers (*guravaḥ*), however, state that although the property of difference (*vaidharmya*) is obtained through the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) applied individually to earth and the other elements, the repetition is performed again in order to make known the difference of the body and so forth by way of their internal subdivisions.

Difference (*vaidharmya*), moreover, is the state of being different (*vidharmā*), which refers to a specific property (*dharma*) that is excluded from others; its abstract state is difference. It is a unique property that establishes the essential nature [of a thing], which is to say, it is a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekyanumāna*).

[The difference of earth from substance: “Earth is that which is connected with the universal ‘earthness’ (*pṛthivītva*). It possesses color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, gravity, fluidity, and momentum. These specific qualities, beginning with color, are established in the section on the classification of qualities (*guṇaviniveśādhikāra*). The seven beginning with number are established by the mention of visibility (*cākṣuṣa*). Gravity is established by the teaching regarding falling. Fluidity is established by the mention of its similarity to water. Momentum is established by the mention of subsequent action. (PDhS)

Since it was mentioned first among those [elements], earth is defined here: "Because of its connection with earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*). "Earth" is the designation of the subject (*lakṣya*). "Because of its connection with earth-ness" is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*), which is the unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*). The "connection with earth-ness" is an inherence (*samavāya*) characterized by earth-ness. Earth is the locus (*dharmin*); "it is distinct from others" is the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). "Because of its connection with earth-ness": that which is not distinct from others is not connected with earth-ness, such as water and so forth; but earth is not thus unconnected with earth-ness; therefore, it is distinct from others. For inherence (*samavāya*) would be an over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*) definition; thus, "earth-ness" is used as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).

But surely, in this way, since "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) alone is capable of effecting the exclusion because it is unique (*asādhāraṇa*), is there not the fault of the reason having an ineffective qualification? No; for its purpose is to dispel the suspicion that [the reason] might be impossible in the subject (*pakṣa*). To explain: if one were to say simply "it is earth because of earth-ness," the suspicion as to whether [earth-ness] exists or does not exist in the subject would not be removed. Therefore, the term "connected" (*abhisambandha*) is effective.

[Objection: But surely, since the relation is already understood from the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) itself—as in "the state of earth" (*pṛthivītva*)—or from the genitive case—as in "the state of earth belonging to earth"—its designation by its own specific term is redundant? [Reply: That is not so. The abstract suffix denotes the state (*bhāva*) through its primary function (*śabdavṛtti*), but it does not denote the relation (*abhisambandha*). Nor is the term "relation" (*abhisambandha*) redundant by relying on an implied function (*gamya-vṛtti*), for if that were the case in the technical treatise (*śāstra*), it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, since the genitive case expresses a non-specific relation, the term "relation" (*abhisambandha*) is used to obtain a specific relation.

But, one might object, since the distinction of inherence (*samavāya*) is unreal due to the difference of its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), how could this definition serve as a means of distinguishing it from other categories? No; for even a conceptual distinction can perform a causal function (*arthakriyā*), just as in the case of the auditory organ (*śrotra*).
