For instance, the auditory organ is a region of space characterized by its conjunction with the ear-cavity; and although that distinction is unreal, it performs the causal function characterized by the perception of sound. The same holds true for inherence. Alternatively, the definition may be "earth-ness as inherent" (*samavetaṃ pṛthivītvaṃ lakṣaṇam*). This is because the compound *abhisambaddha-samavāya* is understood as a *karmadhāraya*, meaning "the inherence which is connected with earth-ness," and thus earth-ness is what is connected to that [inherence].

Now, one might ask: since there is no deviation regarding either member of the compound, how can this be a descriptive determinative compound (*viśe�ṣaṇasamāsa*)? In that case, "connected" (*abhisambaddha*) means "that which is connected," and thus "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) is meaningful as it is seen to be inherent in color and so forth. When it is stated, "and earth-ness," since earth-ness cannot possibly exist without being inherent, there is no deviation.

Now, if it is argued that "earthness" (*pṛthivītva*)—in the form of the exclusion of non-earth—is not inherent (*asamaveta*), and that the term "related to an object" (*arthavat-abhisambandha*) is intended to exclude that [non-inherence], we say: no, because that [exclusion] is unestablished. For the exclusion of a thing by means of a qualifier is observed only when the thing is already established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as for example, the exclusion of non-blue things by the qualifier "blue. Nor is exclusion (*apoha*) established, because the dilemma regarding its subsistence (*vṛtti-vikalpa*) is untenable. Alternatively, since the subverting argument lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge, and because a real universal (*sāmānya*) exists, there is no fault in accepting a *karmadhāraya* compound even though the single word [“earth”] does not deviate [from its referent].

Some maintain that *abhigrahaṇa* means "connection on all sides" (*abhi samantāt sambandha*) for the purpose of pervasion (*vyāpti*), and "connection in a forward direction" (*ābhimukhyena sambandha*) for the purpose of demonstrating the capacity to convey [the probandum] through non-deviation in purely negative concomitance (*kevalavyatireka*).

Now, is the earth—which is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as being excluded from other things—taken as the subject (*pakṣa*), or is it unestablished? If it is unestablished, its status as the subject is improper. If, on the other hand, it is established by valid cognition as being excluded [from others], then the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is redundant. If, however, it is perceived as not excluded [from others], that is incorrect; for the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of entities is indeed excluded, and it is observed that when a subject is apprehended in that very form, it is not apprehended in any other form. This is not so. For the earth is taken as the subject by virtue of worldly convention (*lokaprasiddhi*). Thus, that which is the object of people’s conventional usage as "earth" is what is taken as the subject; hence there is no contradiction.

[Objection: But then there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). In the case of the proposition "earth is distinct from others," the distinction from others is what is to be proven; yet, the status of being a limiting correlate (*avadhibhāva*) is only possible once those [others] are understood through their distinction from earth. Thus, since the understanding of one precludes the understanding of the other, there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that neither exists. [Reply: This is not so. Earth appears in non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) in its excluded form (*vyāvṛtta-rūpa*) by means of the sense organ, aided by the perception of its unique properties (*asādhāraṇadharma*). Likewise, water and the other elements also manifest to us through the very operation of the eye, via the exclusion resulting from the perception of their own unique properties. Even though the distinction is apprehended by oneself, an inference is presented for the sake of convincing another. For indeed, an opponent who holds a contrary view is convinced only by means of inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*).

Now, if "difference from others" is what is to be proven, then since water and the other elements are also different from others, there exists a similar instance (*sapakṣa*); how then can there be an invariable concomitance based solely on negative instances (*kevalavyatireka*)? No, because the meaning of the probandum (*sādhya*) has not been understood. For the meaning of the probandum in the statement "earth is different from others" is that "earth is different from all others without exception. And thus, there is an absence of a similar instance; for water and the rest are not different from their own selves.

Now, if earthness were to differ from its unique property (asādhāraṇadharma), it would have to differ from yet another [property], leading to an infinite regress. If, however, there is no difference, the relationship between the probandum and the probans is untenable. Therefore, it differs by itself; for otherwise, even the case of earth would be sublated by such a state of affairs.

Now, if it is argued that "earthness" is qualified by earth and earth is qualified by earthness, resulting in mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*), this is not so. For earthness, which possesses a recurring nature, appears in non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) through the operation of the senses as excluded from other distinct entities. Thus, although the specific nature of the universal (*sāmānya*), despite its inclusive character, is excluded from others, it is perceived directly by perception itself; yet, for the purpose of communicating it to another, it is stated as a logical reason (*hetu*). Consequently, there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and so forth. Furthermore, one who is entirely in disagreement cannot be a person to be convinced; therefore, knowledge of the subject (*dharmin*) and knowledge of the means of proof (*sādhana*) must be accepted by way of the universal. It is simply that the earth, as distinct from others, is not [yet] understood, and thus the formulation of the proof is presented.

Likewise, the statement "a single sentence, when repeated, expresses a greater meaning" is connected with the intent of defining the word and its referent, namely the sentence "due to the connection with earth-ness. And thus, the universal (*sāmānya*) is the word-referent; because it is unitary, it is the cause for the formation of linguistic convention (*saṅketa*), so say the followers of Jaimini (*Jaiminīyas*). However, as for particulars (*viśeṣas*), since they are related to indefinite directions and locations, they cannot be apprehended in their entirety; therefore, how could they be the objects of linguistic convention?

If linguistic usage proceeds because a convention is established only for as many particulars as are perceived, then linguistic usage would be impossible regarding other particulars, since a convention cannot be established for them. Furthermore, for one who is not a yogi, there is no perception of all particulars individually. Nor can there be an understanding of the rule governing the relationship between signifier and signified—namely, that "this is the name of this" or "this is the denotable object of this"—with respect to things that have not been perceived. And without such an understanding of the convention (samaya), there is no manifestation of meaning upon hearing a word. If it is argued that the convention is established with respect to particulars by taking recourse to a non-different cause (abhinnanimitta), that too is incorrect. Even if a non-different cause exists, the infinity of particulars does not cease; therefore, because the convention is applied to the universal (sāmānya), the universal is the meaning of the word.

Nor should it be said that, having denoted the universal through the perception of the convention associated with it, the word will subsequently apply to the particulars; for this would entail the admission of a discontinuous operation, and since words, actions, cognitions, and so forth cannot function discontinuously, such a view contradicts the Sūtra. Thus, because its power is exhausted precisely upon the cognition of the qualifier, it does not convey the qualified object. As it has been said: "The denotation does not reach the qualified object, as its power is spent on the qualifier."

Now, one might argue that since the cognition of a universal (*sāmānya*) is not itself a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), the cognizer would have no motivation for either engagement or withdrawal because the cognition lacks a specific object. This is not so; for when the cognition of the particular arises through the necessary implication (*anyathānupapatti*) of the cognition of the universal, engagement and withdrawal do indeed occur. For instance, as it is said: "A universal without a substratum would be like a hare's horn" (*Ślokavārttika*, *Ākṛtivāda*, verse 10).
Thus, there must be a cognition of a substratum; enough of this excessive speculation.

All this is incorrect. When there is a non-different cause and material basis (*nimittopādāna*), the meaning of a word is that which possesses a universal (*sāmānyavat*), because of the cause of convention (*saṅketa*). For example, although particulars exist in infinite variety, a single, non-different universal is perceived among them in one instance. Because of the perception of that [universal], even those particulars not being perceived are possessed of that universal; and words, though impermanent, are the objects of convention when accompanied by a specific sequence [of phonemes]. For instance, "Wherever you see such a universal, there this word should be employed; and from such a word, this meaning is to be understood"—in this way, the grasping of convention is possible despite the infinity of particulars. And thus, from hearing a word, the cognition of an object possessing a universal is observed. That [cognition] implies the apprehension of the convention, and convention is established only in this manner and not otherwise.

Now, because one does not perceive particulars such as the *śāvaleyā* (the brindled cow) upon hearing the word "cow," the particular is not the meaning of the word. True. But what is it then? The object conjoined with the universal (*sāmānya*) is perceived, not the particular such as the *śāvaleyā*. And that [particular] is perceived from words such as *śāvaleyā* themselves. Yet, for this reason alone, the universal is not the sole meaning of the word, because both appear in the relationship of primary and subordinate. Likewise, in usages such as "bring the cow," the object possessing the universal is connected with actions such as bringing.

Now, having expressed the universal (*sāmānya*), how can it function with respect to the particular (*viśeṣa*)? [Is this not] a contradiction of the Sūtra? No; it is due to a misunderstanding of the meaning of the Sūtra. For the meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: it is prohibited that a word, having once conveyed a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), should convey a qualifier again—that is, a "cessation of operation" (*viramya-vyāpāra*) is forbidden. It does not mean, however, that having conveyed a qualifier, it does not denote the qualified (*viśeṣya*). Similarly, an action (*karman*), having produced disjunction (*vibhāga*), produces subsequent conjunction (*saṃyoga*); for there is no destruction of that which has not produced conjunction. Nor does the prohibition of cessation of operation mean that having produced disjunction, it then produces conjunction. Likewise, the cognition of the qualifier, having produced the cognition of the qualified, does not initiate another effect. The same prohibition applies to pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth as well.

But was it not said that "the capacity [of the word] is exhausted in the qualifier"? That it "would not denote the qualified" is because capacity has the effect as its domain. And the effect—characterized by the cognition of the qualified, just like the cognition of the qualifier—is observed to be the determiner of that capacity. Now, if one were to claim the non-existence of the effect itself, such a person contradicts even their own self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), since the cognition of the qualified is indeed experienced. Furthermore, the objection regarding the relation of qualifier and qualified applies only to the position where they are the objects of distinct cognitions, not when they are the objects of a single cognition. This is equally applicable to the acceptance that a perceived word conveys its meaning; for if the capacity were exhausted in the cognition of itself, it could not convey the universal (*sāmānya*). If it is argued that the capacity is not exhausted there because the cognition of the universal is observed, then the capacity is likewise not exhausted in the case of the cognition of the particular (*viśeṣa*), since that too is observed. Moreover, the employment of a word is for the purpose of conveying a meaning.

As for what was said—that activity and cessation would occur through the determination of a particular (viśeṣa) because the cognition of the universal (sāmānya) would otherwise be inexplicable—does the comprehension of the particular follow from the inexplicability of the cognition of the universal alone, or from the inexplicability of the cognition of that particular itself? If it were from the inexplicability of the cognition of the universal alone, then since the cognition of the particular would follow from the cognition of the universal alone, there would be no engagement [with the object]. If, on the other hand, it were from the inexplicability of the cognition of a qualified universal, then that particular which is being cognized as a qualifier is already understood from the word itself.

Now, if it is argued that [the universal is known] from another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), does this mean from verbal testimony (*śabda*)? If so, how can it be said that the word-referent is the universal alone, given that the word also denotes the particular? Or is it from another means of valid cognition? No, for one does not experience the operation of another means of valid cognition [in this context]. Furthermore, on the opponent’s view, it is impossible for the universal to be distinct from the particular; thus, if there is no difference between them, it follows that the particular must be apprehended just as the universal is. Otherwise, there would indeed be a distinction between the apprehension of one and the apprehension of the other. If it is claimed that it is accepted by some that [the universal] is both non-different and different [from the particular] in certain respects, we say no. Since difference and non-difference consist respectively of negation and affirmation, they cannot coexist in a single substratum (*dharmin*) that is non-different. For one must state: is it different in the very same form in which it is non-different, or in a different form? If it is argued that it is different with respect to a difference in location while non-different with respect to a difference in nature, and that there is no disagreement here because the opponent accepts difference with respect to a difference in distinct locations, [we reply: [This is the opponent's position: "The universal is different from the particular with respect to a difference in spatial location, but non-different with respect to its own nature. This is what the opponent understands as the distinction.

Now, [the opponent argues that] because it appears as having both a pervasive (anugata) and an excluded (vyāvṛtta) nature, it consists of the cognition of a real entity (*vastu*). This is incorrect. It is precisely what we maintain that [an entity] is pervasive due to its connection with a pervasive universal (*sāmānya*), whereas it is excluded by its own specific form (*svarūpa*); thus, a dual nature is indeed accepted. Furthermore, if there were oneness through identity (*tādātmya*), a dual nature would not be possible; therefore, a relation characterized as inherence (*samavāya*) must be admitted. However, if there is a distinction based on difference in essential form (*svarūpa-bheda*), then without inherence, it would be impossible to designate [an entity] with a fixed qualification. Without a relation such as "earthness belongs to earth," there would be no restrictive rule as to why earth is designated as earth in one state and not in another.

Furthermore, if the word "earth" were to denote "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*), then the meaning of the word "earth-ness" would have to be stated. Moreover, we do not see the utility of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) in the case of non-difference; thus, it is logical that the meaning of the word "earth" is that which possesses the universal. Now, as for the objection: "How can the word 'earth,' which has been conventionally established for one thing, apply to another object?"—he replies: because of the connection with "earth-ness" as the cause, the word "earth" is conventionally established for one thing, and it applies to other objects as well by virtue of that [connection]. Thus, since a convention [restricted to a specific individual] is untenable, the view that the meaning of a word is a particular (*viśeṣa*) is impossible; consequently, the Sāṃkhya position regarding the power (*śakti*) [of words] is also refuted.

Likewise, the refutation [of the opponent's view] is as stated in the *Ślokavārttika* (Śūnyavāda, verse 254): "The potencies (*śaktayaḥ*) of all entities are within the scope of inference based on the necessity of their effects. This is because earth performs its function due to its connection with "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*). Thus, earth-ness itself is the innate potency, whereas any other [potency] consists of the final auxiliary cause (*caramasahakārin*), since the effect is produced when that exists and not produced when it is absent. For instance, even though the threads are present, they do not initiate the effect without the final conjunction of the thread; therefore, that [conjunction] alone is the potency. Now, one might ask: how can one thing be the potency of another distinct thing? But this is the same even if they are not distinct. It is simply that very thing which is the potency of that very thing. If it is argued that if the final auxiliary cause is the potency for the preceding ones, then since that [auxiliary] itself would be incapable and thus not a cause, another potency must be posited, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), we say: this is not so. For the potency of the preceding auxiliary causes is indeed the final auxiliary cause itself, since the effect is produced through their mutual relationship. Furthermore, that very state of being complete is expressed by the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) as "the causal complex" (*sāmagrī*), because only when that is present is the designation "complete" observed.

Now, if it is argued that a supersensible power (*śakti*) is not admitted, then when fire is obstructed by a gem, a mantra, or the like, and does not initiate effects such as combustion (*sphoṭa*), what is it that is being obstructed? It cannot be the fire itself, nor the contact with fire, because both are perceived. Therefore, it must be the power that is obstructed. This is incorrect. For the absence of obstructing factors—such as gems or mantras—is also a cooperative cause (*sahakārī*) for the production of the effect; in their absence, the effect does not arise. Thus, power is simply the conjunction [of causes] as qualified by that absence. Furthermore, it is impossible for there to be an obstruction, non-production, or destruction of a power. Since power would have been produced long ago, its destruction would follow, and since there would be no cause for its re-emergence, it would follow that it could never be produced again. Because that which lacks power does not produce an effect, it is known through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the power of fire is simply the conjunction with fire as qualified by the absence of obstructing factors. In this same way, here too, "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) is the inherent power, while the other [factors] serve as cooperative causes.

It has been stated that the nine substances beginning with earth possess qualities (*guṇavattva*), that they are inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇatva*), and that earth, water, and the self possess fourteen qualities. To this end, he states the passage beginning with "color and so forth" (*rūpādi*) to address the following questions: by which qualities are they possessed of qualities; in the production of what are they inherent causes; what are those fourteen qualities; and what is the definition of a quality? The phrase "possessing color and so forth up to mental impression" (*rūpādisaṃskāravatī*) means that she (earth) possesses [the qualities] starting from color and ending with mental impression (*saṃskāra*). One might wonder: are these presented by the author of the commentary (*vṛttikṛt*) as independent [categories], or are they intended by the author of the Sūtras (*sūtrakāra*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And these, in the section on the classification of qualities," and so forth. These were indeed mentioned by the author of the Sūtras. In which section? That section in which qualities are classified in various ways—that is, in many manners—is called the second chapter (*adhyāya*); therein they were propounded by the author of the Sūtras.

Likewise, by the sūtra "Earth possesses color, taste, smell, and touch" (VS 2.1.1), the four specific qualities are stated. Furthermore, by the phrase "because of the mention of visibility" (*tathā cākṣuṣavacanāt*), he shows the sūtra: "Number, dimensions, separateness, conjunction and disjunction, priority and posteriority, and action are visible because they inhere in substances possessing color" (VS 4.1.12).

The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: a material substance (rūpidravya) that has attained the conditions for perception (upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta) and is endowed with magnitude (mahattva) and other qualities; because they are inherent (samavāya) therein, number and the other qualities are also apprehended by direct perception. Thus, even though the sūtra is intended for another purpose, it declares the existence of number and the rest in a substance possessing color-form (rūpavat). Otherwise, if they were non-existent, there would be no perception of them therein.

The term "categories" (*padārtha*) is plural in order to demonstrate that, apart from the universal "category-ness" (*padārthatva*), there exist other subordinate universals such as "oneness-ness" (*ekatvatva*). The term "dimensions" (*parimāṇāni*) likewise serves to indicate that, relative to the universal "dimension-ness" (*parimāṇatva*), there are subordinate universals such as "atomicity-ness" (*aṇutvatva*). The singular form "separateness" (*pṛthaktvam*) is used to show that, relative to the universal "separateness-ness" (*pṛthaktvatva*), there is an absence of subordinate universals such as "unitary-separateness-ness" (*ekapṛthaktvatva*). The compound "conjunction and disjunction" (*saṃyogavibhāgau*) is formed with a dual ending to indicate that, although there is no subordinate universal apart from the universals "conjunction-ness" (*saṃyogatva*) and "disjunction-ness" (*vibhāgatva*), disjunction nonetheless possesses a dependence upon conjunction. Similarly, the dual form "remoteness and proximity" (*paratvāparatve*) is used to indicate their coexistence, even though there is no subordinate universal apart from the universals "remoteness-ness" (*paratvatva*) and "proximity-ness" (*aparatvatva*).

Likewise, [the sūtra] says: "Because of the teaching on falling" (*patanopadeśāt*). [The sūtra] *Vaiśeṣika-sūtra* 5.1.7 states: "Falling occurs because of gravity" (*gurutvāt patanam*). He shows this sūtra. And just as gravity is the cause of falling, we shall explain that in the examination of gravity (*gurutva-parīkṣā*). "Because of the statement of similarity with water" (*adbhiḥ sāmānyavacanāt*). [The sūtra] *Vaiśeṣika-sūtra* 2.1.6 states: "The fluidity of terrestrial substances such as clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*), lac (*jatū*), and beeswax (*madhūcchiṣṭha*), resulting from contact with fire, is a similarity with water. This shows the sūtra. The meaning of the sūtra is that the fluidity produced in clarified butter and the others through contact with fire is similar to that of water. "Because of the statement of subsequent action" (*uttarakarmavacanāt*). [The sūtra] *Vaiśeṣika-sūtra* 5.1.17 states: "The first action of an arrow (*iṣu*) arises from impulsion (*nodana*); and from the momentum (*saṃskāra*) produced by that action, there arise subsequent and further actions. This shows the sūtra. The first action of the arrow—meaning the shaft—arises from impulsion; and the action, depending upon impulsion, initiates a momentum. From the momentum produced by that action, there arise subsequent and further actions; one momentum initiates multiple actions until the fall. The use of the genitive case in the word "of the arrow" (*iṣoḥ*)—even though the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) of the arrow is already understood—is for the purpose of making known that the action exists even in its constituent parts. Alternatively, since the sense of the genitive is actually present, there is no fault even in expressing it.

“Odor exists only in earth. Color is of many kinds, such as white and so forth. Taste is of six kinds, beginning with sweet. Odor is of two kinds: fragrant and non-fragrant. Its touch, while being neither hot nor cold, is produced by heating (*pākaja*).

“It is, however, of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal. That which is characterized as atoms is eternal; that which is characterized as an effect is non-eternal. It possesses a multiplicity of universals (*jāti*) distinguished by the arrangement of parts such as stability and so forth, and it provides manifold assistance, such as serving for lying down, sitting, and other purposes.”
“And its effect is threefold, consisting of what is designated as the body, the sense organs, and the objects.

“In that regard, the body is of two kinds: born from a womb (*yonija*) and not born from a womb (*ayonija*). Among these, the non-womb-born body of gods and sages—which does not depend on semen and blood—is produced from atoms accompanied by a specific merit (*dharma*). The bodies of punishment for minute creatures are produced from atoms accompanied by a specific demerit (*adharma*).”

“[The body] is born from the union of semen and blood; it is born from a womb. That [womb-born body] is of two kinds: viviparous and oviparous. Among humans, domestic animals, and wild beasts, it is viviparous; among birds and reptiles, it is oviparous. “The sense organ that manifests odor is the olfactory organ (*ghrāṇa*). It is composed of purely earthly atoms, which have not been overcome by water and the other elements and are not mixed with them, and which are present in all living beings.”

“The object, however, is that which is produced through the process beginning with dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth; it is threefold, characterized as earth, stone, and stationary (*sthāvara*). Among these, modifications of clay consist of regions of ground, walls, bricks, and the like. Stones consist of rocks, gems, diamonds, and so forth. Stationary things consist of trees, grasses, herbs, shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and forest giants.”

Since form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory qualities] are differentiators because they are unique [to their respective elements], he states their uniqueness in order to support the point being asserted: "Smell exists only in earth," and so forth. Now, is this restriction regarding smell untenable because it is perceived in water or fire? No; for it is perceived through the relation of inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyukta-samavāya*). To explain: in water, the manifestation of smell is observed due to contact with a perfuming substance (*vāsaka-dravya*), and in fire, it is due to the influence of a particular kind of fuel. If smell were inherent by its very nature in fire, it would be perceived in fire even without a particular fuel, or in water even without contact with a perfuming substance. But such is not the case. Therefore, it is correct that smell exists only in earth.

Form (*rūpa*) exists in earth alone in many varieties, such as white and so forth, but not in water nor in fire. In water, only white is invariably perceived, and in fire, only luminosity; however, in earth, it is of many kinds. For indeed, because earth is differentiated by various types such as cloth and the like, it is observed that some parts are white and some are green.

Now, it may be argued that it is appropriate for earth to possess a connection with multiple forms in view of the difference between its individual instances (*vyakti*); however, as for that which has the form of a globe (*golaka*), there are not multiple forms in it. If it is then claimed that even in that case there is a connection with multiple forms because of the perception that some parts are white, some black, and so on—this is not so. Because the part (*avayava*) and the whole (*avayavin*) are distinct, how could the whole possess such a state [of multiplicity] when only the parts possess the connection with multiple forms? Or, if this were admitted, it would contradict the Sūtra: "In an all-pervading substance (*avibhu dravya*), specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) perceptible by the same sense organ are impossible" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.1.28). Thus, [the opponent's position] would be contradicted.

For it is observed that even many [qualities] perceivable by the same sense organ can coexist in a pervasive substance, as in the case of sounds in space; therefore, the term "non-pervasive" (*avibhu*) is included to exclude such cases. Likewise, since qualities perceivable by different sense organs—such as color (*rūpa*), taste (*rasa*), and so forth—can coexist in a non-pervasive substance, the phrase "perceivable by the same sense organ" (*samānendriyagrāhya*) is used. Furthermore, since many qualities perceivable by the same sense organ, such as number (*saṃkhyā*) and others, are observed to coexist in a non-pervasive substance, the inclusion of the term "specific" (*viśeṣa*) serves to exclude those.

Therefore, there is a contradiction in accepting that many colors exist within a single piece of earth. Even granting this for the sake of argument, we ask: when many qualities such as white and so forth coexist in one place, do they pervade their substrate (*āśrayavyāpitva*) or do they reside in specific parts (*pradeśavartitva*)? If they pervade the substrate, then even when a composite whole (*avayavin*) is perceived together with a single part, its multiple forms would be grasped even when other parts are obscured, precisely because they pervade the substrate. If, on the other hand, they reside in specific parts, then the qualification "pervading the substrate" is nullified.

Now, [the opponent claims] that a single variegated color is "that form. Just as there are specific distinctions such as white, yellow, and so forth, so too variegation is simply a specific kind of color. Regarding this, it has been said:
"If it is argued that this variegated [color] is one, then this is even more variegated than that.
If it is one, how can it be variegated? And if it is variegated, how can it be one? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.200)

"One variegated [color]" means it is exceedingly wonderful. It is not logical that mutually contradictory forms should originate a single form, because they are observed to originate forms of a similar nature, as in "from white, white."

Now, it is determined that in earth and water there exists merely a specific form such as white and so forth, because its perception would otherwise be inexplicable. For otherwise, due to the absence of color (*rūpa*), they would not be perceptible to the eye; since a substance possessing color is what is perceptible to the eye. Nor does the status of being an object of the eye arise from the color of the constituent parts alone; for if one thing were made an object of the eye by the color of another, it would follow that even air would likewise be so perceived. Therefore, because it is an object of the eye, mere color exists in earth.

But surely, if this is so, it contradicts the statement that "the nature of earth is of many kinds," because color-in-general (*rūpamātra*) does not include [specific qualities] such as white and so forth. For it is said that "being of many kinds" means being differentiated by distinctions such as white and so on; yet "color-in-general" is devoid of such particulars—thus there is a contradiction.

All of this is based on an unknown meaning. For it is accepted that color (*rūpa*) exists in the earth in many varieties, such as white and so forth. [Objection: But was it not stated that this contradicts the Sūtra? [Reply: No, because the meaning of the Sūtra has not been understood. And thus is the meaning of the Sūtra: the prohibition is that in a non-omnipresent, non-pervasive substance, there cannot exist specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) that are perceptible by the same sense organ and uniform in form; but it does not prohibit those of multiple varieties. How so? Because in the case of the earth, a nature consisting of multiple forms is perceived. The same applies to taste (*rasa*), which has six divisions.

The coexistence of many forms and tastes that possess a single identical form of object within one [substratum] is not accepted, because it would be redundant. For instance, since the cognition of color is produced by a single white form alone, a second [white form] would be entirely redundant; likewise, [a second taste] would be redundant for the cognition of sweetness produced by a sweet taste.

Now, regarding the existence of a single [quality] such as white and so forth, it has been asked whether its occurrence is pervasive (*vyāpyavṛtti*) or non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*). In that regard, there is no contradiction in its being non-pervasive, because we do not accept the restrictive conclusion that the remaining [qualities] must necessarily pervade their substratum. For this very reason, since a cloth is perceived together with a single part, there is likewise the perception of only that one form. Furthermore, because multiple forms are not perceived as pervading the entire substratum, there is an absence of a variegated appearance (*citrapratibhāsa*).

Now, does the variegated [color] arise from something variegated, or from something non-variegated? If one accepts that it arises from the variegated, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that variegation would also appear in the causes of the causes of the cloth. If, on the other hand, it arises from the non-variegated, then since [the cause] is of a single form, there would be the undesirable consequence that a variegated form would arise everywhere. This is not tenable. For it is observed that causes possessing various forms initiate an effect possessing various forms. And it is not the case that there are no various forms in the causes of those [causes], such that variegation would not be produced. Nor is there any sublation (*bādhaka*) to the fact that because the threads possess multiple forms such as blue and so forth, the cloth also initiates multiple forms; for such a form is acquired through the process beginning with the qualities of the cause. To explain: even though the color in each individual cause is not variegated, it is logical that from a blue [thread] comes blue, and from a yellow [thread] comes yellow. Let it be granted, then, that there is a single variegated form resulting from the initiation of a single form by means of forms such as blue and so forth. Just as "white" and so forth are specific types of color, so too "variegated" is simply a specific type of color. Even if it is not designated by words such as "white," its existence is established because it is designated by its own word.

Now, how can contradictory qualities such as blue and so forth originate a single form? [The opponent asks: "As in the case of white forms. For just as it is observed that many white forms originate a single white form, so too the origination of a variegated form (*citra*) by blue and other colors must be accepted, since it is observed. [The opponent objects: "Since the word *citra* is a synonym for 'manifold' (*nānā*), the claim that 'one thing is variegated' (*ekaṃ citram*) is itself a marvel (*āścarya*). [The author replies: That is incorrect. Just as the designation 'variegated' (*citra*) is applied to manifold forms—as in "the threads are variegated, being connected with blue and other forms"—so too is the designation 'variegated' applied to the cloth produced from them, as in "the cloth is variegated" or "its form is variegated. Moreover, the designation 'variegated' is not necessarily observed only in cases like cloth when they are connected with manifold forms; rather, it necessarily occurs when [an object] is originated by causes possessing manifold forms.

Now, since the variegated form is a single unity, would there not be a variegated appearance even when the whole (avayavin) is perceived while it is joined with only one part, provided that the remaining parts are covered? No; because of the absence of auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*). For it is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the sense faculty, assisted by the perception of various forms in the parts, produces the variegated appearance in the whole. Therefore, when the remaining parts are covered, there is an absence of the variegated appearance in the whole because those forms are not apprehended. Nor does non-appearance entail absolute non-existence, for [an object] may also fail to be perceived due to the absence of auxiliary conditions.

As for what has been stated by some—that mere form (rūpamātra) is known through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for its perception—therein also there is no fault, because an inference is presented for one who is in disagreement. To explain: regarding the earth, even for one who does not believe that variegated color (*citra-rūpa*) exists as distinct from particular qualities such as white due to its heterogeneous nature (*vaijātya*), an inference is [established]: "The possession of color is known from the perception of the earth," and "from perception by the eye. Once the possession of color is established, it is proven that because it cannot be designated by terms such as "white" and so forth, it is denoted by the word "variegated."

By this, taste (*rasa*) is explained. Taste is of six kinds, beginning with sweet, and it exists only in earth. This is because, despite the difference between individual instances, it is found even within a single instance. Thus, even in a single *harītakī* fruit, all six types of taste are perceived. For this very reason, since these six varieties are not perceived elsewhere, taste serves as the differentiator from the other elements.

Likewise, odor is of two kinds: fragrant (*surabhi*) and non-fragrant (*asurabhi*). This applies to a single instance of earth through the distinction of individual manifestations, as previously explained. Now, one might object: since the designation "non-fragrant" could simply be the absence of fragrance, the twofold division of odor is untenable. This is not so; for both types are distinguished by degrees such as "more intense" and so forth. Just as there is the conventional usage of "more intense" and so on regarding fragrant odors, the same applies to non-fragrant odors. Furthermore, this would not be possible if it were merely the absence of fragrance, because an absence cannot possess degrees of intensity.

The touch of this earth, while being neither hot nor cold, is produced by heating (*pākaja*). "Neither hot" is for the purpose of excluding hot touch; "not cold" is for the purpose of excluding [the touch] of wind; and "produced by heating" is for the purpose of excluding [the touch] of air. Now, if one were to say simply that "produced by heating" means "born from contact with fire," there would be no ambiguity; so why include the mention of "neither hot nor cold"? It is for the sake of stating its essential nature (*svarūpa*).

Others, however, maintain that because the hot touch of fire arises from heating, the term "not hot" is included [to exclude that]; whereas the inclusion of "not cold" alone is for the sake of stating its essential nature.

Now, it might be argued that touch is not produced by heating (*pākaja*) because its distinctness (*vailakṣaṇya*) does not appear [in perception], just as it does not for color and the like. That is not so; for even if the distinctness is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the fact that it is produced by heating is established through inference (*anumāna*). And thus: "The touch of earth is produced by heating, because it is a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of earth, like the color and other qualities residing therein."

[Objection: But in that case, there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even the general qualities (*sāmānyaguṇa*) would be produced by heating (*pākaja*), because they are qualities of earth (*pārthivaguṇatva*), just like color (*rūpa*). [Reply: This is not correct. If the general qualities are made the subject (*pakṣa*), the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to conjunction with fire (*agnisaṃyoga*). For instance, the conjunction with fire in an earthly atom is a quality of earth but is not produced by conjunction with fire. Nor does this contradict the status of being a specific quality of earth (*pārthivaviśeṣaguṇatva*). Since a reason that exists in only a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) but is entirely excluded from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) is indeed a means of valid cognition (*gamaka*). Furthermore, since it is not contradicted by perception or scripture regarding the subject, it is not "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*). Nor is it "equal to the point at issue" (*prakaraṇasama*), because its truth is not perceived and thus it is not irrelevant. Therefore, earth is distinct from others because it is the cause of touch and other qualities produced by heating.

The state of being common among things is *sāmānya* (universality), which is therefore based upon difference; thus, he states the difference with the words, “But that is of two kinds. That earth is of two kinds. In what form? He says: “It is both eternal and non-eternal. Eternal is that characterized as atoms, having the nature of atoms. Non-eternal, however, is that characterized as an effect, having the nature of an effect—this is the distinction. Since this distinction exists, the definition of universality (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is established; thus, any suspicion of its impossibility is dispelled.

And in order to dispel the doubt that "since there would be an absence of an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) upon the destruction of every effect, there could be no further production," the statement says: "But it is of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal. It is thus established that when the non-eternal [atoms] are destroyed, the eternal ones again initiate effects in heaven and elsewhere through the process beginning with dyads (*dvyaṇuka*).

But how, one might ask, is earth known to have atoms as its intrinsic nature? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Characterized by its effect" (*kāryalakṣaṇā*). It is characterized—that is, known—by means of its effect. For instance, an effect is preceded by an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*); that cause, too, must be produced by another inherent cause, and so on, until one reaches the primary effect, which is likewise produced by an inherent cause. The producers of that [primary effect] are the atoms. Thus, the inherent cause of an effect has a smaller dimension than the effect itself; the inherent cause of that [cause] also has a smaller dimension, and so forth, until it is understood that the primary effect is composed of atoms possessing the ultimate, minimal dimension.

Now, if it is not admitted that there is a final limit even to those parts—since you do not accept eternal causes—then, because an effect cannot arise without a cause, there would be another inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) for that cause as well; thus, in this infinite regress, there would be no distinction such as "smaller" and so forth among the resulting substances. For instance, it is observed that what is produced from few causes is small, while what is produced from many causes is large. And this [distinction] is not possible in an infinite regress where one does not admit eternal causes, since everything would be indistinguishable in being produced by an infinite number of causes. Just as the earth, in the form of a globe, is produced by an infinite number of causes, so too would effects such as jars be [the same], leading to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of them having a uniform appearance. Furthermore, a uniform appearance is not observed based on number, weight, or dimension, because jars and other things are perceived to have different dimensions and different weights. For instance, there is a diversity: one thing is less than five *palas* while another is more, at ten *palas*, both being produced by many similar causes. And that diversity would not exist in the case of an infinite regress.

Furthermore, even if one does not accept [the existence of] eternal [atoms], it is not the case that the re-emergence of all produced substances (*kāryadravya*) after their destruction during the state of dissolution would be impossible, because non-existence (*abhāva*) cannot serve as an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). We shall explain how this is possible during the state of dissolution in the *Bhūtaparīkṣā*. Therefore, an infinite regress need not be avoided. One must accept that the primordial effect (*ādikārya*) arises from the causes of cloth and so forth, which exist in a progressively smaller scale.

That first effect is produced by an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), because it is an effect; whatever is an effect is produced by an inherent cause, just like a cloth and so forth, and this [first effect] is likewise an effect; therefore, it is produced by an inherent cause. Nor should it be argued that the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) deviates from its concomitance with [having an inherent cause] due to non-existence (*abhāva*), because the nature of being an effect consists in its relation to the existence of its own cause. Likewise, the state of being progressively smaller found in the causes of jars and other things must rest somewhere, because it is expressed by comparative terms such as "more" or "most," just like great dimension (*mahāparimāṇa*). Those in which it rests are the atoms (*paramāṇu*).

Now, atoms possess parts because they are corporeal, like a jar; because they are simultaneously connected with six [other atoms]; because they are designated by spatial directions indicated by terms such as "eastern part" and "western part"; and because they initiate composite effects possessing parts, like threads and the like.

All of this is unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), because the existence of atoms (*paramāṇu*) is not established. If, however, the existence of atoms is indeed accepted, then since you have admitted a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that makes known the existence of atoms, an inference contrary to that [existence] would be invalid due to lacking a subject matter (*nirviṣayatva*). [Objection: Since the opponent accepts that atoms are indivisible, an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpatti*) is being drawn against him; thus, this is a *prasaṅga* argument. [Response: In that case, if the opponent has accepted the atoms through a means of valid cognition, then as long as he maintains the validity of that cognition, the contrary inference cannot arise. If, on the other hand, it is from an invalid means of cognition, then since that is invalid, the existence of atoms is not established; so what is the point of presenting an inference, given that it results in the fallacy of the unestablished locus?

Likewise, there is a contradiction between the two terms in the proposition that "atoms possess parts. For the word *paramāṇu* (atom) denotes a partless, ultimate minute entity (*niratiśayāṇu*), whereas if it were to have parts, it would necessarily possess a magnitude greater than its constituent parts; thus, there is a contradiction. Furthermore, since a thing cannot be an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) if it possesses a magnitude equal to its own parts, those parts would themselves have to be atoms. If those too have parts, they would require further parts, and if those too have parts, they would require yet more—leading to an infinite regress. Regarding this infinite regress, the refutation already stated is that the distinction between "smaller" and so forth would be untenable.

Now, if partless atoms are accepted on the basis of valid cognition so that there may be no infinite regress, then the inference of their having parts would be invalid, because it is sublated by that [perception].

Now, it might be argued that because atoms are partless, they could not have conjunction with six [other atoms], nor could there be designations of direction and location. This is not so, because it occurs otherwise as well. For instance, since conjunction does not pervade its locus (*avyāpyavṛtti*), even when there is simultaneous connection with those situated in directions such as east and west, the atom does not possess parts. Likewise, if there is a designation such as "eastern part" or "western part," that too must be understood as figurative (*bhākta*), since the primary sense is precluded; this is because the atom serves as the substratum for a non-pervading conjunction in a general sense.

As for that [property] of being a commencing cause of something possessing parts—if it means being a commencing cause together with its own parts, then that is unestablished, because [the subject] is partless.

Now, is it the case that a composite effect, which is to be produced by its own parts, possesses the capacity to produce [itself]? That is unproven, because a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is originated from two atoms (*paramāṇu*). For instance, atoms originate dyads, but they do not originate themselves, because they are eternal and because action is contradictory within itself. Furthermore, the example of the threads is devoid of the probans; for it is established by the effect that those [threads] do not originate the effect when accompanied by their parts, nor do they originate it when unaccompanied by their parts.

It is observed that "earth is eternal. And for the purpose of refuting those who maintain non-difference (*abheda*), the statement "it is of two kinds" is made. To explain: when earth is distinguished from another earth, is it distinguished by way of being earth, or by way of not being earth? If it is distinguished from another earth by way of being earth, then it follows that it possesses the nature of earth (*pṛthivītva*). If, on the other hand, it is distinguished by way of not being earth, then that which is so distinguished would not be earth. Now, suppose the distinction arises from a connection with a further particular (*viśeṣa*)? If those particulars [are themselves distinguished] from yet other particulars, there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If, however, particulars are distinguished without [further] particulars, then it follows that earth must likewise exist [without particulars], as stated by the proponent of duality (*dvaitavādin*).

He states the distinction: "And that [difference] is of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal. Earth is eternal and is distinguished from the non-eternal by its lack of form (*nīrūpatayā*); the non-eternal, however, is distinguished from the eternal. Thus, the distinction arises precisely from these internal subdivisions. Now, as for the objection that if one were to admit further distinctions even among those [subdivisions], it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), that is incorrect. For even if one admits a distinction between a unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) and another unique property, since they are included within only six categories—namely, genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), and so forth—there is no fault of infinite regress. Furthermore, this has already been answered by the statement that the excluded nature (*vyāvṛttasvarūpa*) of objects manifests in indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*).

Alternatively, since there is doubt arising from the perception of both unity and multiplicity in that which is characterized by its characteristic, this statement—“But it is of two kinds”—is intended to dispel that doubt. It is not for the sake of refuting the misconception [of] unity, as in the case of space (*ākāśa*). He defines another property of that which is characterized by its effects: “And it is distinguished by stability and so forth, and by the arrangement of its parts. Stability is the state of being stable; those qualities beginning with it, such as softness, hardness, and so on, are the "stability and so forth. Furthermore, the "arrangement of its parts" refers to a specific configuration; it is "distinguished" by these.

The view of the naked ones (Digvāsas) is that because there is no possible sustainer of gravity, the earth would fall perpetually; however, even though it exists [in a state of falling], it is not perceived due to the determination of its prior and posterior parts. This is refuted as follows: by the word "stability" (*sthairya*), stability means steadiness, which is to say, non-falling. If, on the other hand, there were falling, then due to the excellence of gravity, an excellence of falling would be perceived; and because of the earth's excessive falling, a clod of earth or similar object thrown upward would never again have contact with the ground. For instance, while the clod travels upward and then returns slowly, the earth—due to its rapid falling—would have been separated by hundreds of *yojanas* or more, resulting in a lack of contact. Yet, contact is observed; therefore, it is known that the earth does not fall. Precisely for this reason, since falling cannot otherwise be accounted for, it is known that there exists something which sustains gravity. Otherwise, in the absence of a sustainer of gravity, falling would necessarily occur. Since that [falling] does not happen, an obstructive agent is inferred. For if a heavy substance were the obstructer, it too would possess gravity and thus would fall; therefore, the great air (*vāyu*) acts as the obstructer. Indeed, it is observed that even a small amount of air possesses the power to sustain gravity when leaves and such are placed upon it. At the beginning of creation, the air produced was exceptionally great and acts as the sustainer of the earth along with its water and other elements, holding them up like a blade of grass.

Likewise, there is stability; that is, the earth is non-momentary (*akṣaṇikatva*). And the mention of "stability" is for the purpose of refuting momentariness. We shall explain later how such momentariness is not possible.

However, in order to refute those who consider the earth to be partless and not an effect, it is described as "distinguished by the arrangement of its parts. For "parts" (*avayava*) are constituent portions, which are perceived in the earth; their "arrangement" (*sanniveśa*) is a specific configuration that is directly perceptible. Furthermore, because it is distinguished by the arrangement of its parts, it is an effect. To illustrate: the earth is an effect, because it is distinguished by the arrangement of its parts; whatever is distinguished by the arrangement of its parts is observed to be an effect, such as a jar and the like; and the earth is likewise distinguished by the arrangement of its parts; therefore, it is an effect.

The followers of Jaimini argue that even if [the earth] is an effect, the inference is invalid because the property of possessing a specific arrangement of parts is not perceived in things such as cognition (*buddhi*), and thus the reason is irrelevant (*aprayojaka*). This is incorrect, for we accept that a reason which exists in only a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) can still be a means of knowledge. To explain: we say that whatever possesses an arrangement of parts is seen to be an effect; however, we do not say that whatever is an effect necessarily possesses an arrangement of parts. Furthermore, it is not the case that what exists in only a portion of the similar instances lacks probative power; otherwise, the inference from smoke would itself fail to be a means of knowledge. For instance, if the possession of fire were not necessitated by the possession of smoke, then the presence of smoke would not entail the presence of fire. Now, if you argue that because the pervasion is asymmetrical, the pervasion is only "whatever has smoke has fire" and not "whatever has fire has smoke," then likewise, the possession of an arrangement of parts—even though it exists in only a portion of the similar instances—cannot be considered irrelevant.

Furthermore, since the state of having come into being after not having existed (*abhūtvā-bhāvitva*) is not perceived, the earth cannot be an effect. Is this non-perception [of such a state] by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), or by means of inference (*anumāna*)? If it were non-perception by direct perception, then because it is not perceived in certain things like a jar, it would follow that they are not effects. If, however, even in those cases the state of having come into being after not having existed is known through the arrangement of parts (*avayava-sanniveśa*), then it is the same for the earth as well; its state of having come into being after not having existed is understood precisely through its possession of an arrangement of parts. And we shall explain in the *Bhūtaparīkṣā* that being preceded by an agent is understood through the state of being an effect.

Likewise, regarding the effect-characterized [earth], he states another property: "endowed with a multiplicity of lower universals" (*aparajātibahutvopetā*). An "other universal," however, is one such as *ghaṭatva* (pot-ness) or *paṭatva* (cloth-ness) in relation to *pṛthivītva* (earth-ness). Its "multiplicity" is its being incalculable; "endowed with that" means being possessed of that. And thus, there is no excessive disparity in the definition of the atom.

Likewise, regarding the definition by way of function (*kāryalakṣaṇā*), he specifies the function as "beds, seats, and so forth" (*śayanāsanādi*). Because it performs manifold assistance through its various distinctions, it is said to be "the producer of manifold assistance" (*anekopakārakarī*). This is stated for the purpose of refuting—by means of a concessive argument (*abhyupagamavāda*)—the view that accepts existence (*sattā*) through a connection with the category of existence (*sattā*), on the grounds that whatever performs causal efficiency (*arthakriyākārin*) is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*), whereas the absence of causal efficiency is the defining characteristic of non-existence.

Lest it be impossible to fully comprehend the effects of earth due to their infinity, the author states, "And its effect is threefold," (*), thereby asserting a distinction through intermediate subdivisions within the context of the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*). For just as this property exists in the form of the atoms of the effect (*kāryaparamāṇu*), characterized by the distinction between eternal and non-eternal, and just as there is a connection with properties such as stability and a plurality of subordinate genera (*aparajāti*) in this earth which consists of effects, so too is the effect threefold. Thus, even though the effects of the earth are infinite, they fall within the scope of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) because they exist in a threefold state, mutually distinct from one another in the form of the body and so forth. To explain: that which has the designations "body," "organ," and "object" is "designated as body, organ, and object" (*śarīrendriyaviṣayasaṃjñakam*); all of this is to be known as the effect of the earth.

Others, however, maintain that the threefold effect of this [space], characterized by atoms, consists of bodies and so forth, because the word "this" (idam) is sometimes used to refer even to something remote.

In this context, he states the body’s distinction from other things by saying, “The body is of two kinds. Since a particular depends upon a universal, when a particular is being designated, the definition of the universal must necessarily be present; however, he did not state the general definition in order to cultivate the students’ power of inference (*ūhana*). For instance, when the term "body" is mentioned, the definition—that the nature of being a body (*śarīratva*) is the cause for the linguistic usage of "body"—is indeed understood. Likewise, since the state of being a substratum for action that conforms to will is not possible without a body, it is obtained through the meaning of the word "body" itself, and thus is not stated by its own specific term. However, at the beginning of the treatise, because [the definition] is given by way of the body and so forth, there is no lack of over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

Now, the state of being a body (*śarīratva*) is a valid definition because it pervades all bodies and is excluded from other distinct categories. However, "being the substratum of activity that follows the will" is not [a valid definition]. For although this [latter property] is indeed excluded from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), it is non-existent in every instance of the subject (*pakṣa*). To explain: in states such as death, this [property] does not exist; thus, it is under-pervasive (*avyāpaka*). If it is argued that this is the definition of a living body, that is not so, because it is not perceived even in states such as deep sleep or fainting. How then is this a definition? It is so by virtue of its fitness (*yogyatā*). To explain: a body is distinguished from other things because it possesses the fitness to be the direct substratum of activity following the will and because of its connection with the state of being a body (*śarīratva*); whereas that which is not so [distinguished] is neither fit to be the direct substratum of activity following the will nor endowed with the state of being a body, such as the sense organs and so forth.

Some maintain that the body is that whose sharpness or dullness of the sense-faculties, until death, corresponds to the sharpness or dullness of those faculties themselves. For instance, since sharpness can also arise in the sense-faculties through the application of medicine, the phrase "until death" is included. Thus, we observe that for one who is free from disease, the sharpness of the sense-faculties persists until death due to the sharpness of the body. However, in the case of one who is diseased, we see that when the disease is pacified by the application of medicine, the sharpness of the sense-faculties arises precisely from the sharpness of the body. Furthermore, defects such as cataracts and jaundice occur in the sense-faculties precisely because of the dullness of the body; therefore, [the definition] is distinguished by the sharpness of that [body].

It should be understood that the body is composed of earth because, while being produced from constituent parts such as flesh, it is a final composite (*antyāvayavin*). The term "final composite" is used because fingers and the like—though produced from constituent parts such as flesh—are not objects of the conventional designation "body. Furthermore, the property of being a final composite could possibly apply even to what is not a body; therefore, the phrase "produced from constituent parts such as flesh" is included.

For the purpose of defining the specific characteristics of the earthly body, which has already been characterized by its general definition, there is this classification: "The body is of two kinds. In what form? "Born from a womb (*yonija*) and not born from a womb (*ayonija*). Although the womb-born was mentioned first, because the elucidation of the subject matter is intended here, he speaks of the non-womb-born, saying: "Among these, the non-womb-born. Since the word *yoni* is a synonym for cause, he says "independent of semen and blood" so that it might not be considered accidental. Although the word *yoni* is a general term, it is intended here as a specific cause characterized by semen and blood; thus, by its negation, another cause is obtained. That which is produced from another cause without depending on semen and blood is "non-womb-born. Of whom? "The bodies of gods and sages. However, while the body of gods and sages is non-womb-born, it is not exclusively so, since their being womb-born is also heard in scripture.

Others, however, form the compound by eliding one word "deva" in order to prevent ambiguity: *devāś ca devarṣayaś ca devarṣayas*, [meaning] "gods and divine sages," [and then] "of them. In this context, the gods are eightfold, beginning with the Piśācas; even there, since some are heard to be born from a womb (*yonija*), no further qualification need be considered.

Now, he explains from what that body arises: "It is produced from atoms accompanied by a specific merit (*dharma-viśeṣa*). For instance, in the production of that body, the atoms are the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*), their conjunction is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*), and the specific merit is the instrumental cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*). Furthermore, in the production of a substance, conjunction exists in a relation of inherence with the same object as the effect. Now, what is the proof for the existence of a non-womb-born body (*ayonija-śarīra*) for gods and sages? It is scripture (*āgama*). And thus it is said: "Bodies not born from a womb belong to those of wondrous deeds."
O Maudgalya! They are indeed born from the womb, but not born from a mother and father.

For it is thus: those whose actions (*karman*) are wonderful and excellent are so described; by the power of such excellent actions, their bodies are born from a womb (*yonija*). To ensure that this does not amount to a mere negation of the cause [of birth], he says: "born from a womb" means "born from causes. How then is it said that they are "not born from a womb"? He replies: "not born from mother and father. By the terms "father" and "mother," blood and semen are designated metaphorically. Furthermore, excellent action is twofold: in the form of merit (*dharma*) and in the form of demerit (*adharma*). Among these, from merit arise the bodies of gods and sages (*ṛṣi*), and from demerit arise the bodies of minute creatures (*kṣudrajantu*) and bodies of torment (*yātanāśarīra*). Minute creatures refer to lice and the like; bodies of torment refer to the bodies of hell-beings (*nārakīya*). These arise from atoms accompanied by specific instances of demerit. Now, although the bodies of gods and sages are produced from specific instances of merit, they are understood through inference to be "born from a womb. For instance: the bodies of gods and sages are born from a womb, because they are bodies, like our own bodies and so forth. But since that [inference] is sublated by scripture (*āgama*), it is not authoritative. Likewise, because scripture is sublated by inference, the existence of the bodies of gods and sages is not established; consequently, one's own inference would suffer from the fallacy of having an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatva*) and thus would result in being non-authoritative.

Furthermore, the validity of inference cannot be established by undermining the domain of scripture; rather, it is logical that inference should support scripture. For instance: "The bodies of gods and sages are not born from a womb, because they are produced by superior karma, like the bodies of śarabhas and other such creatures. Although there is a distinction in that non-virtuous (adharma) karma constitutes the "superior" cause for the body of a śarabha, whereas virtuous (dharma) karma constitutes it for the body of a god or sage, the property of being "produced by superior karma" remains identical in both cases. Thus, the example is not devoid of the probans (*sādhana*).

He states that [the body] is born from a womb (*yonija*) by saying, "born from the union of semen and blood" (*śukra-śoṇita-sampāta-ja*). It is born from the coming together—that is, the conjunction—of semen and blood. Semen belongs to the father, and blood to the mother. At the very moment of their union, due to the power of the karma of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), there occurs a connection with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). From the conjunction of semen and blood, a substance in the form of an embryo (*majjita*) is produced. Immediately thereafter, through contact with internal heat (*tejas*) dependent on momentum (*vega*), motion arises in the parts; following that, through disjunction, the conjunction that initiates the substance is destroyed; and from the destruction of that [conjunction], the destruction of the substance initiated by it occurs. Then, from another contact with fire, the previous color and other qualities are displaced. And from yet another [contact], new color and other qualities are produced. Thus, when atoms (*aṇu*) in which qualities produced by cooking (*pākaja*) have arisen, motion produced by the contact of the self with the atom, dependent on unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), initiates disjunction. From that, the previous conjunction being displaced, subsequent conjunction gives rise to a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*); in this manner, from dyads triads (*tryaṇuka*) are produced, and by such a sequence, the body is produced. Furthermore, what is eaten and drunk by the mother is brought down by her digestive heat; then again, through contact with internal heat, motion arises in the parts; then, from disjunction, the destruction of conjunction occurs, and from that, the destruction of the substance. From another contact with fire, the destruction of the previous color and so forth occurs, and from another, the production of redness and so forth. Thereafter, by the process beginning with dyads, the body is produced: such is the logical principle (*nyāya*). This same characteristic should be observed for the body until it reaches the state of ashes. Otherwise, if the consumption of food were not the cause of the nourishment of the substratum, it would be purposeless.

Nor should it be said that those parts which have not yet begun a body initiate another body upon obtaining auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), and then yet another body upon obtaining further auxiliary causes; for this would entail the fallacy of the theory of "beginning what has already been begun" (*ārabhyārambhaka-vāda*). If it were accepted that after one substance has been produced, while that [first] substance remains undestroyed, it subsequently produces another substance—this is not tenable. For it would follow that every effect-substance (*kārya-dravya*) must reside within atoms (*paramāṇu*). To explain: a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is produced from two atoms; while that [dyad] remains undestroyed, another [dyad] is produced by those same two atoms together with other atoms. Then, yet another is produced by those joined with still other atoms. This results in the fallacy of corporeal entities occupying the same location. For instance, a dyad produced by two atoms resides in those two atoms; then, another produced by those same two together with others resides in those two and in that [first dyad]. Thus, there would be the co-location of corporeal things. However, it is observed that they are inherent in distinct substrates; for where one corporeal thing is inherent, another cannot be inherent there.

In order to avoid the fault of [the whole] being merely a part of its object, it is said that [the dyad] is produced by two atoms together with other auxiliary causes and resides in one atom alone; and again, it is produced by those same atoms together with others and resides in one [atom] alone. Even so, a product-substance (*kāryadravya*) residing in a single substance would be indestructible due to the absence of a separation from its causes. Furthermore, there is a contradiction in the statement: "a substance without constituent substances" (*adravyaṃ dravyam*) and "a substance with multiple constituent substances" (*anekadravyañca dravyam*). For instance, "without constituent substances" (*adravyam*) means that no substance is found to be either produced or productive. There is no producer for atoms. Space (*ākāśa*) and the like are neither produced nor producers; thus they are "without constituent substances," which is to say, eternal substances. "With multiple constituent substances" (*anekadravyam*), however, refers to that which has multiple substances as its producer, by way of this very nature. Substance is indeed of two kinds: "without constituent substances," which is eternal, and "with multiple constituent substances," which is produced and an effect. This [classification] is contradicted if one accepts a product-substance that consists of a single substance.

Furthermore, it is not logical for a single entity to be a producer through either succession or simultaneity. Because of its unitary nature, it would have to perform everything that is to be done in a single moment, since that which is capable of producing all effects simultaneously has no dependence on other factors. Moreover, once it has performed all effects simultaneously, there would be no reason for it not to do so again.

Now, if they [the later parts] begin [to produce an effect] by observing the previously begun causal substance (*kāryadravya*), then, since that previous substance which has already begun its effect would also be an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), how could [the new effect] reside in only one substance? One must infer numerous faults regarding the subsistence [of multiple effects] in a single prior [substance], such as the impossibility of [one substance] being the originator of both similar and dissimilar classes of effects, and so forth. Likewise, if every causal substance were to reside only in atoms (*paramāṇu*), there would be no such usage as "here, in these threads, is a cloth" or "here, in these *vīraṇa* grasses, is a mat," because the threads and so forth would lack the status of inherent causes. Furthermore, upon the destruction of a causal substance, there would be a lack of perception [of the subsequent effect], because an intermediate effect has not yet arisen.

Now, if it is argued that because each preceding effect is not destroyed by the atoms, subsequent effects are initiated, resulting in a multiplicity of causal substances; and thus, when the final [effect] is destroyed, the preceding ones remain, leading to the perception of multiple effects—[we reply: in that case, it would follow that even upon the destruction of the conjunction of the potsherds, the jar would not be destroyed. For, when the conjunctions of its parts and their parts are destroyed, those parts and their parts lack inherent causality (*samavāyitva*), and consequently, those conjunctions lack non-inherent causality (*asamavāyitva*). This is because we observe that a substance is destroyed either by the destruction of its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) or by the destruction of its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).

Now, if it is maintained that the action produced in an atom causes the destruction of the substance by way of destroying its conjunction, then, if the action produced in the atom that initiates the first substance were to destroy the substance upon the destruction of the conjunction through disjunction, it would follow that—since each preceding conjunction is admitted to be the non-inherent cause for the production of the subsequent effect by acting as a cooperative factor for the subsequent conjunction—the destruction of that [first conjunction] would necessarily entail the destruction of all effects, and thus no effect whatsoever would be perceived.

Now, if it is argued that the conjunction of the final atoms—which has been accumulated by the conjunctions of preceding atoms—serves as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) for the production of a single effect, and that upon the destruction of that [final conjunction], only the intermediate effect (the pot, etc. which was initiated by it is destroyed, and thus remains perceptible; [we reply: even so, the destruction of a jar or similar object arising from the destruction of the atomic conjunction would be beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) for people like us. For instance, when jars placed in a kiln are destroyed due to contact with fire, that destruction occurs through the medium of the motion of the atoms. Yet, the destruction of the jar is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*) following the destruction of the conjunction of the shards; therefore, it is known that the shards possess the status of inherent causes (*samavāyitva*). Enough of this excessive detail.

Therefore, since we observe a process of increase and decrease in the body at every moment depending on the consumption or non-consumption of food, its production must be explained as occurring through the sequence of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth, arising from the transformation of matter (*pākaja*) caused by the preceding substance. And just as transformation occurs in atoms and production follows the sequence of dyads and so forth, we shall explain this in the section on the production of transformation-born qualities (*pākajotpatti*).

Now, he states the internal distinction even for that which is born from the union of semen and blood: "That is of two kinds: viviparous (*jarāyuja*) and oviparous (*aṇḍaja*). To explain: the body, arising in the womb moment by moment according to the principle of the production of things through maturation (*pākaja*), is called viviparous because it is enveloped by the placenta (*jarāyu*) at the time of emergence. It is called oviparous because, although it has emerged from the mother's body, it arises for some time within the interior of an egg, enveloped according to the principle of the production of things through maturation. To whom does the viviparous belong? He says: "Of humans, domestic animals (*paśu*), and wild beasts (*mṛga*)," meaning humans, domestic animals, and wild beasts. Even though those included under the term "domestic animals" are also designated by the term "wild beasts," this is because they are born in the wilderness.
