Others, however, form a compound by eliding one instance of the word *mānuṣa*: *mānuṣāś ca mānuṣapaśavaś ca mṛgāś ca*. In this case, the same fault applies as when those already denoted by the word *mānuṣa* are further denoted by the word *paśu*; thus, the intended purpose must be considered. Likewise, because it is impossible for the word *mṛga* to denote all animals (*paśu*), there is the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*). He states to whom the term *aṇḍaja* (egg-born) belongs: "of birds and reptiles" (*pakṣisarīsṛpāṇām*). [The compound] *pakṣisarīsṛpāḥ* consists of *pakṣiṇaḥ* (birds) and *sarīsṛpāḥ* (reptiles); [the meaning is] "of those. Reptiles (*sarīsṛpāḥ*) are so called because they crawl crookedly (*kuṭilaṃ sarpanti*), such as snakes and the like, according to conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).

Having stated the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) of the body from the body and from things of the same genus, [the author] says, "The sense-organ (*indriya*) is that which manifests odor," in order to define the dissimilarity of the sense-organ. Thus, because there is a plurality of sense-organs, their general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), which pervades them all, is indeed obtained by implication: [it is] being a cause (*karaṇatva*), being supersensible (*atīndriyatva*), being a substance (*dravyatva*), existing in a fixed substratum (*niyatādhiṣṭhānavṛttitva*), and being a generator of immediate cognition (*aparokṣajñānajanakatva*). The inclusion of the term "being a cause" is for the purpose of excluding the agent, the self (*ātman*), since it is possible for the self to generate immediate cognition. The term "supersensible" is used to exclude non-sense-organs such as lamps, which are observed to be causes and generators of immediate cognition. Similarly, the term "substance" is used because the contact between a sense-organ and its object is a generator of immediate cognition despite being a cause and supersensible. Likewise, the term "existing in a fixed substratum" is used because space (*dik*) and time (*kāla*)—due to being the efficient causes (*nimitta*) of all produced things—are causes, supersensible, and substances, yet they possess the quality of generating immediate cognition; however, since space and time are all-pervasive (*vyāpaka*) and thus produce all effects, it is impossible for them to exist in a fixed substratum. Now, one might argue that the self is also excluded by this qualification due to its all-pervasiveness, and therefore the term "being a cause" is redundant. This is not so; for although the self is pervasive, it serves as the substratum of the body by virtue of being the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*). Therefore, the sense-organ is distinct from other things because it possesses the qualities of being a cause, being supersensible, being a substance, existing in a fixed substratum, and generating immediate cognition; whereas that which is not distinct does not possess the aforementioned probans, such as the body and so forth.

He states the distinction of that which is characterized by the general definition [of a sense organ] from those of the same class: "The olfactory sense organ" (*indriyaṃ ghrāṇam*). While being characterized by the general definition of a sense organ, it is distinguished from others because it manifests odor (*gandhavyañjakatva*). Likewise, by stating "the sense organ manifests odor," he demonstrates its existence through its function. For instance: the perception of odor is the effect of an instrument, because it is an action; whatever is an action is seen to be the effect of an instrument, just as the act of cutting is; and this [perception] is an action; therefore, it is the effect of an instrument.

That instrument which effects the apprehension of odor is the nose (*ghrāṇa*), and it is composed of earth (*pārthiva*). This is because, among color, taste, odor, and touch, it invariably manifests odor. Whatever, among color and the rest, invariably manifests odor is observed to be composed of earth, such as substances like musk; and likewise, the nose invariably reveals odor among color and the rest; therefore, it is composed of earth. Now, [an objection may be raised: "The property of invariably manifesting odor is unproven, since [the nose] also manifests the universal of odor-ness (*gandhatva*), the universal of quality-ness (*guṇatva*), and the highest universal (*sattā*). To this, the qualification "among color, taste, odor, and touch" is added.

Now, one might argue that because there is no difference in their being composed of earth (*pārthivatva*), the olfactory organ (*ghrāṇa*) should manifest not only odor but also visible form (*rūpa*) and other qualities, since visible form and the rest are also qualities of earth and because the relation of inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*) is the same for all of them, with no other specific cause [for restriction] present. To this he says: “The olfactory organ is composed of earthly atoms that are not overwhelmed by water and the other [elements]. Therefore, it manifests only odor. How is this known? That the olfactory organ is composed of earthly atoms that are not overwhelmed by some water and so forth is known from the restriction of the effect. For it is observed that through the operation of the olfactory organ, only odor is perceived, and not visible form or the rest. And a restriction of the effect is not possible without a restriction of the cause; thus, its production is known to be from atoms unmixed with some water and so forth, due to a particular unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) which brings about the perception of odor. Otherwise, the perception of odor alone through the operation of the olfactory organ would not occur, yet that is observed. Therefore, since no other cause is possible, the specific mode of production is the cause, and that [specificity] is due to the power of the unseen force. And since the unseen force is the cause of such determination, this is indeed the intention of the author of the Sūtra.

"Earth is the material cause for the cognition of odor because of its predominance and its possession of odor" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 8.2.5). According to this statement, the "cognition of odor" (*gandhajñāna*) is the sense of smell (*ghrāṇa*), since odor is known by means of it. When that [cognition] is to be produced, earth is the material cause (*prakṛti*)—that is, the cause—due to the reason of its predominance.

Just as it is known through the regular perception of odor that a large number of earth-constituents—aided by a specific unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and whose forms are not obstructed by water and so forth—produce the sense of smell, and as it is understood from the statement of their causal status that even a smaller number of water-constituents are not the cause; for this very reason, those [water] constituents possess the quality of being overwhelmed. Likewise, when there is the assistance of a specific unseen force, the nose produces the manifestation of odor alone because it is produced by constituents mixed with a small amount of water and so forth, and because it possesses odor. Since the nose is earthen, it is possible for it to possess color and other qualities as well; however, the excellence intended here is its possession of odor. And due to the excellence of the odor inherent in it, among color and the rest, even though the relation of inherence in the conjunct (*saṃyuktasamavāya*) is no different, it is the manifestor of odor alone.

Alternatively, if it is argued that only a certain portion of earth is the cause for the perception of odor and not all of it—there being no specific reason [for such a distinction]—the following statement is connected: “Because of its abundance and because it possesses odor, earth is the primary cause (*prakṛti*) in the cognition of odor” (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 8.2.5). *Jñapti* means cognition; *jñāna* means cognition having odor as its object. In that regard, earth is the primary cause (*prakṛti*), that is, the cause, because of its abundance and because it is characterized by possessing odor.

Or there is another meaning: because it possesses odor, the nose is necessarily the cause for the perception of odor. When it is stated that "there is no specific cause," this sentence is to be connected with the word "nose"; and that [nose] possesses odor because there is no distinction in its being composed of earth. To the question "Why is it the nose?", he says: "Because of the predominance of the aforementioned form."

Others, however, maintain that [the sense of smell] is originated by pure earth-constituents (*pārthivāvayava*) unmixed with water and so forth, depending upon specific unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), and that this constitutes its "abundance" (*bhūyastva*). Thus says the *Bhāṣya*: "The olfactory organ (*ghrāṇa*) is originated by purely earthy constituents, unoverpowered and unmixed with water and the like. Here, we do not understand the qualification "unmixed," since non-overpowering is possible even when there is some slight contact with water and so forth. Furthermore, when it is said that "abundance" means the state of being more numerous, it does not imply the absolute impossibility of the presence of others; enough of this.

Having described the sense organ as that which manifests odor for all living beings by way of its nature as both general and particular, he states, “The object, however, is composed through the process beginning with dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth,” in order to define the essential nature of the object. Now, one might object: since the process of composition beginning with dyads and so forth also applies to the body and the sense organs, this definition of an object is over-extensive (*ativyāpin*). This is not so. Because the distinction from the object is established by stating the definitions of the body and the sense organs, the qualification “provided it is other than those two” is obtained. For instance, being composed through the process beginning with dyads and so forth, while being distinct from the body and the sense organs, constitutes an object; for such a thing serves to assist in the state of being an object. Furthermore, an object is that which is to be experienced or is perceivable by the senses of those like us.

Now, it may be argued that a triad (*tryaṇuka*), having been produced through the sequence beginning with dyads (*dvyaṇuka*), is not perceptible by the senses of people like us, even though it is distinct from the body and the sense organs; thus, this definition of an object (*viṣaya*) is non-pervasive (*avyāpin*). This is because the qualification "produced through the sequence beginning with dyads" serves to exclude such cases. For instance, the use of the term "beginning" (*ādi*) in the phrase "that of which the dyad is the beginning" includes the triad as well. That which is "this dyad and so forth" (*asau dvyaṇukādiḥ*) and "that sequence" (*sa cāsau prakramaḥ*)—the object produced by that is "produced through the sequence beginning with dyads," meaning produced by dyads, triads, and so on. A triad, moreover, is produced by dyads, and thus belongs to the sequence beginning with dyads. Furthermore, triads can be producers [of larger wholes] either two at a time or in large numbers without restriction. Thus, it is possible for what is produced by them to be an object of the senses.

And because the object, though characterized by its general definition, is infinite due to its internal subdivisions, he states its summary: "It is threefold. In what form? "Characterized by earth, stone, and immobile [beings]. That whose characteristics—that is, whose nature—is earth, stone, and immobile beings is described as such. As for the nature: it is "earth-ness" in earth and "stone-ness" in stones.

One might object: "Is it not the case that the threefold division [of earth] based on clay and so forth is untenable, because objects such as bricks are not included? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In that regard, walls, bricks, and the like—those being jars and so forth—are modifications of clay; thus they are subsumed under the term 'clay' (*mṛt*). As for 'modification,' it is said that when clay assumes a particular configuration, through contact with fire and by means of atomic activity, the prior substance is destroyed and its dark color and other qualities cease; then, through the production of qualities born of baking (*pākaja*), [new substances] are originated. Even though [the new object] is originated by those baked qualities, the universal *mṛttva* (earthness) does not cease; therefore, they are designated by the term 'clay. He shows those things possessing the universal of 'rock-ness' (*pāṣāṇatva*) by saying: 'rocks, stones, gems, diamonds, and so forth. Their specific nature is to be understood from the technical treatises and common worldly usage. He shows those connected with the genus 'stationary' (*sthāvaratva*) by saying: 'stationary beings are grasses, herbs, trees, shrubs, creepers, spreading plants, and forest giants. Grass is well-known to both parties. Herbs are grains and the like, which end with the ripening of their fruit. Trees are those connected with the genus 'tree-ness' (*vṛkṣatva*), such as the *aśoka* and others. In the same way, the distinctions of shrubs, creepers, spreading plants, and so forth, are to be understood. As it has been said:"
Herbs (oṣadhi) are those that perish at the ripening of their fruit; creepers (latā), shrubs (gulma), and climbing plants (vīrudh) are also included.
A fruit-bearing tree is to be known as a forest-tree (vanaspati), while trees (vṛkṣa) are those endowed with both flowers and fruit.
Thus [it is said].

“Water is so called because of its connection with the property of moisture (*āptva*). It possesses color, taste, touch, fluidity, viscidity (*sneha*), number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, weight, and impression (*saṃskāra*). These [properties] are established as before. Its color, taste, and touch are exclusively white, sweet, and cold, respectively. Viscidity and natural fluidity (*sāṃsiddhika-dravatva*) exist only in water. Furthermore, these [waters] are of two kinds, as before, due to their being eternal or non-eternal. Their effects, moreover, are threefold, designated as body (*śarīra*), sense organ (*indriya*), and object (*viṣaya*). The body is exclusively non-uterine (*ayonija*); it is produced from aqueous atoms accompanied by a specific merit (*dharma*) in the world of Varuṇa. Through the support of earthy particles, it becomes capable of experience. The sense organ is the tongue (*rasana*), which perceives the tastes of all living beings; it is composed of water-particles that are not overwhelmed by other particles. The objects, however, consist of rivers, oceans, snow, hailstones, and so forth.”

Now, for the purpose of defining and examining water (*udaka*) as it has been mentioned, he states the section beginning with “*aptvābhisambandhāt*” (*due to the connection with the property of being water*). The connection with the property of being water (*aptva*), characterized by the property of being water, is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*), namely inherence (*samavāya*). For instance, water is distinguished from other things because of its connection with the property of being water; those things which are not so distinguished are not connected with the property of being water, such as earth and the rest. But water is not like that; therefore, it is distinguished [from others]. Alternatively, a linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) is established: the substance under dispute must be designated as "water" because of its connection with the property of being water. Those things which are not so designated as "water" are not connected with the property of being water, such as earth and the rest. But this [substance] is not like that; therefore, it must be designated as "water. The remaining points regarding the objection and resolution concerning the definition are to be understood from the section on earth (*pṛthivī-adhikāra*). In this way, the sentence "due to the connection with the property of being water" should be applied as before, both for the determination of the meaning of the word and for the purpose of refuting the claim that capacity (*śakti*) is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*).

Previously, it was stated that all nine substances—beginning with earth—possess the nature of an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), that they possess the quality of being a substance (*guṇatva*), and that earth, water, and the self (*ātman*) possess fourteen qualities. Regarding this, [the author] explains: "Those in which form, taste, touch, viscidity, natural fluidity, and so forth, up to mental impression (*saṃskāra*), exist are 'possessors thereof' (*tadvatyaḥ*). What among these is the inherent cause for the production of what? By which qualities are they possessed of qualities? Which are the fourteen qualities? Or what is the definition consisting of those qualities? [The answer follows: [They are the possessors of those qualities] beginning with form, taste, touch, viscidity, and natural fluidity, and ending with mental impression.

“*And these [are] as before*” means they are established in the section concerning the assignment of qualities (*guṇaviniveśa*). For instance, in the *Vaiśeṣika Sūtra* (2.1.2), water is established as having five qualifiers: “Water possesses color, taste, and touch; it is liquid and viscous. Since these [qualifiers] distinguish it from others due to their uniqueness, the author says, “*The color, taste, and touch are exclusively white, sweet, and cold,*” in order to demonstrate this uniqueness. Although these are expressed by general terms in the sūtra, they are [specifically] indicated by implication. For instance, in water, the color is exclusively white and non-luminous, the taste is exclusively sweet, and the touch is exclusively cold.

Likewise, viscidity exists only in water, and natural fluidity exists only in water; thus, these qualities possess a unique (asādhāraṇa) character. "Natural" (sāṃsiddhika) means independent of conjunction with fire, but it is not accidental; rather, in an effect it is preceded by the qualities of its causes, and in atoms it is eternal. Number and the other qualities are to be explained as before.

Thus, when a doubt arises regarding the perception of unity or plurality in that which is characterized by its defining marks (*lakṣaṇa*), this statement—“But they, as before, are of two kinds”—is to be explained for the purpose of resolving that doubt, for the purpose of establishing that the generality of water (*aptva-sāmānya*) is the locus of difference, and for the purpose of demonstrating the seed [of the universe] so as to refute the monist (*advaitavādin*) who does not perceive the difference between one body of water and another. [The monist argues that] upon the destruction of all effect-substances (*kāryadravya*) in the state of dissolution (*pralaya*), there would be no re-origination at the beginning of creation, because it is impossible for an entity (*bhāva*) to arise from non-existence (*abhāva*). Just as the earth, being of the nature of atoms (*paramāṇu*), is eternal, while that which is characterized as an effect is non-eternal, so too is water; thus he says, “Because of the state of being eternal and non-eternal. By this form—namely, through eternity and non-eternity—he shows the diversity (*vaidharmya*) of the internal subdivisions, indicating that their twofold nature consists in these two aspects. Furthermore, although effects are infinite, they should be known to be of three kinds. He asks, “In what form? and replies: that which has the designations “body,” “organ,” and “object” is described as such.

Since the general definition of the body has already been stated, its origin alone is now described: "The body is indeed non-womb-born (*ayonija*). This means it is not produced from the union of semen and blood. Furthermore, it is well known from scripture that it arises in the world of Varuṇa from aqueous atoms accompanied by a specific merit (*dharma*). Now, since an aqueous body—by virtue of being a substratum for fluidity—is not fit for specific enjoyment, he says: "It is capable of enjoyment due to the support of earthly parts. For thus, the aqueous parts are the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), their conjunctions are the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and the earthly parts are the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). The same applies to the fiery and the airy [bodies].

But is this not incorrect? For it is heard that the body is composed of the five elements (*pāñcabhautika*). Thus it is said: "It is composed of the five elements because of [the presence of] odor, moisture, digestion, structural integration, and the provision of space" (Nyāya Sūtra 3.1.31).

The claim that the body is composed of the five elements (*pāñcabhautika*)—earth being the cause of the perception of odor, water of moisture, fire of digestion, air of structural arrangement (*vyūha*), and space by virtue of providing room—is incorrect. This is because we do not observe that things belonging to different classes (*vibhinnajātīya*) can function as inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) for the production of a single substance. Furthermore, a body is not perceived as inhering in parts belonging to different classes. If all five were indeed inherent causes, then among these, which part would be the earthen one and which the watery, fiery, or airy? One would expect to perceive the body as inhering in those [specific] parts; however, this is not the case. Moreover, since the inherent causes possess diverse qualities, there would necessarily be a corresponding diversity in the effect. If this were so, then in an earthen part of the body, there would be one of the various colors such as white, and the touch would be produced by heating (*pākaja*). In a watery part, there would be only white color and cold touch. In a fiery part, there would be brilliant color and hot touch. In an airy part, there would be a touch that is neither hot nor cold and not produced by heating. Consequently, because it is composed of parts with diverse characteristics, the body would be perceived as possessing diversity; yet it is not so perceived. Therefore, this [theory] is untenable.

Now, even the constituent part (*avayava*) may be initiated by multiple elements; for instance, a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is initiated by two atoms—one earthy and one watery, then again by one watery and one fiery, and likewise by one fiery and one airy. Similarly, [dyads] are initiated by the air-tanmātra and the sound-tanmātra. And if it is accepted that these produced dyads initiate a body through the process of triads (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth, then the production of color (*rūpa*) and the other qualities would not occur. For according to the sūtra, "And qualities initiate another quality" (VS 1.1.10), it is stated that multiple qualities are the initiators of a [single] quality. This being the case, in a dyad initiated by an earthy and a watery atom, there would be no production of odor (*gandha*), because that [earthly quality] alone, being singular, lacks the capacity to produce [a new quality]. Likewise, in a dyad initiated by a watery and a fiery atom, there would be no taste (*rasa*). Similarly, in a dyad initiated by a fiery and an airy atom, there would be an absence of color (*rūpa*). Likewise, in a dyad initiated by the air-tanmātra and the sound-tanmātra, there would be an absence of touch (*sparśa*). Thus, since odor, taste, color, and touch are absent in the dyads, they would also be absent in their effects (the triads), and consequently, their absence in the body would follow as a logical consequence.

And this [argument] is the same even in the case of those consisting of two elements and so forth. To explain: in a body composed of earth and water, there would be no production of odor; in one composed of earth and fire, there would be no production of odor or taste; in a body composed of earth and air, there would be no production of odor, taste, or color; and likewise, in one composed of earth and ether, there would be no production of the four [qualities].

Nor is space the initiator of a substance, because it is formless (*amūrta*). For it is observed that only a substance possessing form—that is, one possessing touch—is an initiator of another substance. In this same way, the refutation should be inferred regarding atoms and the like as well, insofar as they initiate [effects] through the assistance of other factors.

Likewise, since the commencement of the three [elements] beginning with earth, as well as the four, is asserted, and the causality of all five is accepted, the state of being composed of the five elements (*pāñcabhautikatva*) is thus intended. Furthermore, it is held that only one [element] is the inherent cause (*samavāyin*). For in an earthly body, the earthly element is the inherent cause; in another [body], such as a watery one, it is the other element. Moreover, the perception of moisture in an earthly body occurs through the relation of inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*). As for heating (*pāka*), it arises from contact with internal fire, and that [fire] is never perceived by the sense organ within the body. Rather, it is postulated that when the previous body ceases, a new body is commenced by means of those qualities produced by heating (*pākaja*) which have manifested as distinct qualities. "Configuration" (*vyūha*), however, is a specific arrangement of parts; it certainly does not result from air alone. And the property of providing space belongs only to the absence of corporeal substances, so it is not a mark (*liṅga*) of ether (*ākāśa*); enough of this.

In order to define the essential nature of the sense organs (*indriya*), he says: “And the sense organ is that which manifests taste” (*indriyañca rasavyañjakam*). The perception of taste is the effect of an instrument (*karaṇa*), because it is an action (*kriyā*); whatever is an action is the effect of an instrument, just like the action of cutting, and this [perception] is likewise an action; therefore, it is the effect of an instrument. And that instrument which brings about the perception of taste must be composed of water (*āpya*), because among color, taste, and so forth, it invariably manifests taste. Whatever invariably manifests taste among color and the rest is observed to be composed of water, such as the water within the mouth; and this [organ] is likewise; therefore, it is composed of water. One might object that since the grasping of even *rasatva* (taste-ness) and other qualities is possible through the operation of the tongue, the reason would be inconclusive (*asambhavitva*); hence the phrase “among color and the rest. For instance, the perception of taste in sweetmeats and the like is not perceived by one whose throat is parched. However, when water is present, there is the perception of taste alone among color and the rest; thus, the reason exists in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*). Since this is not possible in what is not composed of water, there is exclusion from the contrary instances (*vipakṣa*). It should be understood that this [reason] also serves to differentiate [the organ] from others due to its uniqueness (*asādhāraṇatva*).

Now, why is it that among the substances such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth, only a specific substance is invariably the manifestor of taste (*rasa*), and [why] the sense organ [is so]? He says: "The gustatory organ (*rasana*) is composed of water-particles that have begun their existence [as a compound] with other particles not being overwhelmed [by them], even when slightly mixed. Thus, it is the manifestor of taste alone. Others, however, say it is composed of pure water-particles that are not mixed with and not overwhelmed by other particles. [As for the statement] "Water is the primary cause (*prakṛti*) in the cognition of taste because of its abundance and its possession of taste" (*Vaiśeṣika Sūtra*); the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on this sūtra is as follows:

"Because of the preponderance [of water]" (bhūyastvāt). When there is a conjunction of many constituent parts that depend upon unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) for the perception of taste, and there is a slight contact with other constituent parts, the production of a specific quality is taught. For this very reason, the suppression of other constituent parts is untenable; it is because the water-parts are more numerous and the others are fewer. Furthermore, "possessing taste" (*rasavattva*) refers to the excellence of taste in the gustatory faculty. Since the meaning was not explicitly stated by the general term, the sense organ is known as "taste-cognition" (*rasajñāna*), meaning "that by which taste is known. When that [cognition] is produced, water is the material cause (*prakṛti*) due to its preponderance, acting as the manifesting efficient cause (*nimitta*). Therefore, this alone is the sense organ, specifically that which invariably manifests taste among [the qualities] such as color-form (*rūpa*).

Alternatively, since the restriction of the effect cannot occur without the restriction of the cause, he asks: by what rule does the apprehension of taste arise specifically from the gustatory faculty? He says: "The cognition [of taste] arises due to the causes of abundance and possession of flavor. Here, the *prakṛti* (material cause) is the gustatory faculty. For instance, even though there is no difference in the nature of the contact (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), the fact that the perception of taste occurs only in a restricted manner would otherwise be inexplicable; thus, a restrictive cause is known. Since no other [cause] is possible, it is postulated that this cause is the excellence and abundance of the flavor.

Alternatively, it is known through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the perception of taste (*rasopalambha*), since no other cause is possible; thus he says "abundance" (*bhūyastva*) to explain what the cause of the excellence of taste is. For even though there is no difference in their being composed of the watery element (*āpyatva*), it is only taste that attains excellence and not color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth; therefore, abundance is the cause for the production of a specific quality. And that [abundance] is due to the power of unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*). Furthermore, unseen merit/demerit serves as the cause for this specific determination.

He defines the object (*viṣaya*). An object is that which is distinct from the body and the sense organs, and is composed through the process beginning with binary atoms (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth; for it is by its very nature as an object that it provides assistance. It consists, however, of rivers, oceans, hailstones, and the like.

“Fire is that which is connected with the quality of luminosity (*tejas*). It possesses color, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, fluidity, and faculty (*saṃskāra*). Their establishment is as before. Its color is white and brilliant; its touch is exclusively hot; its fluidity is occasional (*naimittika*); and its number and other qualities are as previously described.”

“That too is twofold, because of the existence of atoms and effects. The effect consists of the triad beginning with the body. The body is exclusively non-womb-born (*ayonija*); it arises from atoms accompanied by a specific merit (*dharma*) in the world of the Sun (*ādityaloka*). And through the support of earthly particles (*pārthivāvayava*), it becomes capable of experience (*upabhoga*). The sense organ is the eye; it is composed of light-particles (*tejo’vayava*) that are not overwhelmed by other particles, and it manifests color-form for all living beings. The object, characterized as such, is fourfold: terrestrial, celestial, digestive, and mineral. Among these, the terrestrial originates from wood-fuel, has the nature of upward flaming, and is capable of cooking, sweating, and so forth. The celestial has water as its fuel, such as solar and lightning fire. The digestive is capable of transforming consumed food into the state of chyle (*rasa*) and so on. The mineral is gold and the like. In that regard, the perception of taste and so forth occurs through inherence in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*). <PDhS>

Now, for the purpose of examining the definition of fire (*tejas*) following its enumeration, he states the section beginning with: “Because of its connection with *tejastva*,” and so forth. The connection with *tejastva*—that is, inherence (*samavāya*) characterized by *tejastva*—is the definition. To explain: fire is distinct from other things because of its connection with *tejastva*. Those things which are not distinct [from others] do not possess a connection with *tejastva*, such as earth (*kṣiti*) and the rest; but fire is not like that, therefore it is distinct from others. Alternatively, a linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) is being established. Furthermore, this should be explained as before, both for the purpose of making known that the referent of the word "fire" possesses a universal (*sāmānya*), and for the purpose of negating a supersensible power (*atīndriya-śakti*).

And the statement concerning color (*rūpa*) and so forth is for the purpose of demonstrating [fire's] nature as an inherent cause (*samavāyin*) and its possession of qualities. For it is said: "that which possesses those [qualities], beginning with color and ending with mental disposition (*saṃskāra*), is 'possessing them'. "Their establishment is as before" means that just as color and the other specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) were established in the section on Earth under the heading "The Arrangement of Qualities," so too are they here. Likewise, by the aphorism "Fire possesses color and touch" (VS 2.1.3), two specific qualities are mentioned. Since these two are unique, they serve to differentiate fire from others; thus he states their uniqueness: "Color is white and luminous," meaning it has the nature of illuminating. "Touch is exclusively hot," meaning there is no other kind of touch. "And fluidity is adventitious" (*naimittika*). "Number and the rest are as before" means that fluidity is mentioned by the aphorism: "In tin, lead, iron, silver, and gold—which are fiery—the fluidity produced by contact with fire is common to water" (VS 2.1.7).

When doubt arises regarding the perceived unity or multiplicity of that which is characterized by its characteristics, this statement—“That too is of two kinds,” as explained previously—should be interpreted for the purpose of dispelling that doubt, for the refutation of the proponents of non-duality (*advaitavādin*), for the establishment of the universal (*sāmānya*), and for the demonstration of the existence of the seed [of the universe]. To explain: it is not only earth and water that are of two kinds; what then? This [fire] also. For fire, too, is of two kinds. By what form? He says: “Because of its existence as both atom and effect. That which has the nature of an atom (*paramāṇu*) is eternal, while that which has the nature of an effect is non-eternal. Lest there be a lack of full comprehension due to the infinity of effects, he says: “The effect consists of the triad beginning with the body. It is to be known in the form of body, sense-organ, and object; such is the internal distinction (*avāntaravaidharmya*).

Since the general definition of the body has already been stated, its origin alone is now described: "The body is indeed non-uterine (*ayonija*). For that which is non-uterine does not depend upon the union of semen and blood. [It arises] "from atoms accompanied by a specific merit (*dharma*). Here, the fiery atoms (*taijasa-paramāṇu*) are the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*), their conjunctions are the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*), and the earthly and other constituent parts are the instrumental causes (*nimitta-kāraṇa*). This is established regarding the world of the sun through scripture (*āgama*). Now, if the composite whole of fire were momentary, then what is produced from it would not generate specific experiences; therefore, he says: "And through the support of earthly constituent parts, it is capable of experience. Furthermore, since that body possesses the general characteristics [of a body] and is composed of fiery constituent parts, its specific definition (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) should be understood as being distinguished from others.

Now, for the purpose of defining the essential nature of the sense-faculties (*indriya*), he says: "The sense-faculty is that which manifests color for all living beings. The apprehension of color is the effect of an instrument (*karaṇa*), because it is an action (*kriyā*). Whatever is an action is the effect of an instrument, just as the action of cutting is; and this [apprehension] is an action; therefore, it is the effect of an instrument. That instrument which brings about the apprehension of color is the eye (*cakṣus*). And that [eye] is composed of light (*taijasa*), because among color and the other qualities, it invariably manifests color. Whatever invariably manifests color among color and the others is composed of light, just like a lamp; and since the eye invariably manifests color among color and the others, it is therefore composed of light. For if one were to say simply that the eye is the manifestor of color because it is observed to illuminate substances possessing color and so forth, its being an *invariable* manifestor of color would not be established. Therefore, the phrase "among color and the others" is used. What is intended is its invariable manifestation of color specifically among color, taste, smell, and touch.

Now, since the eye is composed of light (*taijasa*), it might be argued that it should also manifest heat, just as it manifests color, because it is luminous and because there is no distinction in its *saṃyuktasamavāya* (inherence in what is conjoined) with respect to them, and because there is no other specific cause [to differentiate]. To this he says: "The eye is produced by light-particles that are not overwhelmed by other constituent parts. Therefore, it is a manifester of color alone. For instance, the eye is produced by light-particles that are conjoined with only a small amount of earthy particles and are not overwhelmed [by them]; thus, it is a manifester of color alone.

Now, what is the proof for such a specific commencement? It is the restriction of the effect. For instance, among color-form (*rūpa*) and the other objects, it is observed that from the operation of the eye, there is the apprehension of color-form alone. And that [apprehension] would not occur without a restriction of causes; thus, since nothing else is possible, a specific production is the cause here. And that [specific production] arises from the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) which brings about the apprehension of color-form, because that [unseen merit] is the cause for the determination of things.

"Because of its abundance and because it possesses color (*rūpavattva*), fire (*tejas*) is the primary cause (*prakṛti*) for the cognition of color" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra). The commentary (*bhāṣya*) on this sūtra is as follows: "That by which color is known is the cognition of color, namely the eye; in the production of that [cognition], fire is the primary cause due to its abundance. Therefore, the sense organ is the illuminator of color alone. Abundance (*bhūyastva*) refers to the state of being a constituent of many particles of fire, which—when assisted by a specific unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*)—act as the originators [of the sense organ] even when there is some contact with other [earthly] particles. Alternatively, "cognition of color" means the knowledge (*jñapti*) of color; among the objects such as color and so forth, the eye is the cause of that very [knowledge]. Why? He says: "Because of its abundance and because it possesses color, as previously explained. By "possessing color," an excellence of color (*rūpotkarṣa*) is intended. Otherwise, since it is composed of fire (*taijasa*), it might also be thought to possess the quality of hot touch (*uṣṇasparśavattva*); thus, the specific mention [of color] would be purposeless. Alternatively, the excellence of color is known from the fact that among color and the other qualities, it is color alone that is perceived, which would otherwise be inexplicable. From what does this [excellence] arise? He says: "From its abundance, as described above."

Now, since the eye possesses magnitude (*mahattva*) and consists of multiple substances (*anekadravyatva*), why is it not perceived by the sense organ? It is because, like a lamp, it lacks a specific quality of color (*rūpa-viśeṣa*); for it is only where a colored substance possesses such a quality that it is perceived through both sight and touch. That specific quality of color, by whose presence there is perception of color in certain objects, and by whose absence there is non-perception even of something large and composed of multiple substances, is the property of color known as *udbhava* (manifestation), which acts as a specific auxiliary cause (*sahakāriviśeṣa*). Indeed, it is observed that fire situated in water is not apprehended despite its magnitude and being composed of multiple substances, due to the absence of this specific quality of color. Conversely, a lamp with manifested color is apprehended even in the dark. For the creation of entities is for the purpose of experience (*upabhoga*). If color were manifested, then even in the dark, the eye would perceive it, and thus the experience of wicked beings would be impossible. Therefore, by the power of unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) that brings about such experience, Prajāpati produced the eye with unmanifested color. Similarly, if the hot touch were manifested, then when many eyes converge upon a pleasing object such as a dancer during the summer season, there would be a burning sensation—as if from excessively hot rays of the sun. Thus, by the power of unseen merit/demerit alone, the non-manifestation of the hot touch is also postulated.

In order to define the nature of the object (*viṣaya*), he says: "The definition of the object" means the essential nature of the object. "Fourfold" means in what form? He says: "Terrestrial, celestial, digestive, and mineral. This is the internal distinction of the object, which is differentiated from the body and the sense organs by its definition as an object. Among these, "terrestrial" (*bhauma*) is that which exists on the earth. It is distinguished from other types of fuel because it originates—meaning it arises—from wood alone as its fuel; thus, it is characterized by its specific fuel. Furthermore, it is distinguished from others by its nature of flaming upwards, meaning it has the inherent property of burning upwards. This is indeed distinct from the other [types of fire] as well. This is for the purpose of refuting the view that "only that which performs a causal function (*arthakriyākārin*) is ultimately real," even if one were to accept reality through a connection with existence (*sattā*), by way of a concessive argument (*abhyupagamavāda*). And the determination of its action consists in its capacity for cooking, sweating, and so forth. He says "water-fueled" (*abindhana*) to distinguish the celestial from its specific fuel: water is its fuel, but it is not water itself. That is solar, meaning connected to the sun. By the word "etcetera" in "lightning etc.," the falling of meteors and so forth are included. Similarly, "digestive" (*udarya*) is that which exists in the stomach. And that is for the purpose of transforming the consumed food into chyle and so forth—that is, for the transformation into chyle, waste, and the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). And "transformation" consists in the cessation of the previous color and other qualities in the atoms, followed by the commencement of substances such as chyle through the process of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) produced by heating (*pākaja*); we shall explain this in the section on the production of qualities born of heating. "And mineral" (*ākaraja*) means gold and so forth, born from a mine (*ākara*). By the inclusion of "etcetera," tin, lead, iron, and silver are also included.

What is the proof for their being composed of light (*taijasa*)? It is scripture (*āgama*). And thus it is said: "Gold is the first offspring of fire; the sky belongs to Viṣṇu, and cows are the daughters of the Sun."

Now, [the opponent argues] that what is born from fire is not of the same genus as it; thus, because this is inconclusive (*anekānta*), it is not a valid proof. For instance, smoke and the like, though born from fire, are not of the same genus as it. That is incorrect. Because the conventional usage of the term "offspring" (*apatya*) is observed only with reference to being of the same genus. To explain: the usage of "offspring" is not seen for every mere effect. What then? It is seen for that which is of the same genus, as in the case of "human offspring. [Objection: If this is so, since the usage of "offspring" is observed only among sentient beings, its application to an insentient thing is untenable. [Reply: No. Since fire has a sentient presiding deity (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*), it is tenable in relation to that [deity]. Alternatively, although the effects of fire are manifold, by specifying a particular one—namely, "gold is the offspring of fire"—one obtains the status of being of the same genus. If one intended to speak without such specification, one would have said, "another effect is the offspring. Or, the specific [nature] may be understood from another scripture (*āgama*); enough of this. Furthermore, because gold is mentioned first, silver and other metals are also understood to be the offspring of fire; otherwise, the qualification "first" would be meaningless. This being the case, the inference that gold and the like are earthy (*pārthiva*) because they are substrates of gravity is invalid, as it is sublated by scripture. For the operation of inference is prohibited regarding matters established by scripture.

Now, if these [substances] are composed of light (*taijasa*), how then is there the perception of taste and so forth? It is through *saṃyuktasamavāya* (inherence in that which is conjoined). For instance, an earthly substance is conjoined with gold and the like; therein, tastes and other qualities inhering [in that substance] are perceived. Thus he says: "In that case, the perception of taste and so forth occurs through *saṃyuktasamavāya*. If it is asked, "Then let liquidity (*dravatva*) also be thus [earthly]; for what purpose is its status as a quality of light postulated?", we say: No. Because a distinction from the earthly is observed. For instance, an earthly substance such as lac is seen to turn into ash through contact with fire. In gold and the like, however, even through an intense excess of contact with fire, only liquidity persists. Furthermore, the non-appearance of hot touch here is due to *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit).

“Air is that which is connected with the nature of air (*vāyutva*). It possesses touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and impression (*saṃskāra*). Its touch is established as being neither hot nor cold and as not produced by heat (*apākaja*), because of its inclusion among the qualities [of air]. The seven [qualities] beginning with number are established by the statement ‘[Air is] imperceptible among those things lacking color. Impression is established by the statement ‘the motion of grass. This [air] is of two kinds, because it exists as both atoms and effects. Among these, that characterized as an effect is fourfold: body, sense organ, object, and vital breath (*prāṇa*). Among these, the body is exclusively non-womb-born (*ayonija*); it arises from air-atoms accompanied by a specific merit (*dharma*) in the world of the Maruts, and it becomes capable of experience through the support of earth-particles. The sense organ is the tactile organ (*tvagindriya*), which pervades the entire body; it is composed of air-particles that are not overcome by earth and the other elements, and it is the perceiver of touch for all living beings. The object, however, is the substratum of the perceived touch; it is characterized by the marks of touch, sound, support, and trembling; its nature is horizontal movement; and it is capable of propelling and supporting clouds and so forth. Although it is imperceptible, its plurality is inferred by its coalescence (*saṃmūrchana*). Coalescence, moreover, is inferred by the upward movement of two air-masses possessing equal velocity and moving in opposite directions, provided they possess parts. That [coalescence] is also inferred by the upward movement of grass and similar objects. The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is one within the body, being the cause of the propulsion of chyle, waste, and the bodily constituents; though single, it receives the designations of *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and so on, due to the difference in its functions.”

Now follows the section beginning with "Because of its connection with the universal *vāyutva* (*vāyutvābhisambandhāt*)" for the purpose of defining and examining air, which has already been mentioned. "Air" is the designation of the object to be defined (*lakṣya*), and "because of its connection with the universal *vāyutva*" is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*). The "connection with *vāyutva*" means inherence (*samavāya*) as characterized by *vāyutva*. For inherence alone would be an over-extensive definition; therefore, the term "*vāyutva*" is included. Furthermore, since *vāyutva* could not be a prover if it were unconnected [to the subject] due to lacking the property of being a predicate of the subject (*apakṣadharmatā*), the term "connection" (*abhisambandha*) is used to indicate that it is a predicate of the subject. Thus, air is distinguished from others because of its connection with *vāyutva*; for those things which are not distinguished [from others] are not connected with *vāyutva*, such as earth and so forth, whereas air is not unconnected with *vāyutva*, and therefore it is distinguished from others. Alternatively, conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is what is being proved. The remaining points regarding the refutation and resolution of objections to the definition should be understood from the section on Earth (*pṛthivī-adhikāra*). Likewise, the sentence should be explained as before in order to demonstrate that the word "air" denotes a general category and to refute the notion of supersensible power (*atīndriya-śakti*).

The statement concerning touch (*sparśa*) and the other qualities is intended to demonstrate that [air] possesses inherence (*samavāyitva*) and quality-possessingness (*guṇavattva*). That which has [qualities] beginning with touch and ending with mental disposition (*saṃskāra*) is called "that which possesses them" (*tadvān*). Because touch is common to many substances and thus lacks the capacity to differentiate air from others, its unique characteristic is stated: "Its touch, while being neither hot nor cold, is not produced by heating" (*sparśo 'syānuṣṇāśītatve satyapākajaḥ*). The term "not hot" excludes hot touch; "not cold" excludes cold touch; and "not produced by heating" distinguishes it from the earthy [touch]. Furthermore, this is established in the second chapter on the classification of qualities by the aphorism: "Air possesses touch" (*vāyuḥ sparśavān*, Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.1.4).

And here, although the term "possessing touch" (*sparśavān*) is a general one, by implication this specific quality is intended: "possessing a touch that is neither hot nor cold and not produced by heat. By the sūtra, "Because they are not visible among those things lacking color" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 4.1.12), number and the other qualities are established.

For instance, since visual [perceptions] occur in substances possessing specific color-form (*rūpa*) while non-visual [perceptions] occur in their opposites, another sūtra has indeed already stated the existence of number and the other qualities even in formless (*arūpin*) entities. Thus, the prohibition [in the present sūtra] merely means that number and the rest, when inhering in formless things, simply do not become objects of visual perception. Similarly, by the statement "because of the mention of the action of grass" (*tṛṇakarmavacanāt*), he shows the sūtra: "Action arises in grass from conjunction with wind" (*vāyusaṃyogāttṛṇe karma*, Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.1.14).

Furthermore, since the conjunction with wind is a dependent cause for the production of the motion of grass, and since [other causes such as] effort are absent, it follows that velocity is the dependent cause; thus, the existence of *saṃskāra* (disposition/impulse) is established.

Likewise, because the generality of "air-ness" (*vāyutva-sāmānya*) is the substratum of its particulars, there arises a doubt regarding whether that which is characterized by a definition capable of establishing it is one or many. To dispel that doubt, to refute the proponents of non-duality (*advaitavādin*), and to demonstrate the actual existence of the seed [of the universal], the statement is made: "And this [air] is of two kinds, due to its existence as atoms and as effects. For thus, that which has the nature of an atom is eternal, whereas that which has the nature of an effect is non-eternal.

He shows the internal difference [between the types of evidence] by stating "characterized as an effect" (*kāryalakṣaṇaḥ*), meaning it has the nature of an effect. He asks, "In how many ways? and answers, "It is fourfold," namely: "the body, the sense organs, the objects, and the vital breath."

He states the origin of the body: "The body is indeed non-womb-born (*ayonija*). And "non-womb-born" means produced without depending on the union of semen and blood. [It arises] "from wind-atom-paramāṇus accompanied by a specific merit (*dharma*). For instance, the wind-atoms are the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), their conjunctions are the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and earth and so forth are the instrumental causes (*nimittakāraṇa*). This is established by scripture (*āgama*) as being "in the world of the Maruts. Now, since wind is characterized by horizontal movement and is momentary (*kṣaṇika*), a body composed of it would not be capable of producing experience; therefore, he says: "And through the support of earthly parts, it is capable of experience."

To determine the essential nature of the sense organs (*indriya*), he says: "The sense organ [of touch] is that which perceives touch for all living beings. To explain: the perception of touch is the effect of an instrument (*karaṇa*), because it is an action (*kriyā*). Whatever is an action is the effect of an instrument, just as the act of cutting is; and this [perception of touch] is an action; therefore, it is the effect of an instrument. Whatever instrument brings about the perception of touch must be composed of air (*vāyavīya*), because it invariably manifests touch among [the qualities] such as color-form (*rūpa*) and so on. Whatever invariably manifests touch among color-form and the rest is observed to be composed of air, just like the wind from a fan; and the tactile sense-organ (*tvagindriya*) invariably manifests touch among color-form and the rest; therefore, it is composed of air. One might object that since the tactile sense-organ is observed to manifest substances possessing touch and so forth, its status as an "invariable manifester of touch" would be unestablished. To address this, the qualification "among color-form and the rest" is added. In the case of the wind from a fan, although color-form and other qualities are absent when it manifests the touch residing therein, the qualification still holds true because of the actual existence of its capacity to manifest touches such as coldness.

Alternatively, since there is no difference in their being composed of air (*vāyavīyatva*), why is it that only a certain [organ] manifests touch? It is the sense-organ of the skin (*tvagindriya*). To this he says: "It is produced by aerial elements that are not overwhelmed by earth and the other [elements], which are assisted by specific unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*), and which are either pure or slightly mixed with other constituent parts. Therefore, the sense-organ is the manifestor of touch alone. And that [organ] is known to be "pervading the body" because touch is perceived everywhere. Its designation is "the sense-organ of the skin" (*tvagindriya*). "Skin" (*tvak*) refers to the dermis that envelops the body; the sense-organ located therein is called "the sense-organ of the skin" by metaphorical usage.

Now, what is the proof for the specific production of the tactile faculty (*tvagindriya*)? It is the restriction of the effect. Thus, among color-form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory objects], the restriction of the cause is known through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the perception of touch alone. And since no other [cause] is possible, it is postulated that this [restriction] is the instrumental cause for its specific production.

And the commentary on this sūtra is as follows: "Because of its preponderance and because it possesses touch, air (*vāyu*) is the material cause (*prakṛti*) for the cognition of touch" (the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra is lost here). "The cognition of touch" (*sparśajñāna*) refers to the sense organ (*indriya*), since touch is cognized by means of it. Regarding that which is to be produced, air is the material cause (*prakṛti*); this is due to the causal factor of its preponderance (*bhūyastva*). Therefore, that very sense organ is the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) of touch alone among [the qualities] such as color and so forth. Regarding the term "because of its preponderance" (*bhūyastvāt*): it is the state of being a producer (*ārambhakatva*) belonging to a majority of air-particles (*vāyvavayava*)—which are assisted by specific unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*)—due to their slight contact with other particles.

Alternatively, cognition (*jñapti*) regarding touch is knowledge (*jñāna*); among those very elements, such as form and so forth, air (*vāyu*) is the primary nature or the cause. Why? He says: "Because of its predominance (*bhūyastva*), because it is specifically characterized (*vyākṛta*), and because it possesses touch (*sparśavattva*). And by "possessing touch," what is intended is the excellence of touch (*sparśotkarṣa*). Alternatively, the excellence of touch is known through the impossibility of perceiving touch otherwise; he asks, "From what does this arise? and replies, "From the causal factor of predominance (*bhūyastva-nimitta*)."

Is this not all incoherent, since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of air? No; because it is apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). For it is observed that from the operation of the sense of touch, an immediate cognition arises, such as: "the wind blows," "the wind is cold," or "the wind is hot. Nor does this arise subsequent to the recollection of the relationship between a mark and the marked (*liṅga-liṅgi-sambandha*) and the resulting inferential consideration (*parāmarśa*); thus, it is not born of inference. Since it arises even without verbal testimony, it is not verbal (*śābda*). Because it conforms to the functioning of a sense faculty, it is produced by the senses (*indriya-ja*). And whatever cognition is immediate is direct perception.

Now, as for the objection that this contradicts the sūtra: “A substance is perceptible because of its magnitude (*mahattva*), its being composed of multiple substances (*anekadravyavattva*), and a particularity of color (*rūpaviśeṣa*)” (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 4.1.6)—it is not so, because the meaning of the sūtra has not been understood. And thus is the meaning of the sūtra: it should be known that when direct perception (*aparokṣajñāna*) exists, the definition consists of all these factors collectively and individually. For wherever there is direct perception, these factors—both collectively and individually—act as causes. Thus, the self (*ātman*) is perceptible by virtue of its magnitude alone; wind (*vāyu*), however, [is perceptible] by virtue of both its magnitude and its being composed of multiple substances. And in cases where a cognition of a substance occurs through both sight and touch, the definition consists of all [the factors] collectively. As for their relative predominance, it should be accepted according to what is observed. For instance, at night, fire is perceived even from a distance due to the excellence of its color (*rūpa*). Although mountains and the like possess magnitude and are composed of multiple substances, they are not perceived [at night]; thus, color has predominance. Likewise, when light is present, mountains and the like are perceived even from a distance. However, one should consider that magnitude has only minor predominance in such cases.

Now, where there is tactile perception (*spārśana-pratyakṣatva*), the operation of vision (*darśana*) is also observed, as in the case of the word "flood" (*ogha*) and so forth; and since numbers and other such qualities are perceptible, the same should apply here as well. But this is not the case; therefore, only touch itself is perceived, just like heat in fire situated in water. Just as in the case of fire situated in water, even though the substratum is not perceived, there is the apprehension of heat, so too here, even though the substratum is not perceived, there is the apprehension of touch alone.

This is not so. Since color (*rūpa*) is unmanifest (*anudbhūta*) in light residing within water, it is logical that only touch (*sparśa*) is perceptible. For wherever the manifestation of color is the cause of perception, there it must necessarily be grasped by the eye as well, and qualities such as number (*saṃkhyā*) and the rest are perceived. However, when color is unmanifest, there is no such apprehension. Furthermore, it is observed in the case of air (*vāyu*) that a specific color is not the cause of perceptibility; thus, it is not grasped by the eye. Therefore, it is logical that number and the other qualities are not perceived [in water].

If it is argued that, in the absence of a specific quality of color (*rūpa-viśeṣa*), there would necessarily be non-perceptibility, we say no; because this is contradicted by the case of the self (*ātman*). For instance, although the self lacks a specific quality of color, it is perceptible to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Furthermore, qualities such as number (*saṃkhyā*) and so forth, though perceptible in general, are not perceptible with respect to the self precisely because they lack a specific quality of color.

Now, it is observed that the tactile perception of a substance occurs only when a specific color-form (*rūpa*) is present, as in the case of a jar and so forth. Furthermore, there is evidence for the fact that synthetic cognition (*anusandhānajñāna*) takes as its object a substance distinct from both color-form and touch, namely: "That very thing which I saw with my eyes, I now touch; or, that which I touched with my sense of touch, I now see. If it is argued that this [synthetic cognition] does not exist in the case of air, and therefore air has touch alone as its object—this is incorrect. For even in the absence of color-form, air is perceptible through tactile perception. If you say, "This is yet to be proven," we reply: No, because if what is already observed were to be proven, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). To explain: it has been stated that the immediate cognition of air arising from the operation of the sense of touch is observed to be produced through the presence and absence of the sense organ. If that were to be proven, then the visual and tactile perceptions of jars and other objects would likewise have to be proven. If you argue that this [cognition] is not to be proven because it conforms to the sense organs, then the same applies to air. Likewise, this synthetic cognition is possible in the case of jars and the like because they are perceivable by two senses; however, it is impossible in the case of air because it is perceivable by only one sense, and thus [you might claim] it is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). [But this is not so.]

Nor does the cognition of a jar and so forth have as its object something distinct from color and the rest merely because of synthesis (*anusandhāna*). What then? Because the cognition of a jar and so forth is of a different character (*vilakṣaṇa*), it has as its object an entity distinct from color and the rest; and in that case, synthesis also possesses validity. It is not the same with the cognitions "the wind blows" and "the wind is cold," which, because they are of a different character from the cognition of touch, must have as their object an entity distinct from that [touch]. Nor should it be said that this is an inferential cognition arising from the perception of touch, for there is an absence of the recollection of an inseparable relation (*avinābhāva-sambandha*) and so forth. To postulate the operation of the recollection of a relation even when it is not being experienced is improper, as it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the cognition of a jar and so forth is also inferential. Furthermore, since this cognition is co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the perception of wind, it has wind itself as its object.

Others, however, establish the perceptibility of air (*vāyu*) even by means of inference, thinking that an object, though perceived directly by oneself, must be established for another person through inference alone. Accordingly: "Air, which is the substrate of the touch perceived by us and others, is perceptible to the tactile sense-organ of us and others, because—while being distinct from that which has unmanifested color—it is the substrate of the touch perceived by us and others; whatever is, while being distinct from that which has unmanifested color, the substrate of the touch perceived by us and others, is perceptible to the tactile sense-organ of us and others, such as a jar or similar objects; and air is, while being distinct from that which has unmanifested color, the substrate of the touch perceived by us and others; therefore, it is perceptible to the tactile sense-organ of us and others."

[Objection: But in that case, would it not follow that all supersensible objects (atīndriya) are perceptible to people like us, by means of the logical reason "because they are knowable" (prameyatva)? [Reply: No, because this is sublated by the very cognition of another person. To explain: another person cognizes, "I have no cognition whose object is atoms (paramāṇu) and so forth. It is only when one possesses direct (aparokṣa) knowledge oneself that it is appropriate to employ an inference to communicate it to another. And such [direct knowledge] exists regarding air, but not regarding atoms and the like. Furthermore, if atoms and the like were objects of the senses of people like us, they would lose their nature as atoms, because we perceive the operation of our senses upon things endowed with magnitude (mahattva) and other such qualities.

Now, once the existence of air has been established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), [the author] says, "The object (*viṣaya*), however, is that which is the substratum of the perceived touch," in order to define its nature. It is described thus because it is both "perceived" (*upalabhyamāna*) and "the substratum of touch" (*sparśādhiṣṭhāna*). For those who maintain that air is imperceptible, the explanation is: "it is both this [air] and the perceived touch, and it is the substratum of that [touch]. In this context, since the treatise is commenced for the sake of instruction for people like us, the qualification "for people like us" (*asmadādi*) should also be understood. Furthermore, "perception" (*upalambha*) is intended here specifically as occurring through the sense organs; otherwise, since perception by other means of knowledge exists even in the case of the body and so forth, the definition of an object as "being the substratum of perceived touch" would be over-extensive (*vyabhicārin*). Thus, because it is the substratum of the touch perceived by the senses of people like us, it is distinguished from other things, or it should be designated as an "object."

Likewise, he states that air (*vāyu*), which is characterized by its objects, is not perceptible to the senses of people like us, but is rather to be understood through inference: "It has touch, sound, support, and motion as its marks" (*sparśa-śabda-dhṛti-kampa-liṅgaḥ*). That of which touch, sound, support, and motion are the marks is described thus. To explain: touch that is neither hot nor cold and is non-repellent must reside in something, because it is a quality (*guṇa*). Whatever is a quality is observed to be dependent on a substrate, just like color (*rūpa*) and so forth. And this [touch] is a quality; therefore, it is dependent. Its being a quality is established because, while possessing generality (*sāmānyavat*) and not being a substance (*adravyatva*), it is invariably imperceptible to the eye (*acākṣuṣapratyakṣatva*), just like taste (*rasa*). The inclusion of the term "invariably" (*niyamena*) is for the purpose of excluding [the fallacy], since imperceptibility to the eye exists in things like a jar (*ghaṭa*). Nevertheless, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in that generality such as "touch-ness" (*sparśatva*) is invariably imperceptible to the eye but is not a quality; hence the qualification "while possessing generality. Generality exists in the triad beginning with substances, so the term "invariably imperceptible to the eye" is used. Since "being invariably imperceptible to the eye while possessing generality" applies to air and the like, the phrase "not being a substance" is added. When this [reason] possesses the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), exists in one part of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), and is entirely excluded from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), it is a means of knowledge (*gamaka*) because its object is uncontradicted and it lacks a counter-argument (*asatpratipakṣatva*).

Now, let it be granted that there is "dependence" (*āśritatva*) for that which possesses a touch that is neither hot nor cold and is not produced by heating (*apākaja*). But what is the proof for its being "not produced by heating"? It is because of the absence of color and other qualities produced by heating (*pākaja-rūpādi-viyoga*). For instance, a touch produced by heating is observed in jars and the like to be accompanied by color and other qualities produced by heating; therefore, if this [wind] were also produced by heating, it would likewise be so. If it is argued that they are not perceived because they are unmanifest (*anudbhūtatva*) despite their existence, that is not correct; for they are absent elsewhere. Indeed, it is never observed that when a touch produced by heating is perceived, color and the rest are absolutely unperceived elsewhere. Furthermore, there is no proof for the existence of color and the rest here, which results in the impossibility of such an experience. Moreover, the assumption of non-manifestation is only tenable if there is actual existence. If it is asked what the proof is for their non-existence, it is simply absolute non-perception. For instance, since the substratum of the intended touch can exist without gravity (*gurutva*), color and the rest—which are invariably concomitant with it—are never perceived through any means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); thus, they do not exist. Likewise, since a touch produced by heating is observed to be concomitant with gravity, if this [wind] were also produced by heating, gravity would necessarily exist there. And if there were a connection with gravity, the holding up of leaves and such things would be impossible, because that [wind] too would be connected with gravity, leading to that same consequence. Nor is it possible for the substratum of a touch produced by heating to be devoid of gravity; therefore, it does not reside in earth, because it is distinct from the touch of earth. Nor does it reside in water or fire, because it is neither hot nor cold. Since it cannot exist elsewhere, that in which it resides is air (*vāyu*).

Likewise, the initial sound "śuka-śukā" (the sound *śuka*), which is inferred as continuous, has conjunction with a substance possessing touch (*sparśavat*) as its cause; because, while being different from sounds produced by disjunction (*vibhāga*) or sounds produced by sound, it is a sound (*śabdatvāt*). Whatever is a sound, while being different from sounds produced by disjunction or sounds produced by sound, has conjunction with a substance possessing touch as its cause—just like the sound produced by the conjunction of a drum and a stick—and this [sound] is likewise such; therefore, it possesses the aforementioned probandum (*sādhya*). [Objection: But since no distinction is perceived between this [sound] and a sound produced by disjunction, the qualification "while being different from that" (*tadanyatve sati*) is doubtful. [Reply: No. For it is observed that among things possessing color and other qualities (*rūpādimat*) and consisting of dense arrangements of parts, disjunction preceded by the disjunction of causes is the originator of sound; whereas the absence of such [disjunction] is a matter beyond dispute. Thus, [the initial sound] lacks the nature of being produced by disjunction (*vibhāgajatvābhāvāt*). Furthermore, if the sound "śuka-śukā" were produced by disjunction, its perception would not occur simultaneously with the trembling of branches and so forth. Yet such [simultaneity] is observed. Nor is it logical for the disjunction of wind from the branches to be the originator of the sound here, because it is impossible for it to be produced by the disjunction of causes. Therefore, the qualification "while being different from that" is indeed free from doubt.

Support (*dhṛti*) is the holding up; it is the staying of leaves and such things in the sky. And this is the effect of conjunction with a substance possessing touch, because it is a support in the absence of effort and other such causes. Whatever is a support in the absence of effort and other such causes is the effect of conjunction with a substance possessing touch, just as water contained in a vessel; and this [staying of leaves] is likewise; therefore, it is the effect of conjunction with a substance possessing touch.

Regarding the "convergence" (*saṃmūrcchana*) of birds that have gathered together, he says: "Convergence, moreover, [occurs] between two winds of equal velocity that possess contrary directional actions. For convergence is a coming together (*sannipāta*), which is a connection. Between what two? "Between two winds. Of what specific nature? He says: "Of equal velocity. Those two whose velocity—that is, their speed—is equal are "of equal velocity. Otherwise, if one had less velocity, there would be no convergence due to being overwhelmed by the stronger one. Likewise, he states that there is no convergence between those with the same directional action: "[between those] possessing contrary directional actions. Those two whose direction and action are contrary are "possessing contrary directional actions. For instance, there is a contradiction between the actions when one moves toward the eastern direction and the other moves toward it from the opposite side.

Others, however, believe that the two [substances] are so described because their actions are in opposite directions. Here, the lack of contradiction must be considered. Now, he asks: from what is this conjunction (*sannipāta*) understood? He replies: "That conjunction is also inferred by the upward movement of the two possessing parts" (*sāvayavinoh*). Those which exist together with parts are "possessors of parts" (*sāvayavinah*); this was stated in order to indicate that their parts are also large, for they too are possessors of parts; otherwise, it would have been said "of the two possessing parts" (*sāvayavayoḥ*).
Others, however, maintain that here the grass and so forth are intended as the possessors of parts, not their constituent parts.

Alternatively, he explains how the upward movement of air itself is perceived: "That too [is known] by the upward movement of grass and other such things. For instance, the upward movement of grass and the like is not possible because they are insentient, nor is it due to momentum (*vega*), since their motion is sometimes slow and momentum is absent at the time of the production of the initial action. Furthermore, since no other capacity is observed, a connection with a substance possessing momentum is inferred. Nor is that [substance] earthy or watery; for if it were so, being a substratum of gravity, another cause devoid of gravity would have to be stated to account for its upward movement. Nor can the upward movement of grass and the like here be due to contact with fire, because fire has the nature of flaming upward, and such flaming is impossible in the absence of specific fuel, which is not observed here. Since no other agent possesses this capacity, it is known that the upward movement of grass and the like results from a connection with air. Since air naturally moves horizontally, it does not move upward; rather, it is postulated that it moves otherwise in the intermediate space, and thus there is an obstruction by another air. For instance, when a stronger air is obstructed by another even stronger air, through their collision it abandons its own horizontal course and moves upward. And by contact with that [upward-moving air], the upward movement of grass and the like occurs. Thus, it is established that the upward movement of air is inferred from the upward movement of grass and the like, and by that, their conjunction. Therefore, there is a plurality [of air].

Now, although the air called *prāṇa* is included among the objects [of perception] because its touch is perceived as being located within [the body], it is mentioned separately in order to indicate its preeminence and because it performs specific purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*). Likewise, it is stated separately because for one who knows reality and is engaged in the practice of yoga (*yogābhyāsa*), the *prāṇa* is extremely beneficial. Thus he says: “*Prāṇa* is that which, existing within the body, is the cause of the impelling and so forth of the fluids, wastes, and constituent elements (*rasa-mala-dhātu*). For instance, if one were to say simply that *prāṇa* is that which exists within the body, there would be an over-extension (*vyabhicāra*) to the fluids and other internal constituents; therefore, it is specified as "the cause of the impelling and so forth of the fluids, wastes, and constituent elements. Even so, if one were to say simply that it is the cause of the impelling of the fluids and so forth, there would be an over-extension to unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) and the like; therefore, it is specified as "existing within the body.
