Unseen merit and the like do not exist within the body, because unseen merit resides in the self (*ātman*), and because God (*Īśvara*) does not possess a location. Thus, that which exists within the body and is the cause of the impelling of the fluids and so forth is distinguished from others, or should be designated as *prāṇa*.

Alternatively, since the general characteristic of air (vāyu) persists, and because it exists within the body and is the cause for impelling the vital fluids and so forth, there is no deviation [from the definition] when it is called "prāṇa."

Now, as to whether this [breath] is one or many, he says: "Being one, it receives the designations of *apāna* and so forth due to the difference in its functions. Alternatively, why is a real (ontological) distinction not accepted? Because of the occurrence of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*). For instance, if the five winds exist in the body by way of pervasion (*vyāpti*), then because they are connected, there would be only one wind; thus, their status as five would cease. If, on the other hand, they do not pervade [the body], even so, since the body would be pervaded by one alone, the others would be impossible. Thinking thus, he asserts their distinction based on the difference in their functions. That very wind which has the nature of exiting through the mouth and nostrils is called *prāṇa*. It is *apāna* because it leads downward impurities and the like. It is *samāna* because it leads [substances] evenly. It is *udāna* because it leads upward. It is *vyāna* because it leads in various ways, that is, in manifold manners.
Thus ends the dissimilarity with wind.

“Now, the procedure for the creation and dissolution of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) is stated. At the end of a hundred years according to the measure of Brahmā, at the time of the final liberation of the currently existing Brahmā, for the sake of the rest of all living beings exhausted by the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) during the night, and simultaneously with Maheśvara—the Lord of all worlds—desiring to withdraw [the universe], there occurs the cessation of the activity of the unseen potencies (*adṛṣṭa*) residing in all souls, which are the causes that bind together the body, the sense organs, and the great elements. Then, from the actions produced by the conjunction of the soul and the atom through the will of Maheśvara, there arise disjunctions of the atoms that are the causes of the body and the sense organs; upon the cessation of their conjunction, their destruction occurs down to the level of the ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*). Likewise, among the great elements—earth, water, fire, and air—in this same sequence, as each subsequent one ceases, each preceding one is destroyed. Thereafter, the separated atoms remain, and the souls remain for that same duration of time, permeated by merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).”

“Then again, for the sake of the enjoyment of living beings, immediately after Maheśvara’s desire to create, motion arises in the atoms of air due to their conjunctions with the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) residing in all souls; from the mutual conjunctions of these [atoms] in the eastern direction, by way of the sequence of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth, a great wind is produced, which remains vibrating in the ether.”

“Immediately thereafter, from those very same atoms of water, by that same process, a great ocean was produced and remains floating about. Immediately thereafter, in that very ocean, from the atoms of earth, through the sequence beginning with dyads (dvyaṇuka), the great earth was produced and remains in a solid state.”

“Immediately thereafter, in that very great ocean, a vast mass of fire, blazing intensely, remains, having arisen from fiery atoms through the process beginning with dyads. When the four great elements have thus been produced, by the mere volition of Maheśvara, a great cosmic egg (aṇḍa) arises from those fiery atoms conjoined with earthly atoms.”

“Having produced from that [Lord] Brahmā—the Grandfather of all worlds, who possesses four lotus-faces—together with the entire universe, He appoints him to the creation of beings. And that Brahmā, thus appointed by Maheśvara, being endowed with extraordinary knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty, and having understood the ripening of the karma of living beings, creates through his mind the Prajāpatis whose knowledge, enjoyment, and lifespan correspond to their respective karmas, as well as the Manus, gods, sages, and classes of ancestors; and from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet, he creates the four castes and other beings high and low, and then endows them with dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty according to their latent dispositions.”
The Procedure for Creation and Destruction.

Now follows the section beginning with the words “of the four,” which is intended for the examination of God (*īśvara*) by way of completing the remaining investigation of the elements (*bhūta*). For, although the definition and examination of the elements were stated in the preceding sections immediately after their enumeration, the procedure for their creation and dissolution was not mentioned. Likewise, God was enumerated and defined above under the guise of an act of salutation; however, because He is the primary [subject], He cannot be examined without an examination of Dharma. Thus, this section is commenced. Furthermore, the procedures for creation and dissolution are set forth together in a single section; for if they were treated in separate sections, there would be as many as four sections, which would contradict the nature of this work as a concise compendium.

Now, one might object: "In this way, is it not improper to set forth similarity (*sādharmya*) at the occasion of discussing dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*)? No. Although the processes of creation and dissolution differ with respect to each individual element, the cognition of similarity arises because they are described together in a single context; it does not exist in an ultimate sense. Furthermore, when dissimilarity is being stated, there is no negation of whatever similarity exists. For example, earth and the other elements possess a twofold nature by virtue of being both atoms (*paramāṇu*) and effects (*kārya*). And as for the effect—namely, the triad beginning with the body—it does not abandon its character of similarity even though it possesses dissimilarity due to mutual differences among its members. (*Note: This refers to the fact that while the three types of bodies differ from one another, they all share the common property of being "effects" of the elements.)*

Now, when it is said "of four," it is not known which ones; therefore, [the text specifies] "of the great elements" (*mahābhūtānām*). The inclusion of the word "great" (*mahat*) is for the purpose of excluding the atom (*aṇu*). [Objection: But in that case, would there not also be an exclusion of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), since it too possesses creation and dissolution? [Reply: No. Because it is the originator of the great, it too is denotable by the word "great. For indeed, since the process of production is prescribed as beginning with the dyad and so forth, and the process of dissolution terminates at the atom, the proposition regarding the rule of creation and dissolution must certainly apply to the dyad as well. And that [proposition] would have been established in this way. Nevertheless, even when it is said "of the great elements," it is not known how many; and even when it is said "of four elements," it is not known which ones. Therefore, [the term] "earth and the others" (*pṛthivyādīnām*) is understood. Furthermore, there is no occasion for ether (*ākāśa*) here, as its inclusion would not fit the context of this explanation. Thus, the "rule" (*vidhi*)—meaning the method or manner—is that by which the creation and dissolution of the four great elements are expressed. Alternatively, "rule" (*vidhi*) means the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); or, by those two which are the means of knowledge, the "rule" refers to the ordainer or the agent. This very sentence, being repeated, has multiple meanings.

The explanation of the process of dissolution (*saṃhāra*) by means of the passage beginning with "by the Brahma-measure" (*brāhmeṇa mānena*) is presented first, despite the deviation from the sequential order, for the purpose of making known the beginninglessness of *saṃsāra*. For indeed, creation is obtained prior to dissolution, and after that, dissolution; thus, there is beginninglessness. He explains how that dissolution occurs: "From the actions born of the conjunction of the atoms with the self through the will of Maheśvara, following the disjunction of the atoms which are the causes of the body and the senses, upon the cessation of their [atomic] conjunctions, there is the destruction of those [bodies and senses] down to the ultimate atom. Regarding those bodies and senses, when the conjunction that initiates the substance ceases within the constituent atoms, the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is destroyed, and consequently, that which was produced by it is also destroyed. Thus he says: "From the actions born of the conjunction of the atoms with the self through the will of Maheśvara, [destruction occurs] from the disjunctions of the atoms which are the causes of the body and the senses, until reaching the ultimate atom. The cessation of the conjunction that initiates the substance results from the disjunctions of the atoms from their own causes; and these [disjunctions] arise from the actions born of the conjunction of the atoms with the self through the will of Maheśvara. To explain: the will of Maheśvara is the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*); the conjunction of the selves with the atoms is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*); and the atoms themselves are the inherent causes (*samavāyin*). Thus, actions are produced in the atoms. At what occasion? He says: "[of the unseen merits and demerits] residing in all selves" (*sarvātmagatādṛṣṭānām*). These are the unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*) residing in all selves. Of what kind are they? "[Of those] which bind the body, the senses, and the gross elements" (*śarīrendriyamahābhūtopanibandhakānām*). Those by which the body, senses, and gross elements are bound—that is, brought about—are so described. Their "function" (*vṛtti*) is the capacity to yield their fruit. When that [capacity] is simultaneously obstructed—that is, destroyed—through experience, that [destruction] occurs "simultaneously with the desire to withdraw" (*sañjihīrṣāsamakālam*). For when the desire of Maheśvara, the Lord of the entire world, arises to withdraw [the universe], and for what purpose? "[For the sake of rest for those weary of *saṃsāra*" (*saṃsārakhinnānām*). For living beings who are weary in *saṃsāra* by way of repeatedly assuming and discarding bodies, it is for the sake of rest, as in the night. Just as those weary from bodily exertion during the day find rest at night due to the absence of such activity, so it is here as well.

And when is there a desire for withdrawal? At the time of Brahmā’s liberation (*apavarga*). For when his term of office has ended, Brahmā is liberated; and that occurs at the conclusion of the hundred-year lifespan of the current Brahmā. By what measure? He says: "By the [measure] of Brahmā" (*brāhmeṇa*). This belongs to Brahmā, therefore it is "Brahmic. Furthermore, know that a divine cycle of four ages (*caturyuga*) consisting of twelve thousand [years] is a *kalpa*.
A thousand of these constitutes a single day of Brahmā.
By means of such days, months and so forth are also to be stated; this is the measure.

Thus, just as at the time of Brahmā’s liberation, simultaneously with Maheśvara’s desire to withdraw [the world], there occurs the destruction of bodies and sense organs upon the cessation of the activity of specific *adṛṣṭas*, so too "there is the destruction of the great elements—earth, water, fire, and air—in this very same order. (**)

Regarding the production of action in atoms, through the process of disjunctions leading to the cessation of existing conjunctions, as each subsequent [action] occurs, each preceding one is destroyed; this is with respect to their production. Whatever has been produced earlier perishes while each subsequent [action] exists. For instance, when the subsequent [action] exists, there is first the destruction of the air, and immediately thereafter that of the water, and so forth.

Others, however, maintain that this statement is intended solely with regard to the order of recitation (*pāṭha*). For instance, just as there is the destruction of the body and the sense organs, so too is there the destruction of the great elements—earth, water, fire, and air—in this very sequence, according to the order of recitation and not by any other sequence. And thus, upon the destruction of the body, the sense organs, and the great elements, there is also the destruction of the qualities and actions dependent upon them. Consequently, the atoms remain separated, no longer serving as the substratum for effects. Likewise, the selves remain permeated and connected with merit, demerit, and mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), as well as with the atoms.

If it is asked: "For what purpose is the mention of 'particularities' (*viśeṣa*) when other categories such as 'universals' (*sāmānya*) also persist?", [the answer is: it is for the sake of making known that the destruction of substances terminates in atoms (*paramāṇu*). Furthermore, since the selves (*ātman*) lack the cause for the destruction of their qualities (*dharma*) and so forth, they persist as permeated by *dharma*, *adharma*, and mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), but not in their bare state alone; otherwise, due to the absence of a causal factor, there would be no further rebirth. Now, as to how long this persistence lasts, he says: "for exactly that length of time," meaning for a hundred years according to the measurement of Brahmā.

Then again, at the end of a hundred years, when the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) that brings about rest has ceased to operate, because living beings experience the ripening of their karma, the "desire to create" (*sisṛkṣā*)—the wish to emanate—arises in Maheśvara for the sake of the prosperity of enjoyment (*bhogabhūtaye*). Immediately after that, actions (*karma*) inhering in the atoms of air arise. From what causes? He says: "from their conjunctions" (*tatsaṃyogebhyaḥ*). These are the conjunctions of those enjoyers with the atoms; this is the indication of the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). And since these [actions] depend on something else in initiating their activity, he says: "depending on the unseen forces residing in all souls that have attained their functional state" (*sarvātmagatavṛttilabdhādṛṣṭāpekṣebhyaḥ*). "Residing in all souls" means residing in all the enjoying souls (*bhogin*); they are "unseen forces that have attained their functional state. They are called such because they are unseen forces obtained through a "function" (*vṛtti*), which is an auxiliary cause (*sahakārikāraṇa*); depending on them is "depending on those," and from those [they arise]. However, the interpretation "those by whom a function has been obtained" is not correct, because in that case the word ending in the past passive participle (*niṣṭhānta*) would have to be placed first according to grammatical rules.

Now, what is this "subsistence" (*vṭtti*) that serves as the auxiliary cause for those unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*)? It is a specific point in time characterized by the absence of the unseen force that brings about cessation; for when that [absence] exists, the effect is produced. To illustrate: according to the measurement of Brahmā, when a hundred years are not yet complete, creation does not occur even though the unseen force that brings about experience is present, because the unseen force that brings about cessation acts as an obstacle. However, when the hundred years are complete, due to the absence of that specific obstructing unseen force, the unseen forces that bring about experience proceed toward creation. Thus, it is understood that their "subsistence" is time characterized by the absence of obstacles. For Maheśvara as well, the desire to create arises only when that [subsistence] is present.

Thus, when the production of effects occurs within the atoms of air, immediately thereafter disjunction follows. Consequently, upon the cessation of [their prior] conjunctions, dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) are produced from the mutual conjunctions of those atoms and initiate triads (*tryaṇuka*), and so forth; in this sequence, a great wind is produced and remains intensely vibrating (*dodhūyamāna*) in the sky, that is, in space. Having been produced at the outset, it becomes the cause for the non-falling of heavy objects due to its connection with an excessive velocity (*vega*). And the capacity of wind to obstruct the falling of leaves and such is observed. Furthermore, since it possesses an exceeding degree of magnitude and is connected with velocity, it is not surprising that it supports the earth together with the oceans like a blade of grass.

“Immediately thereafter” (*tadanantaram*) means immediately after the arising of wind; “in that very same” (*tasminneva*) means in that very wind which serves as the substratum. “From the aqueous atoms by that same sequence” (*āpyebhyaḥ paramāṇubhyastenaiva krameṇa*) means: through the production of action, following disjunctions, upon the cessation of [prior] conjunctions, dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) arise from mutual conjunctions, and from those, a triad (*tryaṇuka*); such is the sequence. “A great ocean” (*mahān salilanidhiḥ*), meaning the sea, has arisen; “floating about” (*poplūyamānaḥ*) means it remains floating excessively.

“Immediately thereafter” (*tadanantaram*) means immediately after the production of water; “in that” (*tasmin*) refers to the receptacle, the ocean; “from the earthly atoms” (*pārthivebhyaḥ paramāṇubhyaḥ*), by the aforementioned sequence, dyads and triads are produced. In this manner, through such a process, the great earth comes into being. And once produced, it “remains in an aggregated state” (*saṃhatāvatiṣṭhate*).

“In that very great ocean,” (*tasminneva mahodadhau*)—in this locative sense—a great mass of fire arises from fiery atoms through the same process of the production of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) as before. And once produced, it remains intensely blazing and exceedingly luminous. Nor should it be argued that the relationship of container and contained is untenable because of the natural opposition between fire and water; for such a relationship is indeed observed, as in the case of the submarine fire (*vāḍava*) and Varuṇa.

Others, however, in order to avoid the contradiction, connect the phrase "in that very great ocean" with the earth [passage]. Subsequently, when that production of the earth has occurred, there arises a great mass of fire from fiery atoms through the process beginning with dyads (*dvyaṇuka*).

Previously, in this manner—as previously stated—“when the four great elements have arisen,” that is, when they exist; “from the mere volition (*abhidhyāna*) of Maheśvara,” meaning from his mere will, and not from the activity of a body or other such means; likewise, from that very cause, a great egg (*mahadaṇḍa*) is produced from fiery atoms accompanied by earth atoms. Of what nature is it? It is “great. For here, the fiery atoms are the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), their conjunctions are the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and the earth particles as well as the volition of Maheśvara are the efficient causes (*nimittakāraṇa*). Thus, dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) having been produced, they begin the great egg through the process of triads (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth. And within that space inside the egg, he produces Brahmā.

To specify what kind [of being], he says: "having four lotus-like faces" (*caturvadanakamalam*). He is so described because he possesses four faces that are like lotuses. Furthermore, he is the "grandfather and lord of all worlds," from the earth up to the world of truth (*satya*). Likewise, he is "together with all the worlds. Having created him, Maheśvara appoints him to the creation of beings, saying: "O Brahmā! Perform the creation of beings."

“And that Brahmā, commissioned by Maheśvara,” is so called because he is endowed (*sampanna*) or possessed (*yukta*) with those things—namely, supreme knowledge (*jñāna*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), and sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). For this very reason, “having known the ripening of the karma of living beings, he creates sons. Of what kind? “Prajāpatis,” lords of progeny; those whose knowledge, enjoyment, and lifespan are in accordance with their karma are so described as “those possessing knowledge, enjoyment, and lifespan corresponding to their karma” (*karmānurūpajñānabhogāyuṣaḥ*). Likewise, “Mānasas,” born of the mind, produced through the mere volition of the mind without physical exertion; therefore, he creates them. Furthermore, he creates the hosts or assemblies of those so called: Manus, gods, seers, and ancestors. Indeed, he creates the four castes—Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—with knowledge, enjoyment, and lifespan corresponding to their karma. From what [parts of his body] does he create them? He says: “From the mouth, arms, thighs, and feet,” respectively. Likewise, he creates “other beings, high and low,” existing in a state of superior and inferior status. And having created these aforementioned ones, “he endows them with virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty according to their dispositions” (*āśayānurūpaiḥ*); for whatever the nature of a being’s karma may be, he brings about for that being a corresponding degree of virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty.
Doubts regarding the proof of God and their resolution.

Is it not the case that all this is incoherent, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of a Lord? No, for his existence is established through inference and scripture. Thus, the inference is as follows: the creation and dissolution of the earth and so forth are preceded by an agent. If it is argued that there is no such inference because creation and dissolution are not observed among the elements (*bhūta*), [we reply] that they are established by virtue of their possessing a structured arrangement (*racanāvattva*). For instance: the earth and so forth are effects, because they possess a structured arrangement; whatever possesses a structured arrangement is an effect, just like a jar and the like; and since the earth and so forth possess a structured arrangement, they are therefore effects.

Nor should it be argued that the reason is "inconclusive" (*aprayojaka*) because the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is observed even in the absence of being composed (*racanāvattva*). For if that were so, it would follow that every reason existing only in a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) would be non-probative. To illustrate: smoke too would be inconclusive, since fire-possessingness is observed even in its absence [in a red-hot iron ball]. If you argue that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is such that "wherever there is smoke, there is fire," then it is exactly the same in our case: "wherever there is composition, there is being an effect. Furthermore, in the case of a jar and the like, the state of "having come into existence after not having existed" (*abhūtvā bhāvitva*), though not perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), is established precisely through the property of being composed; and this is likewise the same in the case of the world's dissolution (*saṃhāra*). Once "being an effect" is established, "having a creator as its antecedent" (*kartṛpūrvakatva*) is then proven. Thus: the subject of dispute has a conscious being as its cause, because it is an effect; whatever is an effect has a conscious being as its cause, just like a jar and the like; and this [world] is an effect; therefore, it has a conscious being as its cause. And since this reason possesses the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), exists in the similar instances, is entirely excluded from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), and has its object uncontradicted (*abādhitaviṣayatva*), it is probative by virtue of being free from a counter-reason (*asatpratipakṣatva*).

But if the probandum (*sādhya*) is "being preceded by a creator who is the substratum of the knowledge of all knowable objects," then the example is devoid of the probandum, because in the case of a jar and the like, we observe that "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is pervaded by being preceded by one who is not omniscient. Furthermore, the reason (*hetu*) is contradictory (*viruddha*): "The subject of dispute is not preceded by an omniscient being, because it is an effect, like a jar. Moreover, if the probandum is "being preceded by one who is not omniscient," then there is a failure to establish what was intended.

This is not so. When the conscious substratum (*bodhādhāra*) as the controller (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*) is the probandum (*sādhya*), there is neither the fallacy of the probandum being absent (*sādhyavikalatva*) nor the fallacy of contradiction (*viruddhatva*). Nor does the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) deviate from a conscious controller; thus, by the power of observing non-deviation, the perceived [state of being an effect] proves a controller capable of producing the earth and other things within the subject (*pakṣa*). Furthermore, one who is ignorant of the material causes and instruments of the earth and so forth cannot be capable of producing the earth and so forth; therefore, knowledge regarding atoms and the like is obtained for that creator. It is observed that all inference, proceeding by the force of grasping a general pervasion (*vyāpti*), establishes a specific probandum by the force of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). Nor can even a vociferous opponent establish a subversion of the general pervasion between "having a conscious cause" and "being an effect" here. If, however, it were not a proof because of the absence of pervasion in terms of a specific [instance], then smoke too would follow as being no proof, since in that case as well, the pervasion of mere smoke is observed with mere fire, from which all specificities have been excluded. Thus, in this case too, a contradiction regarding the specific is indeed possible: "This mountain does not possess the fire restricted to mountains, because it has smoke; whatever has smoke does not possess such specific fire, like a kitchen; and this [mountain] is likewise; therefore, it possesses the aforementioned probandum."

If it is argued that there is no room for contradiction because smoke is observed to be pervaded by fire in general, and thus wherever it is observed, fire is present there precisely because it establishes fire—then this is the same here as well. Since the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is observed to be pervaded by an intelligent agent (*buddhimat*), it establishes such an agent in the subject (*pakṣa*). Now, if it is argued that it is logical because a location containing smoke is seen to be pervaded by fire, and thus [the presence of smoke] establishes the existence of fire in another location as well; then, in that case, the state of being an effect, wherever it is perceived, must likewise be pervaded by an agent capable of producing it. Consequently, it should lead to the inference of an agent capable of producing the earth and so forth, even in the subject.

Regarding this inference—that "that which is not a subject of dispute is preceded by an omniscient being"—since the negation of a specific [quality] implies the acceptance of the remainder through its inherent capacity, it would follow that [the world] is preceded by one who is not omniscient, because the property of being an effect does not deviate from having an agent. Furthermore, if that non-omniscient being were capable of producing the earth, there would be a difference in name only; if, however, he is incapable, how could he be the creator of the earth and so forth?

Now, if it is intended that the specific quality of another’s omniscience is [denied] by means of the reason "being an effect," then for the purpose of refuting that, one might argue: "The positive formulation is 'it is preceded by one who is not omniscient'. In that case, if one accepts that the negation of a specific attribute implies the admission of the remainder, then because such capacity is observed, there would be no contradictory inference regarding the mere agent [of the world]. To this we say: No. How could the capacity to produce the earth and so forth be merely a difference in name? For if there were no capacity, the effect would not arise; yet the effect is observed. Furthermore, if all specific attributes are negated, the universal—being without a substratum—cannot be established, leading to the consequence that the [inference] is invalid due to having no object. And this [inference] is not invalid, because it is impossible to negate the pervasion of the universal. If, on the other hand, there is a negation of a particular specific attribute, then by admitting that specific attribute, the admission of another specific attribute follows, just as when one says, "He does not see with his left eye."

If it is argued that the operation of inference is appropriate because the relationship between fire and smoke is established through direct perception, whereas it is not so here [in the case of the earth], we say no. For here too, since the relationship between being an effect and having a presiding agent is established, inference certainly proceeds.

If it is argued: "Fire is perceived even after [its existence] has been inferred; however, God is not so. Therefore, how can there be an inference [of Him]? We say: No. For even that which is absolutely beyond the senses, such as the eye and other organs, is inferable from perception. Now, if you argue that in this case there is an inference because action is observed to be generally both an effect and having a cause, then [we reply]: there is likewise an inference because the state of being an effect is observed to be generally preceded by an agent. And it must be admitted that since the state of being an effect is pervaded by an agent possessing a body and so forth, what is established here is precisely such an agent, as in the case of a jar and similar objects. For an objection based on the exaggeration (*utkarṣa*) or diminution (*apakarṣa*) of properties between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the example (*dārṣṭāntika*) would result in the destruction of all inference. To explain: the introduction of non-existent qualities like a body is *utkarṣa*; the denial of existent qualities like omniscience is *apakarṣa*. Furthermore, not all properties of the example apply to the subject of the example, for if they did, the very distinction between example and subject would be destroyed. Indeed, just because an axe or similar tool is seen to be the instrument for the act of cutting does not mean the same applies to the act of perceiving color. And just as an inference is made here because action is pervaded by an instrument whose specific nature is set aside, so too it is in the inference of God; thus, the application of the *jāti* (fallacious rejoinder) is untenable.

By this, what was said [by the opponent]— namely, "If it is claimed that some mere cause acts as a presiding controller, that is a proof of what is already established, because that [controller-ship] is established by the actions (karma) of all seeds"— is refuted. (Ślokavārttika, Sambandhākṣepaparihāra 75)
Thus, that [objection] is refuted.

For instance, if an intelligent supervisor is what is to be proven, how can there be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by means of "action" (*karman*), which is insentient? This is because that [action] too, being insentient, requires a supervisor. For it is observed that everything insentient functions only when presided over by a sentient being, just as in the case of threads and so forth, and likewise with action and the like. Nor is the self of beings such as ourselves the supervisor, because that self lacks knowledge regarding that [action]. Furthermore, the knowledge of the self of beings such as ourselves regarding action is not produced by the senses, nor does it have atoms and the like as its object. And in the absence of such knowledge, its capacity to impel [action] is not observed. Moreover, the spontaneous activity of an insentient thing has never been perceived; for if it were to act spontaneously, it would continue to act even once the effect was fully accomplished, since it is devoid of discrimination.

Now, if it is argued that milk proceeds while presided over by something insentient, that is not so; for it does not proceed during the state of death when there is an absence of effort on the part of the cow's calf. Furthermore, since everything not presided over by persons such as ourselves is included within the subject (*pakṣa*), there is no deviation of the probans from the probandum (*sādhya*), which would entail the destruction of all inference. Thus: "Other insentient things are presided over by someone other than us; they are presided over by an intelligent being in the production of effects, because they are insentient; whatever is insentient is seen to proceed only when presided over by an intelligent being, such as threads and the like; and these [things] are likewise; therefore, they possess the aforementioned probandum."

Now, if it is argued that because a creator is observed to possess a body and so forth, God must likewise possess such a state, then what is being proven here if the status of being the creator of the earth and other things is admitted even while possessing a body and so forth? Or, if it is argued that one who possesses a body and so forth cannot be the creator of the earth and other things due to being non-omniscient, then—since there is a deviation of the effect from a creator—one must admit that the status of being a creator belongs only to one who is bodiless. Furthermore, there is no proof for the existence of a body and so forth [in God]. If it is claimed that the very fact of being a creator is the proof, that is indeed contradictory; for by being a creator one would possess a body and so forth, and by possessing a body and so forth, one could not be the creator of the earth and other things.

Nor is this an independent proof (*svatantra-sādhana*), because its locus is unestablished (*āśrayāsiddhatvāt*). For instance, only if the existence of an agent were established would the property of being an agent and the possession of a body and so forth constitute the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*); however, this has not been accepted.

Now, if it is argued that the opponent has accepted an agent such as Earth and so forth, this is merely an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpādana*). For if that acceptance were dependent upon a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then because [the argument] is sublated by that very [cognition], the contrary inference cannot even arise. Nor could there be a sublation of this [inference] by that [opponent's position], since the latter is rooted in that [sublated cognition]. If, on the other hand, the opponent has accepted it without any means of valid cognition, then, since an object of knowledge (*prameya*) is not established without a means of valid cognition, what is the use of the contrary inference? For it would result in the fallacy of having an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*). And this same point applies equally to the other reasons for refuting God (*īśvara*).

Likewise, if there were a connection with a body, an effect that occurs simultaneously in multiple, indefinite locations could not exist due to the necessity of being restricted to a specific location; yet such an effect is observed. Now, if it is claimed that the body is all-pervading, eternal, and supersensible in order to account for the production of an effect in indefinite locations—that is not so, because it contradicts what is observed. Furthermore, the status of being an agent must be accepted as belonging to one who is indeed bodiless. For instance, since a permanent body is impossible, that body would have to be produced by that very agent; why then would it be produced by another body? If another body were admitted, then that [second] body would have to be produced by one endowed with yet another body, and thus, being exhausted in an infinite succession of bodies, no further effect would ever manifest from the Blessed One. If it is argued that the body itself acts as the agent and this is not contradicted even at the time of producing its own effects—[we reply: if that were so, then when the body is destroyed during the state of dissolution, there would be no production of effects at the beginning of a new creation, as the bodiless one lacks agency; therefore, the status of being an agent must be accepted as belonging to one who is indeed bodiless.

If it is argued that because we observe agents to act out of dependence on a purpose, there is an absence of activity in the Lord due to the absence of such a purpose—that is incorrect. For the existence of an agent is established by the existence of the effect; and since He is Himself perfectly complete, His activity is understood to be for the sake of others. Alternatively, this objection does not apply because the Blessed One has the nature of being active. Just as the sun, by its very nature of illuminating, makes objects manifest, so too the other [the Lord], by virtue of being the cause of effects, produces effects.

Now, how can that which is bodiless be a mover by mere will, as is the case with the selves of people like us who move their bodies and so forth? Or, if it is argued that the relationship between the moved and the mover exists only when a body is present, then here too, the relationship between the moved and the mover exists only when an atom is present; thus the cases are equal.

Now, if Maheśvara’s desire to create or desire to dissolve were eternal, there would be the constant production of effects. If, however, they are non-eternal, that [desire] too cannot arise without the will of Īśvara; thus there must be another desire, and since that too is non-eternal, it is dependent on the will of Īśvara. This leads to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), whereby the Lord’s capacity would be exhausted solely in the production of that [successive desire], and he would have no activity toward any other effect. If, on the other hand, the will of Īśvara is produced even without the will of Īśvara, then let it be the same for other effects as well.

Now, if [the entity] is eternal, it must produce its effect even upon obtaining auxiliary causes. If those auxiliaries are also eternal, there would be the constant production of the effect; if they are non-eternal, then that [eternal entity], while bringing about those auxiliaries, must depend upon further auxiliaries. If those [auxiliaries] are also non-eternal, there must again be further auxiliaries, leading to an infinite regress and the persistence of the aforementioned fault.

This is not a fault. For when the existence of previously produced unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) is present, desire performs its function. To explain: even in the production of auxiliary factors, it requires another auxiliary factor, and for that too another; thus, the solution is its beginninglessness (*anāditva*). And it has been stated that desire is an auxiliary factor in both creation and dissolution. Likewise: "The one God, with eyes on all sides, with faces on all sides, with arms on all sides, and with feet on all sides, blows together heaven and earth with his arms and with his wings, generating them. (*Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* 10; *Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad* 3.2).
Thus, [the self] is established by scripture (*āgama*).

Nor is there a lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) in those [scriptural passages] that set forth its essential nature (*svarūpa*), because they possess the capacity to produce valid cognition (*pramā*). For indeed, the authority of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) consists in its being a producer of valid cognition, not in its being a producer of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*). And this [capacity to produce valid cognition] exists here [in the case of scripture] as well. As for engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), these occur for a person because of their desire for what is capable of accomplishing an object, once that object has been determined to be a means to pleasure or pain.

Now, if it is argued that these [statements] possess primacy because they are auxiliary to an injunction (*vidhi*), and not because their purpose is to convey their own literal meaning—that is incorrect. For they are auxiliary to an injunction precisely by virtue of conveying their own meaning. To explain: praise (*stuti*) functions as an incitement to action by conveying its own meaning, while censure (*nindā*) functions as a deterrent by conveying its own meaning. Otherwise, if their meaning were not fully understood, there would be no distinction between what is enjoined and what is prohibited, and engagement or withdrawal would occur indiscriminately. Furthermore, it is observed that even an injunctive sentence impels a person only through the medium of conveying its own meaning. The same would apply to sentences whose primary purpose is to convey their own form (i.e., descriptive or explanatory statements), since there is no difference in their nature as sentences and no specific reason [to treat them otherwise].

Likewise, if statements whose purpose is to convey the essential nature of things were not authoritative, then in the absence of knowledge regarding such matters as "Water is pure; *darbha* grass is a purifier; [this] is impure... [this] is unclean," there would result the contingency of engaging in or desisting from actions indiscriminately, even when these statements serve as auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) to an injunction. But this is not the case, because we observe that people engage only with what is pure and desist from what is impure. Thus, since engagement with the desired and desistance from the undesired are observed once the essential nature of an object is understood through sentences whose purpose is to convey that nature, it is known that such statements—by virtue of generating valid cognition (*pramā*)—act as auxiliaries to an injunction for either engagement or desistance. However, if one were to act without such understanding, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the injunction.

Now, if those [scriptural passages] whose meaning is their own literal form were authoritative, then even statements such as "stones float" would have to be true to reality. This is not so, because in the case of the primary sense, there exists a subverting proof (*bādhaka*). For where there is a subverting proof regarding the primary sense, there figurative usage (*upacāra*) is postulated; but in the absence of such [a subversion], there is indeed authority. And there is no subverting proof whatsoever regarding those [passages] that establish the existence of God. Thus, since the sentences establishing creation and dissolution are authoritative in their literal sense, it is improper to postulate a contrary meaning.

By this, the position of the Śākyas is also refuted. For the Śākyas likewise oppose [this argument] by means of the exaggeration or depreciation of the example and the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭānta-dārṣṭāntika*). And the resolution for that has already been stated; moreover, that is a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*). Whatever effect is observed to be pervaded by a certain kind of agent—such that, upon perceiving it, one who has seen its production forms the cognition "this was produced by someone"—that very thing, when perceived in such a manner, would lead to the inference of an agent of that same kind. As it has been said:
The established [result] follows the presence or absence of the presiding agent, just as it is.
Therefore, that which is inferred from such [properties] as its arrangement and so forth [is not valid].

Furthermore, since the effects such as the earth have never been seen to be inseparable from a creator, how could they lead to the inference of a creator? If it is argued that an inference is possible because of the commonality of the word "effect" despite the difference in the objects themselves, then in that case, since whiteness in smoke has been observed to be pervaded by fire, the whiteness perceived even in a palace or similar structures would lead to the inference of fire there as well. As it has been said:
"When an object is established as distinct, [an inference] based on the non-distinction of a word due to mere similarity of sound [is invalid]."
Inference is not tenable, as [the existence of] fire cannot be inferred from white-colored substances and the like.

(PV 1.14) If it were the case that because some effect is seen to be invariably concomitant with an agent, every such effect—even one whose concomitance with an agent has not been observed—must be preceded by one, then since jars and other products of clay are observed to be preceded by a potter, anthills and the like would also have to be preceded by one. As it has been said:
"Otherwise, because some product of clay is made by a potter..."
If [the existence of] a pot and so forth is established by means of an agent, then the anthill must also be established as its creation.

How then is it said that this effect, such as the earth and so forth, is born of karma? For how can the diversity of the worlds be born of karma? And that [karma] is mental action consisting of consciousness; it is not a different entity from cognition.

All of this is incoherent. It has been stated that the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is pervaded by a creator (*kartṛ*) in a general sense, because such a pervasion is observed in the case of [products like] a jar; therefore, its existence is established even in the case of the earth. Furthermore, it has been said that all inference proceeds by depending upon the apprehension of a pervasion in a general sense elsewhere [than the subject]. It is not a valid objection to claim that no inference whatsoever can possibly depend on the apprehension of a pervasion within the subject itself—such as the claim that "the effects consisting of the earth and so forth are not observed to be pervaded by a creator"—because this would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the total abolition of all inference. To illustrate: the impermanence of sound is accepted on the grounds of its being produced (*kṛtakatva*). Here too, one could argue: "That quality of being produced which exists in sound is not observed elsewhere to be invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvitayā*) with impermanence"; thus, there would be no inference. If you reply that an inference occurs when the pervasion between being produced and impermanence is apprehended elsewhere in a general sense, and not within the subject itself, then the same applies to the inference for God (*īśvara*). Nor is there merely a formal similarity here, since the property of being an effect exists in both cases without deviation. Furthermore, it is not the case that whiteness is an indicator of fire, because it deviates due to its presence even in the absence of fire. Likewise, the fact of being a modification of clay is not a logical mark (*liṅga*) for the prior existence of a potter even in the case of anthills and the like, because of deviation; for that property is present even in things like city walls and bricks, which are not preceded by a potter.

As for this [argument] that the diversity of the worlds arises from karma, that is indeed accepted. Even if karma, being insentient, must proceed toward the production of its effects under the superintendence of a sentient being—and thus the existence of a Lord (*īśvara*) follows—nevertheless, even though karma is [governed] by a sentient being, that [sentient being] does not possess the status of being the locus of that [karma], because its sentience alone is what matters. Furthermore, there is no identity between that [karma] and consciousness, since it will be stated later that [karma] is a quality of the self (*ātman*). Nor is this [inference for the Lord] comparable to the inference based on "originating from the same branch" (*eka-śākhā-prabhavatva*); for in that case, when the ripening of other fruits is to be proven by the reason of originating from the same branch, its lack of validity is appropriate due to the emergence of sublation (*bādha*) by perception, but such is not the case with the inference for the Lord.

Nor should it be argued that agency is pervaded by the possession of a body and so forth, such that in the absence of the latter, the former must also be absent; for if the inference from effect is non-deviant, the existence of an agent is established. Furthermore, the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) cannot serve as a subverting factor here, because one inference cannot be subverted by another inference. Moreover, if the existence of the subject (*dharmin*) is established by the prior inference, then [the subsequent argument] would have a subject already proven by another means (*upakṛtaviṣayatva*); if it is not established, then it lacks the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*).

Now, as for the claim that "because that which is eternal lacks exclusion [from other instances], its causal capacity is difficult to establish" (*Pramāṇavārttika* 1.25), and thus God is indeed not an agent—that is not so, because the refutation of momentariness will be stated later. Furthermore, this doctrine of God has been explained in detail by our teachers, and therefore it is not elaborated upon here.

“Since ether, time, and space are each unitary, there is no lower genus [to subsume them]; therefore, they possess three technical designations: ether (*ākāśa*), time (*kāla*), and direction (*diś*). Their qualities are sound, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction. Among these, sound is not a specific quality of a substance possessing touch, because—while being perceptible—it does not originate from the qualities of its own cause, it does not persist as long as the substance itself, and it is perceived elsewhere than its substratum.”

“Because it is perceptible by the external sense organs, because it is graspable by other selves, because it does not inhere in the self, and because it is perceived as distinct from the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), sound is not a quality of the self. “Because it is graspable by the auditory organ and because it is a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*), sound does not belong to space, time, or the internal organ (*manas*). “By the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), being a quality, sound is the inferential mark (*liṅga*) for the cognition of space. Its oneness is established because there is no difference in its inferential mark, namely sound. Its separateness (*pṛthaktva*) follows from that [oneness]. Its dimension is that of the infinitely great (*paramamahatparimāṇa*) because of the statement regarding its pervasiveness (*vibhava*). Conjunction and disjunction are established because of the statement regarding the causes of sound.”

“Because it possesses qualities and because it is non-dependent, it is a substance (*dravya*). Because there is no possibility of causes that are either of the same or different classes, it is eternal. And it serves as the instrumental cause for the perception of sound by all living beings through its existence as the auditory organ (*śrotra*). “The auditory organ, moreover, is a region of space (*nabhodeśa*) known as the cavity of the ear, which is bound by *dharma* and *adharma* that bring about the experience of sound through its specific instrumental cause. Since it is eternal, deafness occurs due to the deficiency of that which binds it.”

Now, for the purpose of defining and examining space (*ākāśa*), which possesses a general designation, there is this section: "Since space, time, and direction are each unitary, and thus lack subordinate genera, there are three technical designations. He states that these constitute the definition of space and the others without being combined: "Space, time, and direction," corresponding respectively. For, because the word "iti" is connected to each term individually, the designation "space" applies to space, the designation "time" applies to time, and the designation "direction" applies to direction; it is not the case that all three apply to a single entity.

Now, why are these [terms] technical (*pāribhāṣikya*)? Because there is no basis (*nimitta*) consisting of substance, quality, or action. One might argue that the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), such as "space-ness" (*ākāśatva*) and so forth, will serve as the basis; to this he says: "In the absence of a lower genus" (*aparajātyabhāve*). For a lower genus—such as space-ness, time-ness, or direction-ness, which exists in relation to the higher genus of "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*)—is simply not possible, because space and the others are each unitary, whereas a universal must have multiple loci.

Furthermore, since the three technical designations (*pāribhāṣikī-saṃjñā*) do not apply to space (*ākāśa*) and the other [elements], the statement regarding their commonality (*sādharmya*) is not connected [to the context]. This is because, on the occasion of discussing dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), designations function as forms of dissimilarity due to their mutual exclusion; moreover, their mention together in one place is for the sake of the treatise’s systematic compendium (*saṅgraha*). Thus, the designation "space" has descended through a stream from beginningless time and cannot occur elsewhere; therefore, by virtue of its uniqueness (*asādhāraṇatva*), it is a definition (*lakṣaṇa*). And this qualification is obtained by implication. For instance: space is distinct from others, because it is denotable by the word "space" as it has descended through a stream from beginningless time. That which is not distinct from others—such as non-space—is not like this, just as earth and so forth are not; and since space is not like that, it is therefore distinct.

If it is argued that technical designations (*pāribhāṣikyaḥ saṃjñāḥ*) are indeed impossible because the absence of the fourfold cause itself serves as the cause [for their application], then it would follow that they apply only where a cause consisting of substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*karman*), or universal (*sāmānya*) is not possible, and nowhere else; thus, that absence would be the cause. This is not so. For here, what is intended by "cause" is that which is the cause of a cognition colored by its own [referent]. Just as the conventional usage such as "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*) is colored by a substance, a quality, or a universal, this conventional usage regarding space (*ākāśa*) and so forth is not colored by the absence of those; therefore, these are indeed technical designations.

Previously, it was stated that substances possess the qualities of being inherent causes (*samavāyitva*) and having qualities (*guṇatva*). To this end, he explains: "Its qualities are sound, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction. By these qualities it possesses qualities. Among these, it is the inherent cause for the production of certain things; furthermore, sound serves as its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) because of its uniqueness.

[Objection: But surely all of this is unestablished with respect to its substratum (*āśrayāsiddha*), because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of space (*ākāśa*). [Reply: No; for even though it is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), its existence is established by inference (*anumāna*). To the question "What is the inference?", he says: "Sound" (*śabdaḥ*). For instance: sound is dependent on something, because it is a quality (*guṇatvāt*); whatever is a quality is dependent on something, just like color and so forth (*rūpādi*); and this [sound] is a quality; therefore, it is dependent.

Now, [the author] says "it is not a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of that which possesses touch" (*na sparśavadviśeṣaguṇaḥ*) in order to show that it cannot be a quality of earth and so forth. This is because, while being perceptible to us and others, it does not have the qualities of its own cause as its antecedent (*akāraṇaguṇapūrvakatvāt*). Whatever is perceptible to us and others and does not have the qualities of its own cause as its antecedent is not a specific quality of things possessing touch, just like pleasure and so forth; and this [sound] has the aforementioned probans; therefore, it is not a specific quality of things possessing touch.

[Objection: But surely, here, when the negation of specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) is the probandum (*sādhya*), there is the implication of general qualities (*sāmānyaguṇa*), because the capacity of a specific negation to imply the remaining [possibilities] is observed. Or, if it is the negation of general qualities, then likewise there is the implication of specific qualities. [Reply: This is not so, because the determination of the subject (*pakṣa*) and other members of the argument depends upon the counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*). To explain: the opponent has accepted that sound possesses the nature of a specific quality of earth and so forth; it is precisely that which is being negated. Furthermore, the status of being a general quality is simply not desired [by the opponent]. As for the "implication of the remainder," that occurs where both [alternatives] are established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); in such a case, when one is negated, the other remains unnegated. For example, since perception is seen to be produced by both the left and right eyes, when one is negated, the other remains because it is not negated. However, the status of sound as a general quality of earth and so forth is not established for the opponent; therefore, this is not a flaw. For this very reason, although conjunction, disjunction, and so forth—being perceptible to people like us—are preceded by qualities of their causes (*akāraṇaguṇapūrvaka*), they nonetheless do not possess the nature of specific qualities of tangible substances (*sparśavad-viśeṣaguṇatva*). Thus, because they are included within the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), there is no lack of invariable concomitance (*anaikāntikatva*). Color and the rest are the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), and since they are preceded by qualities of their causes, they are indeed devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhana-śūnya*). Nevertheless, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because the color and other qualities of the atoms of earth are not preceded by qualities of their causes, yet they are specific qualities of tangible substances; to exclude these, the qualification "while being perceptible to people like us" (*asmadādipratyakṣatve sati*) is added. Those [qualities of atoms], however, are perceptible only to yogis. Since the treatise is commenced for the sake of instruction for people like us, the qualification "people like us" is indeed obtained.

Others, however, in order to avoid fallacies such as *saṃyoga* (conjunction), extract the qualifying term from the statement of the thesis (*pratijñā*) and connect it with the probans (*hetu*). For instance: "Sound is not a quality of tangible things, because—while being a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) perceptible to us—it is not preceded by the qualities of its cause, like pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth. Here, since there is a connection between the general and the specific, the negation of the general necessarily entails the negation of the specific, just as the negation of "Brahminhood" implies the negation of [specific lineages] such as the Vājasaneyins. Furthermore, it must be considered how a word contained within a compound in the thesis-statement can be connected with the word expressing the probans.

Is it not the case that the reason—"because it does not have the qualities of its cause as its antecedent" (*akāraṇaguṇapūrvakatvāt*)—is unestablished (*asiddha*), since from the perspective of others, sound is admitted to be produced from the qualities of its cause through conjunction, disjunction, and [another] sound? For instance, space is the cause of sound, and its qualities such as conjunction and so forth are the "qualities of the cause"; since these are its cause, it possesses the property of having the qualities of its cause as its antecedent. This is not so, because there has been a failure to understand the intended meaning. The meaning intended here is as follows: the "qualities of the cause" are those qualities residing in the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*); that quality for which these are the preceding cause is "antecedent to the qualities of its cause. For example, the color of a cloth is antecedent to the colors of the threads. But this is not the case for sound, because space, being unproduced (*akārya*), lacks inherent causes and thus lacks qualities residing in inherent causes.

Now, [you may argue] that according to our own view, sound is preceded by the qualities of its cause; thus, for example, the sound of a drum is preceded by the sounds of its constituent parts, and likewise the sound of a conch shell. This is not so, because those [sounds] are not perceived. For instance, at the time of the sound of a conch shell, the sounds of the conch’s constituent parts are not experienced, just as the forms of the threads are not experienced at the time of perceiving the form of a cloth.

If it is argued that there is no perception [of the parts] because they are overwhelmed, we say no; for there is a lack of evidence for their existence. To explain: there is no proof that the sounds of the parts, having arisen long ago, initiate a sound in the whole (*avayavin*). Alternatively, if the non-perception of the part-sounds is due to their being overwhelmed by the sounds of the whole while they still exist, then in the absence of those [overwhelming sounds], they should be perceived—just as the sound of a lute is perceived when the sound of a donkey is absent. For instance, when a lute is being played in the presence of a donkey, the sound of the lute, though existing, is not perceived due to being overwhelmed; yet it is observed to be perceived again once the overwhelming factor is gone. However, such a cognition of the sounds of the whole does not occur.

Furthermore, it is not observed that in cases where effects are preceded by the qualities of their causes, the effect possesses the power to suppress its cause; this is likewise the case regarding the suppression of sound. Rather, it is simply that due to the perception of a loud sound, a faint one is not perceived. Nor can it be argued that the non-perception of the sounds of the parts occurs only at the time of perceiving the sound of the whole, since they were unperceived even previously. Moreover, the quality of being preceded by the qualities of the cause persists as long as the substance exists. Furthermore, one should not say—on the strength of the doctrine of the existence of the effect—that although the sounds of the parts and the whole exist, they are not perceived due to a lack of a manifestor, for that [position] will be refuted later.

Nor should it be asserted that the sounds of parts lack the status of non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) simply because they differ from the sound of the whole; for such a cause is observed among things of the same class as well as among those of entirely different classes. For instance, just as a sound of the very same nature [as its cause] arises in the effect from the most brilliant color residing in the cause, so too is it with taste and the other qualities. Likewise, there is the status of being a non-inherent cause for that which is of an entirely different class, as in the case of the conjunction called "accumulation" (*pracaya*) and number (*saṃkhyā*) in the production of dimension (*parimāṇa*). But sound is not like this. To explain: the sound of a drum is deep, whereas the sounds of its constituent parts possess different characteristics; the same should be inferred for the sounds of conch shells and other such objects.

Nor should it be thought that the proof of the thesis is established by the example of pleasure and so forth, on the grounds that everything consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion; for this is refuted by the rejection of the doctrine of *pradhāna*, and because pleasure and the rest are qualities of the self (*ātman*).

Likewise, sound is not a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of substances possessing touch, because while being perceptible to us and others, it does not persist for as long as the substance exists. Whatever is perceptible to us and others and does not persist for as long as the substance exists is not a specific quality of substances possessing touch, just like pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth. And this [sound] is perceptible to us and others, yet does not persist for as long as the substance exists; therefore, it is not a specific quality of substances possessing touch. Furthermore, those which are specific qualities of substances possessing touch persist for as long as the substance exists while being perceptible to us and others, such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth. Here too, the phrase "while being perceptible to us and others" is included in order to exclude the color and other qualities of the atoms of earth (*pārthivaparamāṇu*). Nor is there a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by means of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the like, according to the reasoning stated previously. Nor does sound persist for as long as the substance exists, because it is not perceived in the same manner as color and the rest.

Likewise, there is another reason: “And because it is perceived elsewhere than its substratum” (*āśrayādanyatropalabdheśca*). The word “and” (*ca*) serves as a conjunction. It is not only for the two reasons previously stated, but also because it is perceived elsewhere than its substratum that sound is not a specific quality of something possessing touch (*sparśavat*). Now, one might object: since space is the substratum of sound, its perception elsewhere is unestablished (*asiddha*), because it is perceived by that very [space]. [Response: This is not so, because we are speaking of the drum and so forth as the "substratum" according to the opponent's own admission. For instance, the sound of a drum is not a quality of that [drum], because it is perceived elsewhere than it. Whatever is perceived elsewhere than something is not a quality of that thing, just like pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth. And whatever is a quality of something is perceived only in that very place, just like color (*rūpa*) and so forth. But sound is not like that; therefore, it is not a quality of that [drum]. [Objection: This is not established, because sound is perceived in that very place, just as the appearance "the sound is in the drum" is seen, like color. It cannot be otherwise. [Response: This is not so, because... [text continues with further logical arguments regarding the nature of perception and the relationship between substratum and quality]. *(Note: The provided source text contains an ellipsis at the end. The translation above reflects the full argumentative structure leading up to the point where the source text breaks off.)*

Nor is there an absence of the auditory organ (*śrotra*) there, because, being composed of *ahaṅkāra*, it exists as a pervasive entity. Nor does it follow that all sounds would be perceived, because by the power of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), the sound acquires its existence only in a restricted location. Alternatively, one may accept that the non-pervasive [sound] has a dimension reaching as far as that location. Where there is no manifestation of a substratum, there the sound itself arrives at the location of the auditory organ by way of the dimension of its own substratum.

This is incorrect. For here, in the cognition "the sound is in the drum," the appearance occurs precisely at the location of the substrate by means of an inference based on a continuum (*santāna*). [Objection: But surely, since there is no specific cause [for distinction], there is simply an absence of certainty; namely, is it the sound residing right there that is perceived, or one inferred through the continuum? [Reply: It is not the perception of that which resides right there, because in some cases, even when separated from its substrate, it appears at the location of the ear. Nor is it the case that qualities possessing touch are perceived when separated from their substrate; thus, the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*).

If it is argued that even though sound is a quality of a substance possessing touch (*sparśavat*), its perception will occur through the arrival of its substratum—just as in the case of odor—we say no. In the case of odor, since its status as a quality of a substance possessing touch is well-established, and because it appears precisely at the location of the olfactory organ without the substratum being severed, it is logical that its subtle support arrives there. However, this is not the case for sound. Thus, it is not logical for the drum-sound, which has a subtle substance as its substratum, to arrive [elsewhere], because it is produced as inherent (*samaveta*) in the drum itself. For what is inherent in one place cannot become inherent in another. Even if one were to argue for its arrival based on the theory of inherence (*samavāya-vāda*), the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) would be that there would be a perception of both the sounds of the drum's parts and the drum-sound itself, since there is no distinction in their inherence in the subtle substance.

Likewise, the sound produced in a drum from the striking of the drumstick does not travel at all, because its substratum remains there. If one were to assume that the sounds produced in the subtle parts of that [drum] do travel because their substratum travels, then the deep resonance of the drum and such would never be heard. Nor should it be thought that, because it is derived from *ahaṅkāra*, the pervasive [sound] can function in the location of the drum and so forth; for the derivation from *ahaṅkāra* has already been refuted previously. Furthermore, since the apprehension of the location of the drum and so forth by the auditory organ is impossible, it follows that there could be no apprehension of the sound as delimited by that location.

Now, if it is argued that for one who knows the convention, when there is an inference of the substratum (the drum) from hearing the sound, the sound appears as delimited by the thought, "This is the sound of a drum"? Then you have arrived at my own path. How so? Because we admit that when the substratum is inferred through the medium of the series [of sounds] from hearing the sound, there is the appearance, "The sound is here in the drum.
Thus, it is established that sound is not a specific quality of a tangible substance, because it is perceived elsewhere than its substratum.

Likewise, when a single musical instrument is being played, because many notes such as *ṣaḍja* and others are perceived, sound cannot be a quality of that [instrument]. For instance, if sound were a quality of the musical instrument, how could there be the existence of many sounds—perceptible by the same sense organ—within a non-pervasive substance? If it were argued that this is like a variegated color (*citrarūpa*), we say no; for in that case, a single effect is produced from various forms. As it has been stated: "Various forms initiate a single effect. However, a single sound is never observed to be initiated by various sounds in this manner. Furthermore, a variegated auditory appearance of a single sound at one time is not possible here, because sounds appear sequentially. Moreover, if one were to accept the production of a variegated sound like a variegated color, it would follow that it should be perceived simultaneously; yet there is no sequential manifestation, since it has already been stated that there is no evidence for its existence [in that way]. And if one accepts its production sequentially due to conjunction (*saṃyoga*), then sound does not possess the specific qualities of tangible substances, owing to its dissimilarity to them. Enough of this excessive detail.

But one might ask: since the proposition (*pratijñā*) is presented here immediately after the statement of the reason (*hetu*), what is the purpose of this reversal of the members of the syllogism? It is simply to demonstrate that there is no such fixed rule in this treatise. For instance, [the author] shows that the "premature statement" (*aprāptakāla*), defined as "the statement of the members of the syllogism in reverse order" (Nyāyasūtra 5.2.11), is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) only in the context of debate (*jalpa*), not in the context of a formal treatise (*śāstra*). Others maintain that it is for the sake of obtaining the illustrative examples (*udāharaṇa*) and other members; however, that is unnecessary, because the meaning can be conveyed even without a slight reversal, since those members are accepted in various ways.

[Objection: Since an object is determined by a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) alone, the presentation of multiple reasons regarding one and the same object is indeed useless. Alternatively, it must be understood—on the grounds that the presentation of another means of valid cognition would otherwise be inexplicable—that the preceding [means] lacks the capacity to determine the object, or that it determines an object not previously known, because it merely restates what has already been apprehended. For if another means of valid cognition were to operate even upon an object already apprehended, there would be the undesirable consequence of never reaching a final conclusion. Therefore, since the objects of the various means of valid cognition are mutually exclusive, the presentation of multiple reasons serves only for the sake of complete comprehension. [Response: This is not so, because we do not maintain such a restrictive rule in all cases. Thus, the observation of multiple methods for a single object in a treatise is not a fault, for such a work aims to benefit others. Furthermore, since those to be instructed have diverse inclinations, multiple reasons are presented so that some might understand through a particular method with little effort. Nor is any of these means invalid here, because they all produce valid knowledge.

Nor does it follow that there must be an infinite regress of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaparamparā*), because even when an object has been determined, one does not necessarily admit the introduction of another means of valid cognition. For instance, there is dependence on another means of cognition only where another means of cognition exists, not where it does not. As, for example, when an object is understood through verbal testimony and one wishes to know it further through inference; or when it is apprehended by inference and one seeks to perceive it through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Likewise, even in the case of direct perception, after an object has been perceived by one instrument, one may perceive it again by another instrument. Similarly, when multiple means of cognition are applied toward a single object that is a source of pleasure, the purpose is the intensification of that pleasure.

Furthermore, the general definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not "the capacity to apprehend an object not previously apprehended," because this would entail the invalidity of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) and other such cognitions. For we shall explain that recognition and inference operate precisely upon an object that has already been apprehended.

Now, one might argue that [the object in question] must be a quality of the self (*ātmaguṇa*), like pleasure and so forth, because it is a particular quality residing in a single location and because it is a momentary particular quality; to this he replies: "Because it is perceptible by the external sense organs," and so on.

Now, if the previous inference were faultless, there would be no occasion for another inference at all. This is not so; for if sound were a quality of the self (*ātman*), it would not be perceived by the ear, and thus both inferences would suffer from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*). To explain: the ear is not the self, because it is not an agent. Nor is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) itself the ear, because that is an external instrument (*bahiḥkaraṇa*). Alternatively, if [the internal organ] were admitted [to be the ear], then as long as there is perception of pleasure and so forth, there ought to be perception of sound; consequently, deafness would be impossible.

Now, [you might argue that] the apprehension of sound belongs to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) because the activity of the [external organs] has ceased. If that were so, then pleasure and other such qualities would not be apprehended. Furthermore, it is never observed that an instrument, such as the eye, whose activity has ceased with respect to one object, can manifest another object elsewhere. Moreover, the auditory organ (*śrotra*) cannot consist of anything from earth up to air, because its capacity is determined to be restricted to the production of the sense of smell and the others. Nor is it possible for space (*dik*) and time (*kāla*) to have the nature of the auditory organ, because the external senses are material (*bhautika*). By the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the auditory organ must be something else; and if that were the case, there would be no apprehension at all of sound, which is a quality of the self (*ātman*), and thus the reason would be unestablished in its substratum (*āśrayāsiddhatva*). Yet sound is indeed apprehended by an external sense-organ; therefore, it is not a quality of the self. And thus: Sound is not a quality of the self, because it is perceptible by an external sense-organ. Whatever is perceptible by an external sense-organ is not a quality of the self, just like color and so forth; and this [sound] is perceptible by an external sense-organ; therefore, it is not a quality of the self. By way of contrast (*vaidharmyeṇa*), however, [the argument applies to] pleasure and the rest. Consequently, sound is not a quality of the self, because it is perceivable by another self, like color and so forth. And qualities of the self are not perceivable by another self, just like pleasure and the rest.

[Objection: Surely, it is impossible for a sound to be perceivable by another self (*ātman*) with respect to its individual manifestation (*vyakti*).
