For instance, that particular sound-manifestation which has arisen and is inherent in one auditory organ does not exist in another. However, with respect to the universal (*jāti*), there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*), because even pleasure and the like are perceivable by another self. [Reply: This is not so. A sound is perceived by another [self] through a nature different from that by which it is produced. Pleasure and the like are not like this. To explain: due to an extremely intense impact, a single sound-manifestation arises pervading a vast portion of space and is indeed perceived by many. Nor is there a contradiction on the grounds of its non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛttitva*), because it does not pervade its own substratum. Furthermore, the acceptance of a continuum (*santāna*) is not contradicted, since we accept the production of sounds distinguished by degrees such as "more intense" and so forth. For instance, due to an extremely intense impact, a single sound-manifestation arises pervading a large, conceptualized portion of space; then, based on experience, there follows a sequence such as "more intense," and so on. Thus, for one who asserts that perceivability by another self is impossible with respect to the individual manifestation, there would follow the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*), because of the acceptance of a continuum.

Furthermore, sound is not a quality of the self (*ātman*), because it does not inhere in the self, just like color and other such qualities; for those which are qualities of the self, such as pleasure and so forth, inhere in that very [self]. Now, if one were to argue that "not inhering in the self" is not distinct from the property to be proven (*sādhya*), he says: "And because it is perceived as distinct from the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*). For instance, sound does not inhere in the self, because it is perceived as distinct from the ego-sense, just like color and other such qualities. Since these [qualities] do not function without a cause consisting of the self—as seen in their actual application—it is postulated that their status as being instrumental to the self (*ātmopakāritva*) is their cause.

Now, [the author] says "because it is perceivable by the sense of hearing" (*śrotragrāhyatvāt*) and so forth, in order to refute the claim that sound might be a quality of space (*dik*), time (*kāla*), or the internal organ (*manas*). Thus, sound is not a quality of space, time, or the internal organ, because it is perceivable by the sense of hearing. Whatever is perceivable by the sense of hearing is not a quality of space, time, or the internal organ, just as the universal "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*) and so forth; and sound is indeed perceivable by the sense of hearing; therefore, it cannot be a quality of space, time, or the internal organ. Furthermore, those things which are qualities of these [three] are not perceivable by the sense of hearing, such as number (*saṃkhyā*) and the like. Moreover, since the sense of hearing has been established as distinct from space, time, and the internal organ, if sound were a quality of those [three], it would follow that it could not be perceived by that [organ]. For instance, since sound is not connected with space and time, there would be no perception of sound as inherent in them.

Since the mind (*manas*) is of atomic dimension (*aṇuparimāṇa*), if sound were a quality of it, there would be the undesirable consequence that deep sounds would not be heard. Furthermore, in the absence of [the mind], sound would fail to arise in certain locations. Nor can the existence of a cause in a particular place be established solely by the effect, since an effect can exist otherwise [than through its specific cause]. Moreover, the perception of specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of atoms by a sense organ has never been observed, as is the case with pleasure and other qualities of all-pervading substances (*vibhudravya*). The mind is indeed of atomic dimension. Thus, if sound were a quality of space, time, or the mind, it could not be apprehended by the auditory organ. This is the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) expressed by the phrase: "And because of the absence of being a specific quality" (*vaiśeṣikaguṇabhāvācca*). That is to say, it is because of its status as a specific quality (*vaiśeṣika*)—meaning a quality belonging specifically to a substance—that this is so. For instance, if space, time, and the mind were taken as the subject of the proposition, the absence of specific qualities would be unestablished (*asiddha*) for them, precisely because they themselves possess specific qualities; thus, the reason is explained by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). When it is stated that space, time, and the mind lack specific qualities, the reason that sound is indeed a specific quality is thereby obtained. Consequently: Sound is not a quality of space, time, or the mind, because it is a specific quality. Whatever is a specific quality is not a quality of space, time, or the mind, just like color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth; and this [sound] is a specific quality; therefore, sound is not a quality of space, time, or the mind.

Others, however, considering that in the thesis "sound is not a quality of space, time, or the internal organ (*manas*)," the absence of being a Vaiśeṣika quality is not distinct from the thesis itself, state another reason (*hetvantara*). For instance: sound is not a quality of space, time, or the internal organ, because it is a mark (*liṅga*) of its possessor (*guṇin*) by virtue of being a quality. Whatever is a mark of its possessor by virtue of being a quality is not a quality of space, time, or the internal organ, just like pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth; and this sound is a mark of its possessor by virtue of being a quality; therefore, it is not a quality of those [three]. Those which are marks of space and time are not marks of their possessors by virtue of being qualities—just as the cognitions of "east," "west," and so on, and the cognitions of "simultaneous" and so on. For these are marks of those two because they qualify them, and [the cognition of pleasure is a mark] of the self (*ātman*) by virtue of being a quality. Likewise, although words such as "simultaneous" and words such as "east" and "west" are marks of those two because they qualify them, they nevertheless infer other substrata (*āśrayāntara*) by virtue of being qualities. Enough of this excessive detail.

And since the same refutation has already been stated regarding [sound] being a quality of the mind (*manas*), it follows by elimination (*pariśeṣa*) that sound, being a quality, serves as the inferential mark (*liṅga*) for the apprehension and delimitation of space (*ākāśa*). Elimination occurs when, after the possibility of one thing has been negated, it cannot apply to any other. Thus, this means of proof is sufficient to establish the object through its non-deviation from negative concomitance (*vyatireka-avyabhicāra*). To illustrate: Sound resides in a substance distinct from earth, water, fire, air, direction, time, self, and mind; because it is a quality while there exists a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that sublates its subsistence in those [others]. For whatever does not reside in a substance distinct from those [eight], and for which there exists a valid means of knowledge sublating its subsistence in them, is not a quality—just like color (*rūpa*) and so forth. But sound is not like that; therefore, it is established that sound resides in a substance distinct from those, and that substance is space (*ākāśa*). Now, is that [space] one or many? He says: "Its oneness is established because there is no distinction in the inferential mark, namely sound. For sound is the inferential mark of space, and because it is undifferentiated, it does not indicate plurality.

Is it not the case that the non-distinctness [of sound] is unproven, because sounds are diverse? For instance, since the diversity of effects cannot exist without the diversity of causes, those sounds distinguished by variations such as intensity and so forth must have a diverse cause; thus, the manifoldness of their substratum is established. And if one were to maintain that there is diversity of effects even without diversity of causes, then there would likewise be no fourfold nature of atoms. One might argue that even in that case, a diverse effect such as earth and so forth will arise from a single cause. [If you reply: "In that case, the diversity of the cause is inferred from the diversity of the effect," then this is equally applicable to the diversity of sound; so enough of this.

That is incorrect. Since a variety of sounds is perceived even through a variety of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), there is no multiplicity in their substratum. Thus, from a most intense impact, a most intense sound arises, and from a mild one, a mild one, and so forth. Nor should it be argued that the same applies to earth and the other elements; for in those cases, the fourfold effects are seen to arise from distinct material causes (*upādāna*), and thus atoms of those respective types are understood to be of exactly four kinds. As for the variety of effects, it arises solely from the variety of causal complexes (*sāmagrī*). In this regard, one should understand—as the case may be—that in some instances there is a difference in the cause, in others a difference in action (*karman*), and in others yet another factor. It is true that here the variety of sound is established even by a difference in the [non-inherent] cause, and thus there is no difference in the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*); however, because this is indistinguishable from the evidence provided by the sound itself, it does not establish [the existence of] multiplicity.

Now, if it is argued that even though plurality is not established, unity cannot be established without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and therefore a *pramāṇa* must be stated—[the author] says: no. Since the existence of number is established by [the category of] substantiality (*dravyatva*) itself, and since there is an absence of a *pramāṇa* for plurality, unity alone is established. Furthermore, having bypassed dimension (*parimāṇa*), which follows immediately after number and has reached its turn, why is there a definition of separateness (*pṛthaktva*) by skipping the proper sequence? To this he says: "Because of following after that" (*tadanuvidhānāt*). Following after that [unity] means concomitance (*sāhacarya*); for wherever there is unity, there necessarily is single-separateness (*ekapṛthaktva*). However, such following after that does not exist in the case of dimension. For instance, the specific following after that is as follows: wherever there is unity, there necessarily is single-separateness. But there is no such specific following after that in the sense that wherever there is unity, there necessarily is minuteness (*aṇutva*) or largeness (*sthūlatva*). Therefore, separateness is defined first.

Thus, he asks from what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) the supreme magnitude (*paramamahat-parimāṇa*) exists in space (*ākāśa*), and answers: "Because of the mention of pervasiveness" (*vibhavavacanāt*). He demonstrates this in the aphorism: "Space is great because of its pervasiveness; likewise is the self (*ātman*); and the mind (*manas*) is atomic due to the absence of that [pervasiveness]" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.1.22–23). By the word "because of pervasiveness" (*vibhavāt*), which is a general term for the cause, its supreme magnitude is intended by implication. For indeed, the supreme magnitude of a pervasive substance is established in cases such as the self; here too, it is proven in the same way: "Space is supremely great, because of its pervasiveness, like the self. And when all non-pervasive things are taken as the subject (*pakṣa*), this is a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekānumāna*). When it is stated that "the supreme magnitude of [substances] beginning with space and ending with the self follows from their pervasiveness," the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is: "those which do not possess supreme magnitude do not possess pervasiveness."

Now, what is this "all-pervasiveness" (*vibhutva*)? It is conjunction with all elemental substances (*bhūta*). Others, however, consider that all-pervasiveness is the inherence (*samavāya*) of sounds produced everywhere in space (*ākāśa*), or, in the presence of that [inherence], the state of being fully manifest. Alternatively, it is established as "supreme magnitude" (*paramamahattva*) because, while not having atomic dimension (*aṇuparimāṇa*) as its locus, it is an eternal substance (*nityadravya*). Likewise, he shows the aphorism: "Because of the mention of the cause of sound, [there are] conjunction and disjunction" (*saṃyogavibhāgau*) [Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.2.36], and "The production of sound is from conjunction, from disjunction, and from sound" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.30). For indeed, since it is stated that conjunction and disjunction are the non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of the production of sound, inherence in space is obtained. Otherwise, in the absence of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), there would be no status as a non-inherent cause; and there is no other non-inherent cause [for sound]. Since space thus possesses qualities (*guṇavat*), it is a substance (*dravya*)—like an atom—because of possessing qualities and because of not being dependent on anything else (*anāśrita*). For instance, an atom is observed to possess qualities and to be independent, and yet it has the nature of a substance; this [possession of qualities and independence] is not possible for that which is not a substance.

Now, as to whether space (*ākāśa*) is eternal or non-eternal, he says: “It is eternal because of the absence of causes, both homogeneous and heterogeneous. To explain: it has no homogeneous inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), because space is a single entity. Nor is there any heterogeneous non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), because in the absence of a homogeneous [cause], its conjunction [which would serve as such] is also absent. Furthermore, since the production of a real effect is not possible without an inherent and non-inherent cause, space is established as eternal due to its being a non-effect (*akāryatva*). And for this reason, it is “the instrumental cause (*nimitta*) for the perception of sound by all living beings. Although space is one, he demonstrates that it performs multiple purposeful actions. Space is not the cause of the perception of sound merely by its existence; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of sound being perceived without distinction by all living beings everywhere, since all sounds would be equally inherent in space. Therefore, he says: “by way of being the auditory organ (*śrotrabhāvena*),” meaning by way of being the sense of hearing.

"What is that ear? he asks, and replies: "The ear, moreover, is a region of space (*nabhodeśa*) designated as the auditory cavity. That by which one hears is the "auditory organ" (*śravaṇa*); it is so called because it is both that [organ] and a cavity. A region of space whose designation is "auditory cavity" is what is meant; it is the ether (*ākāśa*) characterized by its conjunction with the ear-socket (*karṇaśaṣkulī*). Likewise: "It is bound by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) which bring about experience caused by sound. That which has sound as its cause is so described; and that which brings about such experience is "experience-causing"; it is "bound" by those two, meaning it is assisted or conditioned by them.

[Objection: Even so, since the region of space—characterized by its conjunction with the auditory canal and assisted by a specific unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*)—is not something other than that [space], would there not be the perception of all sounds? [Reply: This is not so. If the auditory organ (*śrotra*) is space characterized by conjunction with the auditory canal, then because that [conjunction] does not pervade [the whole of space], there is no apprehension of all [sounds]. Although sounds are co-inherent in the same object as the conjunction with the auditory canal, nevertheless, due to the absence of a specific proximity (*pratyāsatti*), there is no apprehension. For only that sound which possesses proximity to the conjunction with the auditory canal is perceived. And it is not the case that all sounds are thus [perceived], because they do not pervade [the whole of space].

Nor should it be argued that there is no perception at all because [the sound] is produced in a location distinct from the portion of space enclosed by the ear-cavity; for, since the perception of sound would otherwise be inexplicable, it is established—by way of the principle of a continuous series—that [the sound] arrives at the location of the auditory organ. Enough of this.

Now, why is it that the deaf do not perceive sound even when there exists a portion of space obstructed by the conjunction with the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*)? He says: "Because of the absence of a cooperative cause" (*sahakāryabhāvāt*), and so forth. Since the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) which is the cooperative cause for the perception of sound is absent, the perception of sound does not occur; thus, deafness is logically established.

“Time is characterized by the notions of priority and posteriority, simultaneity and non-simultaneity, slowness and quickness. Since there is no other cause for the arising of those notions—which are distinct from previous notions regarding objects—that which is the cause therein is time. It is the cause of the production, persistence, and destruction of all effects, as indicated by its designation. It is the basis for the conventional usage of moments (*kṣaṇa*), instants (*lava*), twinklings (*nimeṣa*), units of eight (*kāṣṭhā*), units of fifteen (*kalā*), hours (*muhūrta*), watches (*yāma*), days and nights, half-months, months, seasons (*ṛtu*), solstices (*ayana*), years, yugas, kalpas, manvantaras, minor dissolutions (*pralaya*), and the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*). Its qualities are number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, and disjunction. (PDhS)

“Because there is no distinction in the marks of time, its unity is established. Its plurality follows from its conformity [to various objects]. From the statement ‘time is the cause,’ its dimension is that of the infinitely great (*paramamahat*). From the statement ‘because of the priority of its cause,’ it possesses conjunction. From the fact that it causes the destruction of those [conjunctions], it possesses disjunction. Its status as a substance and its eternity are established, just like space. Although it is essentially one because there is no distinction in the marks of time, there is a figurative attribution of plurality—like a jewel or a cook—due to the differences in the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) consisting of the commencement, accomplishment, persistence, and cessation of the activities of all effects.”

Now, for the purpose of defining and examining time (*kāla*) as that which possesses the aforementioned general characteristics, there begins the section starting with: "Time has as its inferential mark the cognitions of priority and posteriority, simultaneity and non-simultaneity, slowness and quickness. (*kālaḥ parāparavyatikarayaugapadyāyaugapadyacirakṣiprapratyayaliṅgaḥ*) and so forth.

And here, considering that the very mark (*liṅga*) which establishes the existence of time serves as its differentiator from other things, [the author] did not state another definition. For instance: Time is distinct from others, because it has as its marks the cognitions of priority and posteriority, their transposition, simultaneity and non-simultaneity, and slowness and quickness; whereas that which is not distinct does not possess the aforementioned marks, such as earth and so forth; but time is not like that, therefore it is distinct. Alternatively, a conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is being established: the substance under dispute should be designated as "time," because it possesses the marks of the transposition of priority and posteriority and so forth.

Now, since there is no perception of an obstructing factor, how do these [notions] serve as marks for the existence of time? By virtue of being specific effects. It is observed that a specific effect arises from a specific cause. The notions of priority and posteriority, their reversal, simultaneity and non-simultaneity, and slowness and quickness are specific effects; thus, their being preceded by a specific cause is established. In this regard, the "reversal" (*vyatikara*)—that is, the inversion—of priority and posteriority caused by direction is perceived. For it is observed that where priority is produced with reference to direction, there indeed posteriority is produced; and where posteriority is produced, there indeed priority is produced, which constitutes a different object. Furthermore, a distinction from the causes of conventional usage is possible. Thus, when one observes an elderly person of inferior caste who is situated in a distant direction, and takes a young man of superior caste as the point of reference (*avadhi*), the cognition arises: "This one is prior to, or more remote than, the other. With reference to that [cognition], priority (*paratva*) arises from conjunction with a more distant spatial division of time. Conversely, taking the elderly person as the point of reference, when one observes a young man of superior caste who is situated in a proximate direction, but considers his developed beard and coarse skin, the cognition of proximity arises. With reference to that [cognition], posteriority (*aparatva*) arises from conjunction with a nearer spatial division of time.

In this case, because it differs from the "remoteness" (paratva) produced by direction, that [direction] itself cannot be the cause; nor is it possible for remoteness to be produced by genus (*jāti*), since it belongs to a lower category [than substance]. Furthermore, none of the elements such as earth can be the cause, as their causal capacity has not been established. That which remains as the cause is time (*kāla*).

But surely, since the two bodies are produced on the very same day according to the principle of the arising of qualities produced by cooking (*pākaja*), how can there be priority and posteriority? [The answer is: It is in relation to the revolutions of the sun from the time of birth. For instance, if one person has undergone more revolutions of the sun since birth than another, that person possesses priority; if the other has undergone fewer, that person possesses posteriority.

If it is argued that the revolution of the sun alone may suffice and there is no need for time, we say no. This is because [time] is inferred from cognitions such as "simultaneous" (*yugapat*). Furthermore, cognitions such as "simultaneous" do not arise from the revolution of the sun alone; for they do not occur when all [beings] are in the same solar revolution, nor is there a linguistic designation [for them]. Indeed, the designation is "simultaneous time," not "simultaneous revolution of the sun."

Nor should it be said that action itself is time, because this would entail the impossibility of such notions as "simultaneous" and so forth. For, since action is admitted to have the nature of action and thus possesses no specific distinctions, there would be an absence of such notions, as well as an absence of the distinction between priority and posteriority. Furthermore, action is not perceived as being "time. If action were distinct from the agent and the object and were the producer of specific cognitions, it would be a mere difference in terminology. If, however, it were not distinct [from the agent and object], there would simply be an absence of specific cognitions; enough of this elaboration.

Likewise, simultaneity (*yaugapadya*) is the state of being simultaneous (*yugapadbhāva*). It refers to the performance of actions by many agents simultaneously, or the arising of many effects at once. For instance, we observe cognition based on an agent in the form "these [agents] act simultaneously," and cognition based on an effect in the form "these [effects] were produced simultaneously. Now, it is not the mere agent or the mere effect that serves as the object of these cognitions, because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For even where an effect occurs sequentially, the agent and the action still exist there. This might be understood: we do not know from what specific cause this cognition arises—whether it takes the agent or the effect as its object. That which is the qualifier, distinct from earth and other such things, is Time (*kāla*). Thus, there is no such thing as simultaneity, non-simultaneity, or sequence [without it]. Furthermore, there is cognition based on an agent in the form "these [agents] act non-simultaneously," and cognition based on an effect in the form "these [effects] were produced non-simultaneously. Since in these cases too the objects are specific agents and actions, one must posit a cause distinct from earth and the rest; thus, Time is established.

Likewise, a single agent performs one effect slowly due to distraction or lack of desire, while he performs another quickly due to his eagerness for it. In this case, the cognitions "done slowly" and "done quickly," being distinct from one another, necessitate a distinct cause. Nor is the effect itself the cause, since it is common to both instances; nor is the agent alone the cause, as he too is common to both. Since nothing occurs without a cause, there must be a distinct cause; therefore, he says: "of those" (teṣām), i.e., of the cognitions such as "simultaneous" and so forth; "in their objects" (viṣayeṣu), i.e., in the agents and effects. Of what kind are they? "Distinct from previous cognitions" (pūrvapratyayavilakṣaṇānām); "previous cognitions" refers to those cognitions regarding the agents and effects, and [the new ones] are distinct from them. Since no other cause, such as earth and so forth, is possible for their production, that which is the cause is Time.

Now, since time is of a single uniform nature, it would follow that there could be no distinct cognitions [of temporal distinctions]. If it is argued that time is distinct due to the distinction in actions, and that the distinction in cognitions arises from being qualified by that [distinct] time—then, in that case, there is an unavoidable circularity (*itaretarāśrayatva*). For instance, since an action, by its very nature as an action, lacks any inherent distinction, how could it qualify time? Furthermore, if it is claimed that time is simultaneously qualified by an action, and the action is simultaneously qualified by that time, this is precisely the fault of circularity.

This is not so. For it is accepted that when there is an apprehension of the nature of mutually distinct actions within non-conceptual consciousness (*nirvikalpikā saṃvit*), time as qualified by those [actions] arises, and from that, cognitions such as "simultaneous" and so forth occur. Furthermore, the arising of conceptual cognition (*savikalpa*) from non-conceptual cognition is desired [by us]. Alternatively, the action itself is qualified by its own nature, and time, acting as its auxiliary, produces the cognitions of "simultaneous" and so forth. Moreover, in this case, time is not the qualifier; rather, since a qualified effect arises, there must be a qualified cause.

Others, however, maintain that time is perceptible because the operation of inference and other means of knowledge is not perceived, and since [knowledge] is impossible without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For instance, the cognition of the qualifier is postulated through the inexplicability otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*) of the cognition of the qualified; and since no operation of another means of valid cognition is perceived therein, that [cognition] is indeed perception itself.

[Objection: But surely, even though all causal factors (*kāraka*) have a specific function in the production of the cognition of the qualified (*viśeṣya*), there is no reason for distinction such that only one [factor] is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and not another. [Reply: No. Because in the production of the cognition of the qualified, only one [factor]—namely, the qualifier together with its own object-cognition (*svālambana-jñāna*)—has this specific function; this alone is "conjunction" (*anurāga*). Furthermore, a qualifier is that which generates a cognition colored by itself (*svānurakta-pratyaya*); it does not impart its own form (*ākāra*), nor does it generate a cognition expressed by its own word, because that is impossible. Indeed, the qualifier does not impart its own form. *I,123*

Because the theory of [knowledge possessing] forms has been refuted, it is also impossible for knowledge to be expressed by a qualifying word with respect to the qualified object, since the cognition "a staff in the person" does not arise. If it is argued that there is no status as a qualifier because it is impossible for the staff to impart a specific excellence (*atiśaya*) [to the person], we say no; for its very nature is excellence, insofar as it generates a qualified cognition. And that cognition is the excellence, because when it exists, the effect exists.

Now, if it is argued that there is no evidence for the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) being the objects of distinct cognitions—since the cognition of the qualifier prior to the arising of the cognition of the qualificand does not show it to have that [qualificand’s] form, nor is there a sequential means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—we reply: Furthermore, being the object of distinct cognitions is not pervaded by the relation of qualifier and qualificand; nor is the relation of qualifier and qualificand necessarily sequential. Thus, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in both cases. For instance, although the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*) are objects of distinct cognitions, they do not stand in the relation of qualifier and qualificand; thus, there is a deviation. Nor can the relation of qualifier and qualificand serve as the reason (*hetu*) when "sequence" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), because it is too common (*sādhāraṇatvāt*), since it is excluded from both the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). Nevertheless, if the qualifier and the qualificand were objects of distinct cognitions, the resulting comprehension would have the character of perception (*pratyakṣa*). To explain: the qualifier apprehended through inference, by functioning together with the sense-object contact, would be included within the causal complex of perception (*pratyakṣasāmagrī*); consequently, the comprehension produced by that [complex], namely "this place possesses fire," would be a result of perception.

Furthermore, an inference of fire without a substratum is not possible beforehand. Likewise, when fire itself is being inferred, it is perceived as qualified by "fire-ness" (*agnitva*); thus, there must first be the apprehension of "fire-ness. In that case too, since fire is the qualifier, there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*). If it is argued that the inherence (*samavāya*) of "fire-ness" is the qualifier of fire? Even there, whether "fire-ness" or "fire" is the qualifier, the same fault remains; for since an unqualified entity exists everywhere, its capacity to function as a qualifier is untenable. If it is argued that the mountain is the qualifier of fire? There too, "mountain-ness" and the inherence therein would be the qualifiers, leading to the same fault as before. If it is argued that the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) with fire is the qualifier of both the mountain and the fire? Then there are two things conjoined, and their conjunction [would require another], which leads back to the previously mentioned defect. Therefore, one who accepts inference as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) must admit a single cognition whose object is both the qualifier and the qualified. And because of the perception of the mountain as qualified by smoke, there arises the comprehension of it as qualified by fire.

Now, if the two fingers are the objects of a single cognition—as in the case of the position that they share one and the same cognitive object—how can there be the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*)? [If you say it is] by way of the relationship of primary and subordinate (*pradhāna-upasarjana-bhāva*), then [we ask]: why is that so? If you reply that this is the same even when they are objects of distinct cognitions, then consider this: since there is no difference in their being objects of distinct cognitions, how is there a restriction such that "this is the qualifier" and "this is the qualified"? If you say it is because of the relationship of primary and subordinate, then we agree; for there is no fault in this even when they are objects of a single cognition.

Furthermore, this relationship of qualifier and qualified (viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva) has a single referent and is not included within the category of "dharma" (quality), because it is excluded from each of those [categories]. Nor is it included within the categories such as "substance" (dravya) and so forth, because it is perceived among the six [categories]; for none of these, such as substance and the rest, is perceived among the six.

Now, if it is argued that the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) is an unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) distinction that serves as the cause for a distinct cognition, then, given its unity, the determination that "this is the qualifier" and "this is the qualified" would be untenable, because the state of being qualifier and qualified would be one and the same. For instance, that which is the state of being a qualifier would be the very same as the state of being a qualified; thus, for a single person at one and the same time, that very thing would be both the qualifier and the qualified. But this is not the case. Therefore, the relation of qualifier and qualified is not an unseen distinction within the qualified entity itself. Furthermore, if it is argued that there is no single perceived entity fixed as either qualifier or qualified, even so, the relation between qualifier and qualified would still not exist.

Therefore, the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) should be understood according to the circumstances: in some cases it is conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and in others it is inherence (*samavāya*). Likewise, even in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*), the relationship of qualifier and qualified is simply the connection between the particular [non-existent object] and the eye or other sense organs, because it generates a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭapratyaya*) by means of that [connection] which exists. Nor is the causality of the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) denied here, since it is common to all effects. Nor does the unseen merit/demerit preclude the operation of perceived causes, for if it did, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the body and so forth also being non-existent. For instance, one might argue: "Let the unseen merit/demerit alone be the producer of pleasure and so on; enough with the postulation of the body and such. If, however, the body and so forth are accepted because they are perceived despite the presence of the unseen merit/demerit, then the relationship of qualifier and qualified must likewise be accepted as the connection between the particular [object] and the eye or other sense organs, precisely because it is perceived.

If it is argued that since [the quality] does not reside in the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), how can it be its property? No; for it does not reside in it with respect to the operation of something unseen (*adṛṣṭavat*). Furthermore, if they were the objective supports (*ālambana*) of a single cognition, the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) between "fragrant" and "substance"—which are grasped by different sense organs—would not be possible, for it is never observed that a single cognition is produced by two different sense organs. This is not so. Since there is no subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the qualifier and the qualified being the objective supports of distinct cognitions, this [cognition "fragrant substance"] is a synthetic cognition (*anusandhānajñāna*). For instance, having perceived the odor with the nose, one subsequently synthesizes the substance with the mind through either sight or touch, thinking, "The substance is fragrant. Nor should it be said that every cognition of a qualified object is a synthetic cognition, for in those cases there is no subverting argument. Likewise, if the qualifier and the qualified were the objective supports of distinct cognitions, there would be no memory such as, "I saw a man with a staff," because memory must have the nature of a prior experience (*anubhava*).

If it is argued that, because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the cognition of the person—as in expressions such as "bring the man with the staff"—the cognition of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) has that [staff] alone as its objective support due to the person's connection with a single action, we say: no. Since the person is the primary object of qualification (*viśeṣya*), its connection with the action and its coreferentiality are indeed logically consistent; enough of this excessive detail.

Others, however, maintain that if [the qualifier and the qualified] were the objective support (*ālambana*) of a single cognition, there could be no relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva*), because those two would respectively have the nature of instrument (*karaṇa*) and object (*karman*). For indeed, that by which something is qualified is the "qualifier," which is an instrument; that which is qualified is the "qualified," which is the object. And this [distinction] would not exist if they were the objective support of a single cognition, since both would then be objects. Nor, if its operation were unknown, would it differ from the eyes and other [senses], as there would be no distinction in their being auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*); thus, that [distinct] cognition is postulated. Furthermore, if a staff qualified by "staff-ness" (*daṇḍatva*) were intended to be the qualifier of a person, then for that [staff] too there would be another [qualifier], leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If the staff itself were the qualifier of "staff-ness," there would be mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*), resulting in the undesirable consequence that there is no cognition of the qualified. Yet, such a cognition of the qualified does exist; therefore, by the principle of "otherwise inexplicability" (*anyathānupapatti*), it is understood that there is merely a cognition of the qualifier.

Regarding what was stated—that this cognition of the qualified (*viśeṣya*) prior to its arising does not show the nature of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*)—it must be examined: what is this "nature of the qualifier"? For the nature of being a qualifier does not appear in the stick [as its object] in the same way that "stick-ness" (*daṇḍatva*) and so forth do. Now, if being a qualifier consists in producing a cognition colored by itself, and if that means producing the cognition of the qualified together with a cognition whose object is itself, then there is a contradiction of your own tenets. Nor do we see any sense of "coloring" when two things are objects of a single cognition, since [we have already] refuted such things as their being denotable by the same word. Furthermore, temporal sequence is not the cause of the relation between qualifier and qualified, as that is not admitted. On the contrary, the cognition of the qualified indeed shows the cognition of the qualifier; otherwise, it would be impossible for it to be qualified by that. As for the claim that because it is not apprehended through inference, it must be the result of perception—that is incorrect. For here, due to the presence of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*), we admit that they are objects of a single cognition. However, such a subverting argument does not exist in all cases.

Others, however, maintain that when there is an inference of fire immediately following the perception of smoke, the cognition "this mountain possesses fire" is indeed a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); for otherwise, the demonstrative indication of immediacy as "this" would not be possible. And in this regard, it must be asked: if the subject qualified by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) were itself the object to be proven (*sādhya*), how could this [inference] function as a means of proof?

As for the question of whether this relationship between qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and qualified (*viśeṣya*) is one or many: even if its unity is accepted, there is no lack of distinction between the qualifier and the qualified, because there exists another unique cause [for their differentiation]. For it has been stated that the qualifier is defined by its capacity to produce a cognition colored by itself, whereas the qualified is defined by being the object of the cognition of the qualified; furthermore, the relationship of qualifier and qualified merely acts as a cooperative factor (*sahakārī*) in the arising of the cognition of the qualified, but it is not the cause of their distinction.

Furthermore, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*) alone do not constitute the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*), because that relation is absent in the case of inherence and in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*). If it is argued that even here there is a connection between the qualified object and the sense organ, we say no; for that [connection] does not reside in the qualifier. Nor can its residence [in the qualifier] be claimed on the basis of an operation, as is the case with the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), because conjunction and inherence are never observed elsewhere [than in their own substrates]. For if one were to maintain that conjunction and inherence reside in the qualifier by virtue of an operation, then there would be a perception of non-existence and inherence even without a connection to the qualified object; for it is observed that they produce perception only where they themselves reside. As for the unseen force, however, although it inheres in the self, it is common to the production of all effects; thus, whether conjunction and the like exist or not, the operation of the unseen force alone is indeed admitted. And that [unseen force], while appearing as if connected to both [the self and the object] by virtue of its operation, is not actually connected in the ultimate sense.

Nor is it the case that a metaphorical object cannot serve as a concomitant cause for a sense organ, for the absence of such a concomitance is established by the impossibility of [the resulting] direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) being otherwise. Furthermore, it is observed that even something metaphorically attributed to the auditory organ serves as a concomitant cause for the cognition of sound. As for the claim that this is a synthetic cognition (*anusandhānajñāna*) such as "the fragrant substance," that is incorrect; for if it were so, the same consequence would follow in other cases as well. Moreover, since there is no subverting argument against these two being the objects of distinct cognitions, that very [view] must be accepted.

Nor is there any impossibility of the recollection, "I saw the man with a staff," because even though the impression produced by the cognition of the qualifier acts as a cooperative cause for the cognition of the qualified object, that [recollection] still arises through the production of an [additional] impression.

As for the claim that, even though the qualifier and the qualified share the same objective support within a single cognition, the connection with the action and grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) are possible because the qualified is predominant—that is not correct. For it is precisely the nature of this predominance that must be examined. When there is a shared objective support within a single cognition, one must consider what constitutes this predominance. Furthermore, regarding coreferentiality, since there is no difference in the fact that both share the same objective support within a single cognition, there is no basis for the distinction that it belongs to the cognition of the person and not to the cognition of the staff; thus, there is an absence of a cause for such a qualification.

Now, [it may be argued that] grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) arises because two things having distinct qualifying causes (*viśeṣaṇanimitta*) reside in a single object—as in the cognition "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*), where the staff is the qualifier in relation to the man. However, since there is no other qualifier for the staff when it itself functions as a qualifier, there can be no coreferentiality [between the staff and the man]. This is not so; for we admit the appearance of multiple objects of cognition (*prameya*). To explain: if one admits that even "staff-ness" (*daṇḍatva*) and so forth appear as objects of cognition in the knowledge "not a man with a staff," then the statement regarding coreferentiality holds; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the Sūtra: "From the whiteness inherent [in the cloth], there arises the cognition of whiteness; from that [whiteness], the cognition of the white [cloth] arises, as they stand in the relation of cause and effect" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 8.1.6), which refers to the nature of cause and effect.

Furthermore, there is no mention of a real entity in the case of a metaphorical expression, because there is no sublation of its primary sense. Nor is the distinction in cognition due solely to a distinction in the object of cognition, since it can also arise from a difference in auxiliary causes.

[Objection: If that is so, then just as with the qualifier, a cognition must also be postulated for the relation; for, since the coloring by that [relation] does not appear therein, we must admit its operation even though it is unperceived, just like the eye and other [senses].

Nor is the state of being qualifier and qualified [established] through the metaphorical attribution of non-difference, because the cognition "the staff is in the person" would otherwise be untenable. Now, if...

If it is argued that there is a "synthetic cognition" (*saṅkalanājñāna*) which, having grasped the qualifier, the qualified, their relation, and the worldly state of affairs, and having combined them, cognizes [the object] in that manner and not otherwise—this is not tenable. For there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of such a multitude of cognitions. To explain: only the final cognition of the qualified object is observed to arise; and since that is possible even otherwise, the cognition of the qualifier is lost. Furthermore, there is no proof for the existence of any other intervening cognitions.
Nor is this conceptual cognition devoid of an object, because it conforms to the presence and absence of the [external] object and because no subverting evidence (bādhaka) arises.

Thus, since the apprehended qualifier produces the cognition of the qualified (viśeṣya), and since no operation of a logical mark (liṅga) or the like is perceived, time is an object of perception. True. Likewise, even though they share a single cognitive support (ālambana), cognitions such as "simultaneous" are not marks of time, because time itself is their support by way of being a qualifier. Furthermore, these [cognitions] are results of direct perception (pratyakṣa) due to their conformity with the sense faculties; so, enough of this.

He states the proposition that [the Lord] is the cause for the arising of all effects: "And He is the cause of the arising, subsistence, and destruction of all effects" (*sarvakāryāṇāñcotpattisthitivināśahetuḥ*). Arising is the acquisition of selfhood by entities; subsistence is the capacity to perform a succession of multiple effects; destruction is annihilation. He is the cause of these. Although all of this is already implied by the statement "the cause of all effects," the distinction is nevertheless stated with reference to specific intermediate particulars.

Now, as to how it is known that time is their cause, he says: “Because of its designation” (*tadvyapadeśāt*). For instance, there is a designation by means of time regarding origination, such as “it originated at midday” or “it originated in the afternoon. Regarding duration, there is “it endured until midday” or “and [until] the afternoon. Regarding destruction, however, there is “it perished in the morning” or “it perished at the end of the rainy season,” and so forth. On the other hand, the designation of an effect by means of its cause is, for example, “visual cognition” or “mental cognition.”

Now, it might be argued that designation is indeed possible even without a [real] causal basis, as in the cases "atoms are corporeal" or "the man is stick-bearer. True; nevertheless, since such designation is observed only when a relation exists, and no other relation is possible here, the relation of cause and effect is understood. Or, one might suggest there is conjunction (*saṃyoga*)? No; for that would entail the undesirable consequence that qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*karman*), and so forth could not be designated at all. Yet, designation does exist in those cases too, as in "sound in the forenoon," or likewise "upward motion," and so on.

Now, one might argue that this designation [of causality] will occur through inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*). This is not so; for if [time] were non-existent, it would follow that [the effect] would also be non-existent. Therefore, the relation of cause and effect alone must be accepted as the connection, since that is all-pervasive (*vyāpaka*). Likewise, the perception of an effect such as a flower occurs at a restricted time and not at another time; thus, its status as a cause is known through positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*). For instance, the blossoming of *pāṭala* and other flowers occurs only during the spring season and not at other times; this should be inferred for other effects as well. Similarly, time’s status as a cause is established from the conventional usage, "it awaits the time of production. For indeed, [the effect] is perceived by depending upon a cooperative factor (*sahakārin*), and without the cooperation of time, this usage regarding "production" would not occur.

Likewise, the atom (*paramāṇu*) is not the cause of notions such as "simultaneous" and so forth, nor is it the cause for the conventional usage of time units—such as *kṣaṇa*, *lava*, *nimeṣa*, *kāṣṭhā*, *kalā*, *muhūrta*, *yāma*, day-and-night, half-month, month, season, solstice, year, *yuga*, *kalpa*, *manvantara*, dissolution (*pralaya*), and the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*). For instance, a *kṣaṇa* is the moment of time characterized by an atom’s leaving the space it occupies in the sky.
It is said: "Two of those [atoms] are called a *lava*, and two *lavas* are a *nimeṣa*. Fifteen *nimeṣas* are proclaimed here as a *kāṣṭhā*."
"Thirty *kāṣṭhās* are said to be one *kalā*, and thirty *kalās* are one *muhūrta*. [From the *Purāṇa*.
In this manner, the definitions for the month and so forth, which are well-known, should be understood.

Furthermore, this conventional usage of "moment" (*kṣaṇa*) and so forth, being specific in nature, implies a specific cause. Since no other cause is possible—given the refutation of [causality by] action (*kriyā*) and the like—the existence of time (*kāla*) is established. To demonstrate that it is an inherent substratum (*samavāyin*) and possesses qualities (*guṇavat*), the statement is made: "Its qualities are number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction. In this regard, it is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) for the production of certain things; thus, through these qualities, time is endowed with qualities.

Now, since the existence of number is established by its very nature as a substance (*dravyatva*), the doubt arises as to whether it is one or many; to dispel this, he says: "Its oneness is established because there is no distinction in the marks of time" (*kālaliṅgāviśeṣādekatvaṃ siddham*). The mark of time, which consists of cognitions such as "simultaneous" and so forth, is not distinguished [in its essence]; thus, it does not indicate plurality. [Objection: But this is unproven, because the cognitions of "simultaneous" and so forth are mutually distinct. And a difference in effects cannot occur without a difference in causes; therefore, plurality alone is logical. [Reply: True. From the difference in effects, the difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is indeed known. And that [difference] can also be accounted for through the inclusion of other auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*). How, then, could there be plurality in time? It has been stated in this regard that what is augmented by specific actions produces specific cognitions. Nor should it be argued, as before, that this contradicts the fourfold classification of atoms; for the same response applies. Thus, since there is no proof for plurality and since a substance must be numerable, its oneness is established.

Likewise, it is said: "Separateness [is established] because it conforms to that. This means that there is conformity with unity due to their coexistence; for wherever there is unity, there must necessarily be a single separateness. However, since such coexistence does not exist with respect to specific dimensions (*parimāṇaviśeṣa*), separateness is defined by skipping its place in the sequence, for the sake of clarity in cognition.

Likewise, [it is said]: "Because time is the cause [of such notions], its dimension is that of the supreme great (*paramamahat*). He shows the *sūtra*: "The designation 'time' applies to the cause of notions such as 'simultaneous' and so forth" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.1.25). For indeed, the name or designation 'time' belongs to the cause of notions such as 'simultaneous' and so forth; and since those notions occur everywhere, time is all-pervading (*vyāpaka*). And from that, it follows that it possesses the dimension of the supreme great. Alternatively, one should state—as before—that it possesses the dimension of the supreme great because it is an eternal substance while not being the locus of atomic dimension (*aṇuparimāṇa*).

Likewise, [the author] states: "Conjunction [is established] from the mention of priority of the cause and so forth. He shows the sūtra: "Priority and posteriority in the effect arise from the priority and posteriority of the cause" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.2.22). For we shall explain in the examination of priority that the "priority of the cause" is intended figuratively as the conjunction of time with a substance, because it is the producer of priority.

“Because it is the destroyer of that [conjunction], disjunction [is established]” (*). For since that conjunction is produced, it must necessarily undergo destruction. And since there is no destruction of its substratum in all cases, it is destroyed only by disjunction; thus, disjunction is established. Now, he explains how time possesses substantiality and permanence: “Its substantiality and permanence are established like those of space” (*). That is to say, time is a substance because it possesses qualities and is not dependent [on another]. Furthermore, because it lacks both homogeneous and heterogeneous causes, it is permanent by virtue of not being an effect; such is the meaning of the extended application (*atideśa*).

Now, one might ask: "If time is indeed a single entity, how can there be the conventional usage of [terms] such as 'present' and so forth? To this he says: "Even though its unity is established directly (*añjasā*) by the non-distinction of the marks of time," and so on. Although the unity of time is established directly—that is, in its primary sense—due to the non-distinction of the marks of time, nevertheless, the commencement, the accomplishment of action, the persistence, and the cessation of all effects are what are called its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Due to the difference among these, there is multiplicity. Thus, the future is time characterized by the action of commencement; the present is that characterized by accomplishment, which is the attainment of self-nature (*ātmalābha*); likewise, persistence is the capacity to perform multiple successive effects, and that too is the present, because it pervades the existence of the object for as long as the object endures—so long as the object evolves, it is the present. Similarly, cessation is destruction, and that which is characterized by it is the past.

Now, as to how multiplicity is metaphorically attributed, he says: "Like a gem, or like a cook. Just as a gem, without abandoning its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), is metaphorically designated as manifold due to the difference in limiting conditions (*upādhi*)—such as being called "yellow" or "red"—so too here, the distinction between present and so forth arises through the influence of the limiting condition of distinct actions. Or, just as for a person, without abandoning his own essential nature, there is a distinction such as "cook" and so on due to various actions, so it is here as well. For if the distinction were real, logical contradictions would arise. To explain: if the distinction between the present and so forth were real and [the entity] were all-pervasive (*vyāpaka*), then because a single entity would be connected to multiple times, the consequence would follow that it could not be designated [by any specific temporal term]. For it could not be designated as "present," since it is also connected with the past and the future; nor could it be designated as "past," since it is also connected with the other two. Nor would it be non-pervasive [if it were merely designated as past], since it is connected with the others as well. In that case, one might object: how is it that for multiple persons in the very same location, there arise cognitions of the past, future, and present? These are indeed observed to occur thus. Furthermore, for a single person, the cognition of the "present" occurs in a single location upon perceiving an action currently taking place; for another, the cognition of the "past" occurs in that very same location upon the cessation of the action; and for yet another, the cognition of the "future" occurs upon perceiving an action about to arise. Thus, it is established that the production of various cognitions is due solely to the influence of the action, and not because of any real distinction in the entity itself.

“Space (*dik*) has as its defining mark the notions of ‘east,’ ‘west,’ and so forth. Taking a corporeal substance as a limit, it is that from which there arise in respect to corporeal substances themselves ten notions—namely, ‘this is to the east,’ ‘to the south,’ ‘to the west,’ ‘to the north,’ ‘to the southeast,’ ‘to the southwest,’ ‘to the northwest,’ ‘to the northeast,’ ‘below,’ and ‘above’; that is space. “Furthermore, its qualities are number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction. These are established in the same manner as those of time.”

“Since there is no distinction in the marks [of direction] and since direction is essentially one, the supreme sages have established ten conventional designations—such as ‘east’ and so forth—for the sake of the usage of the Vedas, the Smṛtis, and worldly affairs, based on the specific conjunctions of the blessed Sun as he revolves clockwise around Mount Meru, corresponding to the regions of the directions presided over by the world-protectors.”

“Then, by virtue of devotion, the ten directions are established. Furthermore, due to their being presided over by specific deities, they come to have ten designations: Māhendrī, Vaiśvānarī, Yāmyā, Nairṛtī, Vāruṇī, Vāyavyā, Kauverī, Aiśānī, Brāhmī, and Nāgī.”

Now, for the purpose of examining the definition of *diś* (direction), which has reached its turn [in the sequence], there is the section beginning with: “*Diś* is that which has as its inferential mark (*liṅga*) the cognitions of ‘east,’ ‘west,’ and so forth. Here, “*diś*” is the designation of the object to be defined (*lakṣya*). “Having as its inferential mark the cognitions of ‘east,’ ‘west,’ and so forth” is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*). Thus, “east” and “west” are “east-west”; those of which these are the first are so-called; and these are the “cognitions” (*pratyaya*). That of which these are the “inferential mark” (*liṅga*) is thus described.

In order to explain the summary statement, he says: "Taking a corporeal object as a limit, with respect to corporeal substances that have become objects [of cognition], that cause from which the ten notions—such as 'this corporeal substance is to the east' or 'to the south' of this corporeal substance—arise, is *diś* (space/direction). And thus, space is distinct from other things, because it has the notions of "east," "west," and so forth, as its inferential mark (*liṅga*); for whatever is not distinct does not possess such [notions], just like earth and the other elements. Alternatively, the conventional usage [of the term] is what is to be proven.

But is it not the case that cognitions such as "prior" and "posterior" occur only with respect to corporeal objects by virtue of mutual dependence? Thus, the stated definition is unestablished. This is not so; for if there were mutual dependence, it would follow that both [the notions] would be absent. To explain: if the cognition of "posterior" depends on "prior," and the cognition of "prior" depends on "posterior," then in the absence of one, the other would also be absent, resulting in the non-existence of both. Nor is it without a cause, because it arises at certain times, and because through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the operation of a corporeal substance is perceived, as well as its being the objective basis (*ālambana*) due to designations such as "finger. Furthermore, that [substance] in its undifferentiated state does not have the capacity to produce a cognition, because if it were undifferentiated everywhere, it would follow that the cognitions of "prior" and so forth would be indistinguishable in all cases.

Now, if it is argued that the cause is simply a material substance (*mūrtadravya*) serving as a limit (*avadhibhūta*), we say no; for such a substance is indistinguishable in all cognitions. To explain: if that were the cause, then wherever there is a cognition of "east," there alone would follow cognitions of "south" and so on, because there is no distinction [in the substance itself]. Nor is convention (*saṅketa*) alone the cause, for without a cause, convention cannot apply everywhere. Indeed, a word like "east" (*pūrva*), having been conventionally fixed to one thing in the absence of a single underlying cause, does not apply to another object. If it is argued that there exists a single cause for the application of conventions regarding "east" and other directions, by whose presence the word applies even to other objects, then that [cause] is indeed *dich* (space/direction). If it is further argued that direction, being undifferentiated, cannot produce differentiated cognitions, we say no. We shall explain immediately hereafter that even though direction is unitary, it produces differentiated cognitions by virtue of specific conjunctions (*saṃyoga*).

If it is argued that cognitions of "east" and so forth are objectless because they are conceptual (*vikalpaja*) and arise by the force of mental impressions (*vāsanā*), that is not so; for they are not sublated. A cognition that is not sublated cannot be objectless. It has already been stated that, as in the case of the cognition of white and so forth, the operation of the object—which is pointed out by the finger and so on—is perceived through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Nor is mental impression alone the cause here, because, according to the previous reasoning, it is impossible for it to exist apart from an object of cognition. Therefore, specific cognitions such as "prior" and "posterior" do not occur without a specific cause. Since no other cause in the form of earth and so forth is possible, and given the impossibility of any other cause, that which is the cause in this case is *diś* (space/direction); this follows the logical principle of the qualifier and the qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-nyāya*). Its causality in the production of all things should be understood as being like that of time (*kāla*).

In order to demonstrate that [space] is an inherent cause (*samavāyin*) and possesses qualities, he says: "Its qualities are number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction. Regarding this, he applies an analogy: "These are established as being like time. Likewise, because there is no distinction in the marks of direction and because there is an absence of specific marks, the oneness of space is established.

[Objection: But surely, since the cognitions of "prior," "posterior," and so forth indicate causes that are mutually distinct, plurality alone is logical. [Response: No; for, according to the reasoning already stated, the distinction between cognitions can be accounted for even by the distinction among their auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*). Therefore, since the connection with number is established through its very nature as a substance (*dravyatva*), and there is no evidence for plurality, unity is established.

Because it conforms to that oneness, it possesses single-separateness (*ekapṛthaktva*) by virtue of its concomitance. By the statement, "The term 'direction' (*dik*) denotes the cause of the notions of 'prior,' 'posterior,' and so forth," its supreme magnitude (*paramamahattva*) is established. Thus, since the notions of prior, posterior, and so forth do not occur anywhere without a cause, direction (*dik*) is all-pervasive, and therefore possesses supreme magnitude. Furthermore, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is established by the sutra: "Priority and posteriority [arise] from the priority of the cause and the posteriority of the cause" (VS 7.2.22). For instance, the "priority of the cause" refers to the conjunction of direction and a substance (*piṇḍa*) which produces priority; likewise, "posteriority" refers to the intended producer of posteriority, as we shall explain in the examination of priority and posteriority. Since conjunction is perishable due to being produced, and because the destruction of its substratum is impossible in all cases, it is destroyed even by disjunction (*vibhāga*); thus, disjunction is established—this is the meaning of the extended application (*atideśa*). Likewise, it is a substance (*dravya*) because it possesses qualities and is not itself supported by another. It should also be understood that it is eternal because there is no possibility of causes—whether of the same or different classes—for its production.

Now, he asks how the conventional usage of "east" and so forth with respect to a single direction could be possible, and says: “Even though [direction] is essentially one because there is no distinction in its indicative marks,” and so on. For in that case, although the oneness of direction is established in a primary sense (*añjasā*) since plurality is not established due to the lack of distinction among its indicative marks, nevertheless, there is a transformation of the case ending in the phrase “the conjunctions of the sun with the regions of the directions presided over by the world-protectors. Alternatively, when there is the intention to ask “to whom do those conjunctions of the blessed sun belong?”, the use of the genitive is indeed appropriate, as the relationship [of possession] exists.

Regarding the phrase “of regions of the directions protected by the world-guardians”: these are “tenfold,” meaning of ten types, distinguished as “eastern and so forth. They are “designations” (saṃjñā) established “by the supreme sages. To the question “for what purpose? he says: “for the sake of the practice of Śruti, Smṛti, and worldly convention. That is to say, for the sake of the practical usage of what are called Śruti, Smṛti, and the world. For there is Vedic (śrauta) practice such as “one should sacrifice a gayal in the northwestern direction”; Smṛti practice such as “one should eat facing the east”; and worldly practice such as “our elders used to sacrifice facing the east. [These designations are made] for the sake of establishing such well-known usages.

Now, as to how the Blessed One’s conjunction with the regions of the quarters occupied by the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) occurs, he says: “of one revolving clockwise around Meru. For, as it happens, even for one who circumambulates Meru, there arise specific conjunctions [with the quarters], and by virtue of those, the conventional designations of “east” and so forth are established; this is known through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). To explain: at the time of sunrise, because of the Sun’s conjunction with a particular region of the quarter, the convention “east” (*prācī*) arises—so called because the Sun first (*prāk*) moves toward that direction. Likewise, at midday, due to conjunction with a particular region of the quarter, the convention “south” (*dakṣiṇā*) arises. Similarly, in the afternoon, due to that conjunction, the convention “west” (*pratīcī*) arises. The same should be stated for the “north” (*udīcī*) and other directions as well.

[Objection: In that case, let that very conjunction with the sun be the cause for the conventional usage of "east" and so forth; there is no need for the postulation of [separate] directions. [Reply: No. If the sun itself were the object of the conventional usage of "east," "west," and so on, then by postulating yet another sun [for each], there would be an infinite regress; therefore, it is logical that there must be a different cause. Furthermore, since the revolution of the sun is not possible everywhere, it would follow that the conventional usage of "east," "west," and so forth would be absent in those places. Therefore, one must admit that although direction is a single entity, it is capable of specific conventional usage when augmented by various conjunctions.

Thus, by means of devotion and ritual service, the ten directions are established. Furthermore, due to the appropriation of these ritualized directions by deities, they come to have ten designations: that which is appropriated by Mahendra is the Māhendrī direction, that which is appropriated by Vaiśvānara is the Vaiśvānarī direction, and so it is for the others as well.

“Because of its connection with the nature of self, it is the Self. Since it is imperceptible due to its subtlety, its existence is established by means of the instruments—the ear and so forth—which are themselves inferred from the perception of sound and other objects. For we observe that instruments, such as an axe and the like, are employed by an agent; thus, by the well-known fact regarding sound and other objects, the one who accomplishes [their perception] is inferred.”

“Consciousness does not belong to the body, the senses, or the mind, because they are insentient. Consciousness does not belong to the body, because it is composed of the elements like a jar, because it is an effect, and because it is impossible [for consciousness] in a dead body. It does not belong to the senses, because they are instruments, and because we observe the recollection [of objects] even when the senses are impaired or when the objects are not present. Nor does it belong to the mind, because if it did not depend on other organs, there would be the consequence of simultaneous perception and memory, and because the mind itself is an instrument. By elimination, since it is an effect of the self, the self is thereby established. Furthermore, by means of activity and cessation—which are inherent in the body and capable of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful—the conscious controller of the body is inferred, just as a charioteer is inferred from the movement of a chariot; and [the self is also established] by means of the vital breaths and so forth.”

“How so? Because we observe modified actions in the air enclosed within the body, as in the case of one blowing a bellows. Because of the regular action of closing and opening the eyes, like the operator of a wooden machine. Because it is the cause of the body’s growth, healing of wounds, and the regrowth of broken parts, like a householder. Because of the action of the mind, which connects the instruments that perceive desired objects, like a child throwing a ball in the corners of a house. And because we observe a modification of the sense of taste following the perception of a visual object through the sequence of recollecting its flavor, a single perceiver of both is known, like a spectator looking through many windows. <PDhS>

“The possessor of qualities (guṇin) is inferred from the qualities of pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort. And these [qualities] are not qualities of the body or the sense organs. Why? Because they do not form a single syntactical unit with the notion of ‘I’ (ahaṅkāra), because they exist in specific locations, because they do not persist as long as the substance exists, and because they are not perceptible by the external senses. Likewise, it is because the word ‘I’ is distinct from words such as ‘earth’ and so forth. <PDhS>

“His qualities are cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, mental impression (*saṃskāra*), number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction. Regarding the section on the marks of the self (*ātmaliṅga*): from the beginning with cognition up to effort, these are established [as qualities of the self]. Merit and demerit are established because it is stated that they are not causes for the qualities of other selves. Mental impression is established because it is stated to be the cause for the production of memory. Number is established because of the statement regarding the distribution [of cognitions]. Distinctness is also established for this very reason. Likewise, dimension is established as ‘supremely great’ because of the statement ‘and thus the self. Conjunction is established because pleasure and the rest are produced by contact. Disjunction is established because it is the destroyer of that [conjunction]. <PDhS>

Now, for the purpose of examining the definition of the self (*ātman*), there is this section beginning with “because of its connection with selfhood” (*ātmatvābhisambandhāt*). The definition is either the connection with selfhood, or the inherence (*samavāya*) characterized by the self. For instance: the self is distinct from other things because of its connection with selfhood; whereas that which is not distinct from other non-selves is not connected with selfhood, such as earth and so forth; but the self is not like that, therefore it is distinct. Alternatively, the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is what is to be proven. Thus, the sentence should be construed as before, with the aim of defining the meaning of the term. Likewise, the objection to and resolution of the definition should be stated as before.

But surely all this is incoherent, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of a self (*ātman*). To explain: it is not perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), like color and so forth, because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) cannot be determined. Nor is there any inference (*anumāna*) connected with a self. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Since it is imperceptible due to its subtlety (*saukṣmya*), its comprehension is achieved through the sense organs, such as the ear, which are themselves inferred from the perception of sound and other objects. By "subtlety," what is intended is the absence of magnitude (*mahattva*) and other qualities inherent in a single substance possessing a specific form; it does not mean being possessed of an atomic dimension (*aṇuparimāṇa*). For this very reason, it is imperceptible.

But is this not improper? For that [self] appears in the cognition "I. Thus, the cognition "I am happy," "I am suffering," or "I have desire" is observed. Nor is this preceded by inference, because the operation of recollecting the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the marked (*liṅgin*) is not experienced. Nor is it verbal, since it arises even without words. Nor is this a mistaken cognition (*viparyaya*), because it is not sublated. Nor is it a doubtful cognition (*saṃśaya*), because its form is not experienced as such. Therefore, since it is of the nature of valid knowledge (*pramā*), when other means of knowledge are excluded, its function must belong to perception alone. It does not have the body as its object, because it arises through the operation of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). To explain: the body is not something to be delimited by the internal organ, because it is an external object.

[Objection: But if this is so, then how is the cognition "I am thin" or "I am fat" to be explained? [Response: It occurs through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), because a sublation (*bādhaka*) applies to the primary sense. For instance, just as one has the cognition "my servant," one observes the cognition of difference in the form "my body"; therefore, it is logical that the cognition "I" with respect to the body is merely metaphorical, just like [the cognition] regarding a servant. Furthermore, since metaphorical usage does not proceed without a cause, the fact of being a benefactor to the self (*ātmopakārakatva*) is postulated as the cause. As for the self, however, [the usage] is primary, because it is in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatva*) with the cognition "I am happy. For it is observed that wherever there is the cognition "I am happy," there alone is the cognition "I" perceived. Moreover, we shall explain later that the connection with pleasure and so forth belongs to the self alone, distinct from the body and other such things.

As for the claim that [the self] is like form (*rūpa*) and so forth because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) cannot be determined, that is incorrect, because the intrinsic nature does manifest as "I. Nor is it a fault that one thing is not perceived through the intrinsic nature of another thing, for that would entail the consequence that all objects would be imperceptible. Furthermore, there is no consequence that the manifestation "I" would occur with respect to another person's self, because that other self is not perceptible to oneself.
