And it has been stated that this cognition is born of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and does not originate from another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Nor does the fact that one self is imperceptible to another self entail that one's own self is likewise imperceptible, because that is sublated by self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*). Nor is there the consequence that other properties such as number (*saṃkhyā*) and so forth would be perceptible, because they are imperceptible due to the absence of their manifestation. For it has already been stated that only where a particular form (*rūpaviśeṣa*) is perceptible are number and the rest perceptible.

Now, [it may be argued that] because it is impossible for the self to be both the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) at one and the same time, it cannot be perceived; but that is not so. For this is possible through a difference in defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). To explain: agency (*kartṛtva*) is established by the presence of the definition of an agent, namely, being the substratum of knowledge and desire to act; and at that very same time, objecthood (*karmatva*) is established by the observation of being pervaded by the action (*kriyā*). Thus, there is no fault, since the determination of entities depends upon their defining characteristics. Nor should there be a contradiction between these two in a single substrate at one time, as there is between the agent and the instrument (*karaṇa*). For instance, agency consists in independence (*svātantrya*) while instrumentality consists in dependence (*pāratantrya*); since these two take the form of affirmation and negation, it is logical that they cannot coexist in a single substrate. However, such is not the case with agency and objecthood.

For this very reason, although there is a presence of affection for the self in cognitions such as "my body," the self functions merely as a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*), just as Śrīharṣa is in the cognition "the temple of Śrīharṣa"; for in both cases, there exists an obstructing factor (*bādhaka*). For wherever, despite the presence of affection, there is an obstructing factor to its being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*), there one postulates only the status of a delimiting factor. And in the case of the self, the existence of Śrīharṣa constitutes an obstructing factor, namely, the impossibility of [his] being either the agent (*kartṛtva*) or the instrument (*karaṇatva*).

Nor is it logical that the distinction between agent and so forth, being perceived within a single substratum (*dharmin*), should be merely illusory, because the difference in their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇabheda*) is real. This fault applies only to those for whom there is no difference in defining characteristics. Furthermore, since conceptual cognition (*kalpanājñāna*) has already been refuted previously, the arrangement of causes and so forth is not superimposed through conceptualization. Thus, because the distinctions of agent and so forth have different bases, when that very self is determined—whether by inference or by perception—that same status as an agent involves no fault.

[Objection: But if this is so, since the cognition "I" regarding the self (*ātman*) is a result of perception (*pratyakṣa*), the statement "while it [the self] is imperceptible due to its subtlety (*saukṣmya*)" is incoherent. [Reply: No, for this is stated with reference to the external sense organs (*bāhyendriya*). To explain: when it is asked why the self is not perceptible by the external senses like earth and other elements, the statement becomes coherent. It is not perceptible by the external senses because of its subtlety—due to the absence of a specific quality of form (*rūpa*) inhering in the same substrate, and the absence of magnitude (*mahattva*) which is concomitant with being composed of multiple substances. Thus, even though it is actually perceptible, it is designated as "imperceptible. And that being the case, its comprehension is achieved through the instruments (*karaṇa*) such as the ear and so forth. The phrase "by the ear and so forth" is to be applied to both [cases]. For instance: the apprehension of sound is the effect of an instrument, because it is an action, like the action of cutting. The same applies to the remaining [senses]. Since it is imperceptible by the instruments such as the ear and so forth due to the aforementioned subtlety, its comprehension is achieved by those very [instruments] acting as inferential marks (*liṅga*).

He states an inference for the existence of the ear and the other [senses] as well: "inferred from the apprehension of sound and so forth. This means they are inferred by the activities of apprehending sound, touch, form, taste, and smell; thus, they are "those inferred by those [activities]. For instance: the apprehension of sound has an instrument as its cause, because it is an activity, like the activity of cutting. The same applies to the remaining [apprehensions].

In order to establish pervasion (*vyāpti*), he says: "Because instruments such as axes and the like are seen to be employed by an agent. Just as instruments such as axes are employed by an agent, so too are the ears and other [senses] instruments; therefore, they are employed by an agent. For it is thus: the ears and other senses are instruments, they are employed by an agent, because they are instruments, like axes and the like.

Now, if it is here being argued that the soul is omnipresent because it is the agent [of action], then there is either a lack of the probandum (*sādhyavikalatva*) in the example, or, in the case of the contrapositive, the proving of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). This is not so; for in all inferences, the relationship between the probandum and the probans (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) is established through generality alone. If there were no pervasion (*anuvyāpti*) by way of specific instances, it would follow that all inference would be abolished. Furthermore, we shall explain in the section on that [inference] that inference is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Once the existence of an agent is established, his transcendence of the body and other such things follows by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*). Thus, he is inferred as the "accomplisher" (*prasādhaka*) not merely by means of instruments, but "by means of the manifestation (*prasiddhi*) regarding sound and the rest. Manifestation regarding objects such as sound is consciousness (*vijñāna*); by that, the self is inferred as the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). For instance: knowledge of sound and the like must be dependent upon something, because it is a quality (*guṇatvāt*). Whatever is a quality is dependent, just as color and so forth are; and knowledge is a quality; therefore, it is dependent. Its being preceded by an inherent cause follows from its being an effect, just like color and the like.

Now, fearing that [the argument] might result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by suggesting that consciousness resides in the body and so forth, he says: "Not of the body, the senses, or the mind" (*na śarīrendriyamanasām*). For others hold the view that, just like the vital breath (*prāṇa*), since consciousness exists when the body exists and is absent when it is absent, consciousness is a property of the body alone; the same should be inferred for the senses and so on. To negate this, he states: "Consciousness does not belong to the body, the senses, or the mind. Regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) in the context of worldly convention (*vyavahāra*), the reason (*hetu*) "because of being non-cognizant" (*ajñatvāt*) is not identical to the probandum. Alternatively, this is a presentation of his own established tenet (*svasiddhānta*): according to our system, these [three] do not possess consciousness. One might object: "If the body has no consciousness, then for what purpose did others state that 'the person (*puruṣa*) is the body characterized by consciousness'? Likewise, one might suspect that because [consciousness] follows the presence and absence of the senses, it belongs to the senses. Anticipating this, he says: "Because of being non-cognizant. For such statements do not proceed from one who perceives a contradiction in the case of a knower. Alternatively, some explain: "The mind" (*manāṃsi*) refers to the body and the senses themselves, as they are thought of by means of these [instruments]. They do not possess consciousness because their instruments are non-cognizant; the meaning is that they are composed of insentient causes.

Now, why is it that the instruments (karaṇas) lack consciousness? Because their effects lack consciousness. [Objection: But in that case, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (itaretarāśrayatva). [Reply: No; since both disputants agree that effects such as jars are insentient, the insentience of the instruments is established. And since the atoms which originate the body belong to that same class, if the body is produced from insentient causes, it too must be insentient. The same applies to the sense organs. Furthermore, if consciousness were present in the atoms, then because of the plurality of persons within a single body, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the cessation of practical activities such as recollection.

Furthermore, since positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) regarding the production of consciousness in relation to the body and the sense organs can also be established on the basis of their being its cause, how can they be considered its substratum? If it is argued that this involves the fault of postulating an unobserved entity, we say no; for there is indeed the existence of an object even when it is to be inferred, just as in the case of perception. This is because [the object] is apprehended by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, the existence of an inferable object is certainly present.

In this regard, he states "the body does not possess consciousness" (*na śarīrasya caitanyam*) in order to refute consciousness in the body. Here, however, if consciousness were taken as the subject (*pakṣa*), its being an effect of the elements would be unestablished; therefore, the body itself is taken as the subject. To explain: the body is devoid of the consciousness imagined by others, because it is an element and because it is an effect. Whatever is an element and whatever is an effect is devoid of consciousness, just like a jar; and so is the body; therefore, it is insentient.

Others, however, believe that the intended reason (*hetu*) is simply "because it is an effect of the elements" (*bhūtakāryatvāt*). That is incorrect, because there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) [from the probandum] precisely by what was stated as "because it is elemental" (*bhūtatvāt*). If it is argued that when one says "because it is an effect of the elements," there is a deviation with respect to the Self (*ātman*), we say no; for that [Self] is the very thing yet to be proven (*sādhya*). Deviation occurs only when [the reason] is already established. Furthermore, for one who already accepts the existence of the Self, the presentation of an inference would be entirely useless. Likewise, if one says "because it is an effect" (*kāryatvāt*), there is no deviation, and thus the word "elemental" (*bhūta*) would be redundant. Nor is there a deviation with respect to consciousness (*cetanā*), since consciousness, being devoid of sentience, belongs to the class of similar instances (*sapakṣa*). Therefore, only the two reasons [mentioned above] are logical. As for the transposition of the members [of the syllogism], the refutation has already been stated.

Likewise, [it is said]: “And because [consciousness] is impossible in the dead state. Since consciousness is not perceived in the state of death—just as color and other qualities are not perceived—it is not a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the body. For instance: consciousness is not a specific quality of the body, because it ceases to exist while the body is still present; for those things which cease while the body is present are not its specific qualities, such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth; whereas those which are specific qualities of the body do not cease while that [body] exists, such as color and the like. Nor does the negation of being a specific quality entail the attainment of being a general quality (*sāmānyaguṇa*), because the determination of the subject (*pakṣa*) and so forth depends upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*). For the opponent accepts that consciousness is indeed a specific quality of the body, and it is precisely that which is being negated here. Furthermore, the body itself is not made the subject here, because it would result in a fallacy of the reason having a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇatā*), given the reason: “because consciousness is impossible in the dead state. Likewise, there is the negation of consciousness in the sense organs: consciousness does not belong to the sense organs, because they are instruments (*karaṇa*), like an axe and so forth. It should also be observed that [they lack consciousness] because they are composed of the elements (*bhūta*) and because they are effects (*kārya*). For this reason as well, the sense organs do not possess consciousness: because memory is observed even when they are impaired. Nor is the existence of a quality seen when the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*) has perished. For instance: memory is not a quality of the sense organs, because it arises even upon their destruction; for whatever arises even upon the destruction of something else is not a quality of that thing, just as the color and form of a cloth [do not belong to a jar] even when the jar is destroyed; and likewise, memory occurs even when the sense organs are destroyed; therefore, it is not their quality.

If the senses were sentient, then because an action is not observed without an instrument, there would have to be other instruments [for those senses]. Those instruments would be the senses themselves, and since they are the very objects of dispute, they would be the self; thus, one would have to accept a plurality of persons within a single body. This being the case, just as Yajñadatta does not recognize an object perceived by Devadatta, there would be no recognition by one sense of an object perceived by another sense. Yet such recognition is observed; therefore, the senses are not sentient. Furthermore, if a single sense were accepted as the conscious presiding agent over all the instruments, there would be a difference in name only.

Now, [the opponent might argue] that consciousness (*caitanya*) will belong to the object. To refute this, he says: "And because recollection is observed even in the absence of the object" (*viṣayāsānnidhye cānusmṛtidarśanāt*). For instance, recollection is seen when the object is absent or has perished; yet a quality of that [object] does not persist upon its destruction. Next, [the opponent might suggest] that it will be a quality of the mind (*manas*). To refute that, he says: "Nor is it of the mind" (*nāpi manasaḥ*). Consciousness is a quality [of something else], because it is an instrument (*karaṇa*), like an axe and so forth. If the mind were the agent and yet required another instrument for the perception of pleasure and so on, there would be a mere difference in terminology. That is to say, that which is the instrument for the perception of pleasure and so on would simply be the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and that which is the conscious mind would be the self (*ātman*). If, on the other hand, it does not require another instrument, then: "In the case of not requiring another instrument, there would follow the consequence of simultaneous perception and recollection" (*karaṇāntarānapekṣitve yugapadālocanasmṛtiprasaṅgaḥ*). For if the mind were conscious, there would follow the simultaneous cognitions of color, taste, touch, and sound. This is because, once the eyes and other senses are connected with the mind, they would be independent of any further instruments due to their connection with their respective objects.

For instance, there would be simultaneity of memory because of the independence from instruments. Nor can a single entity produce effects sequentially, since its prior nature has not perished. Nor can it produce everything simultaneously and then cease acting, for there would be no cause for such cessation. Furthermore, if one admits that the prior nature is discarded with each effect, the consequence follows that it is momentary.

Now, could consciousness also belong to the instrument, the mind? That is not so, because "it is itself an instrument" (*svayaṃ karaṇabhāvācca*). For consciousness is the primary action (*pradhānakriyā*), and that [action] inheres either in the agent or in the object; it cannot possibly exist in the instrument, because such is never observed. Indeed, an instrument is never seen to be the locus of the primary action. However, from its own perspective, everything is indeed an agent. Thus, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), since consciousness is an effect of the self, "the self is thereby established. (*tenātmā samadhigamyate*)

What, then, is this *pariśeṣa* (method of elimination)? When the body and so forth, as well as genus (*jāti*) and other categories and objects, have been ruled out as the locus of consciousness, and when that [consciousness] has been established as residing in something else, and since space (*ākāśa*) and the rest cannot be suspected of being multiple due to the understanding of their unity, another substance remains; thus, *pariśeṣa* is a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekyanumāna*). And so: cognition resides in a substance distinct from earth, water, fire, air, space, direction, time, and mind, because it is a quality while there exists a subverting proof against its subsistence in those [others]; for that which does not reside in a substance distinct from those is not a quality when there exists a subverting proof against its subsistence therein, as in the case of color and so forth; but cognition is not like that; therefore, it resides in a distinct substance.

But surely all this is incoherent. Since [the entity] is momentary, the relationship of substrate and superstratum (āśrayāśrayibhāva) is untenable. Furthermore, the existence of things is pervaded by causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). And that [efficiency] is impossible in non-momentary entities, whether through succession or simultaneity. As for successive production: because the nature [of the entity] is uniform, that very same nature which exists at the time of the arising of the first effect must also exist at the time of subsequent effects; thus, there follows the undesirable consequence that all [effects] would be identical. This is because it is impossible to establish a difference in effects without a corresponding difference in their causes.

Now, if it is argued that it is precisely from the difference in effects (*kāryavailakṣaṇya*) that we know a different nature (*svarūpa*) arises for entities in each effect following the cessation of their previous nature, then—since you do not admit the persistence of the [entity's] own nature—it follows that the entity is non-existent. If it is argued that even for a persisting entity, there is causal efficacy in that very same way upon obtaining auxiliaries (*sahakārin*) either successively or simultaneously, we say no. Because those two [auxiliaries] are distinct from it, since they either produce an excellence (*atiśaya*) in it or remove an impediment; and because of this distinction, they are indeed other than it. Even if they were not distinct, how could the production of an effect by an entity be observed while that [entity] remains unchanged? For the production of an action by one thing when another thing has arisen is never observed; thus, there would be no dependence at all upon an object that provides no assistance, and consequently, there would be an absence of auxiliary status. If it is argued that even the capacity of the auxiliaries depends on further auxiliaries, and if that too depends on yet another auxiliary, then there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If it is argued that the auxiliaries possess their capacity intrinsically, without any further auxiliary, then this is the same in the case of the primary entity as well; so, enough of this.

Thus, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), by excluding itself from non-momentary things, excludes existence (*sattva*) which is pervaded by it; therefore, non-momentary things are non-existent. Consequently, since the exclusion of the possibility of non-momentariness in the opponent's position is established through the perception of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*), existence itself is the proof for momentariness. Likewise, because destruction is causeless, there is non-existence immediately after arising; this is momentariness.

Is it not improper [to claim that destruction is uncaused], since the production of the destruction of a jar and so forth is perceived through the operation of a mallet and other such instruments? No; for that operation applies to the conjunction with a spatial part of the self [the jar]. Moreover, if destruction were produced as something distinct from its cause, then there would be no perception of its absence, because its own nature would not have perished. Furthermore, if one were to admit that non-existence itself is the producer of an effect, it would follow that it possesses the nature of a positive entity (*bhāva*).

Furthermore, since there is no difference in their being distinct entities, there is no specific reason why, when that [destruction] has arisen, the non-perception of some entity should occur while it does not for all others. Nor would there be a necessity for its occurrence even if it were dependent upon a cause; for dependence and necessity are contradictory, just as in the case of dyeing a cloth. To explain: dye applied to a cloth comes into being through the presence of causes and does not come into being in their absence. Likewise, the perishability of an object might also depend on the presence of a cause for destruction or on the absence [of a cause]. If, however, destruction occurred without a cause for things whose nature is indestructible, then destruction would follow even for space and other things accepted as eternal. If, on the other hand, the cause belongs to an entity that is destined to perish, then what is the use of postulating such a cause, since destruction occurs necessarily by virtue of the very nature of the thing itself, even without a cause?

If destruction were both an instrument and an effect because it is produced (*kṛtaka*), then upon its destruction, there would necessarily be the re-emergence of the entity. Therefore, [the statement] "nothing happens to it; it simply ceases to be" refers to the non-destruction of the property established as the characteristic of the entity. Furthermore, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for [proving] non-momentariness, because it is a conceptual cognition (*kalpanājñāna*).
All this is based on an ignorance of the subject matter, since conceptual cognition has already been refuted.

Now, it may be argued that in the cognition "this is that very same [object]," unity is untenable due to the manifestation of contradictory aspects. For instance, "that" is a cognition having a past form, while "this" has a present form; and the occurrence of two contradictory forms in a single [cognition] is not observed. This is incorrect. Since the theory of [external] forms has been refuted, the sense faculty—assisted by the recollection of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by prior experience—generates a cognition that manifests both [aspects] as "this is that very same. And because this cognition conforms to the presence and absence of the object, it is incorrect to claim it is without an object.

Now, let it be granted that objects possess stability on account of recognition. But how can they possess causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*)? [The answer is: "When there is proximity of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). For instance, when auxiliary causes are present sequentially, there is sequential production; and when they are present simultaneously, there is simultaneous production. As for what was asked—"What is done by the auxiliary cause for that [permanent entity]?"—nothing at all. What then? Only the effect itself [is produced] upon its presence, otherwise the status of being an auxiliary cause would be impossible. Alternatively, by virtue of its capacity (*sāmarthya*), the completeness of the causal complex (*kārakasākalya*) alone is brought about, because the effect arises when that [complex] is present. As for incapacity, it is the deficiency [of the complex] that is removed, since completeness and deficiency are mutually exclusive states. Nor does the object itself undergo such a transformation through the appearance or disappearance of those two [completeness and deficiency], because those two are not distinct from it.

Nor does it follow that all things act as co-operating causes for one another simply because there is no difference in their being distinct entities; for we observe that only a specific thing produces an effect when it exists, based on the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) between its presence and the production of the effect. Furthermore, the capacity of co-operating causes does not derive from other co-operating causes, since we perceive that even when independent of those others, the collection of such causes produces a single effect provided they are in mutual proximity. This is observed, for instance, in the case of the eye, visible form, light, and mental attention, which produce a single effect when they are in mutual proximity.

Nor should it be argued that no excellence (*atiśaya*) is produced in the final state through the sovereign influence of the others; for since there is no distinction [between the cause and the excellence], such excellence cannot exist, as it is not the case that the very same thing becomes its own excellence. Thus, there is no contradiction even in other effects regarding the production of excellence by things that are themselves devoid of excellence. Alternatively, if it is held that things endowed with excellence produce excellence, then, if one admits that their excellence is likewise produced from something else, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would follow, resulting in the undesirable consequence that the intended effect would never arise. Therefore, we consider it logical that the excellence of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) consists simply in their mutual proximity. Consequently, since the difference in the effect arises from the difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), entities do not possess distinct natures for each individual effect.

Furthermore, this refutation of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) for non-momentary entities—by means of both succession and simultaneity—is capable of implying the admission of the remainder when there is a negation of a specific case; thus, there would follow the consequence of causal efficiency by way of another mode [of existence]. And yet, there exists no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends such [causal efficiency] as being non-existent.

Likewise, because it is accepted that effects are produced through mutual predominance (*parasparādhipatya*), if one accepts that each individual among form and the other [sensory objects] is the simultaneous cause of multiple forms and so forth, then since simultaneity has already been refuted, succession—which is included therein—is also refuted; thus, to state it again by its own name would be a mere tautology. For instance, just as form initiates color, taste, smell, and touch simultaneously, so too do taste and the others; if one intends to speak of them individually, succession exists in that very same context, and therefore only the single case [of simultaneity] should be negated. Furthermore, no such rule is possible that "only a single thing arises from a single cause" and "it initiates that [effect]."

Furthermore, it is not possible for a single entity to produce multiple effects sequentially unless it is admitted that it becomes something else at every moment. Therefore, since non-momentary entities do produce causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)—either successively or simultaneously—when their auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*) are present, they are neither non-existent nor are they manifold; thus, the reason "because of existence" (*sattvāt*) lacks the fault of lack of exclusion (*avyatireka*). Nor does its exclusion apply only to the subject (*pakṣa*), because that [non-existence] would be a different nature from it. As for the claim that, due to contradiction with non-momentariness, the very subject of your position is established as the subverting proof (*bādhaka*) that excludes the suspicion of non-momentariness—this is incorrect, because the cognition of contradiction is impossible without the cognition of the contradictory term. If, however, the non-momentary is indeed cognized as being contradictory to it, then that [non-momentary] is not non-existent, since it performs causal efficiency in the form of being an object of cognition; how then could there be an exclusion of it by this [reason]? Moreover, if the exclusion of the suspicion of non-momentariness were cognized through the subverting proof alone, the reason "because of existence" would be redundant, since that [proof] too would have as its object the exclusion of what is not of that nature. Alternatively, if momentariness itself is proven by the fundamental reason, and if that [momentariness] is distinct from the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and so forth, how can it be determined by inference? For inference has a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object.

Furthermore, it is not logical that the probans "because of existence" (*sattvāt*) possesses the capacity to convey [the conclusion] without positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) in relation to similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), for this would entail the consequence that even an uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) reason is a prover. Moreover, since everything is included within the subject (*pakṣa*), there would be no similar or dissimilar instances at all. If it is argued that because the demarcation of the subject and so forth is superimposed by conceptual construction (*kalpanāsamāropitatvāt*), there is positive concomitance in a similar instance superimposed by conceptual construction, and likewise negative concomitance in a dissimilar instance [superimposed by conceptual construction], and thus it has the capacity to convey [the conclusion]; then, in that case, inference would be merely conceptual (*kālpanika*), depending on a demarcation of the subject and so forth superimposed by conceptual construction. Consequently, momentariness itself would be unreal (*avāstavam*).

Now, [you might argue that] momentariness follows from the causelessness of destruction. That is not so. For even causelessness would involve remaining for some period of time, since there would be no contradiction in its destruction [occurring later]. Nor is causelessness logical, because, just as with an entity (*bhāva*), the operation of a cause is observed in the case of a non-entity (*abhāva*) as well through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). If it is argued that the production of the series of potsherds (*kapāla-santāna*) results from the operation of a mallet and so forth, we say no; for that [series] arises from a contradictory [cause]. Nor can the series of potsherds be an obstruction [to the perception of the jar], for if it were, the jar would be perceived at that time just as it was before. Even if it were an obstruction, once that [obstruction] is destroyed, the jar should be perceived. Furthermore, there is no contradiction between the jar and the series of potsherds, because the potsherds are the very causes of the jar.

Now, as for the claim that there is the perception of a thing’s destruction as a distinct entity (*arthāntara*), that is not so, because of the contradiction in their coexistence. For instance, when a positive entity (*bhāva*) has arisen, the non-existence (*abhāva*) is not perceived; rather, it is observed that at that very time, the positive entity is perceived. [Objection: If this is so, then at the time of a jar, its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is destroyed, which would require another prior non-existence for that [destruction], and yet another destruction for that, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). [Response: Some say that even if such a state exists, there is no fault, because the accomplishment of the effect is observed.

Others, however, maintain that because there would otherwise be no completion of the effect due to infinite regress, the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the jar and the destruction of that prior non-existence are one and the same.

The Gurus, on the other hand, state that since the prior non-existence of the jar is not perceived at the time of the jar’s existence, that very non-perception constitutes its negation; they argue that the prior non-existence belongs to the jar itself, because there is a contradiction between their coexistence.

Now, if it were argued that because non-existence (*abhāva*) is indistinguishable from being a different entity (*arthāntara*), then upon its arising, there would be the non-perception of everything—this is not so. For when that [non-existence] arises, the contradiction between those two [existence and non-existence] is established by the non-perception of one or the other. Just as, despite the lack of distinction in being different entities, it is observed that only a specific cause is the cause of a specific effect and not of all effects—such being the fixed rule—likewise, a contradiction with only a specific existent is observed for non-existence; thus, this is not a valid objection.

As for the claim that if destruction depended upon a cause, its occurrence would not be inevitable—just as with the dyeing of a cloth—this is incorrect. For there is no contradiction between dependence and inevitability, since we do not observe that because something is an exception in one case, it must be so everywhere. Furthermore, even if they were dependent, we observe the rising and setting of the sun, planets, constellations, and stars; yet if they were independent, their setting would have to occur immediately after their rising, because that which is capable cannot be delayed. And indeed, once the sun has risen, its setting necessarily follows.

Now, it has been asked: "If the destruction of an entity (*bhāva*) is admitted, what is the purpose of a cause? To this, [the reply is]: because it is impossible for [an entity] to have destruction as its very nature, destruction necessarily occurs only for that which is susceptible to destruction when a cause is present—not for things such as space (*gagana*). Likewise, an entity arises from its own causes in precisely such a manner that it must necessarily possess a cause for its destruction.

Now, if it is argued that because non-existence (*abhāva*) arises from a cause, it follows that there is no distinction between it and existence (*bhāva*), that is not so; for a difference in essential nature (*svarūpa-bheda*) is logically established. Just as form (*rūpa*) and other qualities, arising from causes, are distinguished from one another due to a difference in their essential natures, so too is non-existence distinguished from existence. Furthermore, the nature of non-existence consists in its being characterized by the sixfold definition of substance (*dravya*) and the rest, and in its being apprehended through its dependence upon existence.

Now, it was argued that because non-existence possesses origination, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the re-emergence (*unmajjana*) of the entity upon its destruction. (To this we reply: That is not so, because the properties of non-existence are distinct from the properties of existence. Just as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), which lacks origination, undergoes destruction, so too does the destruction of a substratum (*dharmin*)—which possesses origination—undergo non-destruction. Furthermore, the re-emergence of the entity does not occur through the destruction of its destruction, because that [destruction of destruction] does not have the nature of the entity nor is it caused by it. For instance, the destruction of the destruction of a jar is neither of the nature of the jar nor is it the cause of it; how, then, could there be the consequence of its re-emergence?

Nor is there a non-existence of an entity, because it is determined by means of valid cognition such as perception. For instance, the cognition "there is no jar on this ground" is born of the senses, since it conforms to the presence and absence of the sense organ. Nor is it without an object, because its objective support is the ground qualified by the absence of the jar.

If it is argued that the perception of the ground as distinct from the jar is itself the non-perception of the jar, and not [non-perception] due to its absence, then—in the absence of any distinction—there would arise the cognition "it does not exist" even when the ground is occupied by a jar. Therefore, the perception of the absence of the jar is itself the non-perception of the jar, and not merely the absence of perception. Furthermore, if destruction were not admitted, then since an entity would persist after [its production] just as it did before, non-perception would not be possible. If it is then argued that because it lasts for only a single moment, it does not persist in the second moment, then that very [momentary nature] is its absence, insofar as it is not perceived in the second moment while it exists [in the first]. Otherwise, since the sense organs and so forth remain in the same state and there is no destruction, there could be no non-perception of a permanent thing.

As for this statement, "He possesses nothing whatsoever; he simply does not exist," this is the talk of a madman. For one whose destruction has not yet occurred, there would have been no perception [of him] even previously, precisely because he would already be destroyed. Furthermore, if there were no contradiction with non-existence, he would remain even later, and thus he would be eternal. Likewise, if momentariness were true, there could be no recollection by another, because the experiencer would have perished; for it is not the case that Yajñadatta can remember an object experienced by Devadatta.

Now, [it might be argued that] there is no recollection because the relation of cause and effect does not exist between different mental continua (*santāna*), whereas within a single continuum there is such a causal relation; thus, a resultant cognition arises possessing all the preceding latent impressions (*vāsanā*) deposited therein, and therefore it is logical that there should be recollection of an object experienced by that [same] agent. This is not so. Even if a causal relation exists, since the state of being distinct remains as it was, how could there be recollection—as in the case of the continua of Devadatta and others? Furthermore, there is no proof for the existence of a continuum, because there is no proof that one cognition is the effect of another cognition.

Now, suppose it is argued that there is "the nature of consciousness [arising] from consciousness. For in this way, an effect that is conscious arises only from what is conscious, just as white [color] arises from white, and so forth. But if this were so, then smoke would not have fire as its cause, because there exists a moment of smoke belonging to the same class [as the preceding smoke]. If, on the other hand, it is maintained that smoke arises even from a distinct moment of fire, then consciousness too will arise from a distinct body and so forth; thus, there is no proof for the existence of another instance of consciousness [in the prior moment]. If it is further claimed that fire is the cause of smoke by virtue of some degree of similarity, then the same applies to the body and so forth in the production of cognition. Likewise, white could arise even from black, because some degree of similarity exists.

If it is accepted that the immediately preceding cause (*samanantara-pratyaya*) must be of an absolutely identical nature, then from a cognition of form (*rūpa-jñāna*) alone another cognition of form would arise, from a cognition of taste (*rasa-jñāna*) alone another cognition of taste, from pleasure alone another pleasure, and from pain alone another pain; thus there would be an infinite regress of continua (*santāna*), and yet no such simultaneous perception occurs. If you argue that these are not perceived simultaneously because moments that have not been experienced do not arise, then one must also accept a continuum for that [non-perception], since its arising is impossible without it. This being the case, it follows that their perception would occur at that very same time, which is not the case. Therefore, there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) such that every cognition is produced by another cognition.

Furthermore, since destruction is non-different [from the experience], it is not logical for memory to occur while that experience persists. If it is argued that the experience does not persist because it is absent in the second moment, we say no; for if there is non-difference, it must indeed persist, as there is no contradiction with itself. But if there is difference, then by admitting a contradiction between coexistence, one enters our own philosophical position. Therefore, memory establishes the existence of a persisting self.

Furthermore, the relationship of cause and effect is not tenable if things are momentary. For instance, at the very moment the effect arises, the cause perishes; and if one accepts that this [perishing] is not distinct from the arising, then there could be no causal relationship between two things that arise simultaneously, just as there is none between the left and right horns of an animal. Moreover, the Vaiśeṣikas maintain that the cause exists in a state of perishing, because destruction possesses a cause. However, for those who argue that destruction is causeless, the state of perishing is indeed possible even apart from the destruction of the entity itself, since that state consists in the completeness of the conditions for destruction.

Furthermore, for one who maintains the doctrine of self-cognition (*svasaṃvidvādin*), there is no apprehension of the causal relation, because the cognition of the cause terminates within itself, and likewise the cognition of the effect does so; thus, the cognition of the cause does not experience the existence of the effect, since at the time of that [effect's] existence, the [cause's] cognition has already passed away. Nor is there a single subsequent cognition that cognizes both the existence of the effect at the time of the cause's existence and its non-existence when the cause is absent.

Now, if it is argued that there exists a conceptual cognition grasping the relation of cause and effect through the sequence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) by means of the cognitions of cause and effect, then—given the admission that this [cognition] is a superimposition of such a form—it follows that the relation of cause and effect remains unestablished due to its lack of validity. For instance, whatever is superimposed upon something is unreal in that regard, just as yellowness and so forth are in the case of a conch shell.

If it is argued that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is the recollection of what was previously perceived, then in that case, there can be no mental impression (*vāsanā*) without the apprehension of a causal relationship. In the absence of that [apprehension], how could there arise a conceptual construction that determines that [past object], given that a mental impression conforms to its corresponding experience? Furthermore, it has already been stated that a mental impression cannot exist apart from cognition itself. Therefore, it remains established that without a persisting synthesizer (*pratisandhātṛ*), there is simply no apprehension of a causal relationship. This theory of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) has been refuted at length by our teachers, and thus it is not elaborated upon here. Consequently, since the relationship between substratum and superstratum is possible only if non-momentariness is accepted, it follows by process of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) that consciousness is dependent upon the self (*ātman*).

Likewise, the self (*ātman*) is known through "activity and cessation" (*pravṛtti-nivṛttibhyām*). Of what kind? "Inherent in the body (*śarīra-samavāyinībhyām*), and capable of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful (*hita-ahita-prāpti-parihāra-yogyābhyām*). "Beneficial" (*hita*) means pleasure (*sukha*), and "harmful" (*ahita*) means pain (*duḥkha*); "attainment and avoidance" refers to those two; "capable of" means competent for that. To demonstrate the pervasion (*vyāpti*), he says: "Just as by the action of a chariot [the existence of] a charioteer, who is the controller of the chariot, is inferred, so too the self is inferred as the controller of the physical frame, the body. For instance: the living body is controlled by one possessing effort (*prayatnavad-adhiṣṭhitam*), because it is the locus of activity and cessation which are inherent in the living body and capable of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful—just like a chariot. Since the property of being the locus of activity and cessation occurs in wind and other such things [where there is no conscious controller], the phrase "capable of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful" is included. Furthermore, the movement of a branch when a living creature is crushed by a mechanical device serves to remove harm from the creature, and for one below it, it brings about the attainment of benefit by providing fruit and the like; thus, for that purpose, the term "inherent in the body" is used. Even so, there is a deviation [from the rule] due to the movement of a corpse fallen into a river current. That [movement] also brings about pleasure for a dog below it, as it is eaten [by the dog] for its use, and it produces pain for an ascetic above it who is bathing due to the foul odor; thus, it removes harm. For that reason, the term "living body" is used.

But even so, this qualification shows that [the reason] exists in things like chariots—which are similar instances (*sapakṣa*)—just as it does in dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*); thus, it would remain inconclusive (*asādhāraṇa*). For a chariot does not possess the quality of being a substratum for action inherent (*samaveta*) in a living body. Now, suppose one argues: "Action inherent in a living body, which is capable of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful, is the effect of an effortful agent, because it is a specific kind of action, like the action of a chariot. Even here, the reason with its qualification does not exist in any similar instance. Furthermore, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*): the aforementioned qualified action in a sleeping person on board a ship is the cause of attaining what is intended and the cause of avoiding what is harmful, yet it is not the effect of an effortful agent. Therefore, the reason must be "being the substratum of action that conforms to will. For instance: "The living body is presided over by an effortful agent, because it is the substratum of action conforming to will, like a chariot (as a substance). Or: "Action is the effect of an effortful agent, because it is action conforming to will, like the action of a chariot."

Likewise, [the phrase] "and by means of breath, etc. (*prāṇādibhiśca*) indicates the sūtra: "Inhalation and exhalation, the opening and closing of the eyes, life, the movement of the mind, the modifications of the other sense organs, as well as pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort—these are the marks of the self" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 3.2.4).

Now, one might ask: "Since the self (*ātman*) is not perceived along with these [signs], how can they be indicative [of its existence]? To this he says: "Because distorted action is observed in the air enclosed within the body, as in the case of one blowing a bellows; thus it is inferred. This is a demonstration of pervasion (*vyāpti*). The formal argument (*prayoga*), however, is: the living body is presided over by an agent possessing effort (*prayatnavad-adhiṣṭhita*), because it is the locus of the air enclosed within the body that undergoes distortion, like a bellows. The term "distorted" (*vikṛta*) is used because other types of air also possess the quality of being a locus for air. Distortion, in this context, refers to the upward and downward movement of air which normally tends to move horizontally. Nevertheless, the word "enclosed" (*parigṛhīta*) is used because air may move upward when struck by another air current. Furthermore, the word "body" (*śarīra*) is used because such upward and downward movement of air entering through the openings of a hollow tree is possible. Finally, the word "living" (*jīva*) is used because such distortion is possible even in a body connected to a corpse (if it were merely physical), but here it must be a living one.

[Objection: Even so, it follows that the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is deficient in its probans (*sādhanavikalatā*), because it is impossible for a bellows (*bhastrā*) to have as its substrate a modified wind (*vikṛtavāyu*) contained within a living body (*jīvaccharīra*). [Response: That is not so, because of the similarity with a bellows. By the word "bellows," the body of a buffalo (*mahiṣīśarīra*) is intended through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*). For just as a bellows is blown by one possessing effort, so too is the body of a buffalo observed; therefore, it possesses the status of being the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of both the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*).

Alternatively, the air modified within the living body is presided over by one possessing effort, because it is air modified within a living body, like the air modified within a bellows. Likewise, the action of the aforementioned modified air is the effect of one possessing effort, because it is the modified action of the aforementioned air, like the action of the air modified within a bellows.

Likewise: "By means of the regulated action of closing and opening [the eyes]," it is said; not by that which arises from a disorder of wind (*vātadoṣa*). "Like a manipulator of a wooden machine," the self (*ātman*) is inferred. This is a demonstration of pervasion (*vyāpti*): for just as a wooden machine, when presided over by one possessing effort, has the action of closing and opening, so too does the living body. Closing (*nimeṣa*) is the action for the purpose of the conjunction of the eyelashes; opening (*unmeṣa*), however, is for the purpose of their disjunction. Thus, the living body is presided over by one possessing effort, because it is a whole (*avayavin*) that serves as the substratum for the action of closing and opening, like a wooden machine. As for the two eyelashes, they are the substrata for the action of closing and opening, like the eyelashes of a wooden machine. Or, the actions of closing and opening are effects of one possessing effort, because they are actions of closing and opening, like the actions of closing and opening of a wooden machine.

Likewise, it is inferred that the self exists because it is the cause of the body’s growth, the healing of wounds and fractures, and so forth, just as a householder [is the cause of such things for his house]. This is merely an exposition of the pervasion (*vyāpti*). Growth is the accumulation of parts. The healing of a wound resulting from contact with weapons and the like, or the healing of a fractured limb, is well known in the world. These [reasons] are intended to be stated individually, for if they were taken collectively, there would be nothing to exclude [from the class of examples]. Thus: "The living body is presided over by one possessing effort, because it is the cause of growth and because it is the cause of the healing of wounds and fractures, etc., like a house. By the word "etc.," the emergence of hair and so forth should be explained as being preceded by the qualities of a person (*puruṣaguṇapūrvaka*), just like specific ornaments in a house. Otherwise, this [emergence] would occur even in the state of death; yet this is not the case. Furthermore, growth, the healing of wounds, and the healing of fractures are effects produced by one possessing effort, because they possess that nature, like trees and the like situated in a house.

But is not all of this inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because [such activity] is observed even in insentient things like trees? For instance, the sūtra states: "Since engagement and withdrawal are observed in the internal self (*pratyagātman*), there is an inference [of them] in another [entity]" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 3.1.19). By this, it is asserted that an action conforming to desire is perceived in another sentient being. To explain: since specific engagement and withdrawal are observed in one's own self as effects of a sentient being, it is logical that when they are observed elsewhere, they too are its effects. However, such [sentience] is absent in trees and the like.

As for this stretching out of the limbs and so forth, it will occur due to the inherent nature of things, just as iron moves toward a magnet; furthermore, since scripture is easily accessible, it can indeed be explained even through figurative interpretation—thus, the reason remains inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). If it is argued that there is no inconclusiveness because of the existence of a presiding agent, we say no; for since such an agent exists even in clods of earth and the like, it would follow that they too should experience growth, healing of wounds, regrowth of broken parts, and so on.

All of this is incorrect, because even trees and the like are included within the category of the subject (*pakṣa*). Nor is there a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the probans from the probandum, nor is there a contradiction with the Sūtra, since activity and cessation are present in that case as well. For instance, the stretching out of limbs occurs when a substance is nearby, not due to the inherent nature of the object itself; otherwise, it would follow that such behavior would occur even in the case of a body [without external causes]. Furthermore, a specific desire for particular substances is known to be taught in the *Vṛkṣāyurveda*, as seen by the appearance of flowers and so forth upon their consumption. Moreover, it is improper to treat the scripture as merely figurative, since no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) exists against its primary sense. Enough of this.

Or, is there an inconsistency because growth is observed in accumulations such as sand even without effort? No, for it is accepted that the effort of Īśvara exists there as well. Since that too is included within the subject (*pakṣa*), it must be established—just like the body—that [growth] is preceded by the qualities of a person.

Likewise, the demonstration of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is as follows: "The self (*ātman*) is inferred by means of the activity of the mind (*manaḥkarman*), which is caused by its connection with the instruments that grasp desired objects, just like a boy who propels a ball in the corners of a house. To explain: just as a boy playing with balls in a house strikes a ball held in his hand against a stationary ball in the middle and thereby connects it with another ball, so too does the self strike the eye and other senses within the body with the mind and joins them with their respective objects. In this context, "desired object" refers to color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth; that which grasps it is the "grasper," namely the eye and other senses. The "connection" is with those [senses], and it is known through the activity of the mind caused by that connection. The formal arguments (*prayoga*) are as follows: 1. The living body is presided over by one possessing effort (*prayatnavad-adhiṣṭhita*), because it is the substratum of the instruments that grasp desired objects, like a house. 2. Or, the mind is impelled by effort, because it is connected to the instruments that grasp desired objects, like a ball held in the hand. 3. Or, the activity of the mind is an effect produced by one possessing effort, because it is an activity connected to the instruments that grasp desired objects, like the activity of a ball held in the hand. 4. Or, the connection of the mind with the eye and other senses is an effect produced by one possessing effort, because it is a connection with the instruments that grasp desired objects, like the connection of one ball with another. 5. Or, the eye and other senses are impelled by one possessing effort, because they are instruments that grasp desired objects, like another ball. 6. Or, the connection with the object is an effect produced by one possessing effort, because it is a connection belonging to that which is connected to the instruments that grasp desired objects, like the connection of a ball situated in a corner.

Likewise, the demonstration of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is as follows: “Because a modification of the sense of taste is observed following the visual perception of an object through the sequence of recollecting the [corresponding] flavor, a single cognizer who perceives both is known, like an observer looking through many windows. To explain: for one by whom a specific flavor has been perceived as invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvitayā*) with a particular form and so forth, there occurs a visual perception of that form, which is the object of the eye. Following that visual perception, there arises a recollection of the flavor, which is invariably concomitant with it. Through that sequence, there is a modification of the sense of taste; that is, after the recollection of the flavor, there arises a cognition of the flavor. Then, when effort is present, due to a continuous series of actions in the mind, a connection with the gustatory faculty occurs. From that, the modification characterized by the flooding of saliva within the mouth is produced—such is the order of production.

The sequence of cognition, however, is as follows: from the modification of the sense organ of taste arises its connection with the mind (*manas*). By that [connection] also, a continuous stream of activity in the mind is inferred. From that, effort (*prayatna*) arises; from that, desire (*icchā*); likewise, recollection (*smaraṇa*); from that, latent impression (*saṃskāra*); and from that, experience (*anubhava*). By means of that experience, there is the experiencer.

In this case, however, because the mental synthesis (*pratisaṃdhāna*) expressed as "mine" is observed everywhere, the fact of having a single agent is determined; for such synthesis is absent in the case of works by different authors. Indeed, memories and so forth arising in Devadatta and others are not experienced by Yajñadatta as "my memory" or "my desire. Furthermore, since the sense organs have restricted objects, if their concomitance were not perceived, there would be no memory of an object perceived by one sense organ by means of another sense organ; and in the absence of that [concomitance], a modification of the gustatory faculty would be impossible. Yet such a modification is observed; therefore, a single cognizer who perceives both is known.

Now, if it is argued that memory arises from the perception of the concomitance between color and taste when the body itself is the substratum for the eyes and the tongue, we say no; because that [body] is also different. For instance, there is a difference [in the body] due to the presence of differences in dimension (*parimāṇa*), just as there is in the case of the *kuvalaya*, *āmalaka*, and *bilva* fruits. Indeed, even while one thing remains with a certain dimension, it is impossible for it to possess a subsequent dimension through the negation of its previous dimension; thus, by the impossibility of the former dimension persisting otherwise, there is a cessation of the previous dimension. And since that cessation occurs only through the destruction of the substrate, there is a difference [between the bodies]. Furthermore, the body cannot be the initiator of another body, because the initiation of another [entity] by a single [entity] is prohibited. Otherwise, due to the contradiction between cause and effect, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving all [the bodies simultaneously]. If it is argued that there is merely a difference in state (*avasthā-bheda*) and not a difference in the thing possessing the states (*avasthāyin*), that is not so. If the "state" is the dimension, then upon the difference in that [dimension], there must necessarily be a difference in the [body] itself. If the "state" is a particular part (*avayava-viśeṣa*), then even if that [part] is destroyed, that which is initiated by it [the body] would be destroyed. Nor can it be color and so forth, because they too are destroyed by the destruction of their substrate. Nor is there any other property (*dharma-antara*) that is either conjoined (*saṃyogin*) or inherent (*samavāyin*). Thus, because the body is different [at each moment], memory and the like are simply impossible.

If it is argued that, when memory arises through the sequence of the transfer of causal impressions (*vāsanā*) into the intellect (*buddhi*), a modification of the gustatory faculty (*rasanendriya*) is thereby produced, we say no. This is because memory has already been refuted on the grounds of the momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) of things. Therefore, memory, desire, and so forth have a single agent, because they are recognized as "mine" (*mameti pratisandhīyamānatvāt*). There is no such recognition among things having different agents. However, among things having a single agent, there is the recognition "it is mine" regarding the movement of a dancer's eyebrows by those who have made a prior agreement.

Now, if it is argued that since the eternal self (*ātman*) cannot be assisted, what purpose do experience (*anubhava*) and the like serve for it? [The answer is: nothing at all. For experience and so forth do indeed provide assistance; for when that [experience] exists, one is designated as "the experiencer" or "the rememberer. Alternatively, its assistance consists in being the effect of that [experience]. Thus, an impression (*saṃskāra*) is produced in it by experience, and memory is the assistance provided by that [impression]; by that [memory] too, its own effect [is produced], and so on, which may be inferred successively. Nor does the experiencer undergo such a state [of change] through the manifestation or disappearance of experience and the like, because [the self] is distinct from them. If it is asked how experience and so forth belong to the self and not to another if they are distinct, [the answer is] due to their connection (*sambandha*). Furthermore, we shall explain that there is no infinite regress, because a connection, even if it does not require another connection, is observed to reside in the related entities.

Furthermore, it is never observed that when one person undergoes an experience, another person is designated as the "experiencer. If it is argued that since it is impossible for experience and so forth to impart a specific excellence (*atiśaya*) to the self, such a designation is untenable, we say no. For this very [experience] is the excellence itself; thus, its prior absence, which is the lack of excellence, ceases. It has been stated previously that the completeness of causal factors (*kāraka-sākalya*) constitutes excellence, while their deficiency constitutes the lack of excellence. Moreover, excellence cannot be conceived if there is no distinction [between the self and the experience]. Enough of this excessive detail.

Likewise, it was stated previously: "The possessor of qualities (*guṇin*) is inferred from its qualities (*guṇas*), such as pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort. For instance, pleasure and the rest must reside in something, because they are qualities, just like color and so forth. Now, one might argue that these [qualities] could be qualities of the body or the sense organs; therefore, he says: "And those [pleasure and the rest] are not qualities of the body or the sense organs. Why? He says: "Because they lack syntactic unity with the notion of 'I' (*ahaṅkāra*). This is because they do not share the same substratum (*asamānādhikaraṇa*) with the cognition of "I," unlike consciousness (*vijñāna*). Those which are qualities of the body or the sense organs—such as color and the rest—are not co-referential with the notion of "I."

Now, as for the claim that [the notion] "I am possessed of form" (*rūpavān*) is logical because such a cognition is observed, this is not so; for this [notion] is figurative (*gauṇa*) due to the existence of a sublation (*bādhaka*) regarding its primary sense. Furthermore, it has already been stated previously that [the body] cannot be the objective support (*ālambana*) of the cognition "I"; thus, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is merely metaphorical (*upacarita*), based on the qualities of the body. However, coreferentiality with the knowledge of memory is observed in the form "I am the rememberer. And it has been stated that memory does not inhere in the body. For this reason as well, pleasure and the like are not qualities of the body or the senses, "because they exist only in a limited location" (*pradeśavṛttitvāt*). Since particular qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) pervade their substratum, while color and the like [do so], there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) by means of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the like when proving the negation of [pleasure etc. being particular qualities of the body; for those [conjunctions, etc. are also included within the subject (*pakṣa*). Likewise, pleasure and the like are not particular qualities of the body or the senses, "because they do not persist as long as the substance exists" (*yāvaddravyābhāvitvāt*), like sound. Whereas those which are particular qualities of a substance, such as color and the like, do persist as long as the substance exists. Nor is there a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by means of the color and other qualities of the atoms of earth, for these too are part of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) by virtue of being the locus of the property to be proven (*sādhyādhikaraṇa*). For instance, when the negation of being particular qualities of the body or senses is to be proven, even those [qualities of atoms] are indeed similar instances, since—like conjunction and the like—they are not particular qualities of those [two]. For this reason as well, pleasure and the like are not particular qualities of the body or the senses, "because they are not perceptible by the external senses" (*bāhyendriyāpratyakṣatvāt*), like consciousness (*vijñāna*). Whereas those which are particular qualities of those [substances], such as color and the like, are perceptible by the external senses. Although gravity (*gurutva*) and the like are not perceptible by the external senses, they are not particular qualities of the body or the senses; thus, there is no inconclusiveness. By the negation of "external senses," what is intended is perceptibility by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Likewise, particular qualities of the body are perceptible, but pleasure and the like are not so. If it is argued that because everything consists of the three *guṇas*, everything is endowed with pleasure, pain, and so forth, and therefore [pleasure etc. are not particular qualities of the Self (*ātman*), we say no; for the negation of the doctrine that [everything] consists of the three *guṇas* will be stated later during the occasion of the refutation of *Pradhāna*.

And just as the self is known through qualities such as pleasure and pain, so too is it known by the word “I. The word “I,” being a single term that is not sublated [by external contradiction], necessarily requires a referent (*vācya*). Nor is earth and the like its denotation, because of its difference from words such as “earth”; thus there is a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). If, on the other hand, the word “I” were to denote objects such as earth, there would be grammatical coreferentiality with those terms, such as “I am earth” or “I am water,” and so forth. But this is not observed. Therefore, it is logical that the application of the word “I” occurs only with respect to the self. For a word functioning with regard to one object does not denote a different object; thus it is a single term that is not sublated. If it is argued that this [word] has no objective domain because the relationship of signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*) between words is untenable, we say no, for that relationship will be explained later.

Thus, while the self (ātman) is established as such, there is a proposition of fourteen qualities for the purpose of demonstrating its substantiality, its status as an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), and the fact that its specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) reside in only one part [of its substrate] and are momentary. He shows this [proposition]: "Its qualities are cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, mental impression (*saṃskāra*), number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, and disjunction. He states that these were indeed propounded by the author of the Sūtras: "In the section on the marks of the self (*ātmaliṅga*), those beginning with cognition and ending with effort are established."

Likewise, by stating "because [the author] declares that merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) are not causes for the qualities of another self," he shows the *sūtra*: "Because the qualities of one self are not causes for the qualities of another self" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 6.1.5). For instance, there might arise the suspicion that since the merit of giving and the merit of receiving are established through a rule of temporal sequence—where one precedes the other—they stand in a cause-and-effect relationship; it is to refute this that the *sūtra* was stated: "Because the qualities of one self are not causes for the qualities of another self. Since merit and demerit are qualities of the self, they could not be the cause for the production of qualities in another self. Indeed, it is never observed that pleasure arises in one self from the pleasure of another self, nor that pain arises from the pain of another.

Now, as for the claim that the pleasure residing in a daughter is seen to produce pleasure in the mother—that is incorrect. It is not so, because [the mother's pleasure] arises from the experience of that [pleasure in the daughter]. For instance, having perceived the brightening of the face and other signs in the daughter, the mother—thinking through inference that "pleasure has arisen in her"—experiences mental pleasure through her own internal experience; it does not arise from [the daughter's] pleasure itself, for that [mental pleasure] arises at a later time even after the former [daughter's pleasure] has perished.

Thus, even by means of a sutra intended to deny that the merit of giving is the cause for the arising of the merit of receiving, the existence of dharma and adharma within the self is asserted; we shall likewise state this during the examination thereof.

“*Saṃskāraḥ smṛtyutpattau*” (Impression [is the cause] in the production of memory). He shows the sūtra: “*Smṛtirvāsanākhyāt*” (Memory arises from that which is called *vāsanā* [impression]). For instance, memory, being an effect, necessarily requires a cause. Nor is direct experience (*anubhava*) the cause, because memory arises even after that experience has perished. If it is argued that the destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) of the experience is the cause because of its presence and absence (positive and negative concomitance), that is incorrect. Because that [destruction] is devoid of degrees, it would follow that memory—which is distinguished by variations such as intensity—could not occur. Indeed, without a degree of excellence in the cause, an excellence in the effect is not logical. Furthermore, practice (*abhyāsa*) would be useless, since it is impossible to produce a degree of excellence in a destruction. Therefore, there exists some uncommon cause inherent in the self (*ātman*) that possesses degrees of excellence, from which memory—inhering in that same self—is produced. Nor is this [cause] merely unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), because that is common to the production of all effects; whereas an uncommon cause inherent in the self is observed in the form of the effects characterized as pleasure and pain. Thus, a different uncommon cause for memory must be stated. To explain: memory, inhering in the self, arises when an uncommon cause is present, because it is an uncommon effect inhering in the self, just like pleasure. Therefore, it is established that when an impression is deposited in the self by means of experience, memory is produced. “Memory arises from that which is called *vāsanā*.”

In this regard, [the principle] "Number [is established] because of the statement of their distinct determination" (*Vyavasthāvacanāt saṃkhyā*) indicates the sūtra: "The selves are manifold because of the distinct determination of pleasure and pain" (Vai. Sū. 3.2.19). What, then, is this "distinct determination"? It is the restriction of pleasure, pain, and so forth. For instance, one person has pleasure, another has pain, and another has desire; thus is it observed as a distinct distribution. If there were only a single self (*aikātmya*), then when one is happy, all would be happy, and when one is suffering, all would suffer; thus, the consequence of a lack of distinct determination would follow, since there would be no cause for such restriction.

If it is argued that there is a difference in the body (*śarīra-bheda*) which acts as the restrictive factor [for the lack of recollection], we say no, because it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [unwanted] recollection. For just as recollection—such as the perception "I was happy in my childhood state"—is observed despite the difference in the body due to the distinctions between the stages of infancy, youth, and adulthood (because the self is one), so too would such recollection follow for all bodies. But this is not the case. Therefore, since recollection, which pervades oneness, excludes itself from the bodies of horses, buffaloes, and so forth, it excludes the oneness pervaded by itself; thus, there is plurality (*nānātva*). To explain: in the case of the bodies of horses, buffaloes, and so forth, the subject (*dharmin*) is the self. The thesis to be proven (*sādhya*) is that [the self] is manifold due to the difference in individuals, even while possessing the nature of being a self. This is because there is no recollection by one body of an object perceived by another body. Where there is oneness, there is recollection, as seen in the bodies of infancy, youth, and adulthood; this is the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). We shall explain below, in the section on inferential knowledge (*laiṅgika-jñāna*), how a reason (*hetu*) is a means of cognition through non-deviant negative concomitance alone (*kevala-vyatireka*). Likewise, even within a single body, recollection is observed due to the oneness of the self, as in "there is pain in my foot" and "there is pain in my head. Nor is it logical that there should be a lack of memory regarding what is perceived in the bodies of horses and so forth, just as there is a lack of memory for what was experienced in a previous birth or experienced in the womb. [The lack of memory in those cases is explained by: the experience in the womb being indistinct, and the impressions (*saṃskāra*) from a previous birth being overwhelmed by the suffering of death. However, there is no such cause for the lack of memory regarding what was experienced in the bodies of horses and so forth.

Now, if it is argued that because no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) can be established for the existence of difference, everything must be conceived as one—[we reply: No. For difference is manifested by perception itself through objects whose natures are mutually excluded. Furthermore, since perception grasps both affirmation and negation, and since it is accepted that when the difference of objects is manifested by non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) perception, a conceptual (*savikalpaka*) cognition arises in the form "this is different from that," there is neither circularity (*itaretarāśrayatva*) nor infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Indeed, the apprehension of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*), as well as of affirmation and negation, is held to be without fixed order. In this regard, that which is the qualifier is apprehended first, while the qualified is apprehended later; however, the relationship between qualifier and qualified is not fixed.

Now, if it is accepted here that difference (*bheda*) is exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), which is mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), then how can exclusion itself be a difference? For exclusion is by its very nature exclusion; those things opposed to it, however, depend upon exclusion. If it is argued that this appearance of difference is superimposed by ignorance (*avidyā*), we say no. For that [appearance] is impossible apart from the Self (*ātman*). If there were separation, then oneness would cease. Furthermore, if ignorance were of the nature of the cessation of knowledge (*vidyā*), how could it, being of a void nature, produce worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) through difference? Nor is the appearance of difference illusory simply because a sublater (*bādhaka*) is not perceived. Nor is it logical for imagined forms to produce real causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). In the case of a rope, the effect—such as fleeing—is produced from the real snake-cognition, not from the imagined object. Moreover, since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the oneness of all things, how can the knowledge of oneness be based on knowledge (*vidyā*)? Just as there is no proof for the oneness of all things without a *pramāṇa*, so too might there be manifoldness (*nānātva*), since the absence of a *pramāṇa* is common to both cases. If it is argued that there is scriptural authority (*āgama*) as a *pramāṇa* for oneness, [we reply that] the cessation of oneness follows from the fact that the *pramāṇas* and so forth are real differences. If, however, there were non-difference, the distinction between *pramāṇa* and *prameya* (the object of knowledge) would be untenable.
