How is it that this Self is self-luminous? If these objects were distinct from the Supreme Self, how could they be manifested, since it is impossible for that which is non-luminous to be manifested? If you argue that they are indeed manifested and not distinct from the Supreme Self because He alone has the nature of light, this is not so. Since things related to distinct natures are perceived through means of valid cognition such as perception, their connection with the nature of existence would have to consist either in being of the nature of light or being of the nature of consciousness. However, that [nature] is not possible in the case of objects; thus, by virtue of their non-existence, it follows that the Supreme Self would also be non-existent, because the nature of one object cannot exist in another object without distinction. Furthermore, if there were only one Self, then upon the liberation of that one, there would be liberation everywhere; thus, liberation would be achieved without effort. Likewise, if one were not liberated, another would also not be liberated, leading to the undesirable consequence that no one would ever be liberated.

Now, if it is argued that the emergence of individual souls (*jīvātman*) from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) constitutes *saṃsāra*, and their dissolution back into that very same [Self] constitutes liberation (*mukti*), we say no. If there is no difference between them, whose would liberation or *saṃsāra* be? Or, if they were non-different, duality would be lost. This same refutation should be applied to the view that liberation belongs to those portions of the self delimited by knowledge (*vidyā*), while *saṃsāra* belongs to those portions delimited by ignorance (*avidyā*). As for atoms (*paramāṇu*), they are the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of effects such as the earth, because a cause is observed to have a dimension smaller than that of its effect. However, the Supreme Self is not such a cause, because He is all-pervading (*vyāpaka*). Furthermore, it is never observed that a material thing arises as inherent in an immaterial material cause. If the Supreme Self were the material cause consisting of multiple atomic dimensions, it would be a mere difference in terminology. As for atoms, they have already been established [by us]. Any statement asserting oneness should be explained with reference to the Supreme Self, since He has already been established through inference based on the existence of effects. Regarding the statement, "This one Self alone is situated in body after body," this is intended to negate multiplicity within a single body. For instance, the Buddhists (*Śākyas*) maintain that there are multiple cognitions constituting the self in a single body; to refute that, it is said that there is one [self] per body and not many. Likewise, there are indeed statements that establish plurality [of selves]. Enough of this excessive talk.

“Separateness also [is established] for this very reason,” meaning that because there is plurality (*nānātva*), there is likewise a plurality of separateness (*nānā-pṛthaktva*). “Likewise, from the statement ‘the self’ [it follows that it has] the dimension of the supremely great (*paramamahat-parimāṇa*)”; he shows this by citing the *Vaiśeṣika Sūtra*: “Space is great because of its pervasiveness; so too is the self” (VS 7.1.22). Just as space is great due to its pervasiveness, so too is the self; thus, its supreme greatness is established precisely through its omnipresence (*vibhutva*). Now, if it is argued that the supreme greatness of the self is unestablished because the self has the dimension of the body—such that the self is small in a small body and large in a large body—that is not so, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of the self apart from the body.

But surely, on this view, because the self possesses the properties of contraction and expansion, when the self perishes even in the infant body, it would not exist as the same self in the state of old age; thus, if there were a difference [of identity], memory would be impossible. Nor can a subsequent dimension come into being without the cessation of the previous dimension; therefore, the cessation of the previous dimension occurs precisely through the destruction of its substratum.

Furthermore, since movement is not possible for that which is all-pervading and formless, there would be no experience [of results] because a connection with a body in places such as heaven would be untenable; therefore, movement is indeed accepted. If that is so, then since it possesses form and a large dimension, its cause must be stated—that from which its production arises—and thus it is subject to the same refutation as the doctrine of elemental consciousness (*bhūtacaitanya*).

Likewise, since merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) are qualities of the self (*ātman*), if their substratum were not all-pervading, there would be no upward flaming of fire, no horizontal movement of air, nor the initial action of atoms and the mind; for these depend upon conjunction with their own substrata. Just as effort depends upon conjunction with the self in the case of the hand’s action, so too merit and demerit could not produce action without conjunction with the self, because they are qualities of the self. Since no other cause exists in that regard, the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) itself is the cause, depending upon conjunction with its own substratum. Therefore, due to its pervasiveness, it possesses supreme magnitude (*paramamahattva*). Furthermore, it is heard that when yoga has manifested as supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), one creates bodies together with sense organs and simultaneously enjoys pleasures; this is possible only if the self is all-pervading, not if it is non-pervasive.

Likewise, "conjunction is established because pleasure and the like are produced by contact. For pleasure and the like, being effects, require a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). Since no other [cause] is possible, the conjunction between the self and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is established.
And since that [conjunction], being a product, must necessarily perish, and since there is no destruction of its substratum, it perishes through disjunction alone; thus, disjunction is established.

“Because of its association with the nature of the mind, it is called *manas*. Even when the self, the sense organs, and their objects are present, since we observe that knowledge, pleasure, and pain arise after having not previously existed, another instrument (*karaṇa*) is inferred. Furthermore, because memory is observed to arise even when the ear and other [external senses] are inactive, and because there exists another object of perception such as pleasure which is not grasped by the external senses, there is an internal instrument (*antaḥkaraṇa*).”

“Its qualities are number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and mental impression (*saṃskāra*). From the statement that effort and cognitions are not simultaneous, its oneness in each body is established. Distinctness is also established for this very reason. From the statement of its absence [of magnitude], it has atomic dimension. From the mention of moving away and moving toward, it possesses conjunction and disjunction. Because it is corporeal, it has priority and posteriority, as well as mental impression. Because it lacks touch, it does not originate substances. Because it possesses motion, it is corporeal. Because it would entail having a common physical form, it is non-cognizant. Because it exists as an instrument, it is for the sake of another. Because it possesses qualities, it is a substance. And because it is governed by the grasp of effort and the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), it moves rapidly. (PDhS)

Now, for the purpose of examining the definition of the mind (*manas*), there is this section beginning with: “The mind [is defined] by its connection with *manastva* (mind-ness)” (*manastvayogānmanaḥ*). Connection with *manastva*—that is, inherence (*samavāya*) characterized by *manastva*—is the definition. To explain: the mind is distinct from other things because of its connection with *manastva*. For whatever is not distinct from others—that is, what is not a non-mind—is not connected with *manastva*, such as earth and the other elements. Alternatively, the object to be proven is the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). The remaining points regarding the refutation and resolution of objections concerning the definition are to be understood as before. Likewise, the focus here is on the determination of the meaning of the term.

Now, since it is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of the mind? He states: "It is inference (*anumāna*), because even when the self, the sense-faculties, and the object are in proximity, one observes the arising of cognitions, pleasure, and pain after they have not previously existed. For instance, the self, due to its omnipresence, is connected with all the sense-faculties, and the sense-faculties are likewise connected with their respective objects. Nevertheless, since cognitions of form and so forth do not arise simultaneously, another instrument [the mind] is inferred.

Now, how is the connection of the sense organs with their respective objects known? It is known through inference. For instance: the olfactory organ (*ghrāṇa*) is conjoined with that which is conjoined with its own pervader, because it is the pervader of what is conjoined with it; for whatever is the pervader of what is conjoined with something is seen to be conjoined with that which is conjoined with its own pervader, just as a cloth, which is the pervader of the threads conjoined with *vīraṇa* grass, is conjoined with the *vīraṇa*. Or, a substance such as camphor, when conjoined with a location, is conjoined with that which pervades what is conjoined with itself, because it is conjoined with what is pervaded by that [location]; for whatever is conjoined with what is pervaded by something is seen to be conjoined with that which pervades what is conjoined with itself, just as *vīraṇa* grass, being conjoined with the threads conjoined with a cloth (which is pervaded by the cloth), is conjoined with the cloth.

Likewise, the gustatory sense-organ (*rasanendriya*) is conjoined with that which is conjoined with its own pervader, because it is the pervader of what is conjoined with it, like a cloth which is the pervader of the threads conjoined with the *vīraṇa* grass. Or rather, a substance conjoined with its location is conjoined with that which pervades what is conjoined with itself, because it is conjoined with what is pervaded by that [location], like *vīraṇa* grass and so forth, which are conjoined with the threads pervaded by the cloth. The same applies to the remaining [senses]. As for the sound of a song, however, it occurs only when there is a connection with the ear through the continuous hearing of that which is in proximity.

If this much alone were the cause of knowledge, pleasure, and pain, then there would be no non-arising of them when these [causes] are present; for it is never observed that an effect fails to arise even when its causes are complete. Therefore, since we observe that even while these [causes] are present, the effect first does not exist and subsequently arises, another cause is inferred—one whose presence or absence determines the arising or non-arising of the effect. [Objection: Perhaps the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) will be the cause in this very case. [Reply: No, because that would entail the non-existence of the ear and other sense organs as well. Furthermore, if it is argued that those [organs] are produced only after a long time due to the non-performance of their means of accomplishment at the present moment, the same fault remains.

Thus, the self, the sense organs, and their objects depend upon other causes, because even when they exist, they do not produce [their effects] until [those causes] arise. For those things which, despite existing, do not produce their effect immediately but produce it later are dependent; for example, threads and the like are dependent on the conjunction with other threads. Others, however, argue that the self depends on sequential causes, because even when all other conditions are complete, it produces its effects sequentially. For whatever produces an effect sequentially, even when all other causes are present, depends on sequential causes; for example, a person skilled in various crafts. Or else, the eyes and other senses depend on sequential causes, because even when they exist, they produce their effects sequentially. For whatever exists and produces an effect sequentially necessarily depends on a sequential cause; for example, an axe or a knife depends on the hand. Thus they state the inference.

Likewise, it is observed that the self (*ātman*), even when in proximity to the sense organs and their objects, performs its function only sequentially. Similarly, the eyes and other senses, being presided over by the self, perform their functions only through a sequence of contact with their respective objects; thus, they depend upon a sequential cause. Furthermore, because memory is observed to arise even when the ears and other senses are not functioning, there must be another instrument (*karaṇa*). For instance: memory is produced by an instrument, because it is an action, like the action of cutting. Nor are the ears and so forth themselves the instrument, since memory is observed to arise even when they are not functioning. Whatever arises even when something else is not functioning cannot be the effect of that thing—for example, a jar produced when the threads [of its cause] have perished. Since memory arises for the deaf and others even when the ears and other senses are not functioning, it is not their effect. Therefore, there must be another instrument.

Likewise, "because there exists another object of apprehension, such as pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth, which is not grasped by the external senses," there exists another instrument (*karaṇa*). For instance: pleasure and the like are delimited by an instrument, because they are objects of apprehension, just like color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth. Nor are the eye and the other [external senses] themselves the instrument, because it has been stated that there exists another object of apprehension, such as pleasure, which is not grasped by the external senses. Just as, since odor is not grasped by the eye, another instrument—the nose—is inferred; and since taste is not delimited by those two [eye and nose], the tongue is inferred; and since touch and likewise sound are not [delimited] by those [three], another instrument is inferred. In the same way, since pleasure and the like are not grasped by the external senses, the mind (*manas*), which delimits them, is inferred.

Once the existence of the mind (*manas*) has been established, the statement “Its qualities are number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and mental impression” (*tasya guṇāḥ saṃkhyāparimāṇapṛthaktvasaṃyogavibhāgaparatvāparatvasaṃskārāḥ*) is intended to demonstrate its substantiality (*dravyatva*) and its nature as an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). Since its substantiality alone establishes the existence of number, one might wonder whether it is one or many; to resolve this doubt, he says: “On account of the non-simultaneity of effort and cognition, its oneness in each body is established. He thus shows the sūtra: “Because of the non-simultaneity of efforts and the non-simultaneity of cognitions, there is one mind in each body” (*Vaiśeṣika Sūtra* 3.2.3). The reason for not using a compound here is to include the non-simultaneity of pleasure, pain, and so forth. The meaning of the sūtra is that the mind is neither one in multiple bodies, nor is it many in a single body. What then? It is one in each body. Why? Because of the non-simultaneity of efforts and the non-simultaneity of cognitions. For if the mind were one and all-pervading, then since it would preside over all the sense organs, cognitions of color and other objects, as well as efforts, would arise simultaneously. But this is not observed.

Now, [the opponent argues: "When the Brahmin Kapila eats a long *śaṣkulī* (a type of pastry), five cognitions arise simultaneously. Likewise, in the case of a teacher, efforts arise simultaneously for uttering a sentence, walking, searching for the path, and holding his water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*). This is unproven. Why? Because there is no well-established example of simultaneity [of multiple cognitions]. The impression of simultaneity should be regarded as a mere illusion caused by rapid succession, like the mistaken perception that one is piercing a hundred lotus petals at once. On the contrary, there are many well-established examples of sequential occurrence. Therefore, it is logical that cognitions arise only sequentially due to the mind’s connection with the sense organs in sequence, given that the mind has an atomic dimension (*aṇuparimāṇa*). If one were to admit that even though the mind is atomic in dimension, there are multiple minds within a single body, then since a particular sense organ would be presided over by a particular mind, there would indeed be simultaneity of cognitions. However, since cognitions are experienced as arising sequentially, the mind in each body is one and atomic in dimension. [Objection: Even so, the mind, having presided over the eye and being connected to multiple objects, might produce cognitions simultaneously. [Reply: This is not so. For we observe that a single instrument possesses the capacity to accomplish only a single action. Indeed, a single instrument is never seen performing multiple actions at one time.

Now, it might be argued that this [position] is untenable because, upon the stroke of an axe, multiple actions are perceived simultaneously among the many blades of grass. We say: no, because [the agent] is qualified by being of the nature of consciousness (*bodha*). Alternatively, the parts of the axe itself possess instrumentality; just as the sharp whole is connected with the grasses, so too its parts are indeed connected with them. Thus, due to the multiplicity of instruments, the simultaneity of actions is logical.

Others, however, maintain that "impacts" (*abhighāta*) are the instruments (*karaṇa*). For instance, they argue that the connections of an axe with blades of grass depend upon momentum, and its constituent parts are indeed mutually distinct. This is not correct, because it is only the axe as connected with the action [of cutting] that possesses the status of an instrument. Otherwise, since even the eye would have different connections based on its various objects, it too would be established as an instrument; and because it is presided over by the mind through the door of the eye, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the simultaneous production of cognitions of jars and other things. But this is not the case, due to the lack of such experience. Therefore, the simultaneous manifestation of jars and so forth is not their simultaneous apprehension. It is logical that the eye is an instrument connected with multiple objects. Consequently, the capacity of an instrument lies in the accomplishment of a single action. And once plurality is established, multiplicity of distinctness (*nānāpṛthaktva*) is indeed established through concomitance (*sāhacarya*), following from that [plurality].

Likewise, he demonstrates this in the sūtras: "Because of the statement of its absence, [the mind] has atomic dimension" (*tadabhāvavacanādaṇuparimāṇam*) and "Space is great because of its pervasiveness; so too is the self. Because of the absence of that, the mind is atomic" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.1.22–23). This means that because of the absence of that [pervasiveness], the mind is atomic.

[Objection: But in that case, since all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) is also absent in things such as a jar, would it not follow that they too possess atomic dimension (*aṇutva*)? [Reply: No, because of the qualification "being an eternal substance" (*nityadravya*). To explain: the mind (*manas*) possesses atomic dimension, because while being an eternal substance, it is devoid of all-pervasiveness. Whatever is an eternal substance and is devoid of all-pervasiveness is observed to be so [atomic], just like atoms (*paramāṇu*) and the like; and this [mind] is likewise devoid of all-pervasiveness; therefore, it has atomic dimension. Although a jar and the like are devoid of all-pervasiveness, they do not have atomic dimension; thus, the term "eternal" is included [in the reason]. Furthermore, since eternality exists even in qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, the word "substance" (*dravya*) is used [to exclude them].

Likewise, [the sūtra] states: "From the mention of moving away and moving toward, there are conjunction and disjunction" (*apasarpaṇopasarpaṇavacanāt saṃyogavibhāgau*). It shows the sūtra: "Moving away, moving toward, the conjunctions with what is eaten and drunk, and conjunctions with other effects—these are caused by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*)" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.2.17). "Moving away" (*apasarpaṇa*) is an action for the purpose of separating from the dead body. "Moving toward" (*upasarpaṇa*) is for the purpose of conjunction with a new body. "Eaten and drunk" refers to food, water, and so forth; their movement through the internal channels is one matter. "Other effects" refers to another body; the conjunction of the mind with that is another. The action of the mind belonging to yogis for all these purposes is caused by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). Thus, even by a sūtra intended for another purpose, conjunction and disjunction are stated. Likewise: "Because of being corporeal (*mūrtatva*), there are priority and posteriority" (*mūrtatvāt paratvāparatve*). This is because they follow upon corporeality. For where there is corporeality, the conventional usage of "prior" and "posterior" is possible for one who perceives it. However, priority and posteriority produced by space (*dik*) do not apply to the mind, because those produced by time (*kāla*) are impossible due to its eternity. Yet, with respect to an effect-substance (*kāryadravya*), priority produced by time is indeed possible for one who perceives it in the mind: "the mind is prior, and the effect-substance is posterior. Nor is there a rule that the usage of priority and posteriority is observed only between things of the same genus. Likewise, there is no priority or posteriority [in the mind itself]. "And impulse (*saṃskāra*)" (*saṃskāraśca*): because of corporeality alone, there is that which is called velocity (*vega*).

Now, why does the mind (*manas*), though mutually connected [with other things], not initiate a substance (*dravya*)? He says: "Because it lacks tangibility (*asparśavattva*), it does not initiate a substance. For it is observed that only a tangible substance initiates another substance, as in the case of atoms (*paramāṇu*). Yet there is no proof for the tangibility of the mind, because no effect belonging to the genus *manastva* (mind-ness) is perceived to possess tangibility. Just as an effect belonging to the genus *pṛthivītva* (earth-ness) is perceived to be tangible, thereby making known the tangibility of the atoms that constitute it, so too there is no such effect belonging to the genus *manastva*; how then can the mind be tangible? Furthermore, if it were tangible, then due to its movement within the body—like the air—it would occasionally fail to connect with a particular sense organ, resulting in the non-perception of objects such as color-form (*rūpa*) over a period of time. And this is not observed except in the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). Therefore, by virtue of lacking tangibility, it does not initiate a substance.

Although corporeality (*mūrtatva*) is established by the determination of its atomic dimension (*aṇuparimāṇa*), he states the proof once more: "Corporeality [is established] because of possessing action (*kriyāvattvāt*). This is because action conforms to that [corporeality]. And that [action] is known through its connection with the sense-faculties. For otherwise, how could the mind, being of atomic dimension, connect with another sense-faculty?

Although the consciousness of the mind was previously refuted, he states yet another objection: "Because it would follow that the body would be common [to both], there would be a lack of cognition. For if the mind were conscious, the body would be an object of enjoyment common to both; thus, in the event of conflicting intentions, the experience of pleasure and pain would be impossible.

Now, as to whether it is for its own sake or for the sake of another, he says: "It is for the sake of another because it is an instrument (*karaṇa*). For an instrument, such as an axe and so forth, is observed to accomplish the purpose of another person. And since the mind is an instrument, it therefore accomplishes the purpose of the agent, which is the Self (*ātman*). Now, as to whether the mind is a substance (*dravya*), a quality (*guṇa*), or an action (*karman*), he says: "It is a substance because it possesses qualities. It is like earth and the other [elements]. Its qualities have already been mentioned.

Now, since the mind has an atomic dimension (*aṇuparimāṇa*), how is it that cognitions of color and other objects arise so rapidly? To this he says: "It moves swiftly" (*āśusañcāri*). And that [swiftness] is "due to the influence of effort and the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). That is to say, its swiftness of movement is due to the influence of being grasped by effort—specifically that which precedes life—and by a particular unseen force (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*). [Thus ends the section on Substances in the *Vyomavatī*, a commentary on the *Padārthadharmasaṅgraha* composed by the venerable teacher Vyomaśiva.
{The Section on Qualities (*guṇaprakaraṇam*)}
The commonality of the general property of quality (*guṇasāmānyasādharmya*) is as follows:
“All qualities, such as color and the rest, possess a connection with the general property of quality (*guṇatva*), reside in substances, are devoid of action, and themselves lack qualities.”

Now, following the order of enumeration, the author states the section beginning with “the connection with the quality-ness (*guṇatva*) belongs to all qualities, such as color (*rūpa*), etc. (*rūpādīnāṃ sarveṣāṃ guṇānāṃ guṇatvābhisambandhaḥ*), in order to demonstrate the pervasive commonality (*sādharmya*) of the qualities—whose occasion has now arrived—by way of their difference from other categories (*padārtha*), as well as the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of those specifically determined qualities from their own internal subdivisions. The "connection with quality-ness" is the inherence (*samavāya*) characterized by that [quality-ness]. To what does it belong? To "color and the rest" (*rūpādīnām*). However, since the word "etc. (*ādi*) grasps an indefinite number of objects, it is not known how many there are; therefore, he says "all" (*sarveṣām*). And he says "qualities" (*guṇānām*) in order to exclude [the inclusion of] upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*) and so forth.

[Objection: But if it is stated thus, "of all qualities," since there would be no deviation [from the rule], the phrase "of color and so forth" (rūpādīnām) would be redundant. [Reply: No. Because, by means of the two qualifiers "connection with the nature of quality" (guṇatvābhisambandha) and "being dependent" (āśritatva), the view that "every quality [possesses these]" is excluded. For it is only color and so forth that possess the connection with the nature of quality as their common characteristic (sādharmya), and not others.

Nor is it logical to claim that the mention of "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth is for the purpose of excluding the three *guṇas* accepted by the Sāṃkhyas, because such [a category] is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, it is observed that what is well-known is excluded by a qualifier, as in the case of "non-blue" being excluded by "blue. Thus, form and the rest are distinct from others, or are to be designated as "qualities" (*guṇa*), because they are connected with the property of "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*). Those things which are not distinct and are not designated as "qualities" are not connected with quality-ness, just like earth and the other [elements]. The remainder is as before.

Likewise, "residing in substance" (*dravyāśritatva*) is a common property (*sādharmya*) of color and the other [qualities]. And this is intended to be expressed with a restrictive emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). For otherwise, since substances and so forth also reside in substances, the common property would be over-extensive (*ativyāpin*), and thus not excluded [from them]. The restriction, however, is that they reside only in substances. Substances, actions, and particularities (*viśeṣa*) reside only in substances, but they do not reside *exclusively* [in them]—for universals (*sāmānya*) and inherence (*samavāya*) reside in substances, but not *only* in substances, because they also exist in qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth. Qualities, on the other hand, reside only in substances and not in qualities and so forth; likewise, they reside *only* in substances and are not non-resident, because a substance devoid of qualities is never perceived. Thus, by means of the exclusion of non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*) and the exclusion of connection with others (*anyayoga-vyavaccheda*), it is to be proven that [qualities] are distinct from others because they reside in substances.

Likewise, those from which the activity characterized by motion has departed are "devoid of action" (*niṣkriya*); their state is "actionlessness" (*niṣkriyatva*). Those in whom qualities exist are "possessors of qualities" (*guṇavantaḥ*); their state is "quality-possessingness" (*guṇavattva*), and its negation is "quality-less-ness" (*aguṇavattva*). Now, it has been stated that both actionlessness and quality-less-ness belong to all five categories beginning with quality; therefore, this is not a common characteristic (*sādharmya*) that distinguishes [the category of substance] from other categories. Nor is there any purpose here in mentioning mere common characteristics, since they have already been stated previously. If it is argued that this is merely a common characteristic distinguished [from others] that coexists with the property of being a quality (*guṇatva*):

Alternatively, this [statement] is intended to demonstrate the distinction [of qualities] precisely from the category of substance (*dravyapadārtha*). For others maintain that qualities (*guṇa*) or action (*karman*) are not entities distinct from substance, since their status as such is established by their lack of activity and their nature as qualities. To explain: substance possesses action and qualities, whereas qualities are devoid of those; thus, they are indeed distinct due to the difference in their attributes (*dharmabheda*).

Now, how can color and the other qualities be devoid of action and devoid of further qualities? Because only a substance (*dravya*) is an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), there is no arising of [qualities] that would have them as their substratum. If it is argued that the status of being an inherent cause is justified because colors and so forth arise as inherent in [other] colors and so forth, that is not so; for they are not perceived. For while there is the cognition "the substance possesses color," there is no such manifestation as "the color possesses color."

Even granting [your position], it is said: if color (*rūpa*) is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) for the production of color, there must be another non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). The color of the cause itself cannot be the non-inherent cause, because that too is the inherent cause for the production of its own resident color. Nor is it observed that the very same thing can be both the inherent cause and the non-inherent cause. Nor is conjunction (*saṃyoga*) [the cause], because it is the non-inherent cause for the production of a substance (*dravya*). If the conjunction of the threads were the non-inherent cause for the production of their color, then prior to that production, such conjunction would necessarily be absent. If conjunction were the cause even for the production of colors within other colors, one must likewise state its absence prior to their production. Furthermore, it cannot be said that another color arises from a single [prior] color alone, because the commencement [of an effect] by a single entity is refuted both successively and simultaneously.

For this very reason, there is an absence of action [in qualities], because action conforms to form (*mūrti*). And that [form] is not possible in qualities, because they are devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*). Furthermore, form is defined as the dimension of a non-pervasive substance. Now, if it is argued that the appearance of motion in qualities occurs through the movement of their substratum, how is that so? It is through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), since a primary [application] is precluded. For, by superimposing upon the qualities—through their inherence in the same object—the motion residing in the substance, people understand that "the qualities move."

Thus, because it is devoid of activity and lacks qualities, color (*rūpa*) is a distinct entity from substance (*dravya*). Now, if it is a distinct entity, how is it designated by means of a specific substratum? It is due to the restriction of its relation. We shall explain in the section on the category of inherence (*samavāya*) that there is no need to postulate another relation for the relation itself, precisely because it is of the nature of a relation. [For some, there is the quality of being corporeal: “Color, taste, smell, touch, priority, posteriority, gravity, fluidity, viscidity, and velocity are the qualities of corporeal substances. (*rūpa-rasa-gandha-sparśa-paratva-aparatva-gurutva-dravatva-sneha-vegā mūrtaguṇāḥ*.)<PDhS>

Now, he demonstrates the specific commonality (*sādharmya*) of these restricted qualities as distinguished from other internal divisions: "The qualities beginning with color (*rūpa*) and ending with velocity (*vega*) are the qualities of corporeal substances (*mūrta*). This means they belong only to corporeal things; it does not mean that corporeal things have only these [qualities], because there are others as well. For instance, color, fluidity, and so forth exist in the three [substances] beginning with earth; gravity and taste exist in two; touch exists in four; odor exists only in earth; moisture (*sneha*) exists only in water; while priority (*paratva*), posteriority (*aparatva*), and velocity exist in all five corporeal substances. [Some, moreover, are qualities of incorporeal things.]
“Intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, mental impression, and sound are qualities of the formless.

(*PDhS*) From intellect up to sound, these are the qualities of the formless. They are the qualities of only those things that are formless; however, they do not constitute the entirety of such qualities, because number and the rest are also qualities of them. Those beginning with intellect and ending with mental impression reside in the self (*puruṣa*), while sound resides in space (*ākāśa*). {Some are qualities of both the formed and the formless.}
“Number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction are qualities common to both.

Number and the others, ending with disjunction, are qualities common to both; that is, they are the qualities of both the corporeal and the incorporeal. Likewise, these alone are the qualities common to both.
[Among qualities, those which reside in more than one are the common ones.]
(“Conjunction, disjunction, duality, dual separateness, and so forth, are dependent upon many.

Now, demonstrating the state of being dependent upon one or many, [the author] says: “Conjunction, disjunction, duality, dual separateness, and so forth, are dependent upon many. By the phrase “and so forth,” numbers beginning with three and ending with the highest number (parārdha), as well as the separateness qualified by them, are included. Furthermore, here dependence upon many is intended with respect to individual instances (*vyakti*), not with respect to the universal (*jāti*); for otherwise, it would follow that even color and other qualities would possess that same status [of being dependent upon many].

Although a genus such as *rūpatva* (color-ness) does not subsist in multiple [individuals], nevertheless, a single instance (*tadvyakti*) of it subsists in only one. And conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth are not like this, because an instance of them is observed to be dependent on many. [This applies] to those distinct from that [genus]:
“The remaining [qualities], however, reside in individual substances. (*Śeṣāstu ekaikadravyavṛttayaḥ*).<PDhS>

"But the remaining ones reside in each individual substance" (*śeṣāstvekaikadravyavṛttayaḥ*). The "remaining" are those other than those previously mentioned; for they reside in only one substance at a time. Indeed, a single individual instance (*vyakti*) inheres in only one [substance], and the same applies to individual instances of taste and so forth. However, this restriction—that they reside in only one substance each—applies to these [qualities] specifically, and not exclusively to them, because there are also qualities that reside in both [substances].

{Enumeration of the Particular Qualities} "Color, taste, smell, touch, viscidity, natural fluidity, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, mental impression (*bhāvanā*), and sound are the particular qualities (*vaiśeṣikaguṇāḥ*). <PDhS>
{The enumeration of general qualities} (“Number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, gravity, occasional fluidity, and velocity are the general qualities.
<PDhS> Now, in order to demonstrate which are the specific qualities and which are the general qualities, he says: “Color and the others, ending with sound, are specific qualities.”

What constitutes their status as *viśeṣaguṇas* (specific qualities)? If it were merely "residing in a single [substance]," that would apply even to gravity (*gurutva*) and so forth. If it were "perceptible by a single sense organ," that would not apply to viscidity (*sneha*), fluidity (*dravatva*), merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and the like. If it were "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇatva*), that does not hold, because universals such as "color-ness" (*rūpatva*) are perceived in multiple locations. If you mean this with reference to individual instances (*vyakti*), then it exists even in gravity and the rest. No; for it is established otherwise. To explain: *viśeṣaguṇas* are those which, while being qualified by a particular inherent in themselves, serve to differentiate their own substrate from other things of the same class. The term "own substrate" (*svāśraya*) is used because it is impossible for color and the like to differentiate their substrate without qualification. Furthermore, since color and the like, when unqualified, do not differentiate their substrate, the phrase "qualified by a particular" (*viśeṣaviśiṣṭa*) is included. Numbers and the like are also inherent in the same object as smell and thus differentiate earth; they are also inherent in the same object as viscidity and thus differentiate water. To exclude these, the term "inherent in itself" (*svasamaveta*) is used. For instance, while a particular such as whiteness is inherent in color and sweetness in taste, viscidity or smell is not inherent in number and the like; thus, there is a differentiation. Nevertheless, since the dimension of an atom (*aṇuparimāṇa*) differentiates atoms, the phrase "of the same class as its own substrate" (*svāśrayaikajātīya*) is used. For example, the dimension of an atom, though endowed with a particular inherent in itself, differentiates its own substrate—the fourfold collection of atoms—from others of the same class, but not from those of a different class. The same applies to the dimension of the infinitely large (*paramamahat*).

Color (*rūpa*), being endowed with numerous qualifiers inherent within itself such as whiteness and so forth, serves to differentiate its own substrate from other members of the same class: it invariably differentiates water by means of the qualification of whiteness, and fire by means of whiteness and luminosity; such distinctions are to be understood exactly as previously stated.

Thus, because they possess qualifiers inherent within themselves and thereby differentiate their own substrates from others of the same class, these alone are "specific qualities" (*viśeṣaguṇa*). This is the restriction: only these are specific qualities. Number (*saṃkhyā*) and the rest, up to velocity (*vega*), are exclusively "general qualities" (*sāmānyaguṇa*). Because they lack the defining characteristics of specific qualities, these alone are general qualities.
“Qualities perceptible by each individual external sense organ.

(*śabdasparśarūparasagandhā bāhyaikaikendriyagrāhyāḥ*) Now, demonstrating that [certain qualities] are perceptible by one or several sense organs, he says: “Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell” are those things grasped by each respective external sense organ; thus they are “perceptible by them. The inclusion of the term “external” is for the purpose of excluding the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), for there is indeed a desire to speak of those [qualities] as being perceptible by two sense organs. Furthermore, the restriction implies that these alone are necessarily perceptible by each respective external sense organ, and likewise that they are not perceptible by multiple sense organs.

{The enumeration of qualities perceptible by two sense organs} (“Number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, fluidity, viscidity, and momentum are perceptible by two sense organs.

<PDhS> From number up to momentum, these are exclusively perceptible by two sense organs. By necessity, these alone are perceptible by two sense organs. The term “external” (bāhya) must be understood as persisting [in the definition] for the purpose of excluding the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

Now, how is it that viscidity (*sneha*) is perceptible by two sense organs? Because a cognition of "smoothness" (*snigdha*) is observed when the skin is active. For just as there is the appearance of "smooth hair" through the activity of the eye, so too, after bathing, a cognition of smoothness is seen through the activity of the skin; thus, by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), its perceptibility by two sense organs is determined. Furthermore, we shall examine whether this [viscidity] is composed of water (*āpya*) or earth (*pārthiva*) in the investigation of viscidity.
{The Enumeration of Qualities Perceptible by the Internal Organ}

“Intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort are apprehended by the internal organ. [PDhS] {Enumeration of supersensible qualities} “Gravity, merit, demerit, and mental impression are supersensible. [PDhS]
From cognition (*buddhi*) up to effort (*prayatna*), these are grasped by the internal organ alone; therefore, they are "grasped by that" (*tad-grāhya*).

Weight (*gurutva*), merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and mental impression (*bhāvanā*) are indeed beyond the senses (*atīndriya*); they exist transcending the sense organs and thus do not become objects of their perception. We shall explain how weight is imperceptible during its formal examination. {The enumeration of those qualities among the qualities which are preceded by the qualities of their causes.}
“Color, taste, smell, touch, dimension, unity, separateness, gravity, fluidity, viscidity, and velocity produced by causes other than heat are preceded by the qualities of their causes.

Regarding the statement that those beginning with color and ending with velocity produced by causes other than heat are preceded by the qualities of their causes: the inclusion of the term “produced by causes other than heat” (apākaja) is for the purpose of excluding the color of the atoms of earth.

But surely even those [qualities] are indeed preceded by the qualities of their causes. For instance, the cause is the atom (*paramāṇu*), its quality is the conjunction with fire in the case of an earth-atom, and the color and other qualities are preceded by that; so how is it that they are not "preceded by the qualities of their causes"? That is not so, because there is a misunderstanding of the intended meaning. And this is the intended meaning: only those qualities that exist in the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) are "qualities of the cause"; those effects which have such qualities as their prior cause are what are intended here by the term "preceded by the qualities of their causes. In this way, the qualities produced by baking (*pākaja*) are excluded.

Now, it might be argued that the color and other qualities of atoms such as water, although not produced by heating (*pākaja*), are nevertheless not preceded by the qualities of their causes. This is not so, because what is intended here is a relative negation (*paryudāsa-pratiṣedha*). For, "produced from heating" means those born from heating; by the negation of that, the state of being preceded by qualities other [than those of the cause] is obtained, thereby excluding eternal substances.

[Objection: Even so, the inclusion of the term "non-produced by heat" (*apākaja*) is useless, because it is impossible to establish the restriction that "these [qualities] are preceded solely by the qualities of their causes. For instance, fluidity (*dravatva*) and velocity (*vega*) are also not preceded by the qualities of their causes. [Response: No. Because the purpose is clarity, the restriction is intended as "only these are preceded by the qualities of their causes," and not "these are preceded by the qualities of their causes alone. For one who does not understand this, there might arise the suspicion of a flaw regarding qualities produced by heat (*pākaja*); thus, the inclusion of "non-produced by heat" is for the sake of clarity. Furthermore, the mention of "oneness" (*ekatva*) and "separateness" (*eka-pṛthaktva*) here is for the purpose of excluding "duality" (*dvitva*), "dual-separateness" (*dvi-pṛthaktva*), and so forth; for those are indeed not preceded by the qualities of their causes.
{The statement that qualities are not preceded by the qualities of their causes}:
“Intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, mental impression (*bhāvanā*), and sound are not preceded by the qualities of their causes.

(*PDhS*) Qualities beginning with intellect and ending with sound are indeed not preceded by the qualities of their causes; that is to say, they are not effects whose qualities are preceded by the qualities of their inherent causes (*samavāyin*). However, it is not these alone [that are so], because conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, duality, and double-separateness (*dvipṛthaktva*) are also not preceded by the qualities of their causes.

Now, one must consider this: even though there is no difference in the fact that [these qualities] do not have preceding qualities as their cause, what is the purpose of not mentioning conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the others in this statement? Alternatively, if it is argued that by specifying only those qualities from color produced by cooking (*apākaja-rūpa*) up to momentum (*vega*) as having preceding qualities as their cause, it is understood that the remaining ones do not have preceding qualities as their cause—then in that case, cognition (*buddhi*) and the others need not be mentioned either; or rather, the statement "the remaining ones do not have preceding qualities as their cause" should be stated as a comprehensive summary of all the sub-varieties. Thus, there is no need for the specific mention of cognition and the rest.

This is not so. The specific mention [of conjunction, etc. is for the sake of clarity. Since it has been stated in various ways in the treatise, [the author] does not mention conjunction and the others by their own names in order to ensure that the students achieve a clear understanding of the meaning and to cultivate their power of reasoning (*ūha*). Others, however, believe that what is intended here is the mention of only those specific qualities that function as single entities (*ekavṛtti*); but we do not accept this, because the objection remains unrefuted.
{The Enumeration of Qualities Arising from Conjunction}

“Intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, mental impression, sound, the dimension of cotton, subsequent conjunction, occasional fluidity, priority, posteriority, and those produced by heating are born of conjunction. (PDhS)

Likewise, regarding the statement that [qualities] beginning with cognition (*buddhi*) and ending with those produced by heating (*pākaja*) are born of conjunction (*saṃyogaja*): here, those beginning with cognition and ending with mental impression (*bhāvanā*) arise from the conjunction of the self (*puruṣa*) and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Sound arises from the conjunction of the drum and space (*ākāśa*). The dimension of cotton (*tūla-parimāṇa*) arises from accumulation (*pracaya*). "Subsequent conjunction" (*uttara-saṃyoga*) is according to the reading of the Sūtra; "conjunction born of conjunction" (*saṃyogaja-saṃyoga*) [is mentioned]; and "accidental fluidity" (*naimittika-dravatva*) arises from conjunction with fire. As for priority and posteriority (*paratvāparatve*), they arise from the conjunction of direction (*dik*), time (*kāla*), and the substance (*piṇḍa*). Regarding "produced by heating," these refer to the color and other qualities of earth-atoms (*pārthiva-paramāṇu*), which are also born of conjunction with fire. Thus, these alone are born of conjunction, yet these are not *exclusively* born of conjunction. For instance, sound is born of disjunction (*vibhāga*), and there is also sound born of sound.
{The Enumeration of Qualities Arising from Action} (“Conjunction, disjunction, and momentum are born of action.

<PDhS> “Conjunction, disjunction, and momentum” are called “born of action” because they are produced from actions; however, these are not *only* born of action. For instance, conjunction arises from conjunction, disjunction from disjunction, and momentum even from momentum.
{The Description of Qualities Arising from Disjunction} (“Sound and subsequent disjunction are born of disjunction.

<PDhS> Regarding the phrase “sound and subsequent disjunction”: those two which are born from disjunction are called “born of disjunction” (*vibhāgaja*). These alone are born of disjunction, but it is not the case that these two are *only* born of disjunction. For instance, sound is produced by conjunction (*saṃyogaja*) as well as being born of sound (*śabdaja*). Furthermore, with respect to the reading of the aphorism (*sūtra*), “subsequent disjunction” is understood specifically as a disjunction born of disjunction (*vibhāgajavibhāga*).

{An enumeration of those qualities that depend on cognition, and those that originate both similar and dissimilar kinds [of qualities]:} “Remoteness (*paratva*), proximity (*aparatva*), duality (*dvitva*), dual separateness (*dvipṛthaktva*), and so forth, depend on cognition. Color (*rūpa*), taste (*rasa*), smell (*gandha*), non-hot touch (*anuṣṇasparśa*), sound (*śabda*), dimension (*parimāṇa*), oneness (*ekatva*), single separateness (*ekapṛthaktva*), and viscidity (*sneha*) originate similar kinds [of qualities]. Pleasure (*sukha*), pain (*duḥkha*), desire (*icchā*), aversion (*dveṣa*), and effort (*prayatna*) originate dissimilar kinds [of qualities]. Conjunction (*saṃyoga*), disjunction (*vibhāga*), number (*saṃkhyā*), gravity (*gurutva*), fluidity (*dravatva*), hot touch (*uṣṇasparśa*), cognition (*jñāna*), merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and mental impression (*saṃskāra*) originate both similar and dissimilar kinds [of qualities]. <PDhS>

Now, he demonstrates which [qualities] depend upon cognition (*buddhyapekṣā*) and which initiate their own kind (*samānajātyārambhaka*): "Remoteness, proximity, duality, dual separateness, and so forth" depend upon cognition for their own production; thus they are called "cognition-dependent. By the word "and so forth," numbers beginning with three and ending with the highest number (*parārdha*), as well as the separateness delimited by them, are included. The restriction, however, is that these alone are cognition-dependent, and likewise, these alone are cognition-dependent; they do not exist without cognition.

Color and the rest, up to viscidity (*sneha*), are initiators of their own kind (*samānajātyārambhaka*). Those whose genus (*jāti*) is the same or equal are "of the same genus" (*samānajāti*); they initiate those [entities], and thus they are initiators thereof. However, these alone are not the initiators of their own kind, because there exist things that initiate both [their own kind and another]. Here, the inclusion of the term "non-hot" (*anuṣṇa*) is for the purpose of excluding hot touch (*uṣṇasparśa*), since that too is an initiator of both. The inclusion of unity (*ekatva*) and singularity-in-separation (*ekapṛthaktva*) is for the purpose of excluding duality (*dvitva*), duality-in-separation (*dvipṛthaktva*), and so forth; for duality and the rest are initiators of a different genus, and duality-in-separation and the rest are not causes at all.

For instance, the qualities beginning with color (*rūpa*) and ending with viscidity (*sneha*), which reside in the parts of water, produce those same qualities in the effect [the whole]. Odor, however, residing in the parts of earth, produces odor in that whole [the earth]. And sound, residing in space (*ākāśa*), produces sound in that very same [space]. As for the qualities beginning with pleasure (*sukha*) and ending with effort (*prayatna*), they are producers of dissimilar kinds. They are called "producers" because they produce only what is of a dissimilar kind, but not because these alone are the producers, since others also exist. Thus, from pleasure arises desire; from aversion arises hatred; from those two arises effort; and from that, action (*kriyā*).

The qualities beginning with conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and ending with mental impression (*saṃskāra*) originate both homogeneous and heterogeneous effects. Those whose genus (*jāti*) is the same are "homogeneous" (*samānajāti*); those whose genus is not the same are "heterogeneous" (*asamānajāti*), by the negation of that [homogeneity]. "Originate those" means they are the originators thereof. These alone are the originators of homogeneous and heterogeneous effects, and no others. Furthermore, these are invariably originators of both homogeneous and heterogeneous effects. To illustrate: from conjunction arises conjunction, and heterogeneous [effects] such as cognition (*buddhi*) and so forth; from disjunction arises disjunction, and the heterogeneous effect which is sound (*śabda*); from number arises number, and heterogeneous [effects] such as dimension (*parimāṇa*); from gravity arises gravity, and the heterogeneous effect which is falling (*patana*); from fluidity arises fluidity, and the heterogeneous effect which is flowing (*syandana*); from hot touch arises hot touch, and heterogeneous [effects] produced by maturation (*pākaja*); from knowledge arises knowledge, and heterogeneous [effects] which are mental impressions (*saṃskāra*); from merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) arise merit and demerit, and heterogeneous [effects] which are pleasure and pain (*sukha-duḥkha*); from mental impression arises mental impression, and the heterogeneous effect which is recollection (*smaraṇa*).

{An Enumeration of Qualities Inherent in and Initiating Activity in Oneself and Others} “Cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, mental impression (*bhāvanā*), and sound initiate activity within their own substratum. Color, taste, odor, touch, dimension, viscidity, effort, and [mental] impression initiate activity in others. Conjunction, disjunction, number, unity, individuality, gravity, fluidity, speed, merit (*dharma*), and demerit (*adharma*), however, initiate activity in both. <PDhS> II.010

Now he demonstrates those [qualities] that originate in what is inherent in both themselves and their own substratum: beginning with cognition (*buddhi*) and ending with sound (*śabda*). They are called "originators inherent in their own substratum" because they originate only that which is inherent in their own substratum. However, these alone are not the only such originators, for there exist others that originate in both [themselves and their substratum]. To illustrate: cognition resides in the self (*ātman*), and therein it becomes the cause of knowledge (*jñāna*) and mental impression (*saṃskāra*). Pleasure and so forth, as well as desire, reside in the self; likewise, aversion arises from pain in that very same place. From desire, memory and effort arise in the self; the same applies to aversion. From mental impression (*bhāvanā*), further impressions and memory arise in the self alone. And sound, while residing in space (*ākāśa*), originates sound in that very same place.

"Form and the others, ending with effort, [operate] elsewhere. This means that they initiate [their effects] only in something else; thus, they are "initiators elsewhere," but not these [qualities themselves]. For instance, form, taste, smell, touch, dimension, and viscidity, while residing in their causes, initiate those same qualities in the subsequent effect. Likewise, effort, while residing in the person, initiates action in something else, such as the hand.

Conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the others, up to and including non-dharma (*adharma*), are initiators in both cases. These very same [qualities] are invariably initiators in both cases. For instance, the conjunction of a drum and space, while residing in space, initiates sound in that very [space]; whereas the conjunction of a drum and a stick initiates it elsewhere. Likewise, the disjunction of a bamboo split and space initiates sound in its own substratum, while the disjunction of the bamboo splits initiates sound in the other [substratum], namely space. Number, as it exists in the cause—such as duality, triad, and so forth—initiates dimension (*parimāṇa*) in the effect, as does the number unity (*ekatva*). Unity, however, initiates duality and the rest in its own substratum. The mention of "single separateness" (*ekapṛthaktva*) is for the purpose of excluding "double separateness" (*dvipṛthaktva*) and the like, because those are not initiators. Single separateness, existing in the causes, initiates single separateness in the effect, while [multiple separateness] initiates double separateness and the like in its own substrata. Weight (*gurutva*), fluidity (*dravatva*), and speed (*vega*), when present in the cause, initiate weight and the others in the effect, while in their own substrata they initiate the actions of falling, flowing, and moving. Dharma and adharma, moreover, initiate pleasure and pain inherent in their own substrata, but in the case of another's substratum, they initiate action.
{An enumeration of the causes of action}: “Gravity, fluidity, velocity, effort, merit, demerit, and particular conjunctions are the causes of action. <PDhS>

Now he states the causes of action (*kriyāhetu*), ending with the specific types of conjunction beginning with gravity (*gurutva*): "The causes of action" [are as follows]. To explain: from gravity comes falling; from fluidity (*dravatva*) comes flowing; from momentum (*vega*) comes motion; from effort (*prayatna*) comes action in the hand and so forth; and from merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) comes action in fire and so forth. As for the specific types of conjunction—namely, impulsion (*nodana*), impact (*abhighāta*), and conjunction-with-the-conjoined (*saṃyuktasaṃyoga*)—these too are indeed causes of action. This is because gravity and the others are also observed to be generators of gravity [and other qualities]. {This concludes the enumeration of the non-inherent causes and other qualities, as well as the statement regarding qualities that are not causes.}

(“Color, taste, odor, non-hot touch, number, dimension, singularity, separateness, viscidity, and sound possess the nature of non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). Intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and mental impression possess the nature of instrumental causes (*nimittakāraṇa*). Conjunction, disjunction, hot touch, gravity, fluidity, and velocity possess the nature of both [types of causes]. Remoteness, proximity, duality, and so forth possess the nature of not being causes. <PDhS> Now, he states the non-inherent, instrumental, and dual-natured causes: “Color and the rest, ending with sound, have the nature of non-inherent causes,” and so on.

Now, what is this so-called "non-inherent causality" (*asamavāyikāraṇatva*)? It is the capacity to produce an effect while being in close proximity [to it]. Whatever is proximate to something else, and whose capacity as a producer has been observed through pervasion (*vyāpti*), that is its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) in the production thereof.

What, then, is this proximity (*pratyāsatti*)? It is inherence in a single substratum (*ekārthasamavāya*). This, however, is divided into two types: that characterized by inherence in a single substratum with the effect (*kāryaikārthasamavāya-lakṣaṇā*), and that characterized by inherence in a single substratum with the cause (*kāryakāraṇaikārthasamavāya-lakṣaṇā*). That which has as its characteristic or mark inherence in one and the same object together with the effect is "that characterized by [inherence with] the effect. For example, in the case of sound’s production of another sound. For the word "effect" (*kārya*) resides in space (*ākāśa*), and the word "cause" (*kāraṇa*) likewise resides in that very same place; thus, for this [sound], proximity is inherence in a single substratum with the effect. Similarly, in the case of the production of cognition (*buddhi*) and so forth, there is proximity for the contact between the self (*ātman*) and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). For that [contact] resides in the self, and cognition and the rest likewise reside in that very same place.

[Objection: But in that case, since cognition and the rest also possess inherence in the same substrate (*ekārthasamavāya*) at the time of producing their own effects, would they not likewise be non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) rather than instrumental causes (*nimitta*)? [Reply: This is not a fault. For conjunction is observed to have the capacity for the production of all effects through its pervasion (*vyāpti*), whereas such is not the case for cognition and the rest individually. This is because their capacity is determined only with respect to the production of specific, restricted effects. However, the conjunction of the self and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) has its capacity observed in the production of the entire range of cognitions and so forth; therefore, that alone is the non-inherent cause. Indeed, cognitions and the like never arise without the conjunction of the mind (*manas*). Thus, since cognition and the rest arise at the conclusion of the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), the conjunction of the mind is the cause therein.

[Objection: Even so, since merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) are the causes for the production of the entire range of cognitions and so forth by way of pervasion (*vyāpti*), would they not be non-inherent causes (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*)? [Reply: No. For it is observed that the specific qualities (*viśeṣa-guṇa*) of all-pervading substances (*vibhu*) arise through a particular kind of proximity (*pratyāsatti*). To illustrate: when a sound (*śabda*) initiates another sound, it initiates it immediately after the very portion of space (*nabhodeśa*) occupied by itself, and not because of inherence in the same substrate (*ekārthasamavāya*) in another location—otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving even what was spoken by Brahmā in a distant place. In the same way, merit and demerit would have to initiate pleasure, pain, and so forth immediately after the very part of the self (*ātman*) occupied by themselves; consequently, these would be absent in places such as heaven (*svarga*). However, since pleasure, pain, and so forth are initiated even in other locations, merit and demerit are merely instrumental causes (*nimitta-kāraṇa*). Therefore, it is established that the conjunction of the self and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-saṃyoga*) alone is the non-inherent cause for the production of cognition and the rest, by virtue of inhering in the same substrate.

Likewise, the effect, such as color and so forth, resides in the cloth; the cloth resides in the threads; and the color and other qualities residing therein reside in those very [threads]. Thus, their proximity consists in the inherence of cause and effect within a single substratum (*ekārthasamavāya*).

[Objection: Even so, the color of the thread (*tantu-rūpa*) would be proximate to the production of taste (*rasa*) and so on, and taste would be proximate to the production of color; thus, they would both be non-inherent causes (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*). [Reply: No, because of the qualification "that which is a producer" (*janakatva*). That which is proximate to the production of something and is its producer is a non-inherent cause. Color is not a cause for the production of taste and so on, because no such conformity (*anuvidhāna*) is observed. For while there is conformity with the form of the cause—such that from a white color a white [taste] arises and from a yellow [color] a yellow [taste] arises—there is no such conformity in the case of taste and so on. Indeed, no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is perceived such that "from a sweet or sour [taste], that color is white or yellow. Therefore, even though there is proximity, there is no status as a non-inherent cause, because that specific characteristic of a cause has been defined.

Nor does this entail the same [logical] consequence for the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), because that lacks the aforementioned proximity. For it does not possess co-inherence in the same object with either the effect or its [own] cause, since that effect inheres in that very [cause] alone.

For instance, color, taste, odor, non-hot touch, dimension, and viscidity are non-inherent causes solely by virtue of inhering in the same object as their effect and their cause. Number, however, such as duality and so forth, is a non-inherent cause in the production of dimension by virtue of inhering in the same object as both the effect and the cause. Likewise, the unity of the cause and the singularity of separateness are [non-inherent causes] in the production of the unity and singularity of the effect. In the production of duality, dual separateness, and so forth, unity, singularity of separateness, and the like are exclusively non-inherent causes by virtue of inhering in the same object as the effect. Thus it has been stated regarding sound as well.

These [qualities] possess only the status of non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), but not exclusively these, since others also exist. Here, the inclusion of the term "non-hot" (*anuṣṇa*) is for the purpose of excluding hot touch (*uṣṇasparśa*), because that [hot touch] functions as a cause in both ways [inherent and non-inherent]. From cognition (*buddhi*) up to mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), they possess the status of instrumental causes (*nimittakāraṇa*). This means they are producers devoid of the characteristics of inherent and non-inherent causes. Nor should it be argued that the qualification [of being devoid of those characteristics] is unestablished, because cognition and the rest are producers of what is proximate; this is due to the reasoning already stated. The restriction, however, is that these are only instrumental causes, but not exclusively these.

For instance, cognition (*buddhi*) is the cause for the production of knowledge (*jñāna*) and mental impressions (*saṃskāra*); pleasure is the cause of desire; pain is the cause of aversion; desire and aversion are the causes of effort (*prayatna*), and that [effort] is the cause of action (*kriyā*); merit and demerit (*dharmādharmau*) are the causes of pleasure and pain; and mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is the cause of recollection (*smaraṇa*).

As for those beginning with conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and ending with momentum (*vega*), there is "causality in both ways" (*ubhayathā kāraṇatvam*). This means they possess the status of being both non-inherent causes (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*) and efficient causes (*nimitta-kāraṇa*). It is by this rule that these alone possess causality in both ways, and thus they have causality in both ways exclusively.

For instance, the conjunction of the drum and space is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) [of sound], while the conjunction of the drum and the drumstick is the efficient cause (*nimitta*). Similarly, the disjunction of the bamboo-split and space is the non-inherent cause, while the disjunction of the bamboo-splits is the efficient cause. Likewise, hot touch is the non-inherent cause in the production [of heat], while it is the efficient cause in the case of qualities produced by heating (*pākaja*). In the same way, gravity, fluidity, and velocity are the non-inherent causes in the production of motion within their own substratum, while they are the efficient causes for motion in other substrata.
By the phrase "the non-causality of remoteness, proximity, dual separateness, and so forth," the term "and so forth" includes triple separateness and other such qualities.

[An objection: But surely these do indeed possess causality in the production of cognition and the like? [Response: True; what is intended here is their lack of causality with respect to anything other than that [cognition]. This qualification should also be inferred for the statement regarding "the originator of its own kind" and so on. It is not that only these [qualities] are non-causes, but rather that they are exclusively non-causes, since even atomic dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*) and others are likewise non-causes.
[This concludes] the enumeration of qualities that are non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*) and qualities that endure as long as the substance exists (*yāvaddravyabhāvin*).

“Conjunction, disjunction, sound, and the specific qualities of the self reside in a limited portion [of their substratum]. The remaining qualities pervade their entire substratum. Unproduced color, taste, smell, touch, dimension, unity, individual separateness, innate fluidity, gravity, and viscidity persist as long as the substance exists; the remaining qualities do not persist as long as the substance exists. (PDhS II,014)

Now, he states for which [qualities] there is existence in a specific location (*pradeśavṛttitva*) and for which there is pervasion of the substrate (*āśrayavyāpitva*): "Conjunction, disjunction, sound, and the specific qualities of the self have existence in a specific location. What is intended is that they do not pervade their substrate; it is not, however, that they exist in a "part" (*avayava*), for that would entail the impossibility of such qualities in things that lack parts (*niṣpradeśa*). For these alone there is non-pervasion of the substrate; for these alone there is existence in a specific location.

"Of the remaining [qualities], there is pervasion of their substratum. Those other than those mentioned are the "remaining" ones; they possess the quality of pervading their substratum. How is this so? When the substratum is perceived, if there is a desire to apprehend them, they are necessarily apprehended. For example, when a cloth is perceived, if there is a desire to apprehend its color, that color is necessarily apprehended. However, for those qualities that do not pervade their substratum, there is no necessary apprehension upon the perception of the substratum, even when there is a desire to apprehend them and the sense-object contact is present. For instance, the conjunction of things located on the far side of a mountain is not necessarily perceived even when that mountain is perceived.

"From those beginning with non-produced [color] up to viscidity (*sneha*), there is 'persistence as long as the substance exists' (*yāvaddravyabhāvitva*). That which exists as long as the substance, and whose nature it is to do so, is "persisting as long as the substance exists"; this means their state of not being destroyed as long as the substratum remains. "The others have 'non-persistence as long as the substance exists'. Those other than the aforementioned are the "others," and they are destroyed even while the substratum exists.
[Thus ends the section on the common properties of qualities.]
The Section on the Distinctive Characteristics of Qualities:
“Because each of all the qualities, such as color and the rest, is connected with its own specific lower universal (*aparasāmānya*), they receive the designations ‘color’ and so forth.”

Now, he states the specific dissimilarity: "Because each of all the qualities, such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth, is connected with its own particular generality (*aparasāmānya*), they receive the designations 'color' and so on," and so forth. Those of which color is the first are "color and so forth" (*rūpādayaḥ*). It is not known how many there are; therefore, he says "of all the qualities" (*sarvaguṇānām*). These "all qualities" (*sarvaguṇāḥ*) are precisely those beginning with color and no others. "Each one" (*pratyekam*) means with respect to each individual one among them. "Because of connection with its own particular generality" (*aparasāmānyasambandhāt*): in relation to the generality of "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*), "color-ness" (*rūpatva*) and so forth are the particular generalities (*aparasāmānya*); because of connection with these, the designations "color" and so forth arise. Due to connection with "color-ness," the designation "color" arises; due to connection with "taste-ness" (*rasatva*), the designation "taste" arises. The same applies to the others as well.

{The dissimilarity of color-form (*rūpa*):} “In this regard, color-form is that which is grasped by the eye; it exists in earth, water, and fire; it is the means for perceiving substances and so forth; it is an auxiliary to the visual organ; it is of many kinds, such as white and others; it is eternal in the atoms of water and so forth; in the atoms of earth, it is opposed by conjunction with fire; in all effect-substances, it is preceded by the qualities of its causes; and it perishes only through the destruction of its substrate. <PDhS>

Since form (*rūpa*) was mentioned first therein, he states "form is that which is apprehended by the eye," and so forth, demonstrating the proof for its existence, its definition, its basis, its differentiation by way of causal efficiency, its permanence, and the causes of its arising and destruction.

In this context, it is color (*rūpa*) alone that is apprehended by the eye, not taste (*rasa*) and the rest. Because the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*)—namely, that "color is apprehended by the eye alone and is not to be determined by other sense organs"—depends on its immediate context, it does not intend to negate the visual apprehensibility of substances (*dravya*) and so forth. For instance, once the visual apprehensibility of substances and the like is established, when there arises a suspicion of such apprehensibility regarding them during the extended application (*atideśa*) in the sūtras: “Color is perceptible because of its inherence in multiple substances and because of its own specific qualities” (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 4.1.8), and “By this, the cognition of taste and the rest is explained” (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra ?), the restriction is intended solely to exclude that [apprehensibility] from those [substances], not to deny its occurrence in substances and so forth. Furthermore, we shall explain in the section on inferential knowledge (*laiṅgika-jñāna*) that the Buddhists (*Śākyas*) intend precisely such a restriction as is being proclaimed here.

The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: that which has multiple substances as its cause is called "multisubstantial" (*anekadravya*). Due to inherence (*samavāya*) with such a [substance], there occurs in some cases the perception of color (*rūpa*), provided that its own specific [causal] conditions are present; and it is precisely that specific auxiliary factor (*sahakāriviśeṣa*) whose absence results in non-perception. Therefore, color is perceptible. And this same principle applies equally to the perception of taste and the other [sensory objects].

“Functioning in earth, water, and fire” (*pṛthivyudakajvalanavṛtti*) is the definition of its substratum; or rather, it is a definition that depends on the preceding term. For instance, since the property of being perceptible by the eye (*cakṣurgrāhyatva*) also belongs to substantiality (*dravyatva*), the qualification “perceived by the eye alone” (*cakṣuṣaiva gṛhyate*) is used as a restrictive specification (*sāvadhāraṇa*). Nevertheless, since the universal of color-ness (*rūpatvasāmānya*) is also perceived by the eye alone, the phrase “functioning in earth, water, and fire” is employed. Furthermore, since the quality of functioning in earth and so forth also belongs to other things, the inclusion of the term “restriction” (*niyama*) is necessary. Therefore, color is distinct from everything else, because while it functions exclusively in earth, water, and fire, it is perceived by the eye alone; whereas that which is not distinct does not possess these characteristics, such as taste and the like.

The phrase “that which causes the apprehension of substance and so forth” (*dravyādyupalambhakam*) is a statement regarding purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*). It is called “that which causes the apprehension of substance and so forth” because it brings about the apprehension of substances and the like; that is, it is the cause of the perception of substance. Similarly, [the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra states]: “A substance is perceptible due to its magnitude, its possession of multiple constituent substances, and a specific quality (*rūpaviśeṣa*); and “[qualities and so forth are also perceptible] due to their inherence in that [substance]. Thus, the specific quality is stated to be a cause for apprehension. This definition should be understood as being dependent upon the preceding term.

The phrase “cooperating with the eye” (*nayanasahakārī*) indicates that [the sense organ] illuminates external form by means of the excellence of its own inherent form.
