Nor is this identical to what was stated previously, because here the excellence of form residing in the instrument (*karaṇa*) is being denoted, whereas in the former case, it was the excellence residing in the object (*karman*).

“Of many kinds, such as white and so forth” is the description of its differentiation. That too is indeed specific [to each substance]. It is “eternal in the atoms of water and so forth,” because of the absence of any cause for destruction. Regarding the statement “it is opposed by contact with fire in the atoms of earth,” this means that its opposition—its destruction—is caused by contact with fire. Furthermore, since destruction is not possible for that which has no origin, and because there is an absence of any other cause for its production or destruction, it arises from contact with fire alone. We shall explain in the examination of color produced by heating (*pākaja-rūpa*) that in all effects, production occurs through the sequence of the qualities of the causes, and destruction occurs solely from the destruction of the substrate.
The dissimilarity of taste (*rasavaidharmya*):

“Taste is perceptible by the gustatory organ; it resides in earth and water; it is the cause of life, nourishment, strength, and health. It is an auxiliary to the gustatory organ and is divided into the distinctions of sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, and astringent. Its eternality, non-eternality, and production are as previously described. (*PDhS*)

“Taste is that which is apprehended by the gustatory organ” (*raso rasanagrāhyaḥ*) is the proof for its existence. “Residing in earth and water” (*pṛthivyudakavṛttiḥ*) is the determination of its substratum, or rather, it is a definition dependent upon the preceding term. For instance, since residing in earth and water applies to other things as well, the phrase “apprehended by the gustatory organ” is included. And since the universal *rasatva* (tasteness) and so forth might also be apprehended by the gustatory organ, the phrase “residing in earth and water” is included. Therefore, taste is distinct from other things, because while residing in earth and water, it is apprehended by the gustatory organ; whereas that which is not distinct from other things such as non-taste does not possess this property, just like smell and the rest.

“*For the sake of life, nourishment, strength, and health*” (*jīvana-puṣṭi-bala-ārogya-nimittam*)—this is the determination of its purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*). Life (*jīvana*), however, is the conjunction of the self—which is accompanied by karma that yields experience—with the mind confined within its own body; its cause (*nimitta*) is [food], because it serves as the cause for the nourishment of the body. Nourishment (*puṣṭi*) is the accumulation of bodily parts. And that occurs through the consumption of specific tastes (*rasa*). For instance, when food is consumed, the destruction of the previous substance occurs through internal heat (*tejas*); then, in independent atoms, through the removal of qualities such as blackness and so forth, the process begins with dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) produced by transformation through cooking (*pākaja*). Thus, the initiation of the body should be understood to occur every moment while food is being consumed. Furthermore, the theory of "the initiated initiating" (*ārabhyārambhaka-vāda*) is not possible, as has been stated in the section on Earth (*pṛthivī-adhikāra*). Strength (*bala*) is vigor; its cause is [food] by way of increasing the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). Health (*ārogya*) is the absence of disease; its cause is also [food], since one hears of it occurring when there is the consumption of specific tastes.
“Accompanied by taste” (*rasanasahakārī*): it was stated previously that [tactile sensation] manifests external taste due to the excellence of the taste inherent within itself.

“Divided into the distinctions of sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, and astringent” (*madhurāmlalavaṇatiktakaṭukaṣāyabhedabhinnaḥ*): this classification is also a definition because of its uniqueness. “Its eternity, non-eternity, and production are as before” (*asyāpi nityānityatvaniṣpattayaḥ pūrvavaditi*): the meaning of the extended application (*atideśa*) is that in water-atoms it is eternal, whereas in earthy substances it is produced through contact with fire and perishes; in effects (composite objects), it is preceded by the qualities of the cause and perishes only through the destruction of its substratum. {The difference from odor}.

“Odor is that which is apprehended by the sense of smell, it subsists in earth, it is an auxiliary to the sense of smell, and it is both fragrant and foul; its production and other characteristics are as previously described.”

“Odor is that which is apprehended by the sense of smell” (*gandho ghrāṇagrāhyaḥ*) is the proof for its existence. “Residing in earth” (*pṛthivīvṛttiḥ*) is the determination of its substratum, or else it is a definition relative to the preceding term. For instance, since being apprehended by the sense of smell belongs to the genus of odor (*gandhatva*) and so forth as well, the qualification “residing in earth” is added. Since residing in earth belongs to other things as well, the phrase “apprehended by the sense of smell” is included. Thus, the definition is: the state of residing in earth while being apprehended by the sense of smell.

“Cooperating with the sense of smell” means that it manifests external odors due to the excellence of its own inherent odor; this is the determination of its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Furthermore, there is the classification: “fragrant and non-fragrant.

“Its production and so forth are as before” means that in atoms, [odor] is produced and destroyed through contact with fire; however, in the case of an effect [odor], it is preceded by the qualities of its causes and is destroyed only through the destruction of its substratum—this is the meaning of the extended application (*atideśa*). [The difference regarding touch.]

“Touch is perceptible by the tactile sense-organ; it resides in earth, water, fire, and air; it assists the skin; it conforms to color; it is of three kinds—cold, hot, and neither-hot-nor-cold. Its eternality, non-eternality, and production are also as previously described.”

“Touch is perceptible by the sense of touch” (*sparśastvagindriyagrāhyaḥ*) indicates that it is to be determined through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, the specification of its substratum in the phrase “subsisting in earth, water, fire, and air” (*pṛthivyudakajvalanapavanavṛttiḥ*) is not redundant with the statement that the four [elements] possess touch; for in the former case, the property of a substance (*dravyadharma*) was being described, whereas here, the property of touch itself (*sparśadharma*) is intended. Alternatively, the definition is dependent upon the preceding term. Thus, since subsistence in earth and the other elements also belongs to other things, the phrase “perceptible by the sense of touch” is employed. Moreover, since the universal (*sāmānya*) such as “touch-ness” (*sparśatva*) is also perceptible by that sense, the phrase “subsisting in earth and the others” is used.

If it were possible for number (*saṃkhyā*) and the other [qualities] to reside in earth and the other substances while also being perceivable by the tactile sense-organ (*tvagindriya*), then a restrictive determination (*avadhāraṇa*) must be made. Therefore, touch (*sparśa*) is distinct from others, because while being perceivable by the tactile sense-organ, it invariably resides in the four substances beginning with earth; whereas that which is not distinct from others does not possess this property, such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "the assistant to the skin" (*tvaksahakārī*): the functional analysis (*arthakriyānirūpaṇa*) is that the tactile sense-organ reveals external touch due to the excellence of the touch residing within itself.

Now, the tactile sense-organ (*tvagindriya*) is the manifester of touch (*sparśa*). Why? Because of *saṃyuktasamavāya* (inherence in what is conjoined). That is to say, a substance is conjoined with the tactile sense-organ, and because of its inherence (*samavāya*) in that [substance], touch is perceived. [Objection: If this were so, then because there is no distinction in the relation of *saṃyuktasamavāya*, it would also manifest color (*rūpa*) and other qualities; or else, some distinction must be stated. [Reply: This is not so, because there is an absence of any intensification (*utkarṣa*) of color and the like corresponding to the intensification of touch. To explain: among color and the other qualities, a regulating cause is known through the fact that the perception of touch alone cannot otherwise be accounted for, since a specific effect cannot arise without a specific cause. In this case, the regulator is either the intensification of touch or the universal of touchness (*sparśatva*) residing in the object. This is not possible for color and the others, because touchness is absent therein. Furthermore, the absence of any intensification of color and the like is established simply by the non-existence of such an effect in the case of the tactile sense-organ. Thus, the author of the Sūtras has also said: "Why does tactile cognition not occur with respect to color and the others? Because of their absence" (*Vaiśeṣika Sūtra*). This means that tactile cognition occurs only where the universal of touchness exists. The negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is thus obtained. Moreover, the absence of touchness is an indicator of the absence of being perceivable by the skin, not its producer. Nor can any other "fitness" (*yogyatā*) be postulated apart from a specific contact (*sannikarṣa*), since it is precisely that [contact] whose operation is observed through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Enough of this.

“*Rūpānuvidhāyī* (conforming to color)” indicates concomitance (*sāhacarya*). It conforms to color; being of that nature, it is "conforming to it. Where there is color, there is necessarily touch. Likewise, there is conformity to taste and smell as well. “*It is threefold through the division into cold, hot, and neither-hot-nor-cold*” is the statement of its classification. “*Its eternity, non-eternity, and production are as previously [stated]*”: the meaning of this extension (*atideśa*) is that in water-atoms and so forth it is eternal, whereas in earthy substances it is opposed by contact with fire; in produced effects, it is preceded by the qualities of the cause and perishes upon the destruction of those causes.

{The manner in which color and other qualities arise from heating (*pākaja*)} (“The method for the arising of color and other qualities in earth-atoms due to heating. <PDhS> Now follows the section on the completion of the investigation [of qualities], beginning with the words “of the color and other qualities of earth-atoms. For although the enumeration and definition of color and the other qualities were previously stated, touch (*sparśa*) was not investigated, even though it had been promised; therefore, this is commenced for the purpose of its investigation. These belong to earth, thus they are "earthly" (*pārthiva*).

But surely, since no distinction [between the earth and its qualities] is possible here, how can there be a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and a secondary suffix (*taddhita-pratyaya*)? For those two are observed only when a distinction exists. No; because what is intended by the word "earth" is earth in its state as an effect (*kāryarūpā*), and the atoms that produce it are indeed distinct from it; thus they are called "earthy" (*pārthivāḥ*). Alternatively, the universal (*jāti*) is intended by the word "earth," and these things related to it are "earthy. Furthermore, the phrase "their color and so forth" (*teṣāṃ rūpādayaḥ*) refers to those atoms and their color and other qualities. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), only taste, smell, and touch are included, not number and the rest, because the connection is solely for the purpose of completing the examination of those [latter qualities].

Therefore, for them, "the method of the production of what is produced by baking" (*pākajotpattividhāna*) is the manner [of proof]. Now, one might object: since the meaning of "production" (*utpatti*) is already conveyed by the root *jan* in the term *pākajāḥ* (produced from baking), the inclusion of the word "production" (*utpatti*) is redundant. This is not so, because of its connection with the subsequent member of the compound. For, that by which the very production of the baked qualities is prescribed is the "prescription" (*vidhāna*), which must be understood as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). We shall explain that the production of color and other qualities, which are distinct from the preceding qualities, in the effect is itself the means of valid cognition.

Alternatively, *pāka* is that by which something is cooked, namely the substance of fire (*tejodravya*); or, *pāka* is that which is cooked, namely the atoms of earth (*pārthivaparamāṇu*). That which is produced from these two is *pākaja*. By the force of the subsequent statement, it follows that the production of the color and other qualities of the atoms of earth occurs through their conjunction with fire, and that there is the destruction of [qualities] such as blackness.

Others, however, thinking that the destruction of the dark color and so forth is obtained through ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), offer this laborious interpretation: "Cooking" (*pāka*) is the conjunction with fire, as in "that by which something is cooked"; "produced by cooking" (*pākaja*) means born from that; thus, the destruction of the dark color and so forth [occurs], and from that very cooking arises the production of specific color and other qualities. But that is incorrect, because the fault of ellipsis and the like has not been avoided. Nor should it be said that the term "production" (*utpatti*) is used for the sake of excluding mere manifestation (*abhivyakti*), because that is an unestablished position belonging to another school. [In this regard, first is the manner of the destruction of the effect-substance.]

“When a substance such as a jar is connected with fire, actions arise in the atoms that constitute it, either from the impact of the fire or from its impulsion. From these [actions] come disjunctions; from the disjunctions, the destruction of conjunctions; and from the destruction of conjunctions, the effect-substance perishes. (PDhS)

Now, he demonstrates by means of the passage beginning with "of an uncooked substance such as a jar" (*ghaṭāderāmadravyasya*) in what manner those things produced by heating (*pākaja*) arise. By the phrase "such as a jar" (*ghaṭādeḥ*), the inclusion of the body and so forth is also intended; for, through the thorough understanding of the production of qualities born of heating in that context, one becomes detached from attachment to them, and for the one thus dispassionate, the highest good (*śreyas*) is attained. The term "uncooked substance" (*āmadravyasya*) is used for the purpose of excluding that which is already cooked.

Although even earth-atoms (*pārthivaparamāṇu*) arise from heating (*pāka*), since it is impossible for color and other qualities to exist therein without a cause, they are nevertheless designated as "dark" (*śyāma*) and so forth in relation to their specific prior forms. Actions arise in those atoms which, through a series, are the originating causes (*ārambhaka*) of the dry substance that serves as the substratum for those [qualities]. Why? "From the impact or the push of fire.

Impact (*abhighāta*), depending on velocity (*vega*), is the cause of a single action that results in mutual disjunction; whereas a push (*nodana*) is the cause of multiple [actions] that do not result in disjunction, as we shall explain in the section on action (*karmādhikāra*).
Others, however, maintain that the beginning of a jar is the dyad (dvyaṇuka), and that the atoms which constitute it are its direct causes.

In that process, regarding the production of action (*karma*): the atoms are the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*), their conjunction is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*), and velocity (*vega*) and so forth are the instrumental causes (*nimitta-kāraṇa*). From these [causes] arise disjunctions (*vibhāga*), which are the opposites of the conjunctions that initiate substances. In that case as well, action is the non-inherent cause, the two atoms possess the status of inherent cause, and the remainder are the instrumental causes. "From disjunctions, there is the destruction of conjunctions. Since no inherent cause or other such cause for these [destructions] is perceived, their production arises solely from an instrumental cause. For indeed, it is never observed that a non-entity (*abhāva*) is produced as something inherent in anything.

For this very reason, there is no non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), because of the absence of co-inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*). However, the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) is observed to be operative in its production through positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*). From the destructions of conjunctions, the effect-substance characterized as a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) perishes. The singular number is used with respect to the genus (*jāti*).
[In atoms, after the destruction of the prior color, the production of cooked color (*pākajarūpa*) and so forth occurs.]

“When that [jar] has perished, the destruction of the black color and other qualities occurs in the independent atoms due to contact with fire and the presence of heat. Then, from another contact with fire and the presence of heat, qualities produced by baking (*pākaja*) arise. “Immediately thereafter, through the conjunction of the self and the atoms depending on the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of the experiencers, action arises in those atoms where the qualities produced by baking have been generated. From their mutual conjunction, a causal substance (*kāryadravya*) is produced in the sequence beginning with dyads (*dvyaṇuka*). In that process, the production of color and other qualities occurs through the succession of the qualities of the causes.”

When that [substance] has perished, the cessation of qualities such as blackness occurs in the atoms due to another conjunction with fire. "Again, due to another conjunction with fire, depending upon heat, qualities produced by baking (*pākaja*) arise. In this case, the atom is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), the conjunction with fire is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and the hot touch is the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).

“Immediately thereafter” (*tadanantaram*) means immediately after the moment of the production of redness and so forth. The effects, which are inherent in the atoms in which the qualities produced by transformation (*pākaja*) have arisen, come into being. He states the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) as “from the conjunction of the self and the atom” (*ātmāṇusaṃyogāt*), [conjunction] depending upon the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). To the question of for whom this unseen force belongs, he says “of those who experience [the fruits]” (*bhoginām*).

When action arises, disjunctions follow immediately; from these, destructions of conjunctions occur. Thereafter, through the mutual conjunction of atoms (*paramāṇu*), dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) are produced. In this process, the two atoms possess the nature of inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), their conjunction possesses the nature of non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and the remaining factors are instrumental causes (*nimitta*). In this sequence beginning with that, the effect is produced. Three dyads initiate a triad (*tryaṇuka*); and by means of triads, their own effects are produced without restriction, continuing until the jar is formed. In all cases, the production of color and other qualities occurs according to the principle of the precedence of the qualities of the cause.
Is it not the case that all this is incoherent, because there is no evidence for this sequence? For instance:
(1) since there is no evidence for the existence of motion in an atom, there is no evidence for the destruction of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) resulting from the non-establishment of its effect;

(2) as for the multiplicity of fire-contact, the destruction of the substance, the cessation of blackness and so forth, the arising of redness and so forth, and the production of that very dyad through a sequence of actions among those things produced by baking—all of this is entirely devoid of evidence.

<3> And because subverting evidence is established. For instance, when jars and other vessels have been placed in a kiln, a potter looking through a hole perceives a sensory cognition (*akṣaja-vijñāna*) that "the jar is being baked. This [cognition] is neither of the nature of doubt nor of error, because it is not characterized by the defining marks of those two, and because no subverting evidence arises.
<4> Furthermore, after the baking is finished, there is the perception of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*)—in the form "this is that very same jar"—which remains unsublated.

[The property of] stability: the state of remaining [in place] due to the non-falling of grass, shards, and so forth that have been placed above. For if atoms were subject to cooking (*pāka*), there would be a falling of the shards and other objects placed above, because atoms would lack the capacity to support them.

<6> And because [the jar] is perceived as having that same location, that same dimension, and that same number. For if atoms in which the qualities produced by heating (*pākaja*) have arisen were to originate a jar or similar object through the sequence of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth, then it would not have that location, that dimension, or that number, due to the absence of a cause for restriction. Yet this restriction is observed: it has that very location, that dimension, and that number. Thus, there is stability in jars and other such objects.

Furthermore, it is not logical for a jar or similar object to arise again after its destruction without an agent and other such factors. If it is argued that this is logical because of the existence of God and so forth—namely, that God is the agent and cause, while the atoms and the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) constitute the action—this is not tenable. For, just as in the case of effects such as the earth and so on, since the capacity [of the cause] would not cease even in the production of a jar and the like due to its independence from the effect (because it is already connected to agents such as ourselves), the activity of the potter would be rendered entirely useless.

<8> And there is the absence of obstruction (*āvaraṇābhāva*). For instance, just as a jar or similar object is destroyed through the sequence of actions in its parts resulting from momentum (*vega*) and contact with fire, so too, when glass, clouds, rock-crystal (*sphaṭika*), and the like are destroyed through the sequence of actions resulting from momentum and contact with the eye, the eye—being connected by means of that which is [otherwise] intervening—possesses the power of illumination; thus, there would be an absence of obstruction. Now, if it is argued that because substances such as rock-crystal are transparent, they do not act as an obstacle to the sense organ, and therefore the perception of even an obstructed object is established, then one must likewise admit that a substance such as a jar, by its very nature, does not act as an obstacle to the substance of light; thus, cooking (*pāka*) occurs within the interior as well, due to the penetration of atoms. Otherwise, there would be an identical perception of both the obstructed and the unobstructed, since the absence of obstruction would be indistinguishable in both cases.

If the substance were destroyed by the entry of atoms, then, since the perception of cold touch on the outer surface would otherwise be inexplicable, the water would escape; consequently, upon the destruction of the support, the [water] would fall away. Alternatively, if it is argued that the water escapes because the substance has pores, then cooking would occur within the interior precisely through those channels due to the entry of fire-atoms; so what is the use of its destruction? Enough of this.

All this is non-substantiating because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). For instance, when a jar is filled with water, due to contact with a swift-moving needle-like substance, motion necessarily occurs in the region of its neck. That motion, once produced, initiates a disjunction (*vibhāga*) that is the opposite of the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) that originated the substance; this is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, upon the destruction of the conjunction, there is the cessation of the substance originated by it, since that [conjunction] itself is the originator of another substance; and upon the cessation of that [substance], there is the cessation of what was originated by it. Thus, due to the presence of the cause of destruction, the jar is destroyed. Otherwise, if there were no destruction despite the presence of the cause of destruction, the effect would indeed be eternal. However, since the jar is perceived, it is certain that other substances are originated by the persisting conjunctions.

And in that case, the perception of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) in the form "this is that very same [thing]" does not cease. Furthermore, the falling of the object placed above, its location in that place, its numerical quantity, its dimension, and the non-perception of an agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) exist there; thus, because of this inconclusiveness (*anekānta*), it is not a valid proof. Moreover, even when a jar is destroyed, neither the non-destruction nor the falling of the water is observed.
[Rather, it is only within the atoms (*paramāṇu*) that the production of color and other qualities occurs.]

“Furthermore, neither the destruction nor the production of color and other qualities is possible in a composite substance (*kāryadravya*), because fire cannot pervade it internally and externally across all its parts. Nor can pervasion occur through the entry of atoms, for that would entail the destruction of the composite substance.”

Now, regarding the claim that qualities produced by heating (*pākaja*) arise in atoms—what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for us and others in this matter? [The answer is: it is the production of another quality in jars and the like that is distinct from their previous qualities. But how can that [production] existing in jars and the like lead one to understand that "qualities produced by heating arise in atoms," since such a thing is not possible there through contact with fire? He states this very point: "And neither the destruction nor the production of color and other qualities is possible in a composite substance (*kāryadravya*). Why? "Because there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) by fire throughout all its parts, both internally and externally. For instance, a composite whole exists within and without all its parts. And since there is no entry of fire into the internal space, there is an absence of connection through pervasion; thus, the consequence would be that no heating occurs.

Now, [the opponent] says that cooking occurs within the interior due to the penetration of subtle fire: "Pervasion is not possible even through atomic penetration. Why? "Because of the destruction of the effect-substance (*kāryadravya*). For instance, since the connection with a substance possessing velocity is observed elsewhere to be the cause of motion, here too it must produce motion in the constituent part (*avayava*). That motion, in turn, initiates a disjunction from another part which is the opposite of the conjunction that originates the substance. Therefore, upon the cessation of that conjunction, the effect-substance originated by it is destroyed; and when that is destroyed, what was originated by it also ceases. Thus, by this sequence, the jar must necessarily perish.

Now, if it is argued that the parts of the jar are being cooked, even there, cooking could not occur within the interior; thus, destruction would result from the penetration of fire-atoms. In this way, as fire-atoms penetrate each successive part, those parts are destroyed, and the independent atoms are what are cooked.

Furthermore, if the previous color and other qualities were to persist in the effect-substance (*kāryadravya*), the production of red and other colors would not occur, because the presence of another quality in that which already possesses a quality is prohibited. Therefore, the cessation of the previous color and other qualities is known through the otherwise inexplicable production of red and other colors. And in the case of an effect-substance, that cessation occurs precisely through the destruction of its substrate (*āśraya*). Thus, the *sūtra* states: “Color, taste, smell, and touch are non-eternal because the substance is non-eternal” (Vai. Sū.), whereby destruction by the destruction of the substrate is declared. Furthermore, the *sūtra* says: “And [destruction occurs] in an effect-substance due to contact with fire” (Vai. Sū. and “By this, the non-eternality [of qualities] in eternal substances is explained” (Vai. Sū.), stating that contact with fire is the cause of the removal of color and other qualities only in the case of eternal substances. Consequently, in an effect-substance, the cessation of the previous color and other qualities is known from the appearance of another quality; and that [cessation] occurs only through the destruction of the substrate, since there is a restriction that contact with fire applies only to eternal substances.

Likewise, even if the potsherds remain and their prior color and other qualities do not cease, the production of redness and so forth would not occur. Therefore, since the effect conforms to the form of its cause, blackness and the like are produced. Thus, it must be stated that even in the case of the causes of those causes, another quality distinct from the previous quality arises; otherwise, it would not occur in their effects either.

Furthermore, that production [of qualities] is not possible while the previous form and other qualities persist, because the commencement of another form within that which already possesses a form is prohibited; thus, the cessation of the previous form and so forth must be asserted. And since that cessation occurs only through the destruction of the substrate, there follows the destruction of the entire effect-substance as well.

Furthermore, even if the original color and other qualities were to persist within the atoms, the production of red and other colors would not occur. Since that [original state] would be absent, even in the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), black and so forth would be produced according to the sequence beginning with the qualities of the cause; thus, the emergence of dissimilar color and other qualities would be impossible. Yet, the appearance of a different quality in the effect is observed; therefore, when the color and other qualities in the atoms cease, red and other colors are produced. Moreover, since the destruction of the substratum is not possible there, it is the conjunction with fire alone that acts as the remover, and because no other cause is possible, it is that very conjunction which acts as the producer.

Furthermore, regarding this statement that "substance possesses apertures": if [the cooking] is with respect to the apertures of the potsherds, there would be no cooking in the interior space of that [substance]. If, on the other hand, it is with respect to the apertures of its constituent parts, there is likewise an absence of cooking in the interior space of those. This same argument must be applied to each successive set of constituent parts, down to the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*).

Now, could it be argued that cooking will occur because there is no intermediate space [between the fire and the object]? No; for even in that case, destruction is necessarily established through contact with a fire possessing velocity (*vega*). Furthermore, the production of redness and other qualities cannot occur without the destruction of blackness and other prior qualities. And it has already been stated that the destruction of those [prior qualities] occurs precisely from the destruction of their substratum. That [destruction of the substratum] results from the destruction of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), that [destruction of conjunction] results from disjunction (*vibhāga*), and disjunction results from action (*kriyā*). Thus, the very manifestation of another quality serves as the proof for the existence of the sequence beginning with action.

In this regard, however, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: the color and other qualities of earth-atom (*pārthivaparamāṇu*) are produced by conjunction (*saṃyogaja*), because—while being distinct from sound produced by disjunction (*vibhāgaja*) and sound produced by sound (*śabdaja*), and while being non-eternal—they are specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of that which is eternal, like pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth. The phrase "being distinct from sound produced by disjunction and sound produced by sound" is included to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). The term "non-eternal" (*anitya*) is used to exclude the color and other qualities of water-atoms and so forth. The term "specific quality" (*viśeṣaguṇa*) is employed to exclude general qualities (*sāmānyaguṇa*). And the exclusion of the non-eternal is achieved by the word "eternal" (*nitya*).

Others, however, state the following inference: "The color and other qualities residing in a jar and so forth are produced by contact with fire through a mediated succession, because, while being directly perceived as belonging to the jar, they arise as existing only when that contact with fire exists, just like the sound of the word 'fire' when it is heard. Nor is the qualifying attribute (viśeṣaṇa) unestablished, according to the reasoning already stated.

As for the claim that there is no evidence for the multiplicity of fire-contact (*agni-saṃyoga*), this is incorrect. Its multiplicity is merely figurative (*upacāra*), based on the difference in its effects. When an action arises in the fire that removes blackness (*śyāma*) and other qualities, it simultaneously initiates a disjunction from the previously occupied space such as ether (*ākāśa*). At that very same moment, there is an action in the fire that produces redness (*rakta*) and other qualities within the constituent part (*avayava*). This is the first moment [1]. Then, from that disjunction, the destruction of the [original] conjunction occurs; and by the action of the constituent part, a disjunction from another part is produced, while by the action of the fire producing redness, a disjunction from the space such as ether is produced. This is the second moment [2]. Next, there is the conjunction of the fire removing blackness with the atom (*paramāṇu*); the blackness and other qualities are in a state of perishing; from the disjunction of the parts, the destruction of the conjunction that originates the substance occurs; the fire destroying the blackness is in a state of perishing; and by the action of the fire producing redness, the destruction of the previous conjunction occurs, while the conjunction with the atom is in the process of arising. This is the third moment [3]. Then, there is the destruction of the blackness and other qualities; the destruction of the fire that destroyed them; the conjunction [of the parts] is in a state of perishing; the conjunction of the fire producing redness arises; and the redness and other qualities are in the process of arising. This is the fourth moment [4]. Finally, there is the production of the redness and other qualities, and the destruction of the fire-conjunction that removed the blackness. Thus, there is a multiplicity of fire-conjunctions. Furthermore, it is not the case that the fire-conjunction which destroys the blackness cannot serve as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*) for the production of color and other qualities simply because it is in a state of perishing.

Others, however, maintain that because one considers the action in a constituent part of the fire that causes the cessation of the dark color (*śyāma*) and so forth to be simultaneous with the action [in the whole], the destruction of its conjunction occurs at the very same time as the cessation of the dark color and so forth.

Now, what is the proof for the existence of a sequence of actions (*kriyākrama*) in those things produced by heating (*pākaja*) once they have arisen? It is simply the production of the effect-substance (*kāryadravya*). For otherwise, in the absence of action, there would be no capacity to originate a substance among those parts which have not reached one another.

Now, is there no proof that atoms initiate [the formation of] dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) alone? That is not so; for in the case of [atoms being] many—just as in the case of [being] one—there exist subverting arguments (*bādhaka*), since it is well-established that only those endowed with the number two (*dvitva-saṃkhyā*) are initiators. To explain: if many [atoms] were initiators, then even those endowed with numbers such as a hundred would likewise be initiators. And if this were the case, and a product such as a jar were initiated by atoms, then upon its destruction, because no intermediate product had arisen, there would be no perception [of parts]. Yet, when a jar is destroyed, its constituent parts are perceived, and in the parts of those, their own parts; thus, it is determined that the initiation occurs through the sequence of dyads and so forth.

Now, is there not a contradiction with the sūtras, namely: "Substances originate another substance" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.10) and "A substance [arises] from conjunctions" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.27)? No; for these are based on the analysis of the compound through the dual and plural numbers. To explain: in the expression "substance and substances" (*dravye ca dravyāṇi*), there is an *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one term). However, the plural number is used in reference to the effect-substances (*kāryadravya*). It is precisely many effect-substances that originate a substance. Furthermore, it is only those [atoms] endowed with the number two that are eternal, but not all eternal things [are such], because [the quality of being eternal] also exists in the case of effect-substances.

Furthermore, a single entity cannot possess the capacity for production through either succession or simultaneity, because it possesses a unitary nature. To explain: a single atom does not produce an effect successively, because that which is capable cannot be delayed; nor does it produce them simultaneously, because once they have been produced, there would be no further cause for non-production.

Moreover, a causal relationship is never observed between things of equal dimension, since the doctrine of momentary flux (kṣaṇabhaṅga) has been refuted; otherwise, the absence of any disintegration of the cause would entail the impossibility of destruction for the resultant substance.

Likewise, "conjunctions" refers to a conjunction, two conjunctions, and many conjunctions. Since their effect is substance (*dravya*), there is no contradiction because, in relation to eternal [substances], conjunction itself is the effect, whereas in the case of a produced substance (*kāryadravya*), there is no such restriction. Thus, atoms endowed with the number two (*dvitvasaṃkhyā*) initiate a produced substance, because they possess the capacity for initiation provided that there exists valid evidence (*pramāṇa*) refuting the positions of unity or plurality. Furthermore, duality is the initiator of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), like a pair of threads; for a dyad is not initiated by many threads, nor by a single one—thus the reason, when accompanied by its qualification, is established.

Now, why do dyads (*dvyaṇuka*), which are endowed with numbers such as duality (*dvitva*) and so forth, not indiscriminately initiate an effect? Because of the occurrence of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*). To explain: if two dyads were to act as originators, then since the cause for the production of atomic dimension (*aṇu-parimāṇa*) already exists [in those two], it would follow that their initiation is purposeless.

Nor should it be argued that a plurality consisting of two dyads is possible in relation to their causal atoms; for [if this were so], plurality not residing in the cause would not be a cause for the production of magnitude (*parimāṇa*). It is observed that plurality residing in the cause is the cause for the production of magnitude. Otherwise, magnitude would exist even in a dyad, since plurality—being independent of a [further] cause—is possible there as well. Thus, it must be maintained that even a dyad produces a large [substance] only when endowed with the number of plurality. However, this must be postulated for the dyad alone, since the capacity of a single [atom] to initiate [a composite] has been refuted.

Now, it is not accepted that those possessing numbers such as four and so forth are the initiators [of a composite] without restriction, because that would entail the consequence that they directly initiate jars and other such objects. Furthermore, upon the destruction of that [composite], there would be no perception of an intermediate effect, precisely because it has not been produced. Nor is magnitude possible without plurality; thus, only those possessing the number three are initiators. For instance, dyads (dvyaṇukas) initiate a substance only when possessed of the number three, because they possess the quality of being initiators while the presence of subverting evidence exists against the positions of duality, quaternary, and so on, just like the triad of threads in the initiation of a three-threaded cloth.

In this context, however, the sequence of actions is described regarding how long it takes for color and other qualities to arise in a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*). Therein, at one and the same time: the destruction of the dyad from its own cause; the state of being in the process of destruction (*vinaśyattā*) of its effect; the production of the fire-contact that eliminates blackness and other qualities; the state of being in the process of destruction of blackness and other qualities; the state of being in the process of arising (*utpadyamānatā*) of the fire-contact that produces redness and other qualities; the production of the disjunction born of disjunction (*vibhāgaja-vibhāga*); and the state of being in the process of destruction of the conjunction of the two atoms with a location such as space. These constitute a single moment.

<2> Then, at one and the same time, there occurs the destruction of the triad (*tryaṇuka*), the state of being about to perish of its effect, the destruction of the dark color (*śyāma*) and so forth, the state of being about to perish of the fire-contact that destroys the dark color and so forth, the production of the fire-contact that produces the red color (*rakta*) and so forth, the state of being in the process of arising of the red color and so forth, the destruction of the conjunction with space (*ākāśa*) and the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), and the state of being in the process of arising of the subsequent conjunction (*uttara-saṃyoga*). These constitute a single moment.

<3> Then, from the destruction of that effect, there follows the state of perishing of that effect; the destruction of the contact with fire that causes the cessation of the black color and so forth; the production of the red color and so forth; the state of perishing of the contact with fire that produces the red color and so forth; likewise, the production of the subsequent conjunction; the state of perishing of the disjunction, the disjunction produced by disjunction, and the action; and the state of being in the process of arising of the motion—all these occur at one and the same time.

<4> Then, at that same time, there occurs the destruction of that effect, the state of being about to perish (*vinaśyattā*) of its effect, the destruction of the disjunctions and the actions producing the disjunctions from disjunctions, the destruction of the contact with fire that produces the red color and so forth, the production of motion, and the state of being in the process of arising (*utpadyamānatā*) of the disjunction—these constitute one single moment.

<5> Then, following the destruction of that effect, there occurs the state of being about to perish of its effect, the production of the disjunction, and the state of being about to perish of the conjunction—these constitute one single moment.

<6> Then, from the destruction of that effect, there is the state of perishing of its effect, the destruction of the conjunction, and the state of being produced of the subsequent conjunction; these constitute one moment of time.

<7> Then, from the destruction of that effect, there is the state of perishing of its effect, the production of the subsequent conjunction, the state of being produced of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), and the state of perishing of the disjunction and the action; these constitute one moment of time.

<8> Then, from the destruction of that effect, there is the state of perishing of its effect, the production of the dyad, the state of being produced of color and other qualities (*rūpa*, etc.), and the destruction of the disjunction and the action; these constitute one moment of time.
<9> Therefore, once the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) has arisen, the production of color and other qualities occurs in the ninth moment according to the sequence beginning with the qualities of the causes.

However, when it is explained that "having regard for a time characterized by the destruction of the effect" means "having regard for a time characterized by the destruction of the substance," such that the disjunction existing in the two causes initiates a disjunction from the portion of space conjoined with the effect, then—by considering the disjunction produced by disjunction (*vibhāgaja-vibhāga*) as occurring simultaneously with the cessation of the black color and so forth—one must consider that the production of color and other qualities in the dyad occurs in the tenth moment.

And thus, upon the destruction of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), there is the cessation of the dark color and so forth; from that, the production of the red color and so forth; then the subsequent conjunction; then the destruction of the action, disjunction, and [prior] conjunction; and finally, when the dyad is produced through the conjunction of atoms, the production of color and other qualities occurs according to the principle of the priority of the qualities of the causes. The rest is as before. This has been stated with reference to two actions in a single atom: one that produces a substance and [the other] that destroys it.
But when it is held that the action destroying the substance occurs in one atom, while the action producing the substance occurs in another, how then does it proceed?

<1> In that process, simultaneous with the destruction of the conjunction that initiates the substance [the dyad], there arises an action in the second atom that initiates a substance; then, from the destruction of the conjunction initiating the substance, follows the destruction of the dyad, the state of being about to perish of its effect, the production of the fire-contact that eliminates the black color and so forth, the state of being eliminated of the black color and so forth, the state of being produced of the fire-contact that produces the red color and so forth, the production of the disjunction born of disjunction, the state of being about to perish of the conjunction of the atom with a location such as space, and the production of disjunction in the second atom [and the state of being about to perish of the prior conjunction]—all these occur at one and the same time.

<2> Then, there occurs the destruction of the triad (*tryaṇuka*); the state of being about to perish (*vinaśyattā*) of its effect; the destruction of the dark color (*śyāma*) and so forth; the state of being about to perish of the fire-contact that destroys them; the production of the fire-contact that produces the red color (*rakta*) and so forth; the state of being in the process of arising of the red color and so forth; the destruction of the contact between space and the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*); the state of being in the process of arising of the contact of that atom with a location such as space; the destruction of the previous contact in the second atom; and the state of being in the process of arising of the contact with the atom—these [events] constitute one single moment (*ekaḥ kālaḥ*).

<3> Then, from the destruction of that effect, there is the state of perishing of its effect; the destruction of the fire-contact that destroyed the blackness and so forth; the production of redness and so forth; the production of the conjunction of the atom with a location such as space; the state of perishing of the disjunction-born disjunction and the action; the production of the conjunction of the second atom with another atom; the state of perishing of the disjunction and the action belonging to that [second atom]; and the state of being produced of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*)—all these occur at one and the same time.

<4> Then, due to the destruction of that effect, there is the state of perishing of its effect; the destruction of the disjunction-born disjunction and the action; the destruction of both the disjunction and the action in the second atom as well; the production of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*); and the arising of the red color and other qualities—these occur at one and the same time. <5> Thereafter, immediately following the production of the dyad, in the fifth moment, the production of color and other qualities occurs through the process beginning with the qualities of the cause.

Likewise, because one considers the action in the second atom at the same time as the destruction of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), the production of qualities born of cooking (*pākaja*) occurs in six moments. Similarly, if one considers the action at the same time as the cessation of the black color and so forth, it takes seven moments; if one considers the action at the same time as the production of the red color and so forth, it takes eight moments; and if one considers the action immediately thereafter, it takes nine moments, and so on—thus should it be considered.

In that regard, first, dyads (dvyaṇuka) are produced from both baked and unbaked atoms; thus, baked and unbaked [dyads] arise. Then, by the process beginning with triads (tryaṇuka), there is the production of a baked and unbaked jar.

Then again, when substances have been destroyed through the sequence of action and so forth, and the atoms are independent with their qualities of maturation (*pākaja*) as yet unproduced, there arises [in them] redness and other qualities. Thereafter, through the sequence of action, upon the production of subsequent conjunctions, dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) are produced. And in that case, by the process beginning with the qualities of the causes, color and other qualities arise only in those very [atoms] that have been matured. By these, a triad (*tryaṇuka*) is begun which is itself matured. Furthermore, in other dyads as well, the production of color and other qualities occurs in this same sequence, and from those [dyads], the production of triads and so forth is to be described, until the production of specific color and other qualities in the jar.

Now, why is it not admitted that action occurs even in atoms where *pākaja* (heat-produced) qualities have arisen, just as in those where they have not, due to the connection with fire? Because it would entail the non-production of jars and the like. For if action were to occur in atoms where *pākaja* qualities have arisen and which have begun a composite effect, then—since dyads and so forth would be destroyed immediately after their production at every moment—the production of jars and the like would never take place.

Now, if you think that when all the atoms have been heated, a jar or similar object is produced through the sequence beginning with dyads (dvyaṇuka), that is incorrect. For it would follow that the potsherds and other fragments placed on top would fall down, since atoms lack the capacity to support [heavy objects]. But this is not the case. Therefore, by the fact that the production of an effect cannot otherwise be explained, it is known that motion arises only in those [atoms] where heat-produced qualities (*pākaja*) have not yet arisen, and not in those where they have already arisen, because the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) that brings about experience acts as the regulator. Enough of this excessive detail.

Now, regarding the hypothesis that dyads, triads, and so forth are first produced in both baked and unbaked states, and then subsequently produced only in baked states—what is the proof for this? It is simply the observation of the effect as being such. For instance, an effect such as a jar is observed to be initially both baked and unbaked, and then subsequently only baked; thus it may be inferred for the causes and causes of those causes as well. Herein lies the formal argument (*prayoga*): a dyad is initially produced in both baked and unbaked states, because it is the originator of a large earthen substance, like a potsherd. Likewise, a triad is initially produced in both baked and unbaked states, because it is the effect of a large earthen substance, like a jar.

Nor can the production of qualities born of heating (*pākaja*) be explained as occurring through the simultaneous production of motion in all atoms, because rapid heating is not observed, and because it would entail the consequence that objects placed on top would immediately fall. If you say that the linguistic usage of "one," "two," "three," and so forth, is the proof, that is not so; for such usage is a conceptual cognition (*kalpanājñāna*). And a conceptual cognition is not capable of establishing the reality of an object, since it occurs even in the absence of that object. To explain: following the sequence of a non-conceptual cognition of the cause, a conceptual cognition arises after memory, yet there is no persistence of the object due to its momentariness; thus, [conceptual cognition] lacks a real object.

Furthermore, there is the occurrence of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*). For instance, when duality and so forth are produced, they do not arise prior to the production of the substance, because that [substance] does not yet exist. Nor do they arise simultaneously, as that would entail the impossibility of the relationship between cause and effect. If, on the other hand, they arise at a later time, then in that case too, does it arise from its own nature (*svabhāva*) or from something contrary to it? If it arises from its own nature, what is the use of duality and so forth, since the substance itself possesses that very nature? But if it arises from something contrary to it, how can it arise from that which is its own nature? For that would entail the production of duality from one or from many, since the possession of that nature would be indistinguishable in all cases.

Furthermore, [the universal] is non-existent because its mode of subsistence is untenable. Does duality, which resides in multiple things, subsist by way of a single part or by its entire self? It cannot subsist by way of a single part, because such parts do not exist. Nor can it subsist by its entire self, because that would entail the impossibility of its subsisting in both [loci]. Furthermore, it is not the case that it subsists in another substance by the very same nature through which it subsists in one; for that would entail the identity of those two. Thus, due to the impossibility of its subsistence, it is non-existent.

Likewise, because that which has reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) is not apprehended by anyone [if it were absent], if duality and so forth existed, they would be perceived by all persons—just like color and other qualities—because they have reached the conditions for perception; yet they are not perceived, therefore they do not exist. Furthermore, because they are perceivable by the same sense-faculty: the very sense-faculty by which a substance is perceived is the same by which number is perceived; thus, number is not a separate entity from it. If there were a difference, then, as with color and the rest, it would follow that number could also be perceived by a different sense-faculty.

For this reason as well, there is no existence [of duality] because it is not perceived due to spatial separation, because the cognition of it does not occur when that [substratum] is not grasped, and because such a perception is logically impossible. To explain: how could duality, which resides in multiple locations, be determined by the sense organ? For two simultaneous contacts cannot be presided over by the mind at once. If, on the other hand, the eye were so presided over, there would follow the undesirable consequence of perceiving multiple objects simultaneously, since the eye, being presided over by the mind, would be in contact with many objects.

Just as the linguistic usage of "one" and so forth occurs with respect to substances due to their connection with number, so too, if one were to postulate another cause for the linguistic usage of "one" and so forth even with respect to qualities such as oneness (*ekatva*), there would follow the consequence of an infinite regress, since the linguistic usage of "one" and so forth would be possible there as well. If, on the other hand, the linguistic usage of "one" and so forth with respect to oneness and the like is due to its being the very nature (*svarūpa*) of that [quality], then it would follow that the same state exists for substances as well. If [you argue that] the linguistic usage of "one" and so forth is due to a universal (*sāmānya*) of oneness and the like, that is untenable because no such universal is possible; furthermore, that [usage] would be a conceptual cognition (*kalpanājñāna*).

All of this is incorrect. For the cognition of "one" and so forth possesses validity, as there is no sublation of the linguistic usage of "one" etc. To explain: the cognition of "one" and so forth is produced by the object, just like the cognition of blue and other objects, because it follows the presence and absence of that object. Nor does its production occur at the very same time as the arising of indeterminate (nirvikalpaka) cognition despite its dependence on the object; for the recollection of linguistic convention (*saṅketa*), which is a cooperative cause, is absent at that moment. Nor is it produced by memory alone, since the operation of the object is also observed therein. Furthermore, memory neither adds excellence nor removes the lack of excellence [in the cognition]; rather, it simply functions as a generator of cognition when the object is present.

Nor is it a valid objection that because the object and the sense organs lack the capacity for deliberation (*avicārakatva*), they cannot produce [cognition] later as they did before; for such an objection is refuted earlier during the demonstration of the whole (*avayavin*) on the grounds that [the cognition] would otherwise be impossible, because there is no perception of [the parts] in different locations, and because in the absence of the perception of those [parts], there can be no cognition of them. Furthermore, it is not logical to claim that a cognition of "one-ness" and so forth is invalid even though it is not sublated, for that would entail the consequence that cognitions of blue and other colors would also be invalid. If you argue that without the blue object, the cognition of it could not have the form of blue, then the same applies to the cognition of one-ness and so forth.

Now, it might be argued that the cognition of oneness and so forth has the form of a word, and since the object does not possess that form, such cognitions are objectless (*nirviṣayatva*). This is not so; for otherwise, it would follow that even the initial cognition of blue is objectless, as it too would have the form of a word. Alternatively, one might claim that the first cognition of blue is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) and born from the object, whereas the subsequent cognition is conceptual (*savikalpaka*) and arises even when the object has ceased because of the intervention of many moments. Since the object is momentary, the presence of the form of a word within that [subsequent cognition] is impossible; thus, its objectlessness is indeed accepted.

That is incorrect, because momentariness has already been refuted previously. Furthermore, just as in the production of non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) cognition, in the production of conceptual (*savikalpaka*) cognition, the operation of the object—acting in conjunction with the sense organ, the recollection of linguistic conventions (*saṅketa*), and [other factors]—is observed through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). To explain: the operation of the sense organ is determined therein because cognition arises as "this" (*idantayā*), and because the object is pointed out by a finger. Otherwise, if there were no operation of the sense organ and the object in the production of a single cognition, there would be neither apprehension as "this" nor designation by means of a finger and so forth. If it is argued that sensory cognition is the cause for the production of conceptual cognition through a sequence involving mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and thus apprehension as "this" and designation by a finger do not arise directly from the object, we say no. There is no proof for such a sequence.

Now, if it is argued that this conceptual construction is made because the existence [of number] is established through mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*), since otherwise the linguistic usage of "one" and so forth would not occur—that is incorrect. For the refutations, such as the dilemma regarding subsistence (*vṛtti-vikalpa*), have already been rejected. Furthermore, once the existence of number is established, it is logical that the linguistic usage of "one" and so forth arises directly from the object itself.

The state of having the form of a word (*śabdākāratā*), however, is simply not possible in determinate cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*), because the refutation of the theory of mental forms (*sākāravāda*) will be stated later. Rather, determinate cognition arises with the verbal expression (*śabdollekhena*) solely because it is produced by the recollection of a linguistic convention; indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), on the other hand, is devoid of such expression, because the operation of the recollection of conventions is absent.

Nor can [the cognition of "one" and so forth] arise from latent impressions (*vāsanā*), because latent impressions have already been refuted. For it was already stated during the demonstration of the composite whole (*avayavin*) that no latent impression is possible apart from the object of cognition itself. As for the latent impression accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas—which is inferred from memory—that is not the cause for the conventional usage of "one" and so forth, because, being an imperceptible cause, it is distinct in nature from memory. To explain: the cognition of "one" and so forth is immediate (*aparokṣa*); it arises as a direct presentation (*idantayā*) through the operation of the sense faculties, whereas memory does not possess this character; thus, [the cognition of "one"] does not originate from latent impressions. Furthermore, even if such a cognition were to originate from latent impressions, it would establish the object only indirectly, since a latent impression is preceded by the experience of an object. Moreover, the latent impression arising from a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) based on words such as "oneness" likewise establishes the object, because it is admitted that a word is preceded by an experience, according to the principle: "When something is seen, one speaks of what has been seen."

As for the claim that oneness and so forth do not exist because they cannot be accounted for in terms of their production (*utpatti*), that is incorrect, since their production is admitted to occur at a subsequent time. Furthermore, regarding the question of whether that [production] arises from its own nature (*svabhāva*) or from something contrary to it: if by "its own nature" you mean the capacity to produce it, then that is indeed accepted. However, if you mean the state of being the substratum of oneness and so forth, that does not exist prior to production, as such a thing is absent before it has arisen. Once the existence of number (*saṃkhyā*) is established through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), its cause of production must necessarily be stated, given that it is produced within a substance that is an effect (*kāryadravya*). In that regard, if the substratum of oneness, duality, and so forth were itself the producer, then that [substratum] would be non-existent [at the time of production]; yet production is observed. Therefore, the substance augmented by other causal factors (*kāraka*) is the cause of those [numbers], and thus the dilemma regarding their production is untenable.

As for the claim that duality and so forth do not exist because they are not perceived despite meeting the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), that is not correct, because the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*). For instance, duality and the like are produced by a specific enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*); it is only for that person who possesses such a cognition that they meet the conditions for perception, not for another person, since they are perceived only by that specific individual. It is accepted that the status of being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) belongs only to a corporeal substance where perception occurs, and not in its absence. Therefore, since those qualities do not meet the conditions for perception relative to all persons, the reason is unestablished.

As for this [argument]: "Oneness and so forth do not exist apart from the substance, because they are apprehended by the same sense faculty"—in that statement of the thesis (*pratijñā*), there is a contradiction between the two terms, as in saying "this exists" and "it does not exist. Furthermore, it is not proper to take oneness and so forth as the subject (*pakṣa*) of the argument, because they are not established (*aprasiddhatvāt*). It is observed that only what is already established, such as sound and the like, is taken as the subject; yet oneness and so forth are not established for the opponent.

Now, if it is argued that a *prasaṅga-sādhana* (reductio ad absurdum) consists in establishing an undesirable consequence for the opponent by means of [their own] pervasion (*paravyāpti*), then in that case: if the opponent's conviction is preceded by a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), the opposing inference cannot arise because it is sublated by that very same [cognition]. If, on the other hand, it is not preceded by a valid means of cognition, then since an object of cognition (*prameya*) is not established without a valid means of cognition, it is improper to take unity and so forth as the subject (*pakṣa*).

Likewise, regarding the argument "because they are apprehended by the same sense organ": since a substance is perceived by whichever sense organ [perceives it], number is perceived by that very same one; thus, the reason (*sādhana*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the distinctions among color and so forth. For instance, by the very same sense organ that perceives white color, yellow and other colors are also perceived, yet there is neither a difference between them nor their non-existence. Furthermore, since for the opponent substance is not established, how can non-difference from it be proven? If, on the other hand, color itself is the substance, then there is no longer "apprehension by the same sense organ," because color is apprehended by a single sense organ while number is determined by two sense organs.

Now, even if the substance (*dravya*) is a collection of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, nevertheless, the property of being perceivable by the same sense organ (*samānendriyagrāhyatva*) remains unestablished, because color-form and the other qualities are each perceivable by their own specific sense organs. Nor does the difference between color-form and the others follow from their being perceivable by specific sense organs, for that would lead to the absurd conclusion (*prasaṅga*) that distinct varieties such as white and so forth are one and the same. What then? [The difference arises] from a difference in appearance (*pratibhāsabheda*), and that indeed exists here as well; for in one case there is the appearance of a substance, while in another there is the appearance of oneness and so forth. If it is argued that since the difference between number and substance is established through perception, the proof of their identity is "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), being sublated by perception—

As for the claim that duality and so forth do not exist because their perception is impossible once they have arisen—that is incorrect. For this duality and so forth are seen as immediate (*aparokṣa*) through the operation of the sense organs. Nor can a sense organ, when not presided over by the mind, possess the capacity for discernment, since that would entail the consequence of simultaneous cognitions arising [at once]. Therefore, the eye is presided over by the mind. [Objection: There is no connection between them; since the mind is connected with things of atomic dimension (*aṇu-parimāṇa*), it cannot be a presider over multiple things simultaneously, and thus there would simply be no perception of duality and so forth. [Response: But there *is* such perception; therefore, it is the eye itself that is presided over by the mind. [Objection: Even so, due to its connection with multiple objects, it would produce multiple cognitions simultaneously. [Response: No, because the instrument (the sense organ) has the capacity to bring about only a single cognition. For indeed, a single instrument does not perform multiple actions at one time. Therefore, it has already been stated that while jars and other objects may be manifested simultaneously, there is no simultaneous grasping of them.

Regarding what was stated—that the linguistic usage of "one" and so forth arises either from a distinct quality (*guṇāntara*) or from its own nature (*svabhāva*)—we reply that it is by virtue of the universal of oneness (*ekatvasāmānya*). To explain: the linguistic usage of "one" and so forth occurs in a substance due to its connection with a quality; in a quality, it occurs due to its connection with a universal; and in a universal as well, it occurs due to its connection with a quality. Nor is there an infinite regress of apprehensions, because we do not admit that the cognition of a qualifier must necessarily be preceded by another cognition [of a further qualifier]. Now, it might be argued that the cognition of the universal of oneness arises through the relation of inherence-in-what-is-inherent-in-the-conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*), because it functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). This is not so, because no such cognition of a qualified object (*viśeṣya*) having multiple qualities is ever experienced. [Reply: No, for the existence of duality (*dvitva*) is established by the fact that its production could not otherwise be accounted for. To explain: if duality were produced according to the process where qualities of the cause precede—as in the case of color and so forth—it would be perceived at the very moment of the first contact with the sense organ, since it would have been produced long before [the subsequent cognition]; furthermore, counting would become useless. But this is not the case. Therefore, it is determined that the cognition whose object is multiple qualities—even though it resides in the self—is the cause for the production of duality, and its destruction follows from the destruction of that [cognition]. Otherwise, if one were to admit that destruction results solely from the destruction of the inherent (*samavāyin*) and non-inherent (*asamavāyin*) causes, then because those two persist for a long time, duality itself would be permanent or even eternal in some cases, since there would be no destruction of those two and no other contradictory quality (*virodhiguṇa*) could arise. Therefore, destruction is postulated to result only from an instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).

Nor does it follow that, in this manner, the destruction of a jar or similar object would result from the destruction of its efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), for such is not observed. In the case at hand, however, since the destruction of duality (*dvitva*) and so forth is observed even while the inherent (*samavāyin*) and non-inherent (*asamavāyin*) causes remain present, its destruction is postulated as resulting from the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*). Otherwise, as has been stated, it would persist like color and other qualities, and thus its apprehension would occur at the very moment of the first contact with the sense organ. Now, if it is argued that although duality and the rest persist, they are not perceived due to the absence of a manifesting agent (*vyañjaka*), whereas perception occurs now because [the object] has arisen—then it is more logical that the enumerative cognition and so forth possess the status of being the producers (*janaka*) [of duality]. Therefore, since the absence of duality is experienced after the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding duality and so forth, and since no other cause for its production is possible, it is stated that the destruction of the enumerative cognition is the cause of its [duality's] destruction.

Now, regarding the hypothesis that first there is the cognition of the generality of duality (*dvitvasāmānyajñāna*), followed by the cognition of the quality (*guṇajñāna*) and then the cognition of the substance (*dravyajñāna*), what is the proof for this? If it is argued that it is because [the quality] is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*), we say no; for if one must further postulate a qualifier even for a qualifier, it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). To explain: in the arising of the cognition "two substances," since the quality is a qualifier, its cognition at the outset is logical; however, since the generality [of duality] is not a qualifier of the quality, its cognition is not logical. Or, if you accept that it is so, then that generality would also have another qualifier, leading to infinite regress? No, because such a rule is not accepted. For a rule—that a qualifier must necessarily have another qualifier postulated—is denied out of fear of infinite regress; it does not mean, however, that there is no qualifier at all for a qualifier. And this is precisely what the author of the *Bhāṣya* intended to convey, since he mentions the generality as a qualifier even for a quality that qualifies a substance.

Now, what is the proof for the claim that the destruction of the cognition of a substance follows from a mental impression (*saṃskāra*)? Since no causeless destruction of an effect is observed, and since the destruction of the cognition of a substance is experienced through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the causality of the mental impression is established. Furthermore, we shall explain later that its existence is proven by memory. {The manner of the production and destruction of triad-ness, etc.:} “By this, the production of triad-ness and so forth is also explained. Triad-ness and the rest are produced from unitary entities accompanied by the cognition of multiple objects; their destruction results from the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*). <PDhS>

Thus, when the causes for the production and destruction of duality have been explained, he applies this analogy: "By this, the production of triad and so forth is explained. For just as duality is produced from two unities accompanied by the cognition of multiplicity, so too is the production of triad and the rest from unities accompanied by the cognition of multiplicity. And when triad and so forth have arisen, there occurs the cognition of their universal (sāmānya); then, the cognition of requirement (apekṣābuddhi) is in the process of perishing; and simultaneously with that, from the universal, its cognition, and their relation, the cognition of the quality (guṇabuddhi) is in the process of arising—this constitutes one single moment.

<2> Then, at one and the same time: there arises the cognition of the quality "triad-ness" (tritva) and so forth; there occurs the production of the cognition of the substance from the quality, its cognition, and their relation; there is the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*); there is the state of the cognition of the universal (*sāmānya*) being about to perish; and there is the state of the quality being about to perish. <3> Thereafter, at one and the same time: there arises the cognition of the substance; there occurs the production of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*); there is the state of the cognition of the quality being about to perish; there is the destruction of the cognition of the universal; and from the destruction of the relative cognition, there is also the destruction of the quality.
<4> From that [mental impression], there is also the [destruction] of the cognition of the substance—this is the meaning of the extended application (*atideśa*).

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), numbers such as one hundred are included; however, in that case, the extension (*atideśa*) of the production of duality is simply impossible. For instance, since there is no simultaneous contact of a hundred substances with the sense organ, and because there is no causal basis for perceiving the unitary qualities (*ekaguṇa*) residing therein, how could the number "one hundred" arise? Nor should it be argued that the number "one hundred" arises from the simultaneous perception of individual unitary qualities drawn forth by the universal of unity (*ekatvasāmānya*), because the relation characterized as *saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya* (inherence in what is inherent in what is conjoined) between the sense organ and the universal of unity occurs in every single substance, and thus exists even in the qualities of other substances.
