If this were so, the consequence would be the production of numbers like "one hundred" everywhere, since there is no distinction in the sense organ’s relation—characterized as *saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*—with the universal of unity, and if one accepts the perception of individual qualities based on its apprehension, then the number "one hundred" and so on would arise in every substance. But this is not the case. Therefore, due to the absence of a causal basis for dependence (*apekṣākāraṇa*), [the number] does not arise. Furthermore, production cannot occur without a cognition of dependence (*apekṣābuddhi*), because otherwise the act of counting would be rendered useless, according to the logic already stated.

All of this is incorrect, because the conventional usage of number is real. Once the existence of numbers such as "one hundred" is established, since that [number] is produced, its cause of production must necessarily be stated; and since no other [cause] is possible, a distinct *apekṣābuddhi* (relational cognition) is postulated.

And thus, when the cognition of a single quality (*ekaguṇa*) arises with respect to one [object], at the moment the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is produced, there is the state of being about to arise for the cognition of a second single quality, and the state of being about to perish for the preceding cognition; this constitutes a single point in time.

<2> Then, at one and the same time: the arising of the cognition of the second quality; the state of the recollection of the previous quality being about to arise; the state of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) being about to arise through a cognition assisted by the previous mental impression; and the destruction of the previous cognition. <3> Then, at one and the same time: the arising of the recollection; the arising of the mental impression; the state of the cognition of the second quality being about to perish; the "relational cognition" (*apekṣābuddhi*) consisting of both the recollection and the direct experience; and the state of duality (*dvitva*) being about to arise.

<4> Then, from the arising of duality, there is the state of being in the process of arising of the cognition of that [duality], as well as the destruction of the cognition of the second unitary quality; this is one moment.

<5> Then, there is the arising of the cognition of the quality of duality, the state of being in the process of arising of the cognition of the substance, and the state of being in the process of destruction of the memory; this is one moment.

<6> Then, there is the arising of the cognition of the substance, the state of being in the process of destruction of the cognition of the quality, the destruction of the memory, from that destruction the state of being in the process of destruction of the duality, and the state of being in the process of arising of the cognition of the third unitary quality; this is one moment.

Then, at that same moment: there is the arising of the cognition of the third unitary quality; the state of destruction of the cognition of substance; the destruction of the cognition of the dual quality; the state of being produced as the recollection of the previous two unitary qualities; the state of being produced as another mental impression (*saṃskāra*) by means of the cognition of the unitary quality assisted by the previous impression; and the destruction of the dual quality. This constitutes one single point in time.

<8> Then there is the arising of recollection, the arising of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), the state of perishing of the cognition of the single quality, and the cognition of recollection and experience [of the two substances] which constitutes the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*); then there is the state of being produced of the quality of triadness and the destruction of the cognition of the substance—this is one moment.
<9> Then there is the arising of the quality of triadness, the state of being produced of its cognition, and the destruction of the cognition of the single quality—this is one moment.

<10> Then there is the arising of the cognition of the quality of triadness, the state of being produced of the cognition of the substance, and the state of perishing of the recollection—this is one moment.

<11> Then, at one and the same time: there is the arising of the cognition of the substance; the state of perishing of the cognition of the quality [of number]; the destruction of the recollection; from that destruction, the state of perishing of the quality of three-ness; and the state of being about to arise of the cognition of the fourth single unitary quality.

<12> Thereafter, there arises the cognition of the single quality of the fourth [substance]; the substance-cognition is in the state of perishing; the cognition of the quality perishes; the destruction of the quality "three-ness" occurs; and the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is in the process of arising. This sequence should be inferred for the [qualities] such as "four-ness" and so on, up until the point where, regarding the final single quality of the final substance, the cognition arises through conceptualization and the memory arises through that mental impression.

<13> Then, there is the simultaneous occurrence of the production of the memory of all the preceding individual qualities, the state of perishing of the cognition of the single quality of the final substance, and the fact that both the memory and the direct experience constitute the "reckoning-cognition" (*apekṣābuddhi*); following this, there is the state of being produced for the number one hundred—this constitutes one moment of time. <14> Then, there is the simultaneous occurrence of the production of the number one hundred, the state of being produced for the cognition of that [number], and the destruction of the cognition of the single quality of the final substance—this constitutes one moment of time. <15> Then, there is the simultaneous occurrence of the production of the cognition of the quality, the state of being produced for the cognition of the substance, and the state of perishing for the memory—this constitutes one moment of time.

Immediately after that, there arises the cognition of the substance [in the form] "these are a hundred"; the cognition of the quality is in the state of perishing; the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is in the state of arising; and the memory perishes. Immediately after that, from the mental impression, the cognition of the substance also [perishes].

Others, however, maintain that the following is the conceptual construction: there is a cognition of one quality (*ekaguṇa*) in one object, by which a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is produced; then there is a cognition of one quality in a second object, by which another impression is produced along with the previous one; this process continues until there is a cognition of the final quality. Then, because that impression has been manifested through conceptualization, a memory arises whose object is all the individual qualities without exception, while the original experience is in the state of perishing—thus they hold that the "cognition of requirement" (*apekṣābuddhi*) generates the number "one hundred. Nor should it be argued that the experience of duality (*dvitva*) and so forth occurring in the interval is contradicted by [the absence of] perception, since only the causal factor is being mentioned. For instance, the impression generated by the experience of the first quality is the cause for the production of the number "one hundred" by way of memory. It is not the case that the experience of duality and so forth functions in this same way; therefore, it is not mentioned here, not because it does not exist.

Now, let it be granted that the number one hundred arises in this manner; however, the question remains as to how its apprehension occurs. For instance, since there is no simultaneous contact of a hundred substances with the sense organ, the number one hundred residing within them would likewise not be perceptible; how, then, could there be the cognition "these are a hundred"? If it is argued that because of the contact of the sense organ with the final substance, the number one hundred inherent in it is produced and is indeed perceived through the relation of inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyukta-samavāya*), then those previously perceived substances, though lacking direct contact with the sense organ, become objects of immediate cognition—namely, "these are a hundred"—by virtue of the very relationship characterized as that between a qualifier and the qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-lakṣaṇa*).

In that case, would even space (*ākāśa*) and other such entities—which are drawn in by the particularity of existence (*sattā*)—also become perceptible? No, because of a failure to understand the intended meaning. For instance, since the immediate cognition "these are a hundred" is observed, an inquiry into its cause is undertaken here. And since no other connection is perceived therein, those things drawn in by the number "hundred" are perceptible solely through the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*). However, space and the like have not been previously perceived in this manner, nor is there any immediate cognition regarding them; therefore, they are not conceived in such a way.

Furthermore, the number "one hundred" is not perceived through the contact of the sense organ with the initial substance, because it arises in the final substance. For instance, by means of counting, one perceives the single quality (unity) of the final substance; then, the number "one hundred" arises as inherent in those substances in which the quality of unity has been perceived. Therefore, since it is impossible for it to exist in the preceding [substances] even when there is contact with them, it is not apprehended therein.

Nor does it follow from this that a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), acting as an auxiliary to experience, must initiate another latent impression—such that a latent impression produced by the experience of a jar, being assisted by a subsequent experience, would also have to initiate a further impression; for the determination of the nature of things is governed by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). To explain: due to the restriction imposed by the unseen force that brings about the enjoyment of the number "one hundred" and so forth, a specific latent impression arises only in this case (the counting process) and not in the case of a jar or the like, because the effect [of such an impression] is absent there. And the postulation of a cause is made on the basis of the existence of an effect. Thus, the unseen force acts as a regulator only where [the effect] cannot otherwise be explained, but it does not constitute a total rejection of perceptible causes. Therefore, even though the unseen force exists, the causality of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) is postulated because counting is observed [to occur]. Otherwise, if the unseen force alone—acting as an auxiliary to the Lord’s cognition or to the quality of unity—were to initiate numbers such as "one hundred," then the number one hundred would arise in all substances. Consequently, like color and other qualities, it would be perceived even without counting, since it would have been produced long ago. But this is not the case.

If it is argued that there is no perception because of the absence of a manifestor, we say no; for this has already been answered by the fact that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of such a manifestor.

Furthermore, things produced by the intellect of one person cannot be perceived directly by another; thus, if [the world] were produced by God, it would not be perceptible to people like us. Therefore, according to the reasoning already stated, [the world] is both produced and perceived; enough with this excessive elaboration.

“In some cases, [the destruction of duality occurs] due to the destruction of its substratum. How so? When an action arises in a component that is the locus of unity, at that very moment the cognition of the universal *ekatva* (oneness) arises; by that action, a disjunction is produced from another component, and the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) arises. Therefore, at the same time that the destruction of the conjunction occurs due to the disjunction, duality (*dvitva*) is produced; from the destruction of the conjunction, the destruction of the substance occurs, and the cognition of the universal arises. Then, at the same time that the relative cognition is destroyed by the cognition of the universal, at that very moment, duality is destroyed due to the destruction of its substratum.”

[The author] states that destruction [of duality] occurs not only from the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), but also "in some cases from the destruction of the substratum" (*āśrayavināśāt*). The question "How so? is asked by one who is unacquainted [with the process]. There, because the destruction of duality has been stated to occur through the destruction of its substratum, [the author], thinking that this will be understood elsewhere by analogy with that case, states the destruction of duality itself: "When action arises in a part of the substratum of the unitary [number]" (*yadaikatvādhārāvayave karma utpadyate*). At the very moment that disjunction (*vibhāga*) is in the state of being produced, knowledge of the generality of unity (*ekatvasāmānya*) arises; at that same time, the enumerative cognition is in the state of being produced. Then follows the production of disjunction, the state of the conjunction initiating the substance (*dravyārambhakasaṃyoga*) being about to perish, the production of the enumerative cognition, the state of duality being produced, and the state of the knowledge of the generality of unity being about to perish. Immediately after that, there is the destruction of the conjunction, the state of the knowledge of the generality of unity being about to perish, the state of the substance being about to perish, the production of duality, and the state of the knowledge of its generality being produced—these constitute one single moment.

Thereafter, the cognition of the universal (*sāmānyajñāna*) arises, the *apekṣābuddhi* (the enumerative cognition) undergoes destruction, and the substance (*dravya*) is destroyed; simultaneously, the quality (*guṇa*) undergoes destruction. Then, from the destruction of the substance follows the destruction of the quality, and from the cognition of the universal follows the destruction of the *apekṣābuddhi*. Since the destruction of the quality is not caused by the destruction of the *apekṣābuddhi*—because they are simultaneous—it is the destruction of the substance alone that is the cause, owing to its prior occurrence.

However, it should be understood that when action (*karman*) in a part that is the substratum of oneness is considered to occur simultaneously with the *apekṣābuddhi*, then the destruction of the quality can also result from the destruction of both [the substance and the *apekṣābuddhi*].

“This rule is appropriate in the case of a killer and the slain. However, if opposition is characterized by non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*), there would be the undesirable consequence that the cognition of the substance does not arise. How so? Because, at the same time as the cognition of the quality [duality], the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) is destroyed; consequently, duality is destroyed, and there would be the undesirable consequence that the cognition of the substance—namely, ‘two substances’—which depends upon that [duality], does not arise. <PDhS>

With the words, “This procedure is excellent,” and so forth, he concludes his own position by means of refuting the opposing view. This procedure for the production of duality and so on is excellent—that is, it is logical—in which position? He says: “In the position of the victim and the executioner. For when there is the arising of one cognition, there is the state of perishing of another.

“However, if contradiction were characterized by non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*), there would be the undesirable consequence that the cognition of the substance could not arise,” this is unsatisfactory. To explain: if contradiction were characterized by non-coexistence, then at the very moment the cognition of the generality of duality (*dvitvasāmānya*) arises, the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) would perish; and at the moment the cognition of the quality [of duality] perishes, the duality itself would perish. Consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence that the cognition “two substances” (which depends upon that duality) could not arise. Furthermore, destruction would be causeless. For at the very time the cognition of the generality of duality arises, the enumerative cognition perishes; because they are simultaneous, the destruction of the enumerative cognition cannot be the effect of the cognition of the generality. And since there is no other cause, it would follow that destruction is causeless. But this is impossible, as has already been stated.

“If [it is argued] that ‘[the cognition] is like that of an inferential mark, arising from mere cognition’—that is to say, one might think: just as in the case of ‘what has not come into being [is the cause] of what has come into being,’ there is inference from mere cognition even in the absence of an inferential mark, so too, despite the destruction of the quality, there would be the cognition ‘two substances’ based on the mere cognition of the qualities.”

Now, even if the quality (*guṇa*) is destroyed due to the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) at the same time as the cognition of the quality, one might still object that—just like inferential knowledge—a cognition of "two substances" will arise from mere cognition alone; thus, he anticipates the opponent's view: "If it is argued that [it is] like inferential knowledge, arising from mere cognition" (*laiṅgikavajjñānamātrād iti cet*). This would be the intended position: just as in this sūtra, where it is stated that an unreal or non-existent mark (*liṅga*) can be the indicator of a real or existent marked object (*liṅgin*), inference is accepted there even in the absence of a physical mark, based on mere cognition alone.

For instance, since it is held that "cognition is inferred by means of cognition," the cognition must necessarily first be apprehended as the inferential mark (*liṅga*). Thereafter follows its state of perishing; then the state of the arising of the recollection of the relation of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*); immediately after that, the arising of the recollection of the relation of invariable concomitance, the destruction of the cognition serving as the inferential mark, the state of the perishing of that [recollection] cognition, the state of the arising of the synthetic reflective cognition (*parāmarśajñāna*), and finally the arising of the synthetic reflective cognition. At this point, the recollection of the relation of invariable concomitance is in a state of perishing, and the cognition of the inferential mark has also been destroyed. Thus, it is observed that the cognition of the knower occurs from the synthetic reflective cognition alone, which is now devoid of its object. By the same logic, upon the destruction of a quality, the cognition of the substance should arise from the mere cognition of the quality.

Others, however, maintain that just as the non-existent act of raining (*varṣakarma*) is the mark (*liṅga*) of the existent conjunction of wind and clouds, so too, even upon the destruction of a quality, there is knowledge of the substance based on the mere knowledge of that [quality]. This is not correct. For it is not the case that the non-existent act of raining is the mark for the existence of the existent conjunction of wind and clouds. What then? The non-production of the act of raining is fallible (*vyabhicārī*). And since that exists by its very nature, how can it be non-existent? If its non-existence is due to its being of the nature of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpatayā*), then a positive entity would also be non-existent by way of its being of the nature of a negation (*abhāvarūpeṇa*), and thus everything would simply be non-existent. Therefore, the non-production of the act of raining is indeed existent as a mark; thus, another example alone is appropriate.

“Because it is a cognition of the qualified (*viśeṣya*). For a cognition of the qualified cannot occur without a connection to a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) based on similarity. Thus says the author of the Sūtras: ‘From the whiteness inherent [in the substance], there arises the cognition of whiteness; from that [cognition of whiteness], there arises the cognition of the white [substance]; these two stand in the relation of cause and effect. <PDhS>

He states the rebuttal to what was said—that there will be a cognition "two substances" similar to inferential knowledge—by saying: "No, because it is a cognition of the qualified (*viśeṣyajñānatvāt*). For instance, since it arises through the coloring of duality, the cognition "two substances" is a cognition of the qualified; therefore, the operation of an existing quality must be postulated here. That is to say, a cognition of the qualified cannot come into being "without a connection with the qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇasambandham antareṇa*). Thus, for its production, the qualifier, the cognition of that qualifier, and the connection between them constitute the causes. Otherwise, since all causes would lack a specific operation regarding the production of the cognition of the qualified, there would be no fixed status of being a qualifier. Therefore, the qualifier, the cognition of that qualifier, and their connection constitute the causes.

And thus the author of the Sūtras says: "From whiteness as an inherent property (*samavāyin*) and from the cognition of whiteness, there arises the cognition of the white [substance]; these two stand in the relation of cause and effect" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 8.1.8). By this, he demonstrates that this very meaning was intended by the author of the Sūtras as well. To explain: the white substance exists; its state is "whiteness," which is the quality of white. From what kind of [whiteness]? From that which is "inherent," i.e., connected by way of inherence (*samavāya*). "From the cognition of whiteness" means from the cognition of the quality of white. From these three causes, the cognition of the white [substance]—the knowledge of the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*), namely "the white substance"—is produced. Furthermore, those two cognitions—the cognition of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the cognition of the qualificandum—are "related as cause and effect," meaning they possess the nature of cause and effect.
“But inferential knowledge does not arise without [the cognition of] difference; therefore, this comparison is unequal.”

Furthermore, inferential knowledge (*laiṅgika-jñāna*) is not colored by its mark (*liṅga*); thus, he says that it arises even in the absence of the mark: "But inferential knowledge does not arise through non-difference [with] the mark," meaning it does not arise with the coloring of the mark. "Therefore, this comparison is dissimilar. This comparison—that "two substances" will be like inferential knowledge—is dissimilar; it is not the same. For instance, there is a coloring by the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) in the cognition of the qualified (*viśeṣya*), whereas in the case of inferential knowledge, there is an absence of such coloring; this is the point of dissimilarity.

Alternatively, this presentation (*upanyāsa*) is flawed. A "presentation" is so called because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) is presented therein; "like that which is inferential" (*laiṅgikavat*) is the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). And that [example] is flawed, because, being devoid of the coloring by the mark (*liṅga*), it is a cognition lacking a qualifier (*aviśeṣya-jñāna*).

Others, however, hold that the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the cognition thereof are the causes of the effect, which is the cognition of the qualified (*viśeṣya-jñāna*); therefore, they believe that there is no cognition of a substance (*dravya*) without its quality (*guṇa*). They maintain that the cognitions of the qualifier and the qualified stand in a cause-and-effect relationship. But not every cognition is of such a nature, for there is a lack of proof (*pramāṇābhāva*).
By this, the cognition of synthesis (*saṅkalanājñāna*) is refuted, because there is no evidence for any other cognition apart from the cognitions of the qualifier and the qualified; enough of this.

"No, [there is no fault], because of rapid production, as in the case of 'space possesses sound. Just as three cognitions arise rapidly in that instance, so too it is in the production of the cognition of duality and so forth; thus there is no fault. <PDhS>

Now, [the opponent objects]: "Before the production of duality, there are two cognitions—the cognition of the universal 'oneness' and the cognition of relative dependence (*apekṣājñāna*). But once duality has been produced, there are five cognitions: the cognition of that universal, the cognition of the quality [duality], the cognition of the substance, the cognition of conjunction, and the cognition of the qualified object. If these arise in succession, why is this sequence not perceived? Since it is not perceived, it does not exist. To refute this, he says: "Not so, because of rapid production" (*na āśūtpatteḥ*). What was stated—that there is no succession—is not correct; for even though succession exists, it is not experienced due to its occurrence with extreme rapidity.

Now, as to where the non-perception of sequence due to rapid production is observed, he says: "Just as in the case of 'space possesses sound' (*yathā śabdavadākāśam*). Here, three cognitions arise rapidly: the cognition of sound, the cognition of space, and the cognition of the relation between sound and space; thus there is a non-perception of sequence. Likewise, in the production of the cognition of duality (*dvitva*) and so forth, the non-perception of sequence occurs precisely because of their rapid occurrence; therefore, there is no fault.

Nor should it be argued that this is a rebuttal based on the fact that cognitions arise so rapidly that their opposition is characterized solely by non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*), such that while the quality (*guṇa*) has not yet perished, the cognition of the substance (*dravyajñāna*) will occur; for since the cause is present immediately, the effect must likewise exist immediately. Thus, the refutation remains intact: the cognition of the substance cannot arise at the very moment the quality is destroyed, as it is dependent upon that quality. If "non-coexistence" is intended to mean simply that two cognitions do not abide together without opposition, then there is no dispute.

“If it is argued that ‘the same fault applies even in the case of the slayer and the slain,’ the following thought might occur: ‘In that case, even in the view of the slayer and the slain, there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-arising of the cognition of the substance. How so? Because at the same time as the cognition of the generality of duality, the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) is destroyed by the mental impression (*saṃskāra*). This is not so; for the cognition of the aggregate is the cause of the mental impression. Since it is the cognition of the aggregate alone—and not the initial perception (*ālocanajñāna*)—that is the cause of the mental impression, there is no fault.”

Now, anticipating the objection that the same refutation applies even to the "killer-and-the-killed" (vadhyaghātaka) model due to the contradiction characterized by non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*), he says this: “If it is argued that the fault is the same even in the killer-and-the-killed model, [we reply: so be it. This is the summary statement (*saṅgrahavākya*). Its elaboration, however, is: “In that case, even in the killer-and-the-killed model, there would follow the consequence that the cognition of the substance does not arise. To explain: if the non-arising of the cognition of the substance occurs when the quality is destroyed at the same time as the cognition of the quality, then why would there be no such arising even in the killer-and-the-killed model? [The opponent replies: Because the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) occurs due to the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) at the same time as the cognition of the universal (*sāmānya*).

For just as the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) produces duality, so too does it produce a mental impression (*saṃskāra*). Consequently, there occurs the state of the [enumerative cognition] being about to perish, and the state of the cognition of the generality of duality (*dvitvasāmānyajñāna*) being about to arise; then follows the arising of the cognition of the generality of duality, the state of the cognition of the quality (*guṇajñāna*) being about to arise, and the destruction of the enumerative cognition; then the state of the quality being about to perish, the arising of the cognition of the quality, and finally, due to the destruction of the enumerative cognition, the destruction of the quality. Because the cognition of the substance (*dravyajñāna*) depends upon that [quality], it would simply not arise. "No," is the rebuttal, "because the cognition of the collection (*samūhajñāna*) is the cause of the mental impression. For it has been stated that the enumerative cognition is destroyed by the mental impression, but that is not so; because the cognition of the collection—characterized by intense practice and attention—is the cause of the mental impression.

He provides an explanation for the statement regarding the "comprehensive cognition" (*saṅgraha*): "Only the collective cognition (*samūhajñāna*) is the cause of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), not the perceptual cognition (*ālocanajñāna*)," which is to say, the "relational cognition" (*apekṣājñāna*). Therefore, there is no fault [in our position]. If it is asked, "What is the proof (*pramāṇa*) for this?"—it is the non-arising of recollection (*smaraṇa*) and the arising of the cognition of the substance (*dravyajñāna*). For instance, the postulation of a mental impression is made only where there is recollection; and since that [recollection] does not exist here [in the case of the relational cognition], [if one were to admit otherwise], the cognition of the substance itself would not occur. But that [cognition] is observed. Therefore, because it cannot be explained otherwise, it is determined that the relational cognition does not produce a mental impression, as there is no other possible way [for it to function].

“If it is argued that ‘there would be the consequence of the simultaneity of cognitions’—that is to say, one might think: ‘In the case of the opposition between cognitions characterized as the slayer and the slain, there would indeed be the consequence of their simultaneity’—this is not so. Because what is prohibited is the co-existence of two [cognitions] while they are not perishing. By the statement regarding the non-simultaneity of cognitions, both the simultaneous production of two cognitions and the simultaneous co-existence of two non-perishing [cognitions] are prohibited. For in the case of the opposition between the slayer and the slain, there is neither the simultaneous production of two cognitions nor the simultaneous co-existence of two non-perishing ones.”

Now, even regarding the case of the "slayer and the slain" (the relationship between a cognition that destroys and one that is destroyed), he anticipates the opponent's intention with the words: “If it be thought that there would be the consequence of the simultaneity of cognitions. The elaboration of this summary statement is: “Indeed, if there were an opposition among cognitions characterized by the slayer and the slain, there would be the consequence of the simultaneity of cognitions. Thus, if the opposition of cognitions is defined by the relationship of slayer and slain, then because the second arises while the first remains, the simultaneity of cognitions follows as an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpādana*).

This is not undesirable, because "the simultaneous existence of two non-perishing [cognitions] is denied" (*). For instance, by the sūtra, "The mind is one in each body, because cognitions are not simultaneous and because efforts are not simultaneous" (Vai. Sū. 3.2.3), the simultaneous production [of cognitions] and the co-existence of two non-perishing cognitions without mutual contradiction are both denied. Regarding the contradiction between the slain and the slayer, however, neither of these two occurs; thus he says, "For in the case of the contradiction between the slain and the slayer, there is no simultaneous production of two cognitions, nor is there the simultaneous existence of two non-perishing [cognitions]. This is not a fault.

[The difference regarding dimension (*parimāṇa*): “Dimension is the cause of the conventional usage of measurement. It is fourfold: minute (*aṇu*), large (*mahat*), long (*dīrgha*), and short (*hrasva*). Among these, the large is of two kinds: eternal (*nitya*) and non-eternal (*anitya*). The eternal [large dimension] is the supreme largeness (*paramamahattva*) existing in ether (*ākāśa*), time (*kāla*), space (*diś*), and the self (*ātman*). The non-eternal [large dimension] exists only in triads (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth. Likewise, the minute is also of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal. The eternal [minute dimension] exists in atoms (*paramāṇu*) and minds (*manas*); it is spherical (*pārimāṇḍalya*). The non-eternal [minute dimension] exists only in dyads (*dvyaṇuka*). <PDhS>

Now, following the order of the enumeration, the section beginning with “Dimension (*parimāṇa*) is the cause of the conventional usage of measurement” is introduced for the purpose of defining and examining dimension, which has reached its turn. “Conventional usage” (*vyavahāra*) is knowledge; alternatively, that by which something is conventionally used is “conventional usage,” namely, a designation. If it were stated simply that “dimension is the cause of these two [knowledge and designation],” there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). To avoid this, the term “measurement” (*māna*) is included. Even so, since the state of being a cause for the conventional usage of measurement exists in space (*ākāśa*) and the self (*ātman*), the qualification “while being a qualifier of substance” (*dravyaviśeṣaṇatve sati*) is added as a further specification. Furthermore, to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) caused by the universal property of “dimension-ness” (*parimāṇatva-sāmānya*), the qualification “while being a qualifier of substance” should be understood as an implicit addition. To explain: dimension is distinct from other things, because, while being a qualifier of substance, it is the cause of the conventional usage of measurement; whereas that which is not distinct from others—namely, non-dimension—is not like this, just like color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth. Alternatively, the conventional usage itself may be the probandum (*sādhya*).

Likewise, this very sentence, being repeated, is connected with the intent of an investigation into its multiple meanings. For instance, human linguistic usage requires a qualifier because it consists of the cognition of a qualified object, like the cognition of "one with a staff" (*daṇḍin*) and so forth. Nor can any one of the [sensory qualities] such as color (*rūpa*) and the rest be its qualifier, because that [usage] is distinct from their [respective] usages; therefore, there must be a cause that is itself distinct. Furthermore, this is not a conceptual cognition (*kalpanājñāna*) arising from latent impressions (*vāsanā*), since such [impressions] have already been refuted previously.

“It is fourfold,” thus is the classification. In what form? He says: “minute, large, long, and short. Now, one might object that this fourfold division is incorrect, since distinctions such as square and so forth are also possible; but that is not so, because it is largeness itself—when accompanied by the perception of a specific arrangement of parts—that brings about the conventional usage of terms like “square” and the rest. For instance, when there is the perception of a specific arrangement of parts, there arises the usage of terms such as “square,” “triangular,” or “circular”; in the absence of that [arrangement], such usage does not occur. Therefore, no other dimension (*parimāṇa*) is established.

[Objection: But in that case, the conventional usage of "long" and "short" will also arise simply from the perception of specific configurations of parts; therefore, enough with the conceptualization of "length" and "shortness. [Reply: No, because length is perceived even when those [configurations] are not perceived. For instance, in very dim light, the appearance of length in a post or similar object is observed even without the perception of the arrangement of parts. And it should be understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the appearance of a square shape does not occur in this way.

In this regard, because there are further subdivisions of both largeness (*mahattva*) and minuteness (*aṇutva*), he states that dimension (*parimāṇa*) is of six kinds: "Largeness is of two types: eternal and non-eternal. It exists "eternally in space, time, direction, and the self. And that is "supreme largeness," for there is no largeness greater than that. "The non-eternal [largeness] exists only in the triad (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth. That which has the triad as its beginning is described thus; it exists in that alone, for it is there that the causes of production are present.

Likewise, the other [type of] magnitude (*mahat*) does not exist even in the slightest degree; rather, there are two kinds [of dimension]: eternal and non-eternal. To which things [does this apply]? He says: "In atoms and minds" (*paramāṇumanaḥsu*). Atoms (*paramāṇu*) and minds (*manas*) constitute "atoms and minds"; [the dimension] exists in them. Its name is "sphericity" (*pārimāṇḍalya*). For indeed, atoms and minds are spherical (*parimaṇḍala*); the state of being so is sphericity, which is simply their dimension (*parimāṇa*). That, moreover, is eternal, because no cause for its production or destruction is perceived. For instance, since atoms lack a cause, there exists neither the number "plurality" nor "accumulation" as a cause for that dimension. Such is the cause of dimension. Furthermore, because atoms are eternal, their destruction is impossible; therefore, their dimension is necessarily eternal. "Non-eternal [dimension] exists only in the dyad" (*anityaṃ dvyaṇuka eva*) excludes any other substratum.

“Even in the case of large objects such as the *kuvalaya*, *āmalaka*, and *bilva* fruits, the conventional usage of ‘atomic’ (*aṇutva*) is figurative, depending on the absence of that [atomic] excellence. Likewise, length and shortness are inherent in the same substratum as produced largeness and atomicity; even in the case of things like sacrificial fuel, sugarcane, and bamboo which are directly long, the conventional usage of ‘shortness’ is figurative, depending on the absence of that [longitudinal] excellence.”

But is this not improper, since the conventional usage of "minute" (*aṇu*) is observed elsewhere as well? No; for in those cases, it is accepted as a figurative usage (*upacāra*) because a primary sense is impossible. Thus he says: "In the case of large objects such as the water-lily (*kuvalaya*), the myrobalan (*āmalaka*), and the wood-apple (*bilva*), the excellence of dimension (*parimāṇātiśaya*) is considered in relation to the presence or absence of that [excellence]. The excellence [of dimension] is either in relation to the water-lily and so forth, or [the comparison] is from that [water-lily] onwards. The presence of that [excellence] exists in the wood-apple and so forth; having regard for its absence in the myrobalan, there is the conventional usage of "minute" applied to the myrobalan. Likewise, the excellence is the superiority of dimension in relation to the water-lily; the presence of that [excellence] exists in the myrobalan; having regard for its absence in the water-lily, there is the conventional usage of "minute" applied to the water-lily. For where there is actual minuteness, the absence of the excellence of dimension should be understood. Since that [excellence] is perceived elsewhere as well, the figurative usage indeed proceeds.

Alternatively, he states what the proof is for the existence of the primary [atom]: "The usage of the term 'atom' is figurative. For just as the usage of the term "lion" with respect to a boy depends upon a primary [referent], so too this usage of the term "atom," being metaphorical, must be preceded by a primary [referent]; thus, the existence of atoms is established. And likewise, the usage of the term "atom" with respect to water-lilies and the like is preceded by a primary [referent], because it is a figurative usage, just like the usage of the term "lion" with respect to a boy.

Furthermore, while there is a distinction between largeness (*mahattva*) and smallness (*aṇutva*) based on whether they are eternal or non-eternal, such is not the case for length (*dīrghatva*) and shortness (*hrasvatva*), because no other substratum for them is possible. To address the doubt as to where these two reside, he says: "Length and shortness" (*dīrghatvahrasvatve*). This means both length and shortness. These two, however, "inhere in the same object as produced largeness and smallness" (*utpādyamahadaṇutvaikārthasamavete*). That is, they inhere in the same object together with those produced largeness and smallness. For instance, produced largeness exists in triads (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth, and length exists in that very same place. In dyads (*dvyaṇuka*), smallness exists, and shortness exists in that very same place. Because atoms are spherical (*parimaṇḍala*), they possess no shortness; and because space (*ākāśa*) and the like are all-pervading, they possess no length, since we observe the application of those terms only in things contrary to those [atoms and the all-pervading].

Now, it was asked: "How can shortness exist even in dyads (*dvyaṇuka*), given that the conventional usage of 'short' is observed elsewhere as well? This is not so; for one accepts that the term is used figuratively (*upacāra*) elsewhere due to the presence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*). Thus he says: "In the case of fuel-sticks (*samidh*), sugarcane, bamboo, and so forth, although they are directly long, there is a figurative usage of 'shortness' with respect to the presence or absence of the excellence of that [length]. To explain: in the case of fuel-sticks and the like, because the causes for the production of length are present, there is direct—that is, primary—length. Since the usage of 'shortness' is observed even in things that are long, a figurative application is postulated because a primary sense is impossible. In this context, the cause is the presence or absence of the excellence of that [length]. The excellence of the bamboo and such, relative to the fuel-sticks and so forth, is the superiority of their length; the existence (*bhāva*) of that [excellence] is its presence in the bamboo and so on. With respect to the absence of that [excellence], there is the usage of 'shortness' in the case of sugarcane. There is a superiority of length in the sugarcane relative to the fuel-stick; with respect to the absence of that [superiority] therein, there is the usage of 'short' in the case of the fuel-stick.

Alternatively, what is the proof for the existence of primary shortness? The usage of the term "short" is metaphorical. For instance, the usage of "short" with respect to *samit* and other [fuel-sticks] is preceded by a primary [usage], because it is a figurative usage, just like the usage of "lion" with respect to a boy.
{The manner of the production of dimension} ("The impermanent [dimension], though fourfold, has its origin in number, dimension, and aggregation. <PDhS>

Having thus stated the fourfold nature [of size], he states the cause of its production: “The impermanent [size], though of four kinds, has number, dimension, and aggregation as its source (*yoni*). Number, dimension, and aggregation constitute the compound *saṃkhyā-parimāṇa-pracayāḥ*; that which has these as its *yoni*—that is, its cause—is the meaning of the sentence: it is produced by number, dimension, and aggregation, both collectively and individually. Thus the Sūtra says: “Large [size arises] from the plurality of causes, from the largeness of the causes, and from a particular kind of aggregation” (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.1.9). The inclusion of the term “impermanent” is for the purpose of excluding the eternal [size]. The phrase “of four kinds” serves to exclude any lesser number.

“In that regard, the number ‘plurality’ (bahutvasaṃkhyā), which has arisen in the dyads and atoms in dependence upon the intellect of the Lord (īśvarabuddhi), produces largeness (mahattva) and length (dīrghatva) simultaneously with the production of color and other qualities in the effect-substance characterized as the triad (tryaṇuka) and so forth, which is composed of those [atoms]. <PDhS>

Because the sequence of the meaning of the sūtra is intended [to be explained], and thus bypassing the order of the enumeration (*uddeśa*), he states the cause for the production of largeness (*mahattva*): “In that regard, the number ‘many’ (*bahutvasaṃkhyā*) produced in the dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) depending upon the intellect of God (*īśvarabuddhi*) brings about largeness and length in the effect-substance (*kāryadravya*) characterized as the triad (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth, which is commenced by those [dyads], simultaneously with the production of color and other qualities. And likewise, since the intellect of God is eternal and has all things as its object, it certainly exists as having each individual quality as its support. Depending upon that [intellect], the number ‘three’ is commenced in the dyads by means of the individual qualities. The phrase “in the dyads” is for the purpose of excluding the atom (*paramāṇu*). It has been stated that a dyad is commenced by two atoms alone, and not by two dyads, because that would entail a useless commencement. Therefore, [the text says] “in the effect-substance commenced by the dyads of atoms. The mention of “substance” (*dravya*) is for the purpose of excluding color and so forth, since they too are commenced by them. Furthermore, the word “substance” (*dravya*) also applies to the universal “substanceness” (*dravyatva*); hence, with the intention of expressing manifestation, the term “effect” (*kārya*) is used to indicate that even that [universal] is commenced. “Characterized as the triad and so forth” means: it is both the triad and the characteristic of the beginning, namely the nature of the cause and the effect. Alternatively, it is the “initial characteristic” because it is perceived at the beginning of all large substances; when that [triad] has arisen, the number ‘three’ residing in the dyads brings about largeness and length simultaneously with the production of color and other qualities.

For it is observed that an effect-entity is preceded by a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*); therefore, since the triad (*tryaṇuka*) has a composite cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), it must have another non-inherent cause. Furthermore, because magnitude (*mahattva*) is absent in dyads (*dvyaṇuka*), the [magnitude of the triad] cannot be preceded by the qualities of its causes. Now, if the magnitude in the triad arises from the atomic dimension (*aṇuparimāṇa*) itself—since an increase in the dimension of the effect is observed to result from the dimension of the cause—then it is seen that threads are subtler than a cloth, and their parts are subtler than those threads. In the same way, the triad will possess a dimension greater than that of the dyad.

That is incorrect. If the dimension of the cause denoted by the word "small" (*aṇu*) were to produce in the effect the same dimension denoted by that very word, then in a triad (*tryaṇuka*), there would only be the dimension of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*). Just as a cloth produced from a collection of threads denoted by the word "large" (*mahat*) is itself denoted by that same word, so too [in your view] a small dimension would arise only from a small dimension. And if one assumes that the dimension in a dyad arises from the dimension of an atom (*paramāṇu*), then since "smallness" (*aṇutva*) would be impossible, how could "largeness" (*mahattva*) arise from it? Furthermore, it is not logical to call something an "atom" if smallness is impossible; for an atom is designated as such because it is smaller than the smallest. Otherwise, the qualification would be meaningless due to the absence of anything to be excluded. Moreover, the conventional usage of "small" occurs in relation to "large," but an atom is not [so defined]. Nor can largeness be the result if the dimension of an atom is accepted as its cause. Therefore, since the conventional usage of "atom" would be abolished in the absence of smallness, the dimension of an atom cannot be the cause.

Furthermore, it is untenable for the dimension of an atom (*paramāṇu-parimāṇa*) to serve as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*) in the production of minuteness (*aṇutva*), or for minuteness to serve as such in the production of magnitude (*mahattva*). This is because we observe that a non-inherent cause must be of an absolutely identical genus (*jāti*). For example, an absolutely homogeneous non-inherent cause is seen in the case where from an extremely white color arises an equally extremely white color; and an absolutely heterogeneous one is seen in the case where sound arises from conjunction (*saṃyoga*). However, this is not the case here: the dimension of an atom is not the cause of magnitude, nor is the dimension of an atom the cause of minuteness. Since it too is a dimension, it is not absolutely heterogeneous. Moreover, "atom-ness" (*paramāṇutva*) is merely a specific sub-class of "minuteness," and "minuteness" is indeed a different genus from "magnitude"; thus, there is no absolute homogeneity of genus.

Furthermore, accumulation (*pracaya*) is not possible here, because the capacity of color (*rūpa*) and other qualities to produce their own effects has been established. Therefore, it is postulated that number alone is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). The proximity is "great" (*mahatī*); thus, largeness (*mahattva*) and length (*dīrghatva*) reside in the triad (*tryaṇuka*), while the triad resides in the dyads (*dvyaṇuka*), and the number three also resides in those very same [dyads]. This constitutes the proximity characterized by the inherence in a single object of both cause and effect.

[Objection: But in this way, because the intellect of God (*īśvarabuddhi*) is eternal and because dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) persist for some time, there would be only permanence; and likewise, number (*saṃkhyā*), as that which inheres in eternal substances, would also be eternal. [Reply: This is not a fault. Because number is an effect, it must necessarily be perishable. Since its destruction is uncaused—given the prohibition against causeless destruction—and because there is an absence of a cause for its persistence (namely, *adṛṣṭa*), its destruction is postulated. Alternatively, the word "God" (*īśvara*) refers to a lord of yogis (*yogīśvara*); since his intellect is non-eternal, the destruction of that number is indeed possible.

To explain: when an action has arisen in a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), at the very moment it begins the process of disjunction, while the [original] conjunction is in a state of perishing, knowledge of the generality of oneness (*ekatvasāmānya*) arises; simultaneously, the "relational cognition" (*apekṣābuddhi*) is in the process of arising. Thereafter, the conjunction [of the two parts] perishes, while the subsequent conjunction is in the process of arising; the relational cognition arises, while the number three (*tritva*) is in the process of arising. Then, the conjunction of the dyad with the two other dyads arises, while the triad (*tryaṇuka*) is in the process of arising; the disjunction and the action are in a state of perishing; the number three arises, while the knowledge of that generality is in the process of arising. Thereafter, the triad arises, while the disjunction and the action perish; the knowledge of the generality of the number three arises, while the qualities of largeness (*mahattva*) and length (*dīrghatva*) are in the process of arising; the relational cognition is in a state of perishing, while the cognition of the quality of the number three is in the process of arising. Then, largeness and length arise, while the relational cognition perishes; the quality of the number three is in a state of perishing, while the cognition of the quality of the number three arises, and the cognition of the substance is in the process of arising. Finally, simultaneous with the cognition of the substance, the number three also perishes.

“In a composite substance produced by two large parts, it is only the largenesses of the causes that initiate largeness, not their plurality, because a greater degree [of size] is observed when the product is initiated by parts of equal number. (PDhS)

He states that "from magnitude, magnitude is produced": "In a composite effect-substance initiated by two or many large [parts], it is the magnitudes residing in the causes alone that initiate magnitude [in the effect]. By "two or many" (*dvibahubhiḥ*) is meant those which are both two and many. By what are they qualified? By being "large. In a composite effect-substance initiated [by them], it is the magnitudes belonging to the causes that initiate magnitude, not their plurality (*bahutva*). Why? Because when an effect is initiated by causes possessing an equal number [of parts], an increase [in size] is observed.

For instance, a single effect may be produced by four gross [atoms], or likewise by four subtle ones. That which is produced by the gross becomes exceedingly large; thus, it is magnitude (*mahattva*) alone that serves as the cause. Since number (*saṃkhyā*) is common to both cases, if it were the cause, there would be no distinction in the magnitude of the result. Furthermore, in cases where two [atoms] act as producers, magnitude alone must be the cause, as multiplicity (*bahutva*) is impossible there.

Others, however, maintain that because number, like dimension, has its causal capacity determined elsewhere through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it must also be a cause here [in the production of magnitude]. As for the observation that a superior quality is seen in one case even when started by [threads] of equal number—this is not intended to negate the causality of number, for that would entail the consequence that dimension (*parimāṇa*) is also not a cause. To explain: just as a superiority of dimension is observed there in comparison to what is started by [threads] of equal number, so too, in comparison to what is started by the coarsest [threads] of equal number, no superiority of that dimension is perceived in what is started by [threads] of the same dimension but unequal number; thus, dimension would also be a non-cause. Furthermore, if this [number] is accepted as a cause because its efficacy is understood through positive and negative concomitance—even though there is no superiority in relation to a larger dimension—then this is the same for number: "when it exists, that [effect] exists; when it is absent, that is absent. If number were not a cause for the production of magnitude here, then in the case where one thing is started by three coarse [threads] and another by four, since the causal dimension is the same in both cases, the resulting dimension should also be the same. But this is not so, because a superiority of dimension is observed in what is started by four. Therefore, number is also a cause. Likewise, it is logical that in a case started by [threads] of equal number and equal dimension, the magnitude is produced by both, because the efficacy of both has been established elsewhere and because they are proximate here. Thus, the dimension of a triad of threads and so on resides in the triad of threads and so on; and in those threads, both that dimension and their number reside in the very same substratum. This constitutes proximity characterized by the co-inherence (*ekārtha-samavāya*) of cause and effect. How then is this statement to be understood: "Only the magnitudes of the causes initiate magnitude, not plurality"? It is for the purpose of negating an exclusive restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). For instance, the claim that "only the magnitudes of the causes initiate magnitude because no superiority is seen in what is started by [threads] of equal number" is incorrect, because plurality also possesses causality according to the reasoning already stated.

Alternatively, this is a demonstration that magnitude (*mahattva*) is a cause [of bulk], based on the observation that no increase [in size] is seen when [two objects] are composed of an equal number [of parts]; it is not a restrictive definition.

“Furthermore, accumulation (*pracaya*), residing in two tufts of cotton, initiates magnitude in the double-tuft (*dvitūlaka*) by depending either on the loose conjunctions of the parts that constitute each tuft, or on the mutual conjunctions of the parts of the two tufts; it does not depend on plurality or [individual] magnitudes, because an increase [in size] is observed when [two objects] are composed of an equal number of parts and an equal weight-measure (*palaparimāṇa*). (PDhS)

He states that accumulation (*pracaya*) is a cause [of magnitude]: "And accumulation, occurring between two tuft-balls, initiates magnitude in the double-tuft (*dvitūlaka*), depending either on the loose conjunctions of the parts that constitute each ball, or on the mutual conjunctions of the parts of the balls. (*)

"Two cotton-clumps" (*tūlapiṇḍau*) refers to two [entities] consisting of a cotton-clump and a cotton-clump. The conjunction existing between them is "accumulation" (*pracaya*). Of what nature is it? It is "dependent upon the loose conjunctions that constitute the clumps. This means it depends upon those things which are both the constituents of the clumps and the loose conjunctions; thus, it is "dependent upon those. Furthermore, it is "dependent upon the mutual conjunctions of the parts of the clumps. The word "or" (*vā*) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), not as an alternative (*vikalpa*), because both [types of dependence] are accepted here as causal factors. That is to say, there is the conjunction of one clump with the parts of the other clump, and likewise the conjunction of the other [clump] with its own parts. Alternatively, it is dependent upon those conjunctions of the parts belonging to each of the two clumps. And this [accumulation] initiates magnitude (*mahattva*) even in a cotton-clump produced from two cotton-fibers. This is the same in the case of three cotton-clumps and so forth. However, proximity (*pratyāsatti*) is greater when it resides in a two-cotton-clump aggregate whose dimension is that of two cotton-clumps, for in such a two-cotton-clump, there is also the conjunction of the two cotton-clumps themselves. In that very case, although plurality and magnitude are present, their status as causes is denied; thus he says: "Neither plurality nor magnitudes" initiate magnitude in a two-cotton-clump and so forth. Why? "Because an excess is observed in that which is produced by [parts] having an equal number, weight, and dimension."

For instance, one [substance] is produced from three cotton-balls weighing five *palas* each, whose constituent parts are in loose conjunction (*praśithilāvayavasaṃyoga*), while another is produced from constituents that are the opposite. In the case of that which is produced by constituents in loose conjunction, an excess of dimension (*parimāṇātiśaya*) is observed; therefore, accumulation (*pracaya*) alone is the cause, not number, weight, or dimension. If those [other factors] were the cause, there would be no distinction between the two cases.

Now, since *pala* (weight) is not a cause of dimension (*parimāṇa*) in all cases, its negation is not tenable where there is no possibility [of its being a cause]. For instance, although there is an excess of *pala* in stones and the like, there is no corresponding excess of dimension; and in the case of lumps of cotton and the like, even in the absence of such [excess of *pala*], an excess [of dimension] is observed. Therefore, because *pala* is merely a specific form of heaviness (*gurutva*), it is not the cause [of dimension]. What is the purpose of its negation in that context? It is for the purpose of negating delusion. Thus, if others, due to delusion, were to maintain that even such *pala* is a cause, that too is not so, because no excess is observed in what is produced by [cotton] of equal *pala*.

Others, however, in order to avoid this very fault, state that the word *pala* is a synonym for the word *samāna*. Thus, "with weights equal in number and equal in measure" means "with those that are equal in number and equal in measure."

Now, is it not improper to maintain that *pracaya* (looseness of conjunction) alone is the cause? For even though plurality (*bahutva*) and magnitude (*mahattva*) have been determined elsewhere to possess causal efficacy, they are here [in this context] proximate. Nor is the observation of a superior degree [of size] in one case—despite being produced from an equal number of *pala*-measurements—proof for negating the causality of plurality and magnitude; for if there were no superiority in relation to something else, it would follow that *pracaya* itself is not a cause. To illustrate: suppose one object is composed of four [atoms] with loose conjunctions of parts, while another is composed of three such [atoms]. Since a superior degree is observed in the object composed of four, number (*saṃkhyā*) is also a cause. Similarly, suppose one object is composed of four large [atoms] with loose conjunctions of parts, while another is composed of those very same [atoms] when they are extremely large. Here, because a superior degree of the effect’s magnitude is perceived through a superior degree of the cause’s magnitude, magnitude (*parimāṇa*) is also a cause. However, where magnitude is produced by things composed of an equal number and magnitude of atoms with loose conjunctions of parts, all three [number, magnitude, and *pracaya*] are causes without distinction, since their efficacy has been established elsewhere and they are proximate here. As for the interpretation of the sentence, it is as explained previously.
“Furthermore, the number two, residing in two atoms, initiates minuteness in the dyad.”

He states the cause for the production of atomicity: "The number two, residing in two atoms, initiates atomicity in the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*). The dimension of the dyad is the effect. Its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) is the dyad itself; therefore, there must be another non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). Since the dimension of the atom has been excluded as a producer, and no other [cause] is possible, it is the number two residing in the two atoms that serves as the non-inherent cause for the production of the dimension of the dyad, by virtue of its inherence in the same object as the effect and the cause. Furthermore, because the word "atom" (*aṇu*) is a general term, it applies to the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*) as well, since it is qualified as "ultimate" (*parama*) while possessing atomicity. The destruction of the number two, however, is to be explained as before.

“Just as largeness arises in a triad and so forth from the plurality of causes, from largeness, and from homogeneous accumulation, so too does length arise. Just as minuteness arises in a dyad from the number two, so too does shortness arise.”

He states the cause for the production of length: “Just as [greatness], length arises from the plurality of causes, greatness, and homogeneous accumulation, as in the case of the triad (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth. For just as greatness arises from the plurality of causes, greatness, and homogeneous accumulation, so too does length. In the triad, length arises solely from the plurality of causes; in the dyad (*dvitantuka*), it arises solely from the length of the cause. In the triad (*tritantuka*) and so forth, length is initiated by plurality, length, and accumulation; such is the meaning of the extended application (*atideśa*). Likewise: “Just as minuteness [in the dyad], shortness arises from the number two. Just as, due to the impossibility of any other cause, the number two is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) for the production of minuteness, so it is for shortness as well.

"Now, what is the mutual distinction between largeness (*mahattva*) and length (*dīrghatva*) as they exist in triads (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth, and between minuteness (*aṇutva*) and shortness (*hrasvatva*) in dyads (*dvyaṇuka*)? In that regard, there is a mutual distinction between largeness and length, because we observe specific linguistic usage such as: 'Let the long be brought from among the large,' and 'Let the large be brought from among the long. However, the mutual distinction between minuteness and shortness is perceptible to those who perceive them."
“Furthermore, these four kinds of dimension, being produced, perish solely through the destruction of their substratum.”

Now, since they are produced from causes of the same genus, one might ask: "What is the mutual distinction between largeness (*mahattva*) and length (*dīrghatva*) residing in triads (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth, and between minuteness (*aṇutva*) and shortness (*hrasvatva*) in dyads (*dvyaṇuka*)? [The opponent argues: "Objects are distinguished by a difference in their causes; therefore, such a distinction does not exist in the case of largeness, length, and so on. This is not so. Since a distinction between largeness and length exists through a difference in their manifestation (*pratibhāsa*), it follows that there must be a difference in the causal complexes (*kāraṇasāmagrī*) that produce them.

For instance, a difference in causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) is known through a difference in their effects. And such a difference certainly exists here due to the difference in appearance; thus he says: "In that case, there is a mutual distinction between largeness (*mahattva*) and length (*dīrghatva*). Why? "Because we observe distinct linguistic conventions, such as 'Let the long one be brought among the large,' and 'Let the large one be brought among the long ones. Otherwise, since there would be no distinction in largeness, there would be no bringing forth of something distinguished by length from among the large, nor of something distinguished by largeness from among the long; yet this is observed. Therefore, length is apprehended as distinct from largeness, and largeness as distinct from length; thus, due to the difference in appearance, they are distinct, just like color-form (*rūpa*) and the other sense-objects.

Furthermore, the property of being produced by the same causes—considering the inherent (*samavāyin*), non-inherent (*asamavāyin*), and instrumental (*nimitta*) causes—is subject to deviation by products of transformation (*vipākaja*); thus, it is not a valid reason for identity. However, if "having the same causes" is understood with respect to the causal totality (*sāmagrī*), this is unproven, because the difference in the causal totality is established by the difference in the effects. Regarding the distinction between atomicity (*aṇutva*) and shortness (*hrasvatva*), [the Sūtra states]: "For those who perceive them, there is a mutual distinction between atomicity and shortness. This is perceived directly by yogins, since they possess the vision of supersensible objects (*atīndriyārtha*). As for the existence of shortness, its status was previously established through figurative usage (*bhāktavyavahāra*); therefore, since it exists, it must necessarily be apprehended by yogins as distinct from other categories. Enough of this.

“Even this fourfold dimension (*parimāṇa*), being produced, perishes solely through the destruction of its substrate. The restriction is intended to exclude other causes [of destruction]. The inclusion of the term “produced” (*utpādya*) is for the purpose of excluding eternal dimensions.

[The Distinctness from Separateness] “Distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) is the cause of the linguistic usage of differentiation (*apoddhāra*). Furthermore, it resides in a single substance and in multiple substances. Its eternality, non-eternality, and production are explained by analogy with number (*saṃkhyā*). <PDhS>

“However, this is the distinction: just as with oneness and so forth, there is an absence of further universals (*aparasāmānya*) in respect to singular separateness (*ekapṛthaktva*) and the like; rather, they are distinguished by number, because we observe linguistic usage qualified by that [number]. (PDhS)

Now, following the order of enumeration, the section beginning with "Distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) is the cause of the linguistic usage of separation" is introduced for the purpose of defining and examining distinctness, which has reached its turn. "Linguistic usage" (*vyavahāra*) means cognition; it is also "usage" in the sense that by means of it one is made known—that is, it is a verbal designation. If it were simply stated that "distinctness is the cause of these two," there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); therefore, the term "separation" (*apoddhāra*) is included. Separation (*apoddhāra*) means extraction or differentiation. Even so, the property of being the cause of the linguistic usage of separation is not excluded from space (*ākāśa*) and the self (*ātman*); therefore, the phrase "while being a qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇatve sati*) must be supplied. Furthermore, the word "substance" (*dravya*) is also [to be supplied] in order to exclude the generality (*sāmānya*) of "distinctness-ness. [The formal argument is: Distinctness is different from other things, because, while being a qualifier of substance, it is the cause of the linguistic usage of separation; whereas that which is not different from others does not possess this property, such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth. Alternatively, the linguistic usage itself may be the probandum (*sādhya*).

Likewise, there is a statement intended for further investigation: the linguistic usage of "extraction" (*apoddhāra*) is indeed a qualified usage; and since that cannot occur without a qualifier, there must be a distinct cause [for it], because it is different from the usage of [qualities] such as color (*rūpa*). Furthermore, this is because one observes the usage "separately" even when color and the other qualities are not perceived.

It should not be argued that the conventional usage "this is distinct from that" will arise from a connection with a *viśeṣa* (particularity), because eternal *viśeṣas* do not exist in impermanent things. If it is then claimed that the connection with an uncommon property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) is the cause for the usage "distinct" regarding impermanent things, that is not so; for such a state of being qualified by that [uncommon property] is not perceived. Indeed, in the conventional usage "distinct," there does not appear any state of being qualified by an uncommon property consisting of substance, form, action, or universal.

As for what was stated—that the qualifier distinct from those [entities] is not "separateness" (*pṛthaktva*), but rather mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*)—if that is the case, then [mutual non-existence] must be the cause. For indeed, the cognitions "this is not this," "this is excluded from that," "distinct," "a different object," and "dissimilar" occur everywhere with that as their sole cause? No; because the linguistic usage "distinct" (as applied to something qualified by numbers such as unity) is a different matter than that [non-existence], since it occurs without a limit in the form of another category (*padārthāntara*). To explain: linguistic usage qualified by mutual non-existence proceeds by taking another category as its limit, but it is not colored by numbers such as unity. Since this [usage "distinct"] is dissimilar to that, it must have a different object as its cause.

Others, however, [assert that] "it produces various cognitions" for the purpose of negating mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*). This is not so. For, since a permanent quality is never perceived in impermanent substances, if that [quality] were destroyed by the destruction of its substrate, there would be no perception of it anywhere at all. Furthermore, if it were impermanent, there would be no cause for the production of a quality that depends on all substances simultaneously, because those [substances] arise sequentially. Moreover, what has arisen as inherent (*samaveta*) in one place cannot become inherent in another, as this is never observed. If a single permanent entity were to reside in many [substances], it would have the nature of a universal (*sāmānya*), such as "substanceness" (*dravyatva*). Nor is a cognition such as "distinctly distinct" ever observed without a limiting term (*avadhi*) referring to a different category of object, in the way that the cognition "this is a substance, this is a substance" occurs. Even in the case of qualities and so forth, a cognition that possesses a limiting term is caused by mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) and is not based on a universal; and it has already been stated that this [cognition of distinctness] is of a different kind.

Now, [the opponent argues that] distinctnesses (*pṛthaktva*), having diverse intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), are distinguished by number. Furthermore, since the production of duality (*dvitva*) and so forth occurs first, and their destruction follows from the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), they cannot persist at the time of dual-distinctness (*dvipṛthaktva*) and the like. Moreover, if dual-distinctness and so forth were produced prior [to duality], they would be destroyed simultaneously with the cognition of the substance; thus, they could not persist at the same time as the production of duality. Consequently, because their causal operation (*vyāpāra*) is untenable at the time of the arising of the cognition of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), duality and the like cannot function as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*).

If it is argued that it is logical for duality and so forth to function as qualifiers because their production in two distinct persons at one and the same time is possible through the mediation of relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), we say no. This is because duality and so forth produced by the cognition of one person cannot be apprehended by another person. And yet, a qualifier must be apprehended; therefore, this objection does not hold, since we accept that what is remembered can serve as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).

For instance, there is one single moment consisting of: the production of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) from its own cause, which produces dual distinctness; the state of being about to arise of the recollection of duality; the state of being about to arise of dual distinctness; then, the arising of the recollection of duality; the arising of dual distinctness; the state of being about to perish of the relative cognition; and the state of being about to arise of the quality-cognition of dual distinctness.

Therefore, considering that the recollection of duality is precisely what generates the cognition of dual distinctness (*dvipṛthaktva*), [the Vaiśeṣikas] maintain that even regarding qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, linguistic usage such as "this is excluded from that" or "this is different" is caused by distinctness; and since qualities and the like are devoid of further qualities (*nirguṇatva*), they consider this [usage] to be merely metaphorical (*upacāra*). Nor is the cognition "distinct" without an object and produced merely by mental impressions (*vāsanā*), because such [unfounded] impressions have already been refuted.

When a doubt arises regarding whether that which is characterized by a characteristic is one or many, he states its classification in order to dispel that doubt: “That, moreover, is either a single substance or multiple substances. That which has a single substance as its substratum is a *ekadravya*; and that which has multiple substances as its substratum—namely, a substance in a state of non-destruction—is a *anekadravya*. Regarding these two types, there is an extended application (*atideśa*): “The eternality, non-eternality, and production of that [separateness] are explained by means of number. For instance, singular separateness (*ekapṛthaktva*) is eternal because it is not produced in eternal things; and in the case of effects, it is preceded by the qualities of the causes and perishes quickly upon the destruction of its substratum—this is the meaning of the extended application. As for dual separateness (*dvipṛthaktva*) and so forth, their production is from relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), like duality and the rest, while their destruction results from the destruction of that [cognition], and in some cases, from the destruction of the substratum. The production of hundredfold separateness (*śatapṛthaktva*) and so forth follows the logic of the production of the number hundred—this is the extended application.

Anticipating the objection that, "In that case, there would be no distinction from the number 'hundred'," he says: "But this much is the distinction: just as with oneness and so forth, there is an absence of any further universal (aparasāmānya) in respect to singular separateness and the like. For just as there exists another universal such as oneness apart from the universal of number (*saṃkhyātva*), there is no such thing for singular separateness and the like.

Now, if it is argued that this [notion of] "concomitant cognition" (*anugatajñāna*) is untenable, we say no; for it is established otherwise. To explain: an uncontradicted concomitant cognition, which has substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*) as its cause, demonstrates the existence of the universal (*sāmānya*). Furthermore, even in the case of distinct entities, a concomitant cognition is possible by virtue of numbers such as unity and so forth; thus he says: "But it is distinguished by number" (*saṃkhyayā tu viśiṣyate*). Why? "Because we observe linguistic usage qualified by that" (*tadviśiṣṭavyavahāradarśanāt*). For example: "this one is distinct," "these two are distinct," "these three are distinct," and so on.
