Now, let there be only one distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) in all substances, just like number, because it is a cognition of a qualifier and thus requires a qualifying [cause]. Nor can any of the [qualities] such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth be its cause, because its conventional usage is different from theirs; therefore, there must be another cause for it.

"The text from here until the end of the section on distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) was originally located in the manuscript within the section on conjunction (*saṃyoga*); however, because it explains the process of producing dual distinctness (*dvipṛthaktva*), this passage appears out of place there. Therefore, although it has been inserted here, it does not fit well due to its displacement from its original location and its corruption in the reading. This must be reconciled by the learned themselves."

Through that action, there arises the cognition of the quality (*guṇabuddhi*); the cognition of the substance (*dravyabuddhi*) is in the process of arising; the memory of duality (*dvitvasmaraṇa*) is in the process of perishing; the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) perishes; the quality of dual separateness (*dvipṛthaktvaguṇa*) is in the process of perishing. Then, from the thought "two separate [things]," there arises the cognition of the substance; the cognition of the quality perishes; the memory of duality perishes; due to the destruction of the relative cognition, the quality perishes; the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is in the process of arising; and then, from that mental impression, the cognition of the substance perishes.

Alternatively, there is the following sequence: first, the arising of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) that produces duality; then the state of duality being produced; then the state of the enumerative cognition that produces dual separateness (*dvipṛthaktva*) being produced; then the arising of the memory of duality; then the state of that cognition [of duality] being produced; then the arising of the enumerative cognition that produces dual separateness; then the state of dual separateness being produced; then the state of the enumerative cognition that produced duality being about to perish; then the arising of dual separateness; then the arising of the cognition of the quality of duality; then, from the quality of duality, from the cognition thereof, and from their inherence in a single substrate (*ekārthasamavāya*), the state of the cognition of the quality of dual separateness being produced; then the destruction of the enumerative cognition; then the state of duality being about to perish; and the state of the enumerative cognition that produced dual separateness being about to perish—this constitutes one moment.

Then, at one and the same time, there occurs the arising of the cognition of the quality of duality-in-separateness (*dvipṛthaktva*), the state of being about to arise of the cognition of the substance, the destruction of the quality of duality, the state of being about to perish of that [substance-cognition], the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) which produced the duality-in-separateness, and the state of being about to perish of the quality of duality-in-separateness.

Then, from that [conjunction], there arises the cognition of two as distinct substances (*dravyabuddhi*), the state of destruction of the cognition of the quality [of duality], the destruction of the quality of dual distinctness (*dvipṛthaktvaguṇa*), and the destruction of the cognition of the quality of duality (*dvitvaguṇabuddhi*). Simultaneously, there is the state of arising of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*). Then, from that impression, there occurs the destruction of the cognition of the substance. However, the distinction here is that the existing quality of duality, acting in conjunction with its own experience, functions toward the production of the cognition of the quality of dual distinctness.

Others, however, maintain that the cognition arises with each individual quality as its object, while the production of duality (*dvitva*) and dual separateness (*dvipṛthaktva*) is occurring. Thus: the production of duality and dual separateness; the state of the cognition of the quality of duality being about to arise; then the production of the cognition of the quality of duality; the state of the cognition of dual separateness being about to arise; the state of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) being about to perish; then the production of the cognition of the quality of dual separateness; the state of the cognition of the substance (*dravyajñāna*) being about to arise; the state of the cognition of the quality of duality being about to perish; the destruction of the relative cognition; the state of duality and dual separateness being about to perish; then the production of the cognition of the substance; the destruction of the cognition of the quality of dual separateness; the destruction of duality and dual separateness; the state of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) being about to arise; and then, from that impression, the destruction of the cognition of the substance. In this process, however, the distinction is that even when the cognition of the substance arises as "two separate [things]" regarding the existing quality of duality, the quality of duality itself functions as an operative factor.

If it is asked: "Since qualifiers are observed only among qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*karman*), and universals (*sāmānya*) that are themselves inherent (*samaveta*), how can duality (*dvitva*) and so forth—which do not reside in dual separateness (*dvipṛthaktva*) and the like—be a qualifier? It has been stated in the *Padārthasaṅkara* that this is due to figurative usage (*upacāra*), because there is a subverting argument (*bādhaka*). Thus says the Sūtra: "Because qualities and actions lack [other] qualities and actions, there is no cognition dependent on qualities and actions" (*Vai. Sū.*). This means that since qualities and actions lack other inherent qualities and actions, there is no primary (*mukhya*) cognition based upon them. [This concludes the discussion of] the dissimilarity of conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

“Conjunction is the cause of the cognition ‘conjoined. It is also the cause of substances, qualities, and actions; for it is said that it functions as such in the production of a substance independently [of other causes], based on the statement ‘from those that were dependent and from those that were independent. However, in the production of qualities and actions, it is dependent [on other causes], based on the statement ‘the specific quality of fire arises from conjunction with that which is inherent [in its substrate].’”

Now, for the purpose of defining and examining conjunction (*saṃyoga*), which has already been mentioned, there begins the section starting with: “Conjunction is the cause of the cognition ‘conjoined’” (*saṃyogaḥ saṃyuktapratyayanimittam*). “Cognition” (*pratyaya*) means knowledge (*jñāna*); alternatively, that by which something is cognized is a “cognition,” namely, a verbal designation (*abhidhāna*). Since all categories (*padārtha*) are causes of both these types of cognition, the term “conjoined” (*saṃyukta*) is employed [to specify]. Nevertheless, since the state of being the cause of the cognition “conjoined” exists in the case of space (*ākāśa*) and the self (*ātman*), the qualification “while possessing the quality of being a specifier” (*viśeṣaṇatve sati*) must be added. Therefore, conjunction is distinguished from other categories because, while being a specifier, it is the cause of the cognition “conjoined”; whereas that which is not distinguished from others—such as non-conjunction (*asaṃyoga*)—is not like this, just as color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth are not. This statement, “Conjunction is the cause of the cognition ‘conjoined’,” is also connected to the purpose of examination (*parīkṣā*).

Now, it might be argued that it is the substance itself, due to its specific production (*viśiṣṭotpāda*), that is the cause for the conventional usage of "conjoined. For instance, when the moment of conjunction arises from the moment of separation, the conventional usage of "conjoined" is observed, and not otherwise. This is incorrect; because if this "specificity" (*viśiṣṭatā*) is not admitted as distinct [from the substance], then, being of the nature of the substance itself, it would be indistinguishable everywhere, and the cognition of "conjoined" would apply to any substance whatsoever. However, if it is distinct, then that very entity by whose existence—distinct from color and so forth—the convention "conjoined" occurs is itself conjunction (*saṃyoga*); thus nothing is contradicted, since conjunction here consists in the state of being joined (*saṃśleṣa*). Nor is this conventional usage caused by mental impressions (*vāsanā*), because such impressions have already been refuted previously.

He states its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*): "And it is the cause of substance, quality, and action" (*sa ca dravyaguṇakarmahetuḥ*). This is the proof for the existence of conjunction (*saṃyoga*). For indeed, there is no production of a cloth without the conjunction of threads, nor of sound without the conjunction of a drum and a stick, nor of the motion of a javelin in the absence of the conjunction of the hand and the javelin; and since this is observed, conjunction must be accepted.

But how is it that this [conjunction] is the initiator of a substance? He says: "It is independent in the production of a substance" (*dravyārambhe nirapekṣaḥ*). Although it depends on causes such as the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) and so forth, it is nevertheless "independent" because it does not depend on subsequent causes. And how is this explained? "It happens thus, and not otherwise. If one asks, "How is this known? [the answer is]: from the statement [of the *Vaiśeṣika-sūtra*], "From those that are dependent and from those that are independent" (VS 4.1.13). This is the meaning of that sūtra: prior to the production of the final conjunction of the threads, the threads, being dependent, do not initiate the cloth. However, since the capacity of those belonging to the same class [of threads] to produce another cloth has been ascertained, they are employed for the sake of bringing about the final conjunction. And once that [final conjunction] has arisen, being independent, they initiate [the cloth] immediately thereafter; thus, conjunction is independent in the production of a substance. For this very reason, there is no other power apart from the final conjunction, because that [power] consists in the nature of the final auxiliary cause (*carama-sahakāri*). This was stated in the section on Earth (*pṛthivī-adhikāra*).

Nor should it be argued that the conventional designation "cloth" arises from the cessation of preceding moments occupying sparse locations and the production of distinct moments occupying dense locations, thereby rendering the postulation of conjunction superfluous; for the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) has been refuted, and the existence of a whole (*avayavin*) distinct from its parts has been established.

“But [the conjunction] is dependent upon the commencement of the qualities and actions,” because it depends on subsequent causes. How is this known? He says: “Because of the statement [in the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra]: ‘From conjunction with that which is conjoined, the specific quality of fire [arises]’ (VS 7.1.9). The meaning of this is as follows: fire is conjoined with an earth atom; there, depending upon the specific quality of fire—namely, the quality of hot touch—the conjunction of the earth atom and fire initiates the qualities produced by baking (*pākaja*). Depending upon the hot touch belonging to fire, it initiates the specific qualities such as color and so forth.

[Objection: But since the hot touch arises after a long time, it does not possess the quality of being posterior; for in the production of a substance, it is indeed accepted that conjunction depends upon previously arisen causal factors—thus, there would be no distinction [between the two cases]. [Reply: No, because [the hot touch] occurs later as qualified by the cessation of blackness and other qualities. Similarly, the conjunction between the hand and the self, depending upon a subsequent effort, initiates action in the hand.

[Objection: Even so, for the production of cognition and other mental states, there is no subsequent cause for the conjunction of the self and the mind; if you say it is the connection with the body, we say no, because its posteriority is untenable. Although there is no cognition despite the existence of the connection between the self and the mind during the state of dissolution, cognition does occur when there is a connection with the body. Nevertheless, since the connection with the mind is admitted to be simultaneous with the connection of the semen and blood [at conception], the previous conjunction must necessarily have ceased; thus, the connection with the body is not subsequent to that [conjunction]. Furthermore, even when the body is fully formed, the connection of the mind occurs through the medium of its own activity, and the same applies to the body; therefore, there is no evidence for a temporal sequence of priority and posteriority between them.

Nor is it the case that the connection between the self and the mind (*ātmamanaḥ-sambandha*) is entirely independent [of other factors], because its instrumental causes—such as pleasure, pain, and so forth—exist at a time subsequent to it. To illustrate: in the production of desire, the connection between the self and the mind has pleasure or memory as its antecedent conditions (*apekṣākāraṇa*), since these occur prior to it; likewise, in the production of aversion and the like, the causality of pain and so forth should be inferred. However, while the necessity of the body’s connection occurring subsequently is denied, its status as a cause is not. Similarly, in the production of action (*karman*), it is not possible for conjunction (*saṃyoga*) to be an instrumental cause that always occurs last. For instance, in the case of a branch or similar object, downward motion occurs due to gravity (*gurutva*) dependent on contact with a stone or other weight above it; and in the current of a river, the movement of grass and water occurs due to fluidity (*dravatva*) dependent on contact with the grass and water. Thus, in these cases, gravity and fluidity do indeed exist as antecedent conditions.

If that is so, then is the statement “it is dependent upon the commencement of a quality or an action” incorrect? No; for we do not accept an exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*). Thus, it is only at the commencement of a quality or an action that [the substance] is dependent, and not that it is *necessarily* dependent, since its independence is also observed.

(“Now, what are its characteristics and how many kinds are there? Conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the reaching together of two things that were previously unjoined. It is of three types: produced by the action of one, produced by the action of both, and produced by conjunction. Among these, that produced by the action of one is the [conjunction] of a thing possessing motion with a thing lacking motion, as in the case of a post with a hawk, or of all-pervading entities with corporeal objects. That produced by the action of both is the meeting of two things moving in opposite directions, as in the case of two wrestlers or two rams. Conjunction produced by conjunction, however, is a conjunction occurring between an effect and a non-effect, preceded by a conjunction between a cause and a non-cause; it belongs to a thing that has just arisen or has arisen long ago and is currently devoid of motion, and it occurs through the conjunctions of the causes with the non-causes. This arises from one, from two, or from many. First, from one: from the conjunction of a thread and a *vīraṇa* grass, there arises the conjunction of a two-threaded cloth with the *vīraṇa*. From two: from two conjunctions of a thread and space, there arises one conjunction of a two-threaded cloth and space. From many: from many conjunctions of threads and a shuttle, there arises one conjunction of a cloth and a shuttle.”)

“If [the question] ‘What are its characteristics and how many kinds does it have? is redundant because the characteristic has already been determined, [we reply: no, for this [question] is justified by the desire to state another characteristic. Even though the characteristic of the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) was stated previously, the doubt still remains: ‘What is its characteristic in its own right? Others hold that this sentence is intended solely for the purpose of examination. Alternatively, they think that this [objection] is mistaken, [asking] ‘What are its characteristics?’, for they believe that a characteristic of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is simply not possible.”

The question "Of how many kinds? is asked for the purpose of distinguishing its varieties. Regarding that, he states the definition: "Conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the reaching together of two things not previously reached. The term "not previously reached" is used because reaching (*prāpti*) can also mean inherence (*samavāya*). Furthermore, it is indeed accepted that a synonymous term may serve as a definition. And since this [conjunction] is perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the definition of conjunction is not subject to the fallacy of having an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatva*) due to the non-existence of conjunction.

“The [conjunction] is of three kinds,” this presentation of its divisions is for the purpose of avoiding the charge that the general definition is impossible. In what form does it have three kinds? He says: “It is produced by the action of one, produced by the action of both, and produced by conjunction. Regarding the term *saṃyoga* (conjunction): among these, that which arises from an action in one [of two things] is "produced by the action of one" (*anyatarakarmaja*). The two examples, “as that of a post with a hawk” and “and of pervasive entities with corporeal ones,” are given with the intention of expressing internal distinctions. For instance, the conjunction between a hawk and a post is produced by both action and [another] conjunction; however, the conjunction of pervasive entities with atoms is produced by action alone. Although there is no difference in the operation between conjunction and action, the designation is made by means of "action" alone for the sake of inclusion, so that it may be understood that the state of being produced by the action of one exists in both cases.

[Objection: In that case, one should say that [disjunction] is produced by conjunction (*saṃyogaja*) and produced by action (*karmaja*), since the others are merely specific instances of those two. [Reply: True. Nevertheless, the mention of "either one" (*anyatara*) and so forth is for the purpose of an exhaustive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*)—to show that there are only these many varieties of that which is produced by action—and it does not aim at negating that conjunction is a cause. Accordingly, from the conjunction of a hawk’s foot with [the ground], depending upon effort, the motion of the foot arises; disjunction is in the process of arising; in the hawk (the whole), motion is in the process of arising from its own cause; then, the disjunction of the hawk’s foot [from the ground] arises; the previous conjunction is in the process of perishing; in the hawk (the whole), motion also arises; disjunction is in the process of arising; then, the conjunction of the hawk’s foot [with the ground] is destroyed; the subsequent conjunction is in the process of arising; the disjunction of the hawk (the whole) [from the ground] arises; and by the motion of the hawk (the whole), a conjunction of the hawk with a post is produced, because both [motions] are determined to have causal capacity given their proximity. Therefore, the hawk and the post are the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*); the motion of the hawk and the conjunction of its foot with the post are the non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). As for proximity (*pratyāsatti*), it is possible even when the hawk’s foot-conjunction is large; we shall explain later that there is no specific reason [to prefer one over the other] when either one is excluded.

That produced by the action of both [substances] is born from the actions of both, as in the case of "two wrestlers" or "two rams. Here too, if one admits that the action of the whole occurs simultaneously with the disjunctions resulting from the actions of the parts, then it must be considered how conjunction is produced both by the conjunctions [of the parts] and by the actions of the wholes. For just as the action of a part produces a conjunction with another part, so too does it produce a conjunction with its own whole; and likewise, the action of the other part produces a conjunction with its own whole, just as it produces a conjunction with the other part—thus there is a triad of conjunctions. And since proximity exists, these are determined to be the cause by virtue of their efficacy. In the case of two rams, they possess the status of inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*). [In this very context, the reading concerning the process of producing double separateness was present in the manuscript. Indeed, in the cognition of conjunction, the conjunction of the parts and the whole—which serves as the qualifier—is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), while the remainder is the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). Furthermore, the state of being produced solely by the action of both should be understood as applying to the conjunction of two atoms.

Others, however, maintain that because the two terms [of the compound] have their case-endings elided and are connected with both the preceding and the following words, the distinction of conjunction produced by action (*karmaja*) will indeed be included. For instance, since both are perceived as causes of conjunction, when action is mentioned by its own name, one of the two conjunctions is necessarily obtained. "The other" and "action" constitute "the other-action" (*anyatarakarma*); that which is born from these two is "born from the other-action" (*anyatarakarmaja*). And that [conjunction] is produced by one action having conjoined with a second; and conjunction is produced by two things together with a second. Likewise, "both" refers to that which is produced by action alone, being generated by either one action or by two. Regarding "produced by conjunction" (*saṃyogaja*), it refers to both cases: that of something just arisen or that of something arisen after a long time. He states its definition as "of that which is devoid of action" (*akriyasya*), and so forth.

This is the rule regarding that which is devoid of action (*akriya*). With what [entities] does it occur? He says: "with non-causes" (*akāraṇaiḥ*). Of what kind are they? "Those conjoined with causes" (*kāraṇasaṃyogibhiḥ*). Those things which possess conjunctions with a cause are so described; the conjunction of that which is devoid of action with those non-causes conjoined with causes is "conjunction-born" (*saṃyogaja*), because there is no other cause for it.

He provides an explanation for the summary statement: "A conjunction residing in an effect and a non-effect, preceded by a conjunction between a cause and a non-cause. Here, "cause" refers to the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*); anything other than that, in relation to its own effect, is a "non-cause. A conjunction residing in an effect and a non-effect is one that is preceded by the conjunction of those two. That is to say, it is a conjunction produced from the conjunction between the effect of the relevant cause and another thing which is a non-effect. Among these, an example of that which has arisen after a long duration will be stated on the occasion of the discussion of disjunction produced by disjunction; therefore, he states an example of that which has just arisen by way of disjunction: "And that [arises] from one," and so forth. "And that" refers to the conjunction produced by conjunction. "[From] one, from two, and from many"—by the word "and" (*ca*), the disjunction [produced] from one into two is indicated.

“First, from the conjunction of one thread with a *vīraṇa* grass stalk, there arises the conjunction of two-thread [cloth] with the *vīraṇa* grass stalk. For instance, when a thread already conjoined with a *vīraṇa* grass stalk becomes connected with another thread, a two-thread [cloth] is produced. And since its conjunction with the *vīraṇa* grass stalk is produced at the same time as the production of its color and other qualities, an inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) must be sought for that production. Now, motion is not possible here, because both [the thread and the *vīraṇa*] are devoid of motion, and because it is established that color and the other qualities possess causal efficacy only toward the production of their own effects. Furthermore, since the production of a real effect is never observed without an inherent cause, the conjunction of the thread and the *vīraṇa* itself—being of the same class and being proximate—is the inherent cause. Regarding this proximity, some hold that it consists of both forms: inherence in the same object as the effect and inherence in the same object as the cause; however, only inherence in the same object as the effect is taken here because of the lack of intervention by the cause. But others maintain that where the qualities residing in the causes themselves initiate the qualities in the effect, only that [proximity] is to be accepted.

Nor does the fact that a single entity is a producer contradict the aphorism, "Qualities produce another quality" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra...), because there is a restriction that only those functions residing in causes produce effects of the same genus. For it is a rule that those functions residing in causes which produce only what is of the same genus do so only when they are possessed of the number of plurality (*anekatva*). Thus, in this way, the two threads and the *vīraṇa* grass are the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*), the conjunction of the thread and the *vīraṇa* is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and the remainder is the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).

The production of the conjunction of a two-thread [object] with *vīraṇa* grass is as follows: "From two conjunctions of a single thread with space, one conjunction of the two-thread [object] with space arises. (**) When a thread already connected to space becomes further connected with another thread, the two-thread [object] is produced. Furthermore, the action of the thread produces a conjunction not only with the other thread but also with the spatial location, because there is no obstructing factor. Once the two-thread [object] has been produced, a conjunction with space indeed occurs simultaneously with the production of its color and other qualities. If one asks what the proof for this is, it is inference.

For instance, a double-threaded cloth (*dvitantuka*) conjoins with that which is conjoined to its own cause, because it is an effect whose cause is conjoined [to that], like a *vīraṇa* grass stalk conjoined with a double-threaded cloth. Or, space conjoins with the effect of that which is conjoined to its own cause, because it is conjoined to that cause, like a *vīraṇa* stalk conjoined with a double-threaded cloth. Once conjunction is established, since it is an effect, its originating cause must be considered. In this case, since the double-threaded cloth and space possess inherent causality (*samavāyikāraṇatva*), there must be another non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). Now, since action cannot occur in the double-threaded cloth at the same time as the production of color and so forth, and given that the conjunctions of the thread and space belong to the same genus and are proximate, they constitute the non-inherent cause. As for proximity, it may take either of two forms; thus, it should be understood as previously explained.

“From many conjunctions of threads and the shuttle, there is one conjunction of the cloth and the shuttle. When the threads are in conjunction with the shuttle, the cloth arises immediately after the final conjunction of the threads. Its conjunction with the shuttle is perceived at the same time as the arising of that cloth and so forth; thus, the cause of its production must be stated. In this case, since no other non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) is observed, the threads and the shuttle possess the status of inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*), while the conjunctions of the threads and the shuttle possess the status of non-inherent causes. The proximity (*pratyāsatti*), however, is to be explained as before.

But is this not improper? For threads are not the cause of the production of a cloth. Furthermore, a conjunction residing in an effect and a non-effect, preceded by a conjunction between a cause and a non-cause, is called "conjunction-produced" (*saṃyogaja*). Thus, when a thread is connected with another thread, a two-threaded [dyad] is produced; then, upon connection with yet another thread, another effect [a triad] is produced. Since the production of the cloth occurs through the intervention of these multiple effects, how can the threads be the cause of the cloth's production? No, for if that which has already begun an effect were to become a producer again upon reaching other auxiliary causes, there would be the doctrine of "production of what is already begun" (*ārabhyārambhakavāda*). And in that case, there would be the co-location of corporeal things in the same or different places. To explain: that which is begun by two threads exists in those two threads; then that which is begun by those two together with another exists in them and in that [other]; and so it should be understood for each subsequent stage.

Furthermore, if [the cloth] were to exist in only one [thread] while being commenced by two [threads] joined with others, there would be the consequence of its subsisting in a single substance (*ekadravyavṛttitva*). Moreover, the cognition "the cloth is here in these threads" would not occur. Upon the destruction of those [threads], there would be no perception of the intermediate product; and the remaining refutations of the theory of "commencement by what has already been commenced" (*ārabhyārambhakavāda*) should be understood from the section on Earth (*pṛthivī*). Therefore, through the destruction of the intermediate product by means of the action of the parts resulting from the connection with space and so forth, the threads—whose conjunctions remain stable during the time of contact with other threads—again commence another effect. This is the logical process until the production of the cloth from the conjunction of the final threads.

Nor is the production of the intermediate effect (avāntarakārya) purposeless, for without it the intended final effect cannot arise. Just as the attainment of a specific destination is not accomplished without the attainment of intermediate stations—even though those stations are not the ultimate cause—their existence is nonetheless accepted; likewise, since the intended effect is not accomplished without the intermediate effect, its existence must be admitted. However, its status as a direct cause is denied, because the final effect arises even when that intermediate effect has ceased. This suffices.

“And how does the production of two [substances] from one [cause] occur? When there is a conjunction between an earth atom and a water atom, and simultaneously another conjunction occurs—of the earth atom with another earth atom and of the water atom with another water atom—then, by means of those two conjunctions, two dyads (dvyaṇuka), one of earth and one of water, are produced simultaneously. Then, at the very same time that color and other qualities are produced in the two dyads according to the sequence beginning with the qualities of the causes, two conjunctions are produced simultaneously: [one] residing in the respective cause and non-cause [of each dyad], and [the other] residing in the respective effect and non-effect [of each dyad]. What is the reason? For it is a logical rule that an effect must necessarily be conjoined with a non-cause that is conjoined with its own cause. Therefore, the earth dyad is connected with the water atom which is conjoined with its own cause; and the water dyad is likewise connected with the earth atom which is conjoined with its own cause. Now, how is there a mutual connection between the two dyads which are already connected to their respective causes and non-causes? Their connection also occurs through two conjunctions born of conjunction.”

Now, he explains how two conjunctions arise from a single conjunction: "When there is a conjunction between two atoms—one earthy and one watery—and simultaneously a second conjunction occurs, namely, of the earthy atom with another earthy atom and of the watery atom with another watery atom, then, due to the connection of those two [atoms] with substances of their own kind, two dyads (dvyaṇuka) consisting of earthy and watery [matter] are produced simultaneously. Immediately after the production of the dyads, at the very same moment when color and other qualities arise in the two dyads according to the principle that the qualities of the cause precede [the qualities of the effect], "simultaneously two conjunctions arise in the respective effects and non-effects, originating from the conjunction existing in the respective causes and non-causes. One atom is the cause of its own effect; the other is the non-cause in relation to it. The same applies to the other case as well. "Originating from the conjunction existing in them" means originating from the conjunction inherent in them. "In the respective effects and non-effects": the other earthy dyad is the effect of its own cause, while the other watery atom is the non-effect; likewise, the other watery dyad is the effect, while the other earthy atom is the non-effect. Two such conjunctions arising in those [two dyads] are produced simultaneously. And since the dyads and atoms possess the status of inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*), another [type of] non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) must be considered. Furthermore, no action is possible here because both [atoms] are devoid of action; therefore, the conjunction of the atoms is the cause, as its causal efficiency is determined by their state of proximity.

Now, as for the conjunction of an earth-dyad with a water-atom, and likewise that of a water-atom with an earth-atom—what is the reason, what is the proof? He states: "The logical principle (*nyāya*) is that an effect must necessarily conjoin with a non-cause that is conjoined with its own cause. This is the proof. For instance, an earth-dyad conjoins with that which is conjoined with its own cause, because it is an effect whose cause is conjoined with that [other cause], like a cloth produced from two threads conjoined with *vīraṇa* grass. Or, a water-atom conjoins with an effect whose cause is conjoined with itself, because it is conjoined with the cause of that [effect], like *vīraṇa* grass conjoined with a cloth produced from two threads. The same should be stated for the other case as well. Since this is so, therefore an earth-dyad is connected with a water-atom conjoined with its own cause, and a water-dyad also [is connected] with an earth [atom].

“Now, regarding the two dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) which are connected through the cause of one and the non-cause of the other” (*iti*). The cause of the one earth-dyad is the non-cause of the other; likewise, the cause of the water-dyad is the non-cause of the other earth-dyad. He explains how there is a connection between those two dyads, which are thus related, by stating: “There is a connection between them also through two conjunctions produced by conjunction” (*iti*). Those two conjunctions residing in the effect and the non-effect, which are produced from a single [original] conjunction—through these two [is the connection]. The two dyads possess the status of inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*), while the conjunctions of the effect and the non-effect possess the status of non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). As for proximity (*pratyāsatti*), it should be understood as before, since it can exist in both forms. And the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth are the efficient causes (*nimittakāraṇa*).

Nor should it be argued that, at the very moment the color and other qualities are produced, a conjunction will arise for the dyad with another atom that is conjoined to its own cause, or even with another dyad, solely from the conjunction of the cause with the non-cause; for at that time, the dyad lacks the state of being conjoined to a cause. Furthermore, a conjunction produced by a conjunction (saṃyogaja) is defined as the conjunction [of one thing] with something that is conjoined to its cause but is not its effect. Therefore, it must first be stated that there is a conjunction of the aqueous dyad with the earth atom, and of the earth atom with the aqueous [atom], so that through their being conjoined to causes, a conjunction produced by conjunction may also occur between the two dyads.

“Non-produced conjunction does not exist, because it is not mentioned separately, like eternal spherical dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*). For instance, after stating that the four kinds of dimension are produced, [the author] says, ‘Eternal is spherical dimension’; similarly, after stating that conjunctions such as those produced by the action of one [of two things] are produced, he would have stated separately that [non-produced conjunction] is eternal, but he did not say so. Therefore, non-produced conjunction does not exist. Conjunction of ether and the other [all-pervading substances] with atoms occurs in their respective locations and is produced by the action of one [of the two]. However, there is no mutual conjunction among the all-pervading substances (*vibhu*) because they lack separable establishment (*yutasiddhi*). This [separable establishment], moreover, consists in the possession of separate motion by both or either one of the two, and inherence in separate substrata.”

Now, having raised the objection that there is an omission [in the *Vibhāga-sūtra*] because it does not mention "non-produced conjunction" (*ajasaṃyoga*), he states the following for the sake of refutation: "There is no non-produced conjunction, because it is not mentioned separately, like eternal spherical dimension (*nityapārimāṇḍalya*). Just as the Blessed Sage, who perceives all objects, having stated that "fourfold dimension is produced," said, "spherical dimension is eternal," meaning that the dimension of the atom exists; so too, having stated the threefold conjunction—namely, that produced by the action of one [of two things] and so forth—as something produced, he would have mentioned "eternal conjunction" separately had it existed. But he did not say this; therefore, there is no non-produced conjunction. Furthermore, it was promised by the Great Sage that he would explain everything that exists in the form of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*).

[Objection: But surely, in this thesis-statement that "there is no unborn conjunction," there is a contradiction between the words, just as in the case of saying "this does not exist" while simultaneously asserting its existence. [Reply: No, because the thesis is stated otherwise. To explain: the opponent has accepted that the conjunction of space and so forth with atoms is eternal; it is only the *unborn* (aja) nature of that conjunction which is denied here, not its existence. The conjunction of space and so forth with atoms is not unborn, because the Great Sage, the Omniscient One, does not teach it separately as being unborn. And whatever is unborn is taught separately as such, for example: "the spherical dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*) is eternal."

Now, if it is argued that conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the opposite of non-attainment (*aprāpti*), that is simply not possible; for since space (*ākāśa*) and the like are all-pervading (*vibhu*), it is impossible for them to abandon their location. Nor can there be destruction here through the destruction of a substratum (*āśraya*), because the substratum itself is eternal. And since there is no other cause of destruction, [space] must be unproduced (*ajanya*). Furthermore, the failure to mention [conjunction] could arise from mere delusion, and thus the argument is otherwise established. To refute this, he says: "The conjunction of space and so forth with atoms, which occurs in specific locations (*pradeśavṛtti*), is produced by the action of one of the two. If it is asked: "How can conjunctions and disjunctions of an atom occur without abandoning space? [The answer is: It is just as Devadatta [experiences them] without abandoning a tree. For instance, when a person ascends from the base part to the upper part of a tree, conjunctions and disjunctions are perceived precisely without abandoning the tree—such as "he is conjoined with the tree at the base," "at the middle," and "at the top. Nor are those conjunctions of the [mere] location itself, because the cognition "conjoined with the tree" is what is actually experienced. If the conjunction were only with the location, the knowledge would have been "conjoined with the location, not with the tree. But this is not the case, since the cognition "conjoined with the tree" is perceived in every state.

Furthermore, if it is argued that because conjunction (*saṃyoga*) subsists in parts (*pradeśavṛttitva*), the conjunction occurs only with the parts and not with the tree as a whole, then those parts themselves are wholes (*avayavin*) in relation to their own constituent parts; thus, there would be a conjunction of their parts, and since they too are wholes, there would be a conjunction of their parts, and so on, until one reaches partless atoms (*paramāṇu*). Since these atoms lack parts, there can be no conjunction, and consequently, the production of effects through the sequence beginning with dyads (*dvyaṇuka*)—such as earth and other elements—is impossible.

Now, even if atoms are partless (*niṣpradeśatva*), if conjunction is still accepted because they possess spatial divisions (*pradeśatva*), then the objection remains exactly as it was: that in the absence of conjunction between dyads (*dvyaṇuka*), the triad (*tryaṇuka*) could not exist. Furthermore, a conjunction residing in atoms does not initiate a substance inherent in dyads and so forth, because if that which resides in a different locus were to be a producer, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, since conjunction has the property of residing in spatial divisions—that is, it does not pervade its entire substratum—conjunction with both parts (*avayava*) and the whole (*avayavin*) is indeed logically possible.

Furthermore, since it is impossible for a subsequent conjunction to occur while the prior conjunction with the tree remains at the root-position, disjunction—which destroys that [prior conjunction]—is also established. Just as in this case, even without abandoning the tree, conjunctions and disjunctions produced by the action of either one (the man) occur, so too, even without abandoning space, conjunctions and disjunctions will occur for the atom; thus, its all-pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) is not a limiting factor.

Thus, since causes for the production and destruction of the conjunction of atoms, space, and so forth are established, their partlessness (*aja-tva*) is not tenable. As for the claim that the author of the Sūtras might have remained silent due to delusion, that is incorrect; for the categories (*padārtha*) taught by him are perceived to exist exactly as described even through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and once correct knowledge is established, false knowledge—which is its opposite—is necessarily eliminated.

Now, [the opponent might argue] that there will be mutual conjunction among all-pervading entities (*vibhu*). For instance, space is conjoined with the self and so forth, because it possesses conjunction with corporeal things, like a jar. To refute this, [the author] says: "But there is no mutual conjunction among all-pervading entities, due to the absence of separate existence (*yutasiddhi*). Wherever there is conjunction, there separate existence is observed. And since that [separate existence] is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of conjunction, when it is absent, it excludes conjunction which is pervaded by it; thus, the probans [of the opponent] is otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*).

“Furthermore,” that *yutasiddhi* (separate existence) consists in “the possession of separate motion by both or by either one, and inherence in separate substrata. Possession of separate motion by both or by either one constitutes the *yutasiddhi* of eternal things. Inherence in separate substrata by both or by either one constitutes the *yutasiddhi* of non-eternal things. A detailed examination of this should be seen on the occasion of the discussion of disjunction (*vibhāga*). Moreover, the possession of separate motion is not possible for all-pervading (*vibhu*) entities because they are incorporeal; nor is inherence in separate substrata possible for them, because they are not effects.
{The manner in which conjunction is destroyed}:

“The destruction of every conjunction, however, results from disjunction inhering in the same object [as the conjunction], and in some cases also from the destruction of its substratum. How so? When, while there is a conjunction between two threads, an action arises in a constituent part (*aṃśu*) that initiates one of those threads, by that action a disjunction is produced from the other part; from that disjunction follows the destruction of the conjunction that initiated the thread; from the destruction of that conjunction follows the destruction of the thread; and upon its destruction, the conjunction with the other thread—which was dependent upon it—is also destroyed. <PDhS>

Since destruction has a cause, from what does the destruction of conjunction arise? He says: "The destruction of every conjunction, however, results from disjunction inhering in the same object" (*). The destruction of a conjunction occurs through the disjunction of those very two things that were conjoined, because while that [conjunction] exists, it is not perceived. [In this context, the commentary on the *Praśastapādabhāṣya* beginning with "In some cases, also from the destruction of the substratum" and ending with "the destruction of the conjunction that initiates the thread" is not seen; therefore, it is inferred that the text has been lost. From the destruction of the conjunction [comes the destruction of the thread]; when the thread is destroyed, the conjunction [with another thread] that was dependent upon it is destroyed. When action is possible in the other thread at the same time as the destruction of the conjunction of the threads, then it should be understood that the destruction of the conjunction occurs through both the destruction of the substratum and disjunction.
{The dissimilarity with disjunction}:
“Disjunction is the cause of the cognition of separation and the cause of the disjunction of sound.”

Now follows the section beginning with “Disjunction (*vibhāga*) is the cause of the cognition of separation,” for the purpose of examining the definition of disjunction. *Pratīti*, *pratyaya*, and *jñāna* are synonymous; that by which something is cognized is a *pratyaya*, namely, a designation (*abhidhāna*). Since other things might also be causes of such [cognition], the term “separated” (*vibhakta*) is included. Nevertheless, in order to avoid over-extension (*vyabhicāra*) to space (*ākāśa*) and the Self (*ātman*), it should be understood that the qualification “while being a qualifier of a substance” (*dravyaviśeṣaṇatve sati*) applies. Thus: disjunction is distinct from other categories because, while being a qualifier of a substance, it is the cause of the cognition of separation; whereas that which is not distinct does not possess this property, as in the case of color (*rūpa*) and so forth. Furthermore, the statement intended for examination is that the cognition of separation cannot arise without a qualified object (*viśeṣya*) unless there is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Nor can this cognition originate from mental impressions (*vāsanā*), since such impressions have already been refuted. Moreover, the production [of entities] in spatially separated locations has already been refuted by the very refutation of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).

If it is argued that there is no separate entity called disjunction (*vibhāga*) because the conventional usage of "separated" occurs simply upon the non-arising or the destruction of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), we say no; for without disjunction, the very destruction of conjunction would be impossible. To explain: since the destruction of qualities (*guṇa*) is observed to result from the destruction of their substratum or from the appearance of a contrary quality, in a case where the substratum is destroyed, there could be no cognition of being "separated" as long as the conjunction has not been destroyed. Yet, the destruction of conjunction is indeed observed. Since action (*karman*) is seen to lack the capacity to destroy a quality, and since there is no other cause for destruction, disjunction must be admitted. Furthermore, the cognition of being "separated" would, in the absence of conjunction, be merely figurative.

He states its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*): "And it is the cause of the division of sound" (*śabdavibhāgahetuśca*). We shall explain that sound arises from the division of bamboo slivers, and from that division, another division arises.
It should be understood that the phrase "of what characteristics and of how many kinds? is to be connected here as well, because the resolution is the same as before.

“Disjunction (*vibhāga*) is non-attainment preceded by attainment. It is of three kinds: disjunction produced by the action of one [of two things], produced by the action of both, and disjunction produced by [another] disjunction. Among these, those produced by the action of one or both are like conjunction (*saṃyoga*). However, disjunction produced by [another] disjunction is of two types: from the disjunction of the cause and from the disjunction of the cause and the non-cause. He states the definition: “Disjunction is non-attainment preceded by attainment. Attainment is conjunction; that which has this as its antecedent is "preceded by that. Non-attainment is disjunction. Mere non-arising of conjunction is not non-attainment, nor is it preceded by attainment.

Now, since non-attainment (*aprāpti*) occurs prior to [the effect], is it a cause, or does it exist only when [the effect] exists? Some maintain that it merely exists when [the effect] exists, but is not a cause. However, we do not understand this. For, just like action (*kriyā*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is observed to have an operation in the production of disjunction (*vibhāga*) through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Indeed, disjunction does not occur in the absence of conjunction associated with action, but it does occur when that [conjunction] is present. Furthermore, there is no subverting argument against conjunction being the cause of disjunction based on its positive and negative concomitance, out of fear of which one might claim it is not a cause. Moreover, it is accepted that qualities are opposed to their own effects, as seen in the case of sound and so forth. And since conjunction is proximate to the production of disjunction, it is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*). The objection and its resolution regarding non-attainment being the definition of disjunction are the same as those concerning conjunction.

“And that [disjunction] is of three kinds: disjunction produced by the action of one [of two objects], disjunction produced by the action of both, and disjunction produced by [another] disjunction. Regarding this, “the disjunctions produced by the action of one or by the action of both are like conjunctions. By this, it is meant that disjunction is generated by action and by disjunction, as in the case of a hawk and a post. For here, when the hawk’s constituent parts are in proximity to the post, an operation is possible through the consideration of action at the same time as the disjunction of its feet from the post; this is what must be reflected upon. Furthermore, in the case of all-pervading substances and corporeal objects, disjunction is produced by the action of only one. Likewise, disjunction is generated by two actions and by disjunctions, as in the case of two wrestlers or two rams. For just as an action produced on the head of one ram effects a disjunction from the other head, so too does it effect a disjunction from its own constituent parts; thus, the triad of disjunctions between parts and the whole is determined to be the cause for the production of the disjunction of the whole, provided there is proximity. Similarly, disjunction is generated by two things devoid of disjunction, as in the case of two atoms; such is the meaning of the extended application (*atideśa*).

Now, that which is produced by disjunction (*vibhāgaja*) is explained. He states that this is of two kinds due to the difference in its causes: "from the disjunction of the cause, and from the disjunction of the cause and the non-cause" (*kāraṇavibhāgāt kāraṇākāraṇavibhāgācca*). [Objection: Since it is observed that even from multiple causes a single effect is produced, it is not logical for there to be a distinction [in the effect] based on the distinction of the causes. [Reply: That is not so, because what is intended is the distinction between the causal complexes (*sāmagrī*). For one complex is characterized by the disjunction of the cause, while the other is characterized by the disjunction of the cause and the non-cause. And because of that distinction in the complexes, a distinction in the disjunction is indeed established; for we observe a distinction in effects such as a jar based on a distinction in their causal complexes, and because they possess contradictory attributes (*viruddhadharma*) and are objects of distinct appearances. To explain: a disjunction preceded by the disjunction of the cause belongs only to that which possesses motion (*sakriya*), whereas a disjunction preceded by the disjunction of the cause and the non-cause belongs only to that which is devoid of motion (*niṣkriya*). Likewise, there is a difference in properties (*dharmabheda*): a disjunction preceded by the disjunction of the cause initiates sound, whereas a disjunction preceded by the disjunction of the cause and the non-cause initiates only another disjunction. Since a distinction is perceived elsewhere due to that difference [of causes], a distinction must necessarily exist here as well.

“In that regard, first, due to the division of the cause: when action arises in a cause occupied by an effect and it effects a division from another part of that [cause], it does not at that time effect a division from a location such as space; but when it effects a division from a location such as space, it does not at that time effect a division from another part—this is the established rule.”

“Therefore, the action of a part initiates disjunction from another part; from that disjunction follows the destruction of the conjunction that originates the substance. When that [conjunction] has perished, due to the absence of its cause, there is the absence of its effect—namely, the destruction of the whole. At that time, the disjunction residing in the two causes, depending on the time characterized by the destruction of the effect or on the independent part itself, initiates the disjunction of the active part alone from the space or other location conjoined with the effect. It does not belong to the inactive part, because of the absence of a cause; for if a subsequent conjunction were not produced, there would be the undesirable consequence of its being unusable.”

“However, the action of that [substance] does not produce disjunction from a location such as space, because the time for its origination has already passed; yet it certainly produces conjunction with another location, since there is no lapse of time for an action that has not yet produced conjunction. <PDhS>

He states the disjunction [resulting] from the disjunction of the cause with the words beginning with “in that which is occupied by the effect” (*kāryāviṣṭe*). This means in that which is occupied—that is, pervaded—by the effect, i.e., in that which has begun its causal activity; [therein] “an action arises in the cause,” not merely in the cause in general. When it “produces a disjunction from another part” (*avayavāntarād vibhāgam*), which is opposed to the conjunction that initiates the substance, “then it does not [produce it] from a location such as space” (*na tadā ākāśādideśāt*). But “when [it produces it] from a location such as space, then it does not [produce] a specific disjunction from another part. “Stability” (*sthitiḥ*) refers either to the state of affairs or to the thesis regarding the investigation of disjunction produced by disjunction.

Is it not the case that all this is improper, since the establishment of a contrary meaning is supported by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? To explain: a specific action of a cause initiates a disjunction from a point of space at the same time that it initiates a disjunction from another part, because it is an action of a part; whatever is an action of a part initiates a disjunction from a point of space at the same time that it initiates a disjunction from another part, just like the action of a petal of a lotus; and this [action under discussion] is such an action; therefore, the probandum is as stated. Likewise, specific parts are disjoined from a point of space at the same time that they initiate a disjunction from another part, because they are parts, like a lotus petal. Furthermore, the disjunction of a part also arises simultaneously with the disjunction from a point of space, because it is a disjunction of a part, like the disjunction of a lotus petal. Other cases may be inferred in the same way. And there is no sublation here, as the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and other criteria are perceived.

This is incorrect, because a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) is established. To explain: wherever an action is observed to produce two disjunctions, there are invariably present the following pervading properties (*vyāpaka-dharma*): the destruction of the substance, the non-destruction of the conjunction that originates the substance, the non-production of a disjunction opposed to that [conjunction], the lack of independence of the part, and the action’s subsistence therein. Since these properties are excluded from the case in question, they exclude the production of two disjunctions—which is pervaded by them—thereby rendering the inference otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*). Nor is this an instance of an inference contradicted by a specific property (*viśeṣaviruddha*), for such properties are non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*). An inference is contradicted by a specific property only where the properties involved are deviant.

Alternatively, since a specific cause is established by a specific effect elsewhere, this [example] is intended to demonstrate that specific effect. In one case, there is a disjunction that is the opposite of the conjunction initiating a substance, whereas in the other, there is merely disjunction. However, it is not the case that there is merely a dissimilarity between the example and the subject of the illustration.

Furthermore, since a specific effect does not deviate from its specific cause, one must admit a distinction in the action (*karman*) regarding both the production of a disjunction that opposes the conjunction initiating a substance and the production of a mere disjunction. For those who maintain that action resides in a single momentary substance, this distinction is postulated as follows: although it is possible for such an action to exist in either case, there is a difference in that in one instance it produces a disjunction with a point of space (*ākāśadeśa*), while in the other it does not. Consequently, if an independent action of a part were to produce a disjunction with a point of space, there would be no production of the disjunction that opposes the conjunction initiating the substance; thus, in the absence of the destruction of the conjunction, there would be no destruction of the substance.

Furthermore, in this case, there would be no destruction of the effect-substance (*kāryadravya*) resulting from the destruction of its parts; for if it were admitted that the action of those parts also produces a disjunction from the locus of space (*ākāśadeśa*), then—since no specific disjunction from another part would arise—the conjunction [with that other part] would not be destroyed, and consequently, that substance itself would not be destroyed. Likewise, if one admits the destruction of each subsequent part through the destruction of its substratum, the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) would remain undestroyed, because its own substratum is eternal.

Now, if the destruction of the dyad (dvyaṇuka) results from the destruction of its conjunction, then one must admit a disjunction that is opposed to the conjunction initiating the substance; for by means of that [disjunction], destruction is possible even in the absence of the destruction of the substratum.

For instance, when the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) has perished due to the destruction of the conjunction that initiates the substance, the destruction of the effect-substance residing therein is indeed possible. Therefore, wherever there is the destruction of a substance, the action of a part does not initiate a disjunction from the point of space (*ākāśadeśa*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: An independent action of a part does not, at the same time as it initiates a disjunction with another part—which is opposed to the conjunction initiating the substance—initiate a disjunction from the point of space; because it is an action of a part, like the action of a lotus petal. Likewise, an independent part does not, at the same time as it initiates a specific disjunction from another part, disjoin itself from the point of space; because it is a part, like a lotus petal. In this manner, an inference should be formulated by taking disjunction and so forth as the subject (*pakṣa*).

In this case, the production of specific disjunctions is ascertained precisely through the non-destruction of the substance; thus, the property of being present in the similar instance (*sapakṣadharmatva*) belongs to the action of the parts of a lotus and so forth. Furthermore, since nothing is observed that initiates a disjunction with a point of space at the same time as it produces a specific disjunction, there is an absence of a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). Therefore, its status as a probans (*gamakatva*) should be understood solely through the non-deviation of positive concomitance (*anvaya-avyabhicāra*). However, when the probandum is established in a general sense—namely, the negation of the capacity to produce a disjunction with a point of space at the same time as the disjunction of the parts—the probans functions through the non-deviation of negative concomitance (*vyatireka-avyabhicāra*) as well.

For instance, an independent action of a part does not initiate a disjunction from a point of space at the same time as it initiates a disjunction from another part, because it is an independent action of a part; that which does initiate such [a disjunction] is not an independent action of a part, as in the case of the action of a lotus petal. Likewise, an independent part does not disjoin from a point of space at the same time as it disjoins from another part, because it is an independent part; that which does disjoin is not an independent part, as in the case of a lotus petal. Furthermore, independence occurs when a substance is destroyed through a sequence of actions, as has been stated previously. And this is not possible in the case of an action such as the contraction of the parts of a lotus, since the destruction of the substance is not observed there.

Now, if the action of the parts of a lotus also initiates a disjunction from a point of space at the same time as the disjunction between the parts, then—inasmuch as this is beyond the senses—an inference must be stated as the means of valid cognition, for there is no establishment of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). In that case, if the state of being an action of a dependent part were the indicator through non-deviation in negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*), because if one is not established, the other cannot be established.

This is not so; for there is no subverting argument against the production of disjunction by the action of a non-independent part with respect to a point of space. To explain: while the action of an independent part possesses the property of producing a disjunction that opposes the conjunction initiating a substance—this being a subverting argument against its producing a disjunction with respect to a point of space—there is no such [subverting argument] in this case.

For instance, the motion of a part of a lotus initiates a disjunction from a point of space, provided that no obstructing factor arises to prevent its initiation, because it is a motion; whatever is such [a motion] initiates a disjunction from a point of space and so forth, just like the motion of an atom when it has not yet initiated an effect. Furthermore, the motion produced in an atom already connected to a point of space such as ether necessarily initiates a disjunction that terminates that conjunction; for otherwise, if the prior conjunction were to persist and no subsequent conjunction were produced, it would follow that no effects could arise through the sequence beginning with dyads.

Others, however, maintain that just as the action of a non-independent part produces a disjunction from a causeless object such as grass at the same time as it produces a disjunction from another part, so too does it act with respect to space and other entities; and they cite the disjunction of grass from a petal of a lotus as a perceptible example. Nor is it the case that the production of a disjunction by a causeless object through the action of an independent part is not established by perception (for the dispute would otherwise be untenable). Furthermore, this is not a fallacious rejoinder (*asaduttara*), because when a *prasaṅgasama* [balancing-the-consequence] argument is expected, it is accepted that an inference may be presented even regarding an example.

Therefore, the independent action of a part initiates disjunction from another part; from that disjunction follows the destruction of the conjunction that originates the substance. When that [conjunction] has perished, there is an absence of the effect due to the absence of its cause—thus, the composite whole is destroyed. Subsequently, the disjunction of the independent part from the locus of space must be asserted. Without that [disjunction], the prior conjunction would persist, and since the subsequent conjunction would not arise, the action would endure for a period of time, and that which inheres in an eternal substance would itself be eternal. But this is not the case, because action is observed to be momentary. Nor can its destruction occur without a cause for destruction, because such [causeless] destruction is denied. Therefore, since no other cause of destruction exists, and because the capacity of the subsequent conjunction alone to destroy the action is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is established as the cause of its destruction.

Furthermore, a subsequent conjunction does not occur while the prior conjunction with a point of space—which acts as an obstacle—remains; therefore, disjunction is determined to be the cause of that destruction. Nor can this [subsequent conjunction] arise from action, according to the reasoning already stated. Since the production of disjunction is never observed without a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and because no other non-inherent cause exists, the disjunction residing in the two causes is the non-inherent cause due to its proximity and its being of the same genus. For where there is nothing of the same genus, it is postulated that something of a different genus is indeed the non-inherent cause. Action, however, even though present here, is not a cause at all because of the existence of an opposing factor. Therefore, "the disjunction residing in the two causes" initiates a disjunction "from the points of space such as ether," which are characterized by their conjunction with the effect. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the self (*ātman*) and so forth are included.

To the question "With reference to what? he says: "The time characterized by the destruction of the effect. The destruction of the effect is the destruction of the substance; [the new substance] arises with reference to that time characterized by such [destruction], and with reference to that independent constituent part which results from its destruction.

Others, however, maintain that because of the general designation "time characterized by the destruction of the effect," [the disjunction] begins at the same time as the destruction of the substance, having depended upon [the destruction of] the conjunction. They say: "or depending upon an independent part. Since its independence occurs after the destruction of the substance, it is figuratively said to be so even previously. Thus, [it means] "depending upon the independent Lord, or depending upon a part."

To whom does this belong? He says: "Of that which possesses action (*sakriyasyaiva*) alone. Now, since there is no distinction in the fact that the disjunction from the cause resides in both [the parts], what is the restrictive rule here that the disjunction from a location such as space belongs to that which possesses action and not to that which is inactive? It is the production of a subsequent conjunction (*uttarasaṃyogotpatti*). For instance, when the destruction of the prior conjunction occurs due to disjunction, the action produces a subsequent conjunction; therefore, both the disjunction and the action cease. However, how could a disjunction produced in an inactive object cease in the absence of a subsequent conjunction? Furthermore, it is not logical for a subsequent conjunction to arise once the prior conjunction has ceased before the disjunction, because the cause—the action—would then be absent. Moreover, if [the object] were to remain unjoined with space and so forth, those [substances] would not be all-pervading (*asarvagata*). Nor is it observed that a conjunction produced by the action of one thing can be the terminator of a disjunction produced by the action of another. Therefore, it is observed that the cessation of a disjunction occurs through a subsequent conjunction, which is the effect of the action belonging to its own cause. "The consequence of non-enjoyability (*anupabhogyatva-prasaṅga*) in the absence of the production of a subsequent conjunction" means the consequence of being purposeless and the consequence of being perishable. For it is only through the production of a subsequent conjunction—by way of terminating the prior conjunction—that its purposiveness and perishability are established.

Alternatively, if one were to admit the disjunction of an inactive [substance] from a location such as space, there would be no production of a subsequent conjunction for that which possesses action, due to the absence of a cause; however, the absence of a cause is not the reason for the prohibition of disjunction-produced disjunction in the case of an inactive [substance], because its inherent and other types of causes are possible. For instance, the inactive parts and space possess the status of inherent causes (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*), disjunction possesses the status of non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*), and the remainder possess the status of instrumental cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*); thus, the existence of causes is established. Therefore, the absence of a cause is the reason for the prohibition of subsequent conjunction. To explain: if one does not admit the disjunction of that which possesses action from a location such as space, then because the prior conjunction—which acts as an obstacle—remains, there is no production of subsequent conjunction. When that is not produced, the disjunction and the action become unenjoyable and purposeless.

Others, however, maintain that there is no disjunction from a location such as space for that which is devoid of action. This is incorrect. Why? Because of the absence of a cause. When it is argued by the opponent that "there is an absence of proof," he states the subverting argument: "If disjunction were not destroyed, it would follow that it could never be experienced, because a subsequent conjunction would not arise."

Now, even if the action of a part does not initiate a disjunction from a location such as space at the same time as it initiates the disjunction from another part, it might nevertheless be argued that it will initiate it after the destruction of its effect. To refute this, he says: "But that action of the part does not initiate a disjunction from a location such as space," because an action that has ceased cannot have further operation. He states this by saying: "Because that time of initiation has passed. "That time of initiation" (*tadārambhakāla*) refers either to the time of that action's initiation of disjunction, or to the time of that disjunction's own initiation; [it is so called] because that time has passed.

Now, if one objects that once the action has ceased, there can be no subsequent conjunction (*uttara-saṃyoga*) because its operation has been prohibited, we say: no, for this prohibition of operation after cessation is not correctly understood. To explain: an action, having produced disjunction, does not again initiate disjunction; and having produced velocity, it does not again produce velocity—but it certainly does initiate a [subsequent] conjunction with another location, since there is no lapse of time for an action whose conjunction has not yet been produced. This is because "lapse of time" means destruction, and since that is absent [in this case]. Furthermore, its destruction is observed even while it exists [at that moment]. Therefore, it must be accepted that action produces a subsequent conjunction. Consequently, its cessation follows from that.

“How also [is disjunction produced] from the disjunction of the cause and the non-cause? When an action has arisen in the hand and, without producing a disjunction from another part [of the body], initiates disjunctions from points of space such as ether, it then initiates conjunctions with other points of space; at that time, those disjunctions of the cause and the non-cause, having regard for the direction toward which the action is oriented for the commencement of its effect, initiate disjunctions of the effect and the non-effect. Immediately after that, from the conjunction of the cause and the non-cause, [disjunctions] of the effect and the non-effect [arise].”

He explains how disjunction (*vibhāga*) also arises from the disjunction of cause and non-cause with the words: “When action has arisen in the hand,” and so forth. Action having arisen in the hand from its own causes, without yet producing a disjunction from another part that would oppose the conjunction initiating the substance, initiates disjunctions from locations such as space (*ākāśa*); by the phrase “and so forth,” the self (*ātman*) and other [substances] are included. Having initiated those [disjunctions], when—upon the destruction of the prior conjunctions—it initiates conjunctions with other locations such as space, at that time, “those disjunctions of cause and non-cause initiate disjunctions of effect and non-effect. The hand is the cause of the body, while space and so forth are the non-causes; these are their disjunctions. The body is the effect of the hand, while space and so forth are the non-effects; they initiate disjunctions from these. Upon their production, the body, space, and so forth possess the status of inherent causes (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*), while the disjunctions of the hand from space and so forth possess the status of non-inherent causes (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*). Since proximity of both types is possible, and no subverting argument (*bādhaka*) arises, this must be accepted. There is no lack of co-referentiality (*vyadhikaraṇatva*) because of the co-inherence in a single object that is the effect, for such a form of proximity is observed in other cases of action.

Now, if it is argued that because a division of the body is perceived at the very same time as the division of the hand and the book through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), action itself must be postulated as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) [of that bodily division], we say: no. This is because the conceit of direct perception is erroneous due to its rapid occurrence, like the piercing of a hundred lotus petals. For just as the perceptual cognition "a hundred lotus petals have been pierced simultaneously" is invalid because it is sublated by an inferential cognition (*anumāna*) that grasps the truth, so too here, the cognition of simultaneity—"there is a division of the body at the same time as the division of the hand"—is invalid because it is sublated by inference. If one asks, "What is this inference?"—it is the fact that an action has distinct substrates. To explain: the action of a specific part does not initiate a division inhering in a substrate other than its own substrate, because it is an action, just like an action admitted by both parties. Nor is there a contradiction of this inference by direct perception, as in the case of the inference "fire is not hot, because it is produced," for the present inference possesses the five required features (*pañcarūpa*). Thus, a defective inference is sublated by direct perception which cooperates with its own object, and a defective direct perception is sublated by inference. Therefore, since the object of inference is unsublated, even in the case of division, the apprehension of simultaneity arises from rapid succession and not from the actual state of things. Furthermore, rapid succession is seen to be a cause of error even when there is an interval of hundreds of moments, as in the piercing of a hundred lotus petals; how much more so when there is an interval of only one or two moments?
