For instance, when there is a destruction of conjunction due to the division between the cause and the non-cause, the admission of a division between the effect and the non-effect involves an interval of one moment (*ekakṣaṇavyavadhāna*). However, in the case of a division preceded by the division of the cause, its occurrence immediately after the destruction of conjunction and the destruction of the substance involves an interval of two moments (*kṣaṇadvayavyavadhāna*). In the case of the parts of a lotus petal, however, when action arises from contact with a swift needle or similar object, the conjunction is destroyed by the resulting division, and upon that destruction of conjunction, the petal is destroyed; then, through contact with another petal, action arises in its parts—this sequence is to be inferred even for a hundred petals. Since it is admitted that the illusion [of simultaneity] is caused by the rapidity of occurrence even when there is an interval of many hundreds of moments, it will certainly occur in the case of an interval of a single moment. Therefore, because the misconception of simultaneity due to rapidity is erroneous, divisions between the cause and the non-cause do indeed initiate divisions between the effect and the non-effect.

“Immediately thereafter” (*tadanantaram*) means after the distinction between what is an effect and what is not an effect has been established. When the prior conjunction has perished, the conjunctions between causes and non-causes (*kāraṇākāraṇasaṃyoga*) initiate conjunctions between effects and non-effects (*kāryākāryasaṃyoga*), but not previously, because the prior conjunction remains as an obstacle. This [conjunction], however, is produced immediately after the disjunction born of disjunction (*vibhāgajavibhāga*), which was previously asserted for conjunctions produced by conjunction (*saṃyogajasaṃyoga*) that have arisen long ago; and it is defined in this very context because it shares the same underlying method.

Now, what is the proof for the disjunction and conjunction of the body with space and so forth? It is inference. For instance: the body is disjoined from that which is disjoined from its own cause, because it is an effect of a cause that is disjoined from that [cause], like a cloth which is an effect of threads disjoined from *vīraṇa* grass. Or, space and so forth are disjoined from that which is an effect of a cause disjoined from itself, because they are disjoined from its cause, like *vīraṇa* grass disjoined from threads. Likewise, the body is conjoined with that which is conjoined with its own cause, because it is an effect of a cause conjoined with that [cause], like a cloth which is an effect of threads conjoined with *vīraṇa* grass. Once the conjunction of the body with space and so forth is established, since the body is at that time devoid of motion and yet possesses the motion of its parts—and because it is denied that an inherent effect can be produced by anything other than its substrate—furthermore, because no production of an entity is observed without a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and since no other possibility exists, its production is postulated as resulting from the conjunction of the cause and the non-cause. In this case, the body is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of the conjunction with space and so forth, while a specific direction (*viśiṣṭā dik*) is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).

“If the division of the effect arises immediately after the division of the cause, and the conjunction of the effect arises immediately after the conjunction of the cause, then surely this entails the fault of the parts and the whole being *yutasiddha* (separately established). No, for there is a misunderstanding regarding *yutasiddhi*. That [fault] consists in two things, or one of them, possessing separate motion; however, that applies to eternal things. For non-eternal things, *yutasiddhi* is defined as inherence (*samavāya*) in separate substrates. In the case of the tactile organ and the body, there is no possession of separate motion, yet there is inherence in separate substrates; thus, their mutual conjunction is established. In the case of an atom and space, even though there is no other substrate, conjunction and disjunction are established because one of the two possesses separate motion. In the case of the thread and the cloth, which are non-eternal, there is an absence of conjunction and disjunction with respect to each other because there is no other substrate. As for direction (*dik*) and the rest, since they lack the possession of separate motion, there is an absence of conjunction and disjunction with respect to each other.”

When the division produced by division (*vibhāgaja-vibhāga*) has been thus determined, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) states an invalid objection: "If the production of the division of the effect follows immediately after the division of the cause, and the production of the conjunction of the effect follows immediately after the conjunction of the cause, [and not simultaneously], then does it not follow that there is the fault of 'separate existence' (*yutasiddhi*) between the part and the whole? This is not correct. Why? Because of a lack of understanding regarding separate existence. The opponent has not correctly understood what separate existence is, which is why he speaks thus. For, separate existence is the fitness for mutual conjunction and disjunction. Indeed, while parts possess the fitness for conjunction and disjunction with other objects, such fitness certainly exists for the whole [with those same objects], but not for [the whole] with [its own] parts; thus, there is no deviation [from the definition]. Or, if such [mutual] fitness did exist, there would be separate existence alone, and consequently, there could be no inherence (*samavāya*). Yet, we shall demonstrate that this inherence does indeed exist.

This general definition, however, is indeed obtained from the specific definition of *yutasiddhi* (separate existence), because the specific is pervaded by the general; thus, he states the specific definition: "That [separate existence], moreover, consists in the possession of separate motion by both or by either one of the two. This is the *yutasiddhi* of eternal things. The possession of separate motion by two atoms is *yutasiddhi*; likewise, the possession of separate motion by either one of the two—namely, ether and an atom—is also *yutasiddhi*. And what is intended here is their fitness for producing mutual conjunction and disjunction. Otherwise, since the motion of the two atoms that originate a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is perceived when the dyad moves, there would be *yutasiddhi* with respect to the dyad.

In the case of impermanent things, *yutasiddhi* (separate existence) is defined as inherence (*samavāya*) in distinct substrates that exist separately. [Objection: Even so, there would be *yutasiddhi* between a part and its whole because of their inherence in separate substrates. For instance, the whole exists in its parts, and the parts exist in their own constituent parts; thus, there is inherence in separate substrates. [Reply: No, for you have not understood our intention. Just as a cloth has inherence in a substrate other than the pot and its substrate, and a pot has inherence in a substrate other than the cloth and its substrate, the whole does not have inherence in a substrate other than its parts. Therefore, there is no *yutasiddhi*. Here too, the phrase "the state of having inherence in separate substrates for both, or for one of the two" continues to apply. For example, it applies to both, as in the case of a pot and a cloth; or to one of the two, as in the case of space and a pot. In this latter case, the pot has no inherence in substrates separate from itself, whereas space does not, because it is non-dependent (*anāśrita*).

[Objection: If that is so, then since the property of having separate motions is possible even in impermanent things just as it is in permanent ones, let that [separate motion] alone suffice; what is the use of this non-pervasive "inherence in joined substrata" (*yutāśrayasamavāyitva*)? [Reply: This is not so. Because in impermanent things there is no positive or negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with having separate motions, [their] yutasiddhi is simply "inherence in joined substrata. Since that exists, he says that this alone is yutasiddhi: "There is no having separate motions between the tactile sense-organ (*tvagindriya*) and the body. However, because there is inherence in those which are joined, "mutual conjunction is established. For instance, since separation between the tactile sense-organ and the body is impossible until death, even though there is an absence of having separate motions, their yutasiddhi is simply "inherence in joined substrata," because their inherence occurs in their own respective substrata while avoiding mutual dependence on each other. Similarly, although a jar or the like, immediately upon being produced, lacks the property of having motion, since conjunction with space and so forth is observed at the same time as the production of its color and other qualities, the yutasiddhi of one of them is simply "inherence in joined substrata."

However, since conjunction and disjunction are perceived even in the absence of inherence in separate substrata in the case of eternal things, he states that "separate existence" (*yutasiddhi*) consists precisely in having separate motion: "But in the case of the atom and space," [conjunction and disjunction] are established "because one of the two has separate motion," even though there is no inherence in separate substrata.

Thus, after demonstrating the positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—namely, that non-eternal things possess inherence in a conjoined substratum (*yutāśrayasamavāyitva*), while eternal things possess the quality of having separate motions—he states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): "In the case of the two non-eternal entities, thread and cloth, because there is no other substratum [for the cloth apart from the threads], there is an absence of conjunction and disjunction between them. Although the threads reside in their own constituent parts (*aṃśu*), nevertheless, within the substance of the cloth, there is no other substratum apart from the threads; thus, there is an absence of inherence in a conjoined substratum. Due to that absence, there is no mutual conjunction or disjunction. Regarding the specific case of having separate motions, since both are possible for a jar and an atom, there is either a restriction to both or a restriction to one. It is as if there were a restriction to both, because there is no specific reason for restricting it to only one. To explain: the quality of having separate motions applies to the eternal atom, while inherence in a conjoined substratum applies to the non-eternal jar; since both are established through positive and negative concomitance in both cases, it is logical to accept them here as applicable. Where there is only a non-eternal thing, even if the quality of having separate motions is present, there is a restriction of inherence in a conjoined substratum—as in the case of a jar and space, or between two jars. Enough of this excessive detail. Therefore, the statement that "separation of the effect follows separation of the cause, and conjunction of the effect follows conjunction of the cause" is the definition of *yutasiddhi* (separate establishment) for one who has not understood it.

{The manner of the destruction of disjunction} “Destruction, however, belongs to every disjunction because it is momentary; its existence lasts until the subsequent conjunction, and thus it is momentary. But it is not like conjunction, where the destruction of a disjunction occurs between the very same two things between which that disjunction existed. Why? Because, unlike the cognition of conjunction, there is no persistence of the cognition of disjunction [after the subsequent conjunction]. Therefore, because its existence lasts until the subsequent conjunction, it is momentary.”

Now he explains destruction with the words: “But destruction [occurs] because every disjunction is momentary,” and so forth. [Objection: But is not momentariness the state of being destroyed very quickly? And if that is what is to be proven regarding the destruction of disjunction, does this not fail to differ from the probandum itself? [Response: No, because it is the linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) that is to be proven. That is to say, disjunction is to be treated as destructible because it is momentary. Alternatively, momentariness may be defined as the possession of a conjunction that causes extremely rapid destruction; therefore, when the destruction of disjunction is to be proven, there is no lack of distinction from the probandum. Now, what is that cause of destruction? It is subsequent conjunction (*uttara-saṃyoga*). How so? “Because its existence has subsequent conjunction as its limit. This means that subsequent conjunction is the limit or boundary for its existence; thus, its existence lasts until that subsequent conjunction occurs, after which it ceases to exist. This is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). “But not like conjunction” refers to its destruction. For instance, while the destruction of a conjunction occurs through the disjunction of those very two things that were conjoined, it is not the case that the destruction of a disjunction occurs through the conjunction of those very two things that were disjoined. What then? Whether it be a conjunction produced by the action of one of those two or by something else, or a conjunction produced by their [prior] conjunction, it is destroyed by that.

Now, one might ask: "Just as conjunction is not destroyed merely by the arising of disjunction, why is it not accepted that disjunction likewise is not destroyed merely by the presence of conjunction? To this he says: "Because there is no persistence of the cognition of 'separated' [as there is] of the cognition of 'conjoined'" (*saṃyuktapratyayavad vibhaktapratyayānuvṛttyabhāvāt*), for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of its [disjunction's] destruction. For instance, when only disjunction arises within a state of conjunction, the persistence of the cognition of "conjoined" is observed—as in "this is conjoined with what was conjoined"—but such persistence of the cognition of "separated" does not occur when only conjunction arises within a state of disjunction. Therefore, the conclusion is: "It is momentary because it has a limit in the form of a subsequent conjunction" (*tasmād uttarasaṃyogāvadhisadbhāvāt kṣaṇikaḥ*).

Others [hold] that disjunction (*vibhāga*) does not exist as an established entity like conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Why? Because it would follow that disjunction is destroyed by the very same two things from which conjunction arises. For just as an established conjunction is removed by the disjunction of those very two things, so too disjunction would have to be removed by the conjunction of those very two things. If it is argued, "This is indeed accepted," that is incorrect; for there is no persistence of the cognition of "separated" following upon another object, as there is in the case of the persistence of the cognition of "conjoined. Indeed, just as the cognition of "conjoined" persists through another object [in the case of conjunction], there is no persistence of the cognition of "separated" through another object [in the case of disjunction]. Furthermore, that cognition of non-attainment (*aprāpti*) should be understood as the absence of conjunction due to the presence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*); otherwise, if a body were to move to another place or die, because it remains [as a substance], it would be perceived even when one part of the body is grasped. But this is not the case. Therefore, the cognition of "separated" is primary (*mukhya*) with respect to a substance in which motion is currently occurring, whereas at other times it is figurative (*bhākta*) due to its similarity to that state.

“In some cases, destruction occurs simply from the destruction of its substrate. How so? When an action has arisen in a constituent part (*aṃśu*) that is the cause of a two-threaded fabric (*dvitantuka*), and it initiates a disjunction from another part, at that very same time an action arises in the other thread. From that disjunction, the conjunction that originated the thread is destroyed; meanwhile, by the action in the thread, a disjunction from the other thread is produced—this is one moment. Then, at the very moment when the conjunction of the threads is destroyed due to that disjunction, at that same moment the destruction of the thread occurs because of the destruction of the conjunction; and when that [thread] has been destroyed, there follows the destruction of the disjunction from the other thread which was dependent upon it.”

“If that were so, then there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of no subsequent disjunction occurring, because of the absence of a cause for disjunction. Consequently, since there would be an absence of conjunction in that which possesses conjunction with another location, a contrary quality (virodhiguṇa) could not arise; thus, action (karman) would persist for a long time, and action inhering in an eternal substance would itself be eternal—this is the fault. How so? When an action has arisen in an atom that is the constituent of a dyad (dvyaṇuka), it produces a disjunction from another atom; at that very same time, an action arises in that other atom as well. Then, at the very moment when the conjunction that initiates the substance [the dyad] is destroyed by that disjunction, at that same moment a disjunction between the dyad and the atom is produced by the action in the other atom. Then, at the very moment when the conjunction of the dyad and the atom is destroyed by that disjunction, at that same moment, due to the destruction of the conjunction, the dyad is destroyed. When that [dyad] is destroyed, the disjunction between the dyad and the atom, which was dependent upon it, is also destroyed. And thus, because no contrary quality can arise, action inhering in an eternal substance would be eternal—is this not the case? [Response: There is no such fault, because disjunction arises from the disjunction of the thread from another part of the thread. Due to the destruction of the substratum, it is the disjunction of the two threads themselves that is destroyed, not the disjunction of the thread from the other part. From this, the subsequent disjunction is produced. Just as there is a disjunction of the body from space resulting from the disjunction of a finger from space, at that very same time the action, having produced the conjunction, perishes; thus there is no fault.”The provided text contains Sanskrit terms with IAST diacritics and discusses technical points of Vaiśeṣika philosophy regarding action (*karman*), disjunction (*vibhāga*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and the nature of substances. The translation aims to preserve the philosophical nuance and the logical structure of the argument.

Having thus established that disjunction is destroyed by conjunction, he explains its destruction through the destruction of its substrate with the words, "In some cases, it is destroyed by the destruction of its substrate," and so forth. Following the question of one who is unlearned, "How so?", he says, "When an action has arisen in a fiber (*aṃśu*), which is a part of the cause of the two-threaded [cloth]... The cause of the two-threaded [cloth] is the thread; its part is the fiber. When an action produced from its own cause brings about a disjunction from another fiber—[and since the conjunction that initiates the substance is destroyed, the thread is destroyed; when that [thread] is destroyed, it initiates a non-opposing [action] dependent upon it]—at that very same time, "an action also arises in the other thread; and from that disjunction, there is the destruction of the conjunction that initiates the thread; a disjunction from the other thread is effected by the action of the thread. These two occur at one and the same time. "Then, at the very moment when, due to the disjunction, there is the destruction of the conjunction of the threads that initiates the two-threaded [cloth], at that same moment, due to the destruction of the conjunction of the fibers that initiates the thread, there is the destruction of the thread. "When that [thread] is destroyed, there is the destruction of the disjunction from the other thread which was dependent upon it," because there is no other cause for its destruction. At that very moment, the two-threaded [cloth] also undergoes destruction, both due to the destruction of its substrate and due to the destruction of its [constituent] conjunction.

Having thus stated that destruction [of the whole] occurs due to the destruction of its substratum, he demonstrates an undesirable consequence: "In that case, it would follow that no subsequent disjunction could arise. Subsequent disjunction refers to the disjunction of the thread from a location such as space; its non-arising [would follow]. This is because of the absence of the disjunction of the causes (*kāraṇavibhāgābhāvāt*). That is, there is no disjunction of the two causal threads. Alternatively, it means that since the cause—which is itself a disjunction—is absent at the same time as the destruction of the substance, there is no arising of the disjunction from the location of space. Nor can the disjunction of the cause initiate another disjunction at the same time as the destruction of the substance while depending on the destruction of a conjunction, because it is not accepted that something in a state of perishing can serve as a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). This objection applies only to the text as it stands literally.

Furthermore, if no disjunction from the space-points of ether and so forth were produced in the thread, then because the conjunction [with those points]—acting as an obstacle—would persist, the action would not produce a subsequent conjunction. To this he says: "In that which possesses a conjunction with another point, there is an absence of conjunction" (*). Thus, since a contrary quality such as conjunction with another point is impossible, the action would have to endure for a period of time. This contradicts the fact that its momentariness is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Likewise, there is the fault that an action inherent in an eternal substance would itself be eternal. How so? He explains: "When an action has arisen in the atom that initiates the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) from its own cause, it produces a disjunction from another atom, which is opposed to the conjunction that initiates the substance; at that very same time, an action arises in the other atom, which does not initiate [the dyad]. Immediately thereafter, "at the very time when, due to the disjunction, the destruction of the conjunction initiating the substance occurs, at that same time, by the action of the non-initiating atom, a disjunction between the dyad and the atom is produced. Then, "at the very time when, due to the disjunction, the destruction of the conjunction of the dyad with the atom occurs, at that same time, due to the destruction of the conjunction that initiates the substance, the destruction of the dyad occurs. When that dyad has been destroyed, "there is the destruction of the disjunction from the atom that was inherent in it. Consequently, in the absence of a disjunction from the cause, no subsequent disjunction is produced; and since the previous conjunction has not ceased, the action does not produce a subsequent conjunction. Thus, due to the impossibility of a contrary quality, the action inherent in the atom would be eternal. He states the rebuttal to the previous objection: "There is no fault, because the disjunction [of the atom] results from the disjunction of the thread from another part of the thread" (*).

[Objection: Surely the disjunction between the yarn and the thread cannot be the effect of the action in the thread, because the thread is not a cause for the production of the two-threaded cloth (*dvitantuka*), just as space and so forth are not. Nor can it be the effect of the action in the thread, because another thread is not a cause for the production of the [first] thread, just as space is not. Furthermore, it has been stated that an action produced in a cause does not initiate a disjunction from another cause simultaneously with the disjunction from its own [immediate] cause, for that would entail the non-production of specific disjunctions. And since an effect cannot exist without a cause, the disjunction between the yarn and the thread is simply impossible. [Reply: This is not so. For we admit that its production arises from a disjunction generated by the action in the thread. To explain: the disjunction generated by the action in the thread, depending upon the time characterized by the destruction of the conjunction, initiates a disjunction from another thread at the same time as the destruction of the [original] thread, just as it does from a location such as space. Then, depending upon the time characterized by the destruction of the thread, and coinciding with the destruction of the two-threaded cloth due to the destruction of its substratum, the mutual disjunction between the two threads itself perishes. However, the disjunction from the other thread—which was produced from the disjunction generated by the action in the thread—does not perish; rather, from that single disjunction from the other thread, a subsequent disjunction arises, namely the disjunction between the thread and space. The example is: "like the disjunction between the body and space resulting from the disjunction between the finger and space. Just as there is a disjunction between the hand and space from the disjunction between the finger and space, and from that disjunction a disjunction between the body and space arises, so too here: from the disjunction generated by the action in the thread, the disjunction between the yarn and the thread arises, and from that disjunction, the disjunction between the thread and space is produced. Once that [subsequent disjunction] has arisen, the action ceases after producing a subsequent conjunction, due to the absence of the previous conjunction which acted as an obstacle. Thus, there is no fault of the action persisting over a period of time.

But in this view, how can there be the cessation of the disjunction between the thread and space [and other things] upon the occurrence of the subsequent conjunction, given that it was not produced even indirectly by the action of the thread? No, for no such rule is observed regarding a disjunction produced by another disjunction. Others, however, maintain that the action arising in a thread produces disjunction from the other thread as well as from the *aṃśu* (fiber) that constitutes its origin, because the *aṃśu* is also an indirect cause. Furthermore, space and so forth are not causes for the production of the two-threaded cloth even indirectly. Thus, the action of the thread does not produce disjunction from the [other] thread at the same time as it produces disjunction from the other parts. Alternatively, the action of the *aṃśu* initiates disjunction from the other thread just as it does from the other *aṃśu*s, because it initiates the effect together with the product of the *aṃśu*. Therefore, due to the destruction of the substratum, only the disjunction between the two threads is destroyed, but not the disjunction from the other thread. Consequently, the disjunction between the thread and space arises, just as the disjunction between the body and space arises from the disjunction between the finger and space.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the disjunction between the hand and space arises from the disjunction between the finger and space, because a disjunction between a cause and a non-cause initiates a disjunction between an effect and a non-effect? [Reply: It is not so, because the body is not the effect of the finger. Therefore, although there is proximity between the disjunction of the finger and space and the disjunction of the body and space, since both reside in space, nevertheless [the former] is simply not the cause [of the latter]. Consequently, since the hand is the initiator of the body, it is logical to speak of the hand itself as the "body" by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). This is merely an illustration: just as the disjunction of the hand and space arises from the disjunction of the finger and space—which is a disjunction between a cause and a non-cause—so too does the disjunction of the yarn and space arise from the disjunction of the thread and its part (*aṃśu*).

“Alternatively, at the same time that the disjunction from another part arises, an action is produced in that very thread. Then, from the disjunction from the other part, there is the destruction of the conjunction that originated the thread; and by the action of the thread, a disjunction from the other thread is produced—this constitutes one moment. Subsequently, from the destruction of the conjunction, there is the destruction of the thread; and from its destruction, there is the simultaneous destruction of the disjunction and the action which were dependent upon it.”

The phrase “Alternatively (*atha vā*)” introduces another method for the destruction of the division through the destruction of its substratum; it is not, however, a refutation of the objection raised in the preceding context, because it demonstrates that action persists for a different duration of time within a substance that itself persists for a different duration of time. Therefore: “At the same time as the production of the division from another part, an action arises in that very thread (*tasminneva tantau*) which is being divided. Immediately thereafter, from the division of the parts, there is the destruction of the conjunction that originated the thread, and by the action of the thread, a division from the other thread is produced—this is one moment of time. Then, from the destruction of the conjunction, there is the destruction of the thread. From the division from the other thread, there is the destruction of the conjunction with it; then, from the destruction of both [the thread and the conjunction], there is the destruction of the two-threaded cloth. And from the destruction of the thread, there is the simultaneous destruction of the division and the action residing therein.

“Or, when there is a conjunction of the threads and the vīraṇa grass, since no new substance is produced, the destruction of the disjunction between the threads and the vīraṇa grass occurs through the previously mentioned method, namely by the destruction of the substratum and by [the subsequent] conjunction. <PDhS>

Now, the statement beginning with “Or, as in the case of the thread and the *vīraṇa* grass” (*tantuvīraṇayor vā*) serves as a response to the objection that what is inherent in an eternal substance must itself be eternal. For just as no new substance is produced from the conjunction of a thread and *vīraṇa* grass because they are of different classes (*vijātīya*), so too no substance is produced from the conjunction of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) and an atom (*aṇu*). This is because one dyad is non-eternal while the other atom is eternal; thus, they are of different classes. Furthermore, a conjunction between things of different classes does not initiate a substance. Therefore, even when a dyad and an atom conjoin, since no substance is produced, the action (*karman*) arising in the atom—because it does not produce a disjunction that opposes the conjunction initiating a substance—initiates a disjunction even from a location such as space, just like the action in the *vīraṇa* grass. Thus, upon the cessation of the prior conjunction, it perishes after effecting a subsequent conjunction, its destruction occurring according to the previously stated rule.

Alternatively, the meaning of the phrase "by the previously mentioned method" is as follows: at the same time that action arises in the fiber (*aṃśu*) which is the constituent of the thread, action also arises in the *vīraṇa* grass. By the action in the fiber, a disjunction from another fiber is produced; by the action in the *vīraṇa*, a disjunction from another thread is produced—this is one moment. Then, from that disjunction, upon the destruction of the conjunction with the fiber, there is the destruction of the conjunction between the *vīraṇa* and the thread due to the disjunction from the *vīraṇa*. Thereafter, from the destruction of the conjunction that initiates the substance, there is the destruction of the thread. And when the conjunction between the thread and the *vīraṇa* is destroyed, there is a subsequent conjunction; then, through both the destruction of the substrate and the [subsequent] conjunction, there is the destruction of the disjunction between the thread and the *vīraṇa*.

Others, however, [hold that] because the word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of comparison, just as in the case of a thread and *vīraṇa* grass, when a conjunction occurs between a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) and an atom (*aṇu*), no substance is produced. And since no substance is produced, how is the destruction of the disjunction between the dyad and the atom—produced by the motion of the atom at the same time as the destruction of the conjunction that originated the dyad—accomplished? It is by the previously mentioned method; that is to say, by the destruction of the substratum. But when, upon the production of motion in an atom, one considers a motion in this very dyad at the same time as the production of the disjunction from another atom, then by the previously mentioned method, there is the simultaneous destruction of both the disjunction and the motion due to the destruction of the substratum. Furthermore, when one considers a motion in the non-originating atom at the same time as the production of motion in the atom that originates the dyad, then its destruction occurs through both the destruction of its substratum and [the subsequent] conjunction, just like the destruction of the disjunction between a thread and *vīraṇa* grass. Enough of this.

The distinction between remoteness (*paratva*) and proximity (*aparatva*): “Remoteness and proximity are the causes for the application of the designations and cognitions ‘remote’ and ‘proximate. They are of two kinds: produced by space (*dikkṛta*) and produced by time (*kālakṛta*). Among these, that produced by space indicates a particular location; that produced by time indicates a difference in age.”

Now follows the section beginning with “remoteness” (*paratvam*) for the purpose of defining and examining remoteness (*paratva*) and proximity (*aparatva*). Regarding the statement “remoteness and proximity are the cause of the designation and the cognition [of ‘remote’ and ‘proximate’],” there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) if only this were said; therefore, the terms “remote” and “proximate” are included. Nevertheless, since being the cause of the designation and cognition of “remote” and “proximate” is not excluded from space (*ākāśa*) and the self (*ātman*), the phrase “while being a qualifier” (*viśeṣaṇatve sati*) must be supplied. Likewise, generality (*sāmānya*) is also the cause of the designation and cognition of “remote” and “proximate” while being a qualifier; therefore, the term “substance” (*dravya*) is included. Thus, remoteness and proximity are distinct from other things because they are the cause of the designation and cognition of “remote” and “proximate” while being qualifiers of a substance; whereas that which is not distinct from others does not possess this quality, such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth. Alternatively, the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is what is to be proven. Here, by the word “designation,” he indicates that both forms of usage and cognition are intended: “designation” in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa-vyutpatti*) refers to the definitions of number and so forth, while in the sense of a state (*bhāva-vyutpatti*) it refers to cognition. Furthermore, the definition of two qualities in a single section is because the production of one depends upon the means for the other; if they were defined separately, the treatise would become too voluminous, and thus they are stated together for the sake of conciseness.

In response to the inquiry as to what the proof for the existence of *paratva* (remoteness) and *aparatva* (nearness) is, the statement that "remoteness and nearness are the causes of the designations and cognitions of 'remote' and 'near'" should be applied with a view toward its critical examination (*parīkṣā*). To explain: the cognition and designation of "remote" and "near" must be preceded by a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*), because they are cognitions and designations of a qualified object (*viśeṣya*), just like the cognition and designation of "one who has a staff" (*daṇḍin*). Nor can color (*rūpa*) or any other such quality be the qualifying attribute, because the usage [of the terms] is distinct from their usage. Furthermore, a cognition that is not sublated cannot possibly exist without a cause. It has already been stated that mental impressions (*vāsanā*) do not serve as the cause in this case. Now, could it be that substance (*dravya*) itself—by virtue of a specific production—generates the usage of "remote" and "near"? That is not so, because momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) has been refuted. Even if one were to grant [the point], if one accepts that "specificity" (*viśiṣṭatā*) is distinct [from the substance] and yet maintains that it generates the usage of "specific," it would be a mere difference in nomenclature. If, however, it is not distinct, then the usage of "remote" and "near" would apply even to objects situated in the same place and of the same age, since there would be no difference in the existence of the substance. Therefore, it is known that there exists a cause for the usage of "remote" and "near" that is distinct from color and the other qualities.

He states that it is of two kinds due to the difference in its causes: "produced by space (*dikkṛta*) and produced by time (*kālakṛta*). Now, one might object: since space and time have been declared to be the efficient causes (*nimittakāraṇa*) of all things that arise, it is impossible to specify any particular [distinctions between them]. This is not so; for the conjunctions of space and time with a corporeal object (*piṇḍa*) are what are denoted by those respective terms, and thus their being produced by them is established. That which is produced by the conjunction of space and a corporeal object is "produced by space," and that which is produced by the conjunction of time and a corporeal object is "produced by time. Furthermore, he states the mutual distinction between these two: "Among these, that produced by space indicates a specific location (*deśaviśeṣapratyāyaka*). That which has a specific location as its indicator is "that which indicates a specific location"; or, that which causes a specific location to be known is distinguished from that produced by time. "And that produced by time indicates a difference in age (*vayobhedapratyāyaka*). That which has a difference in age as its indicator is "that which indicates a difference in age"; or, that which causes a difference in age to be known is distinguished from that produced by space.

“In that regard, the production of [priority and posteriority] based on direction is now described. How so? When there is a greater or lesser number of conjunctions with what is conjoined between two objects situated in the same direction, an observer, taking one as the proximate object, forms the notion ‘this is remote from that’ regarding the substratum of priority; thus, depending upon that [notion], priority arises from the conjunction with a more distant spatial region.”

“Likewise, having established a remote limit, the cognition ‘this is near to that’ arises with respect to the other substratum of posteriority. Then, depending upon that [cognition], posteriority is produced through conjunction with a more remote spatial direction.”

“In that regard, the production [of spatial distance] caused by direction (*dik*) is being explained. To the question “How so? following the inquiry of one who has not yet mastered the subject, he says: “Of two masses situated in a single direction,” and so forth. The term “of two masses” is a specification of the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). “Situated in a single direction” means they are not situated in different directions; this is the presentation of a restriction. “When there is a greater or lesser number of conjunctions with what is conjoined” refers to regions of the earth. These are the conjunctions with that which is conjoined [to the observer]; their state of being more or fewer means that in one mass there is a smaller number of conjunctions with the conjoined, while in the other there is a greater number than that. When that is the case, “for a single observer”—not for a different one—“having made the proximate [mass] the limit (*avadhi*), [the thought arises]: ‘This is distant from that’” regarding the substrate of priority (*paratva*) where priority is about to be produced. “A cognition arises; depending upon that, through conjunction with a remote region of space (*dikpradeśa*), priority is produced. The designation of “remote” and “proximate” applied to the two regions of space is metaphorical (*upacāra*), because they bring about that [cognition].

Taking the remote object as the limit, the cognition of proximity arises with respect to the other object due to the cause that there is a smaller number of conjunctions with the points of space in conjunction with it. Depending upon that cognition of proximity, priority (paratva) arises from the conjunction with another spatial point. In this process, the substance is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), the conjunction of space and the substance is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and the specific cognition is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).

But surely, in this case, the cognition of the distant arises by taking the proximate as its limit, and the cognition of the proximate arises by taking the distant as its limit; thus, because the cognitions of the distant and the proximate are mutually dependent, there follows the undesirable consequence that both would be non-existent. That is not so, because that which appears in non-conceptual (nirvikalpaka) cognition is accepted as the limiting factor (*avadhi*). For instance, when both the proximate and the distant appear through perception itself in non-conceptual cognition, the conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) indeed arises: "This is proximate to that," or "This is distant from that."

Others, however, maintain that the state of being mutual limits between the proximate and the remote—which are established by memory arising from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by non-conceptual appearances—is logically consistent. Therefore, it is established that there is no absence of both [proximity and remoteness] due to their being mutually dependent.

“[Question: How [is it produced] even in the case of two things determined by time? [Answer: When there are a young man and an old man existing at the present time, conjoined with indefinite directions and locations, and in the presence of such qualities as a grown beard, roughness, wrinkles, and graying hair for one observer, having taken the young man as the limit (avadhi), a cognition of remoteness arises regarding the old man. Then, depending on that [cognition], through conjunction with a subsequent point of time, there is the production of ‘remoteness’ (paratva). And having taken the old man as the limit, a cognition of proximity arises regarding the young man. Then, depending on that [cognition], through conjunction with a preceding point of time, there is the production of ‘proximity’ (aparatva). (PDhS)

He explains how priority (*paratva*) and posteriority (*aparatva*) arise even when produced by time, stating: “of two [objects] existing in the present time,” and so forth. This is the rule regarding the production of both priority and posteriority as produced by space and time: “of two [objects] whose spatial location is not fixed. This indicates that for those produced by time, there is no fixed spatial direction; that is, their spatial location is not fixed. The phrase “of a youth and an elder” is intended to show the distinction of age, because the conventional usage of “prior” and “posterior” is not observed among those of equal age. Regarding the phrase “when there is the presence of grown beard, coarseness, wrinkles, gray hair, and so forth”: these are the grown beard, coarseness, wrinkles, gray hair, and others; when there is the presence of these, [the qualities arise]. The presence of the grown beard, coarseness, and so forth, is the cause of the cognition of proximity, while the presence of wrinkles, gray hair, and so forth, is the cause of the cognition of remoteness. “Of one observer”: this refers to the observer who desires to perceive priority and posteriority. “Taking the youth as the limit, a cognition of remoteness arises with respect to the elder. Depending upon that cognition of remoteness, priority arises from conjunction with a more distant point of time. Taking the elder—who is remote—as the limit, a cognition of proximity arises with respect to the youth, in the form: “This one is closer than that elder. Depending upon that [cognition], posteriority arises from conjunction with a nearer point of time. In this process, the proximate and remote objects (*piṇḍa*) are the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*); the conjunction between time and the object is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*); and the cognitions of proximity and remoteness are the instrumental causes (*nimittakāraṇa*).

But is this not improper? For when food is consumed, by the principle of the production of cooked qualities (*pākaja*), since there is no distinction in their arising on the same day, there would be an absence of the notions of "near" and "far," and thus distance (*paratva*) and proximity (*aparatva*) would be impossible. This is not so. From birth onwards, within a single continuum of the body (*śarīrasantati*), these [notions] are possible in relation to the revolutions of the sun (*ādityaparivartana*). To explain: for one person, from birth, there have been many revolutions of the sun, while for another, there have been fewer; in relation to that, the notions of "near" and "far" arise. In the case of an elder, because there have been many revolutions of the sun, there is the notion of "far"; in the case of a youth, because there have been fewer, there is the notion of "near. It is precisely in relation to that, and in dependence upon the revolutions of the sun within the continuum of the body, that the production of distance and proximity occurs. Furthermore, since no other cause is possible, it is accepted that the distinction between these two—distance and proximity—is caused by time (*kāla*), as distinct from that produced by space (*dik*). For a confusion [of the two] cannot possibly arise from that very same cause.

Thus, having established the production of priority (*paratva*) and posteriority (*aparatva*), the connection [of these concepts] is demonstrated by the Sūtra. Accordingly, the Sūtra states: "Priority and posteriority [arise] from two things situated at the same direction and time, which are respectively proximate and remote" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra). Those two things which possess a single direction and time are described as such; the phrase "from those two" indicates the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). The expression "from two things at the same direction" establishes a restriction specifically regarding priority and posteriority produced by direction. Similarly, "from two things at the same time" refers to both cases as being at the present time. For priority and posteriority are not produced from non-existent things, nor from things that are both existent and non-existent. By the phrase "proximate and remote," the fact that the cognitions of proximity and remoteness serve as the instrumental causes (*nimittakāraṇa*)—subserving as they do the inherent cause—is already stated. Indeed, as in the Sūtra: "Priority and posteriority depend upon cognition" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra), the word *apekṣā* here functions in the sense of a cause. Furthermore, the Sūtra: "Priority and posteriority [arise] from the priority of the cause and the posteriority of the cause" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra) demonstrates the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).

Now, an objection may be raised: if priority (*paratva*) and posteriority (*aparatva*) exist in an effect due to their dependence on a cause (space) and a cause (time), then—just like color and other qualities—they would be perceived even without the cognitions of "near" and "far," provided the object has existed for a long time; for instance, in the case of two lumps of matter existing in the same place and at the same age, they should both be perceived [as having these qualities]. But this is not the case. If you argue that they are not perceived because they are unmanifested, that is not so, because there is no evidence for their existence [in such a state]. Indeed, when the cognitions of "near" and "far" do exist, the perception of an object just produced is perfectly possible. Therefore, the conjunction of space with a lump of matter and the conjunction of time with a lump of matter are metaphorically designated as "priority" and "posteriority," because they bring about the manifestation of priority and posteriority. Nor should it be said that the analysis of the production and other properties of priority and posteriority is incoherent because they are mutually dependent; for mutual dependence is never observed in all cases. To illustrate: there is no mutual dependence between a seed and a sprout, since the sprout arises after a lapse of time through the process of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*), etc., once the seed has perished. Similarly, once the sprout has perished, subsequent effects arise only upon the destruction of each preceding one; thus, the seed does not arise from the sprout, and so there is an absence of mutual dependence. Likewise, there is no mutual dependence between father and son, or between merit (*dharma*) and the body, because the non-perception of one being the cause of the other's perception is established. However, this does not preclude their causality in relation to other effects. Enough of this digression.

“Destruction [of distance], however, results from the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), the conjunction, and the substance. First, when distance has been produced, at the time when the cognition of the universal (*sāmānyabuddhi*) arises, there is the state of the relative cognition being about to perish; and simultaneously, from the universal, its cognition, and their relation, there is the state of the cognition of the quality of distance (*paratvaguṇabuddhi*) being about to arise—this is one moment. Then, the destruction of the relative cognition occurs and the cognition of the quality arises; then, from the destruction of the relative cognition, there is the state of the quality being about to perish; and simultaneously, from the cognition of the quality, its relation, and their connection, there is the state of the cognition of the substance (*dravyabuddhi*) being about to arise—this is one moment. Then, the cognition of the substance arises and the quality is destroyed. <PDhS>

Thus, since priority (*paratva*) and posteriority (*aparatva*) possess the quality of being produced (*utpattimattva*), they necessarily undergo destruction; and because that destruction has a cause, its cause must be stated. He says: "But destruction [arises] from relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and the destruction of the substance (*dravyavināśa*). This constitutes three ways; and there is another position [that it arises] from the destruction of all three. Thus, destruction is sevenfold.

Regarding that, he first explains destruction through the destruction of the *apekṣābuddhi* (the relative cognition): "When otherness (*paratva*) has arisen," from its own cause—namely, because it serves as a qualifier—there first arises a cognition of the universal (*sāmānya*) due to inherence in that which is inherent in what is conjoined with it (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*). At the very moment that cognition has arisen, there is simultaneously the "state of being about to perish" (*vinaśyattā*) of the *apekṣābuddhi*, which is the presence of the cause of its destruction; and there is the "state of being about to arise" (*utpadyamānatā*) of the cognition of the quality of otherness (*paratvaguṇa*) from the universal, the cognition of that [universal], and their relation, which is the presence of the cause of its production. This constitutes one single moment. Thereafter, there is the destruction of the *apekṣābuddhi* and the arising of the cognition of the quality. From the destruction of the *apekṣābuddhi*, there is the state of the quality being about to perish, and the state of the cognition of the universal being about to perish. And from the quality, its cognition, and their relation, there is the state of the cognition of the substance (*dravyabuddhi*) being about to arise. This constitutes another single moment. Thereafter, there is the arising of the cognition of the substance and the destruction of the quality due to the destruction of the *apekṣābuddhi*, since no other cause for its destruction is perceived.

“How is it [destroyed] even through the destruction of the conjunction? At the very same time as the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), an action arises in the substratum of priority and posteriority. By that action, a disjunction from the point of space (*dik*) and the object is produced; this is one moment, during which the production of priority occurs from the relative cognition. Then, there is the production of the cognition of the universal (*sāmānyabuddhi*) and the destruction of the conjunction between the point of space and the object. Then, at the very time when the cognition of the quality (*guṇabuddhi*) arises, the destruction of the quality occurs due to the destruction of the conjunction between the point of space and the object. <PDhS>

Following the question of an unlearned person as to how destruction occurs even from the destruction of conjunction, [the author] says: "At the very same time as the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), an action arises in the substratum of priority and posteriority. This is one moment: the disjunction [from the previous location], and the arising of priority and posteriority; the production of the cognition of the universal (*sāmānyabuddhi*); and the state of the conjunction between the direction and the object being about to perish. "Then, from the cognition of the universal, there is the destruction of the conjunction between the direction and the object. From the knowledge of the universal, the relative cognition enters a state of perishing; the cognition of the quality (*guṇabuddhi*) enters a state of arising; and from the destruction of the conjunction, the quality enters a state of perishing. "Then, at the very time when the cognition of the quality arises," because of the destruction of the non-inherent cause—the conjunction between the direction and the object—"there is the destruction of the quality," namely priority. (From the knowledge of the universal, the relative cognition is also destroyed. For this very reason, the destruction of the relative cognition is the cause of the destruction of the quality, because they are simultaneous.)

“How [is it] even from the destruction of the substance? An action arises in a part of the substratum of priority; at the very same time that it produces a disjunction from another part, the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) arises. Then, at the very same time that the conjunction is destroyed by that disjunction, priority (*paratva*) arises. Thereafter, from the destruction of the conjunction comes the destruction of the substance, and from its destruction comes the destruction of the quality (*guṇa*) residing therein.”

He explains how destruction occurs even from the destruction of the substance: "An action arises in the part that is the locus of the otherness (*paratva*). At the time when [the action] begins the disjunction from another part—which is the opposite of the conjunction that initiates the substance—there is the state of the conjunction being about to perish. At that very same time, the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) arises from its own causes, and there is the state of the otherness (*paratva*) being produced. At the time when, due to the disjunction, there is the destruction of the conjunction that initiates the substance and the state of the substance being about to perish, at that very same time the otherness (*paratva*) is produced; there is the state of the cognition of its universal (*sāmānyajñāna*) being produced. Then, from the destruction of the conjunction, there is the destruction of the substance; from the production of the cognition of the universal, there is the state of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) being about to perish, and also the state of the quality of otherness (*paratvaguṇa*) being about to perish. Then, from the destruction of the substance, there is the destruction of the quality dependent upon it; and from the cognition of the universal, there is the destruction of the relative cognition. Because these occur earlier, the destruction of the substratum alone is the cause for the destruction of the quality.

“Also, how [is it destroyed] due to the simultaneous destruction of both the substance and the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*)? When action arises in a part of the substratum of priority (*paratva*), at that very same time the relative cognition arises; by that action, disjunction from another part is produced, and the production of priority occurs—this is one moment. Then, at the very same time that the conjunction initiating the substance is destroyed due to the disjunction of the parts, the cognition of the universal (*sāmānyabuddhi*) arises. Immediately thereafter, the destruction of the substance follows from the destruction of the conjunction, and the destruction of the relative cognition follows from the cognition of the universal—this is one moment. Consequently, from the destruction of both the substance and the relative cognition, there is the destruction of priority.”

How is it that the destruction of priority (*paratva*) and posteriority (*aparatva*) occurs through the simultaneous destruction of both the substance and the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*)? To this he says: “When action arises in a part of the substratum of posteriority—wherein posteriority is about to arise—at that very moment the relative cognition arises, [the state of] posteriority being in the process of arising; and by that action, a disjunction arises from another part which is opposed to the conjunction that originates the substance, [the state of] that conjunction being in the process of perishing, the production of posteriority occurs, and the cognition of its universal (*sāmānyajñāna*) is in the process of arising: these constitute one single moment. “Then, at the very same time that the destruction of the conjunction originating the substance occurs due to the disjunction, [the state of] the substance being in the process of perishing, ‘at that very same time the cognition of the universal arises’; the relative cognition is in the process of perishing. ‘Immediately thereafter, from the destruction of the conjunction comes the destruction of the substance, and from the cognition of the universal comes the destruction of the relative cognition’; [the state of] the quality being in the process of perishing: these constitute one single moment. ‘Then, from the destruction of both the substance and the relative cognition,’ the ‘destruction of the posteriority’ residing therein occurs. Since the individual capacity of each to cause the destruction of the quality elsewhere has been established, and since both exist at a preceding time, their status as causes in this case is determined.”

“How is it [destroyed] even by the destruction of the substance’s conjunction? When an action has arisen in a part of the substratum of ‘remoteness’ (paratva) and produces a disjunction from another part, at that very same time there is the simultaneous arising of the action in the whole (piṇḍa) and the relative cognition (apekṣābuddhi). Then, at the very moment that ‘remoteness’ arises, at that same time, the destruction of the conjunction that initiates the substance occurs due to the disjunction; and by the action in the whole, a disjunction between the whole and space is produced—this is one single moment. Then, at the very moment that the cognition of the universal (sāmānyabuddhi) arises, at that same time, the destruction of the whole occurs because of the destruction of the conjunction that initiated the substance, and from the destruction of the whole, the destruction of the conjunction with the whole follows. Then, simultaneously with the cognition of the quality (guṇabuddhi), the destruction of ‘remoteness’ occurs due to the destruction of the conjunction between the whole and the whole-in-space. <PDhS>

He explains how the destruction of priority (*paratva*) and posteriority (*aparatva*) occurs even due to the destruction of the substance's conjunction: "When action arises in a constituent part [of the substance]—that is, in a constituent part of the substratum of priority—it produces a disjunction from another constituent part, while the [original] conjunction is in a state of perishing. At that very same time, action and the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) arise simultaneously in the aggregate (*piṇḍa*), which is their inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), from their own respective causes; and at that same time, the disjunction between the direction and the aggregate, as well as the arising of priority and posteriority, occur. This is one moment. Then, at the very time priority arises, there is the state of the general cognition (*sāmānyajñāna*) of that quality being about to arise. At that same time, due to the disjunction of the parts, the conjunction that initiates the substance is destroyed; the substance is in a state of perishing; and by the action of the aggregate, a disjunction between the direction and the aggregate is produced, while the [original] conjunction is in a state of perishing. This is one moment. Then, at the very time the general cognition arises, there is the state of the cognition of the quality (*guṇabuddhi*) being about to arise, and the relative cognition is in a state of perishing. Simultaneously with that, from the destruction of the conjunction, the destruction of the aggregate occurs; and from the disjunction, the destruction of the conjunction between the direction and the aggregate occurs, while the quality is in a state of perishing. Then, simultaneous with the cognition of the quality, from the destruction of both the aggregate and the conjunction, there is the destruction of priority; and from the general cognition, there is the destruction of the relative cognition. Precisely because of this simultaneity, the destruction of the relative cognition is not the cause [of the destruction of priority]. Since the destruction of the aggregate and the conjunction have been determined elsewhere to possess causal capacity, they are the causes because they exist at the preceding moment."

“[How is it] also due to the simultaneous destruction of the conjunction and the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*)? When remoteness (*paratva*) arises, at that time there is motion in the substratum of remoteness; then, at the very same time that the cognition of the generality (*sāmānya*) of remoteness arises, the disjunction between the direction and the object is produced by the motion of the mass. Thereafter, the destruction of the relative cognition follows from the cognition of the generality, and the destruction of the conjunction between the direction and the object follows from the disjunction; thus, these occur at one and the same time. Then, from the destruction of both the conjunction and the relative cognition, the destruction of remoteness occurs.”

He explains how destruction occurs even due to the simultaneous destruction of the conjunction and the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*): "When the quality of 'remoteness' (*paratva*) arises" (*yadā paratvam utpadyate*), meaning when the general cognition of the cause of remoteness is in the process of arising; "at that time, in the substratum of remoteness" (*tadā paratvādhāre*), action arises from its own cause, and the disjunction is in the process of arising; "then, at the very same moment when the cognition of the generality of remoteness arises" (*tato yasminneva kāle paratvasāmānyabuddhir utpadyate*), meaning when the cognition of the quality is in the process of arising and the relative cognition is in the state of perishing; "at that very same moment, by means of the action of the body, a disjunction between the direction and the body is produced" (*tasminneva kāle piṇḍakarmaṇā dikpiṇḍavibhāgaḥ kriyate*), and the conjunction with that [direction] is in the state of perishing. "Then, from the cognition of the generality, the destruction of the relative cognition occurs, and from the disjunction, the destruction of the conjunction between the direction and the body occurs" (*tataḥ sāmānyabuddhito 'pekṣābuddhivināśo vibhāgācca dikpiṇḍasaṃyogavināśaḥ*); this is the state of the quality being in the process of perishing—all at one and the same time. "Then, from the destruction of the conjunction and the relative cognition, the destruction of remoteness occurs" (*tataḥ saṃyogāpekṣābuddhyor vināśāt paratvasya vināśaḥ*). Thus it is said.

“How also [is it destroyed] from the simultaneous destruction of the three causes—the inherent, the non-inherent, and the instrumental? When the cognition of relative distance (*apekṣābuddhi*) arises, at that same time there is motion in the constituent part of the mass; then, at the very moment that the motion produces a disjunction from another part, and the cognition of relative distance and the quality of priority (*paratva*) arise, at that same time there is also motion in the mass itself. Then, from the disjunction of the parts, there is the destruction of the conjunction that originated the mass; and by the motion of the mass, a disjunction from space is produced, as well as the arising of the cognition of the universal. This constitutes one moment. Thereafter, from the destruction of the conjunction comes the destruction of the mass; from the disjunction comes the destruction of the conjunction between the mass and space; and from the cognition of the universal comes the destruction of the cognition of relative distance—all this occurring simultaneously. Thus, from the destruction of these three causes—the inherent, the non-inherent, and the instrumental—the destruction of priority occurs.”

He explains how destruction occurs even from the simultaneous destruction of the three factors—the inherent (*samavāyin*), non-inherent (*asamavāyin*), and instrumental (*nimitta*) causes—by stating: "When the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) arises," this is the state of *paratva* (priority/otherness) being produced. "At that time, there is motion in the part of the aggregate (*piṇḍāvayave karma*)," which is the state of disjunction (*vibhāga*) being produced. Then, at the very same moment when a disjunction is produced from another part—one which opposes the conjunction that initiates the substance—there is the state of the conjunction [of the part] being destroyed due to the motion of the part; there is the production of *paratva*; and there is the state of the cognition of its universal (*sāmānyajñāna*) being produced. At that very same time, there is also motion in the aggregate itself arising from its own cause; there is the state of disjunction being produced; then, from that disjunction, there is the destruction of the conjunction that initiates the aggregate, the state of the aggregate being destroyed, and a disjunction is also produced by the motion of the aggregate. <II,102> There is the state of the conjunction between the direction and the aggregate being destroyed, the production of the cognition of the universal, the state of the relative cognition being destroyed, and the state of the cognition of the quality (*guṇabuddhi*) being produced—all at one and the same time. Thereafter, from the destruction of the conjunction comes the destruction of the aggregate; from the disjunction comes the destruction of the conjunction between the direction and the aggregate; and from the cognition of the universal comes the destruction of the relative cognition—all of this occurs simultaneously. Thus, from the destruction of these three—the inherent, non-inherent, and instrumental causes—there is the destruction of *paratva*. For while in other cases the causality of these factors is observed individually, here they occur combined; therefore, it is appropriate to present the multiple possible causes for the destruction of a quality.

{The nature of cognition} (*buddhidharmyam*). Now, for the purpose of defining and examining cognition (*buddhi*), which has reached its proper occasion, there is this section beginning with “Cognition is apprehension” (*buddhirupalabdhiḥ*). The term “cognition” (*buddhi*) is repeated; it serves both as the designation of the object to be defined (*lakṣya-nirdeśa*) and as the designation of the definition (*lakṣaṇa-nirdeśa*). To explain: “cognition” is the designation of the object to be defined. “Cognition, apprehension, knowledge, and conceptualization are synonyms” is the definition.

Now, since they exist in space (*ākāśa*) in the form of synonymous words (*paryāya-śabda-rūpa*), how can they be the definition of cognition (*buddhi*), given that they belong to a different substratum? [The answer is: Because they possess the nature of that [cognition] through the relationship of the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācakabhāva*). Furthermore, the statement of the definition of synonyms here is for the purpose of making known the diversity of definitions. For instance, it is not only the definition consisting of function, instrument, and so forth, because of its uniqueness; it is also of the nature of synonyms.

Now, might there not be an inconsistency (vyabhicāra) because words, by virtue of conforming to human intention, can function even with respect to other meanings? No, because [the reason] is qualified by the fact that it has been transmitted through a stream extending from beginningless time. For instance: "Cognition is distinct from other things, because it is denotable by such synonyms as have been transmitted through a stream from beginningless time; whereas that which is not distinct from others is not thus [denoted], just like color-form (rūpa) and so forth. Alternatively, linguistic usage (vyavahāra) may be the probandum.

Now, one might object: "Are there not other synonyms for *buddhi* as well? Therefore, you must state the specific reason for defining [the self] by means of these alone, while excluding those others. This specific reason is that it is precisely regarding these that there is disagreement; thus, this statement, though intended as a definition, effectively serves to refute those [other views] by its own force.

And so the Sāṃkhyas [maintain]: the first modification of the *pradhāna* is the intellect (*buddhi*), like the swelling of a seed. The *pradhāna* is the state of equilibrium among *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; its modification is disequilibrium. Experience (*upalabdhi*), however, is the arising of a reflection of the self (*ātman*) in the intellect when it has transformed into the form of pleasure and pain; this is enjoyment (*bhoga*). As Āsuri said: "The experience of this [self] is said to consist in a transformation within the intellect through the faculty of distinct vision; it is the arising of a reflection, just as that of the moon in clear water. (Āsuri)

Thus [it is said]. That [intellect] whose modification is the modification of the sense organs into the form of the object of isolated vision is so described. When that intellect exists, the experience (*bhoga*) of the Self (*ātman*) is said to occur. Of what nature is it? It is the arising of a reflection (*pratibimba*), not something real (*vāstava*). Just as the reflection of the moon occurs in clear water, but not in turbid water; likewise, [the reflection occurs] in the intellect when it is augmented by such a specific modification. For if experience were real for the *puruṣa*, there would be a transformation consisting in the cessation of its prior nature and the assumption of another nature. And in that case, because [the *puruṣa*] is insentient, many faults would follow.

Others, however, conceive of experience in another way. As [Vindhyavāsī] says: "The person, whose self is indeed unmodified, causes the mind—which is conscious by its own reflection—to act through mere proximity, just as a crystal [is affected] by an adjunct."
Thus.

Due to proximity, a crystal—which is not of that nature—becomes the appearance of its adjunct (*upādhi*), assuming its own reflection and its own form. In the same way, this *puruṣa*, whose essential nature is unchanging, makes the insentient mind appear as if it were sentient through its own reflection due to proximity; yet, in reality, the *puruṣa* does not possess sentience, because it is immutable. Knowledge, however, is a transformation of the intellect (*buddhi*) by virtue of the senses transforming into the form of the object. Then, perceiving the *puruṣa* to be eager for experience, the intention (*ākūti*) of the intellect arises. From the perception of that intention, the senses undergo a transformation into the form of the object, resulting from the cessation of their previous state. For otherwise, if they did not abandon their prior form, there would be no cognition of the object afterwards, just as there was before. Furthermore, the transformation into the form of the object is to be understood through the determination of specific functions, such as "this is of blue" or "this is of yellow. For otherwise, in the absence of the object's form, there would be no distinction in the transformation, and thus this determination would not exist. Thus, when the senses have transformed into the form of the object, the intellect transforms by assuming that same form.
Likewise, the fifty cognitive states such as non-accomplishment (*asiddhi*) and so forth are merely specific transformations of the intellect (*buddhi*).

Non-accomplishment has eight varieties, contentment (*tuṣṭi*) has nine, and the divisions of error (*viparyaya*) are five; likewise, incapacity (*aśakti*) is of twenty-eight kinds—such are the divisions of non-accomplishment and contentment.

Since there are seventeen [defects] and eleven obstructions of the faculties, making fifty in total, the synonymy of terms such as *buddhi* and the rest is not established, because they denote distinct meanings. Furthermore, words that denote a single object are synonyms only when they possess an identical ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*).

This is incorrect, because these terms are perceived as synonyms through their usage. For instance, *buddhaḥ*, *upalabdhaḥ*, *jñātaḥ*, and *pratītaḥ* are understood to have a single meaning when employed in reference to one and the same object. If they possessed distinct meanings, there would be the cognition that "one who has apprehended (*upalabdha*) is not necessarily enlightened (*buddha*)," or "one who has known (*jñāta*) is not necessarily cognizant (*pratīta*). But this is not the case. Furthermore, since the non-existence of the primary principle (*pradhāna*) will be stated later, there can be no existence of the intellect (*buddhi*), which is its modification. Due to its absence, there is no reflection of the intellect in the Self; consequently, there is no apprehension, nor its transformation, nor knowledge, nor cognition [belonging to the Self]. If experience were not real, there would be no distinction between the transmigrating Self and the liberated one, because the consciousness residing in itself (*svaniṣṭhā cit*) is identical in both cases.

Nor should it be argued that, despite there being no difference in their all-pervasiveness (*vyāpitva*), the reflection occurs only for the intellect (*buddhi*) associated with the transmigrating self (*saṃsāryātman*) due to its specific proximity, and not for any other [intellect]. For the relationship between the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*) and the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) must be examined, since enjoyment itself is unreal. Nor is karma alone the regulator, because karma is produced by the intellect. To explain: karma produced by the intellect would be enjoyable by all persons (*puruṣa*) alike, as there is no specific relationship [of the intellect] with any one person. Furthermore, the intellect cannot be the agent (*kartṛ*) because it is insentient (*acetana*). Indeed, consciousness (*caitanya*) does not engage in the performance of actions. For agency is independence (*svātantrya*), whereas instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) is dependence (*pāratantrya*); since these two consist of affirmation and negation respectively, agency must be admitted to belong to the person (*puruṣa*) alone. Nor does the person incur the state of transformation (*pariṇāmitva*) when acting after previously not having acted, because an effect is produced when the totality of causal factors (*kāraka-sākalya*) is present and is not produced when they are deficient. Moreover, the presence or absence of this totality or deficiency occurs through manifestation (*āvirbhāva*) and disappearance (*tirobhāva*), and thus the Self (*ātman*) does not undergo such change, as it is distinct from them. Therefore, if the person is the agent, it is logical that he possesses real enjoyment (*bhoktṛtva*). Otherwise, how could an indifferent (*udāsīna*) being who does not perform the act of enjoying be a "enjoyer," given that enjoyment consists in the experience of pleasure and pain? Being the substratum (*ādhāra*) of that [experience] is what constitutes being an enjoyer.

As for the claim that the form of the intellect (*buddhi*) arises from its conceiving a desire for human enjoyment, and that this occurs through the perception of that [desire] by the sense organs—this is incorrect, because they are insentient. For both the intellect and the sense organs are insentient; in the absence of perception of intention in them, how could there be a determined transformation into the form of an object?
