As for the person (*puruṣa*), however, there is no "desire for enjoyment" other than his nature as consciousness. Furthermore, regarding this transformation of the sense organs into the form of an object, the fact that they take on the form of the object is not a proof for the restriction of each specific action (*pratikarmavyavasthā*), because that [restriction] exists even without it, according to the reasoning to be stated later. If the intellect undergoes a transformation into the form of the sense organs upon the cessation of its prior form, then, since there is no difference from its own nature, it would follow that the very arising and ceasing belong to the intellect itself. If [the transformations] were different [from the intellect], there would be an absence of recognition and so forth; for one person is not able to recognize an object perceived by another. Moreover, since the modifications of the intellect exist in identity with it, if those [modifications] are manifold, the intellect must also be manifold; otherwise, if the reverse were true, their identity would be lost.

Furthermore, as for these fifty conditions which are specific transformations of the intellect (*buddhi*), they are not preceded by conscious intent (*abuddhipūrvaka*), because those specific transformations are infinite. Nor can they be included within these [fifty] alone, since no restriction to their specific characteristics is observed. Enough of this digression.
("And that [intellect] is of many kinds, due to the infinity of objects and because it is restricted to each respective object. <PDhS>

Thus, it being established that the synonyms such as *buddhi* (intellection) and so forth are intended as definitions once the opposing views have been excluded, a doubt arises because of the perception of both unity and multiplicity in that which is defined by the definition, as well as due to conflicting opinions. To dispel this doubt, the statement “And that [intellection] is of many kinds” is given. Why is this so? Because “of the infinity of objects and because of its restriction to each respective object.”

[Objection: But is it not the case that "the infinity of objects" (*arthānantyam*) is a property of the object (*artha-dharma*), and thus there is a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vyadhikaraṇatvam*)? [Reply: No, because that is established in another way. To explain: "the infinity of objects for cognition" (*buddher arthānantyam*) is a presentation of the object; and the proof for this is "because of having infinite objects" (*anantārthatvāt*). That which has infinite objects is so described; the state of being such is "having infinite objects. Now, "object" (*artha*)—derived from the sense "that by which something is sought" (*arthyate anena*)—refers to the totality of causal factors (*kāraka-sāmagrī*), not to a single part of those factors, since we observe that the effect remains the same even when those factors differ. For instance, a jar or similar thing is seen to be a single entity produced by many causal factors. However, the totality of factors, being restricted to each specific effect, does not deviate from that [singularity of] effect despite the difference in its constituent parts. Therefore, cognition is of manifold kinds because of having infinite objects—that is, because it is produced by a totality of infinite causal factors—just like a jar or the like. And that which is one is not produced by a totality of infinite causal factors, as is the case with a jar. One should not, however, interpret the proof as intending "being produced by a totality of infinite objective causal factors" (*ananta-karma-kāraka-janyatva*) through an objective derivation (*karmavyutpatti*), because that would be redundant given the phrase "because of being restricted to each respective object" (*pratyarthaniyatatvāt*). To explain: cognition is restricted toward each individual object; as manyfold as the objective causal factor is divided according to its various distinctions, so manyfold are the cognitions. Thus, cognition is of manifold kinds because it is restricted to each respective object, like the sense of smell and the other senses.

Others, however, maintain that in the very first sentence, by interpreting the term through the *karmavyutpatti* (the sense of being produced), the property of being produced by an infinite number of objective factors (*karmakāraka*) is indeed obtained as the "means" (*sādhana*). Thus, they believe that what is intended is "being restricted to each respective object" (*pratyarthaniyatatva*), which is precisely "residing in each individual self" (*pratyātmavṛttitva*). For instance, the meaning of "self" (*ātman*) is that in which [something] is sought (*arthyate*); "being restricted toward that" is exactly "residing in each individual self. Since a universal (*sāmānya*) resides in an infinite number of selves, it does not possess the quality of being restricted to each individual self. Therefore, even though this [property of residing in each self] is possible [for cognition], because cognition is a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*), the qualification "provided it is a specific quality" (*viśeṣaguṇatve sati*) must be supplied.

Others, however, maintain that because the diversity of cognitions—such as the cognition of form, the cognition of taste, and so forth—is established by perception itself, the two terms [in the definition] are intended to demonstrate the mutual difference between the cognition of Īśvara and our own cognition; for [the former] has infinite objects, whereas [the latter] is restricted to each respective object. For instance, the cognition of Īśvara differs from our cognition because its objects are infinite, and our cognition differs from the cognition of Īśvara because it is restricted to each respective object. In this regard, one must consider how this specific distinction is obtained, since the multiplicity of cognitions was asserted only in a general sense.

Now, since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of an object apart from consciousness, it is untenable that objects are infinite or that [consciousness] is restricted to each individual object. To explain: consciousness, because its nature is self-luminous, illuminates itself; objects, however, are insentient by nature—how could they be illuminated? If it is maintained that consciousness, when grasped, is the illuminator, then if one accepts that this [consciousness] is also grasped by another consciousness, the intended object would remain unilluminated due to being exhausted in a succession of cognitions. Nor can it be said that even if the preceding cognition is not grasped, the object alone is grasped; for when those [preceding cognitions] are present, the object possesses the characteristics of being graspable. As it has been said:

Without having grasped that preceding cognition—which has attained the status of being an object of apprehension, which is proximate, and which is the producer—how could a subsequent cognition grasp another [object]? (PV 2.515)

Now, is it that even when not grasped, [cognition] reveals its object? If so, then it would reveal all objects arising even in other mental continua (*santāna*). For just as what has arisen within one's own continuum reveals its object even while remaining ungrasped, so too it would be in another continuum, since there is no distinction between them. Alternatively, is it that in one's own continuum, cognition reveals its object only when it is self-cognized (*svasaṃvedya*)? If so, then an entity that is a distinct thing from the nature of consciousness (*bodha*) would never be revealed at all. To explain: if these objects were of the nature of light (*prakāśa*), how could they be separate from consciousness? Because consciousness itself is of that nature, and if they were not of the nature of light, they would never be revealed. Therefore, it is cognition alone that is designated as such because its very essence is light. Indeed, existence (*sattva*) is pervaded by being of the nature of light; and that [nature], being excluded from external objects, excludes existence itself which it pervades. Thus, things distinct from consciousness are non-existent.

Furthermore, since consciousness is by nature consciousness and thus lacks distinction in all cases, it could not possess the quality of illuminating specific objects. Now, if you maintain that cognition possesses a form (*sākāra*) because of the systematic determination of each respective object—such as "this belongs to blue" and "this belongs to yellow"—then let cognition alone be that which possesses the form; enough with the postulation of an external object. As it has been said:
"If the intellect possesses a form such as blue and so forth, what would be the basis for an external object? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.433).

Likewise, since the object does not exist at the time of cognition, and the cognition does not exist at the time of the object, how can there be a relationship of apprehended and apprehender (*grāhyagrāhakabhāva*) between them? For that relationship cannot exist between what is existent and what is non-existent. Furthermore, if the simultaneous arising of both were admitted at one and the same time, there would be no distinction as to which is the apprehended and which is the apprehender. Nor can there be a relationship of apprehended and apprehender when cognition and the object are restricted to their own respective natures, because it is impossible to perceive a dependence upon the object. Similarly, by means of the refutation of the composite whole (*avayavin*), it is established that there is merely an aggregate of form and so forth, and that this aggregate is not something other than the constituent parts. In this state, the object simply does not exist, because the aggregate does not appear as an ultimate reality (*paramārthasat*). As for those atoms which are ultimately real, they do not become objects of our perception, because they are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). And since the effect is not ultimately real, its appearance is itself without any logical mark (*aliṅga*). Therefore, the distinction between apprehended and apprehender is merely a portion of consciousness itself, arising through the power of beginningless predispositions (*vāsanā*). This is what he says:

Although the nature of cognition is undivided, it appears as if possessed of the distinction between the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and self-awareness to those whose vision is distorted;
however, this is not so from the perspective of ultimate reality. Thus he says:
There is nothing other than cognition to be experienced by cognition, nor is there any other experience of it;
due to the absence of the grasped and the grasper, it manifests by itself. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.327)

[Objection: But then, how is the manifestation "I know blue with my eye" to be explained? For instance, "blue" is the object (*karman*), "I" is the agent (*kartṛ*), "I know" is the action (*kriyā*), and "with the eye" is the instrument (*karaṇa*). Since these appear as having mutually distinct forms, is it not the talk of a madman to assert their non-difference? [Reply: This is not so. For this [manifestation] is possible even in the case of one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*), just like the seeing of two moons. Just as for one with ophthalmia a cognition arises in that form even in the absence of an external object, so too, even though the object and other factors are non-existent, a cognition arises in that form due to the power of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*). [Objection: Now, the cognition of hair and so forth by one with ophthalmia is devoid of an object because it is sublated (*bādhyamānatvāt*), but this [cognition of blue, etc. is not so. [Reply: That is incorrect, because the very relationship between the sublated and the sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) is impossible. To explain: cognition is not sublated by an object. For if sublation occurred through what is perceived or what is not perceived, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If sublation were by means of what is perceived, then every cognition would be sublatable; the same would apply if it were by means of what is not perceived.

Now, if it is argued that knowledge is sublated by knowledge itself, even in that case, it cannot be by means of a cognition having a different object, because that would entail the sublation of the cognition of taste and so forth by the cognition of color. If, however, they have the same object, then [the latter] would simply be a producer [of the former], not a sublater. Furthermore, neither the arising nor the destruction of a cognition constitutes sublation, because that would entail such a state for every cognition whatsoever. If it is argued that sublation is the occurrence of falsity due to the shifting toward another object, that is incorrect; for an object takes the form of the direct object (karman) of an action, and since the very object where a cognition arises is its [proper] object, shifting toward another object is unestablished. Since the existence of the relationship between the sublated and the sublater is itself unestablished in the case of consciousness (*vijñāna*), there is no such thing as false cognition. Nor is there correctness in consciousness, due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Now, is it the correspondence with purposeful action (*arthakriyā-saṃvāda*) that constitutes valid cognition? No; for even in that case, if there were a requirement for a further corroborating factor, it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), and without a corroborator, the establishment of correctness is not achieved. Furthermore, even purposeful action does not differ from cognition, because everything that appears is non-distinct from cognition. As it has been said: "Because it is manifest, that which manifests its own nature is like light; just as light is accepted [as self-manifesting], so too is cognition the knower of itself. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.329)
Thus [it is said].
And if the intrinsic nature and so forth of objects were such that the appearance of one was exactly like that of all, then there would be no discrepancy; but this is not the case.
For instance, to those whose senses are afflicted by spells and the like, things such as fragments of clay appear [as other things].
"They appear in one way, even though they are devoid of that [external] form" (PV 2.355).

Now, what is the proof for the claim that there is an appearance in another way for those whose eyes are afflicted? It is the observation by those whose eyes are unafflicted that it appears exactly as it is. Thus he says:
"Because of the observation of those with unafflicted eyes, it appears exactly as it is."
"Just as in deserts, even a large object appears small when it is at a distance" (Pramāṇavārttika 2.356).

He demonstrates this very lack of stability with the second half [of the verse]: when things are thus analyzed one by one by the intellect, their form (*rūpa*) does not remain established. For just as, when threads are analyzed, the cloth lacks stability—since the threads do not exist apart from the fibers (*aṃśu*), and so forth—it should be inferred accordingly. [Objection: How then do the Śākyas engage in activities such as bathing, given that external objects do not exist? [Reply: It is by following worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*). Just as unexamining people proceed by apprehending an external object through the power of ignorance, so too do the examiners; for according to the principle, "In regard to worldly convention, the fool and the wise man are alike."

This is incorrect, because it would follow that there could be no distinction in cognition in the absence of a distinction in the object. Cognitions such as "the cognition of color" and "the cognition of taste," which manifest with mutually exclusive natures, require that a distinction in the object be admitted. Alternatively, if you argue that the distinction in cognition arises from a distinction in latent impressions (*vāsanā*), then even if that impression produces a specific cognition, if it is distinct from the cognition itself, there is merely a difference in terminology. If, however, it is not distinct, then both [the cognition and the impression] would be identical in nature and thus indistinguishable in all cases; consequently, there would be no variety such as "cognition of color" versus "cognition of taste. Nor can the distinction in cognition arise from a distinction in form (*ākāra*), since that too is impossible. To explain: if cognition in general possessed real forms, then the cognition of blue and so forth would be valid (*pramāṇa*) due to having real forms, while the cognition of two moons and so forth would be invalid (*apramāṇa*) due to having unreal forms—thus destroying the distinction between them, since the quality of having a real form would be indistinguishable everywhere. If, on the other hand, the form were unreal, then the admission of any distinction [between cognitions] would be lost. Furthermore, there would be no established rule for victory and defeat between the proponent and the opponent, as there would be no difference in their engagement through what is invalid.

Furthermore, that which is unreal cannot possess identity with consciousness, because oneness is never observed between the existent and the non-existent, like a donkey and a horn. For this very reason, [Dharmakīrti] stated:
"Because they are necessarily perceived together, there is no difference between the blue and the cognition thereof" (Prajñākaramati’s *Bhāṣya*, p. 127).

Thus, this proof for oneness is the speech of a madman. For if non-existent [cognition] were identical with existence, it would possess existence; but if it were identical with non-existence, it would possess that very nature [of non-existence]. Likewise, if "simultaneous apprehension" (*sahopalambha*)—as established by the opponent—is necessarily pervaded by difference alone, then the reason would be contradictory (*viruddha*). Alternatively, if you intend "simultaneous apprehension" to mean either assistance (*sāhāyya*) or simultaneity (*yaugapadya*), even so, because those two are pervaded by difference alone, the reason remains contradictory. Furthermore, there is an instance of deviation (*vyabhicāra*): an omniscient being apprehends another's mind along with his own, yet that [other's mind] is not non-different from it; otherwise, it would follow that everyone is omniscient. Nor can the restriction of apprehension to a single subject be the reason, because it is not the meaning of the word [used in the argument], and because it is indistinguishable from the probandum (*sādhya*). Moreover, since that object consists of multiple parts such as color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, when it is apprehended, the reason is also unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*).

Now, is the restriction to simultaneous apprehension (*ekopalambhaniyama*) due to the non-existence of external objects? That is not so, because it would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). For instance, the non-existence of external objects would be established on the basis of the restriction to simultaneous apprehension, and the restriction to simultaneous apprehension would be established on the basis of that [non-existence]; thus, the absence of one would result in the absence of the other. Furthermore, if you argue that the probans (*sādhana*) is "being apprehended by the very same [cognition]," this is not the case, because the non-existence of cognition by another [person] is unestablished (*aprasiddha*). As for the object, it is indeed apprehended by others at the same moment; therefore, "being apprehended by the very same [cognition]" is unestablished. The examples of the real moon and the unreal moon are deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*) and deficient in the probans (*sādhanavikala*), because there is no apprehension of an unreal moon as being existent, given the contradiction between existence and non-existence.

Likewise, cognition has the nature of the grasper (*grāhaka*), while blue and so forth have the nature of the grasped (*grāhya*); thus, due to a difference in their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), there is a distinction between these two, just as there is between white and yellow. For if they were non-different, then cognition would also be the grasped object of the blue, and the blue would be the grasper of the cognition. But this is not the case; furthermore, due to a difference in causes, cognition is a distinct entity from the blue. To explain: "From cognition comes the nature of being cognition," "from the sense organ comes the determination of the specific object," and "from the object comes the apprehension of the form. Because of these differences in cause, there is indeed a difference among them. Now, if it is argued that there is no difference in causes, what then? It is merely a difference in exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). Cognition is the exclusion of non-cognition; having a form is the exclusion of formlessness; and the determination of the specific object is the exclusion of what is not of that nature. If that is so, then since activity is impossible within the nature of exclusions—such as the blue, the cognition, the eye, the form, the cognition itself, and the determination of the object—they would simply not be causes, because an exclusion is not a real entity (*avasturūpa*). If, on the other hand, the exclusion of non-cognition and so forth is not different from the excluded cognition itself, then, because cognition would possess a single nature, the demonstration of a difference in causes would be incoherent. Therefore, the difference between the blue and its cognition arises precisely from a difference in causes. As for the appearance of a variegated [object], one must consider how a consciousness possessing multiple forms such as blue, yellow, and so forth could exist if it were mere cognition. For instance, if those forms were identical with a single cognition, they would be one; or if they were identical with it, the cognition would be many—an unavoidable consequence.

Now, if it is argued that there are as many cognitions as there are forms (*ākāra*) therein, then, because those [forms] are restricted to specific objects, there would be an absence of variegated manifestation (*citrapratibhāsa*). Nor is the restriction of cognition to each respective object (*pratikarmavyavasthā*) a valid means of proof (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of forms, since this restriction occurs even otherwise. For instance, although there is no difference in being produced by all the causal factors (*kāraka*), blue is designated by its very action (*vyāpāra*) in the form of the object (*karman*), and not because it imparts a form. Even though all [factors] are equally producers, one must state the specific reason why only the object imparts the form. If it is argued that the object alone imparts the form because it functions in the form of the object, then let the status of being the object itself be the cause for the restriction of designation; what is the use of postulating an impossible form? For if blue and so forth imparted an uncommon form, they would lack the nature of consciousness (*bodharūpatā*); if, however, they impart a common form, there would be no restriction of cognition to each respective object.

Now, if it is argued that there is no such fault because consciousness possesses a superimposed form (*samāropitākāra*), that is incorrect. For in the absence of a persisting self (*ātman*), how could a form be superimposed upon the nature of cognition? First of all, that which has not yet arisen or that which has already perished cannot be a superimposer. Nor can it occur at the very moment of arising, because at the time of acquiring its own being (*ātmalābha*), an activity of superimposition is impossible. Therefore, since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of such a form, it is logical to conclude that this distinction [in cognition] arises solely from the specific object itself.

Now, since objects are by nature non-luminous (*aprakāśasvarūpa*), how can there be illumination (*prakāśa*) of them? It is simply the arising of a cognition whose object is that [thing]. For it is the case that when a cognition has arisen with respect to a certain object, that object alone is apprehended and no other; thus, the relationship between object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) acts as the regulator. Therefore, cognition is the illumination of the object, but it is not an illuminator [in the sense of being a separate agent]. The dilemma—whether that which is grasped is the illuminator of the object or that which is not grasped—is irrelevant to the opponent's position, because they accept that the entire collection of causal factors (*kāraka-jāta*), such as the eye and so forth, is the illuminator of the object. Furthermore, in cases where cognition or a specific inferential mark (*liṅga*) is present, the operation of the grasped [cognition] in the determination of the object is indeed accepted. And its own apprehension occurs through the connection between the self and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); it is not necessary for there to be another cognition in that case either, and thus there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

And if cognition has arisen, why is there no manifestation of the object even in another mental continuum (*santānāntara*), given that the absence of self-awareness (*saṃvedana*) is indistinguishable [in both cases]? [This is not so], because a specific relation to one's own self acts as the regulator. For instance, only that self in which that cognition has arisen as an inherent quality (*samaveta*) is the perceiver, and no other, because of the inherence of the intended cognition therein. However, for one who holds that cognition is self-cognizable and lacks a substratum, it must be considered why the manifestation of the object does not occur in another mental continuum. Furthermore, the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) has already been refuted previously on the grounds of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*).

As for the claim that this consciousness is self-cognizable (*svasaṃvedya*)—meaning that there is no cognition of any other object—that is incorrect, because such a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is untenable. To explain: if self-cognizability means that [consciousness] is perceived through the conjunction of the self and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), then that is indeed accepted. However, if that very same cognition is [simultaneously] the instrument (*pramāṇa*), the object (*prameya*), and the result (*phala*), that is not so; for a non-difference among these three is never observed elsewhere. In cases where they are distinct, there are numerous examples, such as a staff and so forth. Therefore, in the case of cognition, self-cognizability does not consist in the non-difference between the instrument and the object, nor in the non-difference between the action and the object. Consequently, cognition is cognized by another cognition, because it is an object of cognition (*vedyatva*), like a jar or similar objects.

Regarding what was stated—that because its nature is luminosity, it manifests by itself alone like a lamp—if by "luminosity" (prakāśakatva) one intends "the nature of consciousness" (bodharūpatva), then the example is deficient in the probans (*sādhanavikala*), since the nature of consciousness is impossible in a lamp. If, however, "luminosity" means "possession of a radiant form," that does not exist in cognition; therefore, the determination (*pariccheda*) of a cognition occurs only through the arising of another cognition which has that [first] cognition as its object.

Regarding what was stated—that objects, whether their nature is luminous or otherwise, are manifested by cognition—if "having the nature of luminosity" means having the nature of awareness (*bodha*), that does not apply to objects, because objects are not of the nature of awareness. How, then, is there manifestation of them? It is through the arising of a cognition whose object they are. When a cognition has arisen with respect to a certain object, the conventional usage is that "this object has been determined. Therefore, since consciousness is formless (*nirākāra*), the relationship between object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) is the determining factor.
The objection, "If cognitions possess forms such as blue and so forth, what would be the basis for an external object? has already been refuted. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.433)

As for the objection that the object and the subject cannot be experienced at the same time, that too is refuted, because we do not accept momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*). For one who maintains momentariness, this fault arises: since the object does not exist at the time of the cognition, and the cognition does not exist at the time of the object, the relationship of grasped and grasper between the two is untenable. Furthermore, since the existence of the whole (*avayavin*) has already been established, it is not the case that a mere collection of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth constitutes the object of consciousness due to its lack of ultimate reality. As for the claim that "consciousness alone exists" because the existence of atoms is proven, that is no fault, as we do not accept that [position]. Therefore, what the Vijñānavādin says—that "the distinction between the grasped and the grasper is due to conceptual construction (*kalpanā*)"—is also refuted, because external objects appear through the eyes and other senses apart from the nature of pure awareness (*bodharūpa*), and because purposeful engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*) have those [external objects] as their objective domain. Indeed, it is observed that when an object is apprehended, those seeking causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) proceed toward it. Nor is activity based on mere delusion, because non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*) is perceived.

Now, if it is argued that activity (*pravṛtti*), cessation (*nivṛtti*), and purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) are indeed non-different from cognition, that is not so; for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the non-difference of cognitions regarding those things which appear as real entities (*vasturūpa*) with mutually exclusive natures (*parasparavyāvṛttātman*). Furthermore, if external objects are not admitted, there can be no occurrence of correspondence (*saṃvāda*). Correspondence regarding the form of an object occurs through the experience of another mental continuum by means of activity and speech; but that is not so, because such a [corresponding] object does not exist. Nor is there correspondence based on the lack of distinction in production, because it would follow that there is a discrepancy when a taste-cognition arises immediately after a color-cognition.

Now, [the opponent argues: since activity and speech in one's own continuum are observed to be preceded by the impulse of one's own mind, it can be inferred that they are likewise preceded by that [impulse] in another continuum; thus, the existence of another continuum is established. [Reply: No, for if the activity and speech being perceived were non-different from one's own mind, it would follow that they could not be preceded by another's mind. And if they are different, then since they are perceived as appearing directed toward the external, how could there not be the existence of an external object?

Furthermore, for one who maintains the doctrine of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), the operation of inference is not tenable in the absence of the apprehension of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). To explain: activity and speech apprehend a preceding mind that possesses the nature of appearing cognition, because they terminate within the self [of that cognition]. Yet, even this causal mind does not apprehend its own causality. Nor can it be said that conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*)—through the sequence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—apprehends the relation of cause and effect by means of both [the activity and the mind], for since the latent impression conforms to the experience [of the cognition itself], how could there be a conceptual determination of that [relation] when the relation of cause and effect has not been apprehended? Nor is the conceptual cognition a superimposition of what is not that nature; if, through a traditional succession, it lacks the object as its domain, then in the absence of the apprehension of the relation of cause and effect, inference simply does not operate. Therefore, since inference proceeds only when there is the apprehension of invariable concomitance—that "this is the pervaded (*vyāpya*)" and "this is the pervader (*vyāpaka*)" of that—one must admit an object other than mere awareness.

As for the claim that the cognition "I perceive this blue" is erroneous—like the sight of two moons by one suffering from ophthalmia—that is incorrect, because it is not sublated. To explain: for one suffering from ophthalmia, once the ophthalmia has been destroyed and the cognition of oneness arises, the sight of two moons appears to be erroneous; however, this is not the case for another person who has not developed ophthalmia. Thus, regarding the cognition of "blue" and so forth, there is no falsity, because no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) apprehending a contrary object can be established.

But was it not already stated: "What sublates what? Knowledge by knowledge"? For instance, water is the object of the cognition of water, as is well-known to all people; when that [cognition] is abandoned and another cognition arises with respect to a different object, such as a mirage, it is sublated by the cognition grasping that [mirage]. It is made known as being characterized by falsity, in the form: "This cognition of water that arose in me is false," or else there is the cessation of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by it. For instance, when the cognition of a mirage occurs, once the mental impression produced by the cognition of water has ceased, even at a later time, the memory "I saw water" does not arise; consequently, there is no movement toward that location. Furthermore, it has been stated that if a sublater were not admitted, the distinction between truth and falsehood regarding cognition would be untenable, and thus the determination of victory and defeat for the proponent and the opponent could not exist.

As for the statement beginning with "those whose senses are afflicted by mantras and so forth," it does not require a rebuttal, because it is admitted that the manifestation itself is otherwise [erroneous] even by its own nature. To explain: objects such as fragments of clay appear otherwise [than they are], yet they do not appear so to those whose eyes are not afflicted in their true form, nor to everyone; this is indeed accepted as false cognition (*mithyājñāna*), since a sublater (*bādhaka*) is established. And the sublater is indeed accepted in the words: "The vision of those whose eyes are unafflicted is exactly like that. Furthermore, in deserts, even a small object is perceived as large when at a distance, while it is small when nearby; by this, its falsity is sublated. Nor is there sublation of this [large appearance] by that [small one], because to every cognizer, in all places, it manifests as not having that [large] form. Moreover, largeness manifests only in a specific location and not elsewhere, and thus it is non-existent. For that alone is the true nature (*svarūpa*) of objects which is non-contradictory and which accomplishes purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) for those whose minds are healthy. Therefore, fragments of clay and the like exist in that very form in which they manifest to those with unimpaired eyes and in which they accomplish purposeful action, but not in another form. Why? Because objects would lack stability. Now, one might argue: "Even though objects are non-existent in the state of dream, a manifestation and a specific purposeful action—the emission of semen—is possible. But if that is so, then it must be explained how the non-existence of objects in the state of dream is known. If you say it is because they are not perceived in the waking state, then it follows that those things which *are* perceived [in the waking state] must exist. Otherwise, the non-existence of objects in the dream state could not be established simply by their non-perception in the waking state. Therefore, one cannot say that because they are perceived, they are non-existent in the waking state just as in the dream state; for although the reason (*sādhana*)—being manifested—is present, the probandum (*sādhya*)—non-existence—is not certain. There is a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*), since being perceived exists in consciousness, yet non-existence does not. Likewise, if objects were non-existent, the reason "being perceived" would lack the property of the subject (*apakṣadharmatva*). In the example, non-existence does not follow from being perceived, but rather from non-apprehension through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); thus the argument is established otherwise. Furthermore, for one who maintains that "all is consciousness," no distinction between the dream state and the waking state is possible, since in both cases the self-cognized knowledge is admitted to persist. And the arguments based on vows have already been refuted previously. Therefore, it is logical that the waking state is the conjunction of knowledge produced by the senses and other means, whereas the dream state is the opposite of that.

As for the claim that things are non-existent because they are analytically separated by the intellect (*buddhi*), that is incorrect; for if those whose forms appear as manifestations of their own respective cognitions were non-existent, it would follow that consciousness itself is also non-existent. To explain: form and other such qualities are established as objects of their own cognitions through the mutual exclusion of their respective natures, and cloth and other such objects are likewise. Therefore, although a cloth does not appear in the cognition of its threads and so forth, it nonetheless exists in the ultimate sense because it is the object of its own cognition. Thus, since cloth and other such objects are the objects of mutually exclusive cognitions and perform specific causal functions (*arthakriyā*), they are indeed ultimately real.

Since the establishment of an object of cognition (*prameya*) does not occur without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the proof for the non-existence of things distinct from consciousness must be stated. Furthermore, if the non-existence of categories were established without a means of valid cognition, their existence might as well be established, because the absence of a means of valid cognition is common to both cases. Now, if it is argued that the "inapplicability of the definition of the apprehended" (*grāhyalakṣaṇāyoga*) is the means of valid cognition [for proving non-existence], we say no. If this [inapplicability] is a property of existence (*bhāvadharma*), it is contradictory; if it is a property of non-existence (*abhāvadharma*), its locus is unestablished (*āśrayāsiddhi*); and if it is a property of both, it is not a valid probans due to being inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*). Moreover, it is a case of a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*). For instance, the inapplicability of the definition of the apprehended is not a property of the apprehended itself; how then could it prove its non-existence? It is also unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*), because the definition of the apprehended actually exists—as will be explained later, largeness (*mahattva*) and so forth constitute the definition of the apprehended. Furthermore, it is indistinguishable from the thesis (*sādhyāviśiṣṭa*), since the inapplicability of the definition of the apprehended is itself what is to be proven. Nor is there any other means of valid cognition [to establish this].

By this, the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*) is also refuted, and thus it is not discussed separately. For instance, if all objects were non-existent, consciousness too would be non-existent because it would lack the forms of the apprehended and the apprehender; consequently, everything would be empty. But that has already been refuted, since the object of knowledge (*prameya*) cannot be established in the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and because both consciousness and objects are established by means of valid cognition. Thus, since the existence of objects apart from consciousness is proven, and because there is an infinity [of objects] and because cognition is restricted to each respective object, it is logical that consciousness is manifold.

Others, however, hold the view that intellect (*buddhi*) is a specific transformation of the self (*ātman*); thus, it is impermanent in its form as intellect, yet eternal in its form as the self. To refute this, they consider the statement "and it is of many kinds" [to be the refutation]. For instance: because intellect is manifold, the self would also have to be manifold due to their non-difference; or, if the self were one, intellect would have to be one. Furthermore, a position of both difference and non-difference is impossible, since the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*) has already been rejected. Therefore, the doctrine of the naked ones (*digvāsas*)—that because intellect is a quality, the self cannot likewise be manifold even though intellect is manifold—is refuted.

“Although it is of many kinds, in brief there are two types: knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*). Among these, ignorance is fourfold, characterized by doubt, error, indecision, and dream. [Objection:

If this is so, then since cognition (*buddhi*) is infinite, how can it be an object of the knowledge of reality? To this he says: “Although it is of many kinds, in brief... This means that one should understand it as being, in summary, of two types. In what form is there this twofold nature? He says: “Knowledge and ignorance.”

Others, however, raise the objection that since knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) are heard of in the Vedānta system, the demonstration of the infinity of the intellect (*buddhi*) would contradict scripture; to refute this doubt, he says: "Although it is of many kinds, in brief," that is, concisely, it is accepted as being twofold: "knowledge and ignorance."

Vidyā (knowledge) is indeed a determinative cognition that is not sublated by differences of place, time, state, and so forth; and avidyā (ignorance) is its opposite. However, being *pramāṇa* (valid means of knowledge) and being *apramāṇa* (invalid means of knowledge) do not constitute being *vidyā* and being *avidyā*, because of the fallacy of over-extension (*vyabhicāra*). To explain: if "pramāṇa" is intended in the sense of "that by which something is correctly cognized," then doubt and the like would also possess the status of a *pramāṇa* insofar as they apprehend the self and the internal organ; thus, there is a fallacy of over-extension. Furthermore, since it is impossible for [the definition] to be the cause in all cognitions such as perception and the rest, there would be a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*). If, on the other hand, the result [of cognition] is intended, then since memory is not the result of a *pramāṇa*, it would not possess the nature of *vidyā*.

The teachers, however, state that *vidyā* (knowledge) is the cognition that is the cause of specific worldly activity (*viśiṣṭavyavahāra*), while its opposite is *avidyā* (ignorance). In this regard, if "specific worldly activity" is intended to mean activity characterized by engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), then there is the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*), because such activity exists even in cognitions such as doubt (*saṃśaya*). Nor is it the case that [the definition] exists in every instance of the subject (*pakṣa*), and thus there is the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*). If, on the other hand, "specific worldly activity" refers to the cognition "I have perceived this correctly despite differences in place and so forth," then even the capacity to produce that [activity] does not exist in all varieties of *vidyā*; thus, there is under-extension. Consequently, since the conventional usage "I have perceived this correctly" is not found in all varieties of *vidyā*, the definition suffers from the very fault of being non-pervasive (*avyāpakatva*).

Others maintain that even there, ignorance (*avidyā*) is fourfold; thus, the definition of the nature of ignorance is presented by skipping its usual order because the illumination of the subject matter is intended, for the purpose of making known that it is to be eradicated—since ignorance is indeed eradicated by knowledge (*vidyā*).

Now, in what form are the four types [of cognition]? They are "characterized by doubt, error, non-apprehension, and dream" as their essential nature (*svarūpa*). But surely there is also inferential knowledge (*ūhajñāna*); its inclusion is found neither in *vidyā* (valid knowledge) nor in *avidyā* (invalid knowledge), because the fourfold enumeration is given for both. This is not correct, because inferential knowledge is not experienced apart from doubt and certainty. If it is argued that there exists, following doubt, a cognitive state of probability (*sambhāvanā-pratyaya*)—such as "this must be a person," based on the perception of a connection in an external location and the exclusion of the alternative of a post—is this not simply a certainty? For it has the form of "that being that. To explain: when there is the possibility of both—"Could this be a post or a person?"—the negation of one results in the persistence of the other which has not been negated. Thus, it is indeed a certainty.

Now, if it is argued that certainty is not tenable because the perceived particulars reside in a different substratum (*vyadhikaraṇa*), that is incorrect, because we accept that these particulars belong to the conjoined object (*saṃyogin*). For just as particulars such as the roosting of crows produce certainty regarding a post (*sthāṇu*) which is their conjoined substrate, so too do they produce certainty regarding a person in the vicinity of the outer wall. Furthermore, since the connection with that [person] is itself a particular inherent (*samaveta*) in the object, there is no question of them residing in a different substratum. If it is argued that there is no definitive conclusion from the evidence (*sādhana*) because the subject is "this is not a post, due to its connection with the vicinity of the outer wall," that is not so; for in relation to its function (*vyāpāra*), it is possible for it to have the person as its object. If, however, this is a distinct cognition (*jñānāntara*), then since inferential knowledge (*ūha-jñāna*) is a non-erroneous cognition of an object, it must be designated as a form of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because its result cannot be established without a means of knowledge. Otherwise, the general definition of valid cognition would become fallible. If it is argued that the contact between sense organ and object (*indriyārtha-sannikarṣa*) alone is the means of knowledge in the production of inferential knowledge, then how can it be a distinct cognition? It would simply be the result of perception (*pratyakṣa*). Enough of this.

Others, however, maintain that although doubt (*ūha*) does exist, it is not mentioned here because it is obtained through its establishment in a related system (*samānatantra*). Nor can perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the other means of knowledge be obtained by this same principle, because the status of being a "related system" is not established in the absence of one's own school’s doctrine. [The Distinction from Doubt] "Doubt, first of all, is a deliberation (*vimarṣa*) characterized by the thought 'what might it be? which rests upon two alternatives; it arises from the observation of mere similarity between two well-known particulars, from the recollection of their respective specific qualities, and from a lack of [definitive] merit (*adharma*). <PDhS>

Now, the section beginning with "First, doubt" (*saṃśayastāvat*) is intended to define the distinction between doubt and the other [categories] by way of analyzing the differentiation of their respective objects.

Doubt (*saṃśaya*) is now explained because its turn has arrived. The phrase "of those two" (*tayor*) is a specification of the objects, meaning "of those two for whom many well-known particulars (*viśeṣa*) exist. However, one should not adopt a *karmadhāraya* compound—interpreting it as "those two who are both well-known and possess many particulars"—because doubt has as its object the substratum (*dharmin*). Now, since only a single substratum exists there, how is it possible for both [particulars] to be its objects? There is no fault here, because of the presentation of the thesis (*pakṣa*). To explain: it is established that doubt occurs precisely where many particulars are well-known; however, this does not mean that both are objects of the doubt simultaneously, because it is impossible for both to exist in that single substratum at one time. Rather, they are objects of the doubt by way of different times. Whatever is possible in a given case regarding the arising of doubt, that is the object of that doubt.

The cause here is stated as "from the perception of mere similarity" (*sādṛśyamātradarśanāt*). This should be explained as meaning the perception of a substratum (*dharmin*) qualified by similarity—that is, a case where "mere similarity" is perceived therein. It is not, however, to be understood as the perception of mere similarity alone; for if that were accepted, the doubt regarding the substratum would be misplaced, since [the doubt] arises from the apprehension of a property (*dharma*). Here, by the use of the word "mere" (*mātra*) in the phrase "from the perception of mere similarity," he demonstrates the non-apprehension of any absolute particularity (*viśeṣa*), because doubt is not observed even when a universal (*sāmānya*) is apprehended along with its particulars. Nor is the non-apprehension of particulars capable of generating doubt without the apprehension of a universal; thus, both are mentioned. Nevertheless, for one standing on a boat, there is no doubt regarding trees and the like even though both [universal and particular] are present; therefore, the phrase "from the recollection of the particulars of both" (*ubhayaviśeṣānusmaraṇāt*) is included. Furthermore, the recollection of particulars is not seen to generate doubt without what was previously mentioned [the perception of the universal and non-perception of the particular]; thus, the complete set constitutes the cause. Therefore, since doubt arises from the perception of a universal, the non-perception of a particular, the recollection of the particulars of both, and from factors such as adharma, it is distinguished from other [cognitions]. This is the definition consisting of its causes. Accordingly, the Sūtra states: "Doubt arises from the perception of a universal, the non-perception of a particular, and the recollection of a particular" (Vai. Sū. 2.2.17). That substratum in which the universal is perceived is so described; the word "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) here refers to a firm means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since doubt is admitted here to be even inferential (*ānumānika*). "From the non-perception of a particular" means from the non-apprehension of a particular and from the recollection thereof, doubt arises.

But is this not improper? For when Devadatta departs, leaving behind his most beloved woman, even though the three conditions [of perception, non-perception, and non-perception of a sublater] are present due to the spatial separation, no doubt is observed regarding her. To explain: even when there is the perception of the generality "womanhood," because of the perception of various particulars such as [her specific] face and so forth, and because of the recollection thereof, a doubt as to whether she is "mine" or "another's" is not seen; for there is the perception of a sublater in the form of a particularity of place and time which negates the opposing position, namely, that another woman cannot exist in that same place and at that same time. Therefore, should not the phrase "due to the lack of establishment of a sublatant or a probative means of knowledge" (*bādhaka-sādhaka-pramāṇāvyavasthātaḥ*) be added in order to exclude this case? No. Because it has already been excluded by the very term "non-perception of particulars" (*viśeṣānupalabdhi*). That is to say, by the term "non-perception of particulars," the non-perception of all particulars is intended. And that [non-perception of all particulars] does not exist here, because the particularity of place and time is ascertained. Thus, considering that there is nothing to be excluded by this [term], the Sage did not state any further particularity.

He states its essential nature: "Doubt (*saṃśaya*) is a deliberation (*vimarśa*) that rests upon two [alternatives], expressed as 'What could it be? (*kiṃ svid...*). Etymologically, *saṃśaya* means *saṃśītiḥ* (the act of doubting); it is so called because by means of this, the self becomes as if asleep. *Vimarśa* means deliberation; it is a cognition such as, "Is this exactly so, or does it not exist thus? It is a deliberation that rests upon both, having the habit of doing so; thus, "doubt is a deliberation resting upon two. And since it is not possible for both [alternatives] to be the object [simultaneously], it should be explained as "resting upon the mention of both" (*ubhayollekhī*). Therefore, deliberation is distinguished from other things, or it should be designated as "doubt," because it has the form of deliberation, or because it rests upon both alternatives as "what could it be? (*kiṃ syāt*).

“And that [doubt] is of two kinds,” thus is the classification. In what form? “Internal and external. Now, one might object: since doubt is fivefold, its twofold nature is untenable? No; for that is established through internal subdivisions of this very [twofold] category. To explain: external doubt is threefold—arising from the perception of common properties (*sāmānya-dharma*), the perception of multiple properties (*aneka-dharma*), and conflicting testimony (*vipratipatti*). Internal doubt is twofold, because apprehension and non-apprehension (*upalabdhi-anupalabdhi*) are determined by the mind. This is indeed the intention of the author of the *Bhāṣya*, since he says: “The common and multiple properties reside in the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), whereas apprehension and non-apprehension reside in the knower (*jñātṛ*); thus there is no contradiction. Furthermore, if the inclusion [under these two categories] were not accepted, then because doubt would also be divided according to whether its objects are perceptible or imperceptible, the claim of its being fivefold would be incoherent. Or, if it is argued that the fivefold division is not mentioned precisely because it is included within this [twofold] division, then, since it is subsumed under the twofold division itself, the number five is not stated, for the latter is merely a subdivision of the former.

Furthermore, a manifold property (*aneka-dharma*) does not indeed become a cause of doubt because it is common [to both sides], since it does not produce the recollection of those contradictory particulars due to its non-apprehension along with them. Nor is the "non-erroneous contradiction" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*) a cause of doubt, because such a thing is impossible; as we shall explain on the occasion of discussing the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). [As it is said: "In the case of a guide who first points out something correctly and then points it out again falsely, doubt arises regarding the three times: 'Is this correct or is it false?'"* *PDhS: "Antastāvad ādeśikasya samyaṅ mithyā coddiśya punarādiśatastriṣu kāleṣu saṃśayo bhavati kinnu samyaṅ mithyā veti ।"* (Prakaraṇapañcikā, p. 180)

Therein, for the purpose of defining the nature of internal doubt (*antaḥsaṃśaya*), [the author states] "First, internal [doubt belongs] to the instructor" (*antastāvadādeśikasya*), and so forth. For instance, having perceived a specific omen, an instructor once correctly predicted, "Rain will occur," but on another occasion, the opposite occurred. When he predicts again in the same manner, while the three times [past, present, and future] do not exist [simultaneously], a doubt arises regarding that cognition: "Is this correct or false? Now, since the cognition does not persist at the time when there is the perception of a common feature (*sāmānyadarśana*) and the recollection of particulars (*viśeṣānusmaraṇa*), how can it be the object of doubt? To explain: in that cognition, the state of having future rain as its object is the common feature; a cognition arises regarding that cognition characterized by such a feature, but that [cognition] is in the process of perishing. Meanwhile, the recollection of the particulars—correctness or incorrectness—is in the process of arising. Therefore, at the time of recollecting the particulars, the cognition has already passed away; how then can it be the object [of doubt]? This is not a fault, because the self (*ātman*) characterized by that [cognition] is the object. Thus, the doubt is: "Am I one who possesses correct knowledge, or am I one who possesses false knowledge?"
Others, however, maintain that even a past object, though no longer existing, can function as an object of cognition.

[As stated: "The external [object] is of two kinds: that which is perceptible and that which is imperceptible. Regarding the imperceptible object, doubt arises from the perception of a common mark (*sādhāraṇaliṅga*), the recollection of both specific features, and the influence of *adharma*. For example, upon seeing only a horn in a forest, one wonders whether it is a cow or a gavaya. <PDhS>

“In what form is the external [doubt] of two kinds? It is ‘with respect to an object of perception and with respect to an object beyond perception. Regarding that which is beyond perception, doubt is first explained as arising ‘from the observation of a common mark. That is to say, from the observation of a mark that has been previously perceived in association with contradictory particulars, and because those particulars are not currently perceived, doubt arises due to the recollection of both sets of particulars and from factors such as direction and time. For example, in a forest, from the sight of a mere horn, because the specific characteristics belonging to it are not perceived and those characteristics are recollected, doubt arises as to whether it is ‘a cow or a gavaya.’”

Now, how is this [inference] different from perception? Perception is the direct apprehension of a subject (*dharmin*) as qualified by a universal, because its specific characteristics have not yet been articulated. Now, what is the universal in the case of the horns of a cow and a gavaya? It is the connection with a similar arrangement of parts; for the arrangement of parts observed in the horn of a cow is exactly the same as that in the horn of a gavaya. However, those specific features of the cow's horn and the specific features of the gavaya's horn which were previously perceived are not perceived here. Therefore, for one who perceives a horn qualified merely by similarity, because the specific features are not perceived and because of the recollection of them, there arises the doubt: "Is this a cow, or is it a gavaya?"

“Even with respect to an object of perception, because one perceives only the similarity of height in a post and a person, and due to the non-perception of specific qualities such as curvature [in the case of a post] or the absence thereof [in the case of a person], when the general characteristics such as ‘post-ness’ are not manifested, and because of the recollection of the specific features of both, the cognition of the self—which is being drawn toward both—is oscillating: ‘Could this indeed be a post, or could it be a person? <PDhS>

“Even regarding an object of direct perception, because one perceives only the similarity of height in both a post (*sthāṇu*) and a person (*puruṣa*), and because specific features such as curvature and so forth are not perceived. By the word “and so forth” (*ādi*), the specific features in the case of the post—such as the perching of crows—and those in the case of persons—such as the head and hands—are included; [the doubt arises] because these are not perceived. “Post-ness” (*sthāṇutva*) is the beginning of that which is denoted by the word “and so forth,” by which “person-ness” (*puruṣatva*) is understood. And that is indeed a universal (*sāmānya*) acting as a particular (*viśeṣa*). Its non-manifestation occurs because its manifestors—the head, hands, and so on—are not perceived. Therefore, “when that is unmanifested, due to the recollection of the specific features of both, with respect to both”—that is, toward the post and the person—“the cognition of the self being drawn [in both directions] wavers” (*dolāyate*); it does not settle upon a single alternative (*ekakoṭi*). As to what its nature is, he says: “Is this indeed a post, or rather a person? (*kiṃ nu khalv ayaṃ sthāṇuḥ syāt puruṣo vā*)?

Now, is this [cognition] one, or rather many? If it is many—such that "it is a post" is one [cognition] and "it is a person" is another—and these arise sequentially, then would there not be a resolution of doubt by defining that which has the form "it is that" as correct knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) and the opposite as false knowledge (*mithyā-jñāna*)? No, because we do not admit its multiplicity. For instance, the cognition "Could this be a post or a person? is a single cognition characterized by the presentation of contradictory objects, since it is produced by a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) marked by the recollection of contradictory particulars. Indeed, a single mental impression (*saṃskāra*), arising from the experience of particulars and assisted by preceding impressions, produces a single remembrance whose object consists of those contradictory particulars.

Alternatively, it may be argued that mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of specific particulars, being regulated by unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) which brings about the experience of doubt, give rise to [a single] impression; therefore, the recollection has multiple particulars as its object. This is because there is no distinction in the arising of doubt regarding the object, and perceptuality is the same in both cases. True. Nevertheless, the distinction is this: in one case, there is the acceptance of doubt regarding a subject (*dharmin*) qualified by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), due to the perception of a mark (*liṅga*) qualified by a universal (*sāmānya*); whereas in the other case, it concerns a perceptible subject possessing a universal but lacking the mark and devoid of the property to be proven. Some degree of similarity is not denied, for the application of the definition of a universal is observed through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), as well as through recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*). For instance, one subsequently recognizes: "A cognition of doubt has arisen in me regarding this"; thus, it possesses an object.
The contrapositive dissimilarity (*viparyayavaidharmya*):
“The contrapositive also has as its object only that which is accessible to perception and inference.”

Now, for the purpose of defining the distinctions regarding the cause, nature, and object of error (*viparyaya*), there is this section beginning with: "Error, moreover, occurs only within the domain of perception and inference. Alternatively, since doubt has been accepted as having perception and inference as its objects, he says, "Error, moreover, occurs only within the domain of perception and inference," so that error might not be rendered impossible due to a lack of an object. Nor does identity follow from the non-difference of the object, because differences in essential nature and differences in causes are possible. Is the restriction—that error occurs only within the domain of perception and inference—not contradicted by the observation of error even regarding scriptural (*āgamika*) objects, where discrepancies are found? No, because [the statement] is intended to exclude the possibility of [error] being without an object.
Some maintain that the statement, "there is a conceit of perception even when perception is absent," should be explained otherwise.

Others, however, hold that it is for the purpose of refuting the conceptual cognition (*kalpanājñāna*) accepted by opponents [that it says]: "Error (*viparyaya*) also has as its object only what is accessible to perception and inference. It does not mean that every [error] has an object, because it is possible for some to be without an object. For that [cognition] in which an object is perceived through positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) has an object; but another is without an object—it is not the case that all [errors] have objects.

Others, however, maintain that error (*viparyaya*) is indeed an object of perception and inference; thus, they claim that a negation of non-existence (*abhavanapratiṣedha*) is intended for the sake of excluding an eternal error. This interpretation is incorrect, because that very [eternal error] is unestablished. Furthermore, since the status of being an object of perception and inference for an eternal entity is not possible without activity, how could there be a negation of its non-existence here? Enough of this.

“First, regarding the object of perception (*pratyakṣa*): when one whose sense organs are afflicted by bile, phlegm, or wind perceives an object incorrectly due to the lack of proximity to the object, there arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind—dependent on the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by that cognition—a cognition of ‘that’ in what is not that, caused also by demerit (*adharma*). This is error (*viparyaya*), such as [perceiving] a horse in a cow.

“Even in the absence of perception, there occurs the conceit of perception (*pratyakṣābhimāna*), as for example: ‘The nocturnal darkness, dark as a heap of powdered collyrium, has a form resembling the sky when the mass of clouds has vanished and the ocean is motionless.’”

First, he states the error regarding the object of perception: "Of those two whose many specific qualities are well-known" (*prasiddhānekaviśeṣayoḥ*). This defines the object: that which has many well-known specific qualities is so described; [the error occurs] with respect to those two. "Of one whose sense faculties are afflicted by bile, phlegm, and wind" (*pittakaphānilopahatendriyasya*): bile, phlegm, and wind are *pittakaphānilāḥ*; one whose sense faculties are afflicted by these is so described; for such a person, error occurs. To the question "From what?", he says: "From an incorrect observation" (*ayathārthālocanāt*), and so forth. That by which something is observed incorrectly is "incorrect observation," namely, the cognition of similarity.

Alternatively, *ālociti* means "observation" (*ālocana*). By a figurative usage (*upacāra*), because it is the cause of a cognition of similarity—which is an observation that does not correspond to reality (*ayathārtha*)—the term "non-corresponding observation" (*ayathārthālocana*) is intended to refer to that [similarity-cognition]. Therefore: "that which is non-proximate" (*asannihita*) and "that which is an object" (*viṣaya*) is called "non-proximate object" (*asannihitaviṣaya*); the cognition thereof is "born from the cognition of a non-proximate object" (*asannihitaviṣayajñānaja*); and that is the mental impression (*saṃskāra*). Because it is an effect of a mental impression, memory (*smṛti*) is intended by the word "impression. The contact between the self and the mind (*ātmamanaḥsaṃyoga*) depends upon that [memory], hence it is "dependent on that" (*tadapekṣa*). From that non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) and from demerit (*adharma*), error (*viparyaya*) arises. What is its nature? It is "the cognition that something is what it is not" (*atasmiṃstaditi pratyayaḥ*). For instance, the cognition "that in what is not that" is distinct from others; it should be designated as "error," because it arises from non-corresponding observation and so forth. That which is not thus, nor produced from the aforementioned causes (such as the cognition "that in that"), is like doubt and the like. An example of this is: "as when there is the notion of a horse in a cow. For just as, for one who does not perceive specific features such as horns from a distance, a cognition arises—"this is a horse in a cow"—due to the perception of a body qualified by similarity to a horse and the recollection of a horse; likewise, there is the cognition of water in mirages, and the cognition of silver in mother-of-pearl.

But is this not improper? For it is impossible for there to exist a causal factor (*kāraka*) that produces erroneous cognition (*viparyayajñāna*). To explain: the sense organs (*indriya*) are produced for the purpose of producing correct cognition, since their nature consists in [apprehending] "this is that"; how then could they produce false cognition? Nor can it be that they produce erroneous cognition by virtue of defects such as cataracts (*kāca*) or jaundice (*kāmalā*), because a defective causal factor does not produce its proper effect. Just as, for example, a rice seed smeared with oil and the like fails to produce a rice sprout and likewise does not produce a barley sprout, so too the sense organs would only produce correct cognition and not generate erroneous cognition. Furthermore, there is no proof that the cognition of silver has mother-of-pearl (*śuktikā*) as its objective support (*ālambana*). Therefore, immediately after the cognition of similarity, a memory arises—deprived of its own form—in the shape "this is silver. To explain: "this" is the cognition of similarity, while "silver" is the memory, which is devoid of the form "that."

This is not tenable, because it would entail the impossibility of the engagement or withdrawal of one who seeks silver. Now, if you argue that one engages because one considers there to be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—thinking "this very thing is silver"—even though the two cognitions are distinct, then this very cognition of coreferentiality between two things that are actually non-coreferential is itself a false cognition (*mithyājñāna*). Furthermore, if you maintain that engagement occurs when there is a perception of similarity in the form "this" and a non-perception of difference in the form "silver," that is not so; for the mere absence of a cognition cannot be the cause of engagement. To explain: one who seeks silver engages only by thinking "this very thing is silver," and not otherwise. The designation of the immediacy (*aparokṣatā*) of the cognition "this" does not constitute a separate cognition. Otherwise, in cases such as "this is color" or "this is taste," there would likewise have to be a lapse of memory (*smṛtipramoṣa*).

As for the claim that there is no evidence for the cognition "this is silver" having a mother-of-pearl shell (*śukti*) as its objective basis, that is incorrect, because recognition and other such cognitions are possible. To explain: "This is a mother-of-pearl shell; it appeared to me as silver. Likewise, since the cognition "this is not silver" has the mother-of-pearl as its object, the cognition "silver" must also have that as its object. Otherwise, without the cognition "silver" having the mother-of-pearl as its object, there could be no negation "this is not silver," because there would be no prior application (*prasakti*) of the term. And if one were to negate what has not been applied, one could just as well say "this is not a jar" and so forth. If that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence of an endless series of negations everywhere. But this is not so. Therefore, through the medium of cognition, silver is negated as having been applied there.

As for the statement that [the world] lacks a cause of production, that is incorrect, because the sense organs and so forth, when assisted by defects (*doṣa*), produce cognition. For just as a sense organ is observed to be the producer of correct cognition through its presence and absence when defects are absent, so too is it the producer of false cognition when defects are present. Since the operation of the sense organs is observed to result in both types of effects, it is determined that the creation of the sense organs is for the sake of both. Furthermore, the falsity of this [cognition] arises from its departure from its own object and its approach toward another object.

If it is argued that its object is indeed an "extraordinary" (alaukika) silver, and thus the approach toward another object is unestablished, that is not so; for if there were a determination (*adhyavasāya*) of extraordinary silver, it would follow that neither engagement nor withdrawal could occur. If it is then argued that one engages because one considers even the extraordinary to be ordinary, how then is false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) possible? Furthermore, on this view, there could be no subverting cognition (*bādhaka-jñāna*) such as "this cognition has arisen in me falsely," nor would recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) and the like be possible. Yet, recognition does occur in the case of mother-of-pearl and similar objects, as does the realization, "the cognition of silver arose in me here," and the apprehension of its falsity; so how can false cognition be impossible?

If this cognition "this is silver" were indeed based upon the silver itself, then since that [silver] meets the conditions for perception, why is it not apprehended by one standing nearby? Whatever object meets the conditions for perception is necessarily apprehended by one standing nearby, even if it is perceived by someone at a distance, because the state of the sense organs and other factors remains the same. Yet this is not the case. Therefore, the cognition of silver and so forth arises with respect to mother-of-pearl and the like.

Others, however, assert that the falsity [of the cognition] consists in this: that very silver which was previously perceived as qualified by a specific place and time is now perceived as qualified by a different place and so forth. That is incorrect, because since that [silver] does not exist here [in the mother-of-pearl], it cannot be its object. Therefore, the object is indeed the mother-of-pearl itself, which is the domain of the sensory operation and is pointed out by the finger and so forth. Otherwise, how could a cognition of silver produced with respect to a different object be sublated by the cognition of mother-of-pearl? For if the objects were distinct, the relationship of sublated and sublator would be impossible. Thus, the cognition of silver, having arisen with respect to the mother-of-pearl, is sublated by the cognition of mother-of-pearl—which has its own object as a cooperative factor—and is made known as being characterized by falsity, due to the [cognition of silver] shifting toward a different object. As for the cognition of silver, its object is silver, as is recognized by everyone; because it arises with respect to mother-of-pearl while abandoning that [silver], it possesses the quality of deviation (*vyabhicāritva*). By this, the view that "this is a conceptual cognition (*kalpanājñāna*) devoid of an object" is refuted, because the object—such as the mother-of-pearl—is established through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Some maintain that by the statement, "Even when perception is absent, there is the conceit of perception," and so forth, he describes error as being devoid of an object.

An example is: “The sky, from which the mass of clouds has departed, having a form like that of the motionless ocean, [is perceived as] the nocturnal darkness, dark as a heap of powdered collyrium. In this, "that sky in which the masses (*paṭala*) of clouds have departed" is what is meant by that description. Likewise, "not moving" is *acala*; it is that which has a form (*vapuh*) similar to or equal to that ocean (*jalanidhi*). Now, because the sky is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), even for one who possesses the aforementioned cognition—that the sky has a form similar to the ocean—it is impossible to grasp its similarity with the ocean; thus, the claim to be perceiving it through direct perception (*pratyakṣābhimāna*) is without an object (*nirviṣaya*). Similarly, "nocturnal darkness" (*śārvaraṃ tamaḥ*) is that which exists in the night (*śarvarī*). What is its qualification? It is "dark as a heap of powdered collyrium. However, since darkness is of the nature of an absence (*abhāva*), it cannot possess a connection with a dark form; thus, it is without an object. Even if one were to admit that it does have an object, there would be no fault, because the object would be the absence of light (*tejas*) as qualified by specific place and time.

Likewise, the visual rays, having turned back from their own substratum, produce the perception of the sky as having a form similar to the aforementioned ocean, [perceiving] their own eyeball-form as such. This is like the grasping of one's own face by rays that have been reflected from a mirror. For just as visual rays reflected from a mirror produce a reversal in relation to one's own face, [perceiving it] as "the face in the mirror," so too here, the rays turning back from afar display their own eyeball as the sky.
“Or even in the domain of inference, there is the inference of fire from vapor and the like which are mistaken for smoke, and [the inference] of a cow from seeing the horn of a *gavaya*.”

He states the error even regarding the object of inference with the words "by means of steam, etc. (*vāṣpādibhiḥ*). Here, by the word "etc.," frost, mosquitoes, whirlpools, and so forth are included. By what kind of things? By those "regarded as smoke" (*dhūmābhimataiḥ*), that is, by those known in the form of smoke, there is the inference of fire. Likewise, the cognition "it is a cow" arising from the sight of a gavaya's horn is an error. In this case, however, the erroneous cognition regarding the inferential mark (*liṅga*) is produced by the sense organ, while that which arises from its operation is inferential.

“Error (*viparyaya*) is the false conviction that ‘this is the highest good’ regarding the doctrines of the Śākyas and others, which are contrary to the vision of the *Trayī* (the three Vedas).
