It is the conceit of self (*ātman*) in the body, senses, and mind; the perception of permanence in things that are produced; the cognition that an effect arises even when its cause is deficient; the cognition that what is taught as beneficial is harmful; and the cognition that what is taught as harmful is beneficial.”

Now, he describes the misconception arising from the practice of false views with the words: “The false conviction that ‘this is the highest good’ regarding the systems of Śākya and others, which are contrary to the system of the *Trayī*,” and so forth. The term *trayī* is a collective compound (*samāhāra*) for three; by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), it refers to the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman* [Vedas]. The *Trayī* itself is the "vision" (*darśana*). The systems of Śākya and others are those contrary to it; by the phrase "and so forth," the systems of the Jains (*Jaina*) and others are included. Regarding these, the thought "this is the highest good" arises. For instance, the knowledge that "everything is momentary" and the knowledge that "it is empty and devoid of self" are considered the "highest good" because they are believed to be the means of achieving it; thus, through the practice of the Śākya system, a misconception occurs. This is because, as has been stated, there are refutations (*bādhaka*) against the position of momentariness and the rest. In these matters, there is a misconception within the vision due to a non-absolute (*anekānta*) cognition. The same should be inferred for other cases as well. Nor should it be said that because the systems of Śākya and others are contrary [to the truth], there is a misconception even in the *Trayī*; for no refutation is applicable regarding the primary objects such as the Self (*ātman*) and so on. In the systems of Śākya and others, however, the refutations stated against categories such as momentariness remain unrefuted.

Others, however, maintain that the *trayī* is the collection of the three means of valid cognition—perception, inference, and scripture—and that this alone is the "darśana" (vision/system), because other systems such as those of the Śākyas are opposed to it and are thus subject to sublation (*bādha*). Alternatively, the Vaiśeṣika system is characterized by that [trayī], while the systems of the Śākyas and others are its opposites; they have been described as such because they are being sublated.

Likewise, "the conceit of self with respect to the body, the senses, and the mind" is error (*viparyaya*). The error of the materialists (*laukāyatika*) is that the body alone is the self. The error of those who maintain that consciousness resides in the senses is that the senses alone are the self. And for those who maintain that consciousness resides in the mind, it is the mind alone.

“The perception of permanence in things that are produced” is the misconception of the Mīmāṃsakas; for they have already established the produced nature of the earth and so forth, yet they perceive permanence in them. Alternatively, this is the misconception of the Sāṃkhyas: the perception of permanence in produced things such as jars, based on the [Sāṃkhya] view that "an entity does not arise [from nothing] nor does it abandon its own self."

It has been stated that for the proponents of *svabhāva* (inherent nature), the cognition that an effect arises despite the absence of its cause constitutes a misconception (*viparyaya*). Accordingly, they maintain that the observed diversity of the earth and other elements occurs by way of inherent nature alone, without a creator. This is incorrect, because it is observed that the state of being an effect is invariably pervaded by having its own creator as a prerequisite. Since it has been established even in the case of the earth and so forth that they are preceded by a creator, this cognition of the proponents of *svabhāva* is a misconception. Likewise, since no effect is ever perceived without a conscious presiding agent, the cognition held by the followers of Jaimini and the disciples of Śauddhodana—that effects such as the earth and so forth exist without a creator—is a misconception.

Furthermore, since merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) have dissolved into the primal matter (*pradhāna*), they cannot function toward the production of an effect because they are no longer manifest; thus, for the Sāṃkhyas, the cognition that an effect arises despite the deficiency of these two factors is a misconception (*viparyaya*).

And for the followers of the Sugata, the cognition that an effect arises despite the deficiency of its cause is a misconception (*viparyaya*). How so? Because of the identity (*tādātmya*) between arising and perishing. Since momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) obtains, at the very moment the effect is produced, the cause perishes; and that [perishing] is not something other than the arising. Thus, there can be no relation of cause and effect between two things that arise simultaneously; therefore, the cognition that an effect arises when the cause is deficient is a misconception.

Likewise, all this activity is preceded by the Supreme Lord, and the propitiation of Him is the means for attaining the highest good (*parama-śreyaḥ*). Furthermore, the Vedas possess authority both in their own form and regarding their meaning. Thus, when the Vaiśeṣikas teach what is beneficial, the Mīmāṃsakas, Buddhists, and Jains possess the misconception that "it is not so"; this is their error (*viparyaya*). However, when they speak out of impudence, claiming that there is no such thing as the existence of Paramaśiva and the rest, then—even though the Vaiśeṣikas are teaching what is beneficial—these [others] possess the misconception that "this which is taught by the Vaiśeṣikas as beneficial is actually harmful"; this is their error.

Alternatively, when the Vaiśeṣikas teach what is beneficial—namely, that there is a plurality of transmigrating selves, that Paramaśiva is distinct from them, and that through his propitiation, the highest good (śreyaḥ) accrues to ourselves and others—the cognition that this is "unbeneficial" is error (viparyaya).

For the dualists (*dvaitavādin*), because they do not accept that [the world] has that [Primal Nature] as its cause, the cognition that it is "beneficial" through their teaching is a misconception (*viparyaya*). While those Vaiśeṣikas are thus instructing that effects such as the earth are commenced by atoms through the process of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth, and have God as their agent, the Sāṃkhyas possess the misconception that "this is not so, because the world is preceded by Primal Nature (*pradhāna*)," since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of Primal Nature.

Now, there exists Primordial Matter (pradhāna) because of its homogeneity, its limited magnitude, the activity of its power, the relationship between the assisted and the assister, and its manifold diversity. To explain: all this effect, such as the body and so forth, is observed to be permeated by pleasure, pain, and delusion. And whatever is thus permeated is seen to arise from a single cause, just as various jars and other objects permeated by clay arise from a single lump of clay. Thus, there is the following inference: the world and other effects arise from a single cause, because they are permeated [by pleasure, pain, and delusion], like a jar and so forth. Furthermore, the property of being a predicate of the subject (pakṣadharmatva) holds for this [inference], because the homogeneity with pleasure, pain, and so forth exists in all bodies and the like. Nor can pleasure and the rest arise from a cause that does not possess their own nature; therefore, the body and so forth consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion, because they produce them, and because we observe that they produce serenity and the like, they possess that very nature. Pleasure and the rest, moreover, are specific transformations of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; they are not different entities from them, since it is logically impossible for an effect to be distinct from its cause. Therefore, *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* themselves, existing in the form of sound and the rest, produce effects consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion; hence, sound and the rest are not separate from *sattva* and the other qualities. And the state of equilibrium among *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* is Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*).

Likewise, because it is limited. Whatever is limited arises from a single cause, just as a sprout and the like arise from a seed. Limitation consists in being an object determined by a specific measure. Thus, the body and other effects arise from a single [cause], because they are limited, like a sprout and so forth.

And because of the operation of power (*śakti*). For a cause is taken up by one seeking an effect through its power; thus, every effect remains established within its own cause in the form of power until the [dissolution of] *pradhāna*. Now, if all effects are non-different from *pradhāna* because they exist [within it], how can there be production and destruction? We reply that since it is impossible for what is non-existent—such as a donkey's horn—to be an effect, there are only the manifestation and disappearance of that which already exists. For an effect, while established in the form of power, subsequently attains the state of manifestation; then, upon disappearance, it remains established in the form of power, and does not cease to exist.

Likewise, since the parts of a chair, which exist in a relationship of mutual assistance to one another, are observed to arise from a single cause, it is established that the body and so forth likewise possess the property of being preceded by a single cause, as such a state is observed in their case as well.

Likewise, since the manifold variety of curd and other products is observed to arise from a single substance, milk, it is established that the diversity of bodies and so forth must also be preceded by a single cause; and that which is the single cause is *pradhāna*. From that [pradhāna] arises the Great One (*mahat*); from the Great One, the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*); from that, the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the eleven organs; and from those, the gross elements.

All of this is invalid, because it is impossible for positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and the like to establish a logical mark (*gamaka*). To explain: if one seeks to prove that the body and so forth are preceded by a single cause, the property of being "concomitant" (*anvitatva*) is not a valid reason, as it is doubtful. If, on the other hand, the reason is "being concomitant with pleasure, pain, and so forth," that is not the case, because it is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*). For it has already been established that pleasure, pain, and the like are qualities of the self (*ātman*), and thus their being qualities of the body and so forth is unproven. Furthermore, the example of the pot and such is devoid of the probans (*sādhanavikala*), because there is no observation therein of anything concomitant that is pervaded by being preceded by a single cause. If it is argued that the property of being concomitant with clay exists in the pot and so forth, that too is unproven; for in the case of the subject (*pakṣa*), the material causes (*upādāna*) of the body and so forth are observed through perception to be manifold and belonging to specific classes. Thus, the probans is also "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*).

Thus, being limited—that is, being the object of a determination of quantity—is unestablished, because bodies and so forth are infinite due to their internal subdivisions. If, on the other hand, "limited" refers to being limited with respect to a class (*varga*), even then the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because from the perspective of others, this applies even to eternal things; for *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are limited, yet they do not have a single cause preceding them, since the *pradhāna* itself consists of those very qualities. Likewise, although atoms and the like lack a single preceding cause, they are limited with respect to their class. Furthermore, in the case of a sprout and so forth, when the previous substance has perished through a sequence of actions in the parts of the seed caused by contact with soil and fire, it arises via the process of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so on; thus, having a single cause preceding it is unestablished.

As for the claim that an effect exists in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*) because efficient causes operate toward the production of an effect, that is incorrect; for potentiality consists in the nature of the final auxiliary condition (*sahakārin*), and thus it is not a separate entity from the effect. Furthermore, cause and effect cannot be identical, because they are the objects of distinct appearances (*pratibhāsa*). Indeed, the difference in appearance is the basis for the conventional usage of difference among things. If one were to admit identity despite the existence of such difference, it would follow that all things are one, and thus there would not be twenty-four principles (*tattvas*). Likewise, there is a difference in essential nature (*svarūpa*) and a difference in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) between cause and effect: the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) is subtle and manifold, while the effect is gross and unitary. Consequently, the effect does not previously exist in its causes, because it is not perceived there. If you argue that it is not perceived because it is unmanifest (*anabhivyakta*), then what is the proof for its existence? If you say "because of its arising," no; for that which already exists cannot arise. If you say that an effect arises while being non-existent, then why would things like a donkey’s horn not arise? [We reply: No, because of the absence of a cause. For those things for which a productive cause exists, only they arise; this is not the case for a donkey’s horn and the like, since the absence of a cause is understood precisely through the absence of the effect. Thus, one must state that a jar does not arise from threads, nor does a cloth arise from a lump of clay, because a specific causal complex (*sāmagrī*) produces a specific effect. Indeed, we observe that the causal complex characterized by threads is the producer of cloth alone, while another complex produces something else; thus, the restriction of the effect to its material causes (*upādāna*) is due to this [specificity], not due to pre-existence. Furthermore, whatever is produced was non-existent prior to its production; however, there is no universal rule (*vyāpti*) that whatever is non-existent must necessarily be produced.

That existence [of a thing] which is based on the reason of "being in the process of arising" is non-existent, because that reason is non-conclusive due to its lack of commonality. For instance, the state of being in the process of arising does not exist in things such as space, which do exist, nor does it exist in things such as a donkey's horn, which do not exist.

Furthermore, this designation—that "the sprout is born" or "make a pot"—must also be regarded as figurative (*bhākta*), because there exists a primary subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*). To explain: if one were to maintain that the existing pot possesses the status of an object (*karman*) and the sprout possesses the status of an agent (*kartṛ*), then its arising would be contradicted; moreover, since it already exists, the operation of the causal factors (*kāraka-vyāpāra*) would be rendered useless. If it is argued that the operation is for the sake of manifestation (*abhivyakti*), that is incorrect, because manifestation itself must already exist. If, on the other hand, it is claimed that manifestation—which is previously non-existent—is produced, then the principle that "the existent arises" (*sad-utpadyate*) is contradicted; for manifestation is simply the perception of the thing's own nature, and such perception arises while being previously non-existent. Nor is manifestation the removal of an obstruction, since no such obstruction is ever perceived. Therefore, since the production of an already existent thing is impossible, the designation of the sprout and so forth as having the agency of producing themselves or the status of being an object is merely metaphorical; thus, the designation is established through another means (*anyathāsiddhatva*).

As for the claim that these [entities] must be preceded by a single cause because they have entered into a relationship of beneficiary and benefactor—that too is incorrect. If "the state of being beneficiary and benefactor" is intended to mean the production of a single effect by things that are mutually dependent, then this reason is inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*), since such a relationship exists among eternal entities; furthermore, the example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*), because the parts of a chair are produced by distinct causal factors.

Likewise, the manifold variety (*vaiśvarūpya*) of curd and other substances is not preceded by the aforementioned single cause, because it is an effect produced from its own constituent parts (*svāvayava*). For instance, curd is produced from its own parts, not from milk. Indeed, when the milk has perished through the process of action in its parts due to contact with terrestrial fire, curd and the like are subsequently produced through the sequence of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth arising from those qualities produced by cooking (*pākaja*). Therefore, manifold variety lacks a single preceding cause. Furthermore, since multiple causes belonging to specific classes are perceived directly in the subject (*pakṣa*), the argument regarding manifold variety is also "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*).

Furthermore, no effect is ever observed to arise from a single cause alone; thus, for a reason that lacks a similar instance (*sapakṣa*), there is the presence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). Therefore, since positive concomitance and the other criteria lack probative force, when the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) is unestablished, the intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest cannot possibly exist. Moreover, the doctrine of *pradhāna* has been refuted at length by our teachers, and thus it is not elaborated upon here. Consequently, this is the error of the Sāṃkhyas: that the world is preceded by *pradhāna*.

Likewise, since the body is subject to differentiation according to its varying dimensions, if one were to accept that the body itself is the self (*ātman*), there could be no recognition (*pratisandhāna*) [of past experiences]. Thus, when the Vaiśeṣikas—who teach what is beneficial by establishing that the self must be understood as eternal and distinct from the body and other such things—encounter the Lokāyatikas, whose knowledge of what is harmful is erroneous, this situation arises. This same logic applies equally to the Saugatas (Buddhists) and the Jainas. For instance, if the self possesses the property of contraction and expansion, it would be subject to transformation; and because of its changing nature, its identity would be compromised, making recognition impossible. Furthermore, while they claim the self is of the nature of consciousness (*bodha*) based on the premise that it is conscious, this is refuted by the fact that if recognition does not arise even in a self that is mere consciousness, then the cognition of what is conducive to the highest good (*śreyas*) cannot exist. Enough of this elaboration.
The dissimilarity with non-determination.

“Non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*) also arises only regarding the objects of perception and inference. Among these, first, with respect to the object of perception, non-determination is merely a state of wondering ‘what is this? due to distraction or lack of interest, whether the object is well-known or unknown. For example, a person from the Bāhīka country experiences non-determination regarding *panasa* trees and the like. In that case, there is indeed determination (*adhyavasāya*) based on [the perception of] existence, substanceness, earthness, treeness, color, and so forth, as well as branches and other features. Even the property of being a *panasa* (*panasatva*), which is inclusive of all *panasa* fruits and exclusive of mangoes and the like, is directly perceived; however, because of the absence of instruction, the cognition of its specific name does not occur.”

Now, for the purpose of defining the causes, nature, and objects of non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*), there follows this section beginning with: "Non-determination also arises regarding the objects of perception and inference," and so forth. Non-determination (*anadhyavasiti*) is non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*); it is a cognition whose nature is indecisive. And that is distinct from doubt and other such states, both because of the difference in its causes and because of the difference in its objects.

“In that regard,” first, the object of perception (*pratyakṣaviṣaya*) is explained. Because [perception] occurs with respect to objects both well-known (*prasiddhārtha*) and unknown (*aprasiddhārtha*), it is distinguished from doubt (*saṃśaya*); for doubt arises only with respect to well-known objects. Now, he asks: for what reason does non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*) occur even with respect to well-known objects? He says: “due to distraction (*vyāsaṅga*) or lack of interest (*anarthitva*). For example, due to distraction, when the mind of an arrow-maker is absorbed in his arrow, there is non-determination—such as “Who is this who has passed by?”—even though a great king has gone by. Due to lack of interest, for an ascetic devoted to his own practice, there is non-determination—such as “Who is this who has passed by?”—even though a great king has gone by.

Furthermore, this is not doubt (*saṃśaya*), because doubt involves the presentation of two [contrary] aspects and arises from the perception of common characteristics and so forth. Therefore, non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*) is distinct from the other [types of cognition], because it is produced by the aforementioned causes. Alternatively, that cognition which is produced from the aforementioned causes should be designated as "non-determination. That which is not distinct [from the others] and is not so designated is not produced from the aforementioned causes, such as doubt and the like.

He states its essential nature: "What is it? It is mere observation" (*kiṃ*); that is, a cognition such as "what indeed? which is devoid of the delineation of a specific name and is thus non-determinative (*anadhyavasāya*).

Regarding objects whose meanings are not well-known, it is said: "Just as a Bāhīka has no determinate cognition (*adhyavasāya*) regarding *panasa* trees and the like. A Bāhīka is [also called] a Hiraṭhaka; because he lacks any conventional designation (*saṅketa*) for *panasa* trees and such, there arises in him a cognition devoid of the mention of specific names, such as "What is this? In that case, there is indeed a determinate cognition (*adhyavasāya*) based on [universal properties] such as existence (*sattā*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), earthness (*pṛthivītva*), treeness (*vṛkṣatva*), color (*rūpa*), and so forth, as well as branches and the like. For instance, there is the certain cognition "This exists" (*sann ayam*). Likewise, there is the very same determinate cognition: "It is a substance," "It is earth," "It is a tree," "It possesses color and so forth," and "It possesses branches and so forth. Similarly, even the property of being a *panasa* tree (*panasatva*) is directly perceived in non-conceptual awareness (*nirvikalpaka-bodha*) as that which is inclusive of various *panasa* trees and exclusive of mangoes (*āmra*) and other species.

[Objection: If that is so, then in what object does non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*) occur? [The author] says: "But solely due to the absence of instruction" (*kevalantu upadeśābhāvāt*), meaning that because of the absence of linguistic convention (*saṅketa*), there arises no cognition characterized by the mention of a specific name, such as "this is a *panasa* fruit. [Objection: If that is so, then non-determination would simply be the absence of cognition; and since it is of the nature of a non-entity (*abhāva*), its inclusion within ignorance (*avidyā*) is untenable. [Reply: This is not so. For it is impossible to deny this [state], since a cognition consisting of non-ascertainment—distinct from doubt and the like—is actually experienced. And because it possesses the characteristics of ignorance, it is included within ignorance.

“Even regarding the object of inference, for an inhabitant of the Coconut Island (*nārikeladvīpa*), upon seeing only a dewlap, there arises a state of non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*), thinking: ‘What kind of living being could this possibly be? <PDhS>

“Even regarding the object of inference, for a resident of Nālikera Island who has not established a convention, when a specific body [of an animal] is not perceived, there arises a state of non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*) such as: ‘What kind of living being might be here? upon seeing only a dewlap (*sāsnā*). For previously, even though the convention had not been grasped, the dewlap was perceived as invariably concomitant with the [concept of] a valid referent; therefore, when that [dewlap] is perceived while the specific body is not, following the recollection of the relationship of invariable concomitance, once the reflective cognition (*parāmarśajñāna*) occurs, there arises a state of non-determination: ‘What kind of living being might be in this place? or ‘What is the name of this living being? [This constitutes its difference from dream-cognition.]”

“Dream-cognition is that mental experience which occurs through the very door of the senses for one whose collection of sense-faculties has ceased [their outward activity] and whose mind has dissolved [within]. (PDhS)

Having thus described the distinctions of non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*) according to its various causes and so forth, he states the definition of dream-cognition (*svapna*) with the words, “of one whose collection of sense-faculties has ceased,” and so on. “Of one whose collection of sense-faculties has ceased” means one for whom the group of senses (*grāma*) has ceased—that is, withdrawn—from apprehending their respective objects. “Of one whose mind is dissolved” (*pralīnamanaska*): that is one whose mind (*manas*) is dissolved—that is, not conjoined with the location of the sense-faculties. “That mental experience which arises through the very door of the sense-faculties is dream-cognition. Mental (*mānasa*) means existing in the mind; since this also includes memory, pleasure, and so forth, the term “experience” (*anubhavana*) is used to exclude those. Furthermore, since experience can also be produced by the external senses, the word “mental” is included. Nevertheless, there is still the fallacy of over-extension (*vyabhicāra*) due to experiences such as pleasure and pain [which are mental]; therefore, the phrase “of one whose collection of sense-faculties has ceased” is added. For the experience of pleasure and so forth is indeed born of the senses, since the mind operates therein. Now, if it is argued that there is still a fallacy because mental experience occurs even during the state immediately following sleep (*svapnāntika*), that is not so; because that state is of the nature of memory, it is already excluded by the very word “experience.”
Others, however, follow the general definition of ignorance for the purpose of its exclusion from this [definition].

Nor should it be suspected that the cognition of blue, yellow, and so forth occurs for one with closed eyes whose collection of sense-faculties has ceased, because when there is proximity to an object, the cognition of it arises through another sense-faculty. For it is only when there is no cognition by means of a sense-faculty despite the proximity of an object that a person is said to have their "collection of sense-faculties ceased. Furthermore, since experience regarding blue, yellow, and so forth is not possible without the operation of the eye, this [dream-cognition] is rightly considered a form of memory (*smaraṇa*), and that is already excluded by the term "experience" (*anubhava*) itself. [Objection: Even if this is so, since dream-cognition is a mental experience for one whose collection of sense-faculties has ceased, there is no deviation (i.e., over-extension) from the definition if it is stated that it is "distinct from the other" [waking cognition]. Why, then, are the two words "of one whose mind is dissolved" (*pralīnamanaska*) and "only through the door of the sense-faculties" (*indriyadvāreṇaiva*) included? [Response: It is for the sake of providing another definition. To explain: "That mental experience which belongs to one whose mind is dissolved is dream-cognition"—this is the second definition. The word "experience" is used because even the state immediately following a dream (*svapnāntika*) occurs for one whose mind is dissolved. And the word "dissolved mind" is used because experience also occurs in relation to pleasure and the like.

Therefore, because it is an experience of a mind that has dissolved [into sleep], it differs from other [perceptions]; likewise, while arising through the very same gateway as the sense organs, it is an experience belonging to the mental faculty (*mānasa*). Thus, dream-experience arises through the gateway of the sense organs; and since such experience also occurs with respect to pleasure and so forth, the phrase "through the gateway of the sense organs" is employed.
{The manner of the arising of dreams}

“How so? When, for the sake of rest at night or for the sake of digesting food, living beings who are exhausted during the day by bodily activities preceded by conscious intent, the mind—due to a continuous series of actions arising from the connection between the self and the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) dependent upon an effort induced by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa)—comes to rest motionless within the region of the self that is devoid of senses in the heart; then it is designated as ‘one whose mind has dissolved’. <PDhS>

“And when that [body] has dissolved, the collection of the sense organs ceases to function. In that state, while the continuity of the flow of *prāṇa* and *apāna* persists, dream-cognition arises through the door of the sense organs—even though the objects are non-existent—having the form of direct perception due to a specific conjunction of the self and the mind and from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) known as sleep. <PDhS>

Now, as to how dream-cognition arises, and how a person becomes one whose collection of sense-faculties has ceased and whose mind is dissolved, he says: "When," etc. When [the mind] stays motionless—that is, devoid of activity—in that region of the self within the heart and not externally; for he is so described as one whose sense-faculties have gone out (*nirgatendriya*), at that time the person is designated as "one whose mind is dissolved.
Others, however, state that the mind stays motionless there in the downward-facing lotus, which is the region of the self devoid of sense-faculties, as accepted in the scriptures.

And that specific connection with the self arises from a continuity of action—that is, a stream of actions. Furthermore, this continuity of action is produced from the conjunction of the self and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is brought about by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and depends upon effort (*prayatna*). To explain: the mind (*manas*) is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), the conjunction of the self and the mind is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and the effort induced by the unseen force is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*); thus, through this continuity of action in the mind, a conjunction with a specific region of the self occurs, which is designated as "sleep."

And when does this occur? "At night," (*niśi*), according to the majority of cases. And for what purpose does it happen? "For the sake of rest (*viśrāma*) or for the sake of digesting food (*āhārapariṇāma*). This is intended to apply both collectively and individually, depending on the differences between persons; for one person it may have one purpose, while for another it may have both. Of what kind of living being? Of one who is "fatigued during the day. Why? Because of physical exertion (*śarīravyāpāra*). But that [exertion] can also belong to one mounted on a boat or similar vehicle, yet no fatigue results from that; therefore, [the text specifies] "due to conscious effort" (*buddhipūrva*). Consciousness (*buddhi*) is the cause for the arising of activity through the mediation of memory and desire, not directly. Nevertheless, in other bodies, conscious activity occurs by way of [divine] command (*niyoga*), yet no fatigue results from that; therefore, [it specifies] "of oneself" (*ātmanaḥ*), meaning of one's own body. In the manner thus described, the mind (*manas*) is said to be dissolved and connected to a region devoid of sense organs. When that [mind] has dissolved, the person becomes one whose collection of senses has ceased, because the senses, when not presided over by the mind, cannot function toward their respective objects. However, life in that state is inferred "by continuity" (*prabandhena*), that is, by constancy, since the stream of inhalation and exhalation continues. For instance, the flow of the stream of inhalation and exhalation is an effect of effort, yet an effort preceded by desire or aversion is not possible here; therefore, an effort preceded by mere life-force (*jīvana*) is inferred, as we shall explain in the section on effort (*prayatna*).

Now, one might ask: from what cause does dream-cognition arise for the self whose mind has thus dissolved and whose collection of sense-faculties has ceased? To this he says: "From a specific conjunction of the self and the mind" (*ātmamanaḥsaṃyogaviśeṣāt*). This refers to that specific conjunction of the self and the mind which has "sleep" as its designation—that is, its name—and from that [conjunction]. And "from latent impressions" (*saṃskārācca*). Latent impression is the cause for the arising of dream-cognition by way of producing memory.

Alternatively, the term "called sleep" (*svāpākhya*) is an adjective qualifying the *saṃskāra*. For that *saṃskāra* which, during the state of sleep, becomes the cause of the cognition of its own [object] by means of memory is what is "called sleep. Therefore, from space, time, and so forth, through the very door of the sense organs, dream-cognition arises in the form of perception—as if it were a direct perception—even though objects such as elephants are non-existent (*asatsu*) and not present.

Others, however, maintain that it is precisely walls and other such things existing in the form of elephants that serve as the objective support (*ālambana*) for dream-cognition. As for the statement that dream-cognition arises even when objects do not exist, that too is said with respect to the actual nature of the elephants and so forth, because they lack existence in that specific form.

This is incorrect, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for walls and the like being the objective supports (*ālambana*). Furthermore, one who has awakened from a dream does not possess a recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) such as, "These walls and so forth appeared to me in the form of elephants and the like. Nor is it possible for the sense organs to function toward walls and the like in the production of a cognition of elephants and the like, since that cognition arises even when their activity has ceased. Moreover, the independent operation of the mind (*manas*) with respect to external objects is strictly prohibited. Therefore, dream-cognition is indeed devoid of an object (*nirviṣaya*).

Now, dream-cognition is not a category distinct from error and the others. For instance, dream-cognition arising as "that" in what is "not that" is simply erroneous cognition (*viparyaya-jñāna*). When it involves the presentation of both alternatives, such as "Is this a post or a person?", it is doubt (*saṃśaya-jñāna*). And when it arises as "What is its name?", it is non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*). Thus, dream-cognition is not a separate entity from these. Its separate mention, however, is due to its being an indicator of auspicious or inauspicious results.

This is not tenable; for some maintain that because of the difference in its causes, it is a distinct entity from error (*viparyaya*) and the others. To explain: erroneous cognition arises regarding the objects of perception and inference for a person whose sense faculties are impaired by bile, phlegm, or wind. Doubt, however, arises regarding the objects of perception and inference for one who perceives a commonality and so forth, and for whom both specific characteristics are well-known. Thus, a cause entirely different from that of non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*) has been stated. But the causes for the arising of dream-cognition (*svapnajñāna*) are the opposite of those. Therefore, there is a distinction based on the difference in causes. If one were to accept non-distinction despite a difference in definitions (*lakṣaṇa*), it would follow that such a state of affairs would apply everywhere. Furthermore, dream-cognition arises even with respect to an object that is absolutely unknown, whereas this is not the case for error and the rest. Therefore, even though the presence of the mention of both [aspects] and so forth exists, since it satisfies the definition of a dream, one must admit that this is indeed dream-cognition, which is distinct from doubt and the other types of cognition.
{The varieties of dreams}:
“That [dreaming] is of three kinds: from the intensity of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), from a disorder of the bodily humors (*dhātu-doṣa*), and from unseen merit or demerit (*adṛṣṭa*).

“In that regard, first, due to the intensity of mental impressions: when one who is lustful or angry sleeps while intensely contemplating a certain object, then that very stream of contemplation arises in the form of a direct perception.”

“Due to a disorder of the elements (*dhātudoṣa*), one who has a wind-constitution (*vātaprakṛti*) or is afflicted by it sees such things as traveling through the sky; one with a bile-constitution (*pittaprakṛti*) or afflicted by it sees such things as entering fire or mountains of gold; and one with a phlegm-constitution (*śleṣmaprakṛti*) or afflicted by it sees such things as crossing rivers and oceans or snow-mountains.”

“That which indicates auspiciousness—whether regarding objects experienced by oneself or not experienced, or objects well-known or unknown—such as mounting an elephant or obtaining a parasol, all that arises from *saṃskāra* (mental impressions) and *dharma* (merit). Conversely, that which is the opposite—such as being anointed with oil or mounting a donkey or a camel—all that arises from *adharma* (demerit) and *saṃskāra*.
Regarding objects that are entirely unknown, it arises solely from the *adṛṣṭa* (unseen force).”

He states the distinction [of dream-cognition] based on its different causes: "But that" (*tat tu*) dream-cognition "is threefold: from the intensity of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), from a disorder of the bodily humors (*dhātu-doṣa*), and from the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). First, regarding dream-cognition arising from the intensity of mental impressions, he says: "A lover" (*kāmī*)—one who is attached to a certain woman, thinking of her with great respect and with excessive effort—or one who, being angry, sleeps while thinking of his enemy with effort. "That very" (*saiva*) continuous stream of thoughts (*cintā-santati*) of the sleeping person arises in the form of a direct perception (*pratyakṣākārā*); it does not arise from the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).

Regarding dreams arising from an imbalance of the elements (*dhātudoṣa*), he says: one of "wind-constitution" (*vātaprakṛti*)—that is, one whose body is composed of atoms initiated by wind as the predominant cause, and who is further afflicted by wind due to the consumption of such food—sees movements through space and so forth. The same should be understood for those of "bile-constitution" (*pittaprakṛti*) and others as well.

He states that dream is caused by the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*): "That dream-cognition which arises regarding objects—whether previously experienced or not experienced, and whether well-known or unknown—that indicates auspiciousness, arises from the unseen. In that regard, whatever indicates auspiciousness, such as mounting an elephant or obtaining a parasol, all of that arises from both mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) and merit (*dharma*). For a mental impression is produced by a prior experience, and it is the cause for the arising of dream-cognition by way of generating memory.

The perverted [cognition] that experiences the impure consists of [the perception of] being anointed with oil, riding a donkey or a camel, and so forth; this arises from unrighteousness (*adharma*) and mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).

Dream-cognition arises solely from the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) regarding things that are entirely unknown and never experienced before—for instance, one sees oneself ascended to the station of Brahmā and other such states.

(Although dream-cognition occurs when the collection of sense-faculties has ceased, it is nonetheless merely memory (*smṛti*) because it involves the reflective examination of a continuous stream of past cognitions. Thus, this ignorance is fourfold.)

Now, as to whether the state of dreaming (*svapnānta*) is simply dream-cognition or something else, he says: "The state of dreaming" (*svapnāntika*) means that which occurs at the end of a dream, at the conclusion of a dream. [He asks: "Even though it occurs for one whose collection of sense-faculties has ceased, nevertheless it is nothing but memory. [He explains: "Because it consists in the reflective observation of a past continuum of cognitions. That which is both past and a continuum of cognitions—because it takes the form of reflecting upon that—it is indeed memory. Thus is the summary: ignorance is of four kinds, having the nature just described.

Others, however, maintain that "this" ignorance (*avidyā*), as explained by me, is fourfold; otherwise, it would indeed be manifold. [This is a statement of its divisions based on its dissimilarity to knowledge (*vidyā*):
"Knowledge (*vidyā*) is also fourfold, characterized as perception, inference, recollection, and scriptural revelation."

Now, for the purpose of defining the nature of knowledge (*vidyā*), there begins the section starting with "Knowledge, too, is fourfold" (*vidyāpi caturvidhā*). To the question "In what form?", he says: "Characterized by perception, inference, recollection, and that of the sages; such is its nature. Perception is *pratyakṣa*; that which arises from the observation of a mark is inferential (*laiṅgika*); remembrance is recollection (*smṛti*); and that which belongs to the sages (*ṛṣis*) is the knowledge of the sages (*ārṣa*).

[Objection: Since verbal knowledge (*śābdajñāna*) is also of the nature of *vidyā* (valid knowledge), what is the purpose of not including it here? [Response: It is to indicate a point of disagreement (*vipratipatti*). For instance, some maintain that verbal knowledge is included within inference (*anumāna*), while others, such as the Vaiśeṣikas, hold it to be a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*); it is for this reason of disagreement that it is not mentioned here. However, even by a statement primarily intended to classify *vidyā*, its cause—the collection of causal factors (*sāmagrī*)—is indeed implied as a subordinate element. But if one were to accept a classification of perception and so forth based on the primary derivation of the term as "the instrument" (*karaṇa*), then the determination of the classification of *vidyā* would become merely subordinate; that, however, is not correct, because the distinction between types of cognition (*buddhibheda*), which was previously promised, is what is being determined here.

{The Definition of Non-conceptual Perception} “Among these, that which arises in dependence upon each sense organ (*akṣa*) is called perception (*pratyakṣa*). The sense organs are six: the nose, tongue, eye, skin, ear, and mind. That [perception] indeed arises with respect to categories of objects such as substance and the rest. First, regarding substance: in the case of a large [substance] possessing many constituent substances, when there is the fourfold contact [of the object] with light and the causal complex consisting of dharma and so forth, there occurs a mere observation of the intrinsic nature (*svarūpālocanamātra*). <PDhS>

In that regard, for the purpose of defining perception (*pratyakṣa*), he says: "It is called *pratyakṣa* because it arises in dependence upon each sense-organ (*akṣam akṣam pratītyotpadyate*). The compound *pratyakṣa* is a *prādi-samāsa* (a prepositional compound) meaning "that which has gone toward the sense-organ" (*pratigatam akṣam*). Otherwise, if one were to accept it as an *avyayībhāva* compound, there would be no distinction of gender or number, such as in the cases: "perceptible form" (*pratyakṣaṃ rūpam*), "perceptible men" (*pratyakṣāḥ pumāṃsaḥ*), or "perceptible woman" (*pratyakṣā strī*). The employment of the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) "each [sense-organ]" (*akṣam akṣam*) is for the purpose of including all the sense-faculties. Now, one might argue: "Is not the inclusion of all sense-faculties already achieved by the general term *akṣa* itself? No, because a general term functions in two ways. For instance, in the prohibition "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed," the prohibition applies with respect to all Brāhmaṇas; whereas in the injunction "Feed the Brāhmaṇas," the assignment applies with respect to specific Brāhmaṇas. Therefore, the use of the distributive repetition is for the sake of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Furthermore, one might object: "Even when the distributive repetition is present, pervasion is not always perceived—as in the examples: 'The village is within the sacrificial altar' (*antarvedyāṃ grāmaḥ*), 'The village is pleasant,' 'The man is pleasant,' or 'There is a specific quality in the man. Here, the distributive repetition is indeed employed. True, yet even so, the distributive repetition is observed only when pervasion applies to a thing associated with a small number.

Others, however, consider the second mention of the word *akṣa* (sense-faculty) to be for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). That knowledge which arises having depended upon—that is, having reached—the sense-faculty (*akṣa*) is perception (*pratyakṣa*). Now, since the knowledge has not yet arisen, there is no reaching by means of the sense-faculty; how then can it be said to arise "having reached" the sense-faculty? There is no fault here, because figurative usage (*upacāra*) is intended. For example, as in the expression: "This child was born after devouring his mother. For this very reason, [the definition] states that it is an effect dependent on the sense-faculties, and that [knowledge] is [the result] of that [contact]; whereas the form and so forth belonging to the sense-faculties are dependent on the sense-faculties, but they are not knowledge.

[Objection: Even so, does this not lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), since doubt (*saṃśaya*) also arises in dependence upon the sense organ? [Reply: That is not so; for even when a specific definition is not stated, the application of the general characteristic of knowledge (*vidyā*) is obtained. And he will state: "That knowledge which arises as non-erroneous (*avitatha*) and non-designatable (*avyapadeśya*) is the means of valid perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*). By the term "non-erroneous" (*avitatha*), the exclusion of erroneous knowledge (*viparyaya*) and doubtful knowledge (*saṃśaya*) is intended. For both doubtful knowledge and erroneous knowledge are indeed erroneous (*vitatha*).

Others, however, following the logic of their own specific system (*pratitantra-nyāya*), maintain that the term "of the nature of ascertainment" (*vyavasāyātmaka*) must be supplied [from the previous sūtra]. Regarding the term "non-verbalizable" (*avyapadeśya*): *vyapadeśa* means "word"; that which is produced by this is *vyapadeśya*. That which is not *vyapadeśya* is *avyapadeśya*, meaning knowledge not produced by words. [Objection: Is this not already excluded by the statement that verbal knowledge does not arise by reaching the sense organ? [Reply: No, because its purpose is to exclude that knowledge which is produced by words acting as an auxiliary to the sense organs. For instance, even while seeing a color with the eye, one who has not previously made a linguistic convention does not know it as "color"; only after the utterance of the word "color" does he comprehend it. Thus, such knowledge is born from both [the sense organ and the word].

But surely, this is untenable because the operation of the auditory organ and the sense of hearing cannot occur at one and the same time. To explain: the ear, presided over by the mind, grasps sound; then, through a sequence of actions, when there is contact with the eye, there is the grasping of form. And it is not possible for the cognition of sound to persist for such a long duration; so how can there be a cognition produced from both? In this regard, a single action arises in the mind when it is connected to the ear, and this action initiates a separation (*vibhāga*). At the very moment that the separation causes the [ear-]conjunction to reach its state of destruction, the cognition of sound reaches its state of arising. Then follows the production of the cognition of sound, the destruction of the conjunction, and the state of the subsequent conjunction reaching its production. Next, there is the production of the conjunction with the eye which is connected to the object, and the cognition of form reaches its state of arising. Finally, the cognition of form is produced by the eye acting in cooperation with the sound that assisted in its own [prior] cognition; thus, the cognition is produced from both.

Alternatively, this restriction—that the operation of a perceived word necessarily consists in the determination of its meaning through a factor that cooperates with its perception—is not mandatory. Even at a later time, when the mind is connected with the eye, because the word "form" has been grasped, there indeed arises a cognition produced by both [the sense organ and the word]. And the postulation of a cause is made based on the existence of an effect; since that [effect] is observed here, its production is considered according to this sequence. Likewise, because of the designation by means of the word, even for one seeing a form with the eye, there is the cognition produced by both, such as: "I did not know [this] form, but I have understood it from the word 'form'. If it were the case that [a cognition] is non-perceptual (*apratyakṣa*) due to the operation of the word, then [a cognition] would not be verbal (*śābda*) due to the operation of the sense organ, and thus it would become the fruit of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is not so. For while the definition of perception includes the qualification "inexpressible" (*avyapadeśya*), the definition of verbal knowledge does not mention the qualification "not born of the senses" (*anindriyajam*); therefore, there is no fixed rule regarding the cooperation [of the senses] in the case of the word. Indeed, verbal knowledge may arise either from the word with the sense organ as a cooperative factor, or from it devoid of that; in every case, that which produces it is the verbal means of valid cognition.

In this context, regarding the statement "that cognition which arises in dependence upon the sense organ is perception," since the explanations mention the contact of the fourfold [senses] and so forth, the sixfold relation is indeed obtained. And that consists of: conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), inherence in what is inherent in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*), inherence (*samavāya*), inherence in the inherent (*samavetasamavāya*), and the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*).

But even so, [the definition] is already delimited by the very term "contact between sense-organ and object. Now, if the sense-organ were the mind (*manas*) and the object were the self (*ātman*), then inferential and other types of cognition would also arise from their contact, and thus they too would be the fruit of perception. No; for it is untenable that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) functions as a sense-organ merely upon the arising of any cognition whatsoever. It has been stated that the definition of a sense-organ is its capacity to produce immediate (*aparokṣa*) cognition, qualified by such attributes as being an instrument (*karaṇa*). Furthermore, inferential cognition does not occur with respect to an object that is grasped by a sense-organ. Thus, when a cognition arises—being non-erroneous (*avitatha*), non-verbalizable (*avyapadeśya*), and determinative (*vyavasāyātmaka*)—with respect to an object in dependence upon a sense-organ, that [cognition] from which it arises is perception. This is the position that takes the fruit (the cognition) as the defining characteristic. These qualifiers, such as "non-erroneous" and so forth, serve to exclude other types of cognition; they are applied by superimposing them onto the intellect (*buddhi*) even after the cognition to be qualified has passed.

However, in the view that these qualify the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there is no direct application of qualifiers such as "non-deviant" (*avyabhicārin*) and so forth. Now, the causal complex arises in dependence upon each respective sense-organ (*akṣam akṣam pratītya*), because it consists in the totality of causal factors (*kārakasākalya*). This totality, moreover, exists only upon the attainment of the final auxiliary condition and not prior to it; thus, it indeed arises [at that moment]. Likewise, since it is by means of this that cognition is known, the causal complex—characterized by the sense-organs and so forth—is itself the "cognition" (*jñāna*). It is non-deviant and of a determinate nature (*vyavasāyātmikā*). By the word "inexpressible" (*avyapadeśya*), the causal complex is designated as such because it is the generator of that cognition; thus, even in the view that these qualify the causal complex, there is an application of the qualifiers? True. Nevertheless, the qualifiers such as "non-deviance" belong to the result (*phala*); they apply to the causal complex only by way of that result. Therefore, the latter is the view that they qualify the result.

The position that the definition is a qualifier of the essential nature (*svarūpa-viśeṣaṇa-pakṣa*) has already been refuted, because the word "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) denotes an instrument (*karaṇa*). To explain: a *pramāṇa* is that by which something is cognized (*pramīyate*), namely, that distinct from the agent and the object by which the act of cognition (*pramā*) is produced. Under the view that the definition is a qualifier of the essential nature, however, the validity of a means of cognition does not consist in its being the producer of what is produced; rather, it consists solely in its possessing properties such as non-deviation (*avyabhicāritva*). But this [definition] is both over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*) and under-extensive (*avyāpaka*). Thus, even a cognition such as the "subsumptive reflection" (*parāmarśa*) possesses this form, yet it is not considered perception, since it is an inference due to being the generator of an inferential cognition. Furthermore, the status of perception is not obtained for the totality of causal factors (*sāmagrī*) intended to be perception; thus, there is the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*).

For the Sugatas (Buddhists), however, there is no distinction between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*); thus, in their system, it is only as a qualification of its own nature (*svarūpa-viśeṣaṇa*) that [the object] is possible. To explain: for the Sautrāntikas, the mental aspect (*ākāra*) is the means of valid cognition, the external object is the object of cognition (*prameya*), and self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*) is held to be the result. Thus, that very [aspect] is what constitutes the conventional usage of "means of cognition" and "result," or it is a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). But this is not tenable, because a non-difference between an action (*kriyā*) and its instrument (*karaṇa*) is never observed. Furthermore, it has already been stated that the form of an object cannot exist within consciousness; how then could that [consciousness] possess the status of a means of valid cognition? Nor is it logical that validity consists in the determination of an object by virtue of the cognition having the form of the object (*meyarūpatā*), because the object is entirely beyond perception (*atyantaparokṣa*), and thus no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with it can be apprehended. If an operation whose connection is ungrasped were to indicate a specific object, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Consequently, the aspect of color (*rūpākāra*) would also establish taste (*rasa*) and so forth, since there is no difference in the non-apprehension of a connection in either case. Moreover, for one who maintains that only the aspect is cognized, the apprehension of a specific object cannot reside in the aspect; for while the object remains entirely beyond perception, and in the absence of a synthesizing subject (*pratisandhātṛ*), positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are themselves entirely beyond perception.
Furthermore, the definition of perception belonging to others has been refuted at length by our teachers, and thus it has not been mentioned here.

Because the word *akṣa* has multiple meanings, he says: “*Akṣāṇi* [means] the sense-faculties (*indriyāṇi*). These, however, are the nose, tongue, eye, skin, ear, and mind; they are not the organs of action (*karmendriya*) as accepted by others. To exclude memory by negating knowledge that lacks an object, he says: “For that,” namely perception, “arises with respect to categories such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth”; therefore, it is not without an object. And here, by the word “and so forth” (*ādi*), qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*karman*), and universals (*sāmānya*) are included. Others maintain that inherence (*samavāya*) is also included.

Others, however, maintain that this is for the purpose of demonstrating the contact between the sense organ and its object; for perception arises with respect to categories such as substance and so forth. Therefore, there exists a relationship such as *saṃyuktasamavāya* (inherence in what is conjoined) and the like, involving the sense organ.

Since perception arises with respect to categories such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth, it is therefore explained [starting] with "substance" (*dravye tāvat*). Of what kind? "Threefold" (*trividhe*): that which has three modes is called thus; in that [substance]. "Large" (*mahati*): in that which is the locus of largeness (*mahattva*). "Apprehension of the essential form" (*svarūpālocanam*): non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) cognition arises. Why? From "the possession of multiple substances, the manifestation of color, light, and the contact of the four" (*anekadravyavattvodbhūtarūpaprakāśacatuṣṭayasannikarṣāt*). This refers to the possession of multiple substances (*anekadravyavattva*), manifested color (*udbhūtarūpa*), light (*prakāśa*), and the contact of the four (*catuṣṭayasannikarṣa*). And [it says] "and when there is the totality of factors such as merit (*dharma*)": "multiple" (*aneka*) and "substance" (*dravya*) make "multiple substance" (*anekadravya*); that which possesses this is "possessing multiple substances" (*tadvat*); its state is "the possession of multiple substances. Here, "color" (*rūpa*) is intended to mean a specific kind of color. Thus the Sūtra states: "A substance is perceptible due to largeness, the possession of multiple substances, and a specific kind of color" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 4.1.6). It was stated in the section on air (*vāyu*) that when non-obscured cognition exists, all these factors—both collectively and individually—are intended as the causes of perceptual cognition. Furthermore, "contact of the four" means: the self (*ātman*) is conjoined with the mind (*manas*), the mind with the sense organ (*indriya*), and the sense organ with the object (*artha*); from that [arises] the contact of the four. And by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "merit and so forth," space (*dik*) and time (*kāla*) are included.

Now, let it be granted that non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpakajñāna*) arises in this way. What is the proof for its existence? It is simply the arising of conceptual cognition (*savikalpakajñāna*). For otherwise, if a qualified object were not perceived, the recollection of the linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) regarding that qualified object would be impossible, and thus conceptual cognition could not occur, since the latter is the effect of the former. Nor is the recollection of the convention alone the cause of that [conceptual cognition], because—as stated by the aforementioned reasoning—the sense organ (*akṣa*) functions as the cause for the arising of conceptual cognition through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), just as it does for the arising of non-conceptual cognition, provided the object is not momentary.

{Definition of Determinate Perception} “Determinate perception arises from the contact of the self and the mind, depending on qualifiers such as genus, particularity, substance, quality, and action—as in the cognitions: ‘a real substance,’ ‘earth,’ ‘horned,’ ‘white,’ or ‘the cow is walking. <PDhS>

Having thus established non-conceptual [perception], he explains conceptual cognition, which is the knowledge of a qualified object (*viśeṣyajñāna*), with the words: "Dependent upon the qualifiers—universal, particular, substance, quality, and action," and so forth. "Universal" (*sāmānya*), "particular" (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*), "substance" (*dravya*), "quality" (*guṇa*), and "action" (*karman*) are what has been stated. These themselves are the qualifiers; that which depends on them is "dependent upon those" (*tadapekṣaḥ*). The particle *ca* (and) indicates a conjunction: not only does the mere observation of the intrinsic nature (*svarūpālocana*) arise from the aforementioned causes, but that which depends on the qualifiers such as universals and the rest also arises from those very same causes.

Is it not the case that the mention of the contact between the self and the mind is redundant, since it is accepted that [the contact] continues everywhere above [the initial stage], except for specific exceptions regarding the fourfold contact? No; it is for the purpose of making known that this [contact] is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) even in the immediately subsequent cognition.

In that regard, "existent" (*sat*) is a qualification by means of existence (*sattā*); "substance" (*dravya*) is a universal (*sāmānya*); "earth" is dependent on a particular (*viśeṣa*); likewise, "horned" is a qualification of a substance; "white" is dependent on a qualification of a quality (*guṇa*); "cow" is dependent on a qualification of a particular universal; and "going" is a cognition characterized by action—these are the examples.
The manner in which direct perception arises with respect to qualities and so forth.

“With respect to color, taste, smell, and touch, [cognition] arises through the contact of their own substratum with the sense organ, due to their inherence in multiple substances and due to their own specific qualities. In the case of sound, which inheres in the auditory organ, its perception occurs through that very [organ] by means of the threefold contact. Number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, viscidity, fluidity, speed, and action are apprehended by both the visual and tactile organs because of their inherence in perceptible substances. The perception of cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort arises from the conjunction of the two: the self and the mind.”<PDhS>

He states that perception occurs with respect to qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth: "In the case of objects such as color, taste, smell, and touch," [perception arises] because of inherence (*samavāya*) together with multiple substances, and "from their own specificities" (*svagataviśeṣāt*). That by which their apprehension occurs in certain objects, and in whose absence there is no apprehension, is the property of color and the rest known as *udbhava* (manifestation); it is a specific auxiliary cause (*sahakāriviśeṣa*), and from that [perception arises]. And "from the contact with its own substratum" (*svāśrayasannikarṣāt*). The sense organ is conjoined with the substance which is its own substratum; through inherence in that [substance], and when the causal complex consisting of merit (*dharma*) and other factors is present, cognition arises, conditioned by the respective sense organ. "In the case of sound, from the contact of three" (*śabdasya trayasannikarṣāt*). The self is conjoined with the mind, and the mind with the sense organ—this is the contact of the triad. "Of that which inheres in the auditory organ" (*śrotrasamavetasya*). The contact between the sense organ and the object has already been demonstrated. Therefore, apprehension occurs by that very auditory organ and not by another sense organ.

Others, however, hold that because "three" and "this contact" [are both present], the compound *indriyārthasannikarṣaḥ* (sense-object contact) is also perceived; therefore, that which is inherent in the auditory organ (*śrotra*) is apprehended by that very same [contact].

[There is] the apprehension of number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, viscidity, fluidity, velocity, and action. Why? Because they are inherent in substances that are perceptible by sight and touch; thus, the apprehension of number and the others occurs through their inherence [in those substances]. The perception of cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort occurs through the contact of both the self and the mind. For cognition and the rest are inherent in the self and are apprehended by the mind which is connected to it.

“The perception of existence, substantiality, quality-ness, action-ness, and so forth—which are inherent in perceptible substrates—by means of the sense organs that apprehend those substrates, is the direct perception (pratyakṣa) of persons such as ourselves. <PDhS>

Regarding universals (*sāmānya*), he states that perception [occurs as follows]: “The apprehension of existence (*bhāva*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), action-ness (*karmatva*), and so forth—which are inherent in perceptible substrates—takes place by means of those sense organs that apprehend their respective supports. Existence, substantiality, and action-ness are what have been mentioned; by the phrase “and so forth” (*ādi*), earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*), throwing upward (*utkṣepaṇatva*), and others are included. That which is both perceptible and a substrate is “the perceptible substrate”; the apprehension of those things inherent in it occurs by means of the sense organs that apprehend its support. By whichever sense organ the apprehension of the support occurs, by that very same organ there is the apprehension of existence (*sattā*) and the rest inherent in it. To illustrate: existence, while residing in a substance, is perceived by both the eyes and the sense of touch through the relation of inherence-in-the-conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*). Those inherent in odors, tastes, colors, and tangibles are perceived by the olfactory, gustatory, visual, and tactile organs respectively, through the relation of inherence-in-what-is-inherent-in-the-conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*). In the case of sound, however, it is perceived by the auditory organ through the relation of inherence-in-what-is-inherent (*samavetasamavāya*). Pleasure and the like are grasped by the mind through the relation of inherence-in-what-is-inherent-in-the-conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*). Quality-ness (*guṇatva*) is likewise. Therefore, with respect to existence and quality-ness, there is cognition by all the sense organs. Substantiality (*dravyatva*) is perceived by the eyes and the sense of touch through the relation of inherence-in-the-conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*). Action-ness (*karmatva*) is perceived through the relation of inherence-in-what-is-inherent-in-the-conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*). The apprehension of color-ness (*rūpatva*) and the like is also similar. “This is the perception of people such as us,” thus concludes the passage.

{The Determination of Yogic Perception} “For yogis who are superior to us, when they are in a state of union (*yukta*), there arises through the mind aided by merit born of yoga (*yogaja-dharma*) an unerring perception of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) regarding their own self, other selves, ether, space, time, atoms, air, and the mind, as well as regarding the qualities, actions, universals, and particulars inherent in them, and inherence. Furthermore, for those who are separated from yoga (*viyukta*), perception arises regarding subtle, concealed, and distant objects through the contact of the four [factors], by virtue of the power of the aid provided by merit born of yoga.”

Likewise, it is explained how and with respect to which objects direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) arises for yogins who are superior to us. In that regard, for those who are "joined" (*yuktāḥ*), remaining in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), a vision of the immediate nature of things is produced by the mind—which is assisted by and has as its concomitant the *dharma* born of yoga—with respect to which objects? With respect to one's own self, another self, space, direction, time, air, atoms, and the mind; these are what have been mentioned, and [perception occurs] with respect to them. Furthermore, not only is there a direct apprehension by yogins through the mind conjoined with their own selves and so forth, but there is also apprehension through "conjunction-inherence" (*saṃyukta-samavāya*) with respect to the qualities, actions, universals, and other particulars inherent in those [substances]; and with respect to inherence (*samavāya*) itself, there is apprehension through the relation of "qualification and qualified" (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) based on conjunction. For this very reason, inherence is mentioned separately, because it is determined by a distinct means of contact. As for the universal residing in qualities, actions, and so forth belonging to atoms and the like, there is apprehension through "inherence-in-what-is-inherent-in-what-is-conjoined" (*saṃyukta-samaveta-samavāya*).

Now, when the yogi perceives his own internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), what is the instrument? It is the conjunction of the self and the mind; in that case, since the mind is the object to be delimited, the mind itself is the instrument. Furthermore, by means of another person's mind, he impels and connects the mind residing in the subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*); and having become connected with it, he perceives it.

“Furthermore, for those who are disengaged [from meditation], knowledge arises through the contact of the fourfold [means], just like the perception of people such as ourselves. With respect to what objects? ‘With respect to subtle, concealed, and remote objects. Subtle objects are atoms; concealed objects are the world of the Nāgas and so forth; remote objects are Mount Meru and the like. Direct knowledge regarding these arises through the power of the assistance provided by *yogaja-dharma* (dharma born of yoga) for those not in a state of meditative absorption (*asamādhi*). For the sense organs of the Lord of Yogis, due to the assistance of this specific *dharma*, there is no obstruction anywhere. The mention of the ‘contact of the fourfold’ is for the sake of illustration, since apprehension occurs even through the contact of three [factors]. For instance, by means of the assistance of *yogaja-dharma*, a yogi perceives—through the contact of three factors—the speech uttered by Brahmā and others, which has reached the location of his ear according to the principle of an unobstructed continuum.”

Now, it may be argued that all this is invalid, because there is a lack of evidence for the existence of yogis and because subverting arguments (*bādhaka*) can be established. Thus: "A yogi is not a seer of supersensible objects, because he is a living being, like us," or "The senses of a yogi do not have all things as their objects, because they are sense organs, like our own senses. This is not tenable; for since yogis are not established in an independent [proof], the reason "because he is a living being" suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*). If, on the other hand, this is an attempt to produce an undesirable consequence for the opponent by means of a pervasion accepted by him (*paravyāpti*), then if that [existence of yogis] is established for the opponent by a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the reasons used to negate them cannot even arise, as they would be sublated by that very same proof. Furthermore, there is no contradiction of a cause merely by its effect; for if there were, the reason would lose its validity due to lacking the property of the subject (*apakṣadharmatva*), as its very root would be undermined. If, however, yogis—who are accepted by the opponent even without a means of knowledge—are being negated, then since the object of cognition (*prameya*) is unestablished precisely due to the absence of a means of knowledge, the inference negating them is useless.

Furthermore, there is an inference for the existence of yogis. To explain: atoms and other such entities, which are not perceived by the direct perception of people like us, are perceptible to someone because they are objects of knowledge (*prameya*), just like a jar and so forth. Since the reason (*hetu*)—being an object of knowledge—is present in the subject (*pakṣa*) of the argument, namely the atoms and so forth, the condition of being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is satisfied. Likewise, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason "being an object of knowledge" by the probandum "perceptibility to someone" is observed in the case of jars and similar things. Moreover, this [reason] is not sublated by either direct perception or scripture, nor is it countered by an opposing argument; thus, because it is non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*), it is indeed a means of valid cognition.

Furthermore, since all inference proceeds by depending upon the apprehension of a universal pervasion (*vyāpti*) and thereby establishes a particularity within the subject (*pakṣa*), the perception of certain things such as atoms is established through a universal [pervasion]. And he for whom atoms and the like are perceptible is a yogin, distinct from people such as ourselves.

Likewise, the gradation of the intellect, which is observed to arise through the force of practice, must terminate somewhere because it is a gradation, just like the gradation of atomic dimensions. Those in whom this gradation finds its limit are the yogins, who are distinct from persons such as ourselves. When this inference is thus presented, the existence of yogins is established; the remaining [opposing] statements are mere words that do not constitute a sublation and are therefore disregarded.
{This concludes the demonstration of the classification of the result of the means of valid cognition, perception.}

“In that regard, with respect to universals and particulars, perception (*pratyakṣa*)—which is merely the observation of the intrinsic nature (*svarūpālocanamātra*)—is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); the objects of cognition (*prameya*) are the categories (*padārtha*) such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth; the cognizer (*pramātā*) is the self (*ātman*); and the result of cognition (*pramiti*) is the knowledge whose object is substance and the rest. When the knowledge of a universal and a particular arises, perception—which is an undifferentiated mere observation—is the means of valid cognition; there is no other means of valid cognition in this case, because [any other] would lack the form of a fruit.”

Having thus explained the perception of both yogis and non-yogis, [the author] now defines the distinction between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) for the sake of instructing the students and for the purpose of dispelling misconceptions, beginning with the words: “In that regard, with respect to universals and particulars, there is merely the observation of the essential nature,” and so forth. Regarding “universals and particulars,” this refers to [categories such as] substantiality (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), action-ness (*karmatva*), and so on. “Merely the observation of the essential nature” means: *ālocitiḥ* (observation) is *ālocanam* (observing), which is indeterminate (*nirvikalpaka*) cognition. “Perception is the means of valid cognition” means that the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) characterized by that [indeterminate cognition] is the means of valid cognition, perception. By the use of the word “merely” (*mātra*), he shows the absence of any other intervening cognition. [The text continues: “The objects of valid cognition” (*prameyāḥ*). They are called “objects of valid cognition” because they are cognized; they are the categories (*padārtha*) such as substance and the rest, which are delimited by the means of valid cognition. “The knower” (*pramātā*) is the self (*ātman*), because it is the substratum of the act of knowing (*pramā*). “Valid cognition” (*pramiti*) is the resulting comprehension achieved through the means of valid cognition and so forth; it is the knowledge whose object is substance and the rest, and it is the result (*phala*). Thus, because they possess characteristics that are mutually exclusive, the means of valid cognition and the others are distinct from one another. In this way, those who maintain their identity are refuted.

Now, since the distinction between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) is accepted, and because the mere observation of the intrinsic nature (*svarūpālocana*) regarding universals and particulars constitutes the form of valid cognition, [the author] asks: "What is the means of valid cognition for its arising? He replies: "In the arising of the cognition of universals and particulars, [it is] undifferentiated," meaning devoid of the cognition of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*).
