It is called "mere observation" (*ālocanamātra*) because one observes by means of it. The collection of causal factors (*kārakasāmagrī*), characterized by the contact between sense organ and object and so forth, is the means of valid cognition (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*), while the objects of cognition (*prameya*) are the universals and particulars. Now, why is another cognition not admitted even in that observation of the intrinsic nature? He says: "In that observation of the intrinsic nature, there is no other means of valid cognition nor another cognition," because it lacks the form of a result and is thus purposeless. For instance, the cognition of the qualified (*viśeṣya*) is permeated by its qualifier; being otherwise inexplicable, it demonstrates the existence of the cognition of the qualifier. However, in the cognition of the qualifier itself, there is no such permeation by a further qualifier. Furthermore, if another cognition were admitted, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), resulting in the non-arising of the cognition of the qualified itself. Yet, the cognition of the qualified is actually observed; therefore, there is no other cognition within the cognition of the qualifier.

Others, however, by using the term "mere" (*mātra*) in the phrase "mere observation of the intrinsic nature regarding universals and particulars," assert that the result of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*)—perception—is formless (*nirākāra*). Here, "universals and particulars" are intended figuratively as referring to substances and so forth, because they are the objects of inclusive and exclusive cognitions respectively. For if the form were denied in this specific cognition, it would imply the admission of a form elsewhere. The rest is as before. Just as a form is not possible in cognition, so it was stated on the occasion of the refutation of the theory of the form of cognition (*jñānākāravāda*).

“Alternatively, that cognition which arises with respect to all objects through the fourfold contact of sense-organ, object, self, and mind—being non-erroneous and non-verbal—is the means of valid perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*). The objects of knowledge (*prameya*) are the categories such as substance and so forth; the knower (*pramātā*) is the self (*ātman*); and the resulting knowledge (*pramiti*) is the observation of qualities, defects, or neutrality.”<PDhS>

The phrase “or rather” (*athavā*) indicates another way of presenting the division between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*), and not for the purpose of an alternative option. The meaning of the statement is that even in the arising of the knowledge of what is to be abandoned (*heya*) and so forth, the knowledge of substance (*dravya*) and the other categories serves as the means of valid cognition. Thus he says: “In all categories (*padārtha*)”—that is, in substances and the rest—"whatever unfailing, non-verbalizable knowledge arises, that is the means of valid cognition consisting of perception; the objects of cognition (*prameya*) are the categories such as substance; the cognizer (*pramātā*) is the self (*ātman*); and the resulting cognition (*pramiti*) is the observation of qualities (*guṇa*), defects (*doṣa*), and indifference (*mādhyasthya*). Here, the observation of qualities is the knowledge of what is to be acquired (*upādeya*), the observation of defects is the knowledge of what is to be abandoned (*heya*), and the observation of indifference is the knowledge of what is to be disregarded (*upekṣaṇīya*).

[Objection: But surely, since the cognition of what is to be acquired (*upādeya*) and so forth arises after an interval of many moments from the arising of the cognition of substance (*dravya*) and so forth, how can it be the fruit of the cognition of substance? [Reply: It is through a causal succession (*pāramparyeṇa*). To explain: previously, one perceives that things belonging to the class of "substanceness" (*dravyatva*) and so forth are means to pleasure and pain; immediately following that cognition, there is a recollection of the inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) that "whatever belongs to the class of substanceness is a means to pleasure. Then follows the reflective cognition (*parāmarśajñāna*) that "this [object] belongs to the class of substanceness," from which comes the certain determination (*viniścaya*) that "this is a means to pleasure. From that, the cognition of what is to be acquired arises; therefore, it is the fruit of the cognition of substance and so forth by way of a causal succession. And this same process applies to the arising of the cognitions of what is to be avoided (*heya*) and what is to be disregarded (*upekṣaṇīya*).

Now, one must state that there is a difference in the object [of this cognition] because the cognition of what is to be acquired (*upādeya*) and so forth arises from the ascertainment of its being a means to pleasure and so forth. Otherwise, it would simply be the result of inference; for the cognition of what is to be acquired and so forth arises through the contact of the sense organ with the object immediately after the ascertainment of its being a means to pleasure, pain, and so forth—which is the result of perception. True; nevertheless, there is a difference in the object due to the difference in the qualifier. The qualifier "being a means to pleasure" etc. belongs to the cognition of the means to pleasure and so forth, and from that [cognition] arises the cognition of what is to be acquired and so forth. [The definition of inferential cognition.]
“[Knowledge] arising from the observation of a mark is inferential (*laiṅgika*).

Following the mention of perception, he states, “arising from the observation of a mark is inferential,” in order to provide the definition and examination of inferential knowledge. Although the observation of a mark may also produce mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), erroneous cognition (*viparyaya-jñāna*), and doubtful cognition (*saṃśaya-jñāna*), there is no over-extension [of the definition], because this is stated as a specific definition following the general definition of valid knowledge (*vidyā*).

Alternatively, the qualifiers "non-erroneous," "of the nature of a determination," and "indescribable" (avyapadeśya) should also be understood as carrying over here [to this definition]. Furthermore, the recollection of the relationship of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) arises from the perception of the mark (*liṅga*) in its form as knowledge; in order to exclude that, the phrase "it arises with respect to substances and so forth" must be carried over. Thus, that cognition—characterized by qualifiers such as non-deviation—which arises with respect to the object of inference (*anumeya*) from the collection of causal factors (*kāraka-samūha*) indicated by the "sub-sumptive cognition" (*parāmarśajñāna*) following the perception of the mark, is "inferential" (*laiṅgika*). Alternatively, the sub-sumptive cognition itself, which arises from the perception of the mark as a cognition possessing the aforementioned qualifiers, is "inference" (*anumāna*) in view of its being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*).
{Definition of the Logical Mark} (“Furthermore, the logical mark (*liṅga*) is that which is related to the object to be inferred (*anumeya*) and is well-known to exist in what is similar to it.”)
And in the absence of that [object], its indicative mark (liṅga) does not exist at all as an inferential means.
"Kāśyapa has declared that whatever is contrary to this— whether by one or two of these [criteria]— is a non-reason (*aliṅga*), being respectively contradictory, unestablished, or doubtful."

What, then, is the mark (*liṅga*)? He says: "The mark, moreover, is that which is connected with the object of inference" (*anumeya*), and so forth. The object of inference is the subject (*dharmin*)—the locus of the property (*dharma*) intended to be communicated—which is qualified by that property. [The mark] is connected to that [subject] by way of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Pervasion, however, is obtained from the word accompanied by the explanatory statement (*vivaraṇavākya*). Otherwise, there would be a mere co-occurrence (*sāhacarya*) with the object of inference for that which exists only in a portion of the subject. For example, [if one were to argue] "atoms are eternal because they possess odor," this [mark] would be excluded by the word "accompanied" (*sahacarita*). Thus, its exclusion is achieved through that term.

Others, however, maintain that because the expression "again" (*punaḥ*) is intended as a distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is obtained in the sense that the mark (*liṅga*) is repeatedly connected with the object of inference (*anumeya*).

Others claim that the exclusion of the *bhāgāsiddha* (partially unestablished) reason is achieved by the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) "only that which is connected with the inferable" (*anumeyena sambaddham eva*). This is incorrect. For, according to the accepted rule of logic that "the restriction applies to what is other than where the particle *eva* is placed," the probans (*liṅga*) would not be pervaded (*vyāpta*) by the inferable. Indeed, it is through the pervasion—the fact that the inferable does not abandon the probans—that the connection [of the probans] with the subject (*pakṣa*) is known. Since there is no such restriction regarding the probans, its occurrence elsewhere is understood; thus, the phrase "well-known in what is associated with that" (*tadanvite prasiddham*) is rendered redundant if it were intended for the purpose of restriction. Furthermore, if one accepts the restriction "only well-known in what is associated with that" (*tadanvite prasiddham eva*), it would follow that a reason existing in only a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) would be non-probative. If, on the other hand, it is restricted as "well-known only in what is associated with that" (*tadanvita eva prasiddham*) for the sake of excluding occurrence in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), then surely the exclusion from the dissimilar is already established by the lack of restriction itself; thus, the phrase "and it is certainly absent when that is absent" (*tadabhāve ca nāsty eva*) is redundant. Likewise, the restriction "connected only with the inferable" (*anumeyenaiva sambaddham*) is contradicted. Alternatively, this may be a restrictive term used in conjunction [with another]. That is to say, once its presence in the subject is established, the restriction serves to exclude it from the dissimilar instances alone. Even so, since a restriction indicates what is already present, absolute exclusion from the dissimilar is obtained from that very restriction; therefore, the phrase "and it is certainly absent when that is absent" is redundant, as it too indicates what is already present. Moreover, when positive concomitance (*anvaya*) has been shown, there is no need to state negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), and when negative concomitance is stated, positive concomitance is not presented. Since the one is implied by the meaning of the other, stating it again with its own word would be a mere tautology. Therefore, the statement "and it is certainly absent when that is absent" cannot serve to express such a meaning, as it is not the literal sense of the words, and because inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) is not the topic at hand—this being the logical principle in that context. Consequently, the exclusion of reasons existing in only a portion of the subject must be stated by some other means, even without a restrictive particle.
However, for those who hold the view that every statement must be restrictive (*sāvadhāraṇa*), this objection is unavoidable and must be inferred in their definition [of the reason]. For example:
"Presence in the object of inference and in what is similar to it, and absence in what is not."

Thus [it is said]: "The subject (*pakṣa*) is that which is to be inferred; its presence (*sadbhāva*) therein, and likewise its presence in what is similar to it (*tattulya*),"—the word *atha* here takes the place of the word *ca*. "Its non-existence (*nāstitā*), that is, its exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), when there is no dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*)," such is the logical mark (*liṅga*). A dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), however, is either something other than that [subject], its opposite, or its absence; all three types are subsumed by the phrase "when it is non-existent," because the nature of being the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) is common to all of them. In this regard, if one restricts [the definition] to "presence only in the subject to be inferred" (*anumeye eva sadbhāvaḥ*), it would follow that an over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇa*) reason is a prover. Nor does this exclude the "partially unestablished" (*bhāgāsiddha*) reason, and furthermore, the other words [of the definition] would be redundant. If, on the other hand, one intends an exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) by saying "presence only in the subject to be inferred," even so, since the presence is not restricted [to that alone], the occurrence of the mark elsewhere is still obtained; thus, the phrase "presence in what is similar to it" (*tattulye sadbhāvaḥ*) would be useless. If it is made for the sake of restriction, then if one restricts it to "presence only in what is similar to it" (*tattulye eva sadbhāvaḥ*), there is a contradiction between the preceding and following parts. If, after the occurrence in the subject has been established, this restrictive particle is added as a conjunction for the purpose of excluding the dissimilar instance and so forth? Even so, the phrase "non-existence when it is non-existent" (*asati nāstitā*) need not be stated, because its meaning is already conveyed by the restriction. Nor is it logical to restrict it to "presence only in what is similar" (*tulye sadbhāva eva*), because it is accepted that even a reason occurring in only a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) can be a prover. If the phrase is intended to mean "it is non-existent only when it is non-existent" (*asaty eva nāsti*) as a restriction? Even so, it would follow that a reason occurring in only a portion of the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) is a prover, for in that case, it is indeed non-existent only in the dissimilar instance. If the restriction is "it is non-existent when it is non-existent" (*asati nāsty eva*)? Even so, since non-existence is obtained elsewhere besides the dissimilar instance, it follows that an over-exclusive reason and the like would be provers. Therefore, under the view that every sentence must contain a restrictive particle, this objection is unavoidable.
Furthermore, the position of restrictive determination has been refuted in detail by our teachers; therefore, it is not elaborated upon here.

Now, even if the exclusion of the *bhāgāsiddha* (partial unestablished) were achieved simply by means of the word "co-occurring" (*sahacarita*) without the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*), nevertheless, this definition applies to both the *viruddha* (contradictory) and the *asādhāraṇa* (uncommon) fallacies as well; therefore, in order to exclude them, it is said: "and it is well-known in that which possesses it. By this, it is meant that it is "well-known in that which possesses it"—that is, in that which is joined with (*anvita*) or endowed with the property similar to the object of inference (*anumeya*). And such is not the case for the contradictory or the uncommon. Nevertheless, since the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) possesses both the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and existence in the similar class (*sapakṣe sattva*), the phrase "and it is absolutely absent when that is absent" is employed. This means that it is absolutely absent in whatever locus (*dharmin*) there is an absence (*abhāva*) of that property similar to the probandum (*sādhyasamānadharmā*). And such is not the case for the inconclusive.

But even so, since the three characteristics (trailakṣaṇya) are established for both the *prakaraṇasama* and the *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*, it follows that they would possess probative force (*gamakatva*). For instance, in the case of "The composite of light is not hot, because it is produced, like a jar," although the three characteristics are present, it is sublated by perception grasping its heat; thus, it is a *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*. As for the *prakaraṇasama*: "Sound is eternal, because no non-eternal property is perceived in it, like space"; and "Sound is non-eternal, because no eternal property is perceived in it, like a jar. Here too, despite the existence of the three characteristics, there is a lack of probative force due to the presence of a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatva*). Therefore, in order to exclude these two, one must infer from the *Samānatantra* (the sister treatise) the conditions of "having an unsublated object" (*abādhitaviṣayatva*) and "having no counter-argument" (*asatpratipakṣatva*), because the word "and" (*ca*) implies the inclusion of unstated elements.

Others, however, maintain that because the matter is already covered by a defect in the thesis (*pratijñādoṣa*), "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*) is not a separate fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*). Thus they say that in the case of the argument "because no distinction between permanent and impermanent is perceived," since it is unestablished (*asiddha*) according to the respective intentions of the disputants, it is included therein. That is incorrect; for even when a defect in the thesis exists, the reason is called "mistimed" because it is presented only after the presentation of a flawed subject (*pakṣa*). Now, if it is argued that because contradiction (*virodha*) exists between sublation (*bādhā*) and invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), there can be no sublation of a three-featured reason (*trilakṣaṇa*) by perception, or else—if such sublation were admitted—the reason would lack its three features—that is not so. For instance, when the non-hotness of a composite of fire is to be proven, although the reason "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) possesses the three features, its invariable concomitance is not established because its object is sublated by the subject presenting a contrary meaning. Furthermore, fire produces causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) for all living beings through a form established by perception, and not through another form; thus, perception is cooperative with its own object. But inference is not like this, and therefore it is sublated.

Now, if it is argued that since the faulty inference is indeed sublated by perception itself, the very defect by which it is faulty should suffice as its refutation, and thus perception’s sublation is redundant—no, for it is precisely through perception that the defect is made known. For instance, by presenting a contrary object, perception demonstrates that the subject matter (*viṣaya*) of this inference is sublated. If it is further argued that when the non-hot nature of an effect is to be proven, the reason "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is not a prover because its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful—due to the lack of evidence regarding whether atoms (*paramāṇu*) are hot or not hot, and therefore it is a case of "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*) reasoning—this is not so. For if someone were to accept the heat of atoms and yet attempt to prove the non-heat of their effects, then for that person the certainty of the negative concomitance would be established. Furthermore, even if the negative concomitance is doubtful, its mention immediately after the presentation of the "hot" alternative does not contradict its being "mistimed. Nor is there a rule that where one defect exists, another cannot; as in the case of a reason that is unestablished due to multiple qualifiers and so forth.

As for the claim that [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*) because the reality [of the object] is not perceived according to the respective intentions of the proponent and the opponent—that is incorrect, because both [parties] are in a state of doubt. To explain: when there is the perception of a general property (*sāmānya*) and so forth, yet the absence of perception of specific features (*viśeṣa*), a doubt arises in the proponent and the opponent beforehand. In that situation, one who is himself doubtful, with the intention of deceiving the other, employs a doubtful reason (*hetu*) for the sake of determining the subject (*dharmin*); likewise, the other is also doubtful. Thus, because both are in doubt, neither has the capacity to point out the other’s unestablished nature. Furthermore, if even one of them were to state through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) the perception of a specific feature—whether eternal or non-eternal—then it would indeed be an unestablished reason, not a "neutralized" reason (*prakaraṇasama*). Nor can there be the employment of a "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) while in a state of doubt; therefore, there is a distinction [between this and the neutralized reason]. Moreover, we shall explain later that a "non-erroneous contradictory" is not possible at all.

Therefore, in order to exclude these two [fallacies], another characteristic—namely, having a non-sublated object (*abādhitaviṣayatva*) and being unopposed by a counter-argument (*asatpratipakṣitatva*)—must be admitted. Otherwise, the statement would consist of only three members rather than five, because those two [remaining] members would be intended solely for the purpose of excluding these [two fallacies].

But even so, the definition is deficient, because it does not encompass the purely positive (*kevalānvayin*) and the purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*) [reasons]. Yet, these two possess the nature of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*). Thus, where the universal itself is the probandum, there the universal itself is the reason. For example: "The particular is denotable (*abhidheya*), because it is cognizable (*prameya*), like the universal. When the denotability of particulars is the probandum, there is an absence of a counter-example (*vipakṣa*), because an undenotable entity is impossible. For if one were to perceive a counter-example by means of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and then establish its exclusion from that through verbal expression, then since denotability and cognizability would apply there, it would become a similar instance (*sapakṣa*) rather than a counter-example; thus, there is no exclusion from a counter-example. Therefore, its capacity to convey knowledge (*gamakatva*) exists solely through non-deviation from positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

Likewise, the living body is not soulless (*nirātmaka*), because that would entail the consequence of its lacking breath and so forth. Whatever is soulless lacks breath and so forth, like a jar or similar objects; yet the living body is not like that. Therefore, it is not soulless. Since [the opponent] accepts that everything is soulless, there is no similar instance (*sapakṣa*) when the negation of the soullessness of the living body is to be proven. Furthermore, the possession of breath and so forth is absolutely excluded from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) alone; therefore, the reason is a prover solely through the non-deviation of its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Nor is this [reason] "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*), for an uncommon reason is not a prover due to deviation, since it is excluded from the similar instances just as it is from the subject and other categories. Now, if it is intended here that by the negation of soullessness there is the presence of a soul (*sātmakatva*), and the self (*ātman*) is not established, then the subject has an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇa*); that is the same even regarding soullessness. Since the self is unestablished, how can there be its negation? Nor is there a negation of something superimposed by conceptual construction, because [the self] is being established as a reality. For one who establishes [the self], the self is established by means of perception and other valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*); with respect to such a person, the fault of the subject having an unestablished qualification does not exist. However, with respect to the person being taught, this is not a fault, because one who has not realized the truth is the one to be taught. But the lack of establishment in the similar instance is not a fault for a negative-only reason (*vyatirekin*), because its status as a prover depends precisely on the non-deviation of its negative concomitance. This very absence of a similar instance constitutes the "similar instance" [for the purpose of the negative concomitance]; if [the reason] were to occur within it, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) would be possible, but if it were excluded, it would simply be "uncommon. As it has been said: [The verse follows: *na hy asati sapakṣe 'nvayo vyatireko vā sambhavati |* (For neither positive nor negative concomitance is possible when a similar instance does not exist.)

"If there is no activity of the reason with respect to that [object], why is its cessation (nivṛtti) desired? Even that [cessation] is not a negation; why then is this cessation being negated? (Pramāṇavārttika 4.224).

The meaning of this is as follows: if, in the absence of a similar instance (*sapakṣa*), there were no exclusion of the reason (*hetu*) from it, then there would have to be its presence therein, because [exclusion] consists in the nature of being absent from that. However, if its presence is negated, then there must indeed be its exclusion. Furthermore, since no other verbal usage is possible apart from affirmation and negation, the consequence would be total silence. This is incorrect, because the absence of the subject (*pakṣābhāva*) is also a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) by virtue of not being the locus of the property to be proven (*sādhya*); and therefore, there is indeed exclusion [of the reason] from it, as in the case of the reason "because of not possessing breath, etc. (*aprāṇādimattvāt*).

Nor is there the objection that because the determination of the subject (*pakṣa*) and so forth is superimposed by conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), the reason (*hetu*) would be both positive and negative (*anvayavyatirekin*) when it occurs in a conceptually constructed similar instance (*sapakṣa*), whereas it would be "uniquely inconclusive" (*asādhāraṇa*) if it were excluded from it; for the determination of the subject and so forth is based on reality (*vāstavatva*). If, however, they were merely conceptual constructs, how could there be a distinction between a valid reason and a fallacious one, since conceptual construction is indistinguishable everywhere? Furthermore, regarding a jar and the like, is the exclusion of possession of breath (*prāṇādimattva*) due to the exclusion of having a self (*sātmakatva*), or is it due to the inherent nature of the thing itself? Thus, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful. Nor is there any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the existence or non-existence of a self in a jar and the like. This is not so; for by the absence of the specific effect—possession of breath and so forth—the absence of its specific cause—possession of a self—is established as excluded in that case, such as in a jar. To explain: in a body possessing breath, the specific relation to a self capable of producing breath and so forth establishes "having a self"; however, the absence of that [self] is known precisely through the absence of the effect, such as breath, in a jar and the like.

[Objection: But if this is so, since an effect is observed to be preceded by a cause, and thus positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is established, how can it be a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*)? [Response: No, because when a specific cause is to be proven by means of a specific effect, there is an absence of positive concomitance. For in the case of a living body, what is to be proven is a specific connection with a self capable of producing breath and so forth; and with respect to that, there is indeed an absence of positive concomitance. Furthermore, as for one who holds the position that "everything is devoid of a self," how could he express any doubt—such as "is the possession of a self excluded in a jar or not"?—since for him there is no locus of doubt at all.

Nor should it be said that the cessation of breath and so forth occurs only upon the cessation of cognition and so forth, as in the case of a jar; for by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), all [mental states] are included. Furthermore, what must be proven is a specific relation with the self (*ātman*) which is capable of producing those [states]; for in the absence of that, how could cognition and the rest arise? This is because, in a living body, the non-existence of the effect would follow from the non-existence of its cause. Moreover, since the causal relationship has already been refuted previously on the grounds of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), cognition does not arise from [another] cognition. Thus, this specific effect, such as breath and so forth, serves as a means of knowledge (an inferential indicator) precisely through the non-deviation of its negative concomitance (*vyatireka-avyabhicāra*) when proving a specific cause.

Now, an objection might be raised that the body could be established as possessing breath and so forth just like a rabbit's horn; however, this is a flaw because it is impossible to apprehend an exclusion (vyāvṛtti) that is dependent on the absence of those [breaths]. Furthermore, if one accepts that breath and the rest have a cause, and one desires the exclusion of a specific cause based on the exclusion of a specific effect, there would be a mere difference in terminology; in the opposite case, however, such [an exclusion] would not exist, as there would be no apprehension dependent on its absence. Enough of this.

[Objection: But if this is so, how is there a subsumption of these two under the definition-statement? [Answer: By means of a division of the statement (*vākya-bheda*). For instance: "That which is connected with the object of inference (*anumeya*) and is established as being present only where that [object] exists, provided there is no counter-example (*vipakṣa*), is the purely positive (*kevalānvayin*); while that which, given its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharma*), does not exist at all because of the absence of a similar instance (*sapakṣa*), is the purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*). However, the general definition is: "When the probans (*sādhana*) exists, the necessary concomitance (*niyama*) of the probandum (*sādhya*) [is the definition]. The state of being a probans (*sādhyasādhanatva*) is expressed by the term "that which makes inferable" (*anumāpakatva*). To define the fallacious mark (*liṅgābhāsa*), he says:
“Kāśyapa has stated that whatever is contrary to this— whether by one or two [of these criteria]— is a non-reason (*aliṅga*), being contradictory, unestablished, or doubtful. (*) Thus.

Kāśyapa stated that what is the opposite of the aforementioned mark (*liṅga*)—whether by one property, two properties, or by the word "or" [implying] three—is a non-mark (*aliṅga*), a mere semblance of a mark. This is the specification of its particular designations: contradictory (*viruddha*), unestablished (*asiddha*), and doubtful (*sandigdha*). Among these, the doubtful, even though both properties may be present, is not excluded from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*); thus, it is the opposite by way of one property. The contradictory, however, even though the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is present, neither resides in the similar example (*sapakṣa*) nor is it excluded from the counter-example; thus, it is the opposite by way of two properties. The unestablished, moreover, becomes the opposite by way of one, two, or three properties.

In that regard, the argument "Sound is eternal because it possesses generality (sāmānya) and yet is visible" is subverted by one [of the three criteria]. For although this reason exists in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) such as a jar, and although it is excluded from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) such as generality, it does not possess the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*). Likewise, the argument "Sound is eternal because it is not an object of cognition (*aprameyatva*)" is subverted by two [criteria]. For non-cognizability is indeed excluded only from the dissimilar instances; it neither exists in the similar instances nor in the subject itself. And an argument is subverted by all three [criteria] as follows: "Sound is non-eternal because it is not an effect. For this reason does not exist in the subject, sound; nor does it exist in the similar instances, such as a jar; nor is it excluded from the dissimilar instances.

“That which is concomitant with the object to be inferred (anumeya) in a particular place or at a particular time, which is well-known to exist in all or some other instance possessing the property to be inferred, and which is known through valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) to be entirely absent in everything contrary to the object to be inferred—that becomes the mark (*liṅga*) which leads to the inference of an otherwise unknown object. <PDhS>

He provides an explanation for the purpose of clarifying the meaning of the preceding summary statement, beginning with: “That which [is] by means of the object to be inferred (*anumeya*)... and so forth. The explanation of the phrase “connected with the object to be inferred” is: “accompanied by the object to be inferred—which is being determined—without abandoning its occurrence [in that place]. “[In a particular place or at a particular time]” means “in every place and at every time. The explanation of the phrase “and well-known in what is associated with that” is: “well-known in another instance, whether in its entirety or in part, which is associated with the property of the object to be inferred (*anumeya-dharma*). The object to be inferred is the *pakṣa* (the subject); the property belonging to it is the *anumeya-dharma*. That which is associated with or joined to that common property is the *sapakṣa* (the similar instance). The rule is that [the reason] must be well-known in all or in part of that. The explanation of the phrase “and in its absence, it simply does not exist” is: “and in everything contrary to the object to be inferred, it is simply non-existent according to valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). That which is contrary to the object to be inferred is the *vipakṣa* (the dissimilar instance), being devoid of the property of the object to be inferred. “In everything” means it is simply non-existent in all of that. By saying “according to valid cognition,” he demonstrates that one must state the exclusion of the probans (*sādhana*) through the exclusion of the probandum (*sādhya*) by means of valid cognition. The explanation of the phrase “that which makes [the object] known through inference (*anumāpaka*)” is: “this mark (*liṅga*) of the aforementioned form becomes the inferencer (*anumāpaka*) of an object not yet established.”
The definition of a fallacious mark (*liṅgābhāsa*) is as follows:

"That which is contrary to one or two of the three characteristics of the mark as previously described does not serve as a mark for the apprehension of the object to be inferred; this very point was stated by the author of the Sūtras: ‘An unestablished [mark], one that is non-existent, and one that is doubtful are non-indicative (*anapadeśa*).’"

The explanation of the second summary statement is: “But that which [differs] from the three-featured mark as previously described... (*). Because it lacks a non-sublated object (*abādhitaviṣayatva*), and because it is accompanied by a counter-balanced opposition (*satpratipakṣatva*), it is the opposite of what is required—whether by one characteristic, two characteristics, or all three—when the cognition of the inferable is to be produced; thus, it does not constitute a valid mark (*liṅga*). “The author of the Sūtras says exactly this,” (*), as indicated by the presentation of the formulated rule: “That which is unestablished (*aprasiddha*), non-existent (*asan*), and doubtful (*sandigdha*) is not a reason (*anapadeśa*)” (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra).

“An unestablished [reason] is not a valid indicator (*anapadeśa*)”: this excludes the contradictory (*viruddha*), because that is unestablished with respect to the similar instances (*sapakṣa*). “That which is non-existent is unestablished”: for that is indeed non-existent as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*). “And that which is doubtful is not a valid indicator”: this includes the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). The mistimed (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*) and the counter-balanced (*prakaraṇasama*) are also included by the term “unestablished” itself, because they are unestablished due to having a non-sublated object and lacking a counter-argument respectively. Alternatively, they may be included according to the logic of the same system (*samānatantra*). {Definition of Positive Pervasion (*vidhi-vyāpti*)}

“However, the rule is: ‘Wherever there is smoke, there is fire; and in the absence of fire, smoke does not occur. Thus, for one who has mastered this convention, from the perception of unambiguous smoke and the recollection of its concomitance, there immediately follows the ascertainment of fire. In this way, in all cases, that which is invariably connected with another in terms of place and time is the mark (*liṅga*) of that other.”

The logical mark (*liṅga*) of the aforementioned nature is the indicator for one who has grasped the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*); therefore, the statement beginning with “But the positive rule (*vidhi*), wherever there is smoke... is intended to demonstrate the essential nature of that inseparable connection. Here, “positive rule” (*vidhi*) means pervasion (*vyāpti*), which is the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*).

Now, if the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) were between two universals (*sāmānya*), it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because a universal stripped of its particulars is already established. Furthermore, there would follow the undesirable consequence that those seeking specific objects—which are delimited by a restricted location—would neither engage in nor desist from action. Nor can there be an invariable concomitance between two particulars, because since particulars are infinite, they cannot be fully known, and thus the concomitance dependent upon them remains unestablished. Moreover, since all particulars whose properties have not been mentioned cannot be apprehended, if the grasp of concomitance occurs only with respect to as many particulars as are perceived, then no inference could arise from the perception of another particular for which the concomitance has not been grasped.

This is not a valid objection, because we accept the apprehension of an inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) between the possessors of the universals. Although specific fires and specific smokes exist in infinite variety, there nevertheless exists within them the encompassing universals of "fire-ness" (*agnitva*) and "smoke-ness" (*dhūmatva*). By virtue of these encompassing factors and through the force of repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*), the apprehension of an invariable relation between fire and smoke is established, even when there is variation in place and other such factors. For instance, when time varies according to distinctions such as morning or midday, and when place varies according to distinctions such as level or uneven terrain, the concomitance of smoke with fire is observed. Consequently, no suspicion arises that smoke might occur in another place or at another time even without fire. For this very reason, there is no possibility of apprehending a pervasion (*vyāpti*) between a potter and a donkey, since the latter is observed even in the absence of the former at other times.

Others, however, maintain that at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), the cognizer possesses a complete knowledge of all objects, just like a yogi. Otherwise, there would be no recollection of the pervasion in the form: "all smoke does not exist without fire. And the lack of distinct perception [of the individual instances] is due to their being mentioned together in a common expression, just as in the case of a single grain of rice placed within a heap of grain.

Thus, because the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*) in the phrase "wherever... there" is intended, for a cognizer who has grasped the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*)—having established the convention that "wherever there is smoke, there is fire, and in the absence of fire, smoke does not occur"—there follows immediately after the perception of unambiguous smoke the recollection of the coexistence (*sāhacarya*), namely: "Wherever I have seen smoke, there was fire. From this "recollection of coexistence," fire is subsequently determined (*adhyavasīyate*) by means of it; this is "the determination of fire" (*agnyadhyavasāya*), which is the knowledge of reflective awareness (*parāmarśajñāna*). And from that, the cognition of fire arises.

Others, however, maintain that there is simply no such thing as the cognition of consideration (*parāmarśajñāna*). That is incorrect; for if the recollection of the relation of invariable concomitance were not fixed [to a specific instance], the apprehension of fire in a restricted location would not occur. Furthermore, the application (*upanaya*) would be redundant, since its purpose is not admitted [by them]. Therefore, "the determination of fire" (*agnyadhyavasāya*) must be explained as the cognition of consideration, either through etymological derivation or by way of metaphorical designation.

Others, however, maintain that the apprehension of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) arises from the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) and from essential nature (*svabhāva*) as the determinants. But that is incorrect. Even in the case of a causal relationship, it must be admitted that the apprehension of invariable concomitance occurs necessarily through the force of repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*). Otherwise, there would arise the suspicion that smoke might occur even without fire in another place or at another time. If it is argued that once the causal relationship between fire and smoke is understood, how could there be the suspicion of smoke occurring without fire—since its causelessness has been refuted and it must necessarily arise from its own cause—that is true; yet even this knowledge that "all smoke is the effect of fire" does not occur without repeated observation, and thus that must be accepted.

Furthermore, smoke is not the unique effect (*asādhāraṇa-kārya*) of fire, because it is admitted that smoke can arise even from other types of smoke. For instance, in cases such as cowherd huts where the fire has long since ceased, smoke is produced from a momentary spark of smoke itself; how then, upon perceiving smoke that is not the effect of fire, could one infer fire? If it is argued that the inference proceeds from the perception of something that *is* the effect of fire, we say no; for without the prior cognition of fire, it is impossible to ascertain that smoke is produced by it. And if that cognition already exists, what is the use of inference? Moreover, just as one perceives the nature of smoke, a resident of the Coconut Island (*Nārikela-dvīpa*) who has never perceived fire does not perceive that smoke is produced by fire, nor is such a usage (of the reason) logically possible. To illustrate: if "possessing fire" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*) regarding a mountain, then "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is indeed inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). If, instead, "possessing fire" were to be proven regarding smoke itself, then too "being an effect" remains inconclusive. Is the reason "being an effect while possessing the nature of smoke"? In that case, the nature of smoke alone would be sufficient, and thus the fault of a superfluous qualifier (*vyarthaviśeṣyatā*) attaches to the reason. Nor does smoke possess the state of being an effect of fire merely through its connection with fire; rather, it arises through a process beginning with dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) produced by baking (*pākaja*), once the previous substance has ceased. Enough of this.

Likewise, there is no relation of identity (*tādātmya*) between the properties of being a tree (*vṛkṣatva*) and being a *śiṃśapā* (*śiṃśapātva*), for if that were the case, it would follow that the relationship of probandum and probans (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) is untenable. To explain: if the locus (*dharmin*) is perceived, then because of its identity with that [locus], both [properties] would be perceived; in that case, how could there be a relationship of probandum and probans? Conversely, if one is not perceived even when the other is, then there could be no identity. Now, if it is argued that because inference possesses both the universal and the particular, there exists a relationship of the signified and the signifier (*gamyagamakabhāva*) consisting in the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropavyāvṛtti*), even so, identity and causality (*tadutpatti*) are simply impossible in that context. Even if identity were admitted, there could be no status as probandum and probans, because it would entail their oneness (*ekatā*). Furthermore, although there is no difference in the identity between the two, just as the property of being a tree is understood through the property of being a *śiṃśapā*, the property of being a *śiṃśapā* should likewise be understood through the property of being a tree.

Furthermore, if one accepts a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*), then there would be no inference of touch from the perception of color, no cognition of sunset from sunrise, and no inference of the rising of Rohiṇī from the rising of Kṛttikā, because identity and causality do not exist [in these cases]. If you argue that the inference of touch from color occurs because they depend on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatā*), that is incorrect, because the relationship of the signified (*gamya*) and the signifier (*gamaka*) is observed between two moments that are simultaneous. For instance, touch is inferred as being co-temporal with the moment of color, not as preceding it; and in that case, dependence on a single causal complex is simply impossible. Moreover, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the fact that color and touch are mutual causes for each other's arising, since the concomitance of the one is not perceived in the other. Enough of this digression.

"Thus, in all cases, the mark (*liṅga*) of the probandum (*sādhya*) is that which is inseparably connected with it in terms of place or time. This is the conclusion. An example of [inseparable connection] in terms of place is as follows: for those ascending Mount Kedāra, the inference of a lightning strike from hearing the sound of a clamor.

Now, this [sound] is not included within the categories of the Sūtra. For the Sūtra states: "That which is an effect, a cause, conjoined, inherent, or contradictory is inferential" (Vai. Sū.). And the sound of a tumultuous noise (*kalakala*) is not the effect of a thunderbolt strike, because it arises from its own causes even in the absence of that [thunderbolt]. Nor is it the cause of a thunderbolt strike, because it is an effect of gravity (*gurutva*) qualified by the absence of an obstructing factor. Furthermore, since both are non-substances (*adravya*), they do not possess the quality of being conjoined (*saṃyogitva*). Because there is no inherence (*samavāya*) between them in a single substratum, and because they do not originate within themselves, they do not possess the quality of being inherent (*samavāyitva*). And because there is no mutual contradiction, they do not possess the quality of being contradictory (*virodhitva*); thus, [the sound of a tumult] is a different category of object.

Now, how is it that the effect (*kārya*) and so forth function as a logical mark (*liṅga*)? It is because of their invariable concomitance (*avinābhūtatva*). To explain: an effect, being perceived as preceded by its cause, serves as a means of cognition. For instance, from the perception of a specific flood in a river, one infers: "It has rained upstream. Thus, when a river-flood characterized by the carrying away of abundant foam, froth, leaves, wood, and so on, is perceived again—given that such a flood was previously observed to be the effect of rain—it is proper to infer: "This river-flood is the effect of rain, because it is a specific river-flood, like a river-flood previously observed [to be caused by rain]. A flood (*pūra*), moreover, is the contact of water with both banks; since it is indirectly the effect of rain, it is also a cause. Furthermore, a cause, being perceived as having been previously observed to produce an effect, serves as a logical mark when it is itself perceived.

And just as the specific rising of clouds [is the cause] for the act of raining: now, since a cause does not necessarily produce its effect—because effects are seen to arise from indeterminate causes—there is an inconsistency. For instance, even when the rising of clouds exists, rain is sometimes not observed. Furthermore, an effect is seen arising from an indeterminate cause; for example, a scorpion is born from a scorpion, from cow dung, and from a snake. Thus, since indeterminate causes can be inferred elsewhere as well, how can there be a cognition of a specific cause from an effect, or of a specific effect from a cause? This is not so, because it is accepted that a specific cause is the indicator of a specific effect. As for one who does not perceive the specific [cause] even though it exists, that is his own fault, not a defect in inference; thus there is no error.

Likewise, smoke is conjoined with fire; yet, since conjunction is equally resident in both members, how can there be a fixed rule that one is the means of proof (*sādhana*) while the other is the object to be proven (*sādhya*)? This is the same even in the case of inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*), for that too is resident in both; how then could such a distinction be established? If it is argued that only that from the perception of which there arises cognition of the inferable is the *sādhana*, and nothing else, this applies equally to the state of being conjoined (*saṃyogitva*), because [the distinction] is determined by a specific internal difference within that which is inseparably related.

And the inherent hot touch makes one understand the fire residing in water. And the contradictory is, for example, a snake distinguished by hissing, which serves as the inferential mark (liṅga) for a mongoose and the like.

“In the treatise (*śāstra*), the mention of ‘effect’ (*kārya*) and so forth is made for the sake of illustration, not for the sake of restriction. Why? Because we observe instances to the contrary (*vyatireka*). For example: the Adhvaryu priest uttering ‘Oṃ’ is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the Hotṛ priest who is spatially separated; the rising of the moon is [the mark] of the swelling of the ocean and the blooming of the night-lotuses; the clarity of the water in autumn is [the mark] of the rising of the star Agastya—and so on. All such cases are established by the mere statement of a relationship as ‘this belongs to that’ (*asyedam*). <PDhS>

Now, regarding the mention of "effect" (*kārya*) and so forth in the Sūtra, he asks whether it is for the sake of illustration (*udāharaṇārtha*) or for the sake of restriction (*avadhāraṇārtha*). He says: "In the treatise, the mention of 'effect' and so forth is made for the sake of illustration, not for the sake of restriction. How is this known? "Because of the observation of deviation (*vyatirekadarśanāt*). For example: "The Adhvaryu priest, while causing the *oṃ śrāvaya* call to be heard, is an indicator (*liṅga*) of the Hotṛ priest who is spatially separated. Now, the word *oṃ śrāvaya* is neither the cause nor the effect of the Hotṛ, because there is an absence of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*). Thus, its occurrence is possible even without the Hotṛ, and the Hotṛ can exist even without it. Furthermore, its inclusion among [the other types of indicators such as] conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth is untenable. Moreover, this invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) of his exists only at the sacrificial ground and not in another location. Likewise, this Adhvaryu priest also possesses that [Hotṛ] despite being at a distance, because he is the agent of the sound *oṃ śrāvaya*, just like a previously observed Adhvaryu. "The rising of the moon is the indicator (*liṅga*) of the swelling of the ocean and the blooming of the night-lily (*kumuda*). The swelling of the ocean is the accumulation of parts; and that [accumulation] is produced from its own constituent parts, not from the rising of the moon. The blooming of the night-lily is also the separation of parts that have begun their effects, which is the result of an action that does not oppose the conjunction that initiates a substance. And here, by "cause," what is intended is the producer of that which is to be manifested (*abhivyaṅgya*), not the cause of cognition, because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of all causes being included [in this category]. "The clarity of water in autumn is the indicator of the rising of the star Agastya. This too is not included among those things that are its effects and so forth. "The clarity of water in autumn possesses the rising of Agastya, because it is a clarity of water, like the clarity of water previously observed when such was the case. By the phrase "and so forth" (*ityevamādi*), one should infer that sunrise and so on are indicators of sunset, and sunset and so on are indicators of sunrise.

Now, as to how these are subsumed under the *sūtra*, he says: "All that is established by the statement of mere relationship, namely, 'this belongs to that'. For instance, by the general formulation, "this is the indicator (*gamaka*) of this [indicated object], and this is the indicated (*gamya*) of this," all logical marks (*liṅga*) are included. However, with respect to specific cases, one should apply it as "this is its effect" or "its cause," and so forth.

Others, however, consider this sūtra to be for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). They offer an alternative interpretation of the statement: "The mention of 'effect' (*kārya*) and so forth in the treatise is for the sake of illustration. To explain: others have said, "It is known that the mention of 'effect' and so forth in the treatise was made for the sake of illustration because of the observation of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). This is not the case; rather, it is for the purpose of restriction, because since everything is included herein, the observation of negative concomitance is unestablished. For instance, when the *hotṛ* priest is present at the sacrificial ground, the *adhvaryu* priest utters the words "Oṃ, let [the sacrificer] cause [the announcement] to be heard" (*oṃ śrāvaya*); he does not do so even in his absence. Thus, how could he not be the cause? Likewise, the rising of the moon is also the cause of the swelling of the ocean because it possesses positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). That is to say, the swelling of the sea occurs when the moon is present, and not in its absence; thus, by the effect, the moon—though hidden behind a mass of clouds—is inferred. For one who has grasped the pervasion (*vyāpti*), the swelling of the ocean is inferred from the perception of the moon's rise in another location as well. The same applies to the blooming of the night-lotus (*kumuda*). Alternatively, it is simply a case of being in conjunction (*saṃyoga*) through the medium of rays. Similarly, the rising of the star Agastya is also the cause of the clarity of the waters, either as a conjoined factor or through the medium of its rays.
And the examination of the merits and defects in both positions must be performed by the investigators themselves. {The classification of inferential knowledge}

“That [inference] is of two kinds: that based on what has been perceived (*dṛṣṭa*) and that based on general observation (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*). Among these, inference based on what has been perceived is the inference [of an object] when there is no difference in genus between the known instance and the object to be proven (*sādhya*). For example, having perceived a mere dewlap in a cow, one recognizes it as a cow upon seeing a mere dewlap in another place. Inference based on general observation is the inference [of an object] when there is an absolute difference in genus between the known instance and the object to be proven, proceeding from the persistence of the commonality of the mark (*liṅga*) and the property to be inferred (*anumeya-dharma*). For example, having observed that the activities of farmers, merchants, and royal servants are productive of results, one infers a result for those belonging to the [four] castes and [four] stages of life who are engaged in activity even without aiming at a visible purpose. <PDhS>

He states the division: "That" [is] inference; "it is of two kinds. In what form? "The perceived (*dṛṣṭa*) and that which is perceived through generality (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*). "In that regard, the perceived is an inference when there is no difference in genus (*jātyabheda*) between the well-known (*prasiddha*) and the object to be proven (*sādhya*). The well-known and the object to be proven are called "the well-known and the object to be proven. When there is no difference in genus between those two—the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the example (*dārṣṭāntika*)—the inference is "perceived. For instance, just as the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is fit for direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in the subject of the example, so too it is in the subject of the example itself; thus, there is no difference in the property to be proven, but not in the genus (*sāmānya*). For example, having understood that a work such as a painting has a Brāhmaṇa as its agent, and subsequently perceiving one whose agent is a Kṣatriya or another, one infers: "This was produced by some agent, because it is a work such as a painting, like a previously perceived painting of this kind. Even though there is a difference in genus, this is indeed "perceived," because the property to be proven is grasped by direct perception both before and after the inference.

Others, however, form the compound *prasiddhasādhyau* as "the well-known and the to-be-proven. In that case, since the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmī*) is already well-known, it is not "to-be-proven," and the subject of the thesis (*dārṣṭāntika*) is not yet well-known; so how can this be? There is no fault, because figurative usage (*upacāra*) is intended. For instance, the subject of the example is figuratively called "to-be-proven" because it serves as the locus for the property common to the to-be-proven; and the subject of the thesis, while not yet established at first, becomes well-known after the inference, and is thus considered "well-known" even beforehand. The rest is as explained previously.

An example of this is as follows: having perceived a dewlap only on a cow, one subsequently recognizes it as a cow upon seeing a dewlap again in another place—even when the specific cow-individual is not present—thinking, "This is a cow, because it possesses a dewlap, like the previously perceived [cow] that possessed a dewlap."

And *sāmānyato dṛṣṭa* (inference based on general observation) is inference when there is an absolute and total difference in genus (*jāti*) between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*), such that the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is different. Thus, the property to be proven is always unestablished (*aprasiddha*) both prior to and after the inference. Now, if the property to be proven is different [from the example], since the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) itself would be unestablished, how can there be inference? To this he says: "Because of the persistence of the generality of the mark (*liṅga*) and the property to be inferred (*anumeyadharma*)" (*liṅgānumeyadharmasāmānyānuvṛttitaḥ*). This means the persistence through the generality of both the mark and the property to be inferred: "Wherever this generality of the means of proof (*sādhanasāmānya*) exists, there this generality of the property to be proven (*sādhyasāmānya*) exists. Upon grasping that, inference indeed proceeds. For example, having observed that the activity of farmers, merchants, and royal servants possesses a result because it has an intended fruit, one infers that the activity of those belonging to the [four] castes and [four] stages of life (*varṇāśramin*) also possesses a result—of what specific kind? Of those who act without aiming at visible purposes such as obtaining alms; thus, the inference of an intended fruit. For instance: the activity of those belonging to the castes and stages of life possesses a result by way of an intended fruit, because it is the activity of one who acts with foresight (*prekṣāpūrvakārin*), like the activity of farmers and others.

Nor is the objection that "this is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) because it depends upon a visible purpose" valid, since this has been refuted by the qualification of the thesis (*pakṣaviśeṣaṇa*) stating "without aiming at a visible purpose. Those who act while aiming specifically at a visible purpose are not made the subject of the thesis. Nor is it being proved that [action] possesses fruitfulness through an invisible result, which would render the example devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*) and the reason (*hetu*) contradictory; rather, fruitfulness is proved in a general sense through an intended result, and since that exists in the activity of farmers and others, there is no fault in the example being devoid of the property to be proven, nor is there any contradiction in the reason.

In all inferences, there is an equal possibility of an inference that contradicts the specific [property]; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of inference as such. If, on the other hand, the lack of validity for inference is indeed accepted, then in the case of a general property (*sāmānya*), one would be proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), whereas in the case of a specific property (*viśeṣa*), there is a lack of concomitance (*anugama*). Furthermore, if the subject (*dharmin*) and the property are intended as a composite whole (*samudāya*) to be proven, the reason (*hetu*) lacks the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), nor is there positive concomitance (*anvaya*), because the composite whole does not exist elsewhere. If it is argued that even though it resides only in one part of the composite, it is figuratively said to reside in the composite itself, then, because the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) would be merely figurative, the ascertainment of the object of inference would be difficult to obtain. For in that case, perception (*pratyakṣa*) would be the primary means of knowledge and inference would be secondary, since it depends upon a figuratively attributed property of the subject. Being secondary means it is not a valid means of knowledge. Even if the property (*dharma*) alone were the object to be proven and positive concomitance existed, the composite whole would still lack the property of being a characteristic of the subject elsewhere. If, finally, the subject qualified by the property being demonstrated is the object to be proven, then there is simply no positive concomitance at all; thus, every inference would be invalid.

That is incorrect, because when the subject (*dharmin*) qualified by the property to be established (*sādhya-dharma*) is the object of proof, the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is logically established; moreover, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) occurs through a property common to the probandum. For the occurrence of the reason in one place is not [the definition of concomitance], whereas negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is its exclusion upon the absence of that [probandum]. Furthermore, since it is observed that cognition of the probandum in the subject arises from the perception of the mark (*liṅga*), such a conceptualization of concomitance is formulated. Moreover, if this were not accepted, there could be no cognition of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) at all, yet such cognition is indeed observed—this is the distinction. In the case of a contradictory [reason], however, when a specific feature restricted [to the subject] is negated, another specific feature must be admitted. But if all specific features are negated, then even the universal (*sāmānya*) restricted to them cannot be established. Alternatively, the universal of the probandum must necessarily be established as pervading the universal of the means of proof (*sādhana*). Therefore, since the universal of the probandum itself—along with its implied particulars—is established through inference, the fruit for those belonging to the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramin*) is established as being unperceived (*adṛṣṭa*) and transcending particularity.

{The Distinction between the Means of Cognition and its Result in the Case of Inferential Knowledge} “In that regard, the perception of the mark (*liṅgadarśana*) is the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*); the knowledge of the object to be inferred (*anumeya*) is the result (*phala*); the fire is the object of cognition (*prameya*); and the self is the cognizer (*pramātṛ*). Alternatively, the knowledge of fire itself is the means of cognition, while the discernment of qualities, defects, or neutrality regarding the fire is the resulting cognition (*pramiti*); this constitutes inference for the sake of one’s own certainty. <PDhS>

For the sake of instructing his disciples, he demonstrates the distinction between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*): "In this context, the perception of the mark (*liṅgadarśana*) is the means of valid cognition; the knowledge of the object to be inferred (*anumeya*) is the result; fire is the object of cognition (*prameya*); and the self (*ātman*) is the cognizer (*pramātṛ*). Now, one might ask: since the perception of the mark has a different locus [from the fire], how can it be the means of valid cognition for the arising of the knowledge of fire? It is so because, with respect to its operation (*vyāpāra*), it has that [fire] as its object. For just as the knowledge of smoke has smoke as its object with respect to its own acquisition of being (*ātmalābha*), so too, with respect to its operation toward the apprehension of fire, it has fire as its object. This is similar to how the eye, which is inherent in its own parts, has color-form (*rūpa*) as its object with respect to its operation in the production [of visual consciousness].

But surely, in this way, the distinction between the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the other factors would be untenable with respect to a single object, because they possess distinct definitions. To explain: the definition of the knower (*pramātṛ*) has been stated as being the substratum of valid cognition (*pramā*); likewise, the object of valid cognition is the knowable (*prameya*); that which produces the valid cognition, distinct from those two, is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and that which is accomplished by it is the fruit (*phala*). Thus, their difference arises from the difference in their definitions.

Alternatively (*athavā*), he states another way of distinguishing between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*): "The cognition of fire itself is the means of valid cognition; the perception of its qualities, defects, or neutrality regarding the fire is the result. When the cognition of fire occurs, through the recollection of the relation of invariable concomitance and the resulting reflective cognition (*parāmarśajñāna*), there arises the awareness that [the object] is a means to pleasure, which constitutes the cognition of what is to be acquired (*upādeyajñāna*). Likewise, when there is the awareness that it is a means to suffering, there is the cognition of what is to be avoided (*heyajñāna*). And for one who has the awareness that "this is neither a means to pleasure nor a means to suffering," there is the cognition of what is to be disregarded (*upekṣaṇīyajñāna*). Furthermore, the fact that the cognitions of what is to be acquired and so forth are results of the cognition of fire should be explained as being mediated by a causal sequence, just as previously stated.

“This is inference for the sake of one’s own certainty” (*ityetat svaniścayārthamanumānam*) is the conclusion, which indicates inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*). [The inclusion of verbal testimony and other means of knowledge within inference.]

“Verbal testimony (*śabda*) and the other means of knowledge are also included within inference because they follow the same procedure. Just as there is inference regarding a supersensible object for one who has established a convention, through the perception of an unmistakable mark and the recollection of its established connection, so too is it from verbal testimony and the rest. Even the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) characterized by *śruti* and *smṛti* depends upon the authority of a speaker; the authority of the tradition arises from his statement. Furthermore, the composition of sentences in the Veda is non-eternal and preceded by intelligence, because it is stated that ‘the act of giving is preceded by intelligence.’”

Now, this section beginning with "The inclusion of verbal testimony (*śabda*) and the others within inference" (*anumāne 'ntarbhāvaḥ*) is intended to avoid the deficiency in the classification of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and to eliminate any deviation from its general definition. [Objection: But since the inclusion of other [means] within inference was not previously stated, is the word "also" (*api*) not redundant? [Response: No, because of its connection with the word "inference. It means that their inclusion is not only in perception (*pratyakṣa*), but also in inference. Furthermore, the classification of the means of valid cognition was already demonstrated previously by the statement concerning the classification of branches of knowledge (*vidyā*). In that context, there might be the suspicion that this [classification] is untenable because verbal testimony and other means of valid cognition actually exist; this section on inclusion is for the purpose of dispelling that doubt. Likewise, when the class of causal factors such as verbal testimony is included within the causal complex of inference, the inclusion of its result within the result [of inference] is understood as a matter of course.

In that context, those things for which sound (*śabda*) and so forth are the first members are called "those beginning with sound. Therefore, their inclusion within inference (*anumāna*) is due to the identity of their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇaikya*). Thus, if one accepts the *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* (possessive) type of *bahuvrīhi* compound, sound itself is included within inference; whereas, if one accepts the *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna* (non-possessive) type, it refers to the others excluding sound.

And regarding the conventional usage of inclusion (*antarbhāva-vyavahāra*), how is the presentation of the reason—“because they possess the same rule” (*samānavidhitvāt*), meaning “because they are endowed with the same definition” (*samānalakṣaṇayogitvāt*)—not distinct from the probandum? For the unity of the definition is something other than that conventional usage. Those things which have a common rule, means, or definition are described as such; their state or essence is the "fact of being so" (*tattvam*); [the reason] is because of that. He states this very point: “Just as inference occurs regarding an object beyond the senses through the perception of a sign whose connection [to the object] is well-known and through the recollection of its established [connection], so too it occurs from words and the like. For just as for one who has grasped the relationship, after the perception of the sign there follows the recollection of the relationship of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), and from these two there arises inference regarding an object to be determined that is beyond the senses—inference being intended here either metaphorically or etymologically as the knowledge of consideration (*parāmarśajñāna*), since it is by means of this that one infers (*anumīyate ’nena*)—so too is the explanation of the subject of the example: “so too from words and the like.”

Others, however, maintain that the knowledge of the application (*parāmarśa*) simply does not exist. That is incorrect; for if the recollection of the relation of invariable concomitance were unrestricted, there would be no cognition in a specific location, and the function of the application (*upanaya*) would be rendered useless, as has already been stated. Therefore, the former [position] alone is logical.

In this context, according to the view that the compound is *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* (where the quality itself is included), verbal testimony (*śabda*) is also subsumed under inference (*anumāna*). Thus, upon hearing a word, when there is a recollection of the conventional agreement (*samaya*), there arises a cognitive reflection (*parāmarśajñāna*), and from that comes the comprehension of an imperceptible object. For example: "This word 'cow' denotes an object possessing a hump and so forth, because it is the word 'cow,' like previously perceived words of this kind denoting such objects"; and also because it conveys an object through the apprehension of a relation, like smoke.
[According to the opinion of Ācārya Vyomaśiva, verbal testimony is not subsumed under inference.]

This is incorrect, because it is impossible to demonstrate that the word *go* (cow) possesses a referent characterized by the hump and other such features. To explain: since a word has no inherent relation with its object other than that of the signifier (*vācaka*) and the signified (*vācya*), the property of being the word *go* is not a valid reason when proving that it conveys a meaning. This is because the status of being a signifier is determined by cognition, and an intrinsic relation is logically untenable. For instance, smoke conveys the inferable object for all living beings through an intrinsic relation; however, a word does not function in this way, as it conveys meaning only in dependence upon a convention (*samaya*) established by human will. If there were an intrinsic relation, the comprehension of meaning would occur even without a convention upon hearing the words of barbarians (*mleccha*) and others. But if the conveyance of meaning depends on convention, let that alone suffice; there is no need for an eternal relation. Nor does the absence of an eternal relation lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because occasional (*naimittika*) words are subject to convention only when a basis such as "substanceness" (*dravyatva*) exists, whereas arbitrary (*yādṛcchika*) words follow the whim of the person. Furthermore, the fixed rule—that whatever possesses a specific sequential order is the signifier and the other is the signified—is established because the knowledge of the convention resides equally in both.

Convention (*saṅketa*), however, is understood from words and from the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*). To explain: the comprehension of convention arises from such statements as "this is the designator (*vācaka*) of this" or "this is the designated (*vācya*) of this. From the usage of elders, for example, when one hears the command, "Devadatta! Bring the white cow with a stick," an unlearned person understands the convention regarding the words "Devadatta" and so forth through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). As for the elders who engage in linguistic usage, their own comprehension of convention likewise arises from another usage; thus, the objection of infinite regress (*anāditva*) is avoided. Alternatively, there exists a primordial being (*ādipuruṣa*), a direct seer, who is the creator of the conventions for certain [words]. Furthermore, since a word in the form of a sentence does not even depend upon convention for the comprehension of meaning, it is unproven that a word conveys meaning by virtue of a [fixed] relationship.

Nor is it the case that the inferential nature of verbal testimony (*śabda*) is being denied altogether, for it serves as a logical mark (*liṅga*) for the cognition of the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*) and of space (*ākāśa*). For instance, while every sound is an inference for the cognition of space, those [sounds] which are the effects of the intention to speak serve as such even for the cognition of that intention. Furthermore, inferential knowledge does not depend upon the fact of being spoken by a reliable person (*āptoktatva*), unlike the knowledge derived from words. To illustrate: when a doubt arises regarding a verbal cognition—asking whether "is this true or false?"—one examines whether it was spoken by a reliable person or by an unreliable one; however, in the case of inferential knowledge, one examines the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth. This constitutes the distinction.

Thus he says: "Even the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) characterized by *śruti* and *smṛti* depends upon the authority of its speaker. It is not only ordinary worldly speech that depends on the authority of its speaker; even that which is characterized by *śruti* and *smṛti* does so as well.

Now, if one accepts the authority of the Veda (*āmnāya*) on the basis of the authority of its speaker, there would be a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*) among many factors. To explain: the fact that a word was spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*) is ascertained through the attainment of the object; yet the attainment of the object occurs only when one acts after having understood the object through the ascertainment [of the word's truth]. Furthermore, since truth and falsehood are observed in human speech, if a human being were to intervene in the Veda as well, there would be suspicion regarding it, and thus it would lack authority. Moreover, since a person who directly perceives supersensible objects (*atīndriyārtha*) is impossible, how could words expressing such things be preceded by [the perception of] them?
