Furthermore, if one were to compose a verbal arrangement after understanding the meaning from another Vedic sentence, that [composition] too would be subject to some contradiction because of its eternality; however, if it were non-eternal, then the author of that [sentence] would likewise have to understand the meaning from yet another sentence, leading to an infinite regress. Moreover, since the non-eternality of Vedic sentences is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how could their authority depend upon a particular speaker?

Furthermore, in the communication of meaning, the operation of a word occurs solely by virtue of its own power of denotation (*abhidhā-śakti*), without depending on its being spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*). And that [power] is inherent to the word itself; it is not produced later by another. Thus, validity (*prāmāṇya*) is intrinsic (*svataḥ*). Nor can the fact of being spoken by a reliable person be established, because it is not an object of perception, inference, or other means of knowledge. However, invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) depends on the word being composed by a defective person, and is therefore extrinsic (*parataḥ*).

Likewise, it is not possible for all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to depend on something else regarding their validity, because they arise from their own causes in the form of the apprehension of an object. If the capacity to determine an object—which was non-existent [prior to the cognition]—were produced in a fully established cognition by some other causal factor, we might accept that validity is extrinsic (*parataḥ*); but since this is not the case, he says:
"Let it be understood that the validity of all means of valid cognition is intrinsic (*svataḥ*). For a power that does not exist intrinsically cannot be produced by another. (Ślokavārttika 2.76)
Furthermore, the capacity of cognition to determine its object is not preceded by the excellence of its causes, because such excellence is absent in the sense organs. As it has been said:
"The operation of causal factors is indeed observed to be distinct from their birth;
lest the same [distinction] apply to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), its birth is what is intended [to be the operation]. (Ślokavārttika, p. 151)

For just as the sense organs have no other function apart from their arising, it is not so with knowledge, because it accomplishes its result immediately thereafter. Moreover, even by the opponent, the validity of the cognition of a qualifier (viśeṣaṇa) and so forth in producing the cognition of the qualified (viśeṣya) and so forth has been observed. Now, if it is argued that even though knowledge has arisen, it does not possess the capacity to determine the object without an awareness of the purity of the causal factors (kāraka), then one must also state the apprehension of the purity of the causal factors in that case as well; thus, there would be an infinite regress. As he says: "Even when knowledge has arisen, if the object is not yet determined..."
As long as the purity of the cause has not been established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there must be an expectation for the arising of another cognition from another cause;
for as long as that purity is not determined, it is equivalent to non-existence. (Ślokavārttika, p. 60)

"If the cause of that [cognition] is also pure, then that cognition possesses validity; if that [cause] is likewise [pure], and so on, nothing would ever be established" (ŚV, p. 61). Now, if even though validity exists in a cognition, it does not become the cause for the practical application (*vyavahāra*) of "validity" without corroboration by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then—since the capacity would be exhausted in a succession of means of knowledge—the practical application of "validity" could not occur with respect to the intended cognition. Thus he says:
"If the validity of each preceding [cognition] were accepted based on the subsequent one, those who desire further means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) would find no finality.
And if the validity of some [cognition] were held to be intrinsic (*svataḥ*), then let that belong to the very first one; thus he says: [ŚV, p. 50].

If it is accepted that for some [cognition] validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*), then what is the basis for hostility toward the first [cognition] being likewise? (ŚV, p. 69) If one were to accept that the validity of the first and subsequent [cognitions] is mutually dependent, there would be the fallacy of circular reasoning (*itaretarāśrayatva*). Therefore, validity is intrinsic, whereas invalidity is extrinsic (*parataḥ*). For instance, only worldly (*laukika*) words lack validity because human defects (*puruṣadoṣa*) intrude into them; however, since those defects are absent in Vedic (*vaidika*) words, there is not even a suspicion of invalidity.

Now, the lack of validity in the sense faculties is due to defects such as cataracts or jaundice, and not by their very nature. For instance, it is when defects such as cataracts or jaundice are present that there is the production of false cognition, and not when they are absent.

Furthermore, in the case of a cognition that makes something known (*jñapti*), its inherent validity as a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—by virtue of its being informative—is not lost; it is only set aside when falsity is apprehended through a sublating cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*). Nor should it be argued that in our position, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) because even the cognition of mother-of-pearl sublates the cognition of non-mother-of-pearl, or that there would be a succession of grasping the purity of causal factors (*kārakaśuddhi*); for the inherent validity of a cognition, by virtue of its being informative, does not lead to an infinite regress merely through the non-perception of defects. As it has been said: "When validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*), then no other [cognition] need be sought."
And falsity ceases effortlessly upon the cognition of defects.
However, as long as the cognition of defects has not arisen, doubt is without basis.
Thus, no further cognition beyond three or four is required. (ŚV, p. 61; ŚV, p. 64)
Thus is the avoidance of infinite regress.

All of this is based on an unknown meaning, because all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are observed to depend on something else both for their own production and for their manifestation. To illustrate: a word produces correct knowledge regarding its object by depending upon being spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*); it is not seen to do so without that [reliability]. Furthermore, as for the objection raised regarding the mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) of many factors, that is not tenable, because we accept that being spoken by a reliable person functions as an auxiliary to the word even while it remains unperceived. Indeed, the apprehension of that [reliability] is intended to occur subsequently, through another means of valid cognition, upon the attainment of the object. For instance, the status of being spoken by a reliable person is determined for worldly words through the attainment of their objects. Others maintain that it is also grasped through perception (*pratyakṣa*). Thus, when a sentence is heard through the operation of the sense of hearing, an uncontradicted cognition is observed, such as "this was spoken by Cāṇakya" or "this was spoken by Kālidāsa. As for Vedic sentences, however, the certainty that they were spoken by a reliable person arises from their non-contradiction regarding their primary meanings.

If it is argued that because two types of speech are observed in human compositions, there might be a suspicion of lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) regarding the Veda as well due to human intervention—that is not so, because of the absence of defects in its author. For it is observed that the word of one who possesses defects such as passion (*rāga*) is itself unauthoritative; yet, there is no evidence for the existence of such defects in the author of the Veda. It has already been stated below that a person capable of perceiving supersensible objects (*atīndriyārtha*) is possible. Therefore, the author of the Sūtras stated: "The authority of the *Āmnāya* (the collection of Vedas) [is derived] from his word."

Now, one might suspect that if sound were impermanent, its authority would depend on being spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*); however, since that [reliability] does not exist, he says: “And because of an inferential mark (*liṅga*), sound is impermanent” (Vai. Sū.). By perception, it is understood that sound is impermanent because it is not perceived prior to its utterance nor after it; this is what is meant by “because of an inferential mark,” which we shall explain in the examination of sound (*śabdaparīkṣā*). Furthermore, there is an inference regarding the impermanence of the Vedas: “The Vedic sentences are impermanent, because they are sentences, like any sentence admitted by both parties. Likewise: “The composition of sentences is preceded by intelligence”; that is, the arrangement of sentences in the Veda is preceded by intelligence, because it is a composition of sentences, like the composition of sentences admitted by both parties. As for the objection based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*)—that the composition of the Veda is observed to be different at all times—that applies equally to all inferences. Similarly: “The word ‘dadāti’ is preceded by intelligence”; that is, the word *dadāti* in the Veda is preceded by intelligence, because it is stated as *dadāti*, like the word *dadāti* admitted by both parties.

Furthermore, this suspicion regarding the lack of validity that arises when there is human involvement does not cease even in the case of [the Veda’s] eternity, because the human listener is involved therein as well, and because invalidity is observed due to defects in him. For it is indeed observed that the listener’s lack of presence of mind (*apratibhā*) and so forth are causes for the arising of false cognition, while their absence is the cause for the arising of correct cognition. Moreover, eternity is not an absolute cause for the validity of the Vedas; for even when that [eternity] exists, invalidity occurs in some instances due to the intrusion of the cognizer’s defects into the listener’s internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

If it is accepted that the validity of a word arises solely through the power of its own denotative capacity (*abhidhā-śakti*), then statements such as "elephants stand on the tip of a finger" would not be invalid. If, however, their invalidity is due to contradiction resulting from being composed by an unreliable person (*anāpta*), then it follows that only that which is composed by a reliable person (*āpta*) is valid. For just as human defects such as passion (*rāga*) function [to cause] invalidity through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), so too do its excellences (*guṇa*) function for validity; thus, both are extrinsic (*parataḥ*).

Furthermore, apart from the phonemes (*varṇa*), their sequence, and the linguistic convention (*saṅketa*), no supersensible power (*śakti*) exists in denotation; for such a power has already been refuted previously, and because [denotation] functions when the nature of the phonemes and so forth is present. Moreover, that [sequence] is dependent on something else, since its connection with specific universals (*jāti*) has an unperceived effect. It has also been stated that there is another cause for the linguistic convention.

As for the claim that direct perception and so forth operate toward the destruction of passion and the like in a person, but not toward the production of knowledge, that is incorrect; for the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are established in the production of right knowledge. A person who perceives reality as it is and is an instructor to his disciples—this combined definition of an authoritative person (*āpta*) is the cause for a teaching that accords with reality, because no such teaching occurs without it. If, despite the presence of positive and negative concomitance, the function of qualities such as perceiving reality as it is were restricted solely to the destruction of passion and the like, then passion and the rest would likewise have the function of destroying these very qualities; thus, both [validity and invalidity] would be extrinsic (*parataḥ*). Therefore, just as in the case of the production of invalidity, one must admit that the operation of perceiving reality as it is and so forth is also necessary for the production of right knowledge.

Likewise, even in the case of the sense faculties, when defects such as cataracts (*kāca*) or jaundice (*kāmalā*) are present, there is only false cognition (*mithyājñāna*). Since correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*) arises when those [defects] are absent, both [types of cognition] are extrinsic (*parataḥ*). Furthermore, the causality of non-existence (*abhāva*) is accepted by others in various ways; for example, in the production of mental cognition through the exclusion of the five means of valid cognition that apprehend an existent object, or in the production of false cognition when any one of the conditions such as "being a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatā*) is missing in the case of a logical mark (*liṅga*), and so forth. If it is argued: "Since a defect such as cataracts is observed to be the cause for the production of false cognition, its absence is simply not observed, and that is not correct cognition," we reply: No, because if that which possesses positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) were not a cause, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Thus, if the absence of a defect, despite possessing positive and negative concomitance, were not the cause for the production of correct cognition, and if [the presence of the defect] were not the cause for the production of false cognition even when it exists, then both would be intrinsic (*svataḥ*). Moreover, since the production of the sense faculties is observed to result in effects of both kinds, it should be understood that they serve both purposes.

Now, it might be argued that since it is accepted that a sense organ produces false cognition when defects are present and correct cognition when they are absent, it would follow that in the absence of both [defects and their opposites], it would produce a cognition devoid of both; however, this is not a valid objection, because a sense organ devoid of both is impossible. For just as there is no sense organ devoid of both, since defects that were previously non-existent arise and subsequently perish; nor is a general property of "cognition-ness" possible that is devoid of its specific instances, because a possessor of a general property must be associated with its particulars—just as the general property of "cowness" has particulars such as the brindled cow (*śāvaleyādi*) as its substratum.

As for this capacity to determine [an object] which is not preceded by the qualities of its cause—that is indeed accepted, because the cognition of experience, having arisen from the sense organ, consists in the determination of the object. And since the causal instrument that produces it, such as the sense organ, depends upon other causal factors, validity is extrinsic (*parataḥ*). However, the totality of causal factors (*kārakasāmagrī*) does not depend on any subsequent cause; therefore, with respect to that, both [the cognition and its validity] are intrinsic (*svataḥ*), and thus false cognition would not be extrinsic.

Now, if knowledge (*jñāna*) is the activity of the knower (*jñātṛvyāpāra*), and that [activity] is independent in the determination of an object, [and thus] intrinsic (*svataḥ*), then this is the same even for false cognition (*mithyājñāna*). Or, if false cognition depends upon a defect (*doṣa*), then right cognition (*samyag-jñāna*) would likewise depend on the absence of that [defect] and so forth. Furthermore, the activity of the knower is not possible, because the apprehension of an object occurs otherwise [than through such an activity]. For indeed, every causal factor (*kāraka*) produces its effect only when its final auxiliary condition (*carama-sahakārin*) is present; there is no activity other than that [presence]. Even if [the cause] were eternal, there would be the undesirable consequence of the production of all effects at all times, since you would have to admit that it is an independent cause. If, however, it were non-eternal, then since a thing devoid of activity cannot be a cause even when it has arisen, there would be another activity, and yet another upon the arising of that, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). But if activity is of the nature of the final auxiliary condition itself, this fault does not arise, because the effect is produced when that [condition] is present and not when it is absent.

As for the objection raised regarding the necessity of apprehending the purity of the causal factors (*kāraka-śuddhi*), that has been refuted by the statement "not so, because [we] do not accept it. Now, if it is claimed that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is known even without its own validity (*prāmāṇya*), that is incorrect, because every object of knowledge (*prameya*) is observed to be determined by a means of valid cognition. Thus, validity itself is determined by a means of valid cognition, because it is an object of knowledge, just like a jar or other such things. Nor does this lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because we do not maintain that validity must necessarily be apprehended in every case. For only in those instances where, upon the arising of a cognition, a doubt arises as to whether "this is correct or false," is there a dependence on another means of valid cognition; whereas when practical activity (*vyavahāra*) extending to the attainment of the object is possible, that dependence ceases, and thus there is no fault of infinite regress or the like.

Furthermore, if it were maintained that validity is self-cognized because it is a property of cognition, then invalidity would likewise be so; how, then, could it be extrinsic? Likewise, upon the arising of false knowledge, one does not act because falsity has been apprehended; and upon the arising of correct knowledge, once there is the determination of its correctness, there is an absence of doubt and the like as to whether "this is correct or false."

Regarding the statement that the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), by virtue of its being a cognizer, rests upon the mere non-perception of defects: if there is no arising of the cognition of a defect—that is, the non-perception of a defect—then neither is validity made known nor is it produced by that [non-perception]. How, then, can there be a statement regarding its "remaining in an unsettled state"? Alternatively, if it were maintained that the cognition of the absence of defects functions as a knower of validity just as the cognition of a defect (which is a subverting cognition) functions as a knower of falsity, then the validity of that [cognition of the absence of defects] would have to be known from something else, resulting in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If the rebuttal is that the apprehension of validity does not depend on such [further cognition] in every case, provided there is no doubt at the time of the arising of the cognition, then validity is not *svataḥ* (intrinsic), because it is admitted to depend on another both in its arising and its cognition.

Now, if it is argued that correctness (*samyaktva*) existing in the causal factors such as the sense organs does not arise in cognitions through the process of the excellence of the causes, but rather [arises] intrinsically (*svataḥ*), then this is equally applicable to invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) as well. For in that case too, the nature of error and so forth does not arise as something already existing in the sense organs and other such factors.

However, since the intended position is that intrinsic validity (*svataḥ prāmāṇya*) is asserted with respect to a means of knowledge whose nature is awakening (*bodhātmaka*), there would be no dispute at all, because this position does not conflict with the assertion that the validity of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) depends upon a specific speaker. This is because, for the sake of supporting this [intrinsic validity], one demonstrates that other means of knowledge possess extrinsic validity (*parataḥ prāmāṇya*). Furthermore, if the intrinsic validity of the injunction were accepted, the effort toward examination—such as the argument "the cognition produced by the injunction is valid, because it is produced by causal factors free from defects, like the perceptual cognition arising from a logical mark (*liṅga*)"—would be pointless. If, on the other hand, the statement of examination is intended to produce correct knowledge by way of dispelling the delusion of others, then if delusion persists even regarding the knowledge produced by that examination, another examination would be required, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). And since that [regress] is avoided precisely by the reasoning already stated, how could it be said that the validity of an extrinsic means of knowledge is either produced or known? Thus, [extrinsic validity] is established.

The remaining refutations and their resolutions have been explained in detail by our teachers, and thus have not been stated here. Therefore, because verbal testimony possesses validity by virtue of being spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*), it is not included within inference.

Now, since there is no necessary connection between words and their objects, [words] lack authority altogether. Thus it has been stated that the listener’s engagement or withdrawal occurs through the superimposition of those [objects] by conflating the perceived object (*dṛśya*) with the conceptualized object (*vikalpya*). The cognizer proceeds acting under the thought that this very form residing in the conceptualization is the external object; it is not through the perception of the actual external object, because at the time the word arises—following the sequence of the speaker’s intention—the object has already passed away due to its momentariness.

Furthermore, because there is no object beyond the scope of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*), verbal testimony (*śabda*) is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For instance, perception has the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object, whereas inference has the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object. Since the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) are of two kinds, the means of valid cognition are likewise twofold; thus, how could verbal testimony be a means of valid cognition if it were a distinct [object]? Moreover, if verbal testimony had the same object as the sense organ, there would be no difference between a blind person and one who is not blind. As it is said: "The object grasped by the sense organs is one thing, while the range of verbal testimony is another."
One whose eyes are impaired understands [the object] from the word, but does not perceive it through direct perception.

The specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of form and so forth, which is perceivable by the sense organs, is one thing; therefore, let it be understood that the domain of a word is something else—the object of *apoha*. For from a word, one whose eyes are different [from those of another] or whose vision is destroyed understands [the object], but does not see it in the manner that perception (*pratyakṣa*) occurs. Or, if they had the same object, then for a blind person, just as for one who is not blind, there would be a non-mediated (*aparokṣa*) cognition from a word. If that were the case, then just as from the contact of a sense organ with fire, so too from the word "burning" there would be a cognition of the actual sensation of burning. Thus he says:
A person who has been burned perceives the burning as one thing due to contact with fire,
whereas the meaning of "burning" is understood quite differently when conveyed by the word "burning."

Therefore, a word does not have the same object as the sense faculty. Likewise, if a word such as "cow" (or "word") had the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object, then because that [particular] is partless, words such as "white" and so forth would also be synonyms. However, if it has exclusion (*apoha*) as its object, this fault does not arise, because [words] are directed toward the exclusion of different superimpositions (*samāropa*).

Furthermore, if words had real objects as their domain, there would be no lack of restriction regarding their meanings based on human whim. As for linguistic usage, it proceeds from the thought: "I have understood this through a word, and I shall cause another to understand it through a word. This relationship between the communicator and the one being communicated will be like two people with cataracts both seeing two moons. Just as one person with cataracts perceives two moons and communicates this to another, who in turn perceives them, so too is this the linguistic usage of all practitioners everywhere. Now, do the investigators proceed while considering the determination of word-meanings to be false? Yes, because they follow worldly convention, according to the maxim: "In regard to worldly usage, the child and the scholar are alike. Moreover, the capacity of even false cognition to convey an object is observed in certain cases; for example, when two people run toward the light of a jewel and a lamp respectively, perceiving it to be a jewel, although there is no difference in the falsity of their cognitions, there is a difference in terms of their successful causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*).

This is incorrect; for when one acts upon the determination of an object through verbal testimony, its validity is established by its non-discrepancy with the object, just like sense-perception. To explain: even in the case of sensory cognition, there is no other means of validating its correctness apart from non-discrepancy with the object; since this [non-discrepancy] also exists in the case of verbal cognition, how could it be invalid?

The connection [between word and object] must also be stated for sound, just as it is for the sense organs, because a specific effect is perceived; and that [connection] is nothing other than the cognition of convention (*saṅketa*) based upon the signified and the signifier, since no other is possible. And although particulars (*viśeṣa*) are infinite, its establishment is indeed possible through the inclusion of a single universal (*sāmānya*), as has already been stated. Furthermore, if words were invalid, the treatise (*śāstra*) intended for the purpose of understanding the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth would be useless, because the nature of the means of valid cognition and the rest could not be understood from it even indirectly.

If validity were intended to consist solely in the indication of the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), then, since all sentences are invariably connected to that [intention], they would all be equally valid without distinction; consequently, there could be no determination of victory or defeat between the proponent and the opponent in a debate. If it is argued that only that sentence which indicates an intention established by a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with the object is valid, and not every sentence, we say no. For, just like words, intentions do not have an absolute necessary connection with objects. Thus, because the object does not persist at the time of the intention due to the sequence of perceiving the object and then recollecting it, [words] proceed only when there is a conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) of an external object, and not "by unifying the perceived and the conceptualized objects through superimposition."

Furthermore, it is not logical to equate the non-perception of the perceptible with conceptual construction; for while the superimposition of duality and so forth occurs upon a perceived object such as the moon because it has been perceived elsewhere, this conceptualization is false because no sublation arises in the comprehension of the word’s meaning.
As for the claim that at the time of the word's production according to the sequence of the speaker's intention, the object does not exist, that is refuted by the non-acceptance of momentariness.

Now, if it is argued that verbal testimony (*śabda*) lacks the status of a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) because there is no object distinct from the general (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*), that is incorrect, because we do not accept a strict restriction (*ekānta*) regarding the means of valid cognition. Thus, the self (*ātman*) is cognized through scripture (*āgama*), and furthermore, through the marks of rebirth and by the power of yoga, it is also perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); this constitutes a convergence (*saṃplava*) of means of knowledge. Yet, there is also restriction (*vyavasthā*) in certain cases, such as the determination of what is pure or impure through scripture, or the operation of the sense organs within their own respective domains. Therefore, since verbal testimony operates even with respect to the objects of perception and other means, the absence of a distinct object cannot be the reason for its lack of validity. Furthermore, the refutation of the determination of two means of knowledge based on a twofold division of objects has been stated at length by the Guru (Praśastamati), and thus it is not discussed here.

As for the argument that if words had the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their object, there would be no distinction between the blind and the non-blind, that is incorrect; for even when the object is the same, there is a difference in cognition due to the difference in the instruments [of perception]. For in the case of the blind person, a cognition having color-form (*rūpa*) as its object arises from the word, but it is not visual. One who possesses immediate visual cognition is not blind. Since a word illuminates an object even when it is remote, whereas a sense-organ [requires] proximity, these two produce distinct cognitions.

As for the claim that the meaning of "burning" (*dāha*) might be understood from the word "burning" itself—just as the sensation of burning arises from the contact of the sense of touch with fire—that is addressed as follows: if "burning" is suffering, then indeed it is perceived from the word "burning. However, this does not entail that the listener becomes a sufferer, because the suffering does not inhere in him. For only one in whom suffering has arisen through inherence (*samavāya*) is a sufferer; it is not the case that suffering inherent in oneself arises simply from the word "burning. What then? One merely cognizes it as being inherent in another person. Furthermore, the burning characterized by blisters and so forth arises from the contact of the skin with fire, not from the word "burning. Therefore, when the effect such as blisters arises from the contact of fuel with fire, the resulting suffering is experienced by the self through its connection with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and thus one is designated as a "sufferer. But the word "burning" causes one to understand the suffering residing in another's self in an entirely different way, namely, without the effect such as blisters having arisen. Thus, this objection is invalid.

Nor does it follow that words such as "white" and so forth would be synonyms because the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is partless; for it has been stated that since the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) are distinct, the difference in cognition constitutes the definition of difference. Therefore, even if words with different grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) refer to the same object, they are not synonyms.
Furthermore, exclusion (*apoha*) is not the meaning of a word, because—as we shall explain—that very thing is impossible.

As for the objection that, if words had real objects as their referents, there would be no lack of fixity of meaning due to the influence of human desire—that is incorrect. For words that function based on a specific occasion (*naimittika*) do not have unfixed meanings because they operate by virtue of that occasion; however, it is indeed accepted that arbitrary (*yādṛcchika*) words have unfixed meanings due to the influence of human desire, since no subverting factor (*bādhaka*) arises [to contradict them]. Furthermore, verbal usage is not like the vision of two moons by one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*). To explain: in the case of the ophthalmic person’s vision of two moons, there is a subverting factor both before and after the onset of the ophthalmia, whereas for one who has not developed ophthalmia, it exists at all times; but such is not the case with verbal usage.

As for the claim that, despite the lack of distinction in being false cognition, there is nonetheless the accomplishment of purposeful action—as in the case of the light of a gem and the light of a lamp—that arises from a lack of understanding. For it is thus: the cognition of one standing nearby that is directed toward the gem itself is what produces the purposeful action, not the cognition of the light. Furthermore, verbal cognition is not erroneous, because, like sensory cognition, its practical efficacy is observed to extend as far as the attainment of the object.

Furthermore, in the absence of a real relationship, the restriction of conceptual determination—whereby from the word "horse" there arises the determination of a horse, and from the word "cow" the determination of a cow—would not be possible; yet this [restriction] is observed. Likewise, even in the case of the word "horse," if the relationship were not apprehended, there would be no cognition of the related object. Enough of this excessive detail. Thus, since the necessary connection based on identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*) has already been refuted, and since words convey meaning by virtue of convention (*samaya*), it is established that they possess validity as a means of knowledge distinct from inference.
The inclusion of gesture within inference:
“Because one observes the comprehension of a well-known dramatic representation through gesture, that too is indeed nothing but inference.”

Now, some maintain that gesture (*ceṣṭā*) is a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). To refute this, he says: "Because it is observed that one who is well-versed in gestures understands [the meaning] through gesture, that too is indeed inference (*anumāna*). One whose gesture—meaning a physical activity (*kāyika-vyāpāra*)—is well-known as being invariably concomitant (*avinābhūta*) with a specific object is described thus. For such a person, there is an understanding of the specific object through that gesture; for example, from a particular joining of the mouth and hands, one understands thirst, because that [gesture] was previously perceived as being invariably concomitant with it. And thus: "This person is possessed of thirst, because he possesses a particular joining of mouth and hands, like Devadatta in such a state. Therefore, since it functions as a means of knowledge by virtue of the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and other [logical requirements], this too is indeed inference. In the same way, other gestures well-known in the *Nāṭyaśāstra* should also be subsumed under inference.
{The inclusion of comparison within inference}:

“Because a person who is unfamiliar with the gavaya is informed about the gavaya by means of a cow through the words of a reliable authority, comparison is nothing other than the word of a reliable authority. <PDhS>

Now, some maintain that analogy (*upamāna*) is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). To refute this, he says: "Because an authoritative person (*āpta*) explains a *gavaya*—which is not yet known—to someone by means of a cow, analogy is nothing other than the word of an authoritative person. This means: because an authoritative person, by means of the well-known similarity between a cow and a *gavaya*, explains a *gavaya* (which is unknown) through its resemblance to a cow; for instance, the intended analogy is "as is a cow, so is a *gavaya*. That is merely the word of an authoritative person and not a separate means of valid cognition. Nor can it be a separate means of valid cognition simply because it takes the form of an analogy, for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of an infinite number of means of valid cognition due to the distinctions between injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and so forth. If it is argued that even though there is a difference in their internal subdivisions, these [injunctions, etc. do not differ from the instruction of an authoritative person, then the same applies to analogy as well.

Alternatively, it is claimed that for one who has learned of the similarity from a statement and is wandering in the forest seeking a *gavaya*, the cognition "my cow is similar to this" is *upamāna* (analogy); but this is incorrect because it lacks a result (*phala*). It has been stated that the result is the cessation of non-cognition (*ajñāna-nivṛtti*), yet cessation is a form of destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*). For instance, whether non-cognition is the non-arising of knowledge or a contrary cognition, in either case its cessation is simply destruction. Furthermore, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which produces valid knowledge (*pramā*). Nor are the cognitions of what is to be avoided (*heya*) and so forth the result, because they arise only after a lapse of time following the determination of pleasure, pain, and so on, once those [cognitions] have passed away. Moreover, similarity cannot be the object of valid cognition (*prameya*), because the cognition of it is not the result. Or, if that were admitted, another means of valid cognition would have to be asserted.

Now, the opponent’s intention is that comparison (*upamāna*) is the cognition "my cow is similar to this [animal]," which has as its result a cognition whose object (*prameya*) is either the individual body delimited by similarity, or the similarity itself delimited by that body. This cognition is not born of the senses (*indriyajam*), because it arises for one standing in the forest with respect to an object (the cow) located in the house. Nor is it born of inference (*anumānajam*), because no operation of a logical mark (*liṅga*) is perceived. Furthermore, the similarity of the cow existing in the gavaya, even if perceived there, is unestablished [with respect to the cow], because it resides in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇatvāt*). Thus, the inference "my cow is similar to this, because this is similar to that" suffers from the very same defect of residing in different loci. It is not born of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), because there is no fact that remains unaccounted for. It is not verbal (*śābdam*), because it arises even without a word [to that effect]. And non-existence (*abhāva*) has a restricted scope. Nor is this a case of memory (*smaraṇam*), because the similarity of the gavaya was never previously experienced in relation to the individual cow. Therefore, the conclusion is that this is the result of a distinct means of valid cognition.

If the individual entity of a *gavaya*, as delimited by its similarity to a cow, is perceived solely through the sensory contact with an object (*indriyārthasannikarṣa*), then this is simply the fruit of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and not the fruit of another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*). In that case, does the sense organ produce such a cognition while depending on memory, or independently? If it produces the cognition independently, then this would occur even for one who has no prior memory of the individual cow. If it depends on the memory of the mere individual, then it would also occur upon remembering the individual bodies of horses and other animals. If it depends on the memory of the individual as delimited by similarity to a *gavaya*, then if it were to depend on mere memory [of that], it would also occur upon remembering elephants and so forth. If it depends on the memory of the cow-individual, then does it depend on the memory of the cow-individual in general, or on the memory of the cow-individual as delimited by similarity to a *gavaya*? If it depends on the memory of the cow-individual in general, it would also occur upon remembering the individual bodies of horses and so forth. If it depends on the memory of the cow-individual as delimited by similarity to a *gavaya*, then a prior experience must be asserted; for without that, there would be no formation of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), and thus memory itself would be impossible. Therefore, even in the absence of a determinate cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*), a prior experience regarding the cow-individual as delimited by similarity to a *gavaya* must be admitted, so that when a latent impression is produced, there may arise from memory the cognition: "This *gavaya* is similar to my cow. Furthermore, if a prior experience of the cow-individual as delimited by similarity to a *gavaya* were well-established, why would there not be the memory: "My cow is similar to this," upon perceiving the *gavaya*? Thus questioned, [the opponent] says: "I perceived something similar to this," but he does not point to another means of knowledge. Thinking this, the venerable Praśasta [sūtra-author] stated [its] inclusion [within perception].

Others, however, maintain that *upamāna* (analogy) is the cognition "this [animal] is like a cow," which arises after one has perceived the similarity from the words of a forest-dweller—such as "as is a cow, so is a gavaya"—and subsequently, while wandering in the forest with that impression (*saṃskāra*) awakened, sees a gavaya characterized by its similarity to a cow; this occurs immediately after the recollection of the relation of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). Following that, there is the comprehension of the relationship between the name and the named, namely "this is the name *gavaya*. The result (*phala*) is the form consisting of the name and the named, or the individual object (*piṇḍa*) delimited by the name; it is the object of knowledge (*prameya*). Nor can the convention (*saṅketa*) be understood from the verbal statement alone, because the individual gavaya is not present to the senses, and because that would contradict the aphorism: "The application of a name is based on perception" (*pratyakṣaṃ saṃjñākarma*). This is not correct, because the convention (*saṅketa*) is understood from the sentence itself. To explain: the meaning of the sentence concerning similarity is this: "That which is similar to a cow is to be designated as a *gavaya*. Having apprehended the convention from that sentence, and perceiving an individual (*piṇḍa*) delimited by similarity, one subsequently employs the designation: "This is a *gavaya*. However, one does not apprehend the convention for every single individual, for that would entail the absurd consequence of having to establish a convention for each and every object. To illustrate: [if it were so], one would have to grasp the convention thus: "Wherever you see cowness (*gotva*), there the word 'cow' must be applied, and from that, this object is to be understood"; and once the convention is grasped, upon perceiving an individual cow, one understands "this is a cow," but not "this is the name 'cow'," for that would lead to the consequence of an absence of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). Nor, however, is there a contradiction with the Sūtra, because the term "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) serves as an indicator for any firm means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). A name is applied to an object determined by a firm means of valid cognition. For example, even though he resides in another country, a father gives a name to his son, saying, "He is named Yajñadatta."

Now, if it is argued that the convention (*saṅketa*) for a genus-word (*jātiśabda*) applies only to an object perceived by the senses (*pratyakṣa*), this is not so; for it would follow that there could be no convention regarding supersensible (*atīndriya*) objects. Yet, we observe that the word "mind" (*manas*) has a convention applied even to the mind, which is supersensible and yet determined by firm means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Likewise, when asked by another, "How do you know that this is a *gavaya*? one points out the very statement, "It was told to me by a forest-dweller," and does not say, "I recognized it through similarity. Furthermore, there is designation by means of a causal factor (*kāraka*); as in the cases, "recognized by the eye" or "recognized through inference," so too comparison (*upamāna*) is a means of valid cognition whose expressed object is devoid of a [previously known] referent. If it is argued that the object of knowledge (*prameya*) consists of the form of the name (*saṃjñā*) and the named (*saṃjñin*), this is not so; for if the apprehension of the relationship is the result, it is illogical for the relata themselves to be the object of knowledge. If it is argued that the very apprehension of the relata—just like the relationship itself—is figuratively (*upacāreṇa*) designated as such because it resides in both, even then the object of knowledge does not consist of the form of the name and the named, since the name is absent therein. If it is argued that one recognizes [the object] by uttering the word oneself, this is not so; for at the time the word is produced according to the sequence of the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), the cognition of similarity—which would be the means of valid cognition—is impossible. If it is argued that the word "gavaya" produced somewhere in the vastness of the world is the object of knowledge, this is not so; for it is illogical for that which is not being heard to be an object of knowledge. If it were by way of non-obstruction (*apratibandha*), then upon the arrival of someone standing at a distance, there would be the arrival of what was spoken by Brahmā.

Furthermore, one does not utter the word "gavaya" at that very moment while standing nearby [the object], because it is not perceived. Now, if it is argued that the word "gavaya" is the object of cognition (*prameya*) as superimposed by memory, no; for there is no cause for such a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Immediately after the cognition of similarity, one understands, "This is the name 'gavaya'," and there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the entry of its memory in the interval. However, if the individual object (*piṇḍa*) were delimited by the name, there would be a cognition of the relation [between the two], because that [cognition] has both as its objective support. Likewise, even by the opponent who demonstrates the distinction of comparison (*upamāna*) from inference (*anumāna*), the statement—"Comparison is established through the synthesis 'as... so...', therefore there is no lack of distinction"—shows that comparison is intended to have the form of a verbal expression (*vākya-rūpa*). And its inclusion within scripture (*āgama*) is not a fault.

{The inclusion of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) within inference}: “Presumptive testimony arises from a perceived object; that too is indeed inference. Now, the statement “presumptive testimony arises from a perceived object; that too is indeed inference” is intended to demonstrate the inclusion of presumptive testimony within inference. It is called *darśana* because it is seen (*dṛśyate*); thus, from a perceived object—that is, from an apprehended thing which cannot otherwise be accounted for—there is the attainment (*āpti*), reaching (*prāpti*), or logical consequence (*prasaṅga*) of another object. As it has been said: “Presumptive testimony is the postulation of an unperceived object based on a perceived one, when the perceived object is not otherwise possible. (*ŚBh*, p. 13) For example, when one observes the fatness of Devadatta while he does not eat during the day, the fact of his fatness—which would be inexplicable otherwise—is established through the presumption that he eats at night. This is the same as inferring fire from smoke; therefore, presumptive testimony is merely a form of inference. Thus, its inclusion within inference is established. 109.12–15.The inclusion of presumptive testimony within inference is established by the following reasoning: when a certain perceived fact is observed, and that fact is logically impossible except under the assumption of some other fact, the postulation of that other fact constitutes presumptive testimony. Since this process involves the cognition of a probandum based on a perceived mark (the perceived fact), it is subsumed under inference. Therefore, presumptive testimony is not a separate means of valid knowledge distinct from inference. 109.15–17.Thus ends the section on the inclusion of presumptive testimony within inference. 109.17.The inclusion of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) within inference (*anumāna*) is as follows: "From a perceived object, presumptive testimony [arises]; that too is indeed inference. (*darśanārthādarthāpattistadapyanumānameva*). Now, in order to show the inclusion of presumptive testimony within inference, there is the statement: "From a perceived object, presumptive testimony [arises]; that too is indeed inference. That which is seen is a "perception" (*darśana*); from that, from an object being apprehended which is otherwise inexplicable, there is the attainment (*āpti*), reaching (*prāpti*), or logical consequence (*prasaṅga*) of another object. As it has been said: "Presumptive testimony is the postulation of an unperceived object based on a perceived one, when the perceived object is not otherwise possible. (*ŚBh*, p. 13) For example, when one observes the fatness of Devadatta while he does not eat during the day, the fact of his fatness—which would be inexplicable otherwise—is established through the presumption that he eats at night. This is the same as inferring fire from smoke; therefore, presumptive testimony is merely a form of inference. Thus, its inclusion within inference is established. 109.12–15. The inclusion of presumptive testimony within inference is established by the following reasoning: when a certain perceived fact is observed, and that fact is logically impossible except under the assumption of some other fact, the postulation of that other fact constitutes presumptive testimony. Since this process involves the cognition of a probandum based on a perceived mark (the perceived fact), it is subsumed under inference. Therefore, presumptive testimony is not a separate means of valid knowledge distinct from inference. 109.15–17. The inclusion of presumptive testimony within inference is established by the following reasoning: when a certain perceived fact is observed, and that fact is logically impossible except under the assumption of some other fact

When an object known through the six means of valid cognition cannot be otherwise [accounted for], one may postulate another unseen factor; this is declared to be presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). (Ślokavārttika 450)

Thus, there are six varieties of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). Among these, that which is preceded by perception (*pratyakṣapūrvikā*) is as follows: having observed an effect characterized by bursting and so forth, the burning power of fire is inferred because it cannot otherwise be accounted for. In this case, there is no apprehension of an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) through another means of knowledge, because power (*śakti*) is not within the scope of any other means of knowledge. Furthermore, a mark (*liṅga*) whose invariable concomitance has not been perceived cannot function as a logical reason at all. Therefore, this is a distinct means of knowledge.

That which is preceded by inference (*anumānapūrvikā*) is as follows: having apprehended fire from smoke, one’s cognition of its specific qualities arises through the impossibility of its otherwise occurring (*tadanyathānupapattyā*). That which is preceded by comparison (*upamānapūrvikā*) is as follows: after seeing a *gavaya* in the forest, one apprehends the cow, thinking "my cow is similar to this," and through the impossibility of its otherwise occurring, one apprehends its capacity for carrying loads, yielding milk, and so forth. That which is preceded by presumption (*arthāpattipūrvikā*) is as follows: the power that delimits the eye is cognized through the impossibility of the perception of form occurring otherwise. That which is preceded by verbal testimony (*āgamapūrvikā*) is as follows: when Devadatta is alive, one apprehends his absence from the house based on the statement "he is not in the house," and through the impossibility of its otherwise occurring, one apprehends his existence outside. Since there is no mark (*liṅga*) invariably concomitant with being outside, this is the fruit of a distinct means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*).

But that which is preceded by non-existence is as follows: having understood Devadatta’s absence in the house through the exclusion of the five means of valid cognition that apprehend existence, one perceives his connection with an external location because that [absence] would otherwise be inexplicable.

He states their inclusion [within inference]: "That too is indeed inference (*anumāna*) and not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). Thus, the claim that the supersensible power (*śakti*) of fire is cognized through its effect, such as the crackling sound (*sphoṭa*), is incorrect; for that [power] has already been refuted previously, except insofar as it is the final auxiliary cause (*sahakārī*). Fire-contact itself, qualified by the absence of obstructing factors, is the power of fire, because the effect is produced when that [contact] exists. As for the intrinsic power (*nijā śakti*) consisting of the nature of fire (*agnitva*), that too is simply perceptible. As for the argument that once there is a cognition of the universal (*sāmānya*) through inference, the cognition of the particular (*viśeṣa*) occurs through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), that has already been rejected by the one who maintains that the particular is what is to be proven (*sādhya*). Regarding analogy (*upamāna*), although it is non-different from recollection, presumptive testimony preceded by it is nothing but inference, because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is grasped beforehand. For example: "The individual cow delimited by similarity is capable of carrying loads and so forth, because it is an individual cow, like a previously perceived cow of this kind. Presumptive testimony preceded by presumptive testimony is also merely inference based on an inferred [fact]. For instance: "The perception of color is an action that requires an instrument, because it is an action, like the act of cutting. Here, the eye is well-known; and that [eye], being inferred, possesses power because it is an instrument, like an axe.

Furthermore, this cognition of Devadatta’s existence outside [the house]—based on the impossibility of his being alive while not being present in the house—is also nothing but inference (*anumāna*), because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has already been apprehended previously. To explain: Devadatta is connected with the external space, because, while being connected with life, he is not perceived in the house, just like Viṣṇumitra. Moreover, even for the proponent of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), Devadatta’s connection with life must be understood from scripture (*āgama*) alone; otherwise, the presumptive testimony would not proceed. And this same principle applies equally to presumptive testimony preceded by non-existence (*abhāva*).

Even through the absence of the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇapañcaka*), when one apprehends the non-existence of the living Devadatta in the house, his connection with the outside region is inferred. In this way, other examples of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) as well must be subsumed under inference itself by demonstrating their invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*); for otherwise, it would be impossible to demonstrate that [the fact] cannot be accounted for in any other way (*anyathānupapatti*) except through such an occurrence.

Now, some maintain that when there is an inference of a hostile entity such as a snake from hearing sounds such as hissing, the resulting cognition of its adversary, such as a mongoose, is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). That, however, is merely an inference based on what has been inferred (*anumitānumāna*), because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) was already grasped previously. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: "The sound of hissing is produced by a serpent, because it is a sound of hissing, like a previously perceived sound of hissing of this kind. Having thus inferred the serpent, one concludes: "The [place] possesses its adversary because of the presence of the serpent, because it is the locus of the agent of the sound of hissing, like a previously perceived location containing a serpent of this kind."
{The inclusion of *sambhava* within inference}:

“*Sambhava* is indeed inference because of its inseparable connection (*avinābhāvitva*). *Sambhava* is accepted by others as a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). To refute that, the statement is made: “*Sambhava* is indeed inference because of its inseparable connection. For where there is a thousand, a hundred necessarily occurs; thus, an inseparable connection is apprehended. And so, [the proposition]: “A thousand [is] possessed of its constituent parts [in the form of a hundred], because it is a thousand, like a previously perceived thousand.”
The inclusion of non-existence within inference:

“Non-existence, too, is indeed inference. Just as an effect that has arisen is a mark for the existence of its cause, so too an effect that has not arisen is a mark for the non-existence of its cause.”

Some maintain that because the non-arising of an effect is perceived as the absence of its cause, this is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting solely of non-existence (*abhāva*). To refute that, [the author states]: "Not only is possibility [a form of inference], but non-existence (*abhāva*) is also nothing but inference. Just as an arisen effect is a mark (*liṅga*) for the existence of a cause because the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) has already been apprehended, so too is a non-arisen effect [a mark] for the non-existence of a cause, because the non-arising of the effect is invariably concomitant with the absence of the cause. And thus: the non-arising of an effect possesses the absence of its cause, because it is a non-arising of an effect, like the non-arising of an effect admitted by both parties.

Now, since the non-existence of a thing is apprehended through the exclusion of the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that perceive existent things, non-existence (*abhāva*) is a distinct means of valid cognition. For just as the operation of a [means of knowledge] pertains to the determination of an existent aspect, so too must the operation of non-existence be admitted in the determination of its absence. As it has been said: "When the operation of perception and the other [means of knowledge] occurs and the existent aspect is apprehended, then the operation of non-existence is also intended toward the aspect of non-existence. (Ślokavārttika, p. 478)

For instance, non-existence (abhāva) is not apprehended by perception (pratyakṣa), because there is no connection (sambandha) with it. That which is connected and present is grasped by the eye and other [senses]. Due to the absence of perception, inference (anumāna) also does not operate, since it depends upon the apprehension of a related term (sambandhin). The same applies to verbal testimony (śabda). Since comparison (upamāna) and presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) are likewise inoperative, the apprehension of the non-existence of an object of knowledge (prameyābhāva) occurs precisely through the absence of the five means of valid cognition. As it has been said: [The verse follows: *na pratyakṣeṇa tāvad abhāvasya grahaṇam, tena saha sambandhābhāvāt | sambaddhaṃ vartamānaṃ ca gṛhyate cakṣurādinā | pratyakṣābhāvād anumānasyāpy apravṛttiḥ, tasya sambandhigrahaṇāpekṣitvāt | evaṃ śabdasyāpi | upamānārthāpattyoś cāvyāpārāt pramāṇapañcakābhāvenaiva prameyābhāvasya grahaṇam iti ||* (Ślokavārttika, p. 160)

"Where the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇapañcaka*) do not arise with respect to the nature of an object, there the status of non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇatā*) serves to bring about the awareness of the existence of that object. (ŚV, p. 473) [Objection:

If that were so, then even in the case of an object that is obstructed, since the five means of valid cognition are absent, it would follow that its non-existence is apprehended. [Reply: No, because there is also the operation of the apprehension of the object and the recollection of its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), and so forth. As it has been said:
Having grasped the existence of the object and having remembered its counter-correlate, a mental cognition of non-existence arises without depending on the sense organs. (Ślokavārttika, p. 482)

Having perceived the existence of an object such as a patch of ground and having recalled its counter-positive, the jar, one understands through the mind alone—without the operation of the sense organs—that "there is no jar here on this ground. Similarly, having seen a temple and gone outside, even though there is a spatial separation by another region and thus no sensory contact [with an elephant], when questioned by another at that very moment, one understands the non-existence of the elephant. As it has been said:
"Even after grasping a mere object and subsequently recalling something..."
In that regard, when questioned by another about existence, one immediately accepts it.
Likewise,
the non-arising of perception and the other means of knowledge is called the absence of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*).
Either the transformation of the self or consciousness [is the object], or else another entity. (Ślokavārttika, p. 475)

All this is incorrect, because non-existence (*abhāva*) is indeed cognized through perception and other means of knowledge. For instance, it is observed that from the operation of the senses, there arises an immediate (*aparokṣa*) cognition: "There is no jar here on the ground. If it is argued that the operation of the senses extends only to the apprehension of the ground and not to its non-existence, we say no; for there is no proof for the prior apprehension of the ground [independently]. Generally, the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is apprehended first, and subsequently the qualified (*viśeṣya*); since the ground is the qualified object, there is no proof for its prior apprehension. However, speaking hypothetically (*upetyavāda*), if it were granted that the recollection of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) occurs upon the apprehension of the mere thing, then even when one perceives a ground occupied by a jar, if that [jar] were recollected, it would follow that there is a cognition of non-existence [of the jar]. Alternatively, if the recollection of the counter-positive occurs upon the apprehension of the qualified thing, then that thing must first be understood as qualified by some qualifier. Is this understood through the senses alone, or through another means of knowledge? If you accept that it is understood through the senses alone, how can non-existence not be an object of perception, given that the state of being qualified is of the same nature as that [perceived thing]? Furthermore, there is no proof for the operation of inference (*anumāna*) or other means in this case.

Furthermore, if the qualified nature [of the ground] were perceived solely through the exclusion of the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇapañcakavyāvṛtti*), then if one were to admit the apprehension of another object even in that case, one would necessarily have to admit the apprehension of the qualified nature itself, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, since the absence of the jar is already cognized when one perceives the ground as distinguished from other objects by means of the sense faculty itself and then recollects the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), there is no need for the exclusion of the five means of valid cognition.

Since the operation of that very [cognition] which reveals the existent portion is perceived through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) even with respect to the non-existent portion, one should not claim that non-existence (*abhāva*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding an object not delimited by the other five means of valid cognition. Nor is there a failure to perceive [non-existence] due to a lack of connection with the sense organ, for the existence of that [organ] is established precisely by its effect. Furthermore, even by the opponent, a connection characterized by "fitness" (*yogyatā*) between the sense organ and the object is accepted on account of the existence of immediate cognition (*aparokṣajñāna*); and that [connection] must be accepted even in the case of non-existence, since the effect is no different in both cases. Likewise, the Vaiśeṣikas also accept a sixfold connection between the sense organ and the object on account of the existence of immediate cognition; thus, the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva*) certainly exists [between the sense organ and non-existence], for it is only when that [relation] exists that immediate cognition arises.

If, however, non-existence (*abhāva*) is apprehended through the exclusion of the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that perceive existing things, how can there be the restriction that "there are only six means of valid cognition"? For such a restriction is untenable if the means of valid cognition itself is not apprehended. Indeed, if the absence of the means of valid cognition that perceive existing things were the object to be determined, there would be no other means of valid cognition to determine it. If one argues that because the absence of the five means of valid cognition is manifold, some [absence] serves as the apprehender of another, then in that case, that [apprehender] would be apprehended by yet another, and that by this one, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore, since individual instances of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇavyakti*) are manifold, if they themselves are not apprehended, the restriction "only six" which depends upon them could not possibly hold. For the Vaiśeṣikas, however, although the individual instances of the means of valid cognition are infinite, there exists a single defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) that encompasses them all; thus, when the means of valid cognition are apprehended [by way of their definition], the restriction is logically justified.

As for the claim that one who has just left after seeing only a temple, when questioned by another, realizes at that very moment the absence of an elephant and so forth—that is not correct, because this is a case of recollection (*smaraṇa*). Even though previously no determinate cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*) such as "there was an elephant" had arisen, nevertheless, a non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) arose regarding the temple as qualified by the absence of elephants and the like. Otherwise, following the question "When I saw the temple, did I see that elephant standing nearby?", there would have been no recollection; yet such recollection is indeed observed. Regarding an object whose prior absence was not determined, one remains in doubt after another's question: "Was Devadatta there or not? I did not look. One does not determine the absence at that time, for even in the case of scripture (*āgama*), the realization of the actual state of an object occurs through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since it is not possible [to know everything] through the instruction of a reliable person (*āpta*) alone. Therefore, since the absence of the elephant and so forth was already perceived previously, it is logical that this is a recollection: "I did not see an elephant there," and so on. Furthermore, the status of absence as an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) has already been established in the section on the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*)."
{The statement that tradition is the instruction of a reliable person:} “Likewise, tradition also, when it is not false, is indeed the instruction of a reliable person. <PDhS>

Now, regarding a traditional report whose original speaker is unspecified—such as "a yakṣa dwells in this banyan tree"—if its correspondence with reality is apprehended through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is not a distinct category from authoritative instruction (*āptopadeśa*). Thus he says: "Likewise, tradition (*aitihya*) that is non-false is indeed authoritative instruction. For, just as the aforementioned means of valid cognition are not distinct [from perception], so too tradition that is non-false—that is, in accordance with reality—is simply authoritative instruction and not a separate means of valid cognition. In the case of the opposite, however, it lacks validity.

“Parārthānumāna is the communication of an object ascertained by oneself through a statement consisting of five members. It should be understood that parārthānumāna is the communication of an object ascertained by oneself to others—those who are doubtful, mistaken, or ignorant—exclusively through a statement consisting of five members.”

Now follows the section beginning with “by means of the five-membered [statement]” (*pañcāvayavena*) for the purpose of explaining the inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) previously indicated. “Inference for others” is the indication of the definiendum (*lakṣya*). “The communication of an object ascertained by oneself by means of a five-membered statement” is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*). “The object ascertained by oneself” (*svaniścitārtha*) is the probandum (*sādhya*). That by which it is communicated is the “communication of the object ascertained by oneself,” namely, the logical mark (*liṅga*). That [mark], when accompanied by a five-membered statement, is inference for others. Alternatively, “communication” (*pratipādana*) may mean the act of understanding; thus, the knowledge whose object is the object ascertained by oneself, which is produced by a five-membered statement—that collection of causal factors from which it arises—is inference for others. This is the explanation of the proponent who maintains that the meaning of the sentence is the probandum. However, in the view where the logical mark (*liṅga*) is the meaning of the sentence, “meaning” (*artha*) is so called because it is sought after (*arthyate*) by means of it; “communication” (*pratipādana*) is that which is communicated. Thus, the logical mark being communicated by a five-membered statement is inference for others. Or else, “communication” is the attainment of the object ascertained by oneself; and that [attainment], when produced by a five-membered statement, is inference for others.

But in this view, how does inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) differ from inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), given that one perceives the logical mark (*liṅga*) through the eye or through a word, and from that [mark] perceives the probandum (*sādhya*)? Whence, then, is the distinction between "for oneself" and "for others"? Nor is it a distinction that one perceives the mark from a word produced by another, because the eye and other senses are also produced by others; furthermore, the difference in the nature of the word is merely a formal distinction (*vaidharmyamātra*). Therefore, the position that the sentence-meaning is the probandum (*sādhyavākyārtha*) must be accepted, as no defects can be established against it. Accordingly, the distinction is simply this: when the mere mark perceived through the eye and so forth leads to the cognition of the probandum, it is inference for oneself, unaccompanied by words; whereas when it is accompanied by words, it is inference for others. By the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*), we perceive that immediately after the consideration of the competent mark, the cognition of the probandum arises in the form "this is indeed impermanent"; thus, the probandum itself is the sentence-meaning. The sentence ends precisely with "therefore. The remainder of the statement is merely for the purpose of communicating one's intention (*abhiprāyanivedana*), and not for the sake of the meaning itself, since no refutation applies to the position that the sentence-meaning is the probandum. Enough of this excessive detail.

This is the explanation of the preceding summary statement: “By means of a five-membered syllogism alone, and not by a two-membered or a ten-membered one. For whom? “For those who are doubtful, mistaken, or untrained. Inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) should be understood as the communication of an object already ascertained by oneself.

Now, it may be argued that because a sentence is partless (*niravayava*), this [analysis] into five members is untenable. Likewise, letters (*varṇa*) cannot convey meaning when combined, because since they occur sequentially and perish instantly, a "collection" (*samudāya*) is impossible. Nor can they do so individually, for if the meaning were understood from a single letter, the utterance of the others would be useless. Yet, we do perceive the comprehension of meaning from a word once it has been uttered. Therefore, since this cannot be explained otherwise, a nature called *sphoṭa*—which transcends the collection of letters—is cognized. Furthermore, it is observed that upon the utterance of the word "cow" (*gaur*), a cognition arises through the operation of the auditory organ that possesses a non-differentiated form. And this cognition, being distinct from doubt and error, cannot exist without a non-differentiated object, just like the cognition of a whole (*avayavin*). Thus, the utterance of letters is not in vain, as it serves to manifest the essential nature of the *sphoṭa*.

This is not so, because the final phoneme, assisted by its own experience and supported by the preceding phonemes, conveys the meaning. For instance, there is a cognition of the first phoneme, which produces a mental impression (*saṃskāra*); then there is a cognition of the second phoneme, which—assisted by the impression of the preceding phoneme—produces another impression. In this sequence, there is a cognition of the final phoneme. When that cognition manifests the previous impressions and the recollection of all the preceding phonemes occurs, the comprehension of the meaning arises from the final phoneme. Nor does this lead to the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of [meaning-comprehension] arising from the impression produced by the experience of a jar or other objects—which, when assisted by another experience, would likewise initiate an impression—because in those cases there is an absence of the specific unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). That absence is known precisely through the non-existence of the effect. In the present case, however, since the effect exists, a specific unseen merit is postulated as the cause.

Others, however, maintain that the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of the preceding phonemes—being regulated by the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) that brings about the enjoyment of the word's meaning—initiate a single recollection of those preceding phonemes; and the final phoneme, assisted by that [recollection], constitutes the word (*pada*). Alternatively, they initiate a single, diverse impression, and from that [impression] arises a single recollection of the preceding phonemes.

Others, however, maintain that even past preceding phonemes and their cognitions possess the capacity for cooperation with the final phoneme, because this is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). For just as the causality of a present entity is known through positive and negative concomitance, so too is it known for a past one. Alternatively, the destructions of the preceding phonemes and the non-existences (*pradhvaṃsa*) of their cognitions, being proximate, act as cooperators with the final phoneme; thus, the presumption (*arthāpatti*) is exhausted. If such a conceptualization were not accepted, the utterance of the phonemes would be utterly useless. Nor does the utterance serve to manifest the *sphoṭa*, because the alternatives of [the phonemes acting] collectively or individually are untenable. It is not manifested by them collectively, because a composite whole (*samudāya*) is not admitted; nor is it manifested by them individually, because if it were manifested by just one, the utterance of the remaining ones would result in futility. If, on the other hand, such a conceptualization is resorted to, it is equally capable of accounting for the comprehension of meaning; therefore, enough with the postulation of the *sphoṭa*. Furthermore, the cognition of a single, undifferentiated form has either the final phoneme or the property of phonemeness (*varṇatva*) as its object.

Alternatively, just as in the case of the perception of letters existing in a dense mass, the cognition [of them] is erroneous and appears as a non-differentiated form; thus, there is no proof of the *sphoṭa*. Since the faults regarding the manifestation of the *sphoṭa* are identical to those regarding the manifestation of sound, they will be addressed in the very same section on the examination of sound (*śabdaparīkṣā*). Enough of this.

The construction of a sentence (*vākya-kalpanā*) proceeds as follows: upon the cognition of a single word, there is the arising of a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), and the state of the recollection of the linguistic convention (*saṅketa-smaraṇa*) being produced; then, from that, the arising of the impression and the recollection of the convention, the state of the comprehension of the word-meaning (*padārtha-pratipatti*) being produced, and the state of the word-cognition (*pada-jñāna*) about to perish.
