Then, the production of the comprehension of the word-meaning, the state of the recollection about to perish, the destruction of the word-cognition, the state of the second word-cognition and its impression being produced; then, the arising of the second word-cognition, the arising of the impression by means of the comprehension of the word-meaning assisted by the preceding impression, the state of another impression being produced, and the state of the recollection of the convention also being produced; the state of the comprehension of the word-meaning about to perish, the destruction of the previous recollection of the convention, then the arising of the impression of the second word-cognition and also the arising of the recollection of the convention; the state of the word-cognition about to perish, the state of the comprehension of the word-meaning being produced, and the destruction of the comprehension of the previous word-meaning—this is the logical sequence (*nyāya*) that continues until the cognition of the final word. By that process of conceptualization (*kalpanā*), through the manifestation of those impressions, a recollection having all word-meanings as its object is generated. And by that [recollection] and by its own experience, the final word itself is the sentence (*vākya*), and from that sentence, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha-pratipatti*) arises.

Now, if it is admitted that prior to the arising of the cognition of the word, a recollection of the word and its object arises by the force of *adṛṣṭa*, then since that [recollection] does not persist from the time of the word-cognition until the time of the recollection of the convention (*saṅketa*), how could there be a comprehension of the sentence-meaning after the comprehension of the word-meaning? Nor can there be a comprehension of the sentence-meaning without the comprehension of the word-meaning, for such a thing is never observed. If, on the other hand, it is argued that after the word-cognition, a recollection is produced by that mental impression (*saṃskāra*) through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), and thus at the time of the recollection of the convention, the word-cognition is in the state of perishing—therefore, because it does not persist at the time of the recollection of the convention, the aforementioned objection remains exactly as it was: that in the absence of the comprehension of the word-meaning, there is no comprehension of the sentence-meaning.

This is incorrect, because the convention (saṅketa) cannot be established for a sentence. A sentence is merely the final word; however, the meaning of that final word is the sentence-meaning. And when, following the preceding phonemes and their cognitions, a recollection is produced through conceptualization (*kalpanā*) and their residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), at that point the cognition of the word is in the process of perishing. Thus, the final phoneme—characterized by the absence of the recollection of the convention—is the word. This is the conceptual construction of a sentence. Otherwise, if one were to accept that the final phoneme is the word as assisted by a diverse recollection arising from the residual impressions via the cognition of the preceding phonemes, then the cognition of the word would occur after the cognition of the word-meaning, due to the intervention of the cognition of the phonemes.

Others, however, [hold that] for the sake of resolving the aforementioned objection, immediately after the cognition of the final word, a single recollection is initiated through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), involving both the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by that [final word] and the latent impression generated by the experience of the linguistic convention (*saṅketa*). From this, the cognition of the word-meaning arises; the cognition of the word is in the state of perishing; and there is no contradiction between the recollection and the experience. Then, from the final word as qualified by that recollection and experience, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning occurs.

Others, however, maintain that although the cognition of the word has perished once the meaning of the word is understood following the recollection of the convention immediately after the cognition of the final word, nevertheless, a further cognition arises regarding that very same [word]. Then, through conceptualization (*kalpanā*), when a recollection arises from its latent impression (*saṃskāra*), the comprehension of the sentence-meaning occurs from the final word. This is incorrect, because it is denied that a word can operate by pausing; having once produced a cognition of its own object, the word does not produce it again.

Others, however, maintain that even at the time of uttering the subsequent words, the first word—namely the *pratijñā* (proposition) and so forth—remains in space as the constituent of the subsequent words until the final word is reached; thereafter, by means of these five words, a sentence (*vākya*) as a composite whole is produced in the location of the auditory organ, and from that, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) arises. But this has been refuted by experience, for there is no experience of each preceding word at the time of each succeeding word, nor is there experience of all of them at the time of the sentence.

Others, however, maintain that there is the cognition of the first word, by which a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is produced; then there is the cognition of the second word, by which another impression is produced through the previous one, and so on until the cognition of the final word. Thereafter, upon the manifestation of the preceding impressions, a memory arises whose object is the four words; and the final word, as qualified by that [memory], constitutes the sentence. Nor is there any contradiction with experience here, because only the instrumental aspect [of the process] has been described.

Others, considering that recollection is not incompatible with direct experience, resort to the following conceptual construction (*kalpanā*): from the cognition of the first word arises the recollection of the linguistic convention (*saṅketa*); simultaneously, the comprehension of the word-meaning begins to arise; then follows the arising of the cognition of the [first] word-meaning, the state of the previous word-cognition being about to perish, and the state of the second word-cognition being about to arise. Then follows the arising of the second word-cognition, the state of the cognition of the word-meaning being about to perish, the destruction of the [previous] word-cognition, and the state of the recollection of the convention being about to arise. In this sequence, when the cognition of the final word occurs, there is the comprehension of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). In this process, there is no need for the recollection of the preceding words and their meanings, because their function has already been fulfilled by the word-cognition itself while it is in its state of perishing. For the cognition of the second word arises as colored (*anurakta*) by the first word, the third word is colored by that [second], and so on, until the final word is colored by all the preceding words; thus, the final word is the "sentence" (*vākya*).

This is incorrect, because the coloring by the preceding word does not appear in the final word. For instance, while the cognition "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) is indeed colored by the staff, the cognition of the second and subsequent words is not similarly colored by the preceding word. Furthermore, this restriction—that the utterance of the second and subsequent words must occur immediately after the preceding word—is not possible, since we observe the comprehension of meaning even when there is an interval of some time between their utterances; therefore, the previous hypothesis alone is logical.

Now, let it be granted that there is such a conceptualization of a sentence; however, its status as a denoter [of meaning] is denied because of the absence of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Rather, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning arises from the word-meanings. For where the word-meanings are established even by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the comprehension of the sentence-meaning is observed even without the sentence. As it is said: "For one who sees a form with the eye, hears the sound of neighing, and hears the sound of the hoof-beats, the cognition arises: 'A white horse is running. (Ślokavārttika, p. 94)

And likewise, having perceived a white form from afar with the eye, or through the sound of neighing, one infers the universal *aśvatva* (horseness); and by perceiving the sound of the hoof-strike, one understands the action of running—even without a sentence, one grasps the meaning of a sentence. Furthermore, even when a sentence exists, there is no comprehension of the sentence-meaning if the word-meanings are not understood, as in the case of a sentence composed by poets whose word-meanings are unfamiliar. Therefore, it is the word-meanings already expressed that bring about the understanding of the sentence-meaning by means of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), compatibility (*yogyatā*), and proximity (*sannidhi*).

This is not tenable, because it would entail the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) of verbal testimony. Thus, a word (*pada*) in its form lacks authority because it is merely repetitive (*anuvādaka*). As it has been said: "A word does not differ from a mere reminder (*smāraka*), for there is no additional [content] [in it]; and whatever additional [content] there might be, that is not within the scope of the word" (*Ślokavārttika*, p. 412).

If a sentence, even through a traditional succession (*pāramparyeṇa*), is not expressive, how could verbal testimony (*śabda*) be a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? If it is argued that verbal testimony is a means of valid knowledge through a traditional succession because the word-meanings denoted by the words are themselves the indicators [of the sentence meaning], then—since the sound perceived by the ear functions toward the determination of the meaning—it would follow that perception (*pratyakṣa*) also possesses the status of a means of valid knowledge regarding the subject matter of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) through such a traditional succession. How, then, can it be said that "the Vedic injunction alone is the means of valid knowledge for *dharma*"? There is no contradiction in the restriction "the Vedic injunction is indeed a means of valid knowledge. Furthermore, if one does not admit that a sentence determines its own meaning, then since no other means of valid knowledge is possible, one must consider whether word-meanings are included within perception and the other means of knowledge.

In this regard, it cannot be included within perception (*pratyakṣa*), because no operation [of the mind] is perceived alongside the contact between the sense faculty and its object. It cannot be included within inference (*anumāna*), because the relation of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is untenable. It cannot be included within presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), because there is no possible object that would otherwise remain unaccounted for. Furthermore, comparison (*upamāna*) and non-existence (*abhāva*) have strictly restricted domains. Since no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is admitted, this [claim of the mind as a separate means of knowledge] is incorrect.

Nor do words fulfill their purpose merely through the cognition of their own individual meanings, because—according to the reasoning already stated—they also function toward the cognition of the sentence-meaning. Furthermore, a "cessation-and-then-renewal" (viramya-vyāpāra) of activity is prohibited; that is, it is denied that a word, having conveyed one meaning, should convey that same meaning again.

As for the claim that the meaning of a sentence is understood even without the sentence itself, that arises from a lack of understanding. For the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence is produced by the sentence itself; it is like the cognitions "a white horse is running," which are brought about through perception and inference. Furthermore, as for the claim that the meaning of a sentence is understood by means of the sentence even when the meanings of the individual words are not apprehended, that is incorrect. Since the final word—assisted by the recollection of the preceding word-meanings—constitutes the sentence, it necessarily conveys the meaning; thus, there is no deviation [from the rule].

The theory of the denotation of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*), however, does not apply to all words; for if the meaning of a word were denoted as already related to the action and its factors by a single word alone, it would follow that the utterance of the remaining words would be useless. Now, if it is argued that only the final word denotes the related meaning, then if that word also did not depend on the preceding words, its utterance would likewise be useless. But if it does depend on them, there is no difference from our own established doctrine. {The Enumeration of the Members and the Difference from the Proposition}

“The members (*avayava*), moreover, are the proposition (*pratijñā*), the application (*apadeśa*), the illustration (*nidarśana*), the connection (*anusandhāna*), and the conclusion (*pratyāmnāya*). Among these, the proposition (*pratijñā*) is the enunciation of the object of inference (*anumeya*) that is not contradicted [by other means of knowledge]. The proposition is merely the enunciation intended to bring the subject (*dharmin*), as qualified by the property (*dharma*) one wishes to demonstrate, within the scope of the application. For example: ‘Air is a substance. <PDhS>

“By the inclusion of the term ‘non-contradictory’ (*avirodhi*), those subject-predicates (*uddeśa*) that contradict perception, inference, accepted scripture, one’s own treatise, or one’s own words are excluded. For example: ‘Fire is not hot’ contradicts perception; ‘Space is dense’ contradicts inference; ‘Wine may be drunk by a Brāhmaṇa’ contradicts scripture; for a Vaiśeṣika who asserts ‘the effect exists [prior to its production]’ (*satkārya*), it contradicts his own treatise; and ‘A word does not convey meaning’ contradicts one’s own words. <PDhS>

What, then, are its members? He states: "The proposition (*pratijñā*), the indicative statement (*apadeśa*), the illustration (*nidarśana*), the application (*anusandhāna*), and the conclusion (*pratyāmnāya*)," because these are parts of the [inferential] sentence. They are not, however, the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) and so forth accepted by others, because those do not have the nature of speech.

Next, following the sequence of instruction, the definition of the *pratijñā* (proposition), which has reached its proper occasion, is stated: “The *pratijñā* is the mention of the object of inference (*anumeya*) that is not contradicted [by perception and other means of valid cognition]” (*anumeyoddeśo ’virodhī pratijñā*). The *anumeya* (object of inference) is the subject (*dharmin*) qualified by the property (*dharma*) one intends to prove. For the state of being qualified by a property exists in all things in relation to properties such as existence; therefore, the term “intended to be proven” (*pratipipādayiṣita*) is included. That subject (*dharmin*) qualified by whichever property is desired to be proven is the *pakṣa* (locus). The mere mention of that [subject], which is not contradicted by perception and so forth, and which expresses a matter not yet ascertained by others, is the *pratijñā*. The statement of the purpose is the presentation of the aim of this [definition]: the purpose is the bringing of the subject within the scope of the reason (*hetu*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: the *pratijñā* is distinct from the other [members of the syllogism], because it is the mention of the object of inference that is not contradicted by perception and so forth; whereas that which is not distinct [from the others] does not possess this quality, just like the example (*udāharaṇa*) and the rest. Alternatively, it should be conventionally designated as the *pratijñā* because it is the mention of the aforementioned object of inference; and that which is not so designated does not possess this quality, just like the reason (*apadeśa*). An example is: “Wind is a substance” (*yathā dravyaṃ vāyuriti*).

But is it not the case that the statement of the thesis (*pratijñā*) is not a member of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*), because even without it, the meaning is understood from the mere statement of the connection? For instance, in the argument: "Whatever is produced is seen to be impermanent, like a pot; and sound is likewise produced," the meaning of the thesis is established by implication alone; thus, its explicit mention is redundant. And here, one must consider what the nature of this "implication" is, since the object of knowledge is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) itself. It is not the nature of perception (*pratyakṣa*), because the object of dispute cannot be determined through the contact of the sense organ with its object. The same applies to verbal testimony (*āgama*). If, on the other hand, this "implication" is simply inference (*anumāna*), then that inference necessarily requires the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth for the comprehension of the object. Consequently, in the absence of the statement of the thesis, there would be no distinction between similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and dissimilar instances (*asapakṣa*), and since the object would not be understood, the [implication] would not be a means of proof. If it is argued that the "implication" of the present inference is some other inference distinct from the one being explicitly stated, we say no; for if that too does not depend upon invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), it lacks probative force, and without the statement of the thesis, its meaning is not understood—thus the previous fault remains attached. Furthermore, at the time of presenting an inference to establish a desired point, we do not observe another inference being employed to establish that very point.

Furthermore, when the pervasion between "being produced" and "impermanence" is stated in a general sense, it cannot be understood from the application of the proof to sound alone that "impermanence is intended for this [sound] specifically," because the statement of the relationship would be identical whether one intends the contradictory or the non-contradictory, which would lead to the undesirable consequence of an inability to discern the specific intent.

Now, regarding the statement of pervasion (*vyāpti*) that "whatever is produced is seen to be eternal," one who speaks thus is a proponent of a contradictory view (*viruddhavādī*), whereas one who states the pervasion as "producedness is pervaded by non-eternality" is a proponent of the truth (*tattvavādī*); such is the determination. This is not so, because it is impossible to establish a pervasion between producedness and eternality. For instance, eternality is not observed in produced things such as jars, nor is producedness observed in eternal things such as space (*ākāśa*). Since this matter is already understood through the defect of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*), how can there be contradiction? Furthermore, when one has proposed the thesis (*pratijñā*) that "sound is eternal" yet asserts a pervasion between producedness and non-eternality, then because he states a pervasion that is the opposite of his intended meaning, the specific determination that "this person is a proponent of a contradictory view" indeed occurs.

[Objection: But surely, even if one intends [the word] to be both eternal and non-eternal, the statement "sound is eternal" is possible; thus, even when there is a formal proposition (*pratijñā*), there would still be no certainty for the proponent and the opponent regarding what is real and what is unreal. [Response: No, because the specific intention is established by the statement itself. Indeed, there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for understanding the intention of speakers apart from their speech. Therefore, by the statement "eternal," it is determined that the intention is indeed [that it is] eternal, since there is no evidence for postulating any other intention. For this very reason, the arbitrators (*prāśnika*) establish the rules for victory and defeat between the proponent and the opponent. Even in cases where they understand otherwise and state the meaning of the context differently due to having diverse intentions, the specific intention must still be inferred solely from the specific nature of the statement, because a different statement does not arise from a different intended meaning. Alternatively, if one were to accept [that intention is not conveyed], then even from a statement about a relation (*sambandha*), there would be no certainty at all—whether the statement of the relation between "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "non-eternality" (*anityatva*) is made with the intention of [proving] eternality, or with the intention of [proving] non-eternality.

Now, if it is argued that because the determination of the relationship between a reason and its absence depends upon a real connection, there is indeed a connection between "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*) even when intended in a contrary way, and therefore [the reason] possesses the capacity to indicate [the probandum]; then, one who demonstrates such a connection even with the intention of [proving] permanence would be a speaker of truth, since there is no other way to demonstrate the connection. Likewise, without the statement of the thesis (*pratijñā*), for specific persons who are doubtful, mistaken, or unlearned regarding specific objects of knowledge, there would be no comprehension of their expectation; thus, for a proponent who proceeds merely to communicate a general object of knowledge to any person at large, he would be a speaker like a madman.

Now, if it is argued that from the dispute (*vivāda*) there arises the understanding that a particular person requires a particular object of knowledge (*prameya-viśeṣa*), then the thesis (*pratijñā*) has indeed been admitted, because a dispute is of that very nature. For a dispute is a thesis that depends upon another counter-thesis; however, when accompanied by a proof (*sādhana*), it is called a thesis. Nor can the aforementioned understanding arise from scripture alone, because at the time of presenting an inference, scripture lacks authority; or, if it were authoritative, what would be the use of an inference? Therefore, one who desires inference for the sake of others must necessarily state the thesis. And as for this [which follows]:
The capacity for the comprehension of an object from another object resides in the statements of the thesis and the reason.

"It is said: 'Therefore, there is no establishment of proof for those two [the thesis and the reason] from their own side with respect to the object' (PV 4.15). In this regard, the capacity of the object to convey the object is not denied. However, the mere statements of the thesis and the reason lack the capacity to determine the object. Yet, when other members [of the syllogism] are present, their capacity is indeed admitted by way of establishing their own respective objects. Otherwise, if even the statement of the reason lacked capacity, inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) would simply not function."

Now, he says that the statement of the reason (*hetuvacana*), although itself incapable [of proving the thesis], is nevertheless employed for the sake of the opponent's understanding because it indicates a capable reason; the proposition (*pratijñā*), however, is not like this:
"The statement of the thesis (*pakṣokti*) is not even indirectly sufficient [to prove the conclusion], because it merely expresses what is to be proven (*sādhya*);
whereas the statement of the reason, though itself incapable, indicates that which is capable. (PV 4.17)

In that regard, the statement of the thesis (*pakṣokti*)—the utterance of the proposition—is not sufficient even indirectly [to establish the object], and thus it is not a member of the proof (*asādhanāṅga*). To state the probandum (*sādhya*) when the probandum is yet to be established is indeed uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*), because it is unestablished (*aprasiddhi*) both in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instance (*asapakṣa*). Likewise, since the statement of the thesis is synonymous with the statement of the probandum, it would be non-distinct from the probandum itself. If, on the other hand, it is argued that the probandum is not stated because it is useless for the proof, that too is unproven (*asiddha*), because [the thesis] establishes the probandum when accompanied by the other members [of the syllogism]. Conversely, [if one claims it is useless], that reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because even the mere statement of the reason (*hetu*) is not a prover [without the thesis]. Furthermore, for one who asserts that the statement of the thesis is not a member of the proof, there is a contradiction (*vyāghāta*), for by that very assertion, the thesis has already been accepted.

Now, if it is argued that the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is not employed for one's own understanding because it is not perceived therein, then likewise, the statement of the reason (*hetu*) should also not be employed, as it too is not observed [in one's own understanding]. If, on the other hand, the statement of the reason is appropriate because the meaning of the reason is perceived, then the statement of the proposition must also be necessary because the meaning of the proposition is perceived. Just as the meaning of the reason is the cause for the understanding of the probandum (*sādhya*), so too is the meaning of the proposition the object (*karman*); since there is no difference between the two in their status as causes, there is no justification for not stating the thesis (*pakṣa*). Furthermore, since we observe that the operation of instruments (*karaṇa*) occurs only when the object has been presented, the statement of the proposition must necessarily be made to present that object. Enough of this elaboration.

"By the inclusion of the term 'non-contradictory' (avirodhi), those subject-matters of inference that contradict perception, inference, accepted treatises, or one's own words are excluded," thus [the author] shows what is to be excluded. For that subject-matter of inference which is not contradicted by perception and so forth is the thesis (pratijñā).

Others, however, provide this explanation: "The thesis (*pratijñā*) is the statement of that which is to be inferred (*anumeya*), provided it is not contradicted by perception and other means of valid cognition. Although there is nothing to be excluded [from the definition] because the object of inference—the probandum (*sādhya*)—cannot possibly be in conflict with perception and so forth precisely because it is fit to be proven, nevertheless, the term "not contradicted by perception and so forth" is used to describe its essential nature in response to the inquiry, "Of what kind is the probandum? This is similar to how the term "contact between sense-organ and object" is used even when the specific object is already understood through the word "perception" alone. But that is incorrect, because the term "non-contradiction" stands in grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the term "statement" (*uddeśa*), and because there is no contradiction between an action (*karman*) and its instrument (*karaṇa*). As the venerable Uddyotakara has stated: "An action is such as it is perceived; it remains such even when it is not being perceived. Since the thesis is indeed an instrument, a contradiction in that context is logical.

Among these, that which contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣavirodhin*) is, for example: "Fire is not hot. This is because heat is manifested by the tactile sense-organ (*tvagindriya*). "The sky is solid" (*ghanam ambaram*) contradicts inference (*anumānavirodhin*), because it is established through inference alone that space (*ākāśa*) is formless and all-pervading. To say it is "solid" (*ghana*)—meaning having dense constituent parts—is indeed a contradiction; for if it were solid, it would follow that people like us could not move through it. That which contradicts an accepted treatise (*abhyupagataśāstravirodhin*) is, for example, when a Vaiśeṣika says: "Every effect exists prior to its production. For in the Vaiśeṣika treatise, it is well-established that "what was non-existent is produced. "Speech does not convey meaning" (*na śabdo ’rthapratyāyakaḥ*) contradicts one's own words (*svavacanavirodhin*); for if speech does not convey meaning, how is it not contradictory to utter speech for the purpose of making that very meaning known?

Now, since there are only three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how can there be such a multiplicity of contradictions? It is in consideration of worldly convention. Although these distinctions belong to what is contradicted by scripture (*āgama*) and what is contradicted by perception (*pratyakṣa*), nevertheless, because people employ designations such as "contradicted by one's own words" (*svavacanaviruddha*) and "contradicted by one's own treatise" (*svaśāstraviruddha*), they are described in that very way. As for inference (*anumāna*), although it is impossible for one inference to be contradicted by another inference, this designation—"the proposition (*pratijñā*) is sublated by inference"—is used because of the superior force of one's own inference. [This concludes] the dissimilarity of the reason (*hetuvaidharmya*).

“‘The indicator’ (liṅga) is the ‘statement of the reason’ (apadeśa). That which is concomitant with the object to be inferred, which is established by its general presence in things of the same class, and which is entirely absent in everything that is not that [class]—that is said to be the indicator. The statement of that is the ‘statement of the reason. For example: ‘because it possesses action and because it possesses qualities. And thus, that [property] exists in the object to be inferred and in all things of the same class; however, action exists in some but not in all [of those], while possession of qualities exists in all of them. Both of these are entirely absent in what is not a substance. Therefore, it is established that the statement of that is the ‘statement of the reason. <PDhS>

Immediately after the thesis (*pratijñā*), he states the definition of the logical mark (*hetu*): "The statement of the mark (*liṅga*) is the indicator (*apadeśa*). Since words have their meaning as their defining characteristic, this is an expression of the definition of the indicator by way of restating the definition of the mark. "That which is concomitant with the object of inference (*anumeya*), which is universally established in all cases of its similar class (*sapakṣa*) in a general sense"—such a property (*dharma*) existing in the subject (*pakṣa*) is established in its similar class, but not as a specific [property], because properties belonging to one thing do not reside in another. The phrase "and in all cases" shows the distinction between the pervading (*vyāpaka*) and the non-pervading (*avyāpaka*). "And in that which is contrary to it"—meaning in every instance of the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*)—it simply does not exist; this shows the absolute exclusion from the dissimilar class. This also excludes the "neutralized" (*prakaraṇasama*) and the "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*) reasons, as explained previously. Thus, "the mark has been stated" is a restatement of the definition. The word expressing that [mark]—a statement ending in the third or fifth case—is the indicator (*apadeśa*). And so: "This [subject] is distinct from others, because it possesses the statement of the mark as described"; whereas that which is not distinct does not possess such a statement, just like the thesis and other members of the syllogism.

In order to demonstrate the nature of that [probans] as both pervading and non-pervading, two examples are given: “as, for instance, because of possessing action (*kriyāvattva*) and because of possessing quality (*guṇavattva*). By the word “and” (*ca*), he shows another mode: namely, by way of possessing action and by way of possessing quality. This restatement is intended to show the connection with their respective definitions. Thus, that possession of action and possession of quality exists in the inferable subject (*pakṣa*); and it exists in all members of the similar class (*sapakṣa*)—possession of quality in all of them, and possession of action in some of them. Furthermore, “both of these do not exist at all in non-substances (*adravya*),” such as *sattā* (existence) and so forth. Therefore, it is established that the statement of that possession of quality and possession of action, as previously described, is the "indication" (*apadeśa*).
An Examination of Fallacious Reasons (*Hetvābhāsa*)

“By this, it is stated that statements which are unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), doubtful (*sandigdha*), or non-ascertained (*anadhyavasita*) are not valid reasons (*anapadeśa*). Among these, the unestablished is of four kinds: unestablished for both, unestablished for one or the other, unestablished in its existence, and unestablished in respect to the object of inference (*anumeya*). Among these, ‘unestablished for both’ is that which is unestablished for both the proponent and the opponent, as in: ‘Sound is impermanent because it possesses parts. ‘Unestablished for one or the other’ is, for example: ‘Sound is impermanent because it is a product. ‘Unestablished in its existence’ is, for example, when vapor is put forward as smoke in order to establish fire by means of smoke; here, the vapor is unestablished as being smoke. ‘Unestablished in respect to the object of inference’ is, for example: ‘Darkness is an earthy substance because it possesses black color.’”

“By this,” it is understood that fallacious reasons (*apadeśābhāsa*) are excluded by implication; thus, they are characterized for the purpose of avoiding them in one’s own statements and for exposing them in the statements of others. Herein is the general definition: those things which appear like reasons (*apadeśa*) to a correct cognition (*samyagmati*) are fallacious reasons. Since even a non-reason (*ahetu*) appears as a reason to a distorted intellect, the phrase “to a correct cognition” is included. On this view, one must consider how a reason unestablished for either party (*anyatarāsiddha*) appears as a reason to a correct cognition. For, since it possesses the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth, it appears as a reason; thus, its definition as a “fallacious reason” (*hetvābhāsa*) is established because it resembles a reason. However, in the case of one for whom it is actually a reason, effort must be made to establish its status as a reason by demonstrating its possession of the property of being a characteristic of the subject and so forth, because the comprehension of that [status] is the cause for the comprehension of the object [to be proven]. Therefore, although a reason unestablished for either party is in fact a reason according to the nature of reality, it nevertheless produces the cognition of being unestablished because it is not recognized by the opponent as a characteristic of the subject; yet once it is recognized through valid means (*pramāṇa*) as a characteristic of the subject, the probandum is established, and thus it is indeed a reason.

Others, however, maintain that fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are those that possess a common characteristic with valid reasons because they do not conform to at least one of the required forms, such as being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*).

Now, he asks: "To how many, moreover, does this lack of being a valid indicator (*anapadeśatva*) apply? He replies: "The lack of being a valid indicator has been stated for [the four types of fallacious reasons: the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), the doubtful (*sandigdha*), and the non-conclusive (*anadhyavasita*). Regarding this, the classification is given as: "Therein, the unestablished is of four kinds. And the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)—namely, "subsisting in the subject (*pakṣa*) that is under consideration"—is obtained by implication. For subsistence in the subject under consideration belongs to the entire range of fallacies, such as those with unestablished qualifiers; thus, this is a general definition that pervades the subject (*pakṣavyāpin*). Nor is it the case that non-subsistence in the subject would be its [general] definition, because that is impossible in the various sub-types such as those with ineffective qualifiers (*asamarthaviśeṣaṇa*).

In what form is it fourfold? He says: "The unestablished for both, the unestablished for one or the other, the unestablished in its existence, and the unestablished in the object of inference. Among these, "the unestablished for both" refers to when it is unestablished for both the proponent and the opponent, as in: "Sound is impermanent because it possesses parts. For the possession of parts is not established for either the proponents of permanence or impermanence regarding sound. "The unestablished for one or the other" is, for example: "Sound is impermanent because it is a product. For a Mīmāṃsaka who perceives recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) and so forth, the fact that sound is a product is unestablished until it is determined through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by way of refuting one of the two positions. Once the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is ascertained, the probandum is indeed understood from that. "The unestablished in its existence" is, for example: "In the cognition of fire by means of the presence of smoke. For one who perceives vapor and the like without determining them as smoke, when the cognition of fire is to be effected, there is the "unestablished in its existence" because the state of being smoke is not certain. "The unestablished in the object of inference" is, for example: "Darkness is a substance made of earth, because it possesses a black color."

Since *tamas* as accepted by the Sāṃkhyas is not established [for the opponent], this [reason] is unestablished in its substratum (*āśrayāsiddha*), but not with respect to *tamas* in the sense of being an absence (*abhāva*). For that [latter *tamas*] is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); thus, when it is made the subject (*pakṣa*), its having the nature of black color is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*), but not unestablished in its substratum.

[Objection: But if this is so, is this classification not improper because it fails to include the various types of unestablished reasons (*asiddha*) such as those with unestablished qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇāsiddha*)? [Reply: No, for they are included within either the "unestablished for both" or the "unestablished for one of the two. Thus, an example of an unestablished qualifier for both parties is: "Sound is eternal, because while being inexpressible, it is perceptible by the external senses; or, while being perceptible by the external senses, it is inexpressible. An example of an unestablished qualifier for one of the two is: "Sound is eternal, because while being produced, it is incorporeal. In the same way, other cases of unestablishedness should be inferred according to the specific intention of the person involved. An example of an unestablished qualifier due to its incapacity (*asamarthaviśeṣaṇāsiddha*) is: "Sound is eternal, because while being knowable (*prameya*), it is produced. By the reverse, there is an unestablished qualifier due to its incapacity (*asamarthaviśeṣyāsiddha*). An example of an unestablished qualifier due to a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇaviśeṣaṇāsiddha*) is: "Sound is eternal, because while being visible (*cākṣuṣa*), it is produced. By the reverse, there is an unestablished qualifier due to a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇaviśeṣyāsiddha*). An example of an unestablished qualifier due to contradiction (*viruddhaviśeṣaṇāsiddha*) is: "Sound is non-eternal, because while being an effect (*kārya*), it is incorporeal. An example of an unestablished qualifier due to being established otherwise (*anyathāsiddhaviśeṣaṇāsiddha*) is: "Sound is eternal, because while being repeatedly practiced (*abhyasyamāna*), it is incorporeal."

[Objection: Even so, just as these [two types] would be included within "unestablished for both" (*ubhayāsiddha*) or "unestablished for one of the two" (*anyatarāsiddha*), they would likewise be included within "unestablished regarding its existence" (*tadbhāvāsiddha*) and "unestablished regarding the object of inference" (*anumeyāsiddha*); how then can there be a fourfold classification? [Response: With respect to their internal subdivisions, "unestablished regarding its existence" is distinguished from "unestablished for both" and "unestablished for one of the two," because the present context concerns inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*). Likewise, "unestablished regarding the object of inference" is also distinguished. Thus, there is a fourfold classification.

Others, however, consider the "unestablished for both" (ubhayāsiddha) to be that case where both the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) are unestablished; they regard the "unestablished for one of the two" (anyatarāsiddha) as being either unestablished in its qualifier or unestablished in its qualificand. But this is not intended by the author of the Bhāṣya, because the examples are presented from the perspective of the proponent (*vādī*).

Others, however, maintain that for *svārthānumāna* (inference for oneself), the distinction is between the "unestablished due to the absence of its existence" (*tadbhāvāsiddha*) and the "unestablished due to the non-existence of the probandum" (*anumeyāsiddha*), which subsumes all [other] varieties; whereas for *parārthānumāna* (inference for others), it is between the "unestablished for both" (*ubhayāsiddha*) and the "unestablished for either one" (*anyatarāsiddha*). Here, however, the intention is precisely to define the distinction of the latter by means of the former, while its independence is denied. "For that which, although not existing in the subject (*anumeya*), is absent in every instance of what is similar to it and present in what is contrary to it, is the 'contradictory' (*viruddha*) because it proves the opposite, such as: 'Because he has horns, therefore he is a horse. (*PDhS*)

He states the definition of the contradictory (*viruddha*) [reason]: "That which, although not present by pervasion in the *anumeya* (the subject), is absent in all of its similar class (*sapakṣa*), yet exists in that which is contrary to it, the *vipakṣa*—that is contradictory because it proves the opposite, such as: 'Because it has horns, therefore it is a horse. Taking a horned object as the subject (*pakṣa*), for one who seeks to prove "this is a horse" on the grounds of "because it has horns," the reason "having horns" is contradictory, because this [reason] is pervaded only by non-horses. This [first type] exists in a portion of the *vipakṣa*. [The other types are: 1. That which has a present *sapakṣa* and pervades the *vipakṣa*: "Sound is eternal, because it is a product. 2. That which lacks a *sapakṣa* and pervades the *vipakṣa*: "Every product has an omniscient creator, because it is knowable. 3. That which has a present *sapakṣa* and exists in a portion of the *vipakṣa*: "A living body possesses a self, because it is a product. Thus, there are four kinds.

“However, that which exists in the subject (*anumeya*) and is common to both similar and dissimilar classes, yet is itself ‘doubtful’ because it generates doubt—such as: ‘Because it has horns, therefore it is a cow.

Some maintain that this is another type of doubtful reason (*sandigdha*), because when two reasons possessing the aforementioned characteristics but contradicting each other coincide in a single subject, a doubt is observed; for example, regarding the corporeality or incorporeality of the mind (*manas*), [the reasons] being possessed of action and being intangible, respectively.

Surely this [reason] is indeed "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*), like the properties of non-visibility and perceptibility, because it cannot belong to either of the two sides of a composite entity; and therefore, we shall state that it is "inconclusive" (*anadhyavasita*).

[Objection: But surely it is taught in various places in the treatise that seeing two ways [of viewing a matter] is a cause of doubt. [Reply: No; doubt arises from seeing a duality of objects. In the production of doubt, the very sight of a duality of objects is the cause. Furthermore, if those two were of equal strength, they would fail to produce a definitive conclusion due to their mutual contradiction, but they would not be the cause of doubt. Moreover, there is no equality of strength between them, because one of the two—the subject of inference—is sublated by scripture (āgama). This, therefore, is merely a variety of "contradiction" (*viruddha*).

“That which exists in the subject (*anumeya*) and, by way of pervasion (*vyāpti*), exists only in both similar and dissimilar classes—that is, in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*)—is the inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*) characterized by doubt. [The phrase] ‘because it generates doubt’ is a statement of its effect (*kāryopanyāsa*) and not its definition (*lakṣaṇa*), because it would be over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*), as it applies even to the sense organs and so forth. As for the examples: “Because it has horns, therefore it is a cow”—when one takes a horned object as the subject and attempts to prove it is a cow based on the reason “having horns,” this reason is inconclusive because it occurs in all three positions (subject, similar, and dissimilar). This [first type] is that which, while pervading the similar class, occurs in only a portion of the dissimilar class. “Because it has horns, this is not a cow”—this is that which, while occurring in only a portion of the similar class, pervades the dissimilar class. And “Sound is eternal because it is intangible”—this is that which occurs in only a portion of both the similar and the dissimilar classes. Thus, there are four types of inconclusive reasons.

Furthermore, the fourfold classification [of fallacious reasons] would be untenable; moreover, the definition of the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason would be under-extensive (*avyāpaka*), because it would fail to include the non-deviant contradictory (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) and the over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇa*). To refute such an objection, the section beginning with “And when two [reasons] are in one [subject]” (*ekasmiṃśca dvayoḥ*) is introduced. Since no doubt is observed when two reasons residing in different subjects are brought together—such as “Sound is eternal because it is a product” and “Space is eternal because it is not a product”—the phrase “in one subject” (*ekasmin dharmiṇi*) is used. Even so, there is still no doubt when two [reasons] are brought together in a single subject, as in “Sound is non-eternal because it is a product” and “It is eternal because it is an incorporeal non-product”; for that purpose, the phrase “of those having the stated characteristics” (*yathoktalakṣaṇayoḥ*) is added.

Nevertheless, even for two such [reasons] that establish non-contradictory meanings, there is no status as a cause of doubt, as in: "Sound is eternal because it is a product" and "Sound is dependent because it is a quality. Therefore, some maintain that this is another type of "doubtful" (*saṃdigdha*) inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*), because doubt is observed when there is a conjunction of two "contradictory" reasons—that is, reasons that establish contradictory meanings. An example is: "As in the case of the possession of motion and the lack of tangibility regarding the mind with respect to its being corporeal or incorporeal. One [argument] is: "The mind is corporeal because it possesses motion, like an umbrella"; the other is: "The mind is incorporeal because it lacks tangibility, like space. Since both are perceived to possess the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) along with positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), a doubt arises as to whether the mind might be corporeal or whether it might be incorporeal.

That is incorrect, because the employment of both [reasons] simultaneously is impossible. To explain: when one means of proof (*sādhana*) is employed, if it is faultless, the probandum (*sādhya*) is established, making the introduction of another [reason] untenable; if, however, it is faulty, then that very [fault] is what must be pointed out regarding it. Nor is it the case that the defect of two inferences consists solely in their proving mutually contradictory objects, for if the existence of both were established in a single locus by a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it would follow that there is no contradiction. Furthermore, non-deviant inferences necessarily determine the object, since non-deviance is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of such inference; in the opposite case, there is simply deviance. For example, the combined application [of two reasons]: "The mind (*manas*) is corporeal (*mūrta*), because while being intangible (*asparśavat*), it possesses motion (*kriyāvat*); and it is incorporeal (*amūrta*), because while possessing motion, it is intangible."

Regarding that, he states that it is "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*): "But surely this is indeed uncommon, like [the reason] 'not being perceptible to the eye' and 'being perceptible,' because it cannot belong to either side of two conjoined things. For just as, when establishing the commonality of the property to be proven (*sādhyasāmānya*) among other qualities in the conventional usage of "quality"—apart from qualities such as color which transcend the senses—the reason "necessarily not being perceptible to the eye" while being a substance does not exist in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) such as color, nor in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) such as a jar, and is thus uncommon; likewise, because neither of the two concomitants—possessing action (*kriyāvattva*) and possessing touch (*sparśavattva*)—is possible on either side, they are uncommon due to their impossibility in either the similar or the dissimilar instance. And to show that this [reason] is not unaccounted for, he says: "And therefore we shall call it 'undetermined' (*anadhyavasita*)."

Or, "like being non-visual and being perceptible" is an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). For instance: sound is a quality because, while being a substance, it is invariably perceptible without being visual, like a blind person and so forth. This [reason], which exists in one part of the similar class (*sapakṣa*), is completely excluded from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*); however, this is not the case for "possessing action" and "possessing intangibility," as he states: "because neither is possible for either of the two sides of the composite. (*saṃhatayoranyatarapakṣāsambhavāt*)

Having thus refuted that the contradictory non-deviant (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*) and the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) reasons are causes of doubt, [the opponent] raises an objection regarding a contradiction with the Sūtra, saying: "But surely (*nanu ca*), in various places in the treatise (*śāstra*), the perception of both ways is taught as a cause of doubt" (II.199). In various places in the treatise, in this or that Sūtra, it is said: "And having seen what has been seen, there is doubt" (*dṛṣṭañca dṛṣṭavat*, Vai. Sū.). Having seen the possession of action (*kriyāvattva*) in the mind, and since it exists again as something similar to what has been seen—namely, the lack of touch (*asparśavattva*)—one sees the mind as connected to two contradictory properties and doubts whether the mind is corporeal (*mūrta*) or incorporeal (*amūrta*). Furthermore, it is stated that the uncommon reason is a cause of doubt because of the perception of both ways: "As it is seen and as it is not seen" (*yathā dṛṣṭam ayathādṛṣṭañca*, Vai. Sū.). Because it is perceived in both ways—being seen in the subject (*pakṣa*) and, conversely, not being seen in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) or the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*)—there is doubt due to this dual perception.

Alternatively, [the opponent argues that] doubt arises because the object has been perceived in two ways—as possessing action (*kriyāvattva*) and, conversely, as not possessing touch (*asparśavattva*). Since it was perceived in both ways along with both properties, doubt occurs. To this, the other [the author] says: "This is not correct, because doubt arises from the perception of a dual nature in the object. The explanation of this is: "In the production of doubt, the perception of a dual nature in the object is precisely the cause" (*saṃśayotpattau viṣayadvaitadarśanam eva kāraṇam*). The term *viṣayadvaitadarśana* means the perception of a dual nature in the object; it refers to the commonality (*sāmānyam*) itself. Or, it refers to that commonality which possesses a "duality" (*dvaita*), meaning a twofold nature; the perception of that is what is meant. Because it is the cause for the persistence of contradictory particulars, it is the cause of doubt, and not the conjunction of contradictory causes, nor the uncommon property (*asādhāraṇadharma*). This is because, since the uncommon property is not perceived together with the contradictory particulars, it cannot logically serve as a reminder of them. Furthermore, the property that causes the recollection of contradictory particulars is the cause of doubt, not merely the mutual opposition of two equally powerful factors. Regarding their equal power, it has been stated [by the opponent]: "Because of the mutual opposition of those two," and "due to the obstruction of one by the other, there would be a failure to produce a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*), but not the cause of doubt"—just as a rice seed smeared with oil does not produce its own sprout. However, this was said while accepting [that position]. In reality, "there is no equality of power between the two," because one of them—the mind—is "immaterial" (*amūrta*); thus, "because the subject of inference contradicts scripture" (*anumeyoddeśasyāgamavirodhitvāt*). Accordingly, scripture states: "Because of the absence of that [grossness], the mind is atomic" (*tadabhāvādaṇu manaḥ*, Vaiśeṣika Sūtra). And "possessing form" (*mūrtatva*) is simply the state of being connected with a non-pervasive dimension.

Now, if this statement is not authoritative (*apramāṇa*), then since the existence of the mind (*manas*) is unestablished, the inference would suffer from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*); thus, the definition [of inference] as previously stated would be untenable. Nor can the existence of the mind be established by the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions (*yugapajjñānānutpatti*) if its corporeality (*mūrtatva*) is not admitted; for if it were incorporeal, it would follow that it could simultaneously preside over all the sense organs, resulting in the simultaneous arising of all cognitions. Therefore, because the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) contradicts scripture (*āgama*), the inference of an incorporeal [mind] does not possess the aforementioned characteristics. This, moreover, is a specific type of "contradictory" (*viruddha*) reason, which was already mentioned at the occasion of discussing the proposition. It is called a "subdivision of the contradictory" (*viruddhabheda*) because it differs from the [simple] contradictory; it is the "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), because it is presented immediately after the presentation of a defective subject (*pakṣa*).

The two sūtras should be explained as being intended to demonstrate doubt by virtue of having a single substratum (*dharmin*) as their object. Thus, a specific entity possessing a restricted universal was once seen accompanied by certain particular features; later, seeing something similar to it that is invariably connected with other particulars, one doubts due to the intervention of time and space: "Is this such-and-such, or is it not so? Likewise, even though they share a single substratum: "As previously seen" means a certain entity possessing a universal was seen together with a particular feature; "not as previously seen" means that very same thing is seen devoid of the perceived particular and instead accompanied by another particular. Because it has been seen in both ways—that is, because it was seen with both [features]—when there is a perception of something devoid of both, yet no recollection of those [previous perceptions], doubt arises. For example, having perceived Devadatta with hair and then again without hair, when one perceives him at a later time with his head wrapped up, the doubt arises: "Is he with hair or without hair?"

“And that which, while existing in the subject (*anumeya*), does not exist at all in either the similar (*tatsamānajātīya*) or dissimilar (*asamānajātīya*) instances, is ‘unestablished for one of the two’ (*anyatarāsiddha*). Because it is a cause for non-ascertainment, it is called ‘unascertained’ (*anadhyavasita*). For example: ‘The effect exists because it arises. This is included under the statement: ‘That which is unestablished is not a valid reason (*anapadeśa*). <PDhS>

“But has it not been stated in the treatise that this ‘particularity’ (*viśeṣa*) is a cause of doubt, because a particularity is observed in two ways—among things of the same class and among things belonging to different classes? No, because it serves another purpose. When it was said that ‘doubt does not arise from observing a particularity in sound,’ this meant that audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) cannot be a particularity of any one of the categories such as substance (*dravya*), but rather it becomes a universal (*sāmānya*) itself. Why? Because it was stated that a particularity is observed in two ways for each individual distinction among substances and so forth, both among things of the same class and among things belonging to different classes; it was not stated as a cause of doubt. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of doubt arising regarding all six categories. Therefore, doubt arises solely from the cognition of a universal.”

Regarding the case where [the reason] exists in the entire similar class (*sapakṣa*), he states that the "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) reason is "indeterminate" (*anadhyavasita*): "That which exists in the object of inference (*anumeya*) and in both its similar and dissimilar classes"—that is, in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*). "But that which does not exist at all [in either]" is "unestablished for one of the two parties" (*anyatarāsiddha*) because it is an indeterminate cause, meaning it does not produce certainty. Therefore, because it lacks that causal capacity, it is "indeterminate. An example is: "The effect exists, because it arises. Since the reason—"because it is produced"—does not apply to the entire effect prior to its production, it is indeterminate with respect to space (*ākāśa*) and the like, and also with respect to a donkey's horn and the like. Thus, it is indeterminate.

Nor is this [reason] uncomprised by the Sūtra; thus he says: "This is an unestablished non-indicator (*aprasiddho 'napadeśaḥ*)," because it is included under the statement of the *Vaiśeṣika-sūtra*. This is because it is unestablished in both the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*). Thus, having refuted that the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) reason is a cause of doubt, he raises an objection regarding contradiction with the Sūtra, saying: "But surely this particularity (*viśeṣa*) has been stated in the treatise to be a cause of doubt, [namely] among those of the same kind (*tulyajātīyeṣu*), i.e., among the similar classes (*sapakṣa*); and among those that are different things (*arthāntarabhūteṣu*), i.e., among the dissimilar classes (*vipakṣa*). Because the 'particularity' (*viśeṣa*), which is the uncommon property, is 'seen in both ways' (*ubhayathā dṛṣṭatvāt*), i.e., seen in the similar class and in the dissimilar class. Anticipating the objection that by this the uncommon reason is said to be a cause of doubt, he says: "No," because the Sūtra has another purpose (*anyārthatvāt*). Since [the Sūtra] concerns the connection with existence (*sattā*) and the denotation of the word 'object' (*artha*), the doubt is: "Is sound substance, quality, or action? It is not merely due to the connection with existence; rather, when the author of the Sūtra says "and because of audibility" (*śrāvaṇatvācca*), the opponent asks: "Since the particularity of audibility is perceived, how can there be doubt regarding sound? Anticipating this, he says: "This is not a particularity of any one of the categories such as substance" (*nāyaṃ dravyādīnāmanyatamasya*). Audibility is not a particularity of substance, quality, or action. "Rather, it becomes a universal (*sāmānya*) only. Why? Because when the fact that sound is a quality is to be proven, a particularity such as whiteness is seen in "those of the same kind," i.e., in color-form (*rūpa*) and so on, as concomitant with being a quality. And a particularity such as upward-thrusting (*utkṣepaṇatva*) is seen in "different things," i.e., in upward-thrusting and so on, as concomitant with being an action; likewise, earth-ness and so on are seen in earth and so on as concomitant with being a substance. "Of the distinctions of substance and so on" means of substance, quality, and action. "Each individually" means one by one. "Because the particularity is seen in both ways" means because it is seen as concomitant with being a substance, being a quality, and so on. And since the particularity of audibility is perceived in sound, there certainly arises a recollection concerning its being a substance and so on. Therefore, by the logic already stated, audibility is a cause of doubt as to whether this particularity of audibility belongs to something that is a substance, a quality, or an action; it is not [a cause of doubt] by virtue of being uncommon (*asādhāraṇatvena*). For if doubt were to follow from the perception of an uncommon property even in all six categories, then the perception of particularities such as upward-thrusting would not be established as a cause of doubt through positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*). It is not [a cause of doubt] because of the perception of that [particularity].

Furthermore, for one who perceives a particular that is excluded from everything else, doubt is not logical because of the absence of recollection of contradictory particulars; even if such recollection were present, there would be no cessation [of doubt], due to the absence of a cause for the arising of a definitive cognition. Therefore, the conclusion is: "Doubt arises precisely from the perception of the common feature (*sāmānya*), and not from the observation of a particular."

Alternatively, because the state of possessing specific qualities (*viśeṣavattva*) is perceived in both ways—without being qualified by either the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) or the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*)—and because that [state] is perceived in sound, there is doubt regarding sound. A unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) is not a cause for doubt, because it would follow that doubt would arise regarding all six categories (*padārtha*). The rest is as before.

“An illustration is of two kinds: by similarity (*sādharmya*) and by dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). Among these, the observation of the concomitance of the general property of the mark (*liṅga-sāmānya*) with the general property of the object to be inferred (*anumeya-sāmānya*) is the illustration by similarity. For example: ‘Whatever possesses action is observed to be a substance, as for instance an arrow. And the observation of the absence of the mark in the opposite of the object to be inferred is the illustration by dissimilarity. For example: ‘Whatever is not a substance does not possess action, as for instance existence (*sattā*). <PDhS>

Now, following the statement [of the reason], there is the section beginning with "The example (*nidarśana*) is of two kinds" (*dvividhaṃ nidarśanam*), for the purpose of defining the nature of the example. "Of two kinds" is the classification; "example" is the etymological derivation and the definition. An example (*nidarśana*)—that is, an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*)—is so called because within it the external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*) between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) is demonstrated (*nidarśyate*). Likewise, an example is that by which the pervasion between the probandum and the probans is demonstrated; thus, an example is the statement of an illustration that establishes pervasion. For instance, an example is distinguished from other [members of the syllogism] because it is a statement of an illustration as described; whereas that which is not so distinguished is not like this, such as the thesis (*pratijñā*) and so forth.

In what manner is it twofold? "By way of similarity and by way of dissimilarity. Here, "by the generality of the inferable" means by the generality of the probandum (*sādhya*). "Of the generality of the mark" means of the generality of the probans (*sādhana*). "The observation of its conformity is the example of similarity": the generality of the probans is the pervaded (*vyāpya*), and the generality of the probandum is the pervader (*vyāpaka*). An example is: "Whatever possesses action is observed to be a substance, such as an arrow. For here, in the pervasion by substanceness, the possession of action exists as the probans. "The observation of the absence of the mark in the opposite of the inferable"—that is, in the opposite of the probandum—is the example of dissimilarity. [For instance: "Whatever is not a substance does not possess action; for example, existence (*sattā*). For in the case of existence, there is an exclusion of the possession of action through the exclusion of substanceness; thus, this is an example of dissimilarity.

“By this, fallacious examples (*nidarśanābhāsa*) are excluded. For instance: ‘Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal; whatever is seen to be incorporeal is eternal, such as an atom, such as action, such as a pot, such as darkness, like space. And [the example]: ‘Whatever is a substance is seen to possess motion. These are the fallacious examples by similarity (*sādharmya-nidarśanābhāsa*), which are: unestablished with respect to the mark (*liṅga*), the object to be inferred (*anumeya*), or both; unestablished with respect to their substratum (*āśrayāsiddha*); non-concomitant (*ananugata*); and conversely concomitant (*viparītānugata*). <PDhS>

“Whatever is impermanent is seen to be corporeal, such as action, such as an atom, such as space, such as darkness, like a jar; and whatever is devoid of activity is seen to be non-substantial. Thus, examples based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-nidarśana*) that are fallacious include those where the mark is not excluded from the counter-example, where both [the mark and the property] are not excluded, where the substratum is unestablished, where there is no exclusion, and where there is an inverted exclusion. (PDhS)

“By this [it is meant that] ‘pseudo-examples’ (*nidarśanābhāsāḥ*) are so called because they appear like examples; they possess properties similar to those [of a true example]. They are ‘rejected’ in the sense that they are examined for the purpose of being excluded from one’s own statements and for the purpose of being pointed out [as fallacies] in the statements of others. For instance: ‘Sound is eternal, because it is incorporeal; whatever is seen to be incorporeal is seen to be eternal, just as an atom. Since the property to be proven—incorporeality—is absent in the atom, this is an example lacking the probans (*sādhanavikala*). In the same proof, ‘just as action (*karman*)’ is an example lacking the probandum (*sādhyavikala*), because eternality is absent in action. ‘Just as a pot’ is an example lacking both, because neither eternality nor incorporeality exists in a pot. ‘Just as darkness’ is one where the property is unestablished (*dharmāsiddha*), because darkness as accepted by the Sāṃkhyas is not established [for the opponent]. ‘Like space (*ambaramvat*)’ is a verbal defect of non-concomitance (*ananugata*), even though it serves as the locus for both the probandum and the probans; for without the statement ‘whatever is seen to be incorporeal is seen to be eternal, just as space,’ the concomitance is not perceived.”

Alternatively, even a correct example does not establish the probandum for one who maintains the non-existence of space until it has been established by means of valid cognition; thus, it is called a fallacy (*ābhāsa*).

Others, however, maintain that the presentation of a correct example at the occasion of discussing fallacies is for the purpose of making known the fallacious nature of those [pseudo-examples]. For such is the actual illustration, and its counterfeits are the pseudo-examples (*tadābhāsa*).

“Whatever is a substance is observed to possess action”—this is a reversed positive concomitance (*viparītānugama*). And thus, for one who speaks in this way, substantiality (*dravyatva*) would be the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and possession of action (*kriyāvattva*) would be the pervader (*vyāpaka*); this constitutes a reversed understanding of the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader. But this is not the case, because in space (*ākāśa*) and so forth, substantiality is perceived even in the absence of possession of action. Furthermore, some hold that even in the case of equal pervasion (*samavyāptika*), if the probans (*sādhana*) is designated as the pervader, there would be no cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*); this is the refutation. Others maintain that while a reversed positive concomitance is a fault in the case of unequal pervasion (*viṣamavyāptika*), it is not so in the case of equal pervasion. Here, the concluding statement, the mark (*liṅga*), the object of inference (*anumeya*), both, and the locus (*āśraya*)—these are the "mark, object of inference, both, and locus" (*liṅgānumeyobhayāśraya*). Those fallacious examples (*ābhāsa*) in which these are unestablished (*asiddha*), non-concomitant (*ananugata*), or reversely concomitant (*viparītānugata*) are so described. Thus: "The fallacious examples of similarity (*sādharmyanidarśanābhāsa*) are those in which the mark, the object of inference, both, and the locus are unestablished, non-concomitant, or reversely concomitant."

He demonstrates the fallacies of the negative example (*vaidharmyanidarśanābhāsa*): 1. "Whatever is impermanent is seen to be corporeal, as action (*karman*) is" is an example where the probans (*sādhana*) is not excluded; for action is indeed incorporeal (*amūrtatva*). 2. In that same probandum (*sādhya*), "as an atom (*paramāṇu*)" is a negative example where the probandum is not excluded, because an atom is eternal (*nityatva*). 3. "As space (*ākāśa*)" is one where both are not excluded, because there is no exclusion of either incorporeality or eternity therein. 4. "As darkness (*tamas*)" is one where the property is unestablished (*dharmāsiddha*), because darkness as accepted by the Sāṃkhyas is not established [for the opponent]. 5. "Like a jar" is one where, although both are not excluded, there is no negative concomitance (*avyatireka*); for without the statement "whatever is not eternal is not incorporeal," the negative concomitance is not understood. Or, for one who denies the existence of the jar, that which is not established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not effect the establishment of the probandum; thus it is called a fallacy. The negative concomitance is: "Whatever is inactive is seen to be non-substantial. For the exclusion of the probans must be stated through the exclusion of the probandum, but not the exclusion of the probandum through the exclusion of the probans; because even in the absence of activity, substantiality—the probandum—is not excluded in space and so forth. Indeed, the absence of the probans is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) and the absence of the probandum is the pervaded (*vyāpya*). This is the summary: the mark (*liṅga*), the object to be inferred (*anumeya*), and both; these are the "mark, object to be inferred, and both. Those fallacies in which these are not excluded are the "fallacies of the negative example where the mark, object to be inferred, and both are not excluded. These are: the one where the locus is unestablished (*āśrayāsiddha*), the one where there is no exclusion (*avyāvṛtta*), and the one where there is an inverted exclusion (*viparītavyāvṛtta*). Thus: "The fallacies of the negative example are those where the mark, object to be inferred, and both are not excluded, where the locus is unestablished, where there is no exclusion, and where there is an inverted exclusion."

"In the case of an illustration (*nidarśana*), there is a connection (*anusandhāna*)—that is, a mental application (*anusandhāna*)—of the general mark (*liṅgasāmānya*) previously observed together with the general property to be inferred (*anumeyasāmānya*) back to the object of inference (*anumeya*). That verbal expression by which the general mark, stated merely as a property of the object to be inferred and whose capacity [to prove] was not yet perceived, is connected to the object of inference because it was observed in the illustration together with the general property of the object to be inferred—that is *anusandhāna*. For example: 'And thus, air possesses motion. And having perceived its non-existence in the absence of the object to be inferred, one concludes: 'But air is not devoid of motion.'"

Having thus demonstrated the illustration (*nidarśana*) together with its appearances, he says, “In the illustration, together with the generality of the object of inference,” and so forth, for the purpose of defining the connection (*anusandhāna*). “In the illustration” means in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). “By the generality of the object of inference” means by the generality of the probandum (*sādhya*). “Of the generality of the mark (*liṅga*) seen together [with the probandum] in the illustration”—that is, in the subject (*pakṣa*), which is the object of inference—“the bringing back (*anvānayana*) is the connection (*anusandhāna*)”; for since “bringing” (*ānayana*) could also possibly refer to the presentation of something else, the word “of the mark” is used. Even so, since there is a presentation of the mark in the illustration, the word “object of inference” is used to exclude that. Furthermore, since the statement of the reason (*hetuvacana*) also presents the mark whose inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) has been grasped in the object of inference, the phrase “of the generality of the mark seen together with the generality of the object of inference in the illustration” is employed. Therefore, the connection is distinguished from other [members of the syllogism], because it consists in the bringing back (*anvānayana*) into the object of inference of the mark whose pervasion (*vyāpti*) was grasped in the illustration; whereas that which is not distinguished [from others] is not like this, such as the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth.

He provides an explanation of the summary statement: "The generality of the mark (*liṅgasāmānya*) is expressed as being merely a property of the object of inference (*anumeyadharma*)," [which means] it is not yet effective; he shows this by the use of the word "merely" (*mātra*). "[It is] one whose power has not been perceived" (*anupalabdhaśaktika*); that is to say, its power—namely, its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*)—has not been perceived. Furthermore, "it is seen together with the generality of the property of the object of inference in the example (*nidarśana*). That verbal expression by which [the mark] is subsequently connected (*anu-sandhīyate*) to the object of inference—the subject (*pakṣa*)—by way of being manifested as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharman*), is called "connection" (*anusandhāna*).

That [example] is also of two kinds: by way of similarity (*sādharmya*) and by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). In that regard, having perceived the existence of the general mark (*liṅgasāmānya*) together with the general property to be inferred (*anumeyasāmānya*) in the instance of similarity, one concludes: "And so this air possesses motion. In the instance of dissimilarity, however, having perceived the non-existence of that possession of motion in the absence of the substance-ness (*dravyatva*) of the object to be inferred, one concludes: "But air is not thus devoid of motion. By the negation of motionlessness, one establishes the possession of motion. The separate mention [of the example of dissimilarity] is intended precisely for the purpose of negation.

Is it not the case that the statement of the application (*anusandhāna*) is useless, since the probandum (*sādhya*) is established even without it, provided the reason (*hetu*) has been grasped as possessing pervasion (*vyāpti*)? No; for without this [application], the condition of having a non-sublated subject (*abādhitaviṣayatva*) is not understood. The statement of the reason, however, merely presents the cause (*kāraṇa*); it does not, for one who has grasped the pervasion, establish internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*). Internal pervasion is understood in the following manner: "Just as the hand possesses action because it possesses action—which is invariably concomitant with substantiality (*dravyatva*) and not contradicted by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—so too does air possess action. In the absence of such [internal pervasion], however, there is no capacity to prove [the conclusion], even if external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*) exists. For example, when the impermanence of sound is to be proven, the argument "it is perceptible to the eye while possessing generality" is [an instance of] a reason whose application is mistimed (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*). Therefore, the statement of the application (*upanaya*) here is not invalid due to being devoid of an object.

Furthermore, without the application (*upasaṃhāra*), there would be no comprehension of the specific property to be proven (*sādhyaviśeṣa*) in that very locus (*dharmiviśeṣa*), because the relationship [between the reason and the property] would not have been established therein.
