Moreover, at the time of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), the statement of that [application] must be made, since the meaning of the application is perceived; this is because inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) proceeds in accordance with one's own realization. Nor is this [application] non-existent in one's own realization, because the cognition known as "consideration" (*parāmarśajñāna*) is experienced immediately after the recollection of the relationship of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). And it has already been stated that if this were not admitted, then because the recollection of the relationship would be unrestricted, there could be no realization in a restricted location.

Therefore, since there is an apprehension following the recollection of the inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) for the immediate designation "this is it," there exists a synthetic cognition (*parāmarśajñāna*); hence, the statement concerning the consideration of the effect (*kārya-anusandhāna*) is for the purpose of introducing that [cognition].

“Re-statement (*pratyāmnāya*) is the repetition of the proposition (*pratijñā*) for the purpose of producing certainty in others regarding that which was indicated as the object of inference and remains uncertain; or, it is the repetition of the proposition for the purpose of producing certainty in others—whose capacity has been established by the other members of the argument, such as the reason (*hetu*), etc.—by means of the completed sentence. Therefore, [sound] is indeed a substance.”

Now, for the purpose of demonstrating the nature of the conclusion (*pratyāmnāya*), there is the section beginning with “when [the subject] has been indicated as being inferable” (*anumeyatvenoddiṣṭe*). “As being inferable” (*anumeyatvena*) means by way of its fitness for inference. “And when it has been indicated but not yet ascertained for others” (*uddiṣṭe cāniścite pareṣām*) refers to those who are doubtful, mistaken, or lacking understanding. Furthermore, “the restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) for the sake of bringing about ascertainment is the conclusion” (*niścayāpādanārthaṃ pratijñāyāḥ punarvacanaṃ pratyāmnāyaḥ*).

He provides an explanation of the summary statement (*saṅgraha*). Regarding the phrase "in the mere property (*dharma*) to be inferred" (*anumeye dharmamātre*), this refers to that which is "to be established" (*pratipādyatvena*), that is, as the probandum (*sādhya*). And regarding the phrase "indicated and not yet ascertained by others" (*uddiṣṭe cāniścite ca pareṣām*), by whom? By those "whose capacity has been imparted by the [other] members, such as the reason (*hetu*) and so forth. This means: those whose mark (*liṅga*) has had its power—namely, its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*)—imparted by them; that is, those who have placed their trust in this proof, thinking, "From this means of proof, the establishment of the probandum will arise. The phrase "the restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) for the sake of bringing about ascertainment is the conclusion (*pratyāmnāya*)" is intended to exclude mere tautology. The words "restatement of the proposition" serve to exclude simple repetition, such as "sound is impermanent, sound is impermanent. The words "for the sake of bringing about ascertainment" are added to exclude such repetition. The words "by others" (*pareṣām*) are used because even from this [conclusion], ascertainment arises for one who is not already convinced. Furthermore, since among those [others] some might attain understanding of the matter through the presentation of a single member [of the syllogism] by way of recollecting the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the inclusion of the phrase "by a complete sentence" (*parisamāptena vākyena*) is made. This refers to that member by whose presence the sentence is completed. Thus, the conclusion is distinguished from the other members because it possesses the aforementioned definition.

[Objection: But since the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) cannot persist because it is perishable, how can there be a "re-statement" (*punarvacana*) of it? [Response: Because of the utterance of words identical to those [of the original]. Just as, even though an action is momentary, one uses the designation "he dances again" because of the performance of a similar gesture (*abhinaya*) previously, so too, because of the employment of words identical to the proposition, the designation "re-statement" indeed occurs. Since the word "again" (*punaḥ*) is intended to imply a further excellence (*atiśaya*), the re-statement of the proposition—that is, of the subject (*pakṣa*)—is perfectly logical.

However, for those who maintain that the meaning of the *liṅga* (the inferential mark) constitutes the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), the *pratijñā* (thesis) is that by which something is proposed; the *pratyāmnāya* (re-statement) is the re-utterance of that [thesis]. An example is: "Therefore, it is indeed a substance" (*tasmād dravyameva*). By this, the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes its non-substantiality is also demonstrated. Now, the statement of the *pratyāmnāya* is redundant, since the intended meaning is established simply from the expression of the relationship. As it has been said:

“Abandoning the *ḍiṇḍika* passion and closing your eyes, consider for a moment: does the comprehension of the meaning occur by this much alone, or not? If it occurs here, what is the use of this mere string of words? It cannot be said that it does not occur, because it is observed. (*Hetubindu*, Baroda, p. 56) This is not so; for it has already been established that, in the absence of the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*), the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are not established, and thus the expression of the relationship [of the reason] is not a means of proof.

“For if this [word] were absent, the other members—whether taken collectively or individually—would lack the capacity to express that meaning. If it is argued that this is not so because the meaning is already understood [from the context], we say no, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). To explain: after the thesis (*pratijñā*), one need only state the reason (*hetu*); since the learned possess the memory of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the understanding of the meaning will follow. Therefore, the completion of the purpose occurs right here. <PDhS>

“How so? By the statement ‘sound is impermanent,’ sound is described as being qualified merely by an unascertained impermanence. By the statement ‘because it follows immediately upon effort,’ the property that serves as the probans for impermanence is denoted. By the statement ‘here, whatever follows immediately upon effort is seen to be impermanent, as in the case of a jar,’ the mere concomitance of the general property of the probans with the general property of the probandum is stated. By the statement ‘the permanent is seen not to follow immediately upon effort, as in the case of space,’ the absence of the probans together with the absence of the probandum is demonstrated. And thus, since sound is seen to follow immediately upon effort, and sound is not, like space, not following immediately upon effort, the application of the general property of the probans—whose capacity has been observed through positive and negative concomitance—is understood to apply to sound. Therefore, by the conclusion ‘therefore sound is impermanent,’ the completion of the intended meaning—that sound is indeed impermanent—is understood.”

“Therefore, it is established that inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) consists in the communication of an object ascertained by oneself to others by means of a statement consisting of exactly five members.”

Now, one might argue: let the meaning be established by the thesis (*pratijñā*) and the other members alone; what is the use of the conclusion (*nigamana*)? For, since the subject matter is established by the statement of the thesis, and since external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*) is proven by the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*udāharaṇa*), and internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*) is demonstrated by the application (*upanaya*), the intended object is necessarily established. True, this is so. Nevertheless, the conclusion must necessarily be employed to restate the meaning that has already been established by the thesis and the other members. Thus he says: "For in its absence... (*na hyetasmin*). It is not the case that all the preceding members together possess the capacity to express that [final] meaning. When taken individually, they have fulfilled their purpose by establishing their own respective meanings as distinct from one another. Therefore, something else must be stated: namely, that it is the final member, acting as a collaborator with the preceding words—whether taken collectively or brought to mind through memory—that possesses the capacity to communicate the meaning of the entire sentence.

Now, it might be argued that when both internal and external pervasion (*antarvyāpti* and *bahirvyāpti*) are stated for the proof, the specific nature of the probandum (*sādhyaviśeṣa*) is indeed understood; to this he replies: "If it is argued that [the specific probandum] is understood because its meaning is already implied, we say no, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For instance, after the proposition (*pratijñā*), one should state only the reason (*hetu*); since the reason is apprehended by itself for the learned, there will be a recollection of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and from that, comprehension will arise. Thus, the statement of the specific [probandum] would be redundant."

Now, if it is argued that one who intends to communicate to another must do so by means of speech alone, and therefore the remaining [members of the syllogism] must be employed; then, for the sake of communicating the meaning of the sentence, the conclusion (*nigamana*) should also be employed. Furthermore, it is not appropriate to employ [the members] according to the intention of the person being instructed, because such an intention is not directly perceived by those who possess human nature, nor is it established with certainty. For instance, one person may understand the meaning from a single member, another from two, and yet another from three; since the capacities of those to be instructed are thus unsettled, it would be impossible to determine their intentions, and consequently, the employment [of all members] would be unjustified. Therefore, one who intends to communicate to another must demonstrate the means by which they themselves attained understanding; thus, the employment of the five [members] is appropriate. To illustrate: having perceived smoke in a particular location, one recalls the relationship of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), and then reflects, "This place is likewise possessed of smoke. Thereafter, one understands the probandum (*sādhya*), concluding, "Therefore, it possesses fire. Since the meaning of the conclusion is also perceived in this process, its presentation for the purpose of instructing another is indeed appropriate. Thus, the employment of the five [members] must be performed; as the author of the *Bhāṣya* stated: "Therefore, the completion of the matter occurs right here."

Others, however, consider the conclusion (*nigamana*) to be for the purpose of demonstrating internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*). According to them, once the pervasion over the subject (*pakṣavyāpakatva*) has been established through synthesis (*anusandhāna*), the conclusion serves to negate the possibility of the opposite consequence.

When it is demonstrated that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which establishes a contrary object is invalid, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the subject (*pakṣa*) is indeed apprehended. However, where there is no refutation of the opponent's position, the reason (*hetu*) lacks the capacity to prove [the conclusion]. For example: "He is foolish because he is his son, like his other sons who are observed [to be foolish]. Here, since there is no subverting evidence against the son's lack of foolishness, and the absence of any means of valid cognition establishing his wisdom is certain, this proof is established otherwise (*anyathāsiddha*).

If it is argued that it is not logical to demonstrate the invalidity of a contrary means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because there is no contradiction with a means of valid cognition for that which is invariably concomitant (*avinābhūta*), we say no; for without that [contrary cognition], the very existence of invariable concomitance would remain unestablished. To explain: if the validity of the means of valid cognition establishing eternality were maintained, there could be no pervasion (*vyāpti*) of "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) by "non-eternality" in sound. Nor is the establishment of one's own position achieved solely through the refutation of the opponent's position, because they belong to different loci (*vyadhikaraṇatva*) and because it would follow that the reason (*hetu*) itself is redundant. However, when the opponent's position is refuted, that which has been demonstrated as having external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*) and is observed in the subject (*pakṣa*) indeed becomes a proof (*sādhana*); thus, the application of the conclusion (*nigamana*) must be made.

Now, if it is argued that the statement of the thesis (*pratijñā*) itself, when accompanied by the refutation of the opponent’s position, constitutes the proof (*sādhana*), we say no; for that [statement] merely expresses the probandum (*sādhya*). Since the term *sādhya* is formed with a suffix denoting either "that which is worthy" (*arhati*) or "that which is possible" (*śakya*), how could its establishment follow from that very statement? Therefore, one who seeks to establish internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*)—just as external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*) is established—must state an additional member of the syllogism specifically for the purpose of demonstrating that the subject is not contradicted (*abādhitaviṣaya*) and that there is no counter-argument (*asatpratipakṣa*).

Now, one might argue that even for the *prakaraṇasama* (neutralized) and *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (mistimed) reasons, there is the capacity to produce knowledge because external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*) exists, and since they pervade the subject (*pakṣa*), positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are present. This is incorrect; it was stated during the discussion on establishing pervasion that non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) depends upon a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*). Therefore, according to the reasoning already stated, the matter is fully resolved right here.

Thus, although the nature of the individual members has been shown in various contexts, the question “How? is asked here with a view toward understanding their nature collectively. “The statement ‘Sound is impermanent’ expresses sound as characterized merely by an unascertained impermanence”; this is the *pratijñā* (proposition). “The statement ‘Because it follows immediately upon effort’ denotes merely the property that serves as the means of proving impermanence, but not its efficacy [in proving it]”; this is the *hetu* (reason). “In this world, whatever follows immediately upon effort is seen to be impermanent, such as a jar”; by this, the mere concomitance (*anugama*) of the general property of the means of proof with the general property of the probandum is stated; this is the *sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta* (example based on similarity). “An eternal thing is seen to be not following immediately upon effort, such as space”; by this, the absence of the means of proof where the probandum is absent is demonstrated; this is the *vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta* (example based on dissimilarity). “And so, sound follows immediately upon effort”; since it is not the case that it does not follow immediately upon effort, the application of the general property of the means of proof—whose efficacy has been observed through positive and negative concomitance—to sound is understood. “Therefore, sound is impermanent”; by this, the completion of the intended object of proof—that sound is indeed impermanent—is understood; thus, the establishment of the intended meaning occurs. Therefore, it is established that “the communication of one’s own ascertained meaning to others is accomplished solely by means of a statement consisting of five members.”

In this context, it should be understood that when a specific instance of sound is taken as the subject (*pakṣa*), "being produced immediately after an effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) is intended as the probans (*sādhana*). Otherwise, if sound in general were included, the probans would be partially unestablished (*bhāgāsiddha*), for not all sounds are produced immediately after an effort.
[This concludes the section on] the difference from certainty (*nirṇaya-vaidharmya*).

“Ascertainment (*nirṇaya*) is a determinative cognition born from the perception of a specific feature (*viśeṣadarśana*), which is opposed to doubt. This very [ascertainment] is either perception or inference. That which arises from the perception of a specific feature as something opposed to doubt is perceptual ascertainment (*pratyakṣanirṇaya*). For example, when a doubt arises—‘Is this a post or a person?’—due to the recollection of the specific features of both while the specific features are not perceived (following the observation of mere similarity in height between a post and a person), the determinative cognition ‘This is indeed a person’ arising from the perception of specific features such as a head and hands is perceptual ascertainment.”

“When a doubt arises as to whether it is a cow or a gavaya upon seeing only its horns, the definitive cognition that ‘this is indeed a cow’ upon seeing its dewlap is inferential ascertainment (*anumānanirṇaya*). <PDhS>

Now, some maintain that *nirṇaya* (ascertainment) is a distinct category of knowledge (*vidyāntara*). To refute this, the section beginning with "born from the perception of a specific feature" (*viśeṣadarśanajam*) is introduced. Following the discussion of inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), the determination of its inclusion [within the categories of knowledge] is presented here as well, for the purpose of making that inclusion known. The term "ascertainment" (*nirṇaya*) is the mention of the object to be defined (*lakṣya*), while the remainder constitutes the definition (*lakṣaṇa*). For an act of determinative cognition (*avadhāraṇajñāna*) can also be a cognition of error (*viparyayajñāna*), yet it does not arise from the perception of a specific feature. Furthermore, since a cognition of doubt (*saṃśayajñāna*) can also be born from the perception of a specific feature, the inclusion of the term "determination" (*avadhāraṇa*) is necessary.

Even so, if it were stated that "ascertainment (*nirṇaya*) is a determinative cognition born from the perception of a distinguishing feature," there would be no deviation [from the definition], and thus the phrase "contrary to doubt" (*saṃśayavirodhī*) would be redundant? No; for its purpose is to define a specific type of ascertainment. Although the definition "a determinative cognition born from the perception of a distinguishing feature" is a general definition that pervades all forms of ascertainment, the phrase "contrary to doubt" is intended to define that ascertainment which is preceded by doubt. Accordingly, the Naiyāyikas have stated: "Ascertainment is the determination of an object through the consideration of the thesis and the counter-thesis" (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.41). This is the definition of ascertainment preceded by doubt. The word *vimṛśya* means "having performed a deliberation" (*vimarśa*); "through the thesis and the counter-thesis" means through the statements expressing them; and that ascertainment occurs through the means of proof (*sādhana*) and refutation (*dūṣaṇa*).

Now, if doubt is dispelled by the perception of a specific feature (*viśeṣadarśana*) and not by a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*), how can it be said that the latter is opposed to the former? This is stated figuratively, because since the cause of a definitive conclusion is opposed to doubt, the definitive conclusion itself is said to be its opposite.

He states its inclusion [within the means of valid cognition] as follows: "This very [conclusion] is either perception or inference" (*etadeva pratyakṣamanumānaṃ vā*); it is not a separate type of knowledge. For that which is produced by the causal complex of perception is perception, while that which is produced by the causal complex of inference is inference. "That which arises from the perception of a specific feature and is opposed to doubt is a definitive conclusion" (*yad viśeṣadarśanāt saṃśayavirodhyutpadyate sa nirṇayaḥ*)—this is the explanation of what was previously stated.

In this context, when a doubt arises—“Is this a post or a person?”—due to the observation of the mere similarity of height between a post and a person, while their specific features remain unperceived and both sets of specific features are being recollected, the resulting determinate cognition that “this is indeed a person” based on the perception of specific features such as a head and hands is a *pratyakṣanirṇaya* (determinate perception), because it arises from the contact of the sense organ with its object. Similarly, when a doubt arises—“Is this a cow or a gavaya?”—due to the sight of a mere horn even when the body is obstructed, because of seeing a horn characterized by similarity, and when there is the recollection of the relation of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), the resulting determinate cognition that “this is indeed a cow” following the stage of reflective cognition (*parāmarśajñāna*) is an *anumānanirṇaya* (determinate inference).

{The distinction of memory}: “Memory is that which has past objects as its domain; it is caused by desire, recollection, and so forth, and by a specific conjunction of the self and the mind dependent on the perception of a sign, and by a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by cognition characterized by intensity, repetition, or interest; it pertains to objects seen, heard, or experienced, and is the cause of subsequent determination, recollection, desire, and aversion regarding what remains. <PDhS>

Now, for the purpose of defining the cause, effect, object, and essential nature of memory (*smṛti*), there is the section beginning with: “from the dependence on the observation of a mark, desire, recollection, and so forth” (*liṅgadarśanecchānusmaraṇādyapekṣāt*). The phrase “observation of a mark, desire, and recollection” refers to those [factors] as they have been stated; by the word “and so forth” (*ādi*), the inclusion of focused attention (*praṇidhāna*) and other such factors is intended. “Dependent on these” means depending upon them; therefore, [memory arises] from that. The statement “from a specific conjunction of the self and the mind” (*ātmamanasoḥ saṃyogaviśeṣāt*) is the indication of the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). The statement “from a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by intense cognition, repetition, and respect, which depend on the observation of a mark, desire, recollection, and so forth” is the indication of the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). The phrase “regarding objects seen, heard, or experienced” means: “seen” is by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); “heard” is by means of verbal testimony (*śabda*); and “experienced” is by means of inference (*anumāna*).
Others, however, say that "seen" means by the eye, and "experienced" means by the tactile faculty.

In this regard, he shows the indicative mark (*liṅga*): "It is the cause of the subsequent determination (*anuvyavasāya*), recollection (*anusmaraṇa*), desire (*icchā*), and aversion (*dveṣa*) regarding the remainder" (*śeṣa*). The "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is that which is to be inferred from the employed indicative mark; "subsequent determination of the remainder" (*śeṣānuvyavasāya*) is the knowledge of reflective consideration (*parāmarśajñāna*), because by means of it the remainder is subsequently determined. Its cause is the recollection of the relation of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). Likewise, from the recollection of a word comes the recollection of a sentence; from the recollection of pleasure comes desire, and from the recollection of pain comes aversion. The phrase "having a past object" (*atītaviṣayā*) is a statement of its essential nature (*svarūpa*). That which has a past object is thus described.

Is this not indeed improper? Since memory is observed even when the object exists, there is an absence of pervasion (avyāpti); and since inference and other means of knowledge have past objects as their domain, there is over-pervasion (ativyāpti).

Now, if it is argued that only *codanā* (Vedic injunction) reveals objects that are past, future, remote, and so forth, and nothing else such as the sense organs, we say no; for inference (*anumāna*) is also observed to reveal objects that are past and so on. Thus, it is inferred that "there will be rain because of the rising of clouds," and from a specific swelling of a river, it is stated that "there was rain upstream. And in this case, perception must be accepted as the grasper of the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*); otherwise, in the absence of the grasping of pervasion (*vyāpti*), inference itself would not function. Nor can the grasping of invariable concomitance be by means of inference alone, for that would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore, if the grasping of invariable concomitance were by means of a present [perception], how could there be inference of past and future objects? For if the grasping of concomitance were by one thing and the inference were of another, it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, the fact that [inference] has the past as its object must be explained figuratively (*upacāreṇa*): for when the experience regarding an object is past, recollection (*smṛti*) arises therein.

Others, however, hold that when the analysis results in the term *atītaviṣayā*—meaning "that [cognition] whose object is past" (*atīto viṣayo yasyānubhavasyāsau atītaviṣayaḥ*)—the sense is "that [cognition] which has that [past thing] as its object" (*sa viṣayo yasyāḥ sā atītaviṣayā*), and thus, upon reaching this point, one should understand that there is an elision of one of the two words "object" (*viṣaya*), whereby the state of having a past experience as its object is obtained.

Now, why is it not accepted that memory (*smṛti*) arises from an object (*arthaja*)? Because it arises even when the object has perished. Nor is it logical that memory must have as its objective support (*ālambana*) that very object characterized by the place and time at which the original experience (*anubhava-jñāna*) occurred; for at the time of recollection, that object no longer exists and thus lacks the status of being a [present] object. Furthermore, since each of the external sense organs is found to deviate in the production of memory, the operation of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is determined [as the cause]. And since it is impossible for that [internal organ] to operate independently upon an external object, it is logical that memory does not arise from an object. Moreover, if memory were necessarily born of an object, then—given that it possesses qualities such as non-deviation—it would have the nature of valid knowledge (*pramā*); consequently, one would have to say that memory is produced from a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Since no operation of inference (*anumāna*) or other means is perceived in its production, if the internal organ were independent in producing it, memory would possess the status of a valid cognition; and if that were the case, memory would be immediate (*aparokṣa*), which it is not. Therefore, memory is simply without an object (*nirviṣaya*).

{The Distinction from the Knowledge of the Sages} “The intuitive knowledge (*prātibha*) that arises—due to the conjunction of the self and the mind and through a specific merit (*dharma*), in the case of past, future, and present objects beyond the senses such as *dharma* and so forth, whether they are recorded in texts or not—belonging to the sages (*ṛṣi*) who are the authors of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*), is called ‘sagely’ (*ārṣa*). This occurs generally among the divine sages (*devarṣi*), and only occasionally among worldly people; for example, when a young girl says, ‘My brother will come tomorrow, for my heart tells me so. <PDhS>

Now, for the purpose of defining the cause, object, and means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) of *ārṣajñāna* (sage-knowledge), there is the section beginning with “of the authors of the sacred tradition” (*āmnāyavidhātṝṇām*). The *āmnāya* is the Veda, characterized by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*; its authors are the composers, and from those sages arises that which is called “intuitive knowledge” (*prātibhaṃ jñānam*), produced by a specific mental impression (*saṃskāra*) known as intuition (*pratibhā*). It arises “according to the nature of the object” (*yathātmanivedanam*); that is, it arises having as its objective support the very essence or intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of that thing. “That they call *ārṣa*” (*tad ārṣamityācakṣate*). In what objects does it arise? “In the past, future, and present. Of what kind? “In supersensible things such as *dharma* and so forth” (*atīndriyeṣu dharmādiṣu*); by the word “and so forth,” atoms (*paramāṇu*) and other such things are included. “Whether recorded in texts or not recorded” (*granthopanibaddheṣvanupanibaddheṣu ca*): [it arises regarding] things like the Self (*ātman*) which are recorded in texts, and things like atoms which are not recorded, [cognizing] that “this much is *dharma*. For what reason is there a cognition of these things according to their actual state? “From the contact of the self and the mind” (*ātmamanasoḥ saṃyogāt*), and from the “specific quality (*dharma*) acting as a non-inherent cause” (*asamavāyino dharmaviśeṣācca*) as the instrumental cause. “But that [knowledge] occurs only occasionally” (*tattu prastāreṇa*); therefore, among sages, that is *ārṣa*. However, sometimes even ordinary people possess such a form of cognition. What is the proof (*pramāṇa*) for this in our case? He says: “Sometimes even among ordinary people” (*kadācideva laukikānām*), that intuitive knowledge occurs. “For example, a young girl says: ‘My brother will come tomorrow. And that is not born of the senses, because it arises even without the operation of the senses.

Now, even though there is no operation of the external sense organs, this [knowledge] has the status of a result of perception (*pratyakṣa*) due to the operation of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). As for the connection with the sense organ, it is the relation of "qualified and qualifier" (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*) between that which is conjoined [with the sense organ] and its qualifier. For it has been stated by others that knowledge arises by taking as its object the self, a location, or a time as qualified by that [external thing]. But that is incorrect, because [if it were so], its immediacy (*aparokṣatva*) would be untenable. Indeed, the postulation of the operation of the sense organs is made only where there is immediate knowledge; and in this case, that [immediacy] does not exist. Furthermore, it has already been stated that the mind cannot operate independently even toward an external object that serves as a qualifier. Nor is it born of inference, because there is no recollection of the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*), and no experience thereof. Nor is it verbal, since it arises even without words. Therefore, this is the result of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Likewise, when a question is asked, one does not point to perception or other [means of knowledge], but rather says, "My heart tells me."

Now, why is it that the knowledge of the sages (*ārṣajñāna*) is not defined immediately after perception and inference? Because ordinary people such as ourselves do not engage in practical activity (*vyavahāra*) by means of it; for that [knowledge] belongs exclusively to the sages by way of its manifestation, and only occasionally to worldly people. {The refutation of the claim that the vision of the perfected ones (*siddhadarśana*) is a separate branch of knowledge (*vidyāntara*):}

“Vision by the perfected ones (*siddhadarśana*) is not a distinct type of cognition. Why? Because the vision of those who have attained perfection through ointments, foot-unguents, swords, pills, and so forth—vision which consists of seeing visible objects that are subtle, concealed, or distant—is nothing but perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, if it is claimed that the vision of the ripening of merit and demerit (*dharmādharmavipāka*), based on the movement of planets, constellations, and so forth, among beings of the celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial realms, is intended [to be a distinct cognition], that too is merely inference (*anumāna*). Finally, if it is claimed that there is a vision regarding merit and so forth that does not depend on a mark (*liṅga*), even that is included within one of the two: perception or the vision of the seers (*ārṣa*); such is the understanding.”

The vision of perfected beings (*siddhadarśana*) is considered by others to be a distinct type of knowledge (*vidyā*); in order to refute this, he says: “The vision of perfected beings is not a separate kind of knowledge. Following the discussion of *ārṣa*-knowledge, the inclusion of this [vision] is now defined for the purpose of showing its subsumption within *ārṣa*-knowledge as well. That vision which arises for perfected beings is indeed perception (*pratyakṣa*). In regard to what objects? He says: “In regard to subtle, obstructed, and remote objects. Subtle objects are atoms; obstructed objects are the world of serpents (*nāgabhuvana*) and so forth, relative to the senses of people like us; however, there is no obstruction for the senses of perfected beings. Remote objects are Mount Meru and the like; [the vision occurs] in regard to these. Of what kind of perfected beings? To exclude liberated souls (*muktātman*), he says: “of those who are both seen and seers. Furthermore, what is the proof of their existence? He says: “of those who are visible. Sometimes, when free from ointments and such, they are perceived even by direct perception. What, then, is their perfection (*siddhi*)? He says: “of those perfected through ointments, foot-unguents, swords, pills, and so forth. By the word “and so forth,” wish-fulfilling gems (*cintāmaṇi*) and the like are included. And because of the power of ointments and such, the senses of perfected beings illuminate subtle and other types of objects; therefore, “that is indeed perception, not a separate kind of knowledge.”

Now, having observed the movements of the luminaries, one might desire another form of knowledge to know whether good or bad fortune will befall living beings; it is for the purpose of negating that [desire] that [the author states] "of celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial [omens]" (*divyāntarikṣabhaumānām*) and so forth. Celestial (*divya*) refers to things occurring in the sky, such as the falling of meteors; atmospheric (*antarikṣa*) refers to things occurring in the intermediate space, such as the burning of the quarters; terrestrial (*bhauma*) refers to things occurring on the earth, such as earthquakes—[these are] of those [three kinds]. Having perceived the "causes, such as the movements of the planets and constellations" (*grahanakṣatrasañcārādinimittam*), the ripening (*vipāka*) of the merit and demerit of living beings—that is, their capacity to yield results—is seen. [This] is not intended to be another form of knowledge, because "that too is merely inference" (*tadapyanumānameva*), since it is produced by the perception of a mark (*liṅga*), the recollection of its concomitance (*anu-bandha*), and so forth.

Alternatively, even that which is intended as the perception of the ripening of dharma and adharma after observing signs such as the movements of the planets and constellations among celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial beings—gods, siddhas, and humans—is nothing but inference.

Now, if it is intended that there is perception of dharma, adharma, and so forth, independent of inferential marks (*liṅga*), then if that arises as a direct manifestation (*aparokṣa*) from the contact of a sense organ with its object, it is simply perception (*pratyakṣa*). Alternatively, if it arises even without the contact of a sense organ with an object due to a particular merit (*dharma-viśeṣa*), it is nevertheless the "vision of the seers" (*ārṣa*); thus he says, "it is included within one of the two: perception or the vision of the seers. The conclusion, "thus is cognition," is intended to demonstrate the destruction of cognition as accepted by the opponent. [This concludes the section on the dissimilarity of pleasure.]

“Pleasure has the characteristic of favor (*anugraha*). When objects such as garlands—which are desired—are present, pleasure arises from the contact of the self and the mind, depending upon merit (*dharma*) and other factors, following the attainment of the desired object; it is produced by the contact of the sense organs with their objects, and it generates favor, attachment, and clarity of the eyes and other faculties. In the case of past objects, it is born of memory (*smṛti*); in the case of future objects, it is born of conceptualization (*saṅkalpa*). However, that which manifests for the wise even in the absence of the recollection of objects, desire, or conceptualization, has its cause in knowledge, tranquility, contentment, and a specific kind of merit.”

Now, immediately after *buddhi* (intellection), in order to demonstrate the nature of the cause and effect of pleasure (*sukha*), [the author] states: "Pleasure is characterized by favor" (*anugrahalakṣaṇaṃ sukham*), and so forth. "Characterized by favor" means having the nature of favor. It is that which, when produced, causes the self to consider itself as being favored. "When there is the proximity of desired objects such as garlands," etc.: these are garlands and the like, and they are also desired objects; their "proximity" (*sānnidhya*) refers to this. The term "desired" (*abhipreta*) is included because undesirable things, such as passion and the like, do not become causes of pleasure. "The perception of the desired" and "the contact of the sense-organ with its object"—it is stated thus because of these two. By the phrase "depending on merit (*dharma*) and so forth," the inclusion of space (*dik*), time (*kāla*), and other factors is intended. "Depending on those" means depending upon them; therefore, from the contact of the self and the mind—which serves as the non-inherent cause—[and] from the perception of the desired and the contact of the sense-organ with its object, depending on merit and the rest, pleasure arises in the self. "Producing favor, attachment, clarity of the eyes, and so forth" is the definition of its effect. "Favor" (*anugraha*) is the act of favoring, which is the cognition whose object is pleasure; "attachment" (*abhiṣvaṅga*) is clinging; "clarity of the eyes and so forth" (*nayanādiprasāda*) is lucidity. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the lucidity of the face and other features is included. This [pleasure] should be understood as distinct from others because it possesses unique characteristics. Furthermore, it is not the case that everything is suffering (*duḥkha*) in its own nature for one who possesses discernment (*vivekin*), since pleasure, which consists of favor, is also experienced. For this very reason, one should not say that the conventional usage of "pleasure" occurs merely in the absence of suffering, because [pleasure] appears as something produced by distinct causes and differentiated by degrees such as "more intense" and so forth. In the same way, suffering also does not consist of the mere absence of pleasure.

Regarding that which has been stated—that pleasure arises from the contact of the sense organs with their objects when the object is present, whereas it arises through memory and mental construction (*saṅkalpa*) regarding past and future objects—it is said: "In the case of past means of pleasure, [pleasure] is born of memory; in the case of future ones, it is born of mental construction. Thus, that which is to be abandoned is demonstrated.

“As for that which arises in the wise when the recollection of objects, desire, and volition are absent—these being what is meant by the compound ‘recollection-of-objects-desire-and-volition’—that is certainly to be accepted. This is the presentation of the cause: “It has as its causes specific knowledge, tranquility, contentment, and dharma. Knowledge (*vidyā*) is the cognition of reality; therefore, there is happiness for those who possess the knowledge of reality. Likewise, tranquility (*śama*) is the destruction of passion and the like; therefore, there is happiness for those whose minds are peaceful. Contentment (*santoṣa*) is the sense of sufficiency regarding sense-objects; therefore, there is happiness from that. And for some, it arises from a specific merit (*dharma*).

Others, however, maintain that tranquility (*śama*) is produced by knowledge, and from that [comes] happiness; the rest is as before. [The Contrast with Pain: "Pain is characterized by affliction. When there is the presence of undesirable objects such as poison and the like, that which arises—caused by the contact of the self and the mind, depending on demerit (*adharma*) and other factors, and having intolerance, affliction, and dejection as its marks—is pain. In the case of past [objects] such as snakes, tigers, or thieves, it is born of memory; in the case of future [objects], it is born of mental construction (*saṅkalpa*).

For the purpose of defining suffering (*duḥkha*), he says: “its characteristic is affliction” (*upaghātalakṣaṇam*). Suffering is that which has affliction as its essential nature. It is called "affliction" because one is afflicted by it, or because one considers oneself to be afflicted. He states the cause: “when there is the presence of undesirable objects such as poison, etc. (*viṣādyanabhipretaviṣayasānnidhye sati*). These are both "poison, etc. and "undesirable objects"; [the phrase means] when there is the presence of those. Since desirable objects and the like are indeed causes of pleasure, the term "undesirable" (*anabhipreta*) is used. “The perception of the undesired and the contact of the sense-faculties with their objects, depending on demerit (*adharma*), etc. (*aniṣṭopalabdhīndriyārthasannikarṣādadharmādyapekṣāt*). This refers to the perception of the undesired and the contact of the sense-faculties with their objects; from that, depending on demerit and so forth—the word "etc. includes space, time, and other factors—[suffering arises]. Therefore, that which arises inherent in the self (*ātman*) from the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) consisting of the contact between the self and the mind (*ātmamanasoḥ saṃyoga*), following upon the perception of the undesired and the contact of the sense-faculties with their objects depending on demerit and so forth, is suffering. It is to be understood as the instrumental cause of indignation (*amarṣa*), affliction (*upaghāta*), and dejection (*dainya*), and thus the differentiator from other things. The phrase “in past snakes, etc. is for the purpose of defining its effects. Indignation (*amarṣa*) is intolerance; affliction (*upaghāta*) is the cognition that takes suffering as its object. Dejection (*dainya*) is a state of wretchedness produced from suffering. All this is to be understood as the differentiator from other things due to its specific (non-common) nature. “In past [objects] such as snakes, tigers, thieves, etc. refers to the instruments of suffering; “born of memory (*smṛtijam*)” [refers to suffering] regarding those [objects], while “born of mental construction (*saṅkalpajam*)” [refers to suffering] regarding future ones.
The dissimilarity with desire.

“Desire (*icchā*) is the longing for what has not yet been attained, whether for one’s own sake or for the sake of another. It arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending upon pleasure and so forth, or depending upon memory. It is the cause of effort, memory, merit (*dharma*), and demerit (*adharma*). Desire (*kāma*), longing (*abhilāṣa*), passion (*rāga*), intention (*saṅkalpa*), compassion (*kāruṇya*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), hypocrisy (*upadhā*), and disposition (*bhāva*)—these and others are varieties of desire. Sexual desire is *kāma*; the desire for food is *abhilāṣa*; the repeated desire for attachment to sense objects is *rāga*; the desire for action that is not immediately proximate is *saṅkalpa*; the desire to remove the suffering of others without regard for one’s own interest is *kāruṇya*; the desire to renounce sense objects due to perceiving their defects is *vairāgya*; the desire to deceive others is *upadhā*; and a desire hidden within is *bhāva*. Varieties of desire arise from the differences in actions, such as the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), the desire to take (*jihīrṣā*), and so forth.”

In order to define the nature of desire (*icchā*) as both cause and effect, [the author states] "for one's own sake or for the sake of another," and so forth. Desire is defined as having the form of a longing for an object not yet attained. The statement "for one's own sake or for the sake of another" is a description of its divisions intended to dispel misconceptions; it is not merely for one's own sake, but also for the sake of another. He states the cause of its arising: "And that [arises] from the contact of the self and the mind. It arises from this non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). From what does it depend? "[It depends] upon pleasure and so forth, or upon memory. The definition of its effects is given by: "It is the cause of effort, memory, merit (*dharma*), and demerit (*adharma*). A pure intention is the cause of merit, while a corrupt intention is the cause of demerit.

To answer the objection—"There are other qualities such as desire (*kāma*) and so forth; why are they not included [in this list]?"—the author defines their inclusion: "Desire (*kāma*), longing (*abhilāṣa*), passion (*rāga*), intention (*saṅkalpa*), compassion (*kāruṇya*), detachment (*vairāgya*), hypocrisy (*upadhā*), disposition (*bhāva*), and so on, are varieties of will (*icchā*); they are its specific instances. Sexual desire is *kāma*, because one is designated as "desirous" (*kāmī*) when that exists, and not merely by the presence of will in general. Longing (*abhilāṣa*) is the will characterized by the desire for consumption; here, "consumption" is intended in a general sense to mean the taking up of any object. Others say that longing is the will directed toward that [consumption]. Passion (*rāga*) is the will to repeatedly delight in objects, for it is by the presence of that [passion] that one is designated as "passionate" (*rāgī*). Intention (*saṅkalpa*) is the will toward an action that is not yet imminent—that is, a future action. Compassion (*kāruṇya*) is the will to eliminate the suffering of others, without regard for one's own interest; it is the will for their destruction. Detachment (*vairāgya*) is the will to renounce objects due to perceiving their defects, since the conventional usage of "detached" occurs when that [detachment] exists. Hypocrisy (*upadhā*) is the will to deceive others. Disposition (*bhāva*) is a will hidden within; although every will is internal and not external, nevertheless, because this [disposition] is somehow understood in relation to something else, it is called "hidden within. Varieties of will arise from differences in actions, such as the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) and the desire to take away (*jihīrṣā*); the desire to do is *cikīrṣā*, and the desire to take is *jihīrṣā*.

{The dissimilarity of hatred} (“Hatred has the nature of burning. That in which one feels as if one’s self were on fire is hatred. It arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending upon pain or depending upon memory. It is the cause of effort, memory, merit, and demerit. Malice, anger, resentment, intolerance, and indignation are the varieties of hatred. <PDhS>

To define hatred (*dveṣa*), he says: “[It is] of the nature of burning. Hatred has the essential character of burning. “That in which existing, one considers oneself as if set ablaze—that is hatred,” this is the explanation of the preceding [definition]. “And that arises in the self from the conjunction of the self and the mind,” due to the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), “depending on pain or depending on memory”; thus it is produced in the self. “It is the cause of effort, memory, merit (*dharma*), and demerit (*adharma*)”; this is the definition of its effects. For just as demerit certainly accrues to one who engages in killing and so forth out of hatred, likewise merit accrues to one who engages in sacrifice and so forth. To define its divisions, he says: “Malice, anger, resentment, intolerance, and indignation are the varieties of hatred”; these are its specific types. Malice (*droha*) is injury toward one’s master. Anger (*krodha*), however, is that upon arising, a transformation of the body, senses, and limbs occurs. Resentment (*manyu*) is that which produces a transformation of the throat and eyes in one who has been wronged but is unable to retaliate. Intolerance (*akṣamā*) is the lack of forbearance. Indignation (*amarṣa*) is the failure to retaliate against an injurer even after the intervention of years and so forth.

Now, how are these—pleasure, pain, desire, and aversion—distinguished from consciousness? [One might argue they are not,] because they are produced by the same causes and are perceived as having an inward-turned form. For it has been stated that objects are distinguished by a difference in their causes. As it is said: "Entities possessing this or that nature are born from causes possessing this or that nature. Therefore, why is pleasure and so forth not cognition, since it is born from causes non-different from those of cognition? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.251)
Thus.

For instance, some entities possess that form—such as grains and the like—while others do not possess that form and are of a different nature. Why? Because they are produced from causes that either possess or do not possess that form. Those produced from a cause possessing the form of grain possess that form; others, however, being of a different character, do not possess that form. To this, it is said: "If that is so, then why is ignorance (*ajñāna*) not accepted as being non-different from the cognition of pleasure and so forth, since it is produced from the same cause? This is not the case. Even if non-difference were to be proven, the argument that things are produced from the same cause is fallacious (*vyabhicāra*), because it fails when considering the inherent (*samavāyin*), non-inherent (*asamavāyin*), and instrumental (*nimitta*) causes. For example, qualities produced by heating (*pākaja*) arise from a single inherent cause, yet they are mutually distinct. Their non-inherent cause, however, is the conjunction of fire with the atoms of earth, which is one and the same for all of them. Likewise, even the single quality of hot touch serves as their instrumental cause. Thus, there is a fallacy even with respect to those [types of] causes. Furthermore, if one considers the causal totality (*sāmagrī*), the production from the same cause is unproven, because such a totality is restricted to each specific effect. As it has been stated: "In one case the causal totality is characterized by a garland and so forth, while in another it is otherwise. Moreover, when the specific genus and the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) are included, there is indeed a difference in the causal totality in every instance. The fact of being perceived as having an inward-turned aspect (*antarmukhākāratā*) is also fallacious with respect to the properties of cognition (*jñānadharma*). It has already been stated that there is a distinction between the property and the substratum (*dharmadharmi*). Likewise, there is a fallacy with respect to the non-arising and destruction of cognition, for while these two are perceived as having an inward-turned aspect, they do not have the nature of pure awareness (*bodharūpatā*). Enough of this over-elaboration.
The dissimilarity with respect to effort.

“*Prayatna* (effort), *saṃrambha* (exertion), and *utsāha* (zeal) are synonyms. It is of two kinds: that preceded by life (*jīvanapūrvaka*) and that preceded by desire and aversion (*icchādveṣapūrvaka*). Among these, that preceded by life is the cause of the continuous flow of the vital breaths (*prāṇa* and *apāna*) in one who is asleep, and at the time of awakening, it is the cause of the internal organ’s reaching toward other sense organs. The production of this [effort] preceded by life arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending upon merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*). The other [kind of effort], however, is the cause of activity capable of obtaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful, and it is that which sustains the body. And that arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending either upon desire or upon aversion. <PDhS>

Now, for the purpose of defining the nature and classification of effort (*prayatna*), he says: “Effort, exertion (*sarambha*), and enthusiasm (*utsāha*) are synonyms. This is the definition, because [effort] is unique [to its own class]. To explain: effort is distinguished from other things because it is denoted by such synonymous terms that have come down through a beginningless stream of tradition; whereas that which is not so distinguished is not thus [denoted], such as color (*rūpa*) and the like. He states that it is of two kinds due to the difference in its causes: “That which is preceded by life (*jīvana*) and that which is preceded by desire and aversion (*icchādveṣa*). That which has life as its preceding cause is "preceded by life. How is this known? He says: “It is that which impels the continuous flow of *prāṇa* and *apāna* in one who is asleep. This activity of the continuous flow of *prāṇa* and *apāna* in a sleeping person must be the effect of effort, because it is a bodily activity, just like the activity of the vital breaths in the waking state. Not only does it impel the flow of the vital breaths and so on, but “it is also the cause of the internal organ’s (*antaḥkaraṇa*) contact with another sense-organ at the time of awakening. For at the time of awakening, since perception occurs through whichever sense-organ it may be, an action of the internal organ—which resides in a part of the soul devoid of senses—must necessarily be admitted for the sake of its connection [with that organ]; and that [action] is the effect of effort, because it is an action of the internal organ that has been grasped, just like that action in the waking state. Therefore, the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) alone is not the cause here, because it is perceived through inference to be the effect of effort. And since no other cause is possible, the unseen force is accepted as the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).

Since existence (*sadbhāva*) is established, he states the cause of production for that which is preceded by life: "From the conjunction of the self and the mind" (*ātmamanasoḥ saṃyogāt*). Production occurs from this non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), depending upon specific merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*). But the other [type of effort], preceded by desire and aversion, is the cause of bodily activity—the activity capable of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful. Likewise, "it is also that which sustains the body. For by it, gravity within the body is restrained and does not initiate falling. He states its cause of production: "From the conjunction of the self and the mind," as the non-inherent cause; "it arises depending upon desire or depending upon aversion."

**The Contrasting Properties of Gravity:** "Gravity belongs to water and earth; it is the cause of the action of falling. It is imperceptible and is to be inferred from the action of falling. It is opposed by conjunction, effort, and momentum. Its eternity, non-eternity, and production are like those of the color and other qualities of the atoms of water and so forth."

The section beginning with “Gravity belongs to water and earth” (*gurutvaṃ jalabhūmyoḥ*) is intended for the examination of the definition of gravity. Gravity is distinguished from other qualities because, while being imperceptible, it is the cause of the action of falling. The inclusion of the term “imperceptible” (*apratyakṣatve sati*) is necessary, as velocity (*vega*) is also a cause of the action of falling. The phrase “of water and earth” (*jalabhūmyoḥ*) serves to specify the substratum. Alternatively, the definition is relative to other terms: gravity is that which exists only in water and earth and is the cause of the action of falling. Taste (*rasa*) also exists only in water and earth, yet it is not the cause of falling; for if it were, one would observe a variation in the effect corresponding to a variation in the cause elsewhere. Since there is no variation in falling despite the absence of a variation in taste in stones and the like, whereas such a variation occurs in long pepper (*pippalī*) and similar substances due to the presence of taste, taste cannot be the cause of the production of falling. Furthermore, if color (*rūpa*) and the rest were the cause, falling would occur even in fire and so forth because they exist there; since this is not the case, a cause distinct from color and the rest is inferred. Therefore, he says: “It is to be inferred by the action of falling” (*patanakarmānumeyam*). For gravity is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of the first instance of the action of falling, whereas for the second and subsequent instances, it is also momentum (*saṃskāra*). And that [gravity] exists only in water and earth.

[Objection: Is it not the case that gravity (*gurutva*) is perceptible, since there arises the manifestation "five palas" or "ten palas" through the operation of the tactile sense-organ (*tvagindriya*)? [Reply: No, because if gravity were perceptible due to its connection with the tactile organ, it would follow that the gravity of earth and other substances would also be perceptible. [Objection: The tactile organ perceives only the gravity residing in the supported object (*ādheya*), and that [gravity] does not exist in the gravity of earth and so forth. [Reply: Even so, it would perceive the gravity of flies and the like, since that too resides in the supported object. Nor can it be argued that it is not perceived because it is indistinct, for there is no distinction in its inherence (*samavāya*) in a perceptible substance. [Objection: Perhaps its distinguishing feature (*vaiśiṣṭya*) is being the cause of downward motion? [Reply: In that case, for one who perceives a specific downward motion through contact with the tactile organ, the cognition "five palas" or "ten palas" would be merely inferential (*ānumānika*).

Now, [the opponent argues that] since no excess of weight is perceived when a cloth is produced from ten *pala*-weights of threads, weight resides only in the cause and not in the effect. This is incorrect, because a fall is observed in both cases. Nor can it be argued that falling occurs solely due to the weight of another substrate even in the absence of inherent weight [in the object], for that would entail the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that air and so forth would also fall. Therefore, since its existence is established by the effect in both cases, weight exists [in the effect as well]. Furthermore, the non-perception of a specific degree of downward bending (*avanativiśeṣa*) in the effect is the same even when there is contact with the weight of flies and other such things. For instance, when threads are being weighed, no specific bending is perceived even upon contact with flies; yet, this does not mean that their weight is non-existent. Enough of this.

Now, if gravity is the cause of falling, why does falling not occur at all times? He says it is "due to obstruction" (*pratibandhāt*), stating: "It is opposed by conjunction, effort, and momentum" (*saṃyoga-prayatna-saṃskāra-virodhi*). Obstructed by the conjunction of the fruit with its stalk, the fruit does not begin to fall; obstructed by effort, gravity does not cause birds situated in the sky to fall; [and] in the case of arrows discharged from a bow, gravity does not cause them to fall because of the obstruction by the momentum (*saṃskāra*) known as velocity (*vega*). This is because falling is observed in fruits and the like once these [obstructions] have ceased.

“And its [gravity’s] establishment regarding eternality and non-eternality is like that of the color and other qualities of water-atoms,” (*). They are called "water-atoms" because they are both water and atoms; thus, it means "like the color and other qualities of those atoms. Just as the color and other qualities of water-atoms are eternal because they are not produced, in the same way, gravity is eternal because it is not produced in eternal substances. However, in non-eternal substances, because it is produced through the process of preceding qualities in the cause, it is non-eternal just like their color; such is the meaning of the extended application (*atideśa*). {The difference from fluidity}.

“Fluidity is the cause of the action of flowing. It resides in three substances. It is of two kinds: natural (*sāṃsiddhika*) and incidental (*naimittika*). Natural fluidity is a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of water. Incidental fluidity is a common quality (*sāmānyaguṇa*) of earth and fire. Regarding natural fluidity, its eternality, non-eternality, and production are like those of gravity. <PDhS>

“If it is argued that [the liquidity of snow and hail] cannot be natural because they are seen as aggregates, we say no. When aqueous atoms conjoined with celestial heat come into mutual conjunction—known as an aggregate—that constitutes the commencement of a substance. Due to the obstruction of the atomic liquidity by this [conjunction], liquidity does not arise in the resulting effects, such as snow and hail.”

“And the occasional [liquefaction] of earth and fire is produced by conjunction with fire. How so? When action arises in the atoms—the causes of substances such as clarified butter, lac, beeswax, and the like—due to conjunction with fire which depends upon velocity, then from the disjunctions produced thereby, there occurs the destruction of the conjunctions that originate the substance; thus, upon the cessation of the effect-substance, liquidity is produced in the independent atoms due to conjunction with fire which depends upon heat. Then, when action arises in those [atoms] due to conjunction with the self which depends upon the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of the experiencers, an effect-substance is produced through the sequence of dyads and so forth from the conjunctions produced thereby. And in that [substance], at the same time as the production of color and other qualities, liquidity is produced through the sequence of the qualities of the causes. <PDhS>

In order to define and examine fluidity (*dravatva*), he says: "Fluidity is the cause of the action of flowing" (*syandana-karma-kāraṇa*). The action of flowing will be explained later. When it is stated that fluidity is the cause of that [action], there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to momentum (*vega*); therefore, the phrase "subsisting in three substances" (*tridravyavṛtti*) is added. Even so, since momentum can also subsist in three substances, the word "necessarily" (*niyamena*) must be supplied. Color (*rūpa*), however, necessarily subsists in three substances, but it is not the cause of the action of flowing. Therefore, fluidity is distinct from other things, because while necessarily subsisting in three substances, it is the cause of the action of flowing.

That [fluidity] is of two kinds; this is the classification. In what form? As innate (*sāṃsiddhika*) and incidental (*naimittika*). To determine the mutual distinction between these two, he says: "The innate is a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of water; the incidental is a general quality (*sāmānyaguṇa*) of earth and fire. This is their mutual difference. Regarding the statement, "The production, eternality, and non-eternality of the innate are like those of gravity," the meaning of the extension (*atideśa*) is as follows: just as gravity is eternal because it is not produced in eternal substances, and non-eternal because it is produced in non-eternal substances—being preceded by the qualities of its causes and perishing upon the destruction of its substrate—so too is innate fluidity.

Now, is it not improper to say that water possesses natural fluidity (*sāṃsiddhika-dravatva*), since it is not perceived in snow, hail, and the like? If it is argued: "Because we observe them as solid masses (*saṅghāta*), their natural fluidity is untenable," this is not so. Since natural fluidity is observed elsewhere in water, and its existence is established in the water-atoms (*āpya-paramāṇu*), it is determined that there exists an obstructing factor which prevents it from arising in snow, hail, and so forth. Because nothing else is perceived, he states that this is indeed contact with celestial heat: "The mutual conjunction of water-atoms conjoined with celestial heat is what initiates the substance. And that [conjunction] is called "mass" (*saṅghāta*); because it obstructs the fluidity of the atoms, fluidity does not arise in the effect, such as snow or hail. The presence of heat, moreover, is inferred from effects such as bursting. Thus, an effect characterized by bursting is perceived due to contact with snow and hail, and burning occurs in the body and in trees. Its melting, however, results from contact with celestial heat. There is motion in the parts; from that, disjunction; from that, upon the cessation of conjunction and the destruction of the substance, the atoms begin a new effect. In that case, once the obstructing contact with celestial heat has ceased, the fluidity of the atoms initiates fluidity in the effect.

Nor is this [cohesion] merely occasional, for, as in the case of clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*) and the like, no subsequent cohesion is perceived here. For just as there is cohesion of that which has become liquid because its liquidity is occasional—as in the case of clarified butter and so on—so too would it be here; yet this is not the case.

“And the occasional [liquefaction] of earth and fire is produced by conjunction with fire. (*Vaiśeṣika Sūtra* 2.1.54) The question “How so? is one posed by someone who has not yet mastered the subject. To this, he replies: “In the causes of clarified butter and so forth,” where the phrase “and so forth” includes those items mentioned in the Sūtra. For instance, according to *Vaiśeṣika Sūtra* 2.1.54–55: “Clarified butter, lac, and beeswax—though they are earthen—are liquefied through conjunction with fire; this is their commonality with water. Tin, lead, iron, silver, and gold—though they are fiery—are liquefied through conjunction with fire; this is their commonality with water. Therefore, when action arises in the atoms that are the causes of clarified butter and the rest, depending upon conjunction with fire and depending upon velocity (*vega*), subsequent disjunctions are produced. From those disjunctions comes the destruction of the conjunctions that initiate the substance; from that destruction comes the cessation of the effect-substance. When that has ceased, through conjunction with fire depending upon heat (*auṣṇya*), liquidity is produced in the independent atoms. Here, the atoms are the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), conjunction with fire is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and hot touch is the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). Immediately after that, when liquidity has been produced, action arises “from the conjunction of the soul and the atom, depending upon the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of enjoyers” (*Vaiśeṣika Sūtra* 7.1.11). Here, the atom is the inherent cause, the conjunction of the soul and the atom is the non-inherent cause, and the unseen merit/demerit of enjoyers is the instrumental cause. Then, once the prior conjunctions have been destroyed by means of those disjunctions, new conjunctions with other atoms arise from those actions. From those conjunctions, dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) are produced. Through that sequence beginning with the dyad, triads (*tryaṇuka*) and further effects are produced. And in those dyads and so forth, “liquidity is produced in the same manner as the production of color and other qualities, by way of the sequence starting from the qualities of the causes”—thus the principle of the production of qualities born of cooking (*pākaja*) is to be observed here. However, this much is the distinction: in that case (the production of color etc.), there is necessarily the cessation of the previous color and so on, but it is not so for liquidity.

{The Dissimilarity of Viscidity} (*sneho 'pāṃ viśeṣaguṇaḥ | saṃgrahamṛjādihetuḥ | asyāpi gurutvavannityānityatvaniṣpattayaḥ |*) For the purpose of defining and examining viscidity (*sneha*), [the author] states: “Viscidity is a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of water; it is the cause of cohesion (*saṃgraha*), cleanliness (*mṛjā*), and so forth. Since color (*rūpa*) and other qualities are also specific qualities of water, the phrase “cause of cohesion, cleanliness, and so forth” is included [to specify viscidity]. Cohesion is the state of being formed into a mass (*piṇḍīkaraṇa*). Cleanliness, however, is clarity (*viśadatva*). Because it is the cause of these, viscidity is distinguished from other qualities.

Is it not the case that the status of moisture (*sneha*) as a specific quality of water is unestablished, since it is perceived in fresh sprouts and the like? No; for its perception occurs through *saṃyuktasamavāya* (inherence in what is conjoined). For water is conjoined with the sprout and so forth, and the moisture inherent in that [water] is apprehended; because when that [conjunction] is removed, it is no longer perceived. Likewise, because the cognition of oiliness is observed in the hair and so forth after bathing. Furthermore, while there is no cognition of oiliness in all water due to a deficiency in the substratum of the conjoined [element], this is not the case for all earth. "Regarding this [moisture], too, its eternality, non-eternality, and production are like those of gravity (*gurutva*). In eternal [substances], it is eternal; in non-eternal [substances], it is preceded by the qualities of its causes; and it perishes upon the destruction of its substratum.
The heterogeneity of *saṃskāra*:

“*Saṃskāra* is threefold: velocity (*vega*), mental impression (*bhāvanā*), and elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka*). Among these, velocity arises from action in the five corporeal substances depending on specific instrumental causes; it is the cause of a continuous series of actions in a fixed direction, is opposed by a specific conjunction with a substance possessing touch, and in some cases arises through a sequence beginning with the qualities of the cause.”

In order to define *saṃskāra*, he says: "Saṃskāra is threefold. In what form? As velocity (*vega*), mental impression (*bhāvanā*), and elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka*). Since division itself constitutes the definition due to its exclusivity, this [statement] is intended to make known the diversity of those definitions. In that regard, while defining the distinction of velocity from things of the same class and its substratum, he says: "In corporeal substances," and so forth. It is not known how many [substances] are meant by "in corporeal substances"; for that purpose, he says "in five. Even so, it is not known which ones; for that purpose, "in corporeal substances" is the definition of the substratum. Alternatively, the definition of velocity is: being a *saṃskāra* while existing only in the five corporeal substances.

He states the cause: "It arises from action depending on a specific efficient cause" (*nimittaviśeṣāpekṣāt karmaṇo jāyate*). Since conjunction and disjunction are produced by action, the qualification "depending on a specific efficient cause" is added. A specific efficient cause consists of impulsion (*nodana*), impact (*abhighāta*), and conjunction with what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasaṃyoga*); it is "depending on" these. Action is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), while the specific cause of its own [action], such as impulsion and so forth, is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*); and the substratum of velocity (*vega*) is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). This is the definition because it is unique [to action]. He states the effect: it is the cause of a continuous series of actions, that is, a stream of actions, in a fixed direction.

Now, one might object that this is incorrect, because even the action called "revolution" (*bhramaṇa*), which has no fixed direction or location, is a cause [of it]. True, this is so; nevertheless, there is no fault, because we do not accept the restrictive determination that [the cause] is exclusively a series of actions with a fixed direction. Others hold that even that [revolution] is indeed a series of actions in a fixed direction. Others, however, provide a different interpretation, considering the restrictive determination that it is a cause of a series of actions with no fixed direction to be merely the preliminary form [of the argument]. He states its cause of destruction: "It is opposed by a specific conjunction with a tangible substance. If it were opposed by mere conjunction with any tangible substance, then an arrow would not continue its flight due to conjunction with the wind, because its momentum (*vega*), which is the cause of that [flight], would be destroyed; therefore, the term "specific" (*viśeṣa*) is used, since its destruction is observed even at the beginning [of the flight] through conjunction with hard parts.

[Objection: Even so, an arrow shot into the sky would not fall, because there would be an absence of that dense conjunction of parts which destroys its velocity. [Reply: No; for through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is observed that even by mere conjunction with a substance possessing touch (*sparśavat-dravya*), destruction occurs during the performance of multiple effects. Thus, since the destruction of the velocity of a shot arrow is observed, a cause must necessarily be stated, because destruction without a cause is prohibited. Therefore, when multiple effects are produced, [the destruction of velocity] is contradicted either by conjunction with air (*vāyu-saṃyoga*) or by the exhaustion of unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa-prakṣaya*). "In some cases, it arises through the process beginning with the qualities of the cause" (*kvacit kāraṇaguṇapūrvaprakrameṇotpadyate*); for example, when water falling downward from mountains and streams comes into conjunction, a single [mass of] water is produced, and just as color and other qualities [arise], velocity also arises from the velocity of the cause.

“However, that which is called *bhāvanā* (mental impression) is a quality of the self (*ātman*) that serves as the cause of memory and recognition regarding objects seen, heard, or experienced; it is opposed to knowledge, intoxication, pain, and so forth. A sharp mental impression arises from a sharp cognition produced by practice, attention, or interest, resulting from the conjunction of the self and the mind with respect to a marvelous object. For example, as in the case of a person from the South seeing a camel. When learning, arts, athletics, and the like are being practiced, a superior mental impression arises from the successive cognitions—which depend upon each preceding mental impression—resulting from the conjunction of the self and the mind with respect to that very same object. By exerting effort and fixing the mind on the eye, one who desires to see an unprecedented object experiences a cognition of intense interest, like the sight of a flash of lightning; depending upon that, a superior mental impression arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind. For example, as in the case of seeing golden and silver lotuses in Devahrada.”

That which is designated as *bhāvanā* (mental impression) is distinct from other qualities because it is a quality of the self (*ātman*). Nor is there any deviation [in this definition] by means of cognition (*buddhi*) and so forth, because *saṃskāra* is defined as a specific sub-class of existing entities. The phrase "the cause of memory and recognition" (*smṛtipratyabhijñānahetuḥ*) serves both as a definition of its function and as a proof for its existence. Memory arises from what is called *vāsanā* (latent impression), as stated in the section on the Self (*ātmādhikāra*). To the question of in what objects memory and recognition are caused, he says: "in those things seen, heard, or experienced," the sense being that these are objects whose nature has been determined.

He states the cause of destruction: "It is opposed by knowledge, intoxication, suffering, and so forth. Here, "knowledge" is intended to mean counter-knowledge; it is opposed by that, just as the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the knowledge of the self and so on is opposed by the practice of the doctrine of no-self (*nairātmya*), because when that [counter-knowledge] is present, there is no recollection of the former. There is opposition by intoxication, because the latent impression produced by an experience in childhood is not recollected in youth when one is overwhelmed by sensory objects. There is opposition by suffering, just as the latent impression produced by the experience of the scriptures is opposed by intense suffering regarding one's wife and so on, because while that [suffering] exists, there is no recollection of the former. By the word "and so forth," the capacity of anger and other such factors to terminate latent impressions is also indicated.

He states the cause of its production: "That which is born from vivid, repeated, and attentive cognitions is called *tatpratyayaja*. From the conjunction of the self and the mind—which acts as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*)—and depending upon a vivid cognition, a vivid latent impression (*saṃskāra*) arises in the self regarding a marvelous object, "as for a Southerner upon seeing a camel. And that [impression] becomes an exceptionally strong cause for memory.
