[From] "repeated practice" (*abhyāsāt*): "When learning, arts, physical exercises, and so forth are being practiced, an excellence of latent impression is produced from each subsequent cognition, depending upon the preceding latent impressions, through the conjunction of the self and the mind. For practice is a subsequent cognition that depends upon each preceding latent impression; depending upon that [practice], an excellence of latent impression is produced in the self from the conjunction of the self and the mind acting as the non-inherent cause. In this regard, regarding learning (*vidyā*), when there is the hearing of words uttered by a teacher, a latent impression is formed. Furthermore, when one subsequently utters them oneself through the sequence of the desire to speak and so forth, that cognition—depending upon the previous latent impression—initiates another latent impression. Again, when those are uttered, that cognition—depending upon the previous latent impression—initiates yet another latent impression. In this way, after three or four repetitions, an excellence of latent impression arises from the experience of the final word, depending upon the [preceding] latent impressions. This must necessarily be accepted; otherwise, practice would be useless. Nor is there the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) serves as the regulating factor. Moreover, that [unseen force] does not exist everywhere, since the effect, namely memory, is not observed everywhere. For only where memory exists does a cognition depending upon a previous latent impression initiate a new latent impression. Regarding internal practice, it should be considered that the very recollection of a restricted object, depending upon each preceding latent impression, initiates a latent impression. Similarly, regarding the arts (*śilpa*), a latent impression arises from seeing a painting drawn by a teacher; then, having produced it oneself, one perceives it. That perception—depending upon the previous latent impression—initiates another latent impression. Then, having painted it oneself, one perceives it; that perception—depending upon the previous latent impression—initiates another latent impression. Thus, through two, three, or more repetitions, an excellence of latent impression is achieved. Regarding physical exercise (*vyāyāma*), when arrows are discharged according to the method taught in the science of archery (*dhanurveda*) by a teacher, a latent impression is produced. When one then practices oneself following that [instruction], another latent impression is initiated by that experience depending upon the previous latent impression. Again, when practicing in the same manner, another latent impression is produced by that experience depending upon the previous latent impression. Thus, from the final experience, an excellence of latent impression arises.

He explains the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) born from the cognition of attention (*ādarapratyaya*) as follows: "For one who, having fixed the mind with effort upon the eye, desires to see an unprecedented object" (*prayatnena manaḥ cakṣuṣi sthāpayitvā apūrvamarthaṃ didṛkṣamāṇasya*). This occurs similarly to the sight of a flash of lightning for one who wishes to see; thus, the cognition of attention is like that sight. Depending upon that [cognition], an excellence of latent impression arises in the self (*ātman*) from the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), which is the conjunction of the self and the mind (*ātmamanasoḥ saṃyoga*). "As, for example, from seeing golden and silver lotuses in the Devahrada lake. For in that case, having learned of the emergence of the golden and silver lotuses from scripture or from popular report, an excellence of latent impression arises through effort at the time of a special pilgrimage.

“Elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka*), however, residing in tangible substances that possess dense structural arrangements and persist over time, restores its own substratum to its original state when it has been altered. The function of elasticity is observed in stationary and moving objects—such as bows, branches, teeth, horns, bones, threads, and garments—which have been bent or compressed. Its eternity, non-eternity, and production are to be understood in the same manner as those of gravity.”

The *sthitisthāpaka* (elasticity) is distinguished from other [qualities] because, while being a *saṃskāra* (latent impression), it exists only in substances that possess touch (*sparśavat*). In what kind of substances? It is said: "in those characterized by a dense arrangement of parts. These are both dense and parts; their "arrangement" (*sanniveśa*) is a specific configuration. Alternatively, "dense" (*ghana*) is an adjective qualifying the arrangement itself, [meaning] "in those characterized by such [an arrangement]. It is called *sthitisthāpaka* because it "establishes its own substratum, which has been altered, back into its original state after a lapse of time."

He states the proof for its existence: "The stationary and the moving," as they have been described; in their modifications—such as bows, branches, tusks, horns, and bones, as well as threads, garments, and so forth—when these are bent, coiled, or rolled into balls, its effect is clearly perceived. For instance, when the action of drawing occurs in a bow or a branch, even after that [action] has ceased due to impulsion (*nodana*) and other factors, an action is still observed; therefore, an inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) must necessarily be postulated, since an entity cannot arise without it. Nor can any one of the factors such as impulsion be considered suitable [as this inherent cause], because there must be another inherent cause, given that action and disjunction are observed not to be causes for the production of [subsequent] action. Furthermore, even when that [initial action] has ceased, provided there is no obstructing factor, an action is observed in the branch and other objects that maintains them in their previous state; thus, it is logical that there must be another instrumental cause (*nimitta*). However, the causality of a specific unseen force (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*) is not denied, as it is common to all things.

“Its eternality, non-eternality, and production should also be understood as being like gravity (*gurutva*). For just as gravity is eternal in eternal things due to the absence of causes for its production or destruction, and in non-eternal things it is preceded by a cause and perishes through the destruction of its substrate—so too is the impression of elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka-saṃskāra*). However, since the impression of elasticity is well-known in its effects, it is postulated to exist even in the atoms that originate those effects.
{The difference in properties}.

“Dharma is a quality of the person; it is the cause of what is dear, beneficial, and liberation for the agent; it is supersensible and opposed to the consciousness of final bliss; it arises from the conjunction of the person and the internal organ when there is a pure intention; and its causes are the substances, qualities, and actions prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti for those belonging to the various castes and stages of life, existing in the form of general and specific requirements. <PDhS>

For the purpose of examining the definition of *dharma*, he says: “*Dharma* is a quality of the person,” and so forth. Since being a quality of the person applies to cognition (*buddhi*) and other faculties as well, he specifies: “the cause of what is pleasant, beneficial, and liberation. Here, “pleasant” means happiness, and “beneficial” means the means to that [happiness]. Liberation is the absolute cessation of the nine specific qualities of the self. Now, since the knowledge of God (*īśvara-jñāna*) is also a cause of these [qualities], he adds: “of the agent. For *dharma* produced by someone is the cause of what is pleasant, beneficial, and liberation only for that very person; however, this is not the case with the knowledge of God, because, being uncreated, there is no agent [for whom it would function as such]. Furthermore, since the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*) is the cause of the aforementioned result for the agent, he adds: “it is supersensible (*atīndriya*). Since even mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) operate only through the mediation of memory, he adds: “it is opposed to the consciousness of final bliss. Final bliss is the bliss at the very end [of life], and [this knowledge] is opposed to its perception.

[Objection: Even so, since it is supersensible (*atīndriya*) and because it is incompatible with the cognition of final bliss (*antyasukha-saṃvijñāna*), there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) when it is stated that "Dharma is distinct from other things"; therefore, the mention of the remaining attributes is redundant. [Reply: No, because it is distinct from the agent (*kartṛ*). The phrase "the cause of what is dear, beneficial, and liberation" is a definition of its specific purposeful activity (*viśiṣṭārthakriyā*). The phrase "a quality of the person" (*puruṣaguṇa*) is for the purpose of negating its being otherwise [i.e., a quality of something else].

Now, what is the proof for [the existence of] qualities in the Person (puruṣa)? It is inference and scripture. For instance: the world, consisting of bodies and so forth, is preceded by the qualities of the Person, because it is a diverse effect, like a chariot and the like. Just as the maker of a chariot and such, depending upon the diverse intention of the enjoyer, constructs its arrangement accordingly, so too does the maker of the body and so forth. Furthermore, prior to the production of the body, intellect and the other qualities do not exist in the self of beings such as ourselves; and since latent impressions (saṃskāra) have their capacity understood only in relation to the arising of memory, [the maker], depending on some other quality residing therein, initiates the diverse body and so forth for the sake of accomplishing that [self's] experience. As for scripture: "As long as merit and demerit (dharma-adharma) exist in the self, so long do life-span, the body, the senses, and objects [endure]," and likewise, "And his actions (karmāṇi) are exhausted."

But for those for whom *dharma* is a quality (*guṇa*) of the intellect (*buddhi*), how could heaven not be caused by action? For instance, in the state of dissolution (*pralaya*), since the intellect has dissolved into primordial matter (*pradhāna*), *dharma* and *adharma* would remain unmanifest; consequently, the transformation of *pradhāna* into the form of the intellect and so forth would not occur, because it is accepted that only manifest action serves as a cause. Nor can it be argued that what is unmanifest at first is the cause, while that which resides in the intellect is manifest, for there is no specific reason [to distinguish them]. Furthermore, if it is accepted that action performed by the intellect and so forth produces the experience of the agent, then—since there would be no restrictive factor—it would produce the experiences of all persons without distinction. Likewise, it would proceed to produce bodies and so forth even for liberated souls, and due to the lack of distinction, the consequence would be their continued state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*). Moreover, the non-perception of the distinction between the qualities (*guṇa*) and the self (*puruṣa*) cannot be the cause of the activity of *pradhāna*, as this has already been refuted previously.

Even for those who believe that *dharma* is of the nature of an atom (*paramāṇu*), there follows the undesirable consequence that its eternity would entail the abolition of all activity and the absence of death and so forth. Furthermore, impermanence is simply not possible in the case of something having the nature of an atom, because as an atom, it lacks the causes for arising and destruction. Likewise, if atoms were designated by the word *dharma*, there would be nothing more than a mere difference in terminology. Alternatively, if *dharma* and *adharma* were qualities of atoms, even so, the experience of all persons would be of a uniform character, since there would be no distinction in their being produced from atoms which serve as the substrata for merit and demerit.

Now, if it is argued that some atoms are substrata of merit (*puṇya*) while others are substrata of demerit (*apuṇya*), and that an excellence of pleasure arises when they are composed of a greater number of substrata of merit, whereas suffering arises from a greater number of substrata of demerit—even in this case, if those two were eternal, it would follow that death and so forth could never occur. Furthermore, their impermanence is not tenable, because we do not observe that the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of atoms can be produced by the activity of beings such as ourselves.

Others, however, maintain that *dharma* is without a substratum (*anāśrita*). To this, the refutation is as follows: even on the view that it is impermanent (*anityapakṣe*), no effect that is a real entity can possibly exist without a substratum. On the view that it is permanent (*nityapakṣe*), there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the abolition of rituals such as sacrifices. If it is argued that the cause is manifested by the ritual action, then because of its momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), the action perishes and the fruit such as heaven would not occur. Nor is the action a manifestor of that [dharma] in the way a lamp is a manifestor of an object; for even when the action exists, [the dharma] is not perceived. If it is argued that the ritual action such as sacrifice produces a capacity (*sāmarthya*) in *dharma*, then that very capacity is *dharma*; and that in which it resides is the Self (*ātman*). Thus, there would be nothing but a difference in terminology. Furthermore, since there is no connection between the formless Self and [the capacity], there would be no fruit resulting from that connection. Enough with this digression. Nor is action identical to consciousness (*bodha*), for if their distinction were not admitted, the diversity of the world would not be possible, as everything would be indistinguishable due to being of the nature of consciousness.

He states its cause of origination: it arises from the conjunction of the person and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which serves as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). By the phrase “born of pure intention” (*śuddhābhisandhija*), he shows that intention is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). That for which the specific means of the various classes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*) are the efficient cause is called "having that as its cause" (*tannimitta*). He explains this very point with the words: “But its means are those prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*. The classes (*varṇa*) are the Brāhmaṇas and so forth; the stages of life (*āśrama*) are studentship (*brahmacarya*) and so forth. For these, the substances, qualities, and actions exist in the relationship of general and particular.

“In that regard, the general duties are: faith in the Dharma, non-violence, concern for the welfare of living beings, truthful speech, non-stealing, absence of fraud, celibacy, avoidance of anger, ritual ablution, use of pure substances, devotion to a specific deity, fasting, and vigilance.”

"In that regard, the general means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) are as follows: ‘Faith in Dharma’ is a specific form of devotion (*bhakti-viśeṣa*), which is the cause. Non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), however, applies at all times for an ascetic (*yati*) and the like, whereas for others it applies only in specific places and at specific times—for example, ‘I shall not kill at a sacred site (*tīrtha*)’ or on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) and so forth. Being beneficial to living beings (*bhūta-hitatva*) also applies to some at all times, while for others it applies in specific places and so on. Truthful speech is a means to Dharma provided it is not undesirable to others; and it has been said: ‘One should not speak a truth that is unpleasant. Non-stealing (*asteya*) is the absence of theft. It has been stated that in certain circumstances, even theft is not a fault—for instance, taking merely enough food for a dying twice-born man (*dvija*). Absence of guile (*anupadhā*) is the lack of malice toward others. Celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is the restraint of the generative organ (*upastha*); and this applies to some at all times, while for others it applies in specific places and times. The avoidance of anger is likewise. ‘Consecration’ (*abhiṣecana*) is bathing. ‘Service with pure substances’ consists of using [pure] seats, garments, and food. ‘Devotion to a specific deity’ is devotion toward a particular deity known through the three Vedas (*trayī*) and understood through inference. Fasting (*upavāsa*) is the state of not eating for a day and night; it is a means to Dharma at specific times and so forth. ‘Vigilance’ (*apramāda*) is the absence of laziness in the performance of prescribed duties."

“Sacrifice, study, and giving are [the duties] of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas. For the Brāhmaṇa, however, there are specific [duties]: receiving gifts, teaching, and officiating at sacrifices, as well as the sacraments prescribed for his own class. For the Kṣatriya, they are the proper protection of subjects, the suppression of the wicked, not retreating from battles, and his own sacraments. For the Vaiśya, they are buying, selling, agriculture, cattle-rearing, and his own sacraments. For the Śūdra, they are dependence on the preceding classes and ritual acts performed without mantras.”

The common means of accomplishing *dharma* for the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya are: sacrifice (*ijyā*), which is the act of worshipping; study (*adhyayana*), which is the recitation of the Vedas; and giving (*dāna*), which is the offering of wealth to a worthy recipient. The specific means of accomplishing *dharma* for the Brāhmaṇa are: receiving gifts (*pratigraha*), teaching (*adhyāpana*), and officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*). Receiving gifts is the acceptance of wealth that is not forbidden by the scriptures; study is the recitation of the Vedas; officiating at sacrifices is acting as a priest in a ritual; and there are also the sacraments (*saṃskāras*) prescribed for one’s own class. The specific means of accomplishing *dharma* for the Kṣatriya are: the proper protection of subjects, the punishment of the wicked, not retreating in battles, and the sacraments prescribed for one’s own class. For the Vaiśya, they are: buying and selling, agriculture, and cattle-rearing, along with the sacraments prescribed for one’s own class. For the Śūdra, they are: always acting under the command of the Brāhmaṇas and others, and performing rites without mantras, being devoid of the syllable *oṃ* and so forth.

“Regarding those belonging to the stages of life (*āśrama*): for the student (*brahmacārin*) residing in the teacher’s household, there is service to the teacher, the kindling of the sacred fire, the practice of begging for alms as prescribed by his own scriptures, and the avoidance of honey, meat, sleeping during the day, collyrium, ointments, and so forth. For the householder who has completed his studies and vows (*vidyāvratasnātaka*) and taken a wife, there is the performance morning and evening of the five great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*)—known as those for beings, humans, gods, ancestors, and Brahman—using wealth acquired through the *śālīna* or *yāyāvara* modes of livelihood, and the performance of the obligatory cooked-sacrifice rites (*pākayajñasaṃsthā*) according to the single-fire rule when capacity exists. There are also the fire-consecration rites (*agnyādheya*) and others belonging to the class of oblation-sacrifices (*haviryajñasaṃsthā*), and the Soma-sacrifices (*somayajñasaṃsthā*) such as the *agniṣṭoma*. During the intervals between these seasons, there is celibacy and the procreation of offspring. For one who has gone out from the village—whether a student or a householder—and dwells in the forest, there is the wearing of bark, skins, and the maintenance of hair, beard, nails, and body hair. For the forest-dweller (*vanastha*), there is eating what is obtained from the wild, water, what is offered in sacrifice, and the remains of food given to guests. For the renunciate (*pravrajita*)—whoever among the three [other stages] possesses faith, having renounced all actions, granted perpetual fearlessness to all beings, and being vigilant in the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*)—the accomplishment of yoga comes from the contemplation of the six categories. And virtue (*dharma*) arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending on these means and the clarity of disposition, without aiming at any visible purpose.”

Now, the means for accomplishing the dharma of those belonging to the stages of life (*āśrama*) are stated. Among them, regarding the student (*brahmacārin*): of what kind? Of one dwelling in the teacher’s household; his conduct consists of "service to the teacher, gathering fuel for the fire, and the practice of begging for alms. Service to the teacher is attending upon him. Gathering fuel for the fire is the bringing of wood for the sake of the sacred fires. Alms is the collection of begged food, specifically the *mādhukarī* (honey-gathering) method of begging; this is its practice. It also includes the avoidance of honey, meat, sleeping during the day, applying collyrium, anointing with oil, and so forth. This constitutes the vow of learning (*vidyāvrata*), which lasts twelve years for each Veda, totaling forty-eight years, until the mastery [of the texts] is achieved.

Next, the means for accomplishing the duties (*dharma-sādhana*) of the householder (*gṛhastha*)—one who has bathed after completing his studies and vows (*vidyā-vrata-snātaka*), who has performed his vows, and who has taken a wife—are described. These are of four kinds: those who subsist by trade (*vārtā-vṛtti*), those who live as householders (*śālīna-vṛtti*), those who wander about (*yāyāvara*), and those who practice severe renunciation (*ghora-saṃnyāsika*). Among them, the *vārtā-vṛttis* perform blameless occupations such as agriculture and commerce as prescribed by the scriptures; they seek self-perfection through a hundred-year cycle of rituals, both performing sacrifices themselves and officiating for others. The *śālīna-vṛttis*, however, seek self-perfection through a hundred-year cycle of rituals by performing sacrifices, officiating for others, giving gifts, and accepting gifts. The *yāyāvaras*, on the other hand, seek self-perfection by studying but not teaching, performing sacrifices but not officiating for others, and giving gifts but not accepting them. Therein, those called *ghora-saṃnyāsikas* perform their duties with water that has been drawn up and purified; subsisting daily on the practice of gathering gleaned grains (*uñcha-vṛtti*), they seek self-perfection through a hundred-year cycle of rituals while performing sacrifices. As an illustration, there are two types of householders. With wealth acquired through the *śālīna* and *yāyāvara* modes of livelihood, they perform the five great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*)—known as those for the spirits (*bhūta*), humans (*manuṣya*), gods (*deva*), ancestors (*pitṛ*), and Brahman (*brahma*)—both morning and evening. "Evening" refers to the afternoon, and "morning" refers to the dawn. Among these, the sacrifice to the spirits (*bhūta-yajña*) is performed with an external offering (*bali*); the sacrifice to humans (*manuṣya-yajña*) with the *hantakāra* (food given to guests); the sacrifice to the gods (*deva-yajña*) by the scattering of flowers and leaves and the satiation of the sacred fire; the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛ-yajña*) by the giving of alms; and the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahma-yajña*) by the study of the Vedas. This is their performance morning and evening. Regarding the rule of the single fire (*ekāgni-vidhāna*), it is said that one fire is maintained from the time of marriage. Now, he shows the mutual differences in the performance of the occasional rites (*naimittika*) through the passage beginning with "of the forms of the *pākayajñas*" (*pākayajña-saṃsthānām*). The forms of the *pākayajñas* are: *(Note: The original text ends mid-sentence here regarding the list of pākayajña-saṃsthās.)*
The Aṣṭakās, the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha, the Śrāvaṇī, the Āgrahāyaṇī,
as well as the Caitrī and the Āśvayujī— these seven are remembered as the domestic rites of cooked food (pākasaṃsthā).

And regarding these obligatory rites, their performance occurs when one has the capacity; however, for one who is incapable, there is no fault even in non-performance. He states this very point: "By old age, indeed, or by death, he is released from this sacrificial session (*satra*). Regarding the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) and the *haviryajña* forms of sacrifice: the establishment of the fires, the *agnihotra*, the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, the *cāturmāsya*, the *āgrayaṇeṣṭi*, the *nirūḍhapaśubandha*, and the *sautrāmaṇī*—these are the seven *haviryajña* forms. The *agniṣṭoma*, *atyagniṣṭoma*, *ukthya*, *ṣoḍaśī*, *vājapeya*, *atirātra*, and *aptoryāma*—these are the seven *soma-yajña* forms. Thus he says: "Of the *soma-yajña* forms, beginning with the *agniṣṭoma*. In this way, other specific sacrifices as well are to be understood exactly as they are well-known in those respective scriptures. During the other seasons, there is the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and the procreation of offspring.

He states the means for accomplishing *dharma* for one who dwells in the forest: “The forest-dwelling of either a celibate student (*brahmacārin*) or a householder. And it has been said: “Or else, one may renounce even from the stage of celibacy. Therefore, the eligibility belongs to either the celibate student or the householder. They, too, are of four kinds: the *vaikhānasas*, the *audumbaras*, the *bālakhilyas*, and the *phenapas*. Among them, those called *vaikhānasas* perform the service of the sacred fire and carry out the rite of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) using herbs that ripen without cultivation and are excluded from villages; thus they seek the Self. Therein, those called *audumbaras*, having risen at dawn, perform the service of the sacred fire and carry out the rite of the five great sacrifices with jujube (*badara*), wild rice (*nīvāra*), and millet (*śyāmāka*) gathered from whichever direction they look; thus they seek the Self. Therein, those called *bālakhilyas* wear matted hair, their bodies are covered with rags and bark, and on the full moon day of Kārttika or during the month of Puṣya and so forth, they abandon food; having acquired sustenance for eight months, they carry out the rite of the five great sacrifices and seek the Self. Therein, those called *phenapas* have raised staffs, are not insane, feed on withered leaves, and dwell wherever they may; thus they seek the Self. He says this very thing: “Wearing bark, deerskin, and maintaining matted hair, beard, nails, and body hair, as well as eating forest water, oblations, and the remnants of food given by guests, [is the duty] of the forest-dweller. Pointing out the stage of the ascetic (*yati*), he says: “Of any one of the three. Of any one of the three—the celibate student, the householder, or the forest-dweller. Of what kind? “Of one possessed of faith,” who has granted perpetual fearlessness to all beings. And it has been said: “One should not harm any living beings. “Having renounced his own duties,” such as the *agnihotra* and others. “Being vigilant regarding the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*). Non-violence and the like are the *yamas*; service and the like are the *niyamas*; being vigilant regarding these. “From the enumeration of the six categories,” that is, from thorough knowledge. “For one who has abandoned the means of worldly yoga (*yoga-sādhana*); for him, yoga itself is the means for accomplishing *dharma*.

By the aforementioned reasoning, they too are of four kinds: *kuṭīcakas*, *bahūdakas*, *haṃsas*, and *paramahaṃsas*. The *kuṭīcakas* carry the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*), the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), a patched garment (*kanthā*), and so forth, and eat at the houses of their kinsmen. The *bahūdakas* eat alms-food at the houses of Brāhmaṇas and dwell in empty houses or temples. The *haṃsas* have the topknot (*śikhā*), the water-pot, and the staff in hand; they stay for one night in a village and three to five nights at sacred sites (*tīrtha*) and the like, thus seeking to purify themselves through fortnightly fasts and other observances. The *paramahaṃsas*, however, carry only a single staff; they are shaven-headed, wear only a loincloth (*kaupīna*), and renounce the topknot, the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*), the water-pot, the mendicant’s bowl, and so on. For them there is neither merit (*dharma*) nor demerit (*adharma*), neither truth nor falsehood. They are all-enduring, equal toward all things, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as the same. In the case of these four, no visible purpose is aimed at; rather, these means of practice depend upon the clarity of disposition (*bhāvaprasāda*) and pure intention (*śuddhābhisandhi*). From the conjunction of the self and the mind, acting as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), arises spiritual merit (*dharma*).

{Non-dharma and its dissimilarity}: “Non-dharma (*adharma*) is also a quality of the self (*ātman*). It is the cause of harm and transgression for the agent; it is supersensible (*atīndriya*); and it is opposed to the cognition of the final moment of suffering. Its means of accomplishment are those things prohibited in the scripture (*śāstra*), which are the opposites of the means of accomplishing dharma, such as violence, falsehood, theft, and so forth. The non-performance of what is enjoined and negligence are also [means]. Depending upon a corrupt intention (*duṣṭābhisandhi*), these bring about the production of non-dharma from the conjunction of the self and the mind.”

Adharma, like dharma, is a quality of the self. It is defined as: "the cause of harm and transgression for the agent, supersensible, and opposed to the cognition of the final moment of suffering. Adharma is distinct from other things because, while being supersensible, it is opposed to the cognition of the final moment of suffering—the remaining [definition] is as before. Its causes, as stated in the treatise (*śāstra*), are the opposites of the means of dharma, namely violence (*hiṃsā*), falsehood (*anṛta*), theft (*steya*), and so forth. Violence is the killing of living beings; falsehood is untruth; theft is robbery. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), other factors contrary to the means of dharma are included: the non-performance of obligatory duties such as the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyāvandana*), failure to practice due to the lapse of the prescribed time, and negligence (*pramāda*), which is laziness. These causes, depending upon a corrupt intention (*duṣṭābhisandhi*) and a corrupt disposition (*duṣṭābhiprāya*), produce adharma in the self through the conjunction of the self and the mind acting as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).

“For one who is ignorant and possessed of passion and aversion, from a predominant *dharma* accompanied by a small amount of *adharma*, there arises a conjunction with desirable bodies, sense organs, objects, pleasures, and so forth, in accordance with one’s disposition, within the worlds of Brahmā, Indra, Prajāpati, the ancestors, and humans. Likewise, from a predominant *adharma* accompanied by a small amount of *dharma*, there arises a conjunction with undesirable bodies, sense organs, objects, sufferings, and so forth, in the states of hungry ghosts and animals. Thus, from such *dharma* and *adharma* combined, the continuous cycle of transmigration occurs again and again among gods, humans, animals, and denizens of hell.”

“However, for one who acts preceded by knowledge without intending a fruit, is born into a pure family, desires to know the means of removing suffering, approaches a teacher, and—upon the cessation of ignorance through the arising of knowledge of the reality of the six categories—becomes dispassionate; because of the absence of passion, hatred, and so forth, there is no production of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) resulting from those [afflictions]; and when previously accumulated [merit and demerit] are exhausted through experience, [the dharma characterized by cessation] produces the happiness of contentment and the exhaustion of bodily [fatigue], and upon the cessation of passion and so forth, that absolute dharma characterized by cessation, having produced the happiness born of the vision of ultimate reality, ceases. Then, due to that cessation, for the self which is now seedless, there is the cessation of the body and so forth. Since the body and so forth do not arise again, liberation (*mokṣa*) is the pacification [of suffering], like a fire whose fuel has been consumed. (PDhS)

Now he demonstrates for whom karma has arisen that brings about *saṃsāra*, and how it is brought to an end: for the ignorant person who possesses false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) have arisen and bring about *saṃsāra*. Regarding this, he says: "From the impelling [merit] which brings about *saṃsāra*—that is, from the preeminent merit accompanied by a small amount of demerit—there is a connection (*yoga*) with those desired things, namely the body, the senses, objects, pleasure, and so forth. With what kind of things? With those corresponding to one's disposition (*āśaya*), that is, corresponding to one's karma. In which places? In the worlds of Brahmā, Indra, Prajāpati, the Pitṛs, the Ṛṣis, and humans. "Likewise, from the preeminent demerit accompanied by a small amount of merit, there is a connection with undesired bodies, senses, objects, suffering, and so forth. In which places? In the states of the *preta*s and the animal realm. He provides the conclusion: "Thus, from that which is characterized by activity—that is, from merit accompanied by demerit—there occurs again and again the continuous succession (*prabandha*) of *saṃsāra* among gods, humans, animals, and denizens of hell."

Having taught that the arising of *saṃsāra* proceeds from the *dharma* that causes it to turn forward (*pravartaka*), he states its cessation through that which causes it to turn back (*nivartaka*) with the words: "But from that which is performed preceded by knowledge" (*jñānapūrvakāttu kṛtāt*). That whose prior [condition] is knowledge is so described; from that [action]. Of what nature? "From that whose fruit is not intended" (*asaṅkalpitaphalāt*). That whose fruit is not intended in the form "May my body, senses, and objects be such-and-such, not otherwise"—from that [action], birth occurs in a pure family. For one thus born, there arises a desire to know the means for the removal of suffering: "By what means is the absolute cessation of the stream of suffering accomplished? For one who desires this, association with a teacher occurs. Having approached him, one understands the means for the reversal of the stream of suffering, namely: "From the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), the highest good (*śreyaḥ*) is attained. Then, from the study of the treatise, the knowledge of the reality of the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*) arises. And for one in whom the knowledge of the six categories has arisen, there is the cessation of ignorance (*ajñāna*). Upon its cessation, dispassion (*virāga*) occurs, because in the absence of a cause, the effect does not arise. For one who is dispassionate, since passion and hatred (*rāgadveṣa*) are absent, those *dharma* and *adharma* which are born from them do not arise; for passion and hatred are perceived as the generators of *dharma* and *adharma*. In their absence, their absence necessarily follows. Furthermore, the destruction of accumulated [past karma] occurs either through the knowledge of reality or through experience. Then, when passion and the rest have ceased, *dharma* characterized by cessation alone produces the happiness of contentment and the exhaustion of the body. Having produced that, the Ultimate Reality (*paramārtha*), which is the Self (*ātman*) of all things, produces the happiness born from the vision of the Ultimate Reality (*paramārthadarśanaja*). Having done that, it ceases. At that time, for that Self whose seed—designated as *dharma* and *adharma*—has departed, there is the cessation of the body and so forth. Since, due to the absence of the seed, the body and so forth do not arise again, "liberation (*mokṣa*) is the subsiding [of the Self], like a fire whose fuel is consumed. Just as a fire whose fuel is consumed remains in a state devoid of flames and so forth, so too the abiding of the Self, completely freed from specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*), is liberation; this was determined in the opening statement.

“Sound is a quality of space (*ākāśa*); it is apprehended by the auditory organ; it is momentary; it is opposed by both its cause and its effect; it is produced from conjunction, disjunction, and sound; it exists in a specific location (*pradeśavṛtti*); and it has causes that are both similar and dissimilar. It is of two kinds: characterized as phonemes (*varṇa*) and characterized as noise (*dhvani*). Among these, the phoneme-characterized [sound] consists of *a*, *ā*, and so forth, while the noise-characterized [sound] is caused by conch shells and the like. Regarding the production of the phoneme-characterized [sound]: from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending upon memory, there arises the desire to utter a phoneme; immediately after that, there is effort (*prayatna*). Depending upon that effort, from the conjunction of the self and the air, motion is produced in the air. That air, moving upward, strikes the throat and other articulatory sites (*sthāna*). Then, depending upon the conjunction of the air with those sites and the conjunction of the site with space (*ākāśa*), the phoneme is produced. The non-phoneme-characterized [sound] is also produced from the conjunction of the drum and the stick, depending upon the conjunction of the drum with space. From the disjunction of the bamboo joints and from the disjunction of the bamboo with space, and from the sound produced by conjunction and disjunction, there is a series of sounds like a series of reeds. Thus, through this series, when [the sound] reaches the region of the ear, it is perceived. (There is no [direct perception of the original sound]). By the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), the existence of the series is established.”

For the purpose of examining the definition of sound (*śabda*), he says: "Sound is a quality of space," and so forth. When it is stated that "sound is [defined] by being a quality of space," there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to number and other categories; therefore, for that reason, it is specified as "perceptible by the auditory organ. Thus: sound is distinct from other things, because while being a quality of space, it is perceptible by the auditory organ. This is for the purpose of examining whether it is momentary (*kṣaṇika*). Alternatively, the definition is dependent upon the preceding term.

But is it not the case that momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) in sound is unestablished, because recognition and the like are perceived? A cognition arises in the hearer which is observed as follows: "The very same sound that I heard before, I am hearing now. Nor is this [cognition] invalid, since no means of valid cognition is found that apprehends its difference [from the previous sound]. Likewise, the permanence of sound is known through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). For if it were impermanent, then after the cessation of the sound experienced at the time of the convention (*saṅketa*), another sound would be perceived; consequently, the comprehension of its meaning would not occur, as the word would not have been subject to the convention. Yet such comprehension is observed; therefore, by the principle of "otherwise it would be inexplicable" (*anyathānupapatti*), the permanence of sound is known.

This is incorrect, because recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) since it apprehends what has already been apprehended; for its general definition is stated as: "A means of knowledge is that which makes known an object not yet cognized. Now, if you argue that recognition apprehends an object not yet cognized, that is not so, because it would follow that an object not previously seen is false. If you then argue that although the object was apprehended in its own nature, it is nonetheless an object not yet cognized with respect to its present time, place, and so forth—[we reply: [this is not tenable].

But even so, there is the consequence of the occurrence of both defects. If one admits that space, time, and so forth are included within the totality of the object of cognition (*prameya-sāmagrī*), then [the cognition] would have an already cognized object, because the object of cognition has not been previously apprehended by this much alone. Nor is the grasping of space, time, and so forth ever observed through the operation of the sense of hearing. If, on the other hand, they are included within the totality of the means of cognition (*pramāṇa-sāmagrī*), then even though the means of cognition is different, since the object of cognition remains in the same state, it would still have as its object something already cognized. Furthermore, this qualification [“of an unapprehended object”] is made with reference to that [object]; otherwise, it would be untenable due to the absence of anything to be excluded, because the totality of the means of cognition necessarily produces a specific cognition. If one maintains that the difference in cognition everywhere arises solely from the difference in the object of cognition, then the momentariness of every cognition would follow. Therefore, for one who asserts that “a means of cognition is that which reaches an unapprehended object,” recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) would indeed be a means of cognition. Likewise, in the case of hair, nails, and so forth that have grown back after being cut, recognition occurs despite the difference [in the individual hairs], owing to similarity. And in the case of universals (*sāmānya*) and the like, it is because of the actual existence of the object; thus, since two types [of objects] are observed, recognition occurs in the case of sound when no difference is perceived. Nor is it non-authoritative because the manifestors are doubtful, since the self-validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) of cognition was already refuted earlier. Moreover, if one admits the apprehension of non-difference through another means of cognition, then let that [other means] suffice; what is the use of recognition? Furthermore, since manifestors are momentary, they vanish immediately after the cognition of the sound; thus, recognition would be without an object. Nor is there eternality of the manifestors, because that would entail the manifestation of the sound at all times.

Now, [it may be argued that] sound persists until the time of recognition because recognition would otherwise be inexplicable. No; for it exists even otherwise. Even though it is impermanent, recognition certainly arises due to similarity. Sound, which is the subject of dispute, does not persist until the time of recognition, because it is the object of the cognition of sound, like a previously experienced sound. Furthermore, recognition is not sufficient to establish permanence, as it occurs even in the case of impermanent things.

Now, is its persistence (*avasthāyitva*) being proved? Even in that case, if there is persistence within a continuum (*santati*), that same refutation applies. However, proving mere persistence (*avasthānamātra*) is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because we admit that [the sound] persists until the time of perceiving the object, through the sequence of perception, convention, and recollection. Or, is it being argued that because there is recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) even when a word previously perceived is separated by years and so forth, its persistence during the interval is being proved? No, for recognition is observed even when there is difference (*anyatva*). For example, Devadatta, perceived in his childhood state, is recognized upon perception in his old age despite the difference. Nor should it be said that here there is merely a difference of states (*avasthābheda*) of the body, because no such thing is perceived apart from the arrangement of parts, size (*parimāṇa*), color, and so forth. For in the childhood state the arrangement of parts is loose, while in the youth state it is otherwise; thus, due to this difference, a difference in the body is inevitable, since we observe the destruction of a causal substance (*kāryadravya*) through the destruction of its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and because we observe a difference in size. The subsequent size occurs only upon the cessation of the previous size, because the commencement of a size in that which already possesses a size is prohibited. This is the same for color and other qualities as well. Furthermore, the destruction of size is due solely to the destruction of the substratum; thus, there is indeed difference. This is because the difference in size among bodies such as those of children is pervaded (*vyāpta*) by difference itself, as seen in the case of a *kuvalaya* fruit and so on. If it is argued that there is a property (*dharma*) denoted by the words "childhood state" and so forth, which is mutually exclusive [of other states], and that if this were distinct [from the body], then even in the old age state one would perceive the child and others [since they would not have ceased], because there would be no contradiction [between the two]; or, if there were a contradiction, how could difference be unestablished?—then even if they are not distinct, the consequence follows that the substratum itself would likewise appear and disappear along with their manifestation and disappearance. Therefore, just as there is the cognition "this is that very Devadatta" despite a difference in the body due to similarity, so too will there be recognition in the case of sound. Thus, since the absence of [sound] is perceived immediately after its perception by the operation of the auditory organ itself, recognition which grasps unity is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).

Even if one accepts the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*) as the locus of manifestation, if sound were manifested there, it would be perceived by persons situated in all locations, because it is all-pervading and its state of being unobstructed is no different everywhere. Likewise, if only certain parts of it are manifested, then since those parts are non-different [from the whole], the manifestation would belong to the sound itself; thus, the same fault remains. On the other hand, if they are different, how could the sound denote its meaning upon the manifestation of those parts? Furthermore, if the absence of sound is determined as a qualifier of the sound, it has already been stated previously that this occurs only through the relation characterized as the qualifier-qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya*) relationship.

If it is argued that the non-perception of sound immediately after its perception is due to the absence of a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) and not due to its non-existence, we say no; for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its existence [as a latent entity], and because an obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) and so forth are themselves unperceived. Indeed, an imperceptible obscuration of something perceptible by the senses has never been observed through any means of knowledge. Even if such an obscuration were admitted, since sound is all-pervasive (*vyāpaka*), there would be perception of it by persons situated in all locations whenever it is manifested in one place, because its all-pervasiveness remains unchanged when it is unobscured. Furthermore, if [the opponents claim] that the parts [of speech] consist of sound and convey specific meanings, this is merely a difference in terminology.

Now, [the opponent argues: "Does not air, possessing momentum and having produced motion due to its contact with the drumstick and depending on its own velocity, reach the location of the ear and become connected with it? It then displaces the stagnant internal airs situated there; thus, in the absence of such obstructions, the ear becomes the perceiver of sound? [The response is: Even so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving all sounds simultaneously, for when the auditory organ is refined (*saṃskṛta*), all sounds are present to it. Nor can it be said that the air impelled for the sake of manifesting the sound of a cow does not manifest the sound of a horse, because no such restriction is observed among manifestors (*vyañjaka*). For example, a lamp produced for the purpose of manifesting a jar manifests other objects situated in the same place and perceivable by the same sense organ. To explain: the ear is not something to be refined by a specific refiner, because it illuminates objects situated in the same place and perceivable by the same sense organ, just like the eye. The phrase "situated in the same place" is used because an object located outside the space occupied by a lamp is not perceived by the eye even if that space is illuminated by the lamp. The phrase "perceivable by the same sense organ" is used because color, taste, and so forth, though situated in the same place, are not perceived [by the eye]. Or, the sounds under dispute are not manifested by specific manifestors, because they are situated in the same place and perceivable by the same sense organ, like a jar and other such things. In this context, those which are not to be refined by specific refiners—such as the eye and a jar—are the similar instances (*sapakṣa*); the reason (*hetu*) exists in them. Conversely, those which are the opposite are the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*); therefore, the reason is entirely excluded from them. Furthermore, it is observed that the eye, refined by a lamp, illuminates a jar and other objects simultaneously. Thus, the ear too would be the perceiver of all sounds at once. And here, just as in the case of "relative cognition" (*apekṣābuddhi*), a single cognition has multiple objects as its support, or the sounds are uttered simultaneously due to rapid succession. [Objection: But even in the case of a single piece of earth, white and other colors are not manifested simultaneously by the eye, even when it is refined; likewise, odor and other qualities are not manifested simultaneously by the nose and other organs. [Response: Even so, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the reason, because a reason that exists in only a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣaikadeśavṛtti*) is still capable of proving the conclusion.

Now, just as the eye is not the simultaneous illuminator of various distinctions such as white and so forth—even though they are apprehended by the same sense organ and reside in the same location—so too would the ear be. And it was accepted during the demonstration of variegated color (*citrarūpa*) that even on the earth there is the state of being the locus of multiple colors. This is true; nevertheless, the non-apprehension of the distinct colors is due to the absence of auxiliary causes. Thus, it has been stated that the sense organ, assisted by the perception of parts possessing various colors, is the grasper of multiple colors in the whole (*avayavin*), because a variegated appearance occurs when those [auxiliaries] are present. But for the ear, which is refined by air, there is no cause for the non-apprehension of all sounds, since they are all in its proximity. Generals (*sāmānya*), however, are manifested by specific manifestors (*vyañjaka*) and do not occupy the same location [as their substrata], precisely because they are omnipresent within their own objects; thus, there is no deviation [in the rule]. Likewise, the manifestation of odor occurs in oil through contact with sunlight; or at the end of summer, in scorched fields, through contact with the first showers from the clouds. Yet, in these cases, there is no identity of location. Or rather, when the showers from the clouds come into contact [with the ground], wind arises from within the earth; through the sequence of motion in the parts, the previous substance ceases to exist, and when another substance is produced via the process of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth through heating (*pāka*), the odor is manifested. Furthermore, whatever is manifested—be it a general property, color, or the like—is observed to remain situated in its very substrate; this would also be the case for sound. But since that is not the case, sound lacks the nature of being a manifested entity.

Likewise, since the sound of a donkey would also be manifested by that which manifests the sound of a lute, the sound of the lute would never be perceived at all if it were grasped [simultaneously]. But this is not the case; for we observe that in some instances the sound of a lute and other such sounds are suppressed by the sound of a donkey. Furthermore, this relationship of the suppressed and the suppressor is not possible on the view that sound is eternal, because distinctions such as "more intense" and so forth would be impossible. The suppression of a faint sound upon the perception of a more intense sound consists in its non-perception. Nor is it tenable that the non-perception of one sound occurs simply because a more intense manifesting agent (*vyañjaka*) causes the perception of another, for it has already been stated that no such restriction is observed among manifesting agents. Moreover, this cognition—"the sound is intense," "the sound is faint"—is co-referential with the cognition of the sound itself, not with the cognition of the manifesting agent; how then could intensity and so forth be attributes of the manifesting agent? Thus, because they are distinguished by differences such as intensity, sounds are non-eternal, like pleasure and other such qualities. Furthermore, since their coming into being after having not existed is observed when the manifesting agent is absent, they are effects and therefore non-eternal, like a jar and other such things. Likewise, while being distinct from the attributes of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), they are non-eternal because they are specific pervasive attributes (*viśeṣaguṇa*), like pleasure and other such qualities. This has been stated in the section on Space (*ākāśa*): "Space possesses non-eternal specific attributes, because, while being distinct from the atoms of water and so forth, it is an element (*bhūta*), like earth and the others. And: "While being distinct from the atom that is the substratum of spherical dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*) and inferable through priority (*paratva*), [space] is a material cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), just like earth and the others."

Now, there is an inference for the status of sound as a quality (*guṇa*): sound is not of the nature of a substance (*dravya*) or an action (*karman*), because it is capable of being apprehended by the sense of hearing, like the universal "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*). Sound is a quality, because, while being distinct from substances and actions, it is related to existence (*sattā*), like color and other qualities. As for the claim that the eternity of words is known through the otherwise inexplicable nature of the comprehension of meaning, that is incorrect; for even if they are non-eternal, the comprehension of meaning occurs provided that similarity (*sādṛśya*) is grasped. Whenever one perceives the *ga*, *au*, and *visarjanīya* [phonemes] in such a sequence, one should understand the object qualified by "cowness" (*gotva*), and it should be communicated; thus, once the convention (*saṅketa*) has been grasped, perceiving a word of that kind, one comprehends and communicates that object.

Thus, impermanence being established, he states the cause of destruction as "that which is opposed to both the effect and the cause. The first sound is opposed by its effect; the last, however, opposes its cause; and those occurring in between are opposed both by their effects and by their causes. "Born from conjunction, disjunction, and sound" is the cause of its production, according to the *Vaiśeṣika Sūtra*: "The production of sound arises from conjunction, from disjunction, and from sound."

It is of two kinds. In what form? As that characterized by phonemes (*varṇalakṣaṇa*) and that characterized by non-phonemes (*avarṇalakṣaṇa*). That which consists of [sounds] beginning with *a* and ending with *ha* is characterized by phonemes. That for which the cause is something such as a conch shell is "caused by that" (*tannimitta*), meaning it is characterized by non-phonemes. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), other instrumental causes are also included.

In this regard, the production of phonemes (*varṇa*) is explained. From the conjunction of the self and the mind, which serves as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and depending upon memory, there arises the desire to utter a phoneme. Immediately after that, there is effort (*prayatna*). Depending upon that effort, from the conjunction of the self and the vital air (*vāyu*), which serves as the non-inherent cause, motion arises in the air, which serves as the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). That air, having produced motion, moves upward and strikes the throat and other [articulatory organs]. By the word "and others" (*ādi*), the palate, lips, and so forth are included. Thereafter, depending upon the conjunction of the air with the articulatory organ, there occurs the conjunction of the organ with space (*ākāśa*), from which the production of the phoneme results. In this process, space is the inherent cause, the conjunction of the organ with space is the non-inherent cause, and the conjunction of the organ with the air is the efficient cause (*apekṣākāraṇa*).

Sound characterized by non-manifestation (avarṇalakṣaṇa) also arises from the conjunction of a drum and space, depending on the conjunction of the drum and a stick; by the phrase "and so forth," direction, time, and other factors are included. Here too, space is the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa); the conjunction of the drum and space is the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa), and the conjunction of the drum and stick, etc., is the instrumental cause (nimittakāraṇa). Likewise, sound is produced in space from the disjunction of the joint and space—which is the non-inherent cause—depending on the disjunction of the bamboo joint [from its preceding part].

It demonstrates that sound is produced from sound: thus, a sound fully established through conjunction and disjunction initiates other successive sounds in all directions. Therefore, from that non-inherent cause—which depends upon its proximity to its own cause—another sound arises in space; this is the continuity of sound, like the succession of waves. For just as a wave produced by the impact of a large stone or similar object initiates another wave, and that in turn initiates yet another, so there is a succession; in this manner, according to the principle of continuity, the sound is perceived when it has reached the location of the auditory organ.

And this is postulated; otherwise, because those [sounds] would be non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti) by virtue of inhering in a different location—distinct from the portion of space characterized by the conjunction with the auditory canal (karṇaśaṣkulī)—there would be no specific proximity (viśiṣṭapratyāsatti), and thus there would be no perception at all. As it has been said: "Since movement of both the auditory organ and the sound is impossible, if a series (santāna) is not admitted, there can be no mutual contact. And since perception occurs only of that which has reached [the sense], a series is postulated."

Now, on this view, if sounds were to produce another sound only in the very portion of space occupied by themselves, there would be no perception of anything at all, because all [sounds] would be exhausted in one and the same place. If, however, they were to do so in a different location, then even the speech of Brahmā would be perceived here in the region of our ears, due to the production of another sound there.

Now, if [the first sound] were to begin [producing another sound] immediately after its own location, even at a distance of a mere atom, then there would be a perception of those [subsequent sounds] only after an interval of hundreds of moments or more. However, that is not observed, since they are heard after an interval of only two or three moments. Furthermore: "The initial sound does not produce another sound, because it is a sound, like the final sound"; or alternatively, "The final sound produces another sound, because it is a sound, like the initial sound. Therefore, they hold that when the existence of a series [of sounds] is refuted, the arrival of the manifesting agent—namely, air—is postulated on the grounds that the perception of sound would otherwise be inexplicable.

And this is not tenable. For the theory of individual manifestation (*vyaktipakṣa*) has already been refuted, and there is no evidence for the arrival of air. Nor is the perception of sound itself a proof [for its movement], since that can be accounted for through the principle of a continuous series (*santāna*). Furthermore, the objection raised here is refuted by the presentation of the analogy of waves. Just as a wave produced by the impact of a large stone initiates another wave in the space immediately adjacent to its own location, and not on the shore or elsewhere, so too sound, depending on its proximity to its own cause, initiates another sound in the immediately adjacent space. Nor does it follow that there would be perception after an interval of hundreds of moments, because only six types of sounds—distinguished by degrees of intensity such as "loud" and so on—are produced. To explain: when a sound arises from the impact of a drum and a stick, one who is nearby perceives the sound as "most intense," while one further away perceives it as "more intense. Then, in succession, the six varieties—"intense," "weak," "weaker," and "weakest"—are experienced. Thus, the defect mentioned regarding the theory of infinite propagation does not apply. Indeed, it is imagined that from the impact of the drum and stick, a single sound arises pervading a vast extent of space, and thus it is perceived by many people; it is not a continuous series (*santāna*) everywhere. As for the argument: "The first sound does not initiate another sound, because it is a sound, like the final sound"—this is not an independent proof, because the categories of "first" and "final" sounds are not established in themselves. Nor is it possible for a reason (*hetu*) to possess the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) or for there to be external concomitance (*bahirvyāpti*) when both the subject of the example and the subject of the thesis are unestablished. If you claim this is a *reductio ad absurdum* (*paravyāpti*) against an opponent, that is not so. If the opponent's concomitance is based on valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then the opposing inference cannot arise because it is sublated by that very same knowledge. If, however, it is not based on valid knowledge, then the proof is "unestablished in its locus" (*āśrayāsiddha*) due to the non-establishment of the object of knowledge, and the example is "unestablished in its subject" (*dharmyasiddha*), because the specific qualifications of "first" and "final" are themselves unestablished when one seeks to deny that a sound initiates another sound. Therefore, once the theory of individual manifestation is refuted, the postulation of a continuous series is made because the perception of sound would otherwise be inexplicable. Furthermore, there is no evidence for the postulation that the final sound is productive [of another], as that would entail the consequence of its being perceived at all times. Consequently, since the destruction of the final sound is observed through valid means—either through its inherence in a single object conjoined with a tangible substance, or through the exhaustion of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) that brings about experience based on its own cognition—and since causeless destruction has been refuted, its destruction is postulated from the aforementioned causes alone. Enough said.
Thus ends the category of quality (*guṇa*) in the *Vyomavatī*, a commentary on the *Padārthadharmasaṅgraha* composed by the venerable teacher Vyomaśiva.
[Now follows] the determination of the common properties of action (*karman*).

“Even though all five—throwing upwards and the rest—are connected with the nature of action (*karmatva*), their specific characteristics are as follows: they reside in a single substance; they are momentary; they subsist in corporeal substances; they are devoid of qualities; they are produced by gravity, fluidity, effort, and conjunction; they are opposed by the conjunction that is their own effect; they are causes independent of [other] conjunctions and disjunctions; they are non-inherent causes; they initiate effects inherent in themselves and in others; they do not initiate effects of their own kind; they do not initiate substances; they possess a restricted genus; and their distinction lies in initiating effects characterized by spatial direction.”

Now, demonstrating the commonality (*sādharmya*) that pervades its own subdivisions by way of its dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) with other categories, as well as defining their mutual differences (*vaidharmya*) and their causes, he says: "Of throwing upwards (*utkṣepaṇa*), etc. It is not merely the connection with *karmatva* (the state of being action) for two or three of them; rather, it is for all five. This is the inherence (*samavāya*) characterized by *karmatva*. Thus, throwing upwards and the others are distinct from other things, or they are to be designated as "actions," because of their connection with *karmatva*. "Existence in a single substance" (*ekadravyavattvam*): That which is both one and a substance is a "single substance" (*ekadravya*). That which possesses this is "existing in a single substance" (*ekadravyavat*). The state of being such is "existence in a single substance. A single action exists in only one substance, and likewise, only one [action] exists in one [substance]. Why is this so? Because when one thing moves, the movement of all [other actions] is not perceived. Even where many [actions] move at the same time, there too there is only multiplicity, because the causes—such as impact (*abhighāta*)—differ according to each substratum. Furthermore, if one were to accept that an impact occurring in one place has a different inherent cause in another place, then [action] would arise in all substances simultaneously, since there is no distinction. Likewise, if action were destroyed in one substance due to a conjunction, then even in another substratum, its destruction would occur if it were a single entity. And if multiple actions were accepted in a single substance, then when facing opposite directions, there would be no movement at all due to mutual obstruction. If they face the same direction, since conjunction and disjunction would be produced by a single action alone, there is no proof for the existence of a second one. Moreover, the destruction of the previous action and the arising of another action following a subsequent conjunction is indeed accepted in some cases. Therefore, wherever there is the appearance of two actions, it should be understood as being due to rapid succession (*āśubhāvitva*). Now, since "existence in a single substance" applies to color (*rūpa*) and so forth as well, the term "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*) is included; nevertheless, the phrase "subsisting in corporeal (*mūrta*) substances" is added to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to cognition (*buddhi*) and the like.

Now, if it is argued that there is no deviation [from the definition] because "action" (karman) is defined as existing only in corporeal substances (mūrtadravya) while being momentary (kṣaṇika), this is true; nevertheless, the other terms are included for the purpose of demonstrating similarity and for the sake of examination. "Produced from gravity, fluidity, effort, and conjunction" means *gurutva-dravatva-prayatna-saṃyogaja*; its state is its "nature" (*tattva*). This is an illustration, since it can also arise from other causes. Furthermore, gravity and the others, though capable of producing other effects when taken individually, do not produce anything else besides action when combined; thus, they are indeed unique [to action]. Nor is this [nature] pervasive across all varieties of action; therefore, it is merely a point of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). Alternatively, what is intended is the state of being produced by any one of the causes beginning with gravity. Likewise, there is the property of being opposed by its own effect, namely conjunction (*saṃyoga*). The term "its own effect" is used because destruction is not observed through mere conjunction [without such an effect]. Since both disjunction (*vibhāga*) and momentum (*vega*) are also effects of action, the inclusion of "conjunction" is to exclude deviation [from the definition] in those cases. Therefore, although being opposed by its own effect—conjunction—is unique to action, it does not pervade the entire class of actions, as action is sometimes destroyed even by the destruction of its substrate; thus, it is merely a point of dissimilarity. Likewise, the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of action is to be an independent cause (*nirapekṣakāraṇatva*) when performing both disjunction and conjunction.

Is it not the case that independence (*anapekṣakāraṇatva*) is intended for disjunction (*vibhāga*), whereas in the case of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), one must depend upon the prior destruction of conjunction that occurs subsequently; thus, independence is unestablished? No, because that [independence] is established with respect to dependence on a real entity (*vastubhūta*) as a cause. Furthermore, it is said to be "independent" because it does not depend on a cause that exists apart from non-existence (*abhāva*). And since this is not possible for anything else, it is unique (*asādhāraṇa*).

The state of being a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇatva*) is its specific property, distinguished from others. For qualities (*guṇa*), there is a twofold nature: being a non-inherent cause and being an efficient cause (*nimitta*). However, for upward motion (*utkṣepaṇa*) and the rest, there is only the state of being a non-inherent cause; they do not possess this twofold nature. Thus, there is an absolute exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), because the intended meaning is the negation of that twofold nature. Likewise, it is the producer of effects inherent in both itself and another substratum. An action, being inherent in a certain substratum, produces disjunction, conjunction, and [other effects] inherent in that substratum and in another substratum. It does not produce effects of the same class (*samānajātīya*); for instance, an action, once produced, is observed to produce disjunction and conjunction, but not another action, since multiple actions in a single substrate have already been previously refuted. It does not produce substance (*dravya*); an action does not originate a substance, because it is impossible for it to be a cause when it is in a state of perishing due to a subsequent conjunction. This is a common characteristic (*sādharmya*) pervading its own divisions. "Connection with a specific genus" means that a specific genus, such as "upward-motion-ness" (*utkṣepaṇatva*) and so on, belongs to all five. Furthermore, the mutual distinction is their being the producers of effects characterized by direction.

“Among these, upward motion (*utkṣepaṇa*) is that action which, arising from gravity, effort, and conjunction, causes conjunction with upper parts and disjunction from lower parts in the limbs of the body and in things connected to them; the opposite action, which causes conjunction with lower parts and disjunction from upper parts, is downward motion (*apakṣepaṇa*).

“Contraction (*ākuñcana*) is that action by which, when a straight substance [is bent], there occurs disjunction of its tip-parts from their respective locations and conjunction of its base-parts with those same locations, whereby the whole becomes curved.”
“Conversely, regarding the production of conjunctions and disjunctions: that action by which a whole becomes straight is extension (*prasāraṇa*).
That which is the cause of conjunctions and disjunctions with points in space in no fixed direction is locomotion (*gamana*).”

He states that very point: "Among these, throwing upward (utkṣepaṇa) is that action which arises from gravity, fluidity, effort, and conjunction—either collectively or individually—as the cause of conjunction with those things situated above and the cause of disjunction from those situated below. From what [causes] and in what [objects] does it arise? It arises from gravity, fluidity, effort, and conjunction, whether combined or separate. That is called "throwing upward" for the sake of illustration, since velocity and other factors can also be its causes. As for the determination of its substratum: it occurs in the limbs of the body, such as the hands and feet, and in objects connected to them, such as clubs and the like.

Action that is the cause of conjunctions and disjunctions contrary to those [previously mentioned] is *apakṣepaṇa* (throwing downward). It is the cause of disjunction with parts directed upward and the cause of conjunction with parts directed downward. *Ākuñcana* (contraction) is the disjunction of the front parts of a straight substance from their respective locations—namely, the regions of space and so forth characterized by them—and the conjunction of those same parts with the root regions, namely, the regions of space and so forth characterized by those very roots. That action, once produced, by which a curved whole becomes straight, is *prasāraṇa* (extension).

That which is the cause of conjunctions and disjunctions with indefinite directions and locations is *gamana* (motion). This means it is the cause of conjunctions and disjunctions with those indefinite directional locations other than the aforementioned ones.

"Thus, all five types of action [occur] in the limbs of the body and in things connected to them, whether they are perceived (*sat-pratyaya*) or unperceived (*asat-pratyaya*). That which is different from these occurs only unperceived; in those and in other things, that is *gamana*. <PDhS>

He states the conclusion: "Thus, this fivefold action is both with cause (*sat-pratyaya*) and without cause (*asat-pratyaya*). *Pratyaya* means cause; and because of the qualification "existent" (*sat*), even when expressed by a general term, what is intended here is specifically that which is called effort (*prayatna*). Alternatively, effort is called the "cause" (*pratyaya*) because it is the effect of a causal chain. Therefore, that action for which there is an existent cause is described as such; that is to say, it is preceded by effort. That which is without cause is not preceded by effort. And that occurs in the limbs of the body and in things connected to them. Whatever is other than this is "without cause," meaning not preceded by effort, because our effort has no operation therein. And that occurs in these and other substances; since it is distinct from throwing upwards (*utkṣepaṇa*) and the rest, it is indeed locomotion (*gamana*).

“It is incorrect that actions are of five types, because there is no difference in their being motion. For every momentary action, having arisen as mere motion, produces conjunctions and disjunctions with points of space—whether above, below, or across—by its own substratum’s atomic-sized parts; thus, the cognition of ‘motion’ is indistinguishable everywhere, and therefore all action is simply motion. [Reply: No, because we observe the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions according to classes. Here [we see] ‘throwing upward,’ elsewhere ‘throwing downward,’ and so on; in all such cases, the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions according to classes are observed. From this, a distinction between universals and particulars is understood as the cause of those [cognitions]. Furthermore, due to the specific prefixes such as *ut-* and others, and because they initiate effects characterized by specific directions, a distinction in their defining characteristics (*upalakṣaṇa*) is also established.”

It is incorrect to maintain that there are only five types of action (*karman*). Why? Because there is no distinction in their movement; the objection is that they are indistinguishable from the act of moving itself. He explains this: "Everything is momentary. Momentariness is common to all actions, and thus there is no distinction based on their essential nature (*svarūpa*). A mere motion, once produced, effects conjunctions and disjunctions of its own substratum. With what [does it conjoin]? With the spatial points (*pradeśa*) above, below, across, and those as small as the interstices between atoms—that is, with as many points as allow for the entry of one atom into another. Nor is there a distinction based on the difference in their effects, since every [action] produces these same effects. Likewise, the cognition of "movement" is uniform everywhere: one moves upward from the front point to the base point, and from the base point back to the front point. Therefore, the conclusion is that everything is simply movement. "No," says the respondent, "because we observe the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions according to classes. As for the claim that "everything is movement," this is not so, because we observe the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions within the classes of throwing upwards (*utkṣepaṇa*), throwing downwards (*apakṣepaṇa*), and so forth. He explains this: "Here is throwing upwards, there is throwing downwards," and so on. Thus, in every class, the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions are observed. For instance, in the class of "throwing upwards," the cognition "throwing upwards, throwing upwards" recurs, while it is excluded from the classes of "throwing downwards" and the rest. Similarly, "throwing downwards" recurs within its own class and is excluded from other distinct types. The cause of this is understood to be a specific universal (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*) such as "throwing-upward-ness" (*utkṣepaṇatva*), which is the cause of the recurring and excluding cognitions.
