It is not the case that there is only one universal, "movement-ness" (*gamanatva*), because there exist mutually exclusive genera (*jāti*) connected to the distinctions of throwing upwards and the rest. Their mutual distinction arises from the specific prefixes (*upasarga*) such as *ud-* and *apa-*. For example, throwing preceded by *ud-* is "throwing upwards" (*utkṣepaṇa*); preceded by *apa-* it is "throwing downwards" (*apakṣepaṇa*); preceded by *ā-* it is "contraction" (*ākuñcana*); preceded by *pra-* it is "extension" (*prasāraṇa*); whereas "movement" (*gamana*) is distinguished precisely by the absence of any prefix. Furthermore, because they initiate effects characterized by specific directions, the distinction in their defining characteristics (*upalakṣaṇa*)—such as throwing upwards—is established. Thus, it has been stated that the definition of throwing upwards is being the cause of conjunction with a point above and the cause of disjunction from a point below, and so forth. And there is a distinction among the defining characteristics themselves, such as "throwing-upward-ness" and the rest.

“Even so, the restriction that there are ‘only five’ is untenable, because in actions such as going out and entering, we observe the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions according to their respective groups. If it is maintained that a difference in genus (*jāti*) is accepted for throwing upwards (*utkṣepaṇa*) and the rest because the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions are observed throughout them in their respective groups, then the same must apply to going out, entering, and so forth. If it is argued that the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions in those [latter] cases are due to a difference in effect (*kāryabheda*), we say no; for then the same consequence would follow regarding the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions in throwing upwards and the rest, as they too differ in their effects. Alternatively, if it is claimed that while the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions in groups is equally present in both cases, there is a specific reason why a difference in genus exists only for throwing upwards and the rest, but not for going out and the rest—we say no, because this leads to the fallacy of the confusion of genera (*jātisaṅkara*). If the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions in going out and the rest were due to a difference in genus, then the confusion of genera would necessarily follow. How so? When two observers see someone moving from one room to another, they simultaneously perceive the cognition of ‘going out’ and ‘entering,’ as well as the cognitions ‘he enters’ and ‘he goes out’ at the doorway. However, when a curtain or similar barrier is removed, there is neither the cognition of entering nor the cognition of going out; rather, there is only the cognition of ‘moving. Similarly, when a bamboo leaf or similar object falls through a tube, many observers simultaneously perceive the cognitions of ‘whirling,’ ‘falling,’ and ‘entering. Thus, there is the fallacy of the confusion of genera. Such a confusion of cognitions is not observed in the case of throwing upwards and the rest. Therefore, the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions in throwing upwards and the rest are due to a difference in genus, whereas in going out and the rest, they are due to a difference in effect.”

Even so, the restriction that there are "only five" is untenable, because among those [motions] exceeding throwing upwards and the rest—such as going out, entering, and so forth—one observes the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions according to their respective groups. Furthermore, if generalities and particularities were present, an undesirable infinity of motions would result. Anticipating the opponent's intention—that the recurrence of cognitions in cases such as going out is due to a difference in effect (*kāryabheda*) and not due to the presence of generalities and particularities—the author says: "In the case of throwing upwards and the others as well, the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions would follow solely from a difference in effect."

Just as "going out" (*niṣkramaṇa*) occurs through the production of conjunction with an external space and the production of disjunction from an internal space, and "entering" (*praveśana*) is the opposite, so too will "throwing upward" (*utkṣepaṇa*) and so forth occur through the production of conjunction with an upper space and the production of disjunction from a lower space. Now, since there is an equal presence of the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions in groups for both "throwing upward" and so forth, and "going out" and so forth, there is no specific reason why a distinction of universals (*jāti*) should belong only to "throwing upward" and the rest, but not to "going out" and the rest.

This is not so, because it would entail the confusion of universals (*jāti-saṅkara*). To explain: since there is a difference in the universals of "going out" (*niṣkramaṇa*) and so forth, when there is a recurrence and exclusion of cognitions, the confusion of universals—the coexistence of contradictory universals—would follow. And that is undesirable, as it is never observed elsewhere. Although [universals] such as "existence" (*sattā*) and "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*), which are divided into higher and lower levels, do exist in a single individual (*vyakti*), nevertheless [contradictory ones like] "cowness" (*gotva*) and "horseness" (*aśvatva*) are not observed [in one]. Here, however, there is the contingency of the universals of "going out-ness" (*niṣkramaṇatva*) and "entering-ness" (*praveśanatva*) occurring in a single individual. How so? He says: "Because two observers simultaneously perceive the cognitions of 'going out' and 'entering' with respect to one and the same individual action. To whose action is this? He says: "Of a person moving from one room to another room. For instance, when there is only one door between two rooms and two persons are stationed on either side, as another person passes through, the cognitions of "going out" and "entering" are indeed observed simultaneously due to the perception of specific conjunctions (*saṃyoga*) and disjunctions (*vibhāga*). Thus, at the doorway, one says "he enters" and "he goes out. For the observer who perceives disjunction within his own room and conjunction outside, the cognition "he goes out" arises; whereas for the one who perceives conjunction within his own room and disjunction outside, the cognition "he enters" arises. But when the curtain or screen is removed—and by the word "etcetera," the removal of other obstructions such as walls—then, because no distinct difference in the effect is perceived, there is neither the cognition of "going out" nor the cognition of "entering. What then? Only the cognition of "going" (*gamana*) arises. Therefore, since there is the contingency of the coexistence of contradictory universals in this single individual action of going, it has been stated that the difference in cognition arises solely from the difference in the effect. Likewise, when a bamboo leaf or similar object falls into a tube, observers situated above, below, and across simultaneously perceive the cognitions of "whirling," "falling," and "entering"; thus, there is the contingency of a confusion of universals such as "whirling-ness" (*bhramaṇatva*) and the rest.

In order to avoid the charge of a fault within his own position, he says: "Nor is such a confusion of cognitions observed in the case of upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*) and the rest, out of fear of which one would have to accept a distinction based on the difference of effects in order to avoid the undesirable consequence of the coexistence of contradictory universals. He states the conclusion: "Therefore, the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions in the case of upward throwing and the rest is due to the difference of universals, whereas in the case of exiting and the rest, it is due to the difference of effects."

“If it is asked how there can be a difference in cognitions simultaneously [regarding the same object], and if it is thought that just as there is no confusion of universals (*jāti-saṅkara*), so too there is no confusion of multiple actions in a single substance—then how could there be simultaneous cognitions of whirling, falling, and entering in respect to a single action? To this we reply: No, because of the difference in the conjunctions and disjunctions with spatial directions belonging to the parts and the whole. For one who perceives the successive conjunctions and disjunctions of the parts with the points of space on their sides, a cognition of whirling arises. One who observes the disjunction of the whole from the upper region and its conjunction with the lower region has a cognition of falling. Furthermore, one who perceives the conjunction at the inner end of a tube and the disjunction at the outer end has a cognition of entering. Thus, it is established that the difference in cognitions such as exiting and so forth results from the difference in their effects.”

He anticipates an objection: "How can there be a difference in cognitions simultaneously? To explain this: it has already been stated that just as there is no confusion of universals (*jāti-saṅkara*), so too there is no confusion of multiple actions in a single object. Therefore, since there is an absence of causes for a single action, how can there arise for observers simultaneously distinct cognitions—such as revolving, falling, and entering—which are mutually exclusive, given that an effect cannot arise in the absence of its cause? To this we reply (and so forth), providing the refutation: Your claim that the cognitions of revolving and so on simply do not arise due to the absence of causes is incorrect. This is possible because of the difference in the conjunctions and disjunctions of the parts and the whole with respect to spatial directions. "Parts and whole" refers to the members and the composite; [the cause is] the difference in their conjunctions and disjunctions characterized by spatial directions. He explains this very point: for the observer who perceives the conjunctions and disjunctions of the parts with successive points of space on the sides, the cognition of "revolving" arises. But for one who observes the disjunction of the whole from an upper point of space and its conjunction with a lower point, the cognition of "falling"—specifically "the leaf falls"—arises. Furthermore, for one who sees the conjunction within the interior of the tube or the pit and the disjunction from the exterior point of space, the cognition of "entering"—specifically "the leaf enters"—arises. Therefore, it is established that the difference in cognitions such as exiting and so on results from a difference in the effects, not from a difference in universals (*jāti-bheda*).

Others, however, maintain that since actions are innumerable due to their divisions such as whirling (*bhramaṇa*), ejecting (*recana*), flowing (*syandana*), and upward flaming (*ūrdhvajvalana*), there is no obstacle to establishing a distinction between the cognitions of "going" (*niṣkramaṇa*) and so forth based on a difference in genus (*jāti*); therefore, this [view] is not their own opinion. Nor do they believe that whirling, ejecting, and the like are included within "going" alone. But this is not correct, because it will be stated that "going" is a synonym for "action" (*karma*) in general, and because the logical obstacle of the consequence of a confusion of genera (*jātisaṅkara*) is firm.

“Let it be that there is a difference in the cognition [of motion] regarding upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*) and so forth due to a difference in their generic properties (*jāti*), whereas for going (*gamana*) and so forth, it is due to a difference in their effects (*kārya*). Now, is ‘going-ness’ (*gamanatva*) a synonym for ‘action-ness’ (*karmatva*), or is it another universal (*sāmānya*)? From what source does this doubt arise? Because, just as there is the cognition of ‘action’ in all [the types] beginning with upward throwing, there is no distinction in the cognition of ‘going,’ it is understood to be a synonym for ‘action-ness. But since it is designated by a specific name (*viśeṣasaṃjñā*) like upward throwing and so forth, one might think it must be another universal? No; because it is a synonym for ‘action-ness. Just as ‘selfhood’ (*ātmatva*) and ‘personhood’ (*puruṣatva*) are synonyms, ‘going-ness’ is indeed a synonym for ‘action-ness. Now, for what purpose was the term ‘going’ specifically mentioned? It is not so, because it is for the sake of including whirling (*bhramaṇa*) and so forth. The mention of ‘going’ is made to include whirling, falling (*patana*), flowing (*syandana*), and others which are not included by the terms ‘upward throwing’ and so forth. Otherwise, it would follow that only those four which were stated by specific names would be the objects of the knowledge of both the general and the particular. Alternatively, let there be another universal called ‘going-ness’ which resides only in whirling and so forth—those causes of conjunctions and disjunctions with indefinite directions and locations. The word ‘going,’ however, should be regarded as being applied figuratively (*bhākta*) to upward throwing and so forth, on the basis of the commonality of being the agent of conjunctions and disjunctions of its own substratum.”

Let it be that there is a distinction between *utkṣepaṇa* (lifting) and the others due to a difference in their genus (*jāti*), but not so for *niṣkramaṇa* (going out) and the rest. Now, one must consider whether *gamanatva* (the nature of going) is a synonym for *karmatva* (the nature of action)—like the synonyms "jar" (*ghaṭa*) and "pitcher" (*kalaśa*)—or whether it is a distinct universal (*sāmānya*), like *utkṣepaṇatva* and the others. For what reason is this doubt? This is the Teacher’s question. But that [doubt] is untenable; for when a question is posed by one who is already in doubt, it is proper to provide its resolution, rather than to further provoke doubt, since the determination of the cause of that doubt has already been established previously through common characteristics (*sāmānyadharma*) and so forth. This is not a fault. Thinking that once the knowledge of the cause of doubt is attained, the application of the means to eliminate it can be accomplished without effort—just as a physician who has diagnosed the cause of a disease proceeds accordingly—the Teacher asks about the cause. Thus he says: because the cognition of "going" (*gamanapratyaya*) is no different from the cognition of "action" (*karmapratyaya*) in all instances of *utkṣepaṇa*, *bhramaṇa*, and so on, it is understood to be a synonym for *karmatva*. For just as the practice of designating "the action of lifting" (*utkṣepaṇakarma*) and "the action of throwing down" (*apakṣepaṇakarma*) shows that *karmatva* pervades all specific varieties, so too, because we observe the usage "it goes upward" (*ūrdhvaṃ gacchati*) and "it goes downward" (*adho gacchati*), "going" (*gamana*) also pervades all specific varieties; therefore, it is known to be a synonym for *karmatva*.

And it is not the case that there is absolute certainty here; for he says that since it is designated by a specific name (*viśeṣasaṃjñā*) like "throwing upwards" (*utkṣepaṇa*) and so on, it must therefore be a lower generality (*apara-sāmānya*). Indeed, when counting [the types of action] upon the observation of a specific instance, the designation of a general term is not seen at that moment, just as the designation "substance" (*dravya*) is not used at the time of designating "earth" and so forth. Therefore, because both forms of properties are perceived and because no specific [differentiating] features are perceived, one might raise the doubt: "Is 'going-ness' (*gamanatva*) a higher generality, like 'action-ness' (*karmatva*), or is it a lower generality, like 'throwing-upward-ness' (*utkṣepaṇatva*) and so forth? One should not entertain such a doubt. Because "going-ness" is a synonym (*paryāya*) of "action-ness," just like "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) or "personhood" (*puruṣatva*); for the logical principle is that wherever there is the cognition of "action," there is the perception of the cognition of "going. Now, why was "going" mentioned by its specific name? [The answer is: because we do not see the presentation of a general name at the time of a specific name. No; it is for the purpose of including rotation (*bhramaṇa*) and the rest. It is intended to include rotation, falling (*patana*), flowing (*syandana*), and so forth, which are not covered or subsumed by the terms "throwing upwards" and so on, and to make known their status as "actions. Otherwise, if "going" were not mentioned, only those four specifically named actions—throwing upwards and so forth—that were stated would result in being the objects of both the general and specific names. The general name would be "action" (*karman*), and the specific names would be "throwing upwards" and so on; consequently, only those four would be the objects of these names, and rotation and the rest would not be included. Why is this so? Because only those things that are the objects of specific names would also be the objects of the general name. Therefore, "going" is mentioned in order to make known that rotation and the rest are also "actions," just like throwing upwards and so on. And under this view, there is no fault even if rotation and the rest are connected with a lower generality (*apara-jāti*), because infinity is admitted in relation to them. As for the statement that rotation and the rest are included by the mention of "going," that has been explained otherwise.

Alternatively, let there be another lower-level generality (*sāmānya*) called "going-ness" (*gamanatva*), which resides only in [motions] such as whirling (*bhramaṇa*)—which are causes of conjunctions and disjunctions with points in space and directions that are not fixed—and not in upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*) and so forth. If so, how is it that the linguistic usage of "going" (*gamana*) applies to those [other motions]? To this he says: the word "going" should be regarded as figurative (*bhākta*) with respect to upward throwing and the rest. Why? Because of the common ground for metaphorical application (*upacārabīja*): namely, the commonality of being the agent of conjunctions and disjunctions with their own substratum. Just as an upward throw, once produced, effects conjunctions and disjunctions of its own substratum with other objects, so too does going. Nor does it follow from this very reason that, just as there is the linguistic usage of "going" in upward throwing and the rest, there should also be the linguistic usage of "upward throwing" and so forth in "going"; for the postulation of a cause proceeds from the actual existence of the effect. Furthermore, the linguistic usage of "upward throwing" and so forth is not observed in "going," in the same way that the linguistic usage of "going" is observed in upward throwing and the rest; therefore, this objection is not valid. Now, given the presentation of these two positions, what is intended here by the Teacher (*ācārya*)? By stating that the five [motions] possess distinct, specific genera, he intends that "going-ness" is indeed another lower-level generality.
Others, however, believe that since the real refutation was not stated under the view of the highest generality (*parasāmānya*), that very [view] is what is intended.

[As it says: “The rule for action possessing true cognition: How so? When one desires to raise or lower the hand during activities such as sacrifice, study, giving, or agriculture, then an effort arises in the portion of the self where the hand is located. From the conjunction of the self and the hand, depending upon that effort and gravity, action occurs in the hand; and as in the hand, so too in all limbs of the body, such as the feet, and in the body itself. (PDhS)

Previously, action (*karman*) was described as having both a true basis (*sat-pratyaya*) and a false basis (*asat-pratyaya*). Regarding that, he explains how the rule for action with a true basis is established: "In those things desired to be done" (*cikīrṣiteṣu*), meaning in acts one wishes to perform, such as sacrifice, study, giving, agriculture, and so forth—the word "etc. including eating and other activities. When, during sacrifices and the like, one desires to raise up or lower down the hand in order to take hold of sesame seeds and other materials, then an effort (*prayatna*) arises in that portion of the self (*ātman*) where the hand is located. In the production of that [effort], the self is the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*), the contact between the self and the mind (*ātma-manas-saṃyoga*) is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*), and the desire (*icchā*) is the instrumental cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*). Then, depending upon that effort and gravity (*gurutva*), an action arises in the hand—which serves as the inherent cause—due to the contact between the self and the hand, which serves as the non-inherent cause. This applies to all limbs of the body, such as the feet and so on, as well as to the body itself. Just as the contact between the self and the hand is the non-inherent cause and the effort is the instrumental cause in the production of the hand's action, so too, in the production of actions inherent in all bodily limbs and the body, the contact with the self is the non-inherent cause and the effort is the instrumental cause; this is the meaning of the extended application (*atideśa*).

"How is it [produced] even in those things connected to that [body]? When one, having grasped a pestle with the hand, forms the desire, 'I shall lift up the pestle with my hand,' immediately thereafter an effort arises. Depending upon that [effort], at the very same time that an action of lifting arises in the hand due to the conjunction of the self and the hand, an action also arises in the pestle due to the conjunction of the hand and the pestle, depending upon that very same effort. Then, when the pestle has been lifted high, the desire for that purpose ceases. Again, a desire to throw down arises; immediately thereafter an effort arises. Depending upon that [effort], from the aforementioned conjunctions, actions of throwing down occur simultaneously in both the hand and the pestle. Then, by the final action of the pestle, a conjunction called 'impact' (*abhighāta*) is produced between the mortar and the pestle. That conjunction, depending upon the velocity residing in the pestle, produces an action of upward-leaping in the pestle independently [of further effort]. That action, depending upon the impact, initiates a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) in the pestle. Depending upon that [impression], the conjunction of the hand and the pestle produces an action of upward-leaping in the hand as well, independently [of effort]. Even though the previous latent impression has perished, nevertheless the conjunction of the pestle and the mortar—which produces a potent action—becomes capable of assisting in the initiation of that [new] latent impression because it is a specific kind of conjunction."

“Alternatively, that very potent prior impression (saṃskāra) remains without being destroyed due to the impact; therefore, there is no further commencement of an impression in what already possesses an impression. Consequently, at the very same time that the action of upward motion occurs in the pestle—being independent [of external causes] and dependent on the impact and the impression—at that same time, the action of upward motion also occurs in the hand—being independent [of external causes] and dependent on that very same impression and the conjunction of the hand and the pestle. <PDhS>

Following the question of an unlearned person as to how action occurs even in objects like the pestle (*musala*) which are connected to that [hand], he says: Having grasped the pestle with the hand, one forms an intention. Of what kind? Of the form, "I shall lift up the pestle with my hand. Immediately after that, an effort arises in the portion of the self (*ātman*) possessing the hand, corresponding to that [intention]. At the very same time that action arises in the hand—which serves as the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*)—due to the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of the conjunction between the self and the hand depending upon that effort, there also arises action in the pestle—which serves as the cause—due to the non-inherent cause of the conjunction between the hand and the pestle, depending upon that same effort. Then, when the pestle has been lifted high, the intention for that purpose—the intention to lift it up—ceases. From its own cause, there again arises an intention for throwing it down (*apakṣepaṇa*). Immediately after that, an effort arises in the portion of the self possessing the hand, corresponding to that [new intention]. Due to the two aforementioned conjunctions—the conjunction of the self and the hand, and the conjunction of the pestle and the hand—depending upon that effort, actions of throwing down occur simultaneously in both the hand and the pestle. Then, by the final, concluding action of the pestle, a conjunction called "impact" (*abhighāta*) is produced between the mortar (*ulūkhala*) and the pestle. That conjunction, acting as a non-inherent cause and depending upon the momentum (*vega*) residing in the pestle, produces an upward-thrusting action (*utpatana-karma*) in the pestle that is "without cognition" (*apratyaya*), meaning not preceded by effort. That action, acting as a non-inherent cause and depending upon the impact, initiates a residual impression (*saṃskāra*) in the pestle, which serves as the inherent cause. Depending upon that [impression], the conjunction of the pestle and the hand produces an upward-thrusting action in the hand as well, which is "without cognition," meaning not preceded by effort.

One might object: "Since the previous momentum (*saṃskāra*) is destroyed at the same time that action arises in the pestle due to the conjunction of the pestle and the mortar, the pestle does not initiate a new momentum because of the absence of a contributory cause (*apekṣākāraṇa*). In the absence of such momentum, how could the conjunction of the hand and the pestle produce an upward-moving action in the hand that is not caused by prior effort? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even though the previous momentum has perished, nevertheless, the conjunction of the pestle and the mortar is capable of producing a potent action. Why? Because of the presence of a specific type of conjunction (*saṃyogaviśeṣa*). Therefore, it is capable of assisting that action. 'Assistance' (*sācivya*) means the state of being an associate; it is capable of providing aid in that regard."

Alternatively, he presents another position: that the very same potent latent impression (*saṃskāra*) from the previous [action] remains, not perishing upon the impact (*abhighāta*). Since there can be no further commencement of a latent impression in that which already possesses a latent impression while the former potent impression persists, at the very moment when the upward-moving action occurs in the pestle due to the impact dependent on the latent impression, at that same moment, the upward-moving action also occurs in the hand due to the conjunction of the hand and the pestle, dependent on that very same latent impression. This action in the hand is likewise independent of cognition (*apratyaya*).

(“The rule for motion in objects released from the hand. How so? When, having grasped a javelin (*tomara*) with the hand, the desire to throw it arises, immediately thereafter an effort (*prayatna*) occurs. Depending upon that [effort] and the aforementioned two types of conjunction, simultaneous actions of drawing back occur in both the javelin and the hand. Once the hand has been extended, the effort intended for drawing it back ceases. Immediately thereafter, the desire ‘I shall throw it sideways, upwards, far, or near’ arises; immediately thereafter, an effort corresponding to that [desire] arises. Depending upon that [effort], the conjunction between the javelin and the hand, termed ‘impulsion’ (*nodana*), comes into being. From that, an action produced in the javelin—depending upon that impulsion—initiates a momentum (*saṃskāra*) within it. Thereafter, through both momentum and impulsion, actions continue to occur as long as there is no separation between the hand and the javelin. Then, once the impulsion has ceased due to that separation, actions corresponding to the [original] effort occur in the upward, sideways, distant, or near directions by virtue of momentum alone, until the javelin falls. <PDhS>

Regarding the "method of motion" (*gamanavidhi*)—that is, the manner of motion—in the case of objects released from the hand, such as a *tomara* (javelin), he explains how this occurs: when one grasps a *tomara* with the hand and forms the desire, "I shall throw the *tomara* with my hand," immediately thereafter an effort (*prayatna*) arises corresponding to that desire. Depending upon that [effort] and the aforementioned two types of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), namely the conjunction between the self and the hand and the conjunction between the hand and the *tomara*, there simultaneously arise the actions of drawing back in both the *tomara* and the hand. When the hand has been extended and thrown far away, the effort intended for that drawing back—that is, the effort for the purpose of pulling back that *tomara*—ceases. Immediately after that, a desire arises: "I shall throw it sideways, upwards, downwards, far, or near," specifically, "I throw it sideways," "upwards," "downwards," "far," or "near. Immediately after that, an effort arises corresponding to that [desire], being weak if the distance is near and intense if it is far. Depending upon that [effort], the conjunction between the *tomara* and the hand is called "impulsion" (*nodana*); because the impelled (*nodya*) and the impeller (*nodaka*) move together—the *tomara* being the impelled and the hand being the impeller—their conjunction depends on effort. From that, an action produced in the *tomara* depending on the impulsion initiates a momentum (*saṃskāra*). Here, the *tomara* is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), the action is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and the effort is the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). Then, through that momentum and the impulsion, actions continue to occur until the mutual disjunction of the hand and the *tomara* occurs by means of an action intended for their separation. Once the impulsion has ceased due to that disjunction, actions corresponding to that [momentum] arise from momentum as the non-inherent cause, continuing until the falling down—that is, until the fall. Because momentum is distinguished by degrees such as more intense and so forth, the actions likewise become so.

“Likewise, the process of motion in the case of objects released from a machine is as follows. How so? A strong man who has practiced exercise, having steadied the bow with his left hand, fixed an arrow with his right, and grasped the string together with the arrow by means of his fist, forms the desire to draw it back, thinking: ‘I shall draw this strung bow. Immediately thereafter, there is an effort (*prayatna*). When, depending upon that [effort] and the conjunction of the self and the hand, the action of drawing arises in the hand, at that very moment, depending upon that same effort and the conjunction of the hand, the string, and the arrow, an action arises in the string and the arrow. Depending upon the conjunction of the string and the two ends of the bow (*koṭi*), two actions arise in the two ends of the bow—this all occurs simultaneously. When the bow has been drawn back to the ear, the cognition arises: ‘It must not go further than this,’ whereby the effort intended for that drawing ceases. Thereafter, the desire to release [the arrow] is born; immediately after that, there is an effort. Depending upon that effort and the conjunction of the self and the fingers, an action arises in the fingers. From that, there is a disjunction between the string and the fingers. From that disjunction, the conjunction [of the fingers and the string] is destroyed. When that [conjunction] is destroyed, because of the absence of an obstacle, the *sthitisthāpaka* (elastic) impression (*saṃskāra*) residing in the bow causes the bow, which had become curved, to return to its original state. At that time, depending upon that very impression and the conjunction of the bow and the string, an action arises in the string and the arrow. That [action], depending upon its own cause, produces an impression in the string. Depending upon that [impression], the conjunction of the arrow and the string becomes a propelling force (*nodana*). From that, the first action in the arrow initiates an impression in the arrow, depending upon the propelling force. From that impression, aided by the propelling force, as many actions occur as there are until the disjunction between the arrow and the string. Once the propelling force has ceased due to that disjunction, subsequent actions continue solely from the impression in the arrow until its fall. These many actions occur sequentially. Why? Because of the multiplicity of conjunctions. However, the impression is single, because in the interval there is no cause requiring a further action.”

Likewise, regarding the process of movement in arrows, stones, and so forth discharged from a machine: how [does it occur], and what kind of person employs them, and in what manner? To this he says: one who is strong, has practiced physical exercise, and is proficient in the use of missiles and machines; having steadied the bow with his left hand and fixed the arrow with his right—this is said with reference to the majority of cases—he grasps with his fist that bowstring which is "with an arrow" (*saśarā*), meaning it exists together with an arrow, and forms the intention: "I shall draw this bow with the arrow fixed. That which exists together with a string is "with a string" (*sajya*); that which is both *sajya* and an arrow is thus described as *sajyeṣu*. He thinks: "I shall draw this bow with the arrow fixed."

Furthermore, the word *enam* (this) should not be construed with the word *dhanus* (bow), for since the latter is neuter in gender, it would have to be *etad dhanuḥ* (this bow). Now, if it is somehow accepted that it has both genders—either because it is listed among the *ardharca* group or because such usage is observed—even then it would have to be *enaṃ dhanuṣam*, not *enaṃ dhanuḥ*. Others maintain that even when the masculine gender is intended, the second case ending does not occur because the object (*karman*) is already expressed by the particle *iti*. Immediately following that, there is effort (*prayatna*). Depending upon that [effort], from the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*) consisting of the contact between the self and the hand, acting upon the hand as the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*), at the very moment the action of drawing (*ākarṣaṇa*) arises, simultaneously, depending upon the non-inherent cause consisting of the contact between the hand, the bowstring (*jyā*), and the arrow, acting upon the bowstring and the arrow as the inherent causes, an action arises. Depending upon the contact between the bowstring and the two ends of the bow (*koṭi*), which are non-inherent causes qualified by the contact between the hand and the bowstring, two actions arise inherent in the two ends of the bow. And the action inherent in the bow, depending upon the contact between the hand and the bowstring—which is a qualified non-inherent cause arising from the contact between the bowstring and the bow—all this occurs simultaneously at one and the same time, due to the simultaneity of the causes.

Thus, when the bow has been drawn from ear to ear, there arises a cognition that "it must not be drawn further than this. Consequently, the effort intended for that drawing ceases. Thereafter, a desire to release [the arrow] arises. Following that, an effort corresponding to that desire occurs. Depending upon that effort, and with the contact between the self and the fingers serving as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), an action (*karman*) arises in the fingers for the purpose of releasing. From that arises the disjunction between the finger and the bowstring; from that disjunction follows the destruction of their conjunction. When that conjunction is destroyed, because the obstacle is removed, the elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka-saṃskāra*) inherent in the bow initiates an action that restores the curved bow to its original state. In this process, the bow is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), the elasticity is the non-inherent cause, and factors such as unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) are the efficient causes (*nimittakāraṇa*). At the very moment that an action has been produced in the bow—which was made curved by the action of drawing—in order to restore it to its state, an action arises in the bowstring and in the arrow due to the contact between the bow and the string (and the contact between the string and the arrow) acting as non-inherent causes, depending upon that very elasticity. Once produced, that action, depending on its own causes, initiates an elasticity within the string. Depending upon that [elasticity], the contact between the arrow and the string becomes a "push" (*nodana*), because they move together; from that, the first action arises in the arrow. Depending upon that push, it initiates an elasticity in the arrow. In this case, the arrow is the inherent cause, the action is the non-inherent cause, and the push is the efficient cause. From that elasticity, aided by the push, successive actions continue to arise in the arrow as long as there is disjunction between the arrow and the string. Upon the arising of that disjunction, the string and arrow are the inherent causes, the action in the arrow is the non-inherent cause, and the rest are efficient causes. Then, once the push has ceased due to the disjunction, the subsequent actions arise solely from the elasticity of the arrow until it falls—that is, until the fall occurs. These many actions occur sequentially. Why? Because of the multiplicity of conjunctions. If those actions were not destroyed even while the conjunctions persist, the arrow would never fall.

Now, if it is argued that even a single action, having produced multiple conjunctions, perishes due to a deficiency in its capacity, then—because the *saṃskāra* (impression/disposition) would persist as something whose effect has not yet been initiated—it would follow that there is another distinct action altogether; this is clearly untenable. Furthermore, the *saṃskāra* cannot be the producer of conjunction, such that its destruction would occur due to a deficiency in capacity when performing multiple effects. Since those [conjunctions] are the effects of action, it is logical that the destruction of actions themselves occurs upon their production from that [conjunction]. Nor can it be said that the action is non-different from the *saṃskāra*, because difference is defined by the difference in cognition (*pratyaya*). Thus, one observes the cognitions "he moves with speed" and "he is endowed with speed," as well as "he is endowed with motion. Therefore, speed (*vega*) is a distinct entity from action, just like conjunction. If there were no difference, then even in the case of slow movement and so forth, the cognition "he moves with speed" would occur; but this is not the case.

If it is argued that action is inferred from the perception of conjunctions and disjunctions, we say no; for there is no difference in the existence of direct (aparokṣa) cognition regarding action as there is regarding conjunction itself through the operation of the sense organs. Just as the conjunctions and disjunctions of an object with other locations are perceived directly, so too is action.

Furthermore, as for the claim that the cognition "it moves" is inferential when conjunction and disjunction are perceived in different locations—that is not tenable; for in the case of a tree trunk standing upright in the current of a river, no such cognition of movement is observed despite the presence of those [conjunctions and disjunctions], whereas in the case of an arrow shot into the sky, such a cognition is observed even in their absence. And as for the statement that the conventional usage "it stays" arises from its production at each moment in one location, while the conventional usage "it goes" arises from its existence in another location—that too is not tenable, because the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) has been refuted.

Now, it is true that there are many actions (*karma*) because of the multiplicity of conjunctions (*saṃyoga*). However, it is not the case that the impression (*saṃskāra*) is likewise multiple due to the multiplicity of conjunctions, because [the impression] does not perish merely through conjunction. Or, if it were to perish, there would be no production of further actions, due to the absence of a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). Nor can the conjunction between the self and the arrow, depending on the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), be the non-inherent cause; for such a hypothesis is only resorted to when other causes are not perceived through perception and inference. Furthermore, velocity (*vega*) is indeed perceived by the operation of the senses alone; its denial is impossible.

Now, regarding the hypothesis that when an action arises from a residual impression (*saṃskāra*), there is the state of destruction of the [original] velocity and action due to the subsequent conjunction, and the state of arising of another velocity and action; and that consequently, there is the production of those two and the destruction of the former two—what is the fault in this? It is this: that which is in a state of destruction lacks the status of being an *asamavāyikāraṇa* (non-inherent cause). For instance, the previous action does not initiate another residual impression, nor does the previous velocity initiate another action, because both, being in a state of destruction, lack the status of being an *asamavāyikāraṇa*. Furthermore, it has already been stated that no other *asamavāyikāraṇa* for the action is possible in the interval. Moreover, the action produced from a residual impression does not initiate another residual impression, due to the absence of a required auxiliary cause (*apekṣākāraṇa*). Nor can the previous residual impression serve as that auxiliary cause, because the initiation of a residual impression in that which already possesses a residual impression is prohibited; thus, just as the cessation of the previous action must be admitted simultaneously with the arising of the new action due to the subsequent conjunction, so too must the cessation of the previous residual impression be asserted. Furthermore, mere conjunction is not the auxiliary cause for the initiation of a residual impression by an action, because it is observed that in slow motion, even though conjunction exists, the action does not initiate a residual impression. Indeed, it is perceived that in slow motion, despite the presence of conjunction, the action does not produce a residual impression. Therefore, there is only one residual impression in the interval, because of the absence of any auxiliary cause for further action.

[Objection: If that is so, then since the *saṃskāra* (impression/disposition) is of a single nature, how can there be the production of actions distinguished by degrees such as "more intense" and so forth? [Response: It is due to a difference in auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). And that [difference] is to be known only through the difference in effects. In this regard, because what is perceived is not found [to account for the phenomenon], that which is called the "unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*) is postulated. Furthermore, since the destruction of velocity (*vega*) is well-established by the observation of the fall of a discharged arrow, and since that [destruction] must have a cause and no other cause for destruction exists, its destruction is postulated as resulting from the exhaustion of its capacity when it performs multiple effects. And that capacity is precisely a specific kind of "unseen" force that brings about multiple actions. This must be admitted even by one who maintains that there are multiple *saṃskāras*; otherwise, if another *saṃskāra* were produced again, the arrow would simply never fall. Therefore, by the aforementioned reasoning, there is only one *saṃskāra*.
(“Thus, action has been described as having a real cause and an unreal cause with respect to those things presided over by the self.

He states the conclusion: “Thus, action has been described as having a real cause and an unreal cause with respect to those things presided over by the self through effort, and [action] with respect to those not so presided over.”

“In external unanimated [substances] consisting of the four great elements, action in the form of motion arises solely from impulsion (*nodana*) and so forth. Among these, impulsion is a particular kind of conjunction that depends on gravity, fluidity, momentum, and effort, either collectively or individually; it is the cause of action that effects mutual non-separation. From that, action occurs in all four great elements, as for example in the earth known as mud.”

Now, [the term] "in the four great elements" (*mahābhūteṣu*) is used to exclude external things that are not connected to the body and to exclude space (*ākāśa*) and the like; and "without a cause" (*apratyayam*) is used to exclude [action] preceded by effort. Action, which is merely motion, arises from impulsion (*nodana*) and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), impact (*abhighāta*), conjunction with what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasaṃyoga*), gravity (*gurutva*), and the rest are included. Among these, impulsion is explained: a particular kind of conjunction (*saṃyogaviśeṣa*) which depends on gravity, fluidity (*dravatva*), effort (*prayatna*), and velocity (*vega*), either collectively or individually, is impulsion—the cause of action that effects mutual non-separation. If one were to say simply that "conjunction is impulsion," there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); therefore, the phrase "cause of action" is added. Since impact (*abhighāta*) occurs in the same way, the phrase "effecting non-separation" is included [to distinguish it]. Nevertheless, since an action once produced necessarily generates separation, the word "mutual" (*parasparam*) is added. Even so, since conjunction with what is already conjoined (*saṃyuktasaṃyoga*) is also a cause of action that effects the separation of two conjoined things, the phrase "depending on gravity, fluidity, effort, and velocity, either collectively or individually" is included. In this regard, when one takes water in the hollow of the hand and throws it with force, all [four factors]—gravity and the rest—are present; thus, the conjunction of the water with the hollow of the hand depends on them. In the case of individual dependence: a conjunction depending on gravity is impulsion, as when a substance exceedingly heavy is placed upon a fine branch of a tree, it becomes the cause of the branch's downward motion. A conjunction of grass and water depending on fluidity initiates motion in the grass. A conjunction of wind and a tree depending on velocity is the cause of movement in trees and the like. A conjunction of the hand and a mace depending on effort produces the action of the mace. When one thrusts a foot into mud with effort, then the conjunction of the foot and the mud, depending on both effort and gravity, causes the mud to sink down. When a stone or similar object falls with velocity and comes into conjunction with mud, then the conjunction of the stone and the mud, depending on the gravity and velocity residing in the stone, is impulsion. When someone falls with velocity into a well or similar place, then the conjunction of Devadatta and the water, depending on gravity, effort, and velocity, becomes the cause of downward motion. And when grass and such move downward due to contact with a stream of rain, then it should be understood that it depends on gravity, fluidity, and velocity, and so forth. Therefore, action arises in all four great elements from the aforementioned impulsion. To provide an illustration, he says: "as in the case of the earth called mud, from the conjunction of the foot and so forth, according to the aforementioned qualifications."

“*Abhighāta* (impact) is that particular kind of conjunction which, depending on velocity (*vega*), is the cause of a single action that results in disjunction. From this as well, action arises in the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). For example, when stones and other such hard objects strike one another. Likewise, in the case of earth known as mud, which is being pushed or struck by feet and the like, there is a conjunction that depends on either *nodana* (pushing) or *abhighāta* (striking), or depends on both; this is *saṃyuktasaṃyoga* (conjunction with what is conjoined). From this as well, action arises in earth and the other elements. Furthermore, action is produced even in those parts that are neither pushed nor struck.”

He states [the definition] in order to distinguish *abhighāta* (impact) from other [types of contact]: "That particular kind of conjunction which depends on velocity (*vega*) and is the cause of a single action that brings about mutual disjunction—that is *abhighāta*. Since impulsion (*nodana*) and other such factors are also causes of actions that bring about disjunction, he uses the phrase "of that which brings about mutual disjunction" [to exclude them]. Nevertheless, in order to avoid the fallacy of over-extension (*vyabhicāra*) to the conjunction of the self and the mind (*ātmamanaḥ-saṃyoga*), he adds the term "depends on velocity. For the conjunction of the self and the mind does not depend on velocity in order to produce mutual disjunction.

[Objection: But then the word "of one" (*ekasya*) is redundant, since action is perceived in both cases due to impact (*abhighāta*). [Reply: True. Nevertheless, the word "of one" is for the purpose of indicating the first action—that subsequent actions arise from momentum (*vega*) alone—whereas impact and so forth are the cause of many subsequent actions. Others, however, believe that the restriction "of one alone" applies only to the cause, meaning it is the cause of only one [action]. In this way, the qualification "of one" should also be explained in the case of impact. An example is as follows: in stones and such, [the action arises] from the impact of a stone and so forth. To define conjunction through conjunction (*saṃyukta-saṃyoga*), he says: "likewise, when [the earth] is being impelled by feet and so forth," and so on.

Since impact (*nodana*) is also a cause of action produced by mutual non-separation, that conjunction which depends on either impact or collision (*abhighāta*), or depends on both, is "conjunction with the conjoined" (*saṃyuktasaṃyoga*). In some cases it depends on impact, in some on collision, and in some on both. An example is as follows: in the case of earth known as mud—of what specific kind?—when the earth is being pushed or struck by feet and so forth, action arises even in those parts that are not pushed, nor are they directly connected with the foot, nor are they struck, nor are they directly connected with stones and the like. In this case, the spatial parts (*pradeśa*) are the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*); the conjunction with the parts connected to the foot and so forth is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*); and the conjunctions with the foot and so forth are the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).

“Falling is that downward motion which occurs due to gravity when there is an absence of conjunction, effort, or velocity that counteracts gravity in the case of earth and water; as has been stated regarding the pestle, the body, and so forth. Among these, the first [motion] is due to gravity, while the second and subsequent ones are due to both gravity and momentum (*saṃskāra*).”

He states [the definition] for the purpose of defining falling: "Falling is that downward motion which results from gravity. [The phrase] "from gravity" is used to exclude the case of air, for it is possible for air to move downward after having entered upward into tree hollows and the like. The mention of "earth and water" is a definition of the substratum. The substratum of falling is the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*); gravity is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*); and the absence of contact, effort, and velocity—which would otherwise counteract gravity—indicates the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*). An example is "in the case of a pestle, a body, and so forth": due to the absence of contact between the hand and the pestle, the pestle falls; due to the absence of effort, the body falls; and due to the absence of velocity, the arrow falls. Among these, the first falling arises solely from gravity as its non-inherent cause. Once produced, that [first falling], depending upon its own cause, initiates a momentum (*saṃskāra*). Thereafter, the second and subsequent instances of falling arise from both gravity and momentum as their non-inherent causes.

“The downward flow of water that has become a stream from high ground to low ground is due to its fluidity (*dravatva*). How so? The fluidity of the whole (*avayavin*) is obstructed by contact with the banks on all sides; the fluidity of the parts (*avayava*) is also obstructed by that same [contact], as it inheres in the same object [as the whole]. The fluidities of the successive parts are obstructed by conjoined-conjunctions (*saṃyukta-saṃyoga*). But when a breach is made in the dam to some extent, then because the fluidity of the whole is obstructed on all sides, there is no initiation of action [in it]. However, for the fluidity of the part situated near the dam, and for the successive fluidities of the other parts, there is the attainment of function (*vṛttilābha*) due to the absence of an obstructer. From that, there is a gradual gliding of those very [parts] that are conjoined. Then, upon the destruction of the previous substance, a long substance is initiated by the parts remaining in a continuous series. And therein, fluidity is produced through the sequence beginning with the qualities of the causes. And when the conjoined causes move in a continuous series, the action that arises in the whole is called 'flow' (*syandana*).”

He states [the definition] for the purpose of defining flowing (*syandana*): "The downward movement from a higher level to a lower one of waters that have become a stream is 'flowing' because of fluidity (*dravatva*). The phrase "of waters that have become a stream" is used because even stones and the like move downward from a higher level; thus, the term "waters" is employed to exclude such cases. Furthermore, since a similar flow is possible for snakes and other creatures, the word "waters" is specified. Nevertheless, even waters do not move downward from a higher level when firmly grasped by the hand; therefore, the phrase "that have become a stream" is included. Moreover, the term "waters" is used in view of their predominance, but it is not intended as an absolute restriction to water alone, as this property also exists in oil and other substances. Thus, that movement of the aforementioned nature is "flowing," and it arises from fluidity.

To explain how this occurs, he poses another question for one who is unacquainted with the details, out of a desire for a comprehensive understanding: "The fluidity of the whole is obstructed by its connection with the surrounding embankment," and so forth. By means of a connection on all sides—that is, a connection everywhere with the embankment (setu)—the fluidity of the whole (*avayavin*) is obstructed; it does not produce motion in the water, nor does the fluidity of the parts (*avayava-dravatva*) initiate a downward flow. He explains that the fluidity of the parts is also inherent in the same substrate (*ekārthasamaveta*); for wherever there is fluidity of the parts, there too is the connection with the embankment, and thus it is obstructed by that very [connection]. However, the fluidities of the successive parts are obstructed by "connections of the connected" (*saṃyukta-saṃyoga*). A connection of one part with the part connected to the embankment, and by that [connection] yet another, and so on—by these successive connections of the parts, their respective fluidities are obstructed and do not initiate action. But when the breach of the embankment is made, then, because the fluidity of the whole is no longer obstructed on all sides, there is no initiation of action [from the whole]; rather, this is the meaning: due to the large magnitude associated with the whole, it does not exit through the space of a minute aperture. However, the fluidity of the part situated near the embankment initiates its own effect, because the obstructing connection has ceased. Thereafter, the successive fluidities of the parts gradually attain their functional state and produce their effects. For instance, when the part situated near the embankment moves, a disjunction from the adjacent part occurs, whereby that [original] conjunction ceases. Then, due to the absence of the obstructer, the fluidity of the second part initiates action. When the conjunction of the third part ceases, the fluidity residing therein initiates action. In this manner, the successive parts attain their functional state, and consequently, those very parts which are conjoined flow forward.

Although the movement [of water] occurs when the obstructing conjunction is destroyed, it is nevertheless stated that there is a sequential gliding of those very parts already in conjunction, in order to indicate that. Then, upon the destruction of the conjunction that initiates the substance, the prior substance is destroyed; subsequently, a long substance is initiated by the constituent parts which remain in a continuous series despite having been obstructed. In that substance, fluidity (*dravatva*) arises through the sequence beginning with the qualities of the causes. The fluidities of the constituent parts serve as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) for the production of fluidity in the composite whole. In that context, the action that arises in the composite whole during the continuous or sequential movement of the causes is termed "flow" (*syandana*).

“Action [arising] from impression (*saṃskāra*) has been explained in the case of arrows and the like. Similarly, when conjunctions and disjunctions with specific directions and locations arise on the sides of the parts of a wheel and so forth, that action of the whole which is caused by its own impression and results in conjunctions and disjunctions with non-specific directions and locations is called ‘revolution. Such are the various types of motion. <PDhS>

He states the conclusion: [motion] has been described as arising from *saṃskāra* (impetus) in the case of actions such as those of arrows, and also from gravity (*gurutva*) and other causes. Likewise, he says that revolution occurs solely from *saṃskāra*: "In the case of wheels and the like, when conjunctions and disjunctions with specific directions and locations arise for their constituent parts. For the directions and locations occupied by the wheel are indeed specific; when conjunctions and disjunctions are to be produced with them, an action arises in the whole (*avayavin*). Why? From *saṃskāra*. An action produced in the wheel from the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of the initial conjunction between the staff and the wheel—which depends upon the conjunction between the hand and the staff—initiates an *saṃskāra* that depends upon its own specific cause. Thereafter, through both *saṃskāra* and impulsion (*nodana*), further actions arise repeatedly from *saṃskāra* alone. Regarding the production of the initial action in the constituent parts, the non-inherent cause is the conjunction of what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasaṃyoga*), which depends upon impulsion; once *saṃskāra* has been produced from that, *saṃskāra* itself [is the cause]. That revolution is an action whose cause is conjunction and disjunction with non-specific directions and locations; it thus produces conjunctions and disjunctions with non-specific directions and locations.

“However, action occurs in the wind called *prāṇa* due to the conjunction of the self and the wind, depending on an effort preceded by desire or aversion; for in the case of one who is awake, [action] is observed to follow desire, whereas in the case of one who is asleep, it depends on an effort preceded by the [mere] maintenance of life. Although ether, time, space, and the self possess the nature of substances, they are devoid of action because they lack corporeality (*mūrtatva*). Corporeality is the dimension of a substance that is not all-pervading, and action conforms to that [corporeality]; since that [corporeality] does not exist in ether and the others, there is no connection with action for them.”

He demonstrates the distinction [of the action] by means of its different effects. To the question, "From what does the action in the air called *prāṇa* arise?", he says: it arises from the conjunction of the self (*ātman*) and the air, which serves as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), depending upon effort preceded by desire and aversion. To the question, "Of what kind [of person]? he says: "of one who is awake. Why is this so? Because we observe its conformity to desire; that is, exhalation occurs from the desire to exhale, and inhalation occurs from the desire to inhale. However, in the case of one who is asleep, action arises in the air called *prāṇa* from the conjunction of the self and the air—which serves as the non-inherent cause—depending upon the effort that precedes mere living. What is the proof for this? It is the inference that the action in the air of a sleeping person arises from the effort that precedes living. For instance: the movement of the air in a sleeping person is produced by effort, because it is a movement of the air held within [the body], just like the movement of that same air during the waking state. And where no other cause is perceived through either perception or inference, there the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) alone is the cause. Here, since it is established through inference that it is produced by effort, and since there is an absence of effort preceded by desire and aversion in one who is asleep, it is determined that it is produced by the effort that precedes living.

Having thus explained action (*karman*) in the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) through impulsion and so forth, he states the reason for the absence of action in space (*ākāśa*) and the other [categories]: "Space, time, direction, and the self (*ātman*), despite having the nature of substances (*dravya*), are devoid of action because they are incorporeal (*amūrta*), like universals (*sāmānya*) and the rest. For just as universals and the like are inactive due to their incorporeality, so too are space and the others. Indeed, possession of action is pervaded by corporeality; and that [corporeality], being excluded from space and the others, excludes its own pervader—possession of action—from them as well. He expresses this very point: "Corporeality is the dimension of a substance that is not all-pervading, and action conforms to it. Wherever there is action, there is corporeality. And that corporeality does not exist in space and the others. Therefore, they have no connection with action.

(“In the case of the embodied soul, the action of the mind for the purpose of connecting with other sense organs occurs—during the waking state—from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending on an effort preceded by desire and aversion, because we observe the perception of various objects through different sense organs according to one’s intention; and at the time of awakening from sleep, it depends on an effort preceded by the life-force (*jīvana*). The action of departing (*apasarpaṇa*) and the action of approaching (*upasarpaṇa*) arise from the conjunction of the self [with the mind], depending on the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*). How so? When there is the exhaustion or mutual suppression of merit and demerit, which are the auxiliaries of the life-force, due to experience, then, because of the deficiency of those auxiliaries of the life-force, there follows a deficiency in the effort preceded by them. Upon the cessation of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), the action of departing arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, aided by the other two—merit and demerit—which have acquired their functional state, and this action becomes the cause of separation from the dead body. Thereafter, having departed from the body, it becomes connected with a subtle body (*ātivāhika-śarīra*) produced by those very same merit and demerit; and having transmigrated to heaven or hell, it becomes connected with a body corresponding to its latent dispositions (*āśaya*); the action for the sake of that connection is called ‘approaching. Furthermore, for yogis, there is the movement of the mind projected outside to a desired location and its return. Likewise, at the time of cosmic creation (*sarga*), the action for the purpose of connecting with a newly formed body is caused by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). Similarly, whatever other action among the great elements has no perceptible or inferable cause, yet is capable of producing benefit or harm, that too is caused by the unseen force. For example: the action of atoms at the beginning of creation; the upward and horizontal movements of fire and wind which cause the agitation of the great elements; the movement of consecrated gems toward a thief; and the attraction of iron toward a magnet. <PDhS>

Now, if the action of the mind conforms to its form (*mūrti*), then because of its corporeality (*mūrtatva*), a connection with action must be stated. To this he says: when the mind is embodied, i.e., confined within the body, that action which arises for one who is awake in order to connect with another sense organ—whence does it arise? He says: from the conjunction of the self and the mind as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), depending upon an effort preceded by desire and aversion. Why is the mind of one who is awake acted upon by such an effort? To this he says: because we observe the perception of other objects through other sense organs according to one’s intention (*abhiprāya*). "According to intention" means without overstepping the intention. Since we observe the perception of an object through whichever sense organ there is an intention to grasp that object, it is known that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is the substratum of an action conforming to desire. Therefore, since an uncontrolled sense organ cannot grasp an object, a connection with the mind is established. And because that [action] conforms to desire, it is an effect produced by an action generated by an effort preceded by that [desire]. But as for the action of the mind of one who is asleep—which has dissolved in a region of the self devoid of sense organs—in order to connect with another sense organ at the time of awakening, that arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind as the non-inherent cause, depending upon an effort preceded by the life-force (*jīvana*). For instance, the action of the mind of one who is asleep is an effect of effort, because it is an action of the internal organ that has been grasped, just like its action during the waking state. The action of departing (*apasarpaṇa*) and the action of approaching (*upasarpaṇa*) arise from the conjunction of the self and the mind as the non-inherent cause, depending upon the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). Departing is the action for the sake of separation from the dead body; approaching is the action for the sake of conjunction with the embryonic body. When, then, does that departing occur, and how does it happen? He says: "When [there is the exhaustion] of the two factors that cooperate with the life-force," etc. Life-force has been explained. When there is the exhaustion of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) which cooperate with it, due to the experience of pleasure and pain—that is, their consumption—then, because of the absence of karma to be experienced through that body, even though there exists karma that would produce another body for experience, the body simply falls. Or, "mutual suppression" is the presentation of another possible alternative. For instance, there may be suppression of the karma that has begun to produce the current body—which was set in motion to grant experience—by a more powerful, fully ripened karma that grants experience in another body, just as a weak sound is not perceived when there is the perception of a loud sound. Thus, when the karma that assists the life-force is deficient, and the effort preceded by it is also deficient, there is the cessation of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). When they cease, then by those two, merit and demerit, which have obtained their "function" (*vṛtti*)—meaning they have acquired their auxiliary causes—the action of departing arises, having the conjunction of the self and the mind as its auxiliary cause, and serving as the cause of separation from the dead body. Then, having departed from that body, it connects with the subtle body (*ātivāhika-śarīra*) produced by those very same merit and demerit. Having transferred there, it goes to heaven or hell, and having gone, it joins with a body corresponding to its latent impressions (*āśaya*); the action called "approaching" is for the sake of that conjunction. The subtle body is accepted on the authority of scripture, because it is grasped by the internal organ. Furthermore, it is not only from the unseen force that this occurs; it also applies to the mind of yogis which is projected outward. This refers to the repeated going to and returning from intended places by a mind projected to external regions. Likewise, at the time of creation, action caused by the unseen force serves to connect [the soul] with a new body. Not only this, but also whatever action exists among the gross elements (*mahābhūta*). What is its specific nature? It is that whose cause is not perceived through perception or inference, meaning it is capable of producing benefit or harm. That too is caused by the unseen force. He states this very point: as at the beginning of creation, action arises in atoms for the purpose of producing bodies and so forth; and the upward flaming of fire and the horizontal movement of air, which are capable of benefiting or harming living beings. Also, the agitation of the gross elements—the shaking of the earth, mountains, temples, and so on; the movement of gems toward a thief; and the attraction of iron toward a magnet.
Thus ends the category of action (*karmapadārtha*) in the *Padārthasaṅgrahaṭīkā* composed by the venerable Vyomaśivācārya.
[Now follows] the definition of the category of generality (*sāmānyapadārthanirūpaṇam*).

“Generality (*sāmānya*) is of two kinds: the higher and the lower. It pervades its own entire domain, is non-different in nature, and subsists in many individuals. It produces a cognition that conforms to its own essential form across one, two, or many [individuals], and it exists continuously in its substrata as a non-differentiated essence, serving as the cause of inclusive cognition (*anuvṛttipratyaya*). How so? When a continuous stream of cognitions arises with respect to each individual object based on the generality, and through the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by repeated cognitions and the retrospective examination of the preceding series of cognitions, that which persists as the recurring factor is the generality.”

Now, for the purpose of examining the definition of generality (*sāmānya*), there is the section beginning with "generality is twofold: higher and lower," and so forth. Here, because the classification was stated previously, the author demonstrates that by indicating a lack of fixed order, the suspicion of a causal relationship between the definition and the classification of generality is removed; this serves the same purpose as [the statement] "substance is earth, water, fire, and so forth. The phrase "pervading all its own objects" serves to remove misconceptions.

For others think as follows: every universal is omnipresent. Thus, "cowness" exists even in horse-bodies, and "horseness" exists even in cow-bodies and so forth. Non-perception, however, is due to the absence of a manifestor (*vyañjaka*). Wherever there is the presence of a manifestor, there is manifestation; for example, cowness is manifested in cow-bodies, and horseness in horse-bodies.

And that [position] is incorrect. For there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of "cowness" (*gotva*) in the bodies of horses and so forth. Indeed, when existence is established, one may postulate non-perception due to the absence of a manifestor (*abhivyañjaka*). Now, as for the argument that "the universal (*sāmānya*) is connected with all things because it is all-pervasive (*vyāpaka*), like space (*ākāśa*)," what is the proof for this? In that case, if "inherence in all things" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), the example is deficient in the property to be proven, because space does not inhere in everything. If, however, "being conjoined with all things" is the property to be proven, it would follow that the universal has the nature of a substance (*dravya*), which is not tenable; for [inherence] is perceived in qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*karman*), and conjunction (*saṃyoga*) occurs only between substances and nowhere else, as well as because of the absence of separate establishment (*yutasiddhi*). Conjunction belongs only to those things that are separately established. If, then, you are proving merely a "connection" (*sambandha*) with the universal, even there it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because a "conjunction of conjunctions" (*saṃyuktasaṃyoga*) exists everywhere [between the universal and its substrates]. To explain: space and so forth are conjoined with the substratum of "cowness," and everything corporeal is conjoined with that [substratum]. Likewise, if "all-pervasiveness" (*vyāpakatva*) means being conjoined with all things, that is unestablished (*asiddha*). For in the subject (*pakṣa*), that very [property] is "omnipresence" (*sarvagatatva*), and thus there is no distinction from the property to be proven. Furthermore, space and so forth, though pervasive, are not connected with all things; thus, the reason is inconclusive (*anekānta*). If you argue that "connection with all things" is proven by the reason "because of being present everywhere," that too is incorrect. For in the case of space and so forth, there is no connection with qualities, actions, and the like, despite their presence there. Moreover, if we do not accept a specific kind of connection, we do not perceive any "presence" (*sannidhya*) of an entity in another. Therefore, a universal is omnipresent only within its own domain: "cowness" exists only in the bodies of cows, and "horseness" (*aśvatva*) only in the bodies of horses, because they are perceived only there.

He demonstrates the definition as "that which is non-different in nature and subsists in many. "Non-different in nature" means having a single essence (*ekasvabhāva*). "Subsisting in many" refers to that which has its occurrence in multiple locations. It is a universal (*sāmānya*) because it exists in many places while being one; nevertheless, in order to avoid over-extension (*vyabhicāra*) by such things as composite wholes (*avayavin*) or numbers, the qualification "while being eternal" (*nityatve sati*) must be understood as implied. Even so, the color and other qualities of water-atoms and the like are both eternal and subsist in many places; therefore, the qualification "while being one" is added. However, those [qualities] exist in many places while being many; thus, to exclude them, the phrase "while being one" is specified. Furthermore, since inherence (*samavāya*) exists in many places while being both one and eternal, the qualification "while existing through a mode of subsistence distinct from itself" must also be supplied.

Others maintain that everything is obtained within this very sentence and no word needs to be supplied (*adhyāhāra*). For instance, it is described as that which has neither difference nor manifoldness (*nānātva*) nor destruction; thus, by the phrase "that very thing is its self" (*tadevātmā svarūpam asya*), it is understood to be non-dual in nature (*abhedātmaka*), unitary, and indestructible. Furthermore, by the *bahuvrīhi* compound "that which has a presence in many places," the distinction between the locus of existence (*vṛtti*) and that which possesses existence (*vṛttimat*) is indeed demonstrated. Therefore, being unitary and eternal, and yet existing in many places through inherence (*samavāya*), the universal (*sāmānya*) is distinguished from other things.

Is it not the case that this definition is unestablished with respect to its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of a universal? Furthermore, that which is a subsequent cognition (*anugatajñāna*) does not demonstrate the existence of a universal, because it is a conceptual cognition (*kalpanājñāna*). Thus, a subsequent cognition arises by the force of beginningless predispositions (*vāsanā*), but there is no real universal. As it has been said:
"By which cognition, appearing as a single object, the nature of other things is concealed through its own form, [that cognition] arises depending upon distinct entities. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.67)

The meaning of this is as follows: entities (*bhāva*) are distinct, having natures that are mutually excluded from one another; their distinct form is "concealed" or covered by a cognition (*dhī*). By what kind of cognition? By one in which a single object appears—namely, its own internal aspect appearing as if it were external, since that [cognition] is devoid of an external object. By that [cognition], those things whose diversity has been concealed have their distinctions hidden; thus, through concealment, these distinct entities appear as if they were non-distinct by means of some [single] form. (Pramāṇavārttika 3.68)

The meaning of this is as follows: although entities are inherently distinct, through that conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), they appear as if non-distinct while their diversity remains concealed; yet this is not so from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). How then is it called a "universal" (*sāmānya*)? To this he says:
"It is proclaimed as an existent universal by virtue of that intention;
it is non-existent in the ultimate sense, just as it is conceptualized by that [convention]. (PV 1.71)
