Although from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*) a universal (*sāmānya*) does not exist, it is proclaimed as existing "by virtue of that intention" (*tadabhiprāyavaśāt*) and by virtue of appearing in a single form. Yet, it is not a universal, because individuals (*vyakti*) have distinct forms and nothing else appears; thus he says:
"Individuals do not follow one another, and no other following entity appears."
If it were not distinct from cognition, how could it become a different object? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.70)

Therefore, it is cognition (*buddhi*) itself—which arises depending on objects that are excluded from others—that, being conceptualized, conforms to the nature of its own latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Thus, concealing their distinct forms, it determines its own undifferentiated form and, by synthesizing them, displays them. And because these entities existing within cognition—though accomplished by a single means—are manifested as if they were external, they are called a "universal" (*sāmānya*). Furthermore, because this [cognition] occurs with respect to entities distinct from itself, it is said to have "particulars" (*viśeṣa*) as its object, though not in an ultimate sense. Consequently, both the universal and the particular consist of an inclusive and exclusive nature respectively; there are no external objects for those who possess discernment. And how can the activity of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) occur with respect to those [external things]? Indeed, it is the investigators (*parīkṣaka*) who analyze in this way according to their [mental] class (*jāti*), but not the common practitioners (*vyavahartṛ*). The latter, however, regarding their own cognition—which possesses an inclusive form—as having an external form, proceed and communicate after unifying the perceived object and the conceptualized object. But a permanent, unitary, inclusive universal distinct from particulars does not appear [to them].
Furthermore, it has been said:
"A word expresses a portion of the object; in that regard, it is called 'exclusion of others' (anyāpoha).
That form does not exist in the object itself; how then can a word, by expressing that [form], be said to possess the object? (Pramāṇavārttika 3.167)
Thus.

Furthermore, because its mode of subsistence (*vṛtti*) is untenable, there is no such thing as a real universal (*sāmānya*). Thus, a universal residing in one place does not subsist therein by means of only a part, because such a part does not exist; nor does it subsist by its entire self (*sarvātman*), for that would entail the consequence that it could not reside elsewhere. Likewise, if it were admitted that it resides in another place by the very same form in which it resides in the first, then all individual objects (*piṇḍa*) would result in being one and the same. If, on the other hand, it resides by means of a different intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), then due to the difference in intrinsic nature, the universal itself would result in being manifold. Moreover, it has already been stated that once one intrinsic nature is excluded, it is contradictory for a single entity to subsist in multiple locations. Since a single entity lacks any other unconditioned intrinsic nature that is restricted to a specific connection with particular places, times, and states, it cannot be conjoined with anything else that possesses those specific spatial and temporal distinctions.

In this context, "particularity of place" refers to cities and the like; "particularity of time" refers to spring and the like; and "particularity of state" refers to childhood and the like. That which is restricted to these—meaning established in them in its entirety—and which possesses the aforementioned nature and is also "one," has a "conjunction" (saṃsarga), that is, a relation, with them. Through that conjunction, there would be no "separation" (viraha)—that is, dissociation—from another nature not included within or encompassed by the stated nature. The meaning of the reason (*hetu*) is: "because it is devoid of that [other nature]. The phrase "of one that resides in many" is the indication of the subject (*dharmin*). The phrase "no connection with another [entity] possessing particularities of place and so forth" is the indication of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). "Like color and so forth" is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Whatever is devoid of another nature as described above, it has no connection with another entity possessing particularities of place and so forth, just like color and the like. And since this [absence of such another nature] exists in the case of the universal (*sāmānya*) and so forth, this is a perception of the contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*). Furthermore, if the universal were one and connected with all [individuals] through its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), it would follow that all individual objects (*piṇḍa*) would occupy the same place, time, and state. This is because the universal would have as its essential nature a subsistence in individuals qualified by those specific places and so forth. Moreover, when it is perceived in a single individual qualified by a particular place and so on, there would necessarily be a perception of it in its entirety as qualified by every locus, because it is of a single nature. Furthermore, if one does not admit that it resides in many, then, like color and so forth, it would have only a single substratum, and thus it would lack the nature of a universal.

Furthermore, it has been stated that the universal possesses no other intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) by which it could subsist in multiple locations. Nor is there any cause for a restriction regarding the universal’s connection with a specific substratum. Thus, when "cowness" (*gotva*) is being connected, it cannot be connected with a cow, because prior to its connection with cowness, the individual body (*piṇḍa*) cannot possibly possess that nature. If, on the other hand, it were connected with a non-cow, then it would also be connected with a horse, since prior to the connection with cowness, the state of being a non-cow is common to all [non-cows]. Moreover, it is a marvel to claim that the universal such as cowness does not inhere in the place where a cow-body and so forth reside, yet it is connected with that which resides in such a substrate.

The entity (*bhāva*) exists where it is; it is connected with that [individual], but it does not pervade the possessor of that space (*tad-deśin*). This is truly a great marvel! (PV 1.155) Likewise, when an individual (*piṇḍa*) moves, there is no movement of the universal (*sāmānya*), because it is inactive (*niṣkriyatva*). Nor is there staying [in place], because that would entail the consequence that the individual is devoid of it. There is neither movement nor staying by way of parts, because it is partless (*niraṃśatva*). Nor is it connected [to a new individual] after having come from behind, because it was previously unperceived as being devoid of that [universal]. Thus it has been said:

It does not go there, nor was it there before, nor does it exist there afterwards; nor does it possess parts. It does not abandon its former substratum—oh, what a succession of calamities! (Pramāṇavārttika 3.151)

This [objection] is incorrect; it is resolved by noting that it was stated by those who have strayed from the path of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) due to the blindness of their hatred for universals (*jāti*). For indeed, since a recurring cognition is perceived as being uncontradicted through the operation of the eyes and other senses, a recurring cause must necessarily be asserted. Nor can mental impressions (*vāsanā*) alone be the cause, because they have already been refuted previously. Furthermore, if mental impressions were both the cause of specific cognitions and external [entities], there would be a mere difference in terminology. If, however, they were included within consciousness itself, then—since they would be indistinguishable everywhere by virtue of having the nature of consciousness—the variety of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) would not occur; [one would not experience] a conceptual construction in the form of a cow upon seeing a cow-individual, nor a determination of a horse upon seeing a horse-individual, and so forth. Moreover, a determination that is uncontradicted even by differences of place and so on cannot possibly be without an object; thus, the claim that "the other's form is concealed by its own form" (*pra. vā. 1.69*) is already refuted.

As for the claim that "particulars do not follow [one another], and nothing else that follows appears," this is incorrect, because it does appear through a cognition of recurrence (*anugata-jñāna*). For just as the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) exists because it appears in an excluded form (*vyāvṛtta-rūpatayā*), so too the universal (*sāmānya*) exists because it appears in a recurrent nature (*anugata-svarūpatayā*). If the non-existence of the universal were to follow from its non-appearance in a cognition of exclusion, then the non-existence of the particular would likewise follow from its non-appearance in a cognition of recurrence. Therefore, just as the existence of blue and other such things must be accepted because they appear in an uncontradicted cognition, so too the existence of the universal must be accepted because it appears in a cognition of recurrence; for the subverting arguments, such as the dilemma regarding its subsistence (*vṛtti-vikalpa*), lack the status of valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇatvāt*). To explain: the argument that "it does not exist because its subsistence is untenable" is not an independent proof (*svatantra-sādhana*), because it is inconclusive (*anekāntāt*). For in the case of an independent proof, one would have both the existence of color-form (*rūpa*) and the like, and the fact that their subsistence is untenable. Likewise, in the case of the opponent's position, space (*ākāśa*) and the like exist even though their subsistence is untenable. Furthermore, the reason is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*), because subsistence is indeed real in the form of inherence (*samavāya*). The specific negation—that it does not subsist "by way of a part" or "in its entirety"—is improper, because no other mode of subsistence is possible. Moreover, since the universal has a non-different nature, the terms "part" (*ekadeśa*) and "entirety" (*sarva*) do not apply to it, as these two are observed to apply only to distinct things. The universal subsists by way of inherence, not by way of a part or by way of its own nature, because that "part" and that "own-nature" are themselves of the nature of non-subsis-tence. Furthermore, whatever is the own-nature of the universal in one individual (*piṇḍa*), that very same is in another individual, because the capacity to produce a recurrent cognition is possible everywhere. Thus it is said: "Because its own-nature is seen to persist across one, two, or many individuals, it is the cause of its own cognition. The own-nature of the universal is persistent and non-different; therefore, it is the cause of the recurrent cognition, the cognition of recurrence.

Furthermore, the non-difference of the universal does not entail that individual objects (padārtha) exist in that same way [of being non-different], because they are distinct from it. For this very reason, the fact that the universal is perceived in one individual qualified by a particular place and so forth does not entail the perception of it as qualified by every [other] particular; for there is no perception of it as connected to those [other particulars] due to their connection with indefinite places and directions. And just as the particulars are perceived successively, so too is the universal qualified by them. For when there is the perception of cows standing in a village or a city, qualified by particular states such as youth and so on during the springtime, then the universal qualified by those [states] is perceived; at other times, however, it is perceived as qualified by others. Thus, the capacity of the universal to produce a cognition that conforms to all individuals is its nature which is everywhere non-deviant. Therefore, the universal—being non-different in essence and subsisting in many [individuals]—must be accepted on the basis of its perception through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). For just as color, though being one and subsisting in one [substratum], is perceived by direct perception, so too is the single universal [perceived] in many [substrata].

As for the argument stated—that because a single entity, whose nature is qualified by specific locations and so forth, subsists in many places, it cannot be conjoined with another entity that possesses a different location and so forth—therein the qualification of both the reason (*hetu*) and the subject (*dharmin*) is superfluous. For, since the universal lacks any other nature not delimited by its connection with one [particular], there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) when the negation "it is not conjoined with another particular" is to be proven; therefore, the qualification of "location and so forth" is useless for both the probandum and the probans. This is because a qualification is meaningful only when there exists something to be excluded.

Now, if there is an absence of any other nature as previously described, how can there be a connection with something else (*anyayoga*) for the universal (*sāmānya*) and so forth? Or, if there is a connection with something else, how can there be an absence of any other nature as previously described? If it is argued that the necessary connection between those two is established elsewhere, such as in the case of color (*rūpa*), we say no, because of the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). For instance, although the substratum of color lacks any other nature not delimited by its connection with color, it is observed to have a connection with taste (*rasa*) and so forth; likewise, who can prevent the universal from having a connection with another substratum? This is because, like the substratum of color, there is no difference in the universal’s lack of any other nature as previously described. And it has been stated that the substratum of color is indeed a substance (*dravya*).

Now, if it is argued that because the universal (*sāmānya*) is one, its inherence (*samavāya*) in multiple locations is denied, then—given the admission that "whatever is inherent in multiple locations is itself multiple"—the reason would be a prover by virtue of its non-deviation from the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Consequently, it would follow that color (*rūpa*) and other qualities, which are inherent in a single [substratum], must be one; yet this is not the case. Alternatively, if it is argued that because it is one, its inherence occurs in only one location, that too is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). For although space (*ākāśa*) and so forth are one, they lack inherence in only one location. Even if it were asserted that "from inherence in multiple locations follows the consequence of being multiple," there would still be an absence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) in the form "whatever is one is inherent in only one location," since this is absent in the case of space and the like despite their being one. Furthermore, the claim that "oneness follows from inherence in one location" is also inconclusive due to the example of color, sound, and so forth. Since oneness is of the nature of a specific universal (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*), when that is the probandum, the reason lacks both positive and negative concomitance and is therefore not a prover. Thus, the internal mode of the relationship between probandum and probans for an unqualified reason has been refuted. Likewise, even for a qualified reason, there is inconclusiveness due to space and the like; for although space is conjoined with another thing possessing specific locations and so forth, it is observed to be devoid of any other such stated nature.

As for the example given—that the light of a lamp, which is qualified by specific spatial and other attributes, does not have a connection with anything else possessing those same spatial and other attributes—even there, since destruction is admitted to occur through a sequence of part-movements following its production, a connection with something else possessing spatial and other attributes is indeed possible after the lapse of multiple moments of time. Furthermore, the lamp-light does not possess probative force merely because the presence of the probandum and the probans is observed therein, as this would demonstrate a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason. Likewise, the absence of any other nature (*svabhāvāntaraviraha*) in the universal (*sāmānya*) is unestablished, because the other substratum that serves as its qualifier is itself a different nature from it. Moreover, the relationship of qualifier and qualified between the substratum and the superstratum is perceived, as in the cases "the existent substance" (*sad-dravyam*) and "the existence of the substance" (*dravyasya sattā*). Therefore, even the absence of any other nature remains to be proven. Furthermore, in the reductio argument (*prasaṅga*) stating that a single entity existing in many places cannot have a connection with anything else possessing spatial and other attributes, there is a contradiction with one's own words. For if one denies its connection with another, it cannot be said to exist in many places. If you argue that "existing in many places" is a synonym for "universal" and so forth, even then, the denial of "existing in many places" is untenable, because the definition of a universal—given its eternity and oneness—is precisely "existing in many places. Moreover, since the universal’s existence in many places is established by perception, inference is invalid as it is sublated by that perception. Indeed, it is observed that a recurring cognition arises from the operation of the senses upon one, two, or many individual objects. This cognition is not erroneous; for when non-discrepancy is established through the corroboration of perception and scripture, the error that pervades it must also cease.

Nor can there be a recurring cognition (*anugata-jñāna*) arising from exclusion (*apoha*) alone; for since exclusion consists in differentiation (*vyāvṛtti*), it is a non-entity and thus lacks causal efficacy. If it were indeed causally efficient, it would follow that it is a real entity (*vastu*) because it performs a purposeful action (*arthakriyākāritva*). Now, if you do not admit an exclusion that is distinct from the excluded objects themselves, then—since those objects possess mutually exclusive natures—they could not produce a recurring cognition.

Regarding the statement that "cowness is the exclusion of non-cows," there would be a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*): without first apprehending the essential nature of cows, the status of others as non-cows cannot be established; and without that establishment, the essential nature of cows cannot be apprehended. Furthermore, if the status of non-cows were established for all others relative to a single individual cow, then it would follow that all other individual cows would also be non-cows, since they too are distinct from that one individual cow.

Now, if it were the case that everything other than the entire aggregate of cows (*gopiṇḍa*) lacked the nature of being a cow, that would be incorrect. For if the basis for categorization is absent, and the name "cow" is not apprehended in relation to the entire aggregate of cows, it would be impossible to apprehend anything else as being a cow. Furthermore, for those things that possess a common, non-different basis, once the essential nature of a cow is established, the exclusion of others from it is indeed cognized. If it is argued that the recurring cognition [of "cow"] arises from the commonality of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), we say no; because even causal efficiencies are mutually distinct and thus do not produce a recurring cognition. If, on the other hand, you maintain that there must be a common, non-different basis that governs these causal efficiencies, then that very thing is the universal (*sāmānya*).

And what is this "purposeful activity" (*arthakriyā*), by the similarity of which a "concomitant cognition" (*anugatajñāna*) is said to arise? If it is of the nature of carrying [burdens] and so forth, then since that is possible even for humans and others, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a concomitant cognition such as "cow, cow" arising with respect to them as well. Nor is this [activity] present in every instance within the class [of cows], which would lead to the absence of a concomitant cognition altogether. If it is argued that the universal is simply the cognition itself, which possesses both a concomitant and an excluded form, then this is the maxim of "the horse forgotten by one mounted on it. For a concomitant cognition is not possible without a concomitant cause, and causes such as mental impressions (*vāsanā*) have already been refuted.

As for the claim that when this [universal] moves upon its substratum, it possesses action during motion and lacks a substratum during stationariness—that is incorrect. For, given the existence of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*), the cognition of "motion" is merely figurative (*bhākta*). Furthermore, possession of action is pervaded by corporeality (*mūrtatva*); and since that [corporeality] is excluded from universals and the like, it excludes the possession of action which is pervaded by itself. Thus, universals and the like are devoid of action, because action is perceived in objects only when corporeality is present, as established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). That very [corporeality] is the capacity [for action]; and due to its absence, there is an absence of action in space (*ākāśa*) and so forth, not because of an obstruction by omnipresence (*vibhutva*), for if that were the case, it would follow that qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*karman*), and so on, would also possess action. Moreover, if the universal were to move because some substratum of the universal moves, then it would also remain stationary when that [substratum] remains stationary; thus, one would incur the insurmountable predicament that "it neither moves nor stays. Therefore, because of the inherence in a single object of conjunction and disjunction, the motion residing in the substratum is superposed upon the supported [universal], and one understands that "the universal moves."

As for what was stated—"It does not go there, nor did it exist there before, nor does it exist afterwards, nor does it possess parts"—that is a description of the nature of the universal (*sāmānya*), not an intent to negate it. If the universal were non-existent due to the non-perception of its substantial form (*dravyasvarūpa*), then everything would be non-existent, because the non-existence of anything other than that [substance] is indistinguishable everywhere. Furthermore, since the universal persisting through particulars is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself, its non-perception is unproven (*asiddha*). Moreover, if the universal were non-existent, how could there be direct perception whose object is the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) and inference whose object is the universal? Now, if...

"Because it manifests only the object as such, independent of what is not that form, and because it is not established through differences in gender, it is called 'existent' as a universal (*sāmānya*).

— [Dharmakīrti] Thus: "Because it illuminates only the mere thing, which is independent of what does not have that nature, and because it is not fixed by differences in grammatical gender, it is declared to be a 'universal' (*sāmānya*) that is 'existent' (*sat*).
[Dharmakīrti]

This is its meaning: water and other such things, which are distinct from fire capable of burning, cooking, and so forth, do not possess that nature. Because smoke makes known "mere fire"—which is excluded from those [non-fire things] and devoid of specific qualities such as being produced from grass or leaves—it has a universal (sāmānya) as its object. Likewise, the cognition of smoke also has as its object "mere smoke," which is excluded from non-smoke and devoid of specific qualities such as being produced from grass.

This is not tenable. For if a universal (*sāmānya*) is not admitted, the denotation of the "mere" (*mātra*) would be impossible. Nor is exclusion (*apoha*) itself the meaning of the denotation of the "mere," because it is a non-entity (*avastu*) and thus lacks causal efficiency (*ajanakatva*). If, on the other hand, it were an entity, then a real universal would have been admitted; so who is opposing you when you are acting in accordance with your own position? Furthermore, there is no causal capacity in individual fire-instances, since the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) that grasps them is unestablished. Nor is it observed that the cognition of the totality of fire arises from the perception of smoke. Now, if one particular instance among those produced from grass and so forth (*tārṇādīnām*) is the object of the denotation of the "mere," then how can inference have a universal as its object? Moreover, there is no uniform cognition regarding individual fire-instances based on their performing a specific purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), because—according to the logic already stated—actions themselves are mutually distinct. By this, what was previously stated [is refuted].

The claim that "because the cognitions of the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*) are indirectly connected to the real entity (*vastu*), they do not deceive even though they are devoid of the appearance of that [entity]" (PV 2.82) is thereby refuted; for if those two [cognitions] lack a universal (*sāmānya*), there can be no indirect connection to the real entity either.

Nor does a conceptual cognition (vikalpa) having the form of the exclusion of non-fire arise from a conceptual cognition having the form of the exclusion of non-smoke, because the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between those two is not established. Non-fires are not cognized apart from the cognition of fire; and if that [fire] is not cognized, there can be no cognition of fire, as this would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). Furthermore, it was stated during the demonstration of pervasion (*vyāpti*) that smoke is not a signifier by virtue of being an effect. Therefore, since the establishment of invariable concomitance belongs to things possessing universals (*sāmānyavat*), one who desires inference must necessarily admit the universal. Otherwise, in the absence of a real universal, the existence of entities would not be established, and due to the failure to grasp conventions, neither inference nor verbal testimony would possess the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Yet, they do possess such validity. Consequently, as was stated previously, for one proceeding toward the cognition of an object, when non-discrepancy is confirmed through the correspondence with purposeful action (*arthakriyā-saṃvāda*), there follows the cessation of error, which is pervaded by that [non-discrepancy]. Thus, it is said: "It is the cause of the cognition of the persistence of its own nature."

He provides an explanation of the summary statement: "Existing by way of inherence (*samavāya*) in substrates such as the individual bodies of brindled cows and the like—by means of its own nature without distinction, in a single form, continuously without cessation, and without abandoning the preceding body—it is the cause of the cognition of persistence (*anuvṛtti-buddhi*). The term "in substrates" is the explanation of "in one, two, or many"; the phrase "by means of its own nature without distinction" is the explanation of the word "non-different in essence. The question "How so? is either an inquiry from one who lacks proficiency or a challenge from one who holds a contrary view. Thus, at the time of perceiving a single individual body, the universal (*sāmānya*) does not appear as something persisting. Even at the time of perceiving a second body, because the first body is no longer being grasped, there is simply an absence of a persisting cognition. Furthermore, even in cases where a single cognition has multiple bodies as its object, there is still no perception of a persisting cognition. To this objection, he states the rebuttal: "In each individual body, [the universal] depends upon the universal," and so forth.

The production of cognitions occurs in a continuous and uninterrupted succession, one after another. When this occurs, "practice" (*abhyāsa*) consists of each subsequent cognition depending upon the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by each preceding experience. The impression generated by that [practice] gives rise to the examination (*pratyavekṣaṇa*) of the series of past cognitions. That which is both past and a series of cognitions is the "past series of cognitions," and the examination of it is recollection (*smaraṇa*). Recollection has two objects: that which is known as "cognition" (*jñāna*), and the act of knowing itself, "cognizance" (*jñapti*). It is through such recollection—expressed as "I previously perceived something similar to this"—that it is known there exists something that persists throughout; that is the universal (*sāmānya*). Furthermore, through recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) in the form "this is similar to that," that similarity which produces a non-differentiating cognition with respect to distinct things is established as the universal.

“In this regard, existence (*sattā*) is the highest generality (*param sāmānyam*), being solely the cause of the recurring cognition [of ‘being’]. Just as in the case of leather, cloth, woolen blankets, and so forth—which are mutually distinct—there occurs a recurrence of the cognition ‘blue, blue’ due to their connection with a single substance that is blue; likewise, among substances, qualities, and actions, which are mutually distinct, there occurs a recurrence of the undifferentiated cognition ‘existent, existent. And since that [recurrence] must arise from something other [than the individuals themselves], that which is the other thing is established as existence (*sattā*). Because the recurrence of the cognition ‘existent, existent’ follows from its connection with existence, it is therefore a generality indeed.”

He defines exclusion (*bheda*). Among these, existence (*sattā*) is the highest generality (*para-sāmānya*). And here, the proof has already been stated as "because its scope is vast. That existence, however, is indeed a generality. Why? Because it is the cause of the cognition of recurrence (*anuvṛtti-pratyaya*) alone. Although it is also the cause of the cognition of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti-jñāna*) from non-existence and so forth, nevertheless, among things that possess generalities, it produces only a recurrent cognition, not an exclusive one. Therefore, it is indeed a generality.

In this context, once the existence of the universal (*sāmānyamātra*) has been established, he states an inference for the existence of *sattā* (Being) for the sake of clarity; or rather, while perception was discussed previously, inference is now being stated. Therein, he explains the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) in order to support the pervasion (*vyāpti*): just as in the case of mutually distinct and differentiated objects such as leather, cloth, and woolen blankets, there occurs a recurrence of the cognition "blue, blue" due to the connection with another entity, namely the substance *nīla*, so too in the case of substances, qualities, and actions which are mutually distinct, there occurs an undifferentiated recurrence of the cognition "existent, existent" (*sat, sat*). This is the definition of the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*). And that recurrence of cognition must arise from a connection with another entity; that other entity is established as *sattā*. From the connection with *sattā* arises the recurrence of the cognition "existent, existent"; therefore, it is indeed a universal. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: the cognition "existent, existent" regarding substances, qualities, and actions is based on a recurring cause distinct from the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), because it is a recurring cognition among distinct things, like the cognition "blue, blue" in the case of woolen blankets and the like due to the connection with the substance *nīla*. Furthermore, when it is to be proven that [the cognition] is based on a recurring cause distinct from the qualified object by means of a universal, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by means of cognitions such as "cook" (*pācaka*), since these too belong to the class of similar instances (*sapakṣa*). To explain: in the cognition "cook," the cause is either the act of cooking or the proficiency therein, because even when the action has ceased, the convention "cook" persists. Likewise, in the cognition "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*), the staff is the cause; and in the cognition "white," the quality is the cause. Thus, in every case, the cause is indeed something distinct. However, since the staff and so forth are mutually different, one must admit a single, non-different cause as the unifying factor (*upagrāhaka*) for the arising of a recurring cognition; otherwise, they would simply not produce a recurring cognition. Therefore, one must state that there is "staff-ness" (*daṇḍatva*) in staffs, and that universal in white things and so forth.

Regarding this universal (sāmānya), the inclusive cognition "this is a universal, that is a universal" has as its cause inherence (samavāya) in multiple loci while being unitary and eternal. In this same manner, other causes should be inferred in all similar cases.

“Furthermore, substance-ness (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), action-ness (*karmatva*), and so forth, are both universals (*sāmānya*) and particulars (*viśeṣa*) because they are the causes of inclusion (*anuvṛtti*) and exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). Among these, substance-ness is a universal because it is the cause of inclusion among earth and the other substances which are mutually distinct; it is a particular because it is the cause of exclusion from qualities and actions. Likewise, quality-ness is a universal because it is the cause of inclusion among color and the other qualities which are mutually distinct; it is a particular because it is the cause of exclusion from substances and actions. Similarly, action-ness is a universal because it is the cause of the cognition of inclusion among upward throwing and the other actions which are mutually distinct; it is a particular because it is the cause of exclusion from substances and qualities.”

“Thus, because earthness, formness, the state of being upward motion, cowness, potness, clothness, and so forth—which reside in both living and non-living things—serve as the causes of inclusive cognition (*anuvṛtti*), their status as generalities and particulars (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*) is established. However, these [higher categories] such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and the rest are primarily generalities because they have a vast range of objects; yet, because they differentiate their own substrates, they are designated as ‘particulars’ (*viśeṣa*) figuratively.”

Furthermore, by the phrase "substance-ness, quality-ness, action-ness, etc.," the term "etc. includes earth-ness and so forth. Because they are the causes of inclusive (*anuvṛtti*) and exclusive (*vyāvṛtti*) cognitions, they constitute both universals (*sāmānya*) and particulars (*viśeṣa*). He explains this very point: therein, substance-ness (*dravyatva*) is a universal because it is the cause of an inclusive cognition regarding earth and the other substances, which are mutually distinct and possess excluded natures; it is a particular because it is the cause of an exclusive cognition [distinguishing them] from qualities and actions. Just as with substance-ness, quality-ness (*guṇatva*) is also a universal because it is the cause of an inclusive cognition regarding color and the other qualities, which are mutually distinct; it is a particular because it is the cause of an exclusive cognition [distinguishing them] from substances and actions. Likewise, action-ness (*karmatva*) is a universal because it is the cause of an inclusive cognition regarding upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*) and the other actions, which are mutually distinct; it is a particular because it is the cause of an exclusive cognition [distinguishing them] from substances and qualities. In this way, the status of being both universal and particular is established for earth-ness, color-ness, upward-throwing-ness, cow-ness, jar-ness, cloth-ness, and so forth—whether residing in living beings or non-living things—because they are the causes of inclusive and exclusive cognitions; such is the extended application (*atideśa*). Those residing in bodies connected to life, such as cow-ness and horse-ness, and those residing in non-living supports, such as earth-ness and the like, are established as having the status of both universal and particular because they are the causes of inclusive cognition within their own class and the causes of exclusive cognition from other classes.

Furthermore, since a single entity is not observed to possess two forms, how can that very same thing be both a universal (*sāmānya*) and a particular (*viśeṣa*)? [The response is: There is no contradiction here, because one of these is ultimate (*pāramārthika*) while the other is figurative (*aupacārika*). Regarding this, he explains whether these—namely *dravyatva* (substance-ness) and so on—are universals or particulars by way of their primary function: "These, such as *dravyatva*, are primarily universals by way of their primary function (*mukhyavṛttyā*) because their scope is extensive (*prabhūtaviṣayatvāt*). For it is not possible for particulars to have an extensive scope, since they reside in each individual substance. They are called 'particulars' only figuratively (*bhaktyā*), by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāreṇa*), because they distinguish their own substratum. The nature of particulars is to produce the cognition of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*); since that is perceived here as well, the metaphorical usage indeed applies. That is to say, the universal such as *dravyatva* distinguishes its own substratum from other substrata—that is, it excludes it—and for this reason it also receives the name 'particular.'"

“Because of the difference in their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it is established that these [universals] are distinct categories from substance, quality, and action. For this very reason, they are eternal. They are distinct from one another because of their restricted occurrence within substances and so forth, and because of the difference in their cognitions. Each universal is a single entity because its defining characteristic is non-different across its own substrates, and because there is no further defining characteristic of particularity (*viśeṣa*). Although universals are not limited in space, they nevertheless pervade all things within their own respective domains due to the restriction of their indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*) and the restriction of the causal complex (*kāraṇasāmagrī*). Furthermore, in the intervals between substrates, they are not designated because of the absence of the modes of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*). (PDhS)

Now, as to whether substantiality (*dravyatva*) and the like are entities distinct from substance, quality, and action, or whether they are their very natures, [the author] says: "Because of the difference in their definitions, their status as categories distinct from substance, quality, and action is established. This has been stated by the phrase "of a non-different nature and residing in many. For this very reason, they are eternal; since they are categories distinct from substance and the rest, for that very reason they are eternal, because a state (*bhāva*) consisting of substance, quality, and action is observed to be non-eternal.

[Objection: Is it not the case that permanence consists in the state of being unoriginated (*anutpattimat*), and not in being a distinct category of entity from substance and so forth, since the triad beginning with the universal (*sāmānya*) is also to be proven as permanent? [Response: This is not so. Because it appears as having a nature related to [the universal] that is distinct from substance and the rest, it is a different category of entity; and for this very reason, it is permanent, because the causes of its origination and destruction are impossible. To explain: there is no cause of origination for the universal, because its substrata cannot exist simultaneously, and thus it lacks an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*); this has been established in the *Padārthasaṅkara*.

Now, in order to refute the claim that there is only one universal characterized as "existence" (*sattā*), which produces distinct cognitions due to differences in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), he says: "Because of the restriction of occurrence in substances and so forth, and because of the difference in cognition, there is mutual otherness. The restriction of occurrence is such that "substanceness" (*dravyatva*) exists only in substances, and "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) exists only in qualities, and so on. As for the difference in cognition: in the case of substances, there is the knowledge "substance, substance" by virtue of substanceness; and in the case of qualities, there is "quality, quality" and so forth due to the connection with quality-ness. Therefore, because of the difference in cognition and the restriction of occurrence in substances and so forth, there is mutual otherness [among the categories]. Otherwise, since the universal would be one and the same across all categories, there would be neither restriction of occurrence nor difference in cognition.

Now, let it be granted that there is mutual difference [between substance-ness, quality-ness, etc.]. Nevertheless, since the cognition "this is a substance" arises with respect to its own substrates by virtue of substance-ness (*dravyatva*), and the cognition "this is a quality" arises with respect to qualities, one might wonder: is that [universal] one or many? To dispel this doubt, he says: "Substance-ness is one in each of its own substrates; quality-ness is one among qualities; and so too for the rest. Why is this so? Because there is no difference in their definition (*lakṣaṇa*), that is, because there is no difference in their inclusive nature (*anugatasvarūpa*). Alternatively, "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*) means that by which something is defined; it refers to the inclusive cognition such as "substance, substance. Precisely because there is no difference in that [cognition], there is substance-ness among substances and quality-ness among qualities; otherwise, there would be no inclusive cognition at all.

Now, even though there is a multiplicity of distinct forms (*rūpa*), there exists the cognition "form, form. This is true; for the cognition of blue and so forth, which establishes their distinction, is logically possible. But in this case (regarding universals), he says that they are one because of the absence of any defining characteristic of difference, stating that no such means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) exists here to establish a distinction. Now, a cause must be stated for why a jar or the like, arising in a single location, is connected with its specific universal; otherwise, because universals would not be restricted to a particular location, they could not be connected with a fixed substratum (*dharmin*). To this he replies: "Even though universals are not limited to a specific location, nevertheless, due to the restriction of the indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) and the restriction of the causal complex (*kāraṇasāmagrī*), they are all-pervading within their own respective domains. An "indicative mark" is that by which something is indicated; it is simply the recurring cognition itself. For instance, the recurring cognition "substance, substance" occurs only regarding substances, not regarding qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth; therefore, substantiality (*dravyatva*) is indeed all-pervading within its own domain, since there is no proof for its existence in other domains. The same applies to quality-ness (*guṇatva*) and so on. Alternatively, the "indicative mark" is that which manifests the universal; due to the restriction of that [mark], the universal is all-pervading within its own domain. For example, an individual body characterized by a dewlap is connected with "cow-ness," while one characterized by a mane is connected with "horse-ness"; in this way, the manifesting factor should be understood as being invariably present everywhere.

Now, let it be granted that because [the universal] is perceived only in its own substratum due to the restriction of the manifestor (*vyañjaka*), "pervading all its own substrata" must be stated as the reason here; for in the absence of a restrictive factor (*niyāmaka*), there would follow the impossibility of a connection with a restricted substratum. Thus he says: "And because of the restriction of the causal complex (*kārakasāmagrī*), [the universal] pervades all its own substrata. To explain: a cow-individual (*gopiṇḍa*)—produced by a causal complex characterized by the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) that brings about the experience of being connected with the genus "cowness"—is not another, such as a horse-individual. Due to that restriction, only that [cow-individual] is connected with "cowness," and no other. Likewise, a horse-individual is connected with "horseness" because it is produced by a causal complex characterized by the unseen merit that brings about the experience of being connected with the genus "horseness. The same applies elsewhere as well. Therefore, what was said—"Wherever that entity exists, it is connected with that, but not otherwise"—is refuted, since the perception of [the universal] as inherent only in its restricted substratum is established, yet no cause for such restriction has been stated.

As for the objection, "Is this cow connected with 'cowness,' or rather is it a non-cow?", that is not worthy of a response, because the completion [of the entity] and its connection [with universals] occur at the same time. The very acquisition of its own nature by the individual (piṇḍa) consists in its connection with its own causes, such as existence (sattā) and so forth; prior to that, it possesses neither the form of a cow nor the form of a non-cow, since its very existence would otherwise be impossible.

Now, if it is argued that just as gems, mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth—produced from their own causes—are capable of accomplishing specific purposeful actions, and likewise cow-individuals are produced from their own causes alone as being capable of generating the cognition "cow" (gauriti-jñāna) without producing the cognition of a horse or other animals; then, that capacity by virtue of which, when present, they produce the inclusive cognition "cow"—is that [capacity] a distinct entity, or merely a difference in designation? If it is non-distinct [from the individuals], there follows the undesirable consequence of the absence of an inclusive cognition. Therefore, since an inclusive entity appears through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), every objection raised against the universal (*sāmānya*) is simply unproven.

Now, one might object: "If [universals] were all-pervading within their own substrates, then a universal would also be perceived in the space between two individual cows; yet this is not the case. Therefore, how can they be said to be all-pervading within their own substrates? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And because there is no occurrence of either conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*) in the intervening space, they are non-designatable. Since the universal such as "cowness" is perceived through the relation of inherence-in-the-conjoined (*saṃyukta-samavāya*), it is designated as "cowness"; however, that relation does not exist here [in the intervening space]. Therefore, they are "non-designatable. Furthermore, what is this so-called "intervening space" where the undesirable consequence of perceiving the universal is raised? If it is the absence of corporeal substances, then the universal such as "cowness" cannot exist there, precisely because it is an absence (*abhāva*). If, on the other hand, it is the supersensible ether (*ākāśa*) inferred from sound, or a substance such as a jar situated in the intervening space, even in those cases there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the inherence of "cowness" and the like. Thus, its non-perception is logically consistent. Enough of this.
Thus ends the section on the category of Generality (*sāmānya*) in the *Padārthasaṅgraha-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Vyomaśivācārya.

[Now follows] the definition of the category of Particularity (*viśeṣa*). “Those which exist in the ultimate limits (*anteṣu bhavāḥ*) are the ‘ultimate’ (*antyāḥ*); they are called ‘particularities’ (*viśeṣāḥ*) because they differentiate their own substrata. They reside one in each individual eternal substance—which, being devoid of destruction or origination, consists of atoms, space, time, direction, self, and mind—and they are the cause of the cognition of absolute exclusion. (*PDhS*)

“Just as for people like us, a distinction in cognition regarding cows and the like—such as ‘a cow,’ ‘white,’ ‘swift-moving,’ ‘thick-humped,’ or ‘with a large bell’—is observed to be caused by similarities in form, quality, action, parts, and conjunction [with other things]; likewise, for yogins who are superior to us, since no other cause is possible, those causes from which there arises a distinction in cognition for each respective substratum—‘this is distinct,’ ‘that is distinct’—and through which recognition occurs even when atoms are remote in space and time, such as ‘this is that very same atom,’ are the ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣas*). <PDhS>

“If, moreover, for yogins there were a cessation of [erroneous] cognition and recognition through the dharma born of yoga (*yogaja-dharma*) without the ultimate particularity (*antyaviśeṣa*), what would follow? It is not so. Just as from a dharma born of yoga a cognition of white arises regarding what is not white, or recognition occurs regarding that which has never been seen before—if such were the case, it would be false. Likewise here too, without the ultimate particularity, neither the cessation of cognition nor recognition can occur for yogins through the dharma born of yoga.”

For the purpose of examining the *viśeṣas* (particularities), he says: "Those existing at the ends (*anteṣu bhavāḥ*) are the *antyās*; they are called *viśeṣas* because they differentiate their own substrata. Because they are situated at the end of production and destruction, eternal substances are denoted by the word "end" (*anta*). For instance, taking atoms as the limit, there is the production of effects such as dyads (*dvyaṇuka*), and likewise for earth and so forth, production continues up to ether (*ākāśa*) and the rest; according to this reading, even those [ether, etc. are denotable by the word "end. Similarly, atoms and so forth are situated at the end of destruction. Thus, a substance is destroyed only until it reaches the state of atoms; according to the reading, the destruction of earth and the rest also continues until ether and the rest. Those existing in them—that is, residing in them—are designated as "the final ones" (*antyāḥ*). To explain the root meaning: the verbal root *bhū* is used in the sense of existence (*sattā*) or perception, as in the current usage: "Devadatta exists (*bhavati*) in the house, he sits there. He provides an elaboration of this summary statement with the words "in those devoid of destruction and commencement," and so on. Therein, the explanation of the term "end" is "only in eternal substances," specifically referring to atoms, ether, time, space, self, and mind; this designation of a specific name is for the sake of clarity. He explains the meaning of the suffix (*pratya-ya*) with the words "residing one by one in each substance. A single particularity resides in each individual substance; many do not reside in one, because that would lead to redundancy (*vaiyarthyaprasaṅga*). For if a single particularity alone had already produced the cognition of exclusion (*vyāvṛttapratyaya*), other particularities would be redundant. Nor does one reside in many, because that would entail the status of a universal (*sāmānyarūpatā*). The explanation of the second term is "causes of the cognition of absolute exclusion. Because they reside only in eternal substances—by excluding both non-connection and connection with others—they are distinguished from other things due to their residence in the eternal. The definition has already been stated previously.

Now, what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of particularities (*viśeṣa*)? It is inference (*anumāna*). In this regard, he defines an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) for the purpose of establishing pervasion (*vyāpti*): Just as in the case of cows and other animals, we observe that for people like ourselves there is an exclusion of cognitions (*pratyayavyāvṛtti*) from horses and the like; and even though they possess identical form and qualities, this exclusion from homogeneous [individuals] is caused by their specific action, parts, and conjunctions. Among these, the exclusion of cognition based on genus (*jāti*) is seen when one thinks, "This is a cow," and therefore it is distinct from horses and so forth. Even though they belong to the same genus, the exclusion of cognition as "white" occurs in relation to those connected with qualities such as blackness. Similarly, the cognition "one who moves swiftly" is caused by a specific action (*kriyā*), for by virtue of that being present, the object is distinguished even from homogeneous individuals possessing similar qualities. The cognition "fat" is caused by the accumulation of parts (*avayava*); by virtue of that being present, the object is distinguished even from those of the same genus possessing similar qualities and actions. The cognition "humped" (*kakudmān*) is caused by a specific part, for by virtue of that being present, it generates a distinct cognition from others. The cognition "possessing a large bell" (*mahāghaṇṭa*) is caused by conjunction (*saṃyoga*), because when that exists, it generates an excluded cognition.

To explain the application of this analogy, he says: for yogis who are superior to us, there is observed a differentiation of cognition regarding eternal atoms that possess identical form, quality, and action, as well as liberated souls and minds—[a cognition] such as "this one is distinct," "this one is distinct. Since no other cause for this is possible, it arises solely from a connection with *viśeṣa* (ultimate particularity). Thus, atoms which are the substrata of identical form, quality, and action are connected with *viśeṣa*, because they are the objects of differentiated cognition, like cows and the like. Nor should it be argued that in the case of cows and so forth, the differentiators (*viśeṣa*) are merely universals (*jāti*), qualities, or actions; for [the atoms] are specified by being the substrata of identical genus, quality, and action. Furthermore, all fiery atoms are made the subject of the proposition (*pakṣa*) as being connected with the nature of fire (*tejastva*), possessing identical qualities, and connected with identical actions; therefore, the differentiation of cognition among them cannot be caused by those [qualities]. Likewise, luminous color, hot touch, dimension, unity, separateness, and so forth, being common to all, are not causes for differentiated cognition. Action also, because atoms struck by wind move toward a single direction, is common to all and thus is not a cause for the apprehension of distinction. Therefore, since a *viśeṣa* consisting of the intrinsic nature of the substance itself is impossible, that cause from which the differentiation of cognition arises are the "ultimate particulars" (*antyā viśeṣāḥ*). Similarly, liberated souls and liberated minds require a *viśeṣa* because they are the objects of differentiated cognition. Since the connection with a body is absolutely absent, the specific qualities such as intellect (*buddhi*) etc., do not serve as causes for differentiated cognition in the soul, as they are impossible [there]. For the mind also, being devoid of connection with a body, its qualities such as number and so forth are common to all; thus, without a *viśeṣa*, there is no cause for the production of differentiated cognition. The differentiated cognition regarding things qualified by the aforementioned attributes has *viśeṣa* as its cause, because it is a differentiated cognition, like the differentiated cognition of cows and the like.

Now, since atoms and the like are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), what is the proof that they are objects of differentiated cognition (*vyāvṛttajñāna*)? It is inference alone (*anumāna*). For instance: atoms and the like are objects of differentiated cognition, because they are substances (*dravyatva*), just like cows and so forth. Furthermore, atoms and the like are objects of doubt (*saṃśaya*), because they are related to existence (*sattāsambandhitva*), just like a post (*sthāṇu*) and so forth. And where there is doubt, there must necessarily be a definitive determination (*nirṇaya*). Atoms and the like are related to specificities (*viśeṣasambandhin*), because they are objects of definitive determination, just like a post and so forth. Therefore, he says this: those causes from which, in the absence of any other cause, arises the differentiation of cognitions such as "this is distinct" and "this is distinct" with respect to each substrate—those are the ultimate specificities (*antyaviśeṣa*). Likewise, regarding an unperceived atom remote in space and time, the cognition "this is that very same one" is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is observed in cases such as Devadatta when there is a connection with specificities. Thus, because atoms and the like are objects of differentiated cognition and because they are recognized, they are related to specificities. Moreover, for yogins there exists the recognition of an atom previously perceived: "This is that very same atom which was perceived during the spring season while situated in Pañcapura."

If it is argued that the cessation of doubt or the occurrence of recognition arises either from mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) or from distinctness (*pṛthaktva*), and that there is no other specific property (*viśeṣa*) besides these, we say: no. For even when those two are perceived, doubt is observed regarding a post (*sthāṇu*) and similar objects. To explain: even when mutual non-existence and distinctness are perceived, doubt such as "Is this a post or a person? is seen to arise due to the perception of common features and so forth; and conversely, even when distinctness is perceived, a definitive determination such as "This is indeed a person" is seen to occur upon perceiving specific features like a head, hands, and so on. Therefore, a specific property (*viśeṣa*) distinct from mutual non-existence and distinctness must be asserted in the case of atoms and other such entities.

Others, however, maintain that mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) merely produces the cognition of what is being negated, whereas the cognition of differentiation (*vyāvṛtta-jñāna*) is distinct from that; therefore, they consider it to be the effect of a different cause. Furthermore, they hold that the conventional usage of "separate" (*pṛthak*) is due to the quality of separateness (*pṛthaktva*), and not due to differentiation.

Now, [it might be argued that] for yogis, there is the exclusion of [erroneous] cognition and recognition due to the dharma born of yoga (*yogaja-dharma*). To address this, he asks: "If, moreover, for yogis there were the exclusion of cognition and recognition through the dharma born of yoga even without the ultimate particularity (*antyaviśeṣa*), what would be the fault? He replies: "In that case, it would not be so. Just as from a dharma not born of yoga, a cognition of white arises regarding what is not white, and recognition occurs regarding something never before seen; if such a cognition of white regarding what is not white, or recognition, were ever to occur for yogis, it would be false. Likewise, here too, without the ultimate particularity, neither the exclusion of cognition nor recognition can possibly arise from the dharma born of yoga.

Now, since ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣa*) are the objects of distinct cognitions just like atoms, if another particular were required to connect with them, there would be an infinite regress—another particular for that one, and yet another for that one. Nor is there any specific reason why, although they are equally objects of distinct cognitions, this connection with an object belongs only to atoms and not to the particulars themselves. Or, if such a reason were admitted, then just as there is a distinct cognition regarding the particulars even without a connection to further particulars, it would likewise occur in the case of atoms. Thus he asks: "Why is it not assumed that the distinction of cognition occurs *per se* (by its own nature) in atoms, just as it does in ultimate particulars? To refute this, he says: What was stated—that there is an absence of particulars in atoms and a further particular in particulars—is not so. Why? Because of their identity (*tādātmya*), that is, because particulars have that very nature. For those things whose nature is non-distinct require a particular for the production of a distinct cognition, such as atoms and the like. But particulars do not lack that nature; therefore, due to their identity, particulars do not require a further particular characterized by the same definition. And in this case, where something is not of that nature—that is, where the nature is not identical—a cognition based on another cause is observed, as in the case of jars and the like [requiring] a lamp. For instance, in the case of jars and the like, which are not luminous by nature, cognition is seen to arise from a lamp through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); but it is not the case that cognition arises from a lamp in the case of the lamp itself, because the lamp, being luminous by nature, illuminates even without [another] lamp. Nor can it be said that illumination should occur in jars and the like even without light, for it is not observed. He shows an example from scripture (*āgamika*): Just as the impurity of dog-meat, horse-meat, and so forth is inherent (*svata eva*), while other things like sweetmeats become impure through contact with them; yet dog-meat does not become impure through contact with another impure thing, for it is not observed. Nor is food and the like inherently impure like dog-meat, precisely because it is not observed to be so. In the same way here, due to identity—that is, because they have the nature of the particular—the exclusion of cognition occurs *per se* in ultimate particulars, and through connection with them, it occurs in atoms. This is the conclusion.

Now, are particulars (*viśeṣa*) eternal or non-eternal? Because no cause for their production or destruction is perceived, they are indeed eternal. For particulars have their own substratum as their inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), and there is no non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) or other such cause; thus, even if destruction were admitted, there would be no cause for the production of the cognition of differentiation (*vyāvṛttijñāna*) regarding particulars again. If it is argued that the cognition of differentiation arises from another particular, that is not so, because there is no proof for its being something else. Enough with this excessive detail. [Thus ends the category of Particulars in the *Padārthasaṅgraha-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Vyomaśivācārya.]
{The Definition of the Category of Inherence}

“*Inseparably established* (*ayutasiddha*) entities that stand in the relation of the supported and the support—the connection which is the cause of the cognition ‘it is here’ is *inherence* (*samavāya*). Whether they exist as cause and effect, or not as cause and effect, substances, qualities, motions, universals, and ultimate particulars are inseparably established by virtue of standing in the relation of the supported and the support; from this [connection] arises the cognition ‘this is here,’ and from this [connection] comes the non-separation (*aviṣvagbhāva*) of those things that are not all-pervading and whose distinctness is already known. This is the relation called inherence. How so? Just as the cognition ‘curd is in the bowl’ is observed when a connection exists, so too there is the cognition ‘cloth is in these threads,’ ‘mat is in these vīraṇa-grass fibers,’ ‘quality and motion are in this substance,’ ‘the universal quality-ness is in this quality,’ ‘the universal motion-ness is in this motion,’ and ‘ultimate particularities are in this eternal substance. From the observation of such cognitions, it is known that a connection between these exists. (PDhS)

“Nor is this conjunction [possible], because the related entities are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*), because the causes such as the action of one of the two are impossible, because no termination by disjunction is observed, and because it exists only between that which is the locus and that which is to be located. (PDhS)

“And that [inherence] is a distinct category from substance and the others, because its definition is different, just like existence (*bhāva*). Just as existence, by producing cognitions corresponding to itself in its own substrates such as substanceness, exists as a distinct entity from its own substrates and from one another; so too, because the cognition ‘it is here’ is observed in the five categories, inherence is a distinct category from them. Nor is it manifold like conjunction, because its indicative mark is non-different from that of existence and because there is an absence of any specific indicative mark [for plurality]. Therefore, like existence, inherence is one everywhere.”

“[Objection: ‘If inherence (*samavāya*) is one, then because the relation between substances, qualities, and actions with their qualifiers—such as substanceness (*dravyatva*), qualityness (*guṇatva*), and actionness (*karmatva*)—is a single entity, there follows the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a confusion of categories (*padārthasaṅkara*). [Reply: No, because of the restriction of locus and located (*ādhārādheyaniyama*). Although inherence is one and independent everywhere, nevertheless, there is a restriction of locus and located. How so? Substanceness exists only in substances; qualityness only in qualities; actionness only in actions—and so forth. Why? Because of the observation of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*): since the cognition based on inherence, namely ‘here [it is]’, is observed to occur positively (*anvaya*) everywhere, it is understood that inherence is one everywhere. However, because the cognitions based on substanceness and the other qualifiers are observed to occur negatively (*vyatireka*), the specific restriction is known. Just as there is a restriction of the relation of container and contained (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*) despite the oneness of the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) between a bowl and curd, so too, although inherence is one, there is a restriction of locus and located due to the difference in the powers of the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*). (PDhS)

“Even though its relata are non-eternal, inherence (*samavāya*) is not non-eternal like conjunction (*saṃyoga*), because, like existence (*bhāva*), it is without cause. Just as it has been stated that existence is eternal because no cause for it is perceived through any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), so too is inherence. For no cause whatsoever for this [inherence] is perceived through any means of valid cognition. But by what kind of occurrence (*vṛtti*) does inherence reside in substances and the other categories? Conjunction is not possible, because, being a quality (*guṇa*), it depends upon a substance; nor is inherence [itself] [the mode of occurrence], because it is unitary, and there is no other mode of occurrence. [Reply: No, because of identity (*tādātmya*). Just as for substances, qualities, and actions, there is no further connection with existence (*sattā*) for that which is of the nature of existence, even so for inherence—which is indivisible and of the nature of occurrence—there is no other occurrence. Therefore, its occurrence is within itself. For this very reason, it is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), because, like existence and the like, it lacks occurrence in perceptible objects, and because there is no self-cognition regarding its own nature. Therefore, inherence is inferable from the cognition ‘here’ (*iha-buddhi*).”
"Having pleased Maheśvara by means of the power of his yogic practice, he composed the Vaiśeṣika Śāstra; homage to that Kaṇabhuj.
Thus ends the commentary on the six categories, beginning with substance, composed by the teacher Praśastapāda.

Now begins the section beginning with "of those that are inseparable" (*ayutasiddhānām*) for the purpose of examining the definition of inherence (*samavāya*). The definition has already been explained: inherence is the relationship between things that are exclusively inseparable (*ayutasiddha*) and which stand in the relation of the supported and the support (*ādhāryādhārabhūta*). Now, he states for which inseparable things this relationship exists: "of substances, qualities, actions, universals, and particulars. This is stated to show that there is no restriction [to only certain types]; for it applies both to effects and causes, such as cloth and its parts, and to non-causal entities, such as universals and their loci. Furthermore, this is the rule: "inseparable things that exist in the state of being the supported and the support. That cause from which the cognition "this is here" arises is the relationship called inherence. Thus says the Sūtra: "That from which the cognition 'this is here' arises in respect to cause and effect is inherence" (*Vaiśeṣika-sūtra* 7.2.26). "Here" (*iha*) refers to the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), and "this" (*idam*) refers to the located (*ādheya*); without a relationship between these two, the cognition "this is here" does not occur. The phrase "and of those that are not all-pervading" (*asarvagatānām*) is intended to dispel the suspicion of a restrictive rule. For instance, since inherence is observed even in the case of all-pervading entities like space (*ākāśa*) in relation to their own qualities and so forth, the statement "of those that are not all-pervading" must be explained as being for the purpose of dispelling the suspicion of a restrictive rule. Thus, the restrictive rule that "inherence belongs only to all-pervading things" is untenable, because inherence is seen even among things that are not all-pervading. Because the word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of including what is unstated, it follows that [the rule applies] to both non-all-pervading and all-pervading things. Regarding the term "of those whose distinctness is apprehended" (*adhigatānyatvānām*): those for whom distinctness (*anyatva*, i.e., manifoldness) is apprehended are so described; this excludes identity (*tādātmya*). Nevertheless, since cows, horses, and so forth also have their distinctness apprehended, the phrase "existing in a state of non-separation" (*aviṣvagbhāvena avasthitānām*) is used. Non-separation (*aviṣvagbhāva*) means non-distinctness of location (*deśāpṛthaktvam*), but not non-difference, because a difference in essential nature (*svarūpa*) is perceived. To explain: threads are related to different classes and possess different essential natures; if they were separate, the cloth would likewise be so. Thus, there is indeed mutual distinctness due to the imposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) and the difference in appearance (*pratibhāsabheda*). Likewise, color and other qualities also differ due to the imposition of contradictory properties. Since this [distinction] exists between the threads and the cloth, there is indeed distinctness. The Sūtra should also be explained in this way: because of the absence of unity and separateness between cause and effect, and because of their mutual difference in appearance, unity and separateness do not exist [between them]. Therefore, that relationship from which the cognition "this is here" arises for those things whose distinctness is apprehended and which exist in a state of non-separation is the relationship called inherence. "How? is a question posed by one who is unlearned, or a challenge from one who is mistaken. And thus, [the opponent claims] there is no proof for the existence of inherence.

All of this is incoherent. Now, if it is argued that "cognition" (*buddhi*) here is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [we reply] no; for that cognition does not have inherence (*samavāya*) as its objective support, because its domain is the substratum. As it has been said:
"And by this cognition 'here,' inherence is not apprehended;
this cognition, which apprehends the substratum, is not established in inherence."

Now, could it be that [the relation] has as its cause a connection (*sambandha*)? That, however, must be characterized by identity (*tādātmya*), because objections arise against the position of inherence (*samavāya*). To explain: inherence is not possible between two things that have not yet come into existence, for a connection is never observed in the absence of things to be connected. If, on the other hand, inherence is a connection between two things already established, then there would be separate establishment (*yutasiddhi*). Furthermore, if one does not admit a further connection for inherence itself, then since there is no distinction in being "other than everything else," there would be no reason for the restriction that this connection belongs only to these two related entities and not to other categories of things. Alternatively, a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) functions toward the production of the cognition of the qualified (*viśeṣya*), and a logical mark (*liṅga*) functions toward the production of the cognition of the marked (*liṅgin*); but in the case of inherence, such a nature is absent, and thus there is a lack of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its apprehension. For instance, the cognition "the cloth is here in these threads" qualifies the substratum as colored by the superstratum, but it is not colored by inherence; therefore, due to the absence of self-awareness (*saṃvedana*) regarding inherence, inherence is indeed non-perceptual (*apratyakṣa*) within this "here"-cognition. However, in indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*), when there is a cognition of the contact between part and whole, inherence is indeed perceptual. It is simply that, since the "here"-cognition is observed elsewhere to have a connection as its cause, inference proceeds here as well based on the observation of that [connection]. Since this is so, the conclusion is that inherence is inferable from the "here"-cognition, but it is not perceptually manifest within the "here"-cognition itself.
And at the conclusion of the book, out of satisfaction, the teacher again offers salutation to another guru:
"Salutation to that Kaṇabhuj, who, having pleased Maheśvara by the power of his yoga practice, composed the Vaiśeṣika Śāstra."
Thus has this been composed by Śiva, named Vyoma,
which overcomes opposing views and is capable of accomplishing its own purpose.
The functioning of the final moment of the continuum is the sublation...
[Thus ends the Vyomavatī, a commentary on the Padārthasaṃgraha composed by the venerable teacher Vyomaśivācārya.]
